content: An id could hold both a memory and a tombstone: `write_memory` cleared the id's keywords and links and said nothing about tombstones, so a memory arriving from an older file for an id this store had forgotten left **both rows** — and the next export wrote a file Scatterhoard's own reader refuses. Fixed 2026-08-26 by clearing the tombstone in the shared writer. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `an-id-can-hold-both-a-memory-and-a-tombstone`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order, at the reduced depth.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Read every open entry and ask whether it is still open. Raised 2026-09-07 by the human partner, after the migration caught two entries whose claims about current behaviour had gone stale without anything reporting it. **The candidate set is bounded and countable today: 13 open of 85 in ISSUES.md, 20 open of 48 in BACKLOG.md.** For each, ask whether it is fixed or built, whether it is **partly** so and should be split with the done half closed, and — the case the migration surfaced — whether its premise still holds against the current code and served text. **Built when every open entry has been read against the system as it now stands, and each is closed, split, or confirmed open with the date it was confirmed.** The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `audit-open-entries-for-closure`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Filed at the human partner's request while finishing the BACKLOG.md migration, after a second stale current-state claim was caught by hand.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only.

**Filed as its own entry rather than folded into `re-derive-the-issue-common-causes`**, under the split rule: they can finish at different times for different reasons, one producing a taxonomy of causes and the other producing status changes, and neither shipped alone leaves a trap. **They should still be done in one sitting**, because both require reading every entry and the closure pass improves the other's input — a taxonomy built over entries that are silently already fixed counts the wrong population. Same relationship as `linking-has-no-trigger` and `cross-link-the-multi-slug-memories`.

*Confirmed open with the date it was confirmed* is the part that makes it repeatable rather than a one-off: an entry that survives the audit undated looks exactly like one nobody has checked.

content: The *Common causes* analysis in `TRACKING.md` counts against the first nine issue entries and has never been re-run against the eighty-four filed since, so the section is dated in place rather than believed. Built when each cause carries a count re-derived from the memory set with the command that produced it, retired causes are retired, and any new cause the eighty-four surfaced is written up. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `re-derive-the-issue-common-causes`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Unifying the tracking files into TRACKING.md; sweeping up the two entry heads whose text named a file that had just been deleted.
why: Superseded 2026-09-08 for the file rename alone: the analysis moved from `ISSUES.md` into `TRACKING.md` when the three tracking files were unified, and the standing, readiness and built-when are unchanged. Correcting it rather than leaving it is `correct-when` applied to the ordinary case -- the memory describes where something is, that thing moved, and the row generated from this opening would otherwise send a reader to a file that no longer exists.

content: An interface checked as its author wrote it rather than as a client receives it fails in the client's transformation, which no test saw. In this project the tool schemas were correct as published and broken on arrival: a top-level `oneOf` that a flattening client presented as a tool with no arguments, every alternation stripped by one host so an object `scope` arrived as a string, action prose that told a flattening client `amend` took only two arguments, and a refusal for fields the schema never declared, so a validating client dropped them before the server could refuse. **The structural fix is to test the surface through the transformations real clients apply** — flattened, stripped, validated — and publish only what survives them.
context: Re-deriving the common causes of defects across all 104 issues, and moving them from a hand-written section of TRACKING.md into memories the index is generated from.
why: Not in the original analysis, though its seam observation — that all nine early issues sat at the MCP boundary — was pointing at the same place from the inside. The narrower claim here is about what the boundary is tested against. No general form in `coding-lessons` yet; a candidate, since any published schema is read through someone else's parser.

content: The index generator skipped tombstones, so forgetting a supersession chain's middle reopened the entry's first version as a current row and crashed the slug check. Fixed 2026-10-19, the day it was found: `parse` in `scripts/genindex.py` reads a tombstone's `ancestry` as a step of the chain and never as a row, and `born_at` dates a first version that is no longer in the file from the time its ULID carries. Four self-check cases, each failing without its guard. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-index-generator-skips-tombstone-ancestry`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Exporting after the publication review's decisions, when regenerating TRACKING.md crashed on a pronoun memory's forgotten predecessor.
why: Head of an issue cluster, filed fixed. Misleads: the regenerated index showed `unify-the-tracking-files` open again beside its built head, and the slug check failed with a `KeyError`. It became reachable when the publication review forgot chain middles for the first time. The store resolved the chain correctly throughout. `memory_file::read` once had the same defect (`01M1X4GG6HF908MXQXKEMXTZ8B`), and the per-change recall surfaces it for the sentence that would have written this code.

content: In SQLite, `INSERT OR REPLACE` deletes the old row before inserting, so with `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` it fires `ON DELETE CASCADE` on every child table. In Scatterhoard this destroyed the reconciliation base on every amendment, because the `bases` table had been given a cascading key by analogy with its sibling tables. Cascading is right for derived data (a vector recomputed from content) and wrong for a record of agreement between two replicas, which must survive the memory being rewritten in place.
context: Filed 2026-08-05 as amending-destroyed-the-reconciliation-base, severity Corrupts; the schema comment in src/store.rs now says why bases has no foreign key.
why: Copying a schema clause from neighbouring tables reads as consistency and is really an untested assumption that the new table has the same relationship to its parent. The analogy held for four tables and broke on the fifth, and the break was invisible locally — the clause is correct in isolation and wrong only given what the row means.

content: **A detail a person's sharing preferences keep out of every set is kept out of the personal set too.** Decided 2026-10-21 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *the preferences start from a template*. The template therefore carries an explicit carve-out listing what may still go into the personal set, which the person can read and remove. `route-where`, which sends anything about the person to the personal set, has to give way to a preference that says never.
context: Building the sharing preferences served at session start. The first gemma test of the framing came back inconclusive, and that raised whether the template governs the personal set.
why: People use Scatterhoard in many places, and in some a detail can get a person arrested: being gay, in the human partner's example. Someone who wrote that their sexuality is never stored, and then mentions it to a model, is relying on that. If it lands in the personal set it is on their disk and in every backup of it. The first local-model test showed how it happens: following `route-where`, gemma sent the person's employer to `local` in every run.

content: **Upstream `uuid` committed a fix for the v7 ordering bug in https://github.com/uuid-rs/uuid/pull/915**, reported by the human partner on 2026-10-03. That is the bug behind `generated-ids-can-sort-out-of-creation-order`, which the human partner had reported by hand. Whether the fix is in a published release, and which one, was not checked when this was recorded. `issue` in `src/memory/id.rs` stays regardless: it holds the ordering whatever a given version of the crate does, and a later dependency bump changes nothing about it.
context: Starting on recall-is-latin-script-only, the last open issue, right after fixing the slug-collision check.
why: Closes the loop on the upstream report, so a later session that sees the wrapper knows the crate was fixed and does not report it again. It is also not a reason to remove the wrapper, which the earlier record already argued. The release status is left explicitly unknown rather than assumed from the commit.

content: **Measured 2026-09-08 and the best separator found so far: comparing a query against each set's `hoard-scope-topics` charter, rather than against the corpus it summarises.** Raw cosine, query against charter: on-topic queries score **0.295 to 0.472** against their best-matching set, while *how to replace a bicycle inner tube* peaks at **0.057 across all four charters** and gibberish at 0.176 — the first clean gap any candidate has produced. **It also routes**, which is the more useful function: *who may serve on the board committee* scores 0.310 against the `governance-docs` charter and 0.101, 0.108 and 0.057 against the other three, a threefold margin naming the right set. **A charter is a different object from a centroid** — an authored statement of what a set is for, not the average of its text — which is why it can succeed where `cos(query, centroid)` failed at scale by measuring register. **It does not solve the hard case.** *premier league offside rule interpretation* scores 0.310 against the `governance-docs` charter, identical to the genuinely on-topic board-committee query, and *why a slow build might not be the tests* picks `local` over `coding-lessons`. Re-run `probe_whether_set_charters_can_place_a_query` in `tests/probes.rs`.
context: Prototyping scoring variants on the live corpus, after the human partner asked to drive to a design proposal before filing.
why:
Recorded because it is the first candidate on this problem that is not a statistic over similarity scores and not a summary of the corpus, and it came from reading results rather than from computing anything — the prototype run surfaced three sets' charters at the top of a routing query, which is what suggested charters are semantically reachable at all.

Superseded 2026-09-11 UTC only to re-key it: it carried the reserved `hoard-scope-topics` as a subject keyword, which delivered it among the set charters at every session start. It now carries `about-hoard-scope-topics`, per `keyword-standards`; the claim is unchanged.

content: Found 2026-08-03 in the first session driving the fixed surface: storing `keywords: ["MemoryView", "STANDARDS"]` and recalling the memory returned `keywords: ["memoryview", "standards"]` — the same *undetectable through the only interface that exists* argument that made `recall-returns-a-partial-memory` a Corrupts. **Matching itself was correct**: both spellings hit, so case-insensitive search worked and should stay. The defect is that normalisation was applied to the **stored value** rather than to the index — the lookup key and the record were being conflated. The site is `Keyword::new` in `src/memory/text.rs`, which ended `Ok(Self(trimmed.to_lowercase()))`; the neighbouring `MemoryText` deliberately does *not* normalise and says why — *"normalising inside it would change what was recorded"* — and the same argument applies to a keyword, which is recorded content and only incidentally a lookup key.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery, and the diagnosis in one line: one column serving as both record and index. The neighbouring type had already made the argument and it had not been carried across, which is why the fix is a separation rather than a behaviour change.

content: **`coding-lessons` can be adopted by a project, as decided under `set-adoption`; built 2026-09-28 in three steps.** First, its charter was rewritten: the test is *would hold on a different codebase*, and three kinds of memory attach to a lesson by linking to it. Second, an adoption guide was written in the set, an overview and six numbered parts under `coding-lessons-adoption-guide`, with a signpost. Third, this repository's `AGENTS.md` carries the opt-in sentence and nothing else about lessons, making Scatterhoard the first project to adopt it. Whether it works in practice is tracked in `EARLY-VALIDATION.md`, and that is what the release gate now waits for. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `adopting-coding-lessons`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Finishing adopting-coding-lessons with the human partner, and setting what counts as proof of it before publication.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded to record that it is built. The human partner reviewed the charter and the guide before export, and asked that `AGENTS.md` be trimmed to the opt-in sentence so the first adoption tests the guide alone. Closed as built rather than left open, because leaving it open would say the work is unbuilt when what remains is proof, and the project keeps proof in `EARLY-VALIDATION.md`.

content:
**Two tests decide whether rationale belongs in served convention text, and the second is the one that does the work.**

1. **Does it describe a hazard, or an arrangement?** An arrangement is editor-facing. The sharpest instance: a sentence indexing the clause list — *"the third is the one a plausible description can most easily talk you out of"* — is always editor-facing, because it describes how the text is laid out rather than what can go wrong, and it rots silently when the clauses are reordered. Likewise anything explaining why a rule is *worded* as it is.
2. **Does it orient, or does it persuade?** **Served rationale must help a session recognise the case; it must not argue for having the rule.** A session reading a convention has already accepted it — the argument is spent.

**Test 2 matters because persuasion passes test 1.** It describes a real hazard and is still nearly useless at the moment of use. The model to copy is `recall-when`'s *"the moments that most need recall are the ones that least feel like it"*: it says **when to notice**, which is the hard part. The criterion lives in `src/conventions/catalog.rs`'s module header, where editing the file reaches it without anyone having to search.
context: The human partner asking which side of my own trim criterion the reinforcement sentence I had just written fell on, and then asking that the updated criterion be stored where the next convention change would find it. Split 2026-09-24 from the trims it had been bundled with, in step 2 of the out-link work, because the bundle was over the length limit.
why: **Test 2 was found by having the first draft caught**, 2026-09-09, when the human partner asked which side of test 1 a sentence I had just written fell on — it passed test 1 and failed a test not yet written down. That says something about the criterion's reach: test 1 filters the obvious cases and will pass a great deal that should not ship. Anything reading as *this rule is important because X* is persuasion; anything reading as *the case looks like this* is orientation. Not marked `hoard-signpost`: the catalog header reaches an editor by construction.

content: A `PreCompact` hook runs this project's session close-out instead of the default summarisation: [scripts/precompact-checkpoint.sh](scripts/precompact-checkpoint.sh), wired per machine in `.claude/settings.local.json` on both the `auto` and `manual` matchers. **Two things it structurally cannot do, and the design accepts both.** A shell script cannot write what was decided, what is open or what the next step is, so it writes the mechanical half — git state and every count re-derived by running its command — and asks for the rest through the hook's `additionalContext`. And **a `PreCompact` hook cannot be proven to fire from inside a turn**, because the event only occurs outside one; the script was verified by piping a synthetic payload to the exact command line the hook runs. If a compaction passes with no `checkpoints/*-precompact.md` appearing, the likely cause is the settings watcher not having picked up `.claude/`, which opening the hooks menu once reloads. Two further decisions: it does **not** block the compaction, since auto-compact fires when the window is full and refusing would wedge the session; and it does **not** run `cargo test`, leaving that line unfilled with its command beside it, because an absent number a human will fill beats a stale one nobody re-checks.
context: Asked on 2026-09-06 to rig auto-compaction to write a checkpoint and run the normal close-out, while migrating the tracking files.
why: The two limits are the part a later session would otherwise rediscover: the script cannot supply the prose, and its firing cannot be demonstrated from within a session. Both shape what the hook was built to do rather than being defects in it.

content: **`gemma4:12b` handled reports about other people well, but often left `says` out, and did not count a model as a person.** Tested 2026-10-25 with `scripts/local_model.py classify --says --context 4 --runs 3`, on 59 corpus memories. Results: 117 right, 19 missed, 2 false alarms, and 39 refused because a sentence about a person had no `says`, mostly sentences about the person in shared sets, where it changes nothing. Every report about someone else cleared, and their health and employer were caught. Its misses: a judgement of a model labelled `project` (3 of 3), "jbrown is careless" read as a report (2 of 3), and a husband quoted as `my family` rather than `my sexuality` (3 of 3). A control with the pre-change questions missed 11 of the older 144 answers, against 11 here, on different memories.
context: Building the reports-or-judges question and the keep-outs for other people into the uncommitted judgement gate, before the first export of the scatterhoard set.
why: This decides how a missing `says` is handled, since a refusal that changes no routing only costs a small model a round trip it may never get past. The control suggests the extra question did not make the mention questions worse. Misses move between memories from run to run, so three runs cannot settle that. The logs are in that session's scratchpad, `says-run2` and `final-control`.

content: Fixed 2026-09-02: `referenced_from_other_sets` gathers the rows across every loaded store, as `claims_against_hit` already did for disputes — the shape of the fix existed in this codebase, applied to one label family, reading cross-set rows *"into a report rather than into resolution, which is the whole distinction the design turns on."* **In its own field, `referenced_from`, not folded into `incoming`** — which the design had settled for `disputed_by` and which this nearly got wrong: `incoming` is what this memory's *own set* says about it, and merging a reference from elsewhere would make the two indistinguishable at the moment a reader needs to tell them apart. **And it names a `Scope` where a claim names a `SetName`**, which is the whole reason personal sets are included here and skipped there: a claim naming `local` would reach holders for whom `local` is a different set, while this is derived at read time from the stores one machine holds, appears in no export, and reaches nobody else. *A backlink derived this way is visible only on a machine holding both sets and travels in neither export — correct rather than a limitation, since the edge is one holder's private association and a shared set must not gain content from a personal one.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A fix that reuses an existing cross-store report shape, with two distinctions that look like details and are not: a separate field so provenance stays legible, and a `Scope` rather than a `SetName` so the personal-to-shared direction — the only legal one — is exactly what it shows.

content:
A cluster of memories spanning the personal/shared boundary can only be assembled from the personal side, and that constrains any convention telling people to accumulate related memories.

Two rules combine. A shared memory must not link into a personal set, because the reference dangles for every other holder of the shared set; the reverse resolves, since the only person with both sets is the one who wrote it. And `route-where` sends memories to sets by *subject*, so a cluster about one topic routinely spans sets by construction rather than by accident -- an observation about a person to `local`, the general lesson to `coding-lessons`, the project instance to the project's own set.

So the hub of a cross-boundary cluster has to be a personal memory pointing outward. **Measured 2026-09-02: the derived backlink does not close the loop** -- a cross-set edge is invisible from the target's side (`a-cross-set-link-has-no-derived-backlink` in ISSUES.md), so the cluster is reachable from the personal half alone until that is fixed.
context: Found while linking the seed for question shapes that surface defects to two earlier seeds, during the record-shape batch. The measurement was one memory writing three links in a single call -- one within its set, two crossing out -- with only the same-set backlink appearing at the far end.
why:
Hit while trying to connect three accumulation seeds that had routed to three different sets. The instinct is to link a new memory to the older one it resembles, which is whichever direction the two happen to sit in -- and half the time that is the shared-to-personal direction, which is the illegal one. Nothing refuses it: the link is stored and simply dangles for everyone else, so the mistake is invisible from the machine that made it.

This bears on `investigation-pipeline` in particular. A convention saying *accumulate related memories against a seed* will produce cross-boundary clusters as a matter of course, because its own routing rules require it -- and unless it says which end to start from, the cluster gets assembled in the one direction that cannot be followed by the people the shared half exists for. That is a drafting requirement rather than an implementation detail, and it is the kind of thing that is obvious once and then forgotten.

content: **Built 2026-09-18: evaluation mode, as `hoard_sets` action `evaluate`.** It reads a file's own header, names the copy `eval-<set>-<label>` from that and the user's label, and loads it as **a database file in `reviews/` under the home** — not in memory, because a tool sharing a machine with a local model must be sparing with it and nothing portable can say how much there is. The copy is loaded again at every start, so `drop` is the single way one goes. It adopts the file's identity but is never a holder of it: `settle_identity` and `other_holder_of` both leave evaluation stores out, so a review neither withholds the reviewer's own set nor stops it importing its own file, and dropping that set does not withhold the reviews of it. An unscoped recall does not search it; every memory it returns carries `evaluation: true`, taken from the load mode, in summaries and `hoard_lookup` alike, with a response note explaining the mark. Its cross-set links are surfaced as `cross_set_targets` — label, set name, target id, identity, and every loaded scope answering to that identity with its mode — and never resolved. It logs no query, so it calibrates nothing; it drops with no safety copy; it pulls no watch marks. **The `eval-` ban sits at three boundaries** — `create`, a file's header, and a link written into a store — **not in `SetName::new`**, which is also how a loaded set is named. Design in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md); tests across `tests/sets.rs`, `tests/memory_model.rs`, `tests/memory_file.rs`, `tests/store.rs` and `tests/floor.rs`, with eighteen recorded mutations. **Left unbuilt:** a cap on how long `evaluate` may run.
context: Building evaluation mode; the human partner reversed the in-memory storage after the first version shipped.
why: Supersedes the head written the same day, which said the copy lives in memory — the human partner reversed that before the session ended, and a head describing storage that no longer exists is the first thing a later session would build on. The rest is unchanged, including the two things most likely to be got wrong from the design alone: that a review copy is not a holder of the identity it carries, and that the prefix ban is not in the constructor.

content: **Whether memories should carry a claim digest, and how near-duplicates get found.** Raised 2026-08-30 by the human partner, from the observation that a record's checksum cannot detect two memories saying the same thing: `Record::canonical` serialises the whole record, `id`, `created` and `modified` included, so two independently authored records with identical claims never share a checksum. A **claim digest** over the claim-bearing fields alone -- `content`, `why`, `context`, `keywords`, `confidence`, `origin`, `links` -- would match exactly where identity and attribution are the only differences. **This is two mechanisms with one purpose.** The exact digest is cheap and complete, and its immediate case is mechanical: accepting an absorption fork produces pairs differing in precisely those three fields and nothing else, so the digest finds them by construction. The larger case is the one `recall-before-storing` admits it cannot reach -- *a near-duplicate written later in different words survives every mechanical check there is* -- which needs near-duplicate detection over embeddings, and that is neither cheap nor complete. **The human partner expects to build them together**, because doing the exact half alone would be re-walked by the approximate half. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `claim-digest`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The two-mechanisms framing is in the head rather than a member because it is what stops the entry being read as a small mechanical task: the exact digest looks like an afternoon's work, and building it alone is explicitly not the plan.

content: **How to inspect a memory set without adopting it.** Raised 2026-08-26 by the human partner, from a maintainer reviewing a contributor's branch: today the only way to read a set is to import it, and **import is adoption** — checking the branch back out does not undo it, and every later import reports those memories as `Anomaly`, a state no supported operation produces. **Much of this was settled 2026-09-16.** The mode is a property of **how the server loaded the set**, never of the set or its file, and there are three: evaluation (read-only, no watch list, its own temporary name, droppable with no safety copy), read-only distribution — filed separately as `read-only-distribution` — and read-write. An evaluation load is **opt-in for recall**: searched when its scope is named, excluded from an unscoped search, which answers controlling and knowing together and keeps the union centroid from being shifted by a set nobody adopted. **Still open:** how a mode is chosen at load; whether a hit should carry a set's identity, so two copies of one set are visibly copies; whether `scope` should address more than one set, since *mine and theirs as one ranked list* is currently inexpressible; and **promotion to read-write**, which needs the rule that at most one writable holder of an identity may be loaded and that identity resolution answers from it — the fix `two-sets-can-share-an-identity` is waiting on. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `evaluation-mode`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing out the evaluation-mode discussion after deciding opt-in recall, at the end of the session that built the merge driver.
why:
Head of the question cluster, superseded because its standing had gone stale in all three of the parts it listed as open: the first was answered by the three-mode narrowing, the second by the opt-in decision, and the third turned out to dissolve — promotion is a write to a *different* set rather than something a read-only set must support, leaving a loader rule rather than a promotion mechanism.

Kept open rather than resolved: what remains is genuinely undecided, and a question closed while its residue is unfiled is how work goes missing here.

**The promotion clause is the one to read carefully.** It names a rule that belongs to an issue rather than to this question, deliberately — the duplicate-identity defect exists today by a path that has nothing to do with evaluation mode, and whoever fixes it settles promotion as a side effect. Stating it here keeps this question from being closed on the assumption that promotion is unexamined, and keeps the issue from being fixed without anyone noticing it decided something for this one.

content: **The served text around the tools is a lever on a weak model's performance, separate from what memory supplies.** Rewording one refusal took `gemma4:12b` from 0 to 10 recoveries out of 10 (`the-missing-query-refusal-gives-no-example`), and rewording a paging line took it from always stopping after page one to never stopping (`max-chars-is-not-a-bound`). Neither change touched what the memory holds. This is not what `how-much-scatterhoard-lifts-a-small-model` would test directly, but it bears on any measurement of it: a weak model that misreads a tool's documentation cannot benefit from the memory behind it, so poor results could come from the text rather than the memory. **A related line of tests, proposed by the human partner:** how weak models respond to the rest of the tool surface. That covers each tool's and each parameter's description, and each refusal, tested with `scripts/local_model.py` (`retry` for refusals, `agent` for descriptions).
context: Right after fixing the missing-query refusal with gemma's help; the human partner asked to connect it to the open question about how much memory lifts a small model.
why: Recorded at the human partner's request, to connect the refusal fix to the open question. Two things a later session designing the capability measurement should know. Served-text quality has to be controlled for, or held fixed, or the measured lift mixes two effects. And the cheaper tests of the tool surface are a line of work in their own right, with the harness already built. Two instances on one model, so 0.75.

content: **The embedding input's composition is not the fault, and a built-in control is what settled it.** `embedding_input` in `src/embedding.rs` embeds content, then `why`, then keywords; the composition was fixed by a 2026-07-31 ablation over 45 memories and 20 queries and never varied since, while the corpus grew to 871 and `why` fields grew into multi-paragraph essays about the act of recording. Re-run 2026-09-08 over all four compositions on the live union at forty queries: class medians move by at most **0.008** between compositions, and the count of in-domain queries inverted below the best off-corpus query is **1 of 15 in every one of them**. `why` is 34.5% of the embedded text on average, over half in 114 memories. Retrieval does rise with a memory's `why`-share — mean top-10 appearances 0.34 → 0.65 across quartiles under the live composition — **but it rises with `why` removed from the input entirely, 0.42 → 0.60**, so `why`-share is a proxy for something else and not a cause. Worst hub is 4 of 40 under every composition. Re-run `probe_whether_why_belongs_in_the_embedding_input` in `tests/probes.rs`.
context: Chasing the swinging-verdicts observation, before the off-corpus class turned out to be two populations.
why:
Recorded because it is a plausible-looking candidate that had to be killed rather than left available, and because of *how* it died. The hypothesis was that `why` is meta-discourse in one register shared across the whole corpus — "Recorded because…", "Superseded 2026-08-25 to…" — and that a variable share of shared register in each vector would make every sample of the corpus behave differently. The quartile series looked like confirmation. The content-only arm, included as a control precisely so the series could be falsified, showed the same rise, which means longer-`why` memories are retrieved more for reasons that have nothing to do with `why` being embedded.

The general form is worth more than the result: a monotone series across quartiles of a suspected cause proves nothing unless the same series is computed with the cause removed. Without that arm this would have been recorded as an eighth mechanism and a fix would have been proposed for it.

Also worth keeping is that the original ablation was a 20-query pilot on 45 memories, which is below this project's own recorded bar of forty queries. It happened to be right, which is a good reminder that a pilot being under-powered is not the same as its answer being wrong.

content: Noticed 2026-08-31 while settling that identity is a function of a set's origin. The note said nothing was wrong **in a voice that suggests something is**, permanently, on both live shared sets. The entry's plan was to re-aim it at the set's *own records* — a set whose recorded name differs from the names in its own memories is a half-finished rename, which is exactly the state both shared sets had been in, unrecorded, until it was reconstructed by inference. **Fixed 2026-09-02, and not by that plan**: building it showed the comparison has little left to find, since `rename` is atomic so the tool cannot leave a set's name disagreeing with its records, and a set legitimately holding two contributors' identity records is not a fault to report. **What the note carries instead is the state a caller is *about to run into***: this set holds identity records and this machine has not said which is yours, so the next write will be refused. `Server::must_ask_who_you_are` answers it read-only, consulting the same three layers `author_for` does, so the durable map keeps a re-added set quiet in the window between coming back and being written to. The two live shared sets now report nothing, which is what a healthy set should say.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A planned fix abandoned on building it, because the condition it would have detected had been made unreachable by another change. The replacement reports what will block the caller next rather than what merely differs — a better rule for any advisory note.

content:
**The non-match floor is built, 2026-09-11 into 2026-09-12**, in four pieces: a local query log, the `used` label that says which of its queries the set could answer, a level each store calibrates from its own log, and a recall that reads that level against **raw** content similarity. Designed in `documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md` under *Proposed 2026-09-11* and the three sections after it; contracts in `tests/query_log.rs` and `tests/floor.rs`.

What ships: one log row per store a session's recall was scored against, carrying no query text and never exported, bounded at 100 rows of each kind; a query labelled by its `scope` argument or by the session going on to look up, link to, correct, or pass back a memory it returned; `hoard_sets calibrate`, which sets the level at the **5th percentile** of the labelled window less a 0.05 margin once 20 new labels have arrived since the last calibration; `hoard_sets uncalibrate`, which removes a level outright; a floor belonging to one store and one model, cleared when the model changes; and `hoard_recall` reporting when a floor silenced everything, with `ignore_floor` to ask again.

**The rule was corrected the same day it shipped.** The first version took the minimum over the whole log and let recall write the floor down on a contradiction — a ratchet that could only fall, and that one scoped question the set could not answer destroyed permanently. Only calibration writes the level now.

**Still open, and deliberately**: whether the window size of 100 is right, which the sweep could not settle because both stores hold fewer labelled queries than that and their corpora were frozen while the real ones grew; whether the percentile and margin generalise past two stores of one project; and whether a walk-reached memory whose origin cleared the floor should survive a floor its own content similarity fails, which today it does not. `explicit-calibration-pass` holds the alternative shape the human partner asked to keep in reserve. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `calibrated-non-match-floor`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Finishing the floor with the human partner, after they asked how often recalibration would need to run and the answer turned out to be that it could never raise a level at all.
why:
Head of the backlog cluster, superseded the same day it was written because the level's rule changed underneath it: the earlier head described a minimum over everything and a floor recall could write, and both are gone. Standing stays built — what changed is how the level is computed, not whether the mechanism exists.

The evidence lives in the resolved question `floor-calibration-source` and in the sweep recorded beside this entry.

content: **How to inspect a memory set without adopting it.** Raised 2026-08-26 by the human partner, from a maintainer reviewing a contributor's branch: import is adoption, and checking the branch back out does not undo it. **Designed 2026-09-16 in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md) as a special case of read-only, and built after it** (`read-only-distribution`). Settled: an evaluation load comes from a file, once, through a `hoard_sets` action with no `create` step. Only one is loaded at a time. It gets a temporary name the software chooses, which says it is an evaluation copy. It is searched only when its scope is named, and every hit is marked, because the LLM is exploring the set and its memories are not settled. It pulls no watch marks, drops without a safety copy, and does not count as a holder of its identity outside its own searches. It lives in memory, with a size limit to be set by timing a full embed rather than guessed. **Still open:** the size limit itself, and whether a hit also carries its set's identity so two copies of one set are visibly copies. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `evaluation-mode`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Writing the load-modes design document after fixing two-sets-can-share-an-identity, once the human partner reordered the work to build read-only before evaluation.
why: Supersedes the head because its open parts have mostly moved. How a mode is chosen is answered for read-only by `create`, and for evaluation by its own action. Addressing more than one set is answered by one at a time. The promotion clause is now owned by read-only. The order of work also changed: evaluation now waits on read-only, which the old head did not say, hence the `depends_on` link. Kept open for the size limit and the identity-on-hits question, and because nothing is built.

content: Found 2026-08-11 by exporting `local` to see whether it would be refused. It was not, and it should not have been. **A model reading the schema was told the backup route for personal memories does not exist**, against a design that had deliberately settled *"a memory set that cannot be backed up is one bad disk away from being gone."* The intended meaning was that local memories are never *shared* — a statement about the review gate rather than about writing a file. **Fixed 2026-08-11**: the description reads *"never shared to a repository, so it never goes through export review — but it can still be exported, which for this scope means writing a backup."* **Pinned against a live export of `local` in the same test**, so the string cannot drift back into denying a capability the tool offers.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A description that denied a capability the same tool provides, found by trying the thing the text said was impossible. The fix pins the wording against an actual exercise of the capability, so prose and behaviour cannot drift apart again.

content: Building a Scatterhoard test corpus by working back through past sessions would produce a link graph shaped by the labelling pass, not by ordinary use — the same condition that made corpus/link-label-findings.md rich in MOTIVATED_BY and SUPPORTS where live storage produces almost none. That makes such a corpus the wrong instrument for tuning traversal weights, and the right one for testing fan-out, hubness and expansion bounds, which depend on volume and shape rather than on how the labels came to be there.
context: Raised 2026-08-14 when the human partner offered building such a corpus as an option for testing the traversal design. Not decided either way; recorded so the instrument's limits travel with the proposal.
why: Weights tuned on a deliberately-labelled corpus would be fitted to an artifact of how the corpus was built, and would then be applied to a graph that does not look like it. The distinction is worth holding because the corpus is expensive to build and the failure would be invisible: the numbers would look measured rather than guessed.

content: `by_keyword` entries carried no `why`, so on the degradation path — the configuration most likely to be someone's first encounter with Scatterhoard — every recalled memory arrived without its reasoning. Fixed 2026-08-03 with the `MemoryView` convergence. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `keyword-path-drops-reasoning`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **A caveat written into the record at the moment of measurement did not survive being cited.** The 2026-08-03 absolute-floor measurement said in its `context` line *re-measure on a larger store before building on this*. Each later reference carried the conclusion and dropped the condition, and by the time it reached the 2026-09-08 list of ruled-out mechanisms it read as a settled negative. A caveat that lives only in a `context` line is not attached to the claim in any way a later session will feel.
context: Testing the human partner's prediction that the swinging verdicts would subside once their cause was found, by re-running the ruled-out mechanisms against form-controlled query sets. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the memory was over the length limit.
why: Split from the re-measurement that exposed it, because the shape outlasts the number: it is how the absolute floor spent a month ruled out on evidence that never supported the ruling, and the same thing will happen to any caveat kept apart from its claim.

content: **History from before drafting, 2026-08-12: the measurement that produced the convention.** Across both live sets, **37 memories carried five distinct confidence values** — 0.8 once, 0.85 eight times, 0.9 seventeen times, 0.95 eight times, 1.0 three times — and **nothing below 0.8 had ever been written**. Refreshed 2026-08-13 before drafting and the finding strengthened: 44 memories, still exactly five values, still nothing below 0.8, mean 0.888; the seven added since introduced no new value. A field whose whole observed range is the top fifth of the scale carries almost no information, and a reader cannot tell whether that reflects well-founded memories or a session with no idea what the number means. **One constraint on the wording came from Corrections**: changing confidence on an identical claim is a recalibration of apparatus rather than a new belief, so the convention must not push a session toward superseding when it becomes more or less sure.
context: Migrating the confidence-guidance entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the measurement it was argued from.
why:
Irreproducible: the corpus was 37 memories and is now near 500, mostly through migration, so re-running the distribution today answers a different question. This is the baseline any later claim that the convention worked would have to be measured against, and it existed only in the entry body until 2026-09-07.

**One thing the entry said is now wrong and is deliberately not carried forward.** It cited the Golden Rule as already giving the field a job — *an uncharitable generalisation should be recorded as the low-confidence claim it usually is* — as the clearest existing statement of what a low number is for. That clause has since been contradicted by the same document's demand D: where the unknowns are significant the generalisation is **not recorded at all**, rather than recorded and discounted. The shipped convention reflects the corrected position, not the one the entry was drafted against.

content: `hoard_sets export` compares its records with the file it is replacing and refuses to write if that would drop records the file holds, or if the file cannot be read — so another session's work, or records a pull brought in, can no longer vanish in an export. Built 2026-09-14 as `Replaced` in `src/mcp.rs`, reported as `replaced_file` (new, changed and removed records) on every export that goes ahead; nothing persisted and no new field on any record. Widened twice while building, both by the human partner: from counting only new records to all three, and from reporting a removal to refusing it. The way through a refusal is importing first, or moving the file aside for an intended overwrite. Contract in `tests/sets.rs`; the approval recording `tests/snapshots/sets_export.json` shows the first-export shape; mutations under `replaced file:` in `scripts/mutations.py`. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `export-reports-what-the-file-did-not-hold`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building the export refusal straight after committing the export delta report.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because the built behaviour changed: export now refuses a removal rather than only reporting it. The opening sentence is the generated index row, so it states what export does now. The refusal decision and its reasoning are their own memory under this entry's keyword.

content: Sending `scope`'s spelling as a link's `target_set` was refused with *"a set name must not contain ':'"*, naming no field and no fix. Fixed 2026-09-30 in `Link`'s parser in `src/memory/link.rs`: `target_set` is read as text and validated there, so every refusal names the field, and `shared:<name>` is answered with the bare name to send and why the two fields differ: `scope` needs the prefix to tell a shared set from `local`, while `target_set` only names shared sets. The field's schema description now gives the bare spelling too. The cluster's other observation, `target_set` sent for a link within the caller's own set, was already answered by canonicalisation at the write. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-set-name-refusal-does-not-say-how-the-other-field-spells-it`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through open issues with the human partner, after fixing the catalog's byte count.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed as its fixed-when asked: the refusal names the field, gives the corrected spelling, and says how the two differ. Tested by taking the remedy, resending the spelling the refusal recommends and requiring it be accepted, per the coding-lessons lesson on refusals that name a remedy. Two tests in `tests/mcp.rs` and two mutations. Also changed: the `tools_list` snapshot, at the two places the description is served.

content: **The export review checks each memory against the keep-out items in the person's own sharing-preferences file, as worded there, with exceptions applied per set.** Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. In a shared set the server clears a memory only if it is about the project and mentions nothing kept out there. In `local` it clears one that mentions nothing kept out. A memory about someone else always goes to the person.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public, after deciding clear takes per-memory answers.
why: The file is the one source of truth the person can read and edit, so a keep-out they add is checked without any change to Scatterhoard. Exceptions keep working because the model applies them per set. The rejected alternative was a fixed list built into the server, which would ignore what the person adds and copy the template by hand: the `a-fact-restated-by-hand-drifts` cause, with fifteen issues filed under it.

content: Fixed 2026-08-10: each store records its author in `meta`, `Store::author_or_claim` fills in an absent one from the process default and **never displaces a present one**, and every write path goes through `Server::author_for`. **The near-miss worth recording: reading claimed the store.** Adoption was first written into the path that opens a store, which would have made the identity a store settles on a race between two processes' *startup* — the same accident one step earlier, and invisible because both orders produce a plausible result. `recall_does_not_claim_a_store_for_the_reader` exists because of it. **The rule that came out of it is more general than this defect and is now design**: a process may fill in what a shared store does not know; it may not overwrite what the store already says — the same conclusion [Embeddings](documents/design/embeddings.md) reached for the embedding model, arrived at independently.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A fix that nearly reintroduced the defect one layer earlier, and the general rule the near-miss produced. That two independent lines of reasoning reached the same fill-but-never-overwrite rule is what makes it design rather than a local fix.

content: **An evaluation copy adopts its file's set identity but is never a holder of it.** `settle_identity` and `other_holder_of` both leave evaluation stores out, so a review neither withholds the reviewer's own set nor stops it importing its own file, and dropping that set does not withhold the reviews of it. **The `eval-` name ban sits at three boundaries** — `create`, a file's header, and a link written into a store — **not in `SetName::new`**, which is also how a loaded set is named. Built 2026-09-18.
context: Moved 2026-09-24 out of the entry's head, which was over the length limit, in step 2 of the out-link work.
why: The two things about evaluation mode most likely to be got wrong from the design alone, moved out of its head: both look like oversights, and fixing either would break reviews.

content: **Whether a set carries a UUID, minted at creation and travelling in the file header. Resolved 2026-08-30, built 2026-08-31, and the cutover is complete.** Proposed 2026-08-26 by the human partner as a candidate answer to the trust questions gathered on the set-lifecycle list. The name stops being identity; the identity never changes for a set. **The migration was a hard cut, chosen because the window was still open in a precise sense:** the memory file is committed, so anyone cloning already has the *file* -- what nobody has is a *store built from it*, and the hazard was two stores independently minting rival identities for one set. *Mint on import* fails because every importer of a legacy file mints a different identity, manufacturing the collision the change exists to prevent; *auto-mint at export* is the same hazard one door over. **Verified 2026-09-07: all four sets on this machine carry an identity**, three of them sharing a mint prefix from the single cutover operation and the fourth created afterwards. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `set-uuid`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

**Marked resolved on migration although the file still had it unchecked**, 2026-09-07. The entry records the decision, the build and the cutover design, and closes on *which the three existing sets still have to be run through* -- a present-tense claim that was true when written and is not now. `hoard_sets status` shows every set carrying a `set_id`, so nothing is outstanding. This is the `audit-open-entries-for-closure` work arriving through migration rather than through the audit: checking the entry's own present-tense claims is what exposed it, and no separate pass was needed.

The three rejected mint strategies are kept in the head because the hard cut is a one-time operation that cannot be repeated, and a later session meeting a set without an identity will be tempted by exactly the two options that were rejected.

content: **The recall nudge cannot tell the per-change recall from any other recall of the same shape, observed 2026-10-19.** Before pseudonymising `tests/probes.rs`, a behaviour change, the session made no per-change recall. The nudge logged `recalled` at both writes, because the publication review had made several unscoped `ignore_floor` summary recalls since the last commit, none about the change. `is_habit_recall` in `scripts/recall_nudge.py` checks the call's shape (a query, no scope, `ignore_floor`, summary) and nothing about whether it concerns the change. Before the `genindex.py` fix on 2026-10-20 the recall was made properly. It surfaced the cause the defect belonged to, but did not change the fix.
context: Gathering the evidence for the `coding-lessons` release gate, after the publication review's commits.
why: An observation under `adopting-coding-lessons`, item 5, and against the nudge's experiment. Its log reads 53 of 58 code writes as preceded by a habit recall, and this shows that figure counts calls with the right shape, not recalls about the change. So it is an upper bound on the habit. It matters most in sessions doing memory-heavy work, where survey recalls with the habit's settings are common. Whether to tighten the detector, for example by requiring the recall to fall after the last edit, is not decided.

content: **Observation for `charter-rewrite-intake-measurement` and `meta-observation-convention`, 2026-09-14, in `scatterhoard` — the set whose gloss was rewritten.** Over one fix, a session read code and design documents and worked out material of the method-and-path kind: how a set comes to hold an identity and when adoption may replace one, that the broken link it was fixing cannot arise from a renamed copy, that the links table's key ignores the target set, and that identity matching may reach the local set. Each changed what it recommended. It stored none of it as a memory of its own until the human partner asked whether the conventions had prompted it to. Some had gone into the reasons of a decision memory; the rest existed only in the conversation. The conventions had been loaded at the start of the session. The same session did store decisions, issue heads and entry standings promptly throughout, and wrote a *worth remembering* list before each commit. **The investigation ended in a question handed back to the human, not in a commit or an export**, so none of `capture-before-ending`'s event triggers occurred at its end.
context: The human partner asked, after a long investigation of set identity and link formats, whether the conventions had prompted recording any of it, and proposed rewording capture-before-ending around handing control back.
why:
A data point for two open items, and the same one serves both.

**For the charter investigation**, it counts against the hypothesis for this session: the conclusions were recorded and the paths were not, until prompted from outside. One session doing tracked work, where decisions and entry standings have their own prompting in `TRACKING.md` and discoveries made in passing have none — an observation to classify with the others, not a verdict.

**For `meta-observation-convention`**, it is a second instance of the 2026-09-07 failure after that question was filed, and it lands on the seam that question's findings predicted: the event triggers fired where events occurred, and material worked out on the way to a hand-back had no trigger. It is evidence for the candidate recorded then — the moment before handing back to the human — which the human partner proposed again on 2026-09-14 as a rewording of `capture-before-ending`.

Supersedes the first version of this observation, which linked only the charter investigation: the connection to `meta-observation-convention` was visible once both were recalled, and `recall-when` asks for it to be made then. Recorded as what happened rather than as a conclusion about the session's habits, per `store-when`'s rule for memories about a person, a model included.

content: Scatterhoard's own `checkpoints/` files out-compete its memory sets at the boundary they share, and the checkpoints are gitignored. On 2026-08-13 the session captured seven memories in three separate bursts — so `capture-before-ending` fired three times — and none recorded that day's raise of the catalog budget to 18,000. The capture at 22:49 was followed at 22:51 by a checkpoint carrying a whole section titled "The budget is 18,000, and the standard for the next raise is recorded". The fact was in hand two minutes after the capture ran, and went to the one place designed not to outlive the session.
context: Found 2026-08-24, tracing why the corpus held a withdrawn 16,000 figure for eleven days after the budget was raised to 18,000.
why: This rules out the two explanations that looked most likely. It is not a missing trigger: three fired that day. It is not `store-when`'s enumeration, which named "a decision and what it rules out" and under which the *first* budget raise was captured the day before. What separates the two raises is that the first was learned while restoring from a checkpoint and the second was made by the session itself while doing something else — and a decision the session made reads as session narrative, which is what a checkpoint is for. So the split is by the shape of the thing rather than by its durability, and the durable half loses whenever a fact reads like bookkeeping. Checkable by comparing the memory timestamps in the exported sets against checkpoints/2026-08-13-2255.md.

content: **The recall-before-writing habit asks unscoped, with `ignore_floor`, `detail: summary` and a tight limit.** Decided 2026-09-28 by the human partner. A scoped recall labels its query as one the set should answer, and calibration lowers the floor towards what labelled queries scored. The habit asks speculatively and mostly finds nothing relevant, so scoped habit queries would drag `coding-lessons`' floor down to noise for every other query to that set. Unscoped, a query is labelled only when the session goes on to use a returned trigger (looks it up, links to it, or passes it back as already known), and the label lands in the trigger's own store. So the floor learns only from triggers that genuinely matched. **Watch**: whether real trigger hits score below that set's floor, and whether calibrating after habit use moves the floor. Checkable in `Store::calibrate` and `Store::note_used` in `src/store.rs`.
context: Designing how projects that opt in to `coding-lessons` catch failures before they are written, after the trigger experiment.
why: `ignore_floor` was chosen first, because the experiment's correct trigger hits scored below `coding-lessons`' floor (`01M3JTCXF1…`). The human partner then asked whether floor-waived queries still feed calibration. They do: the waiver is not logged, and a scope label is what counts, which is what made scoping the problem. The cost accepted is that an unscoped recall ranks across every loaded set, so a project set of long memories may crowd triggers out of a tight limit. That is the short-memory effect between sets, and is not measured yet.

content: **The catalog has 24 characters free, derived 2026-09-23** — `CATALOG n=11 ids=177 body=17799 total=17976 free=24` from `cargo test --test conventions report_catalog_size -- --ignored --nocapture`. Both of this question's gates now read differently: the restructured wording has been lived with for a month, and the room is gone rather than short, so the next convention drafted forces the question rather than fitting under it. The standing objection — a budget raised whenever it binds is not a budget — is still unspent, and the cheaper answer worked last time by trimming 363 characters of justifying reinforcement. Derive again before using this; the figure is written here dated because it is an audit reading, not a fact to quote.
context: Auditing the open questions for closure, the day after the file-position column went in.
why: This cluster's own rule is never to write a headroom figure down, because six of them went stale in the original entry. Written anyway, dated and with the command beside it, because the audit's finding *is* the reading: 24 free is a different situation from the 320 the migration recorded, and a sweep that said only "still open" would have hidden that. The rule it bends is about quoting figures forward, which this explicitly refuses.

content: **Re-measured 2026-09-08, and the expectation that a linked memory is semantically distant from its source is wrong: links overwhelmingly join memories that are already close.** With the query falling exactly on a link's source — the best case for traversal from that seed — the median target sits at the **1.13th percentile in `scatterhoard`** (711 memories, 89 measurable edges of 119, so about rank 8) and the **4.13th percentile in `coding-lessons`** (121 memories, 78 edges, about rank 5). The 2026-08-15 figure was 2.9% over 23 edges. **Both sets now clear their own crossover**: `scatterhoard`'s is 445 against a size of 711, so traversal is finally returning memories a top-5 content cut would not, which was not true in August. **The two sets differ in the direction that matters more than density:** `coding-lessons` links reach nearly four times further in similarity terms, so its edges bridge ideas the embedding would not have connected, where `scatterhoard`'s mostly join neighbours. Re-run `probe_where_a_link_target_sits_now` in `tests/probes.rs`.
context: Probing the gap cut, when the human partner asked whether the cutoff belongs after link-walking because linked memories would drop sharply in similarity.
why: Recorded because the intuition it corrects is a strong and reasonable one — a `related_to` or `contradicts` edge *could* point anywhere, so it feels as though it usually would — and the corpus says authors mostly link what is already adjacent. That has a consequence for what traversal is worth: an edge joining two memories the embedding already ranks side by side adds nothing a larger limit would not, which is exactly what the crossover measures. It also reframes link density as the wrong quantity to optimise: `coding-lessons` is four times denser *and* its links reach four times further, and the second is what would make traversal earn its cost. Kept with the caveat that the source's own vector is a best case — a real query lands near a seed, never on it — so these percentiles bound how close targets are, not how close they will look in use.

content: **A third way an unanswerable query scores high: one term of art in an otherwise off-domain question.** *why does bread go stale faster in the fridge* scores **0.476** against the `scatterhoard` set — the highest of thirty substance-shaped probes, above the worst answerable query at 0.361, and 0.165 clear of the next probe. **The cause is the single word `stale`**, which is a term of art here: stale mutations, a memory gone stale, the convention `split-when-partly-stale`. Confirmed by minimal pair rather than inferred — swapping it for *dry out* drops the score to **0.366, a fall of 0.110**, where two control pairs (*crack*/*split*, *boil*/*froth*) move only 0.038 each. This is distinct from the rule-shaped collision: that one is a genuine similarity of subject matter, this one is lexical, and a static bag-of-tokens model has no way to notice that the domain around the word is wrong. **Design consequence: a calibration probe set needs screening against the store's own vocabulary, not merely against its topic**, and the statistic taken over it must be robust — this single probe is exactly what makes the max rule unusable while p90 survives.
context: Expanding the calibration probe set from twelve to thirty, which is what exposed the collision.
why:
Recorded because it is the first confirmed mechanism for a false confident hit on this entry, as opposed to a characterisation of when they happen. The entry itself named the suspect — *the vocabulary of a static bag-of-tokens model* — after the embedder was cleared on four counts; this is that suspect caught in the act, with a controlled comparison rather than a plausible story.

It matters more for probe-set design than for scoring. An off-domain probe set is easy to write and feels safe, and the failure is invisible from the outside: nothing about *why does bread go stale faster in the fridge* looks like a question about Scatterhoard. Screening candidate probes against the store's keyword vocabulary would have caught it in a second, and no amount of thinking about topic would.

Confidence 0.9 rather than higher because the minimal-pair test isolates the word convincingly but was run on three pairs against one corpus. The mechanism is standard for static embeddings, which is what keeps it from needing more.

content: Fixed 2026-09-06 by re-keying fifteen memories the same day it was filed, each superseded by a replacement carrying `about-hoard-scope-topics` or `about-hoard-watch` in place of the reserved term, its claim otherwise unchanged. **Verified by recalling all three reserved terms together**: `hoard-scope-topics` returned four memories and all four were charters, `hoard-author` four and all four identity records, `hoard-watch` nothing at all. Before the pass those three returned twenty-two, nine of them impostors. The one live watch was re-keyed too — it had carried `hoard-watch` alongside `hoard-collect`, and `hoard-watch` marks nothing now — and `hoard-collect` still returns it.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix with its verification, which is the part worth keeping: the check was an enumeration of every reserved term rather than a spot check of the ones that had been edited.

content: **Optional and add-on are different trust propositions, not just different provenance -- and the shared serving mechanism is what makes it tempting to treat them alike.** Bundled-optional ships in this repository and is reviewed like source; it differs from the built-in catalog **only by being off by default**. Add-on is third-party prose installed at arm's length. **The likely consequence is that add-ons need explicit per-`id` opt-in** rather than *everything in the directory is included* -- which doubles as the answer to how a user discovers what they have enabled. **The line between built-in and optional is expected to move**, and the human partner declined to pre-commit to a taxonomy; the candidate test held provisionally is *a convention belongs built-in if a user who does not know it exists would be worse off*, to be judged against real candidates rather than settled in advance.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the two categories share a mechanism and differ in the only thing that matters for safety, which is precisely the shape of mistake that gets made once and then defended as consistency.

The per-`id` opt-in consequence is worth recording separately from the reasoning that produces it: it is a concrete surface decision that falls out of the trust distinction, and it solves a second problem -- discoverability of what is enabled -- which would otherwise be designed for on its own.

The provisional test is recorded as provisional, with its own caveat attached, because a memory stating it flatly would harden a judgement its author deliberately left soft.

content: Scatterhoard scores recall similarity against the centroid of the union of all loaded memory sets, not per-set centroids. This is what makes scores comparable when more than one set is loaded.
context: Decided 2026-07-31 during design of recall scoring; re-affirmed 2026-08-02 as a constraint on any fix to the cold-start score problem.
why: Per-set centroids would make a 0.4 from one set and a 0.4 from another different measurements, and nothing in the result would say so. The union centroid keeps one scale across every loaded set.

content: **Measured over the two live sets, it is real but not yet biting**: 16 superseded memories carry 3 non-`supersedes` in-links between them, all `related_to`, all in `coding-lessons` — and `related_to` is the label that survives re-pointing best. Read that with the graph-shape measurement in the `scatterhoard` set: the claim-bearing labels are rare in live writing generally, so **the absence of a harmful instance is partly the absence of the labels that would cause one**. **Why it will matter more than the count suggests**: supersession already outnumbers amendment eight to one in these sets, and the proposal under discussion — correction restricted to records that never entered service, supersession taking the whole update load — moves every claim change onto the mechanism with the silent hazard.

why: A measurement that finds almost nothing and does not exonerate: the harmless result is explained by the rarity of the labels that would make it harmful, and a design change under discussion increases the exposure.

content:
**Semantic recall is Latin-script only, and for some text a memory cannot be stored at all.** Raised 2026-09-09 by the human partner asking whether an English calibration set could serve a Chinese or Hindi user. It cannot, and the reason is upstream of calibration. `potion-base-32M` is distilled from `baai/bge-base-en-v1.5`, whose WordPiece vocabulary is **58,548 of 63,091 tokens Latin (92.8%)** — 492 CJK characters against the three to five thousand common usage needs, **71 Devanagari**, 111 Cyrillic. `model2vec-rs` **discards `[UNK]` before pooling**, so unrecognised text contributes nothing rather than noise, and `Vector::new` refuses the direction-less result.

**Three failure modes, measured.** One question against an unrelated statement in the same language, where near zero is healthy:

| language | unrelated-pair similarity | storable |
|---|---|---|
| English | **0.071** | yes |
| Spanish / French | 0.158 / 0.162 | yes |
| German | 0.276 | yes |
| Japanese | **0.721** | yes |
| Hindi | **0.880** | yes |
| Russian | **0.908** | yes |
| **Chinese** | — | **no: `store failed: embedding failed`** |

So Chinese fails hard at the write. Russian, Hindi and Japanese store and then **cannot be told apart** — every query matches everything, because the script has collapsed onto the few tokens the vocabulary holds. Keyword search is unaffected; it matches on `toNFKC_Casefold` and is script-agnostic.
context: The human partner asking whether a calibration set drawn from English non-fiction could calibrate a floor for a Chinese or Hindi user.
why:
Filed as an issue rather than a question because nothing here is a design choice awaiting a decision: a store that refuses a memory in one of the world's most-written languages, and returns everything for any query in three others, is behaving wrongly by any reading. What to *do* about it is a design question and a large one — a multilingual model, a script check at the write door, an honest refusal that says why — but the defect stands independently of that.

**The severity is that it misleads rather than blocks, for two of the three modes.** Chinese blocks loudly, which is the better failure. Russian, Hindi and Japanese store successfully and recall confidently, and nothing anywhere reports that the similarity numbers are meaningless — a user in those languages gets a memory system that appears to work and returns arbitrary results. That is the same shape as `an-unanswerable-query-returns-confident-hits`, one layer down and far worse.

**It also answers the calibration question conclusively.** A floor cannot be calibrated for a Hindi store because there is nothing to calibrate: the separation the floor would sit inside does not exist at 0.880. The probe set is irrelevant to that. Any work on multilingual calibration is downstream of a model that separates meanings in the script at all.

The measurement is thin in one respect worth stating: one sentence pair per language, chosen by me. The Chinese refusal and the vocabulary counts are facts; the exact similarities would move with other sentences, though not by enough to change the reading.

The placement argument is decision-placement applied to a safeguard: aggregation harm is a property of the set, since a dossier can be assembled entirely from individually answerable, work-serving memories, so no rule examining one memory at a time can see it and routing is the only layer that can. The transparency argument on the other side is real -- a charter is visible and reviewed like any other memory -- and is the thing to revisit if the trade ever looks wrong. Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claim is unchanged.

The other is the transfer case, where an abstract lesson is unreachable by content, the kind the human partner wanted kept. 11 failures is enough to rule out large headroom and not enough for a rate, hence 0.75.
