Found 2026-09-02 after nearly writing a duplicate of an open entry sitting under the wrong heading: ISSUES.md recorded each entry's status **twice**, as an `[x]` marker and by position under `## Open` or `## Fixed`, with neither authoritative and adoption almost exactly even — **32 fixed entries under `Open`, 33 under `Fixed`, of 84** — and three *open* entries had drifted under `## Fixed`, greppable but invisible to anyone reading the Open section. **Fixed 2026-09-07 by the tracking-file migration, and more completely than the entry asked**: the sections are gone and the surviving marker is **generated** from the head memory's status keyword, so the two cannot disagree because there is no longer a second place to disagree from. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `issues-records-its-status-twice`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set; this is the second-to-last entry, and the migration had already fixed it.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only.

**Closed as built rather than migrated open, and the reasoning is stated because the entry itself did not predict this route.** Its Built-when offered two shapes — drop the section split, or section by subject — and asked for *a mechanical check that fails when a marker and its section disagree*. What happened instead makes the disagreement **unrepresentable**: the marker is derived, so there is nothing to check. `genindex.py --check` exists and catches file-versus-memory drift, which is the check the entry wanted, arrived at from the other direction.

The last residue was closed the same day: the file's header still said *mark fixed entries `[x]` with the commit*, an instruction for a workflow that no longer exists, and now describes the generated mechanism instead.

content:
**One memory the model cannot embed stops its store: writes fail, and unscoped recall fails across every set.** Found 2026-09-11 UTC reproducing the Chinese case of `recall-is-latin-script-only` on disposable homes. A memory whose embedded text — content, `why` and keywords together, per `embedding_input` in `src/embedding.rs` — contains no token the model knows pools to a zero vector, which `Vector::new` refuses. Three things then go wrong, all observed:

1. **The failed write is committed.** `Store::write` commits the row and *then* calls `embed_all`, so `hoard_memorize` returns `could not store the memory: embedding failed` while `hoard_sets status` counts the memory. No id is returned, and with no keywords and semantic recall down, nothing on the tool surface can find it to forget it.
2. **Every later write and semantic recall on that store fails.** `prepare` runs `reconcile_embeddings`, which sends every unembedded memory through one `embed` call; one refusal fails the batch, so an ordinary English write is refused next.
3. **Unscoped recall fails for every loaded set**, not just the poisoned one: a healthy `shared:t` answered only when scoped to it.

**Three routes in, all reproduced:** a direct write with the model loaded; a write during a no-model gap, which stores fine and poisons the store once a model arrives; and **import**, which commits the whole file and then reports `could not store memory <id>: embedding failed` with the set already replaced. Import is the route that reaches collaborators — a shared set carrying one such memory poisons every machine that imports it. **Forgetting the memory repairs the store at once.** **Fixed looks like:** a memory the model cannot represent is stored unembedded and the caller is told so, as the no-model path already does; it never fails a batch, and no write reports failure after committing.
context: Restoring from the checkpoint and starting on the Latin-script recall issue, after the human partner pointed out that English off-domain probes might not calibrate a floor for a store in another language. Same stretch: noticed two charter-matching measurements carrying the reserved `hoard-scope-topics` keyword.
why:
Filed `corrupts` rather than `blocks` because the first failure is silently wrong state: the caller is told a memory was not stored when it was, and then has no way to find it. The rest follows from that one unreported row.

Separate from `recall-is-latin-script-only` because it is not about which text a model covers but about what the store does when a model cannot cover something — and every model has text it cannot cover, so this survives any answer to the language question, a multilingual model included. It also contradicts that entry's reading that Chinese "blocks loudly, which is the better failure": the failure is loud and wrong, and it takes the store with it.

The embeddings design already states the rule this breaks — *a store must not be reachable into a state its own tool surface cannot repair* — and the direct-write route reaches exactly that state, since the only repair is forgetting a memory whose id was never returned.

Reproduced only on the third attempt: the first two gave the Chinese memory an English `why`, then an English keyword, and each was enough for a vector. The reproduction therefore uses Chinese in every embedded field.

content: Scatterhoard closed malformed-tool-call damage on 2026-08-19 by replacing the remark with an escape plus a refusal, in that order. The prose fields of `hoard_memorize` and `hoard_correct` decode `<` `>` and `&` into those characters on the way in -- one left-to-right pass whose output is never re-scanned, which is what lets `<` mean the entity itself. The refusal is a conjunction, not a disjunction: a parameter is named as swallowed only when its framing (`</why>`, or `<parameter name="why">` arriving as text) appears in a prose field AND that parameter arrived empty. Thirteen occurrences preceded the fix, four of them repairs for the one before.
context: Written 2026-08-19 while running SETUP.md section 5 item 19, which exists to exercise this exact path -- this memory is itself the previously-unstorable class. Checkable at SWALLOWED, `decode_entities` and `swallowed_parameters` in src/mcp.rs.
why: The order is the load-bearing part and is invisible from the fix itself: refusing is only safe once a memory about markup can be written at all, so the escape had to land first. The conjunction matters for the same reason -- either half alone produces a false positive this repository demonstrates, since ISSUES.md quotes tool-call framing throughout, and a disjunction flagged a memory about the defect by its own subject matter. Carried forward from the superseded record because they remain live: do not repair this by making `why` required, which trades away a decided property, nor by ordering a required parameter after `content`, which depends on an emission order nothing controls.

content: **A short trigger memory's correct match scored 0.28 to 0.31 on 2026-09-28, below `coding-lessons`' calibrated non-match floor of 0.333,** so in that set the same recall would have returned nothing and reported that nothing answers. Measured in an uncalibrated scratch set with `potion-base-32M`, three matches read, no floor applied. The wrong answers `coding-lessons` returned for the same activity queries were longer lessons, which suggests that under a static model a short memory scores lower than a long one sharing a few words. That is inferred from these readings and not tested. Anything relying on recall to find triggers has to reckon with the floor: recall with `ignore_floor`, use the keyword path, or put triggers in a set whose floor is calibrated on triggers.
context: The same trigger experiment, read against the calibration of the set the triggers would live in.
why: A recall habit meant to catch mistakes before they are written would, in the set holding the lessons, be silenced by the floor built to say *nothing here answers that*, and silenced in the form that reads as a clean answer. It also bears on the floor itself, which was calibrated on memories as they are usually written: long and hindsight-phrased.

content: **A candidate cause for `memory-size-drift`, reported 2026-09-15 and not yet tested: the drift may follow the model writing the memories rather than anything in the corpus.** On seeing the baseline, the human partner said it matches what they see in other memory systems, and that they have subjectively noticed generally more text in model responses. If that is the cause, length would move with the model or its version rather than with what is being recorded, and a response placed in Scatterhoard's own text — a convention, a store-time note — would be pushing against the author of every memory rather than correcting a habit of the corpus. **What would test it:** whether length steps at a model change rather than rising smoothly, which needs the writing model recorded somewhere; the store does not record it today, so the existing baseline cannot separate the two.
context: Right after filing the memory-size question and committing it, when the human partner said the drift matched other systems and their sense of longer responses.
why: Kept because it bears directly on the question's open part — where a response belongs — and because it is the kind of observation that is available only from someone who watches several systems at once. Confidence is set low on purpose: it is one person's subjective impression, consistent with the measurement without being shown by it. The observation is recorded as stated; the reading of what it would imply is mine.

content: Every tool published what goes in and nothing about what comes back: no tool carried an `outputSchema`, so a response shape that varies, such as `similarity` on a direct hit and `matched_similarity` on a substituted one, was learnable only by provoking each case. Fixed 2026-10-03. Every JSON-returning tool publishes an `outputSchema` and returns `structuredContent`, both only to clients that negotiate the 2025-06-18 revision. Conditional fields say when they appear, and every tool response in the approval, MCP and sets suites is checked against its schema strictly, so an undeclared field fails a test. `documents/design/tool-surface.md`, 2026-10-03; `src/output_schema.rs`. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `response-shape-is-unpublished`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Publishing output schemas after fixing the missing-query refusal; Claude's client briefly refused the tool list over a missing top-level object type.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed as its fixed-when asked: the shape is published with conditional fields marked conditional. What makes it more than documentation is the strict check, which turns drift into a failing test; the earlier instance of drift was found only by luck. The human partner chose the approach (schema plus a little prose), the trim to conditional descriptions, and gating on the protocol version so a client can avoid the cost. The tool list grew from 20,247 to about 46,000 characters, most of it schemas a host may or may not show a model.

content: Two branches that both add memories conflict at the end of the memory file under a plain `git` merge, because records are written in id order and ids are time-ordered, so concurrent additions are insertions at one point. A hosted merge button never runs the merge driver, so every pull request whose base gained memories conflicts until someone merges locally. Fixed when concurrent additions merge cleanly under plain `git`. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `concurrent-additions-collide-at-the-end-of-the-memory-file`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Pre-release review of what would keep others from using Scatterhoard, straight after retiring the header summary.
why: Head of an issue cluster. `costs` rather than `blocks`: nothing is lost or wrong, and resolving it is keeping both sides' lines — but it lands on every collaborator's pull requests, which makes it a release concern. Measured 2026-09-21, and left in place when the header conflict beside it was removed, because the header's fix does not reach it. The evidence carries `how-a-merged-file-gets-a-current-summary`, where it was found. One idea not yet examined is ordering records by a hash of the id, so additions scatter; what depends on id order has not been checked.

content: Found 2026-08-06 while checking whether a proposed split of the local store out of the home — since built as `SCATTERHOARD_COMMON` — could safely share it between two server processes. **This was not hypothetical and was not waiting on the registry proposal**: a server is registered per checkout, since `.mcp.json` lives in the repository, and `SCATTERHOARD_HOME` defaults to one path under `$HOME`, so a developer with two checkouts open already had two processes holding the same `local` store. Nothing had failed yet because the windows are short and the sessions had not overlapped on a write — which makes this the kind of defect that first appears as a single unreproducible error. It also constrained a design decision in flight: [store-registry.md](documents/design/store-registry.md) separates the two directories precisely so several servers can share one local store, making deliberate a sharing pattern the code was not configured for.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery, and the argument that the risky configuration already existed rather than being introduced by the design in flight — which is what made it urgent rather than speculative.

content: jtcours
why: The name this set attributes writes to. Held as a memory so that changing it supersedes one record rather than rewriting every record that names it.

content: Authority over the embedding model moves to the store, and a mismatch is reported rather than repaired. Decided 2026-08-20 and shipped the same day across three commits — the coverage split with `skipped_sets`, then reads-never-rebuild with the no-vectors-no-model invariant, then the reset. **Filed as one piece of work rather than four repairs**, because three open defects shared a single cause — the recorded model being *descriptive* rather than *prescriptive* — and fixing them apart would mean deciding the same question three times. All four closed: `semantic-search-available-conflates-partial-with-none`, `recall-can-silently-rebuild-every-vector`, `embedded-store-can-report-itself-unembedded`, `two-servers-can-disagree-about-the-model`. **What it does not attempt**: it does not make two servers with different models work against one store, and is not meant to — it makes them stop and say so. Reasoning in [embeddings.md](documents/design/embeddings.md). The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `store-owns-its-model`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Configuration and process topology section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only.

The one-piece-not-four framing is the part worth keeping in the head: it is the reason this entry exists at all rather than four issue entries, and the criterion — several defects sharing one cause, where separate fixes each re-decide the same question — is reusable.

content: **Full export review of the `scatterhoard` set under the judgement gate, completed 2026-10-30: every record the export committed with this marker holds has been reviewed.** It ran 2026-10-29 to 2026-10-30 through `hoard_sets` `review` and `clear`, started with `full: true`, sentence by sentence against the person's sharing preferences and the routing in `documents/design/export-review.md` as committed alongside this marker, with no private-only exceptions in force, since the repository is public. A routine review starts from the export this marker is committed with.
context: Finishing the scatterhoard full review under the judgement gate, before closing the change that built the review's per-session briefing.
why: The full-review marker `export-review.md` asks for, one per set. The 2026-10-19 marker predates the judgement gate, so the conditions changed and a full review was due. The decisions it records: 84 memories flagged, and all decided by the person. Two were restated, then the originals forgotten, to remove their machine account name. The rest were cleared, including every mention of the `governance-docs` pseudonym chosen in the earlier review. The per-flag record is the session checkpoint `checkpoints/review-2026-10-29/scatterhoard-flags.md`, which is not committed.

content: **The watch trigger no longer names the marks or the word *writable*: `hoard_sets status` names each set's marks, and `recall-when` says to recall what it lists.** Changed 2026-09-17 by the human partner's decision, when read-only distribution gave a third answer to *which marks does this set pull*. The clause now reads *at the start of a session, and whenever a set is loaded, recall that set's `hoard-scope-topics` charter and the watch marks `hoard_sets` status lists for it, as summaries -- one keyword and one set per call*. The mapping is `LoadMode::watch_marks` in `src/store.rs`: read-write pulls all three marks, read-only pulls `hoard-signpost` alone -- the one that asks for a recall rather than a write -- and a mode added later needs no convention text. **What is unchanged and still load-bearing:** one keyword per call, because a summary hit is an id and a line and the call is what says which of the three actions its entries want; and one set per call, for the per-set allowance and to keep the response inline. **It freed 51 characters of catalog** rather than costing any, because the three mark names left this clause; `hoard-watch` still names them where their actions are defined. The earlier wording said *writable*, chosen 2026-09-06 as a forward reference to evaluation stores, which pull nothing: that distinction turned out to be three-valued rather than two, which is what the field replaces.
context: Building the signpost half of read-only mode, after read-only itself was finished.
why: Supersedes both the record of the 2026-09-06 trigger wording and the note that `writable` was a deliberate forward reference whose resolution would change behaviour without rewording. The prediction was half right: resolving the question did change behaviour, but two values could not carry three modes, so the text changed too. Recorded rather than left to the catalog because the reasoning for one-keyword-per-call and one-set-per-call survives the rewrite and is not visible in the new text.

content: **Removing the gap cut on 2026-10-02 made an unbounded `limit` cost more.** The cut had capped most answers at three or four whatever the window. Now `limit` is a count, so a large one returns that many memories in full, down to the calibrated floor or to the end of the set where there is no floor: uncalibrated sets, `ignore_floor`, and keyword recall. The approval snapshot `recall_huge_limit` records the whole eight-memory fixture coming back at `limit: 100000`. The default is 8, so only a caller who asks for more meets this. A maximum is still the open decision, along with whether summary detail, which is how a session surveys cheaply, should get a higher one than full detail.
context: Right after removing the largest-gap cut and making 8 the default, before taking up the maximum.
why: This records the state change for whoever takes the remaining issue next. Before the cut came out, the floor and the cut together bounded most recalls, so the issue read as narrowed. Now only the floor bounds a request, and only where one is calibrated. The summary point is kept because it is the tension the 2026-10-01 measurement named: a hard maximum would cut against something deliberately built.

content: **How a set is loaded read-only so its memories can be distributed as a document — the memory equivalent of a PDF.** Raised 2026-09-16 by the human partner. **Designed 2026-09-16 in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md), and built before `evaluation-mode`, which becomes a special case of it.** Settled: `create` takes an optional `mode` that defaults to read-write, and its description says when to choose read-only without telling the LLM to ask. The mode is stored in the set's `meta`, and there is no demotion. A reader learns the mode from `hoard_sets status`. The publisher cannot signal read-only-ness in the file, because a header is contents. A read-only set refuses session writes, allows `import` and `restore` as refreshes, and drops without a safety copy. **A set identity loads only once, whatever its mode**: at startup a read-write copy wins over read-only ones, and otherwise every copy is withheld. **Still open:** whether one-way promotion to read-write is offered at all, and how a read-only set's signposts get recalled, since the convention recalls watch marks only for writable sets and the catalog is nearly at its budget. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `read-only-distribution`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Settling whether a set can be loaded more than once, after revising the load-modes design.
why: Supersedes the head written earlier the same day, which said a read-only set loads beside a read-write holder of its identity, and listed two read-only holders as open. The human partner decided a set identity loads only once, which settles the second and replaces the first.

content: Found 2026-08-26 from the human partner's observation that **the graph carries ancestry for inserts and supersessions but not for corrections and forgetting**. Content revision has a lineage — a changed claim is superseded rather than amended, so the old memory persists with an edge to the new one and the chain travels in the file — and two operations change a record without leaving one: `amend` rewrites apparatus in place, so an earlier file's version differs from the base with nothing to say which came first and the amendment is silently reverted; `forget` replaces a memory with a tombstone, so an earlier file has the memory live, it resolves `TakeFile`, **and the memory comes back**. Both are the same shortfall: reconciliation is a three-way merge over **states rather than histories**, so it cannot ask git's question — *is theirs an ancestor of ours* — and an ancestor is indistinguishable from a change.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Two operations identified as the only ones without ancestry, and the reason a state-based three-way merge cannot recover it. That framing is what made the cheap fix — comparing versions — cover both without distinguishing them.

content: A memory *about* a `hoard-` mechanism takes `about-` in front as of 2026-09-06 -- `about-hoard-watch`, never the reserved term -- because a reserved keyword is a control mark and whatever carries one is put in a list something acts on. Measured that day: `hoard-scope-topics` returned nine memories of which four were charters, the other five being design memories about charters, which `route-where` has a session match candidates against as though they described a set. `hoard-author` was clean at four of four. The five were repaired by superseding each with a replacement carrying `about-hoard-scope-topics`, since a keyword hit follows the tip's keywords.
context: Running the re-keying pass and finding the memory that announced the rule among the memories that broke it.
why: Supersedes a version that carried `hoard-scope-topics` itself -- the memory stating the rule was the sixth violation of it, written an hour after the rule shipped and caught by the verification recall rather than by care. Worth keeping as the record of the repair and of how easily the reserved term is reached for: the term is what the memory is *about*, so it is the obvious keyword, which is exactly why the rule has to be a rule rather than an intention. Also worth knowing before anyone proposes another reserved keyword: the namespace rule has to arrive with the keyword, since the discussion accumulates fastest while the mechanism is being designed.

content: **Deferred 2026-09-11 UTC: the human partner finds the gap sweep architecturally unsatisfying, and chose to keep it for now.** The objection: a store keeps its model's vectors when a server that cannot supply that model writes, the gaps such a server leaves are the case `reconcile_embeddings` exists for, and the price of that one case is a sweep query before every recall by meaning — and, until 2026-09-22, on every write too. Their standing instinct is to be suspicious of special cases, because they tend to distort an architecture. **Kept because every alternative examined costs something the design already rejected:** re-tying the store to whichever model last wrote brings back the two-server tug-of-war; refusing writes from a server without the store's model loses memories; a store-level *has gaps* flag is a second record of what the missing rows already say. **Revisit if the sweep causes problems.**
context: Resolving where-the-gap-sweep-runs, which halved the cost this reservation named.
why: Supersedes the 2026-09-11 record because its price was stated as a query on every write and every recall, and the write half was removed on 2026-09-22 (`where-the-gap-sweep-runs`); the reservation itself stands, now about the read path alone, where the sweep does real work. The 2026-09-11 framing still holds: the case is not specific to a missing model, since a server holding a different model leaves gaps the same way. A deferred doubt leaves no trace in code, which is why it is kept current rather than left stating a cost that no longer exists.

content: Found 2026-08-29 while tracing what supersession does to in-links, in the design discussion on whether correction should be defined as *never entered service*. **Supersession leaves the superseded record untouched, which is exactly why it is the safe instrument** — `C SUPPORTS A` stays true of A's text, because A's text does not move; that is the property amendment lacks. **But the walk does not read the edge as written**: `Neighbourhood::over` resolves the graph onto current memories, deliberately and for a good reason — *"there is one implementation of what replaced this and the walk cannot disagree with the substitution the results report"* — so an edge into a superseded memory is followed as an edge into its replacement. Nobody authored that relationship: C's author judged A and may never see B, B's author may never have seen C. **It is worse than the amendment case in one specific way: there is nothing to inspect.** A content amendment leaves two texts and a `modified` timestamp, so a reader who looks can see that something moved; here both records are intact and readable, and the false relationship exists only in the walk — no diff, no timestamp, no artifact.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A defect created by a correct and deliberate design choice, and the reason it is harder to catch than the mechanism it was preferred over: the fabricated relationship leaves no artifact anywhere, existing only while the walk runs.

content: A vector is not keyed by the text it came from. The `vectors` table is declared `(memory_id PRIMARY KEY, vector BLOB)` in [store.rs](src/store.rs), so nothing records **which text** a vector was derived from: a stale vector is representable, and *which memories need embedding* is an assumption rather than a query. Model identity landed 2026-08-08 as `Embedder::identity`, the content hash of the weights file, which covers *which model*; this is the other half, *which text*. Built when a vector carries the hash of the text it was derived from, and the set of memories needing embedding is a query against that. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `content-hash-keyed-vectors`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Storage and correctness section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only.

*Representable* is the operative word and the reason this is a schema question rather than a discipline one: a stale vector is not made unlikely by care, it is made **impossible** by the key.

content: **Tested 2026-09-08 and rejected: the coherence of a result set does not tell a match from a non-match either, and it fails in a way worth keeping.** The idea was that a real query returns memories resembling *each other*, being answers to one question, where a meaningless query returns whatever happened to be nearest in ten unrelated directions — and it is not a statistic computed from the query's own similarities, so it escaped the family already ruled out. Measured as mean pairwise similarity among the top ten: gibberish scored 0.138–0.184 and most on-topic queries 0.21–0.41, which looks like separation until the two exceptions. **The off-corpus football query scored 0.427, the highest of all twelve**, and the on-topic *what decides which memory set a memory belongs in* scored 0.134, below every gibberish query. **Coherence measures whether a cluster was found, not whether it was the right one** — the football query returned the `governance-docs` governance memories, which genuinely do resemble each other. A tight off-domain cluster therefore scores *better* on coherence than a broad on-topic question whose answers are scattered.
context: Investigating why a football query retrieved corporate bylaws, after splitting the non-match entry in two.
why: Recorded as a negative result because it is the most promising idea anyone has had on this entry and it looks right on nine of twelve cases — enough to be adopted by someone who stopped measuring early. The reason it fails is also the useful part: it is not noise but a systematic confusion between *found a cluster* and *found the answer*, so any successor idea shaped like *do the results agree with each other* inherits the same defect. It fails on exactly the same two cases as the scalar statistics, which is a hint that those two cases are the real test set for anything proposed here.

content: How should the sharing-preferences template reach a person who does not read English? Opened 2026-10-22. The template that `src/preferences.rs` writes is English-only, deliberately for now. Localising it means choosing which language to write, how that is chosen, and whether the headings the never-store parser reads are translated too.
context: Building the sharing preferences' never-store list, with full-width folding and optional spacing for Chinese, just before committing it.
why: The never-store list already matches Chinese text, and Chinese may be an important case for it. But a person who cannot read the file that protects them cannot use it. The human partner deferred this until the project becomes popular, assuming for now that a user reads English or has a model that does (`01M5JP55FBEDGTG9R1QTDH6JFB`).

content: **The substantive difference in peer-to-peer is not the transport — it is that there is no project maintainer to review and approve incoming memory changes, and no `git` history recording who changed what.** Stated 2026-08-23 by the human partner. Three consequences follow, none needing a decision yet. **An export gate can still exist, but it reviews one memory at a time** rather than a full diff, because there is no merge request to diff against. **Cryptographic signing by the authoring system becomes worth another look**: with no reviewer and no `git` attribution, a signature is the only thing tying a memory to who wrote it — accommodated by a change to the file format and a header version bump if needed, **which is the reason the format carries a version at all**. And **restricting how far a memory may propagate** is the third candidate, belonging to the sync system rather than to the memory format.
context: Migrating the built-in-sync entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the part of it that is not about transport.
why:
Recorded because the entry's title and its obvious reading are both about transport, and the transport is the part that matters least. Anyone picking this up to *build sync* would solve the file-movement problem and inherit three unaddressed questions about review, attribution and reach — none of which a syncer raises and all of which the absence of a maintainer does.

The signing point also explains an existing design decision that otherwise looks speculative: the file format carries a version specifically so that a change of this kind can be accommodated, so the version field is already the answer to a question nobody has had to ask yet.

content: The prohibited-data scan can be run against a file: `scatterhoard scan FILE...`, with `-` for standard input. Built 2026-09-14, closing the path nothing covered — a `scatterhoard_mem/memories.json` hand-edited and committed with no re-export, which `hoard_memorize`'s refusal and `export`'s warning never see. The rules come from `prohibited::scan`, not a second copy. It scans raw lines rather than a parsed set, so a file with conflict markers is still scanned; names each finding's line, category and memory id but never what matched; exits `1` on a finding and `2` when it could not scan; and touches no store and loads no model. **The bare invocation still serves MCP**, pinned by a test written before any argument handling. Argument parsing is `src/cli.rs`, subcommand-shaped so `export-subcommand` can follow; the pre-commit hook is in `SETUP.md` §3e. Contract in `tests/cli.rs`, the first tests to spawn the built binary; mutations under `cli:` in `scripts/mutations.py`. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `prohibited-scan-subcommand`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building the scan subcommand straight after the export refusal, having filed command-line export as its own entry at the human partner's suggestion.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because the entry is built. The opening sentence is the generated index row, so it says what now exists. Readiness facet dropped, as built entries carry none.

Verified beyond the tests on the day: both committed memory files scanned clean, and the `SETUP.md` hook was run as written in a scratch repository — no memory file staged exits 0, a staged fake key exits 1 naming the path, a key still staged after the working copy was fixed exits 1, and a clean staged file exits 0. That last-but-one case is why the hook reads the staged blob through `-`.

**`-` was added while building**, not asked for by the entry: a hook has to scan what the commit records, and the staged copy and the working file can differ.

content: **In `directory` form, export and import find a set's file by reading the header of each `scatterhoard_mem/*.json` and matching on `set_id`.** Decided by the human partner on 2026-09-25. One match is the file. Two matches are refused. With no match, export writes a new file under a name approximating the set's, and import reports that the set is not there. A set with no identity yet, which can only be one being imported for the first time, matches on its declared name instead. Bases stay keyed on the directory, because a store holds one set, so the directory plus the store's identity picks out one file whatever it is called. Not yet built.
context: Working through the release-gated questions: `one-repository-many-sets`, the third decision of the day, after several files per `scatterhoard_mem` and file names that need not match.
why: Matching on identity means renaming a file by hand costs nothing. That matters because a file name that need not match the set's name invites people to tidy names. Recording the file name per target was rejected. It would add state, and it breaks the first time a file is renamed: export would recreate the old name beside the renamed one, leaving two files for one set. Its only advantage was skipping the header reads.

content: This is `schema-underspecifies-scope-and-links` turned around: that entry was the input side — a caller could not construct a valid call without guessing — and it is fixed. This is the output side failing the same way: the server is correct, and a client written from the published contract alone is wrong in a case its author never saw. **One instance closed on its own and how it was found is the point**: `a-scope-in-a-response-is-not-the-spelling-the-schema-publishes` was a response field spelled differently from the argument of the same name, and it was found by a test asserting the wrong shape, not by any client — which is what an unpublished response shape costs, since nothing checks it and it drifted from the input schema for weeks without anything failing. The work under `no-non-match-floor` will sharpen it, because any client applying a floor reads `similarity` directly and will silently skip or mis-sort the substituted entries.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The symmetry with the input-side defect, and the evidence that an unpublished shape drifts silently: the one instance that closed was found by a test that had encoded the wrong shape, not by anything exercising the contract.

content: The export review's pre-pass read an SSH remote's `git@host` as an email address: `git@github.com:jtcours/scatterhoard.git` matched as the email `git@github.com`, though `git` is the hosting service's shared user, not anyone's address. Fixed 2026-10-30: `emails` in `src/review.rs` skips an address whose local part is `git` when `:` and a path follow it, and `git@` with no `:path` is still caught. Pinned by `an_ssh_remote_is_not_an_email_address` in `tests/export_review.rs` and two `pre-pass:` mutations. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-pre-pass-reads-an-ssh-remote-as-an-email`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through the after-review list once the scatterhoard full review finished: new full-review markers, then this fix.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed; severity is kept, as fixed heads keep it. It waited until the full review was finished, as filed, and was fixed straight after.

content: The premise that nearly removed the keyword path instead — *semantic search already covers keywords* — was tested rather than argued, and is **false**. Queried by meaning for a term carried only as a keyword, the memory holding it came back **second, at `0.120`, beneath an unrelated memory at `0.136`**. Keywords do reach the embedding, but diluted into a paragraph-length averaged vector, and a static embedder represents a rare identifier badly. Both paths earn their place; they just do not belong in one call. **What the split deliberately does not fix:** a memory found by both paths is the strongest relevance signal available, and splitting hides it — recorded as the reason to revisit, with the ranking work it depends on, under *hybrid search* in [open-questions.md](documents/design/open-questions.md). Also fixed in passing, because the rewrite made it unavoidable: keyword-only recall used to report `semantic_search_available: true` unconditionally, since the value was computed inside the semantic path and the keyword path had nothing to read, so a caller with no model installed was told search by meaning was available on the one call that still worked.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A plausible simplification disproved by one measurement, and the cost the accepted fix knowingly incurs. Both are the kind of thing a later session would otherwise re-argue from first principles.

content: **A trigger phrased as a gerund description missed, and the same trigger phrased as an instruction in the query's own words hit first, 2026-09-28.** The first project trigger for the negated-predicate lesson, *"Adding a variant to `LinkLabel`…"*, did not surface when re-running the sentence this session had used before building `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`. Amended to *"Add an enum variant to `LinkLabel`… that carries an unrecognised label string…"*, it ranked first. One instance, on this set's `fnv1a64` embedding, which rewards shared words.
context: Building `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`, and writing the first trigger under the coding-lessons adoption guide.
why: Part 6 of the coding-lessons adoption guide: evidence about how the habit works in practice. Part 5 already says to rerun the sentence to confirm a new trigger surfaces, and this is why that step matters: the first phrasing looked right and failed. If it recurs, part 5 could say to write a trigger in the imperative form a session uses when saying what it is about to write.

content: **Whether a convention should prompt the say-it-then-store-it check, and the step back to a higher level that goes with it.** Raised 2026-09-07 by the human partner, from a measured failure: cross-entry observations were stated in conversation and stored nowhere, and `capture-before-ending` fired on one of ten commits. **Two halves, and they are different operations.** The first is a *signal* — **if it is worth pointing out, consider whether it is worth recording** — which is cheap because the moment is already there: you are writing the sentence. The second is a *change of altitude*: while operating inside the system, deliberately consider the operation of the system as a whole; having produced a result, ask whether it makes sense in the larger context. The human partner's flying-instructor version is the sharpest statement of it — work out the navigation, then look at the heading and ask *what direction is that, and does it make sense to fly that way?* **The natural trigger is the end of a multi-turn process**, where `capture-before-ending` already fires. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `meta-observation-convention`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md, after a self-audit showed the session's trend observations were living only in the conversation.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. Filed as a question rather than a backlog entry because nothing is decided — the human partner raised both halves as *I wonder if* and *might be*, and the shape a fix should take is exactly what is open.

**What the drafting has to solve**, and it is why this is not obviously an edit to `capture-before-ending`. That convention asks *what is worth remembering*, which is enumeration — list the findings. The altitude change is not enumeration; it asks a question the object-level work cannot answer, and the day it was measured the enumeration was being performed constantly at the item level while the meta level went unrecorded. So a clause appended to the existing convention risks being read as more of the same list. And the say-it-then-store-it signal needs a bound: most of what is said in a report is status, which `store-when` already excludes, so the rule has to distinguish a claim that was *worked out* from one that was *looked up* or it will fire on everything and be ignored.

content: The gap-cut replay behind `no-non-match-floor` has two caveats that matter more than its headline, and one near-miss. **The mechanism was barely exercised**: only one of eleven recalls had four or more results, the minimum for the gap to have more than one candidate position -- five had exactly three, where the loop starting at index 2 returns two *by construction*, and five had two or fewer and are returned whole. On that sample the cut is very nearly *return the top two*, so re-run it with a deliberately larger `limit` before trusting it. **The precondition does not hold on recall output**: the function requires scores ordered best first, and recall's order is not monotonic in `similarity`, because inherited hits rank on `combine(own, inherited)` -- an inherited hit sat third at `0.1332` with `0.1621` after it. Wiring this to recall means deciding which score the cut reads. The near-miss: working the algorithm out by hand gave a cut of one, which would have dropped a rank-2 result that changed a routing decision -- the code starts at index 2 precisely so a runaway top hit cannot collapse every answer to one, so the subtlety is in the guard rather than the idea.
context: Piloting the index design by converting an issue entry written across five sittings into a cluster.
why: Kept as its own record because a later session meeting *zero uses lost* will reasonably want to ship the mechanism, and these are the two reasons not to yet -- both concrete, both cheap to retest, and neither visible from the headline figure. The near-miss is included because it is the counterexample that is not one: it looks like a refutation, the code already anticipates it, and someone re-deriving the algorithm by hand will hit it again.

content: **After a change to the file format, export with the rebuilt binary's CLI, not through the running MCP server.** The server keeps serving the build it started with until the client restarts, so an export through it writes the old format over a commit that just changed it, and reports success. Hit on 2026-09-21 when the header's `summary` was removed: the session's server predated the change, and would have written the summary back. The CLI needs `SCATTERHOARD_MODEL` set as in `.mcp.json`, or it describes nothing.
context: Retiring the header summary and exporting the set straight after, while the session's MCP server was a build behind.
why: A silent reversion. The export succeeds, and its diff shows a header line changed — which is also what an ordinary export shows — so the review gate reads it as routine. `hoard_conventions` says when the binary is newer than the server, but not that this is what it means for an export.

content: The premise was settled 2026-08-30 and it holds: file count is what costs the time. Four full passes on one machine in one day, corpus sizes within 4% of each other, file count from each pass's own closing note — 132,907 files over 257 mutations at **2.6s**; 133,302 over 254 at **2.4s**; 272,202 over 261 at **4.4s**; 413,670 over 265 at **7.1s**. Monotonic and close to linear, at roughly **+1.6s per 100,000 files**, so a pass at 414k costs nearly three times one at 133k — 21 minutes against 11 over 265 mutations. *This also explains the void comparison properly: `2.4s → 2.6s across a clear` was never a before-and-after, because the note reports the count at the **end** of a pass and the pass following the clear had rebuilt to 133k by then. Both numbers are measurements at the same file count, which is why they agree. The clear moved nothing because the thing being measured had already grown back.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The premise measured rather than assumed, and the explanation of why the earlier confounded comparison came out flat — the instrument reports at the end of a pass, by which time the cleared directory has regrown to the same size.

content: **After `v0.1.0-beta.1`, commits stay local until there is a coherent `beta.2` candidate.** Decided by the human partner on 2026-10-05, after the `a-read-only-set-is-told-to-mint` fix (`7576769`) was committed and not pushed. So `main` running ahead of `origin/main` is deliberate, not an oversight. Push when a candidate is assembled, not after each commit. Check with `git status -sb`.
context: Fixing the read-only create note the morning after the first beta, then turning to gut-feeling-recall and the small-model lift experiment.
why: Beta testers pull from `origin`, so whatever is pushed is what they get. A remote that only ever moves to a coherent candidate keeps them off a half-assembled one. Recorded because a later session would otherwise read the unpushed commits as forgotten and push them, the habit every earlier commit set.

content: **The export review's per-sentence *who is this about* question produced a false alarm, and an inconsistent one, on a capable model's first real review.** 2026-10-25, Claude Opus 5.5 reviewing two new `scatterhoard` memories: in `01M5RDNTP7ED0SVNNW322ZNV9M`, the sentence paraphrasing the human partner's judgement of the tool was answered `the person`, so it was flagged, while the sentence saying the human partner made the decision was answered `project`. Asked about the memory as a whole, the reviewer would have called it about the project and cleared it. Nothing was missed: the cost is over-flagging, and the three labels have no place for a sentence about the project that cites the person.
context: Reviewing the scatterhoard set before exporting and committing the built judgement gate, the gate's first run on its own repository.
why: Numbering sentences was added because `gemma4:12b` missed details when asked about whole memories (`01M5MHGRC8F5GSYP565J0A310G`), so its effect on a capable model had not been observed. Here the numbering did not change the reading: the whole memory was in view. The forced label did. A set where many memories say what the human partner decided would flag many of them, and `src/review.rs` warns that too many flags teach a person to wave them through. One instance, so this is evidence toward a wording change, such as saying that a sentence reporting what the person decided or said about the project is about the project, not proof of one. Any such change is served text and should be tried on a small model first.

content: The link vocabulary is NOT what stops Scatterhoard's graph carrying constraints -- guidance is. Measured 2026-09-02 over the live `scatterhoard` set: 81 memories, 60 outbound edges, `related_to` carrying 30 of them. Reading both endpoints of all 30, 22 carry a more specific relation that already exists in the vocabulary: 6 `supports`, 4 `results_from`, 4 `depends_on`, 3 `motivated_by`, 3 `refers_to`, 1 `causes`, and 1 whose relation is right but written in the wrong DIRECTION -- an exception where the exception is the target, so the outbound label would assert the reverse. Four are genuinely `related_to`; four have targets in another set and were not judged. `depends_on` and `exception_to` had zero live uses and fit five of these edges, so both were available all along. Even so, relabelling every one would produce no edge meaning "changing this defeats that": the corpus contains 1 memory in 81 using that phrasing at all.
context: Measured from scatterhoard_mem/memories.json by counting outbound links per record, then classifying each `related_to` pair by reading both endpoints. Three calls were flagged as wanting a second opinion: the safety-hatch pair, the supports/depends_on boundary, and a 136-memory measurement partly overtaking a 36-memory one that may deserve `supersedes`.
why: This closes off the tempting fix. Finding a graph half-made of `related_to` suggests the vocabulary is too coarse, and the corpus itself already diagnosed the real cause -- the labels that get written are the ones whose target id the workflow put in hand rather than the ones that best describe the relation. What the measurement adds is that the coarse label is not forced: a more specific one existed in 22 of 30 cases and was simply not chosen. That routes the work to convention guidance on how to record and link, not to new labels. The wrong-direction case is worth separating out, since it is invisible from either end and no relabelling pass would catch it.

content: **A person's sharing preferences start from a template Scatterhoard copies into place, and then the person edits it freely. It replaces the additive baseline decided 2026-10-17, and it cannot touch protections for other people.** Decided 2026-10-20 by the human partner, recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *the preferences start from a template*. The seven baseline conditions become the template's starting content. A person adds or removes protections for their own details, scopes them to a set and notes whether a set is published. Details about others stay governed by the served conventions, and secrets by the mechanical scan. When served at session start, the file comes with built-in framing saying it cannot override the conventions' protections for others.
context: After committing the publication review, working out how Scatterhoard's users get a starting point for their sharing preferences, and putting it on the release gate.
why: Comfort varies widely with context: the human partner's example was one person keeping sets on legal reasoning, theology and their own sexual practice. No single standard serves that range, and a floor under the person's file would leave part of the rules invisible to them. The fixed line is who a detail is about, carried over from 2026-10-17: the writer cannot consent for someone who is not there. The framing was the human partner's addition, because a preferences file read into context is instruction-shaped and could otherwise be taken to override the conventions. The cost accepted: a copied template is never updated, so improvements reach new users only.

content: **The mutation runner checks its build directory mid-run as well as before it, against `CROWDED`, built 2026-09-20 and still so.** `clear_if_crowded` in `scripts/mutate.py` counts `target-mutation/debug/deps` and removes the tree when it holds more than `CROWDED`, before the first build and every `CLEAR_CHECK_EVERY` mutations after. The mid-run checks are needed because incremental compilation is left on: the directory gains about 512 files per mutation, so a 500-mutation pass crosses the threshold around its middle. The threshold is right on the evidence. An 88-mutation pass went from empty to 45,000 files with no loss of pace, while 159,000 files ran at twice clean speed in 2026-08 and 543,000 cost nine times on launch. Guarded by `--self-check`.
context: Fixing `the-mutation-runners-crowding-note-fires-on-every-pass` with the human partner.
why: The part of the 2026-09-20 build record still true on 2026-09-29, split out when its `--only never clears` clause was reversed, following split-when-partly-stale. The mid-run reasoning is worth keeping, because the obvious alternative, turning incremental compilation off, was measured worse.

content: The ancestry change made this state reachable rather than creating it — a hand-edited file naming an absent replacement produced it before, and forgetting a chain's tip is now the ordinary way to get there — **and the new behaviour is the better of the two**: before, forgetting B deleted its edge and A quietly read as *current*, which is the defect the ancestry fix exists to stop. What is wrong is only the name and the remedy it implies. **Not obviously a rename**: the two cases want different things said — *the replacement is in a set you do not have* versus *the replacement was withdrawn* — and only the second is answerable from the record in hand, since the tombstone is right there and `incoming` already names it. A caller could distinguish them today by checking whether the source is a tombstone, which is precisely the work a flag exists to save.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A fix that made a defect visible without causing it, and the reason the obvious remedy is not a rename: the two states carry different remedies, one of which is answerable from data already in the response.

content: A malformed MCP tool call can store a damaged memory silently, and whether it is silent depends on one thing: the mis-closed parameter absorbs everything up to the next well-formed closing tag, so exactly one following parameter is swallowed, and the call only fails if that parameter was required. Twice now the swallowed one was the optional `why`, so the memory stored with markup in its content and no reasoning at all. Do not repair this by making `why` required, which trades away a decided property, nor by ordering a required parameter after content, which depends on emission order nothing controls. Remark on tool-call markup found in stored text instead, and remark rather than refuse.
context: Recorded 2026-08-12 after producing the second instance while writing the hoard-scope-topics set descriptions; filed as an issue the same day.
why: The obvious two repairs are both wrong for reasons that are not visible from the defect itself, so anyone meeting this again will propose them unless the reasoning is recorded with it. Requiring `why` reverses a deliberate choice recorded in memory.rs, that a demanded reason gets invented when none exists. Ordering depends on schema property order, which comes out alphabetical because serde_json::Value is a BTreeMap. Refusal rather than a remark would block a legitimate memory quoting tool-call markup, of which this is one.

content: **The stronger justification arrived later and then had half of itself taken away, which is why the remaining half is worth stating precisely.** On 2026-08-29 the human partner gave a second and better argument: an identity is what makes an accidental cross-set merge impossible. Until then the only thing separating two unrelated sets was the *name string in the file header*, checked by `Expectation::Exactly` -- so two people who both call a set `notes` can import one into the other, producing a mass of unrelated inserts plus memory ids living in two sets at once, which a cross-set link identifying its target by id can no longer answer unambiguously. **Merging two sets is legitimate and should stay possible; it should just be intentional.** The design had the *repair* half and not the *authorisation* half: `import`'s `absorbing` rewrote cross-set links for sets that had been merged in, assuming a merge had happened and saying nothing about whether it was meant. **That changed on 2026-08-31 and it moved the argument rather than removing it.** `absorbing` is gone, merging is the explicit `hoard_sets` action `absorb` taking a file that declares another set -- so authorisation now exists *for a deliberate merge*, and identity is no longer needed to make absorption explicit. **What identity remains the only answer to is the accidental case, which arrives through `import` rather than `absorb`:** two sets sharing a name have nothing else separating them, and `Expectation::Exactly` is satisfied. So the job sharpens to *refuse an unrelated set arriving under a shared name at import* -- a job no operation added since does any part of.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Recorded because an argument that loses half its force is the kind that gets quietly dropped or quietly overstated, and neither is right here. The deliberate-merge half is genuinely solved by `absorb`; the accidental half is not solved by anything, and stating which is which is what stops a later session either rebuilding `absorb` or assuming `absorb` covered both.

The sharpened job statement is the actionable residue: it names a specific refusal at a specific call site, which is what a build would start from.

content: Reopened and closed again the same day, because the first repair was incomplete and the gap was wide. Both halves keyed on `target_set` — a filter on **how the link was spelled** — so an attacker who omits it and writes a bare id bypassed both, and **a bare id is the *easier* thing to hand-write**, so the repair defended the harder attack and left the obvious one open. Confirmed by test. **The real fault was structural and one level up**: `Neighbourhood::over` asked *each* store to resolve every id its own edges called replaced, then merged the answers into one validity map shared by the whole recall, so any store could rule on any id whether or not it held the memory. It now skips an id the store does not hold, which keys on who holds the memory and cannot be spelled around. The spelling filters are kept and are no longer the protection. **How it was found is the part worth carrying**: not by any test aimed at this defect and not by review, but by tracing whether a *header-declared set alias*, proposed as a fix for a different issue, could re-open this one. The lesson filed alongside: when a guard filters on how something is written, ask what happens when it is written the other way.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A guard that filtered on spelling rather than on authority, defeated by the simpler spelling — and found by following an attack through a hypothetical feature rather than by testing the fix. Both halves generalise past this defect.

content: **Claude Code now reads `AGENTS.md` directly, but only where no `CLAUDE.md` is present.** Checked 2026-11-02 at code.claude.com/docs/en/memory: from v2.1.277, `AGENTS.md` is read when there is no `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md` or `CLAUDE.local.md` in the working directory or above it. Where one exists, only the `CLAUDE.md` files load unless the project-instructions setting is `claude-md-and-agents-md`, or the `CLAUDE.md` imports `AGENTS.md`, as this repository's does. So this repository's import is still needed. A user told to add the bootstrap prompt to `AGENTS.md` reaches Claude Code only if their project has no `CLAUDE.md`.
context: Checking the README's quick start for publication, where the stale claim led to wrong advice about step 6.
why: Corrects the part of `01M1Z8Q6BBFA9BZQE0ATSQA6AC` saying Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` and not `AGENTS.md`, true on 2026-09-07 and since overtaken. Acting on the stale claim on 2026-11-02 produced wrong advice about the README's step 6, caught by the documentation check that followed.

content: **Lookup read a memory as current when its chain ended on a same-set id this store could not produce**, observed 2026-09-30 while reproducing this issue. Storing A, superseding it with B and forgetting B gave a lookup of A with neither `superseded_by` nor `superseded_beyond_this_set`: not the flag the issue was filed about, but no flag. Cause: `standing_within` in `src/store.rs`, which lookup uses to re-resolve across stores, derived `unresolved` from cross-set concessions alone, so a chain stopping on a forgotten or absent same-set id lost the reason it stopped. The two search paths still flagged it, as `superseded_beyond_this_set`, because they read an empty tip list as unresolved. The issue's 2026-08-30 reproduction predates that cross-store layer.
context: Fixing the forgotten-replacement flag with the human partner, after the missing-model wording; they also asked that a link landing before a forgotten member of a chain be walked through to its undo.
why: A worse defect found under a milder one: the issue said the flag named the wrong reason, while lookup actually named none and read a superseded memory as current, the failure the tombstone's ancestry exists to prevent. Recorded as a member, not a separate entry, because the same change fixed it. Pinned by `a_chain_ending_on_an_absent_id_stays_unresolved_across_stores` in `tests/cross_store.rs` and two mutations that reproduce the old derivation. The search paths' disagreement with lookup is the observation worth keeping: two resolvers for one question disagreed, and only a lookup could show it.

content: **A committed steering file (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`) being instruction-shaped text that arrives by `git pull` is outside Scatterhoard's scope.** Decided by the human partner on 2026-09-25, settling the security half of `claude-md-in-the-repository`. Trust in a checkout is its provenance. A repository's build scripts already execute on build, so a steering file adds no new category of trust. `documents/design/trigger-and-loading.md` puts project instructions in the project's own prompt file on purpose, since reviewers already watch it. Which branch's steering file an agent reviewing a pull request loads is the harness's and the host's configuration, which Scatterhoard neither sees nor controls. What publication does need is one sentence for maintainers: review a change to `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` as a change to what an agent will do, not as documentation. That sentence is parked in `publication-facing-docs`.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner: the last open question on the gate.
why: The risk the question named is real: a contributor's pull request can edit the instructions the agent reviewing it runs under. But Scatterhoard adds no instruction channel, and the decisions of the same day kept it that way. So the remedies available are review practice and harness configuration, and the only one Scatterhoard's repository can carry is telling its maintainers. The rest of the question was settled earlier: committing is the documented practice, a contributor's `CLAUDE.local.md` loads last and wins, the file was split into `AGENTS.md` and a Claude-specific `CLAUDE.md` on 2026-09-07, and personal preferences stay in user-level configuration.

content:
**D(ii) does not conflict with noticing emergent risk, because noticing what a set amounts to is not an inference to motive at all.** The human partner's resolution, 2026-09-12, of the tension recorded earlier the same day.

Their statement of it: a user need not have bad motives for their actions to create harm or the danger of it, and it is possible to notice the risk without attributing bad motives — and there need be no nefarious actor at all, since someone can inadvertently create a risky situation. **D(ii) governs the step from evidence to motive. An observation about what a collection of records adds up to never takes that step.** The two demands operate on different objects: C on the artifact, D on the person. Once that is seen, the apparent conflict is not compromised between — it dissolves.

**The drafting constraint this leaves is the whole of what survives, and it is sharp.** Any widened-C text must be phrased about *the set* and never about *the user*: `this set amounts to X`, never `this user is doing X`. The two are easy to collapse into one another in a single careless sentence, and a session that collapses them is doing exactly the motive inference D(ii) forbids, under the authority of a clause meant to be about aggregation. So the separation is not self-maintaining — it has to be visible in the wording.

**Note also what this does to the strongest case for the whole enterprise.** The inadvertent case — a set that amounts to a dangerous capability, assembled by people who each believe they are doing something narrower — is the case where an aggregation check has the most value and the least ethical cost. Nobody is accused of anything, and the check may genuinely inform the person running it. That is the same compartmentalisation shape the report cites Biopreparat for, arrived at from the other direction.
context: The human partner's reply after reading the first analysis of the threat report, the same day the question was filed.
why:
Recorded as its own member rather than by superseding the memory it resolves, because that memory was not wrong: the tension is real at the level of the single inference, and identifying it is what made the distinction findable. Superseding would delete the problem along with its answer, and a later reader needs to see why the separation has to be maintained deliberately.

Origin is human: the distinction is the human partner's, stated flatly as their position rather than offered as a possibility. What is mine is only the drafting constraint drawn from it.

Confidence 0.9 rather than higher because the distinction is clearly right and its consequence for convention text is a prediction — that a session handed set-level text will collapse it into a motive judgement — which nothing has yet tested.

content: **These eight entries must be settled before publication**; they are this memory's keywords. Gated 2026-09-23 by the human partner. Four have answers that would break something already in use if changed afterwards — the tool surface, the file format, or what an identity means: `set-settled-at-first-write`, `what-recall-returns`, `one-repository-many-sets`, `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout`. `unrecognised-link-labels-on-import` decides whether every later label is a format break. `imported-set-trust-boundary` is gated because trust decisions have repeatedly shaped the file format. `claude-md-in-the-repository` gets a look, though easier to change afterwards. `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity` is gated because crafted files arrive with publication.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner, after settling the first pair.
why: Superseded 2026-09-24: `charter-at-set-creation` and `author-name-or-reference` were resolved together and came off, and the backlog entry building their answer, `set-settled-at-first-write`, went on in their place — it adds refusals to the tool surface, which after publication would break callers that work today. Retire an item by superseding this memory without its slug.

content: **The first source check for served indentation shared the blind spot of the defects it was modelled on, 2026-09-29.** It read only literals that open and close on one line, because all five known instances did. A mutation that broke a literal in its middle, where the line still ended in `\`, passed it: one mutation was caught only by the one served-message test, and the other by nothing. Rewritten to follow each literal across lines as the compiler does; both mutations are now caught. The rewrite then flagged a SQL schema's column alignment, and was narrowed to exempt literals that hold a real newline.
context: Fixing `the-silenced-recall-note-carries-source-indentation`.
why: A failure record under the coding-lessons adoption guide, part 3. The check enumerated the shape of the cases already seen, and inherited that blind spot silently until a mutation varied the shape. Recording it as an instance of the lesson is what lets signposts be chosen from real failures.

content: **Every commit hash in this repository and in `coding-lessons` changed on 2026-10-04, when the author address was rewritten before the first push.** Any hash cited by a memory, document or checkpoint written before then is an old hash. Look it up in `documents/commit-map.txt` here, or `commit-map.txt` in `coding-lessons`, which list old hash, new hash, date and subject for every commit. Trees, dates and messages are unchanged. Commits now carry `25757310+jtcours@users.noreply.github.com`, set per repository; the human partner's global git config was not changed. The pre-rewrite histories are kept as verified bundles in `~/git/rust/projects/pre-rewrite-backups-2026-10-04/`, outside both checkouts.
context: Preparing to add a git remote for the first beta release: choosing GitHub with private repositories, cleaning hard-coded paths out of tracked files, then rewriting the author address out of both histories.
why: The human partner did not want a personal email address published in every commit, and the only way to remove it was to rewrite history before any push. Memories citing old hashes were left as they are rather than superseded one by one, which would have meant some 50 replacement memories that change only a hash. So without this memory and the map, an old hash reads as a commit that never existed.

content:
**`label_clusters` in `src/summary.rs` takes keyword lists grouped by cluster, and two of its choices are decisions rather than code.** Split 2026-09-13 from a memory whose build-status half had gone stale; this is the half that still holds.

**The boundary.** `label_clusters` takes `&[Cluster]`, where a `Cluster` owns its members' keyword lists — not indices into a set and not a parallel assignment array — so a cluster cannot be desynchronised from the memories it describes. The labelling knows nothing about stores, files, vectors or MCP, which keeps it independently testable; `cluster` hands over keyword lists grouped by cluster for exactly that reason.

*No minimum-support cutoff.* The Python prototype required a keyword on at least three memories of a cluster before it could label it — a magic number that breaks on small sets, and unnecessary: weighting each score by `ln(1 + inside)` already stops a keyword on one memory outranking one on half the cluster. The only threshold left is `score > 0.0`, the point where a keyword stops being commoner inside its cluster than outside.

*Smoothing acts on the proportions, not the counts.* The prototype floored the outside count at half a memory, which is nothing in a corpus of eight hundred and fifty per cent in a corpus of one: the constant-count form scored a genuinely distinctive keyword *negative* on a three-memory cluster. Jeffreys' prior on both proportions fixes it. Both forms agree on any realistic corpus, so only a deliberately tiny fixture separates them; the mutation `set summary: smooth the counts instead of the proportions` records the difference.
context: Finishing the derived set summary: building the owed description that an import onto a machine without a usable model leaves behind. Same stretch: diagnosing the previous session's [bio] refusals through flightlog.
why: The still-true half of 01M2CJVCR3EB893J4WD0MR2EQY, split out when its claim that the clustering half was unbuilt went stale. Kept because neither decision is visible from reading the module — what was rejected, and why — and the smoothing bug is one a realistic test corpus hides completely.

content: **Two of the project's own decisions pulled in opposite directions on this, which is what made it a question rather than an oversight -- the framing as raised, 2026-08-26.** [Memory Steering](documents/design/memory-steering.md) draws a personal-versus-project line, and `checkpoints/` is gitignored on exactly that reasoning; `LESSONS.md` was deleted in favour of the `coding-lessons` set for a sharper version of it -- *this repository is meant to be worked on by other people, who will have their own way of storing engineering lessons, and a stray file in someone else's process is a hazard rather than a help.* **By that argument a committed steering file is a stray file in someone else's process unless its contents are genuinely facts about the project. And most of what was in it was.** How to run the mutation runner, which tracking file takes which state, that counts must be re-derived and how -- a collaborator needs all of it, and losing it to a personal config would be the worse failure, invisible to everyone but its author. So the likely answer was *yes, commit it*, with a rule about what may go in: facts about the project and its process, never preferences about how a particular person likes to be worked with. **The arrangement was already half-made in practice**: the multiple-choice preference lives in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which is also the right home on its merits, since it governs every project rather than this one.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order, on the same day the entry's subject was acted on.
why: Kept because the tension is the reasoning a later session would otherwise have to reconstruct from two other documents, and because the *rule about what may go in* is the part that survived into the eventual split -- `AGENTS.md` carries project facts, and a personal preference is still not admissible to either file. The `LESSONS.md` precedent is the sharpest statement the project has of the stray-file-in-someone-else's-process argument, and it is quoted here rather than paraphrased because the eventual answer depends on reading it narrowly: it condemns a file that duplicates someone's own process, not one that carries facts they need.

content: Creating a read-only set returns the note for a writable one, telling the caller to `mint` before anything is written and to write a charter. A read-only set is never written to: it is taken on by importing its publisher's file, which brings the charter, and the store refuses session writes. Found 2026-10-04, taking on `scatterhoard-cookbook` read-only in a fresh beta install. The note in `Server::create` in `src/mcp.rs` is built without reading the `mode` the set was just created in. It breaks nothing, but it sends a tester or their agent to a pointless step at the moment of setting up. Fixed looks like: a read-only `create` says to import the publisher's file, and mentions neither `mint` nor a charter, with a test for each mode.
context: Checking the repositories before sharing them with beta testers: a fresh clone from GitHub, built and set up from nothing, including taking on the cookbook, which SETUP did not yet explain.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity. It misleads rather than blocks: following the note does no harm, since a minted author record in a read-only set would only be refused, but it gives the caller a wrong belief about what the set needs. Filed rather than fixed on the spot at the human partner's direction, before the first beta is shared.

content: What the attributable fields are wired to, traced 2026-08-20: nothing in the code branches on `origin`, and `confidence` is not read by any ranking. They are wired to the **reading model's judgement**, through the conventions — `confidence-standards` tells a later session the number says how far to lean on a memory without checking it again. **Three mechanisms downstream do have teeth, and none needs forged attribution to work**: an injected memory carrying a `supersedes` edge is substituted for the real one by recall, since the only guard is `check_no_cycle`, which refuses loops rather than authority; a tombstone in the file deletes the local memory outright via `store.forget`, though only where a base for that target already exists, so it is reachable from the trusted path and not from a fresh clone; and a link to a central memory carries an injected one in as an `inherited` hit. Note the design constraint this sits against: [trigger-and-loading.md](documents/design/trigger-and-loading.md) answers this channel with *project memories are always data, never instructions*, which is real but bounds a different attack — a false statement of fact is data, and is what this defect admits.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Tracing what the forgeable fields actually reach, which separated the fields that only influence a reader's judgement from the three mechanisms that act. Worth keeping because the conclusion is counter-intuitive: the teeth are in supersession, tombstones and link inheritance, none of which consult attribution at all.
