content: **One behaviour was settled in advance of the design, 2026-09-06 by the human partner, and the served convention is already written against it.** An evaluation store does **not** get its watch list pulled, unless asked for specifically, or perhaps at the moment it is switched to read/write if that capability exists. **That is why `recall-when`'s trigger says *whenever a **writable** set is loaded*** -- the condition is already phrased against a distinction this question has not yet drawn, so resolving it turns the clause mechanical without rewording it. **Until then every store is writable and the clause reads as *whenever a set is loaded*.** So the convention is currently a no-op distinction that costs nothing and will start doing work the day evaluation loading exists.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Recorded because it is easy to read `recall-when`'s *writable* as redundant and trim it -- the catalog is under a character budget and the word currently distinguishes nothing. It is a deliberate forward reference, and removing it would have to be undone by the change that makes it meaningful.

Worth having as a technique as well as a fact: settling one downstream behaviour before designing the feature let a convention be worded once rather than twice, which is the cheap half of a decision that is otherwise entirely open.

content: **This issue's chosen fix is a note, not a floor**, decided 2026-09-24 by the human partner: when every calibrated set declines a question and only sets without a floor answer, recall says so, and the caller can re-ask with a `scope`. Filed as `note-when-only-uncalibrated-sets-answer`. The issue stays open until that is built.
context: Settling the backup calibration shape with the human partner, straight after filing the two backlog entries.
why: Recorded under the issue's slug so a session recalling the issue finds its decided fix, rather than reopening the floor investigation the day's measurements closed for small sets.

content: The moment the two counts disagree is the worst available one: the gap appears at the export gate, the one place [Export Review](documents/design/export-review.md) asks a human to scrutinise what travels into a repository. An unexplained extra record in a file about to be committed is precisely what that review exists to catch, so the tooling spends the reviewer's attention on a discrepancy that is not one — and trains them to wave it through next time. This is the `coding-lessons` two-scales lesson in a new place, and the same shape as the cold-start similarity score: `0.0` from a one-memory store and `0.0` from a thousand-memory store are not the same measurement, and nothing in the result distinguishes them. Here the collision is in a *name* rather than a scale, which makes it cheaper to fix and easier to miss.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The cost is not the confusion but the habituation: a review gate that raises a false alarm at the moment of scrutiny teaches its reader to discount the next one. That is why this was filed as Misleads rather than Costs.

content: Found 2026-08-07 while reading `forget` to work out what the cross-process refresh had to rebuild. **Nothing leaked the content**: resolving a hit reads SQL, finds no such memory, and drops it. **What leaked was scan width.** Recall scans a fixed multiple of the requested limit and discards hits that resolve to nothing, so enough departed vectors ranking ahead of a surviving memory push it past the end of the scan — and recall answers with nothing at all, for a store that plainly contains a match. Two forgotten memories are enough at `limit: 1`. It also defeated, in its own small way, the reason `forget` deletes the row outright rather than flagging it: a principal reason to forget is that sensitive data reached the memory, and several hundred floats derived from that text are a copy of it. The database no longer held it; the process did.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery, and the two costs kept apart: the visible one is an empty answer over a store that contains a match, and the quiet one is that a vector is a copy of the text it came from, which is what forgetting is for.

content: **First replay for `gut-feeling-recall`, 2026-09-29: breadth held, phrase extraction was noisy, and valence as defined failed.** It was run offline on the set exported at `7a61a8e`, before the forget decision, with TF-IDF over content and why standing in for the live embedding. Query: the before-writing sentence that missed on 2026-09-28. Its 40-nearest neighbourhood held 5 memories carrying the decision, the best at rank 4; a mundane control held none. But TF-IDF also *ranked* one 4th, where the live embedding did not, so this does not separate aggregation from a better ranking. *Resurrects forgotten* ranked about 82nd among phrases, behind the project's memory-writing boilerplate (*day filed*, *checked tests*). Heat, counted as issue-cluster membership, severity or a corrective link, marked 79% of the set hot: neighbourhood 0.89 against control 0.87.
context: Filing `gut-feeling-recall` and running the first falsification attempt the same hour.
why: Evidence for the question, deliberately including what failed. The next steps follow from the failures. Heat needs to count only things that went wrong, such as failure records and reversed decisions, not topic membership, since this project's memory is mostly about defects. Phrases need a stoplist for how the corpus is written, or a contrast against it. The confound needs the same replay through the live embedding, on a snapshot loaded for evaluation. The script was a scratch file and is not kept.

content: **Measured before the work, 2026-08-21: SETUP.md §5 is the project's most productive defect source — twelve found through it, none caught by the test suite** — which is why its untested corner was the expensive gap rather than a tidiness one. **And every item was written by running it**, which is the part worth repeating: item 22 found `amending-a-claim-is-refused-where-no-client-can-reach-it` while being drafted, because attempting the thing produced a refusal that could not be the documented one.
context: Migrating the setup-smoke-items entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is why the section is worth maintaining.
why:
The twelve-to-nothing ratio is the argument for spending effort on a hand-run checklist at all, and it is the kind of figure that stops being quotable once nobody remembers when it was taken — it dates to 2026-08-21 and counts defects found by exercising the tools from a real client rather than by automated coverage.

*Written by running it* is the transferable half. A checklist item composed from the code documents what the author believes; one composed by performing the step documents what happens, and the difference surfaces immediately, as it did here — the defect was found in the act of writing the item that would have described it wrongly.

content: **`gemma4:12b` through Ollama's `/api/chat` returns an empty `content` when the prompt invites tool calls but the request offers no tools**, so a hand-written probe scores every run as a miss. Observed 2026-10-30: a system prompt saying "describe any tool calls you would make", with no `tools` in the request, gave empty content with `eval_count` 64 and `done_reason: stop`, on 20 of 20 runs with thinking off and most runs with it on. The tokens were generated and the visible text was empty. Rewording the system prompt to "you have no tools in this conversation; reply in plain prose" fixed it at once. Check a probe's replies are non-empty before reading its score.
context: Testing the new pseudonym sentence in the export review's flag guidance on gemma4:12b with a scratch probe, after the full scatterhoard review finished.
why: An empty reply scores as a clean negative, so a probe that is broken this way reports that the wording under test failed when the instrument did. Here it would have recorded a working sentence as ineffective. The mechanism is inferred, not confirmed: the likeliest explanation is that the model emitted tool-call syntax that Ollama parsed out of `content`, with no `tool_calls` field to receive it.

content: **The tracking system is the recipe that is ready now,** named by the human partner on 2026-09-28 as one that could be generalised to other task-like items. It has run this project's issues, backlog, questions and causes since 2026-09-07. Its parts: one head memory per entry carrying a `hoard-proj-<kind>-entry` mark, the entry's slug and a status keyword; members that carry the slug; a Markdown file with generated regions between `BEGIN`/`END GENERATED INDEX` markers, one row per head; `scripts/genindex.py`, which rebuilds the regions from the exported set, fails with `--check` when file and memories disagree, and refuses to drop rows; `depends_on` rendered as "blocked by"; and a causes region ranked by `causes`/`instance_of` links. The `hoard-proj-` prefix it relies on is already served to every user by `keyword-standards`, so nothing in the pattern is private to this project except the script.
context: Filing the question of where user-facing recipes live, straight after the human partner raised it.
why: A candidate recipe for `where-user-facing-recipes-live`, and the one that answers its *when* half: it has been used, so writing it up generalises a working mechanism instead of copying untested design. What needs deciding is how much of it travels: the script itself, or a description of what any generator must do, which is the check, the refusal to drop rows and the markers. Checkable in `TRACKING.md`'s own instructions and in `scripts/genindex.py`, including `--self-check`.

content: **The sharing preferences stay markdown, rather than moving to TOML or YAML.** Decided 2026-10-31 by the human partner. YAML misreads silently -- an unquoted `no` becomes false, and a colon turns the template's own exception into a mapping -- which is the defect the bare-line fix addressed. TOML is strict but fails for the whole file, bringing back the lockout that refusing a file would cause. The human partner's observation: reading markdown as precise instructions amounts to a small markup language of our own, acceptable as long as nothing in it surprises the person.
context: Fixing the dropped bare-line issue in the preferences file, after restoring from the 2026-10-30 checkpoint and restarting the server.
why: A structured format is the obvious fix for imprecise parsing and will be proposed again. What decided it is the failure mode per line versus per file for an audience that may not code, which neither the code nor the file shows.

content: **With ten triplets per language and 29 rivals, the paraphrase-rank test separates the models but not by a wide gap, and Japanese is where the gap closes.** Measured 2026-10-04 with `probe_whether_each_language_ranks_a_paraphrase_first` in `tests/probes.rs`, counting first places out of 10. Under `potion-base-32M`, English scored 10, and the other languages scored 0 to 4: Japanese 4, Spanish 3, German 2, French and Hindi 1, Russian and Chinese 0. Under `potion-multilingual-128M`, every language scored 5 to 9: English and German 9, Spanish and French 8, Russian and Chinese 7, Hindi and Japanese 5. The mean margin over the best rival was negative for every non-English language under base-32M and positive for every language under multilingual. Japanese came closest to the line on both measures, at −0.036 and +0.003.
context: Restoring from the 2026-10-04 checkpoint. Widening the paraphrase triplets from three to ten per language and turning the lost scratchpad rank harness into a probe. Earlier the same session, the human partner decided the check asks the agent for sentences in languages it has none for.
why: This is the evidence a threshold for the declared-language check has to be set against. The ten-per-language rank test separates the models, but by one place at Japanese (4 against 5), so any fixed bar sits on that boundary. Reporting the score rather than a pass or fail, as already proposed, is what this supports. The per-triplet grid the probe prints shows which triplets fail across languages.

content: Should `restore` refuse a file whose `set_id` is not the set's? Today it replaces the set's contents with any file declaring the set's name and keeps the store's own identity, so the result is another copy's records under this set's identity. Import and export refuse that mismatch since 2026-09-26, and the design's list of where it is refused names only those two. Against refusing: `restore` is the rescue tool, written for a caller with less context than usual, and a mismatch may be exactly the damage being repaired. For: it builds the diverged copy the import refusal exists to stop, and the next export over the shared file would then be refused anyway, later and further from the cause. Checkable in `restore_set` in `src/mcp.rs`, which reads no identity from the file. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `restore-from-a-file-of-another-identity`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building the release gate's directory-form group: identity-mismatch refusal, just committed, with the reserved directory accepting the local set next.
why: Head of a question cluster. Found 2026-09-26 while building `identity-mismatch-refusal`, by asking which other readers of a set's own file compare identities; only `restore` does not. Filed as a question rather than an issue because the rescue-tool argument makes the answer genuinely open, and the human partner decides refusals of this kind. Possibly release-gated, since adding a refusal after publication breaks a restore that works today; that is for the human partner to say.

content: **Whether a fixed result count is the right shape for a default at all. Resolved by implementation: it is not, and the shape changed -- verified 2026-09-07.** Raised 2026-08-16 by the human partner from how widely relevant-set sizes vary: across 24 labelled queries the answer key ran from **1 memory to 36**, so a fixed default returned memories nobody wanted at one end and a fraction of the answer at the other. The obvious alternative was already ruled out -- a score threshold needs a floor, and `no-non-match-floor` plus the cold-start question leave no constant anyone can defend. **What shipped is neither.** `limit` is now a **window** rather than a count: for a semantic search the cut falls at the largest gap between consecutive scores inside it, so a question with two good answers returns two. The constant is `DEFAULT_WINDOW = 20`. **Keyword search keeps a plain count**, deliberately -- it does not traverse and has no scores to find a drop in. **And the dissolution the entry anticipated also arrived:** `recall-already-known` is built, so a caller can page past what it holds, and a page size does not have to be right when there is a way to ask for the next one. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `fixed-result-count`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

**Marked resolved on migration although the file had it open**, 2026-09-07, on the same basis as `set-uuid`: the entry asks which of two shapes a default should take and names a possible dissolution, and the code answers all three. Both of the entry's closing sub-questions -- *what default* and *whether a default matters once paging exists* -- are settled by what is built.

The keyword-search exception is recorded in the head rather than dropped, because it is the one place a plain count survives and someone re-reading the resolution would otherwise take it as universal. It is a reasoned exception, not an oversight: there are no scores there to find a gap in.

content: **The finding that produced this question is itself the argument for it -- noted 2026-08-03.** It was an **investigation across nine observations**, and nothing in the convention catalog would have prompted recording either the observations or the conclusion drawn from them. **So the question arrives with its own evidence attached:** a project's most valuable knowledge was assembled by hand from nine scattered noticings, and the memory system that exists to hold such things did not ask for any of them. **That connects it to the conventions for observations, puzzles and investigations** -- since served 2026-09-04 as `hoard-watch` -- which cover the accumulating half. What this question adds is the *duplication-specific* half: recording authoritative sources when they are established, and recalling before writing anything that might become a second copy.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the provenance is unusually strong evidence and is easy to lose: the question is not a good idea somebody had, it is the generalisation of a defect analysis that found a single dominant cause, and the analysis happened without the tool's help despite the tool existing.

The relationship to the watch convention is recorded because the two look like duplicates -- both about accumulating findings -- and are not: one is about noticing over time, this is about checking before writing. Merging them would lose the recall half, which is where the duplication actually gets prevented.

content: The documents a published repository needs, written roughly concurrently with first publication. At least a minimal `README.md`, plus whatever the hosting site expects. The human partner writes the human-facing parts. Filed 2026-09-25. Two things are already known to be needed. Second, one sentence for maintainers, parked here until drafting: review a change to `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` as a change to what an agent will do, not as documentation. `CONTRIBUTING.md` is its own entry, `contributing-and-branching-docs`. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `publication-facing-docs`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing `claude-md-in-the-repository`, the last open question on the release gate, with the human partner.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, filed at the human partner's request so the need is tracked rather than remembered. It gives the maintainer sentence from `claude-md-in-the-repository` somewhere to live until the documents are drafted. Deferred until first publication, the same trigger `contributing-and-branching-docs` waits on, because a README written long before release goes stale before anyone reads it. Nothing blocks it, so it is linked to that entry rather than marked as depending on it.

content: Ids change spelling, and prefix lookup goes away. Shipped 2026-08-20, both halves together as required: the id's text form became **Crockford base32** — 26 characters, no separators, ULID's encoding, the bits unchanged so it is `MemoryId`'s parse and display plus a migration rather than a new identifier — and **`hoard_lookup` stopped accepting a prefix**, taking a whole id or refusing, with recovery becoming a separate, explicitly selected **substring** search. **The two had to land together, because the second is only safe once the first has removed the instinct it defends against.** `MemoryId` carries a hand-rolled Crockford codec with no new dependency, and `Store::reencode_ids` migrates a store written in the previous spelling — **not optional**: without it every id in an existing file stops matching and the store answers nothing while looking healthy. Closes `lookup-prefix-selectivity-is-time-correlated` by subtraction rather than by repair. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `crockford-base32-ids`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Configuration and process topology section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only. Reasoning in [memory-data-model.md](documents/design/memory-data-model.md) and [recall-mechanisms.md](documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md).

*Answers nothing while looking healthy* is the failure worth having in the head: a missed migration here does not error, it returns empty results from a store that reports itself fine.

content: **The data-directory move was run end to end on 2026-09-30, on a disposable home with the real binary and model.** Moving `local.sqlite3` into a new directory, with every server stopped, then setting `SCATTERHOARD_COMMON` there keeps the store whole: same set identity, same memory count, recall finds everything. Moving the one file is enough, since stores use SQLite's default rollback journal, not WAL. Setting the variable without moving reads a fresh store at the new path: 0 memories and no `set_id` at all until its first write, which then mints a different one. So the symptom check is identity missing or changed, not merely changed. Merging a split back fails: `a-split-local-store-cannot-be-merged-back`.
context: Testing the move procedure for the first scatterhoard-cookbook recipe, after the human partner settled that recipes live in a published set.
why: The verification the cookbook rule requires before a recipe is published, and the facts the recipe will rest on. Kept with this issue, since it is what turns the stranded-store question into a recipe rather than a detector. The missing identity before a first write is the detail a symptom recipe would otherwise get wrong.

content: The migration follows the settled rule and was checked against the live stores before it could run on them: copies of all three were opened with the new code — 88, 66 and 99 rows across 3, 2 and 2 targets, byte-for-byte unchanged. Four of the seven stored targets existed and were already canonical; the other three are scratch directories from finished sessions, which keep their spelling. So the migration is a no-op on this machine, which is what the design predicted when it measured the same thing on 2026-08-11. *Whoever builds it inherits the rule [never keep a reconciliation base you cannot prove](documents/design/store-registry.md). The trap is specific: **two raw keys that canonicalise to one key are a collision, not a merge.** Where their rows disagree about a `memory_id`, neither is the other's ancestor, and keeping either supplies a wrong base for the file the other described. Drop both — dropping degrades to a reported conflict, while guessing returns `TakeFile` and overwrites a memory in silence.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Running a migration against copies of the live stores before letting it touch them, and the collision rule for the case it would hit elsewhere. The rule matters because merging two bases looks like the helpful choice and silently produces a wrong ancestor.

content:
**Measured 2026-09-12 on this project's own two sets: cluster representatives fail, distinctive keywords work, and neither reports what the project is *for*.** Spherical k-means over the stored 512-dimensional L2-normalised embeddings read straight from the `vectors` table, pure Python, about four seconds for 829 memories — so the cost of computing this at export is negligible.

**Three labelling schemes, tried in order.**

*Nearest-centroid memory, shown as its opening line* — the version proposed in conversation. **It fails.** A cluster's most central memory is still one specific claim (*Two of the three changes shipped 2026-09-02, in the required order…*), not a description of a theme. Reading eight of them tells you nothing about the set.

*Distinctive keywords per cluster, by log-odds against the rest of the set* — **this works.** On `scatterhoard` at k=8 it returned: store and set lifecycle; corrections and supersession; vectors, tombstones and embedding internals; conventions and the catalog budget; the non-match floor, calibration and scoring; issue tracking; reserved marks and the backlog; graph traversal and hybrid search. That is a fair and near-complete description of the corpus. `coding-lessons` at k=6 was likewise fair.

*Distinctive content terms instead of keywords* — **noticeably worse.** These memories are argumentative prose, so domain terms drown in reasoning vocabulary (*leaves, carry, longer, someone, happened*). Fixable only with a general-English background corpus to weight against, which is more machinery than the idea warrants. This matters because keywords are a user-controlled field and content is not, so the gameable labelling is the one that reads well.

**The finding that reaches furthest: the summary reports preoccupations, never stated purpose.** Nothing in the `scatterhoard` output says *a memory system for LLMs*. That is [`store-when`](documents/design/conventions.md) working exactly as written — *do not record what a glance at the code would answer* — so a project's identity is precisely what a well-kept corpus never contains. **No derived view of a disciplined set can report what the project is for.**

**That may not be the loss it first appears.** What it does report is machinery, and machinery is diagnostic: *similarity, centroid, non-match floor, hybrid search, supersession, graph traversal* reads unmistakably as retrieval over versioned linked records. By the same token *terminal guidance, propellant grain, IMU drift* would be legible without any statement of intent. Machinery may be the better signal precisely because nobody writes it down in order to be understood.

**Two caveats on the numbers.** `k` was chosen by hand at 8 and 6; a real implementation needs a rule for it. And the eight clusters came out unusually even, 18.7% down to 6.9%, with no dominant theme — a set with one overwhelming preoccupation would look different, and nothing here says how different.
context: Testing, on this project's own two sets, whether a derived set-level summary at export would actually be legible — the human partner asked what such a summary would say for `scatterhoard` and whether it would be accurate.
why:
Recorded because it is a measurement with a negative result inside it, and the negative result is the useful half: the version proposed in conversation does not work, and a session picking this up would otherwise build it.

The finding about `store-when` is the one worth carrying furthest. It is not a defect in the summary technique — it is the corpus behaving exactly as the conventions intend, and it means no derived view of any well-kept set can report stated purpose. Any design resting on the summary showing what a project is *for* is resting on something the conventions actively prevent.

At 0.8 because the mechanism and the numbers are solid but the sample is two sets from one project, both unusually prose-heavy, which is a weak basis for predicting how a corpus of ordinary engineering notes would read.

content: **Whether the gap sweep should run on writes, or only on recall by meaning.** Raised 2026-09-11 by the human partner while `one-unembeddable-memory-stops-the-store` was being fixed. `prepare` in `src/store.rs` runs `reconcile_embeddings`, and its only callers are `write` and `recall_across_with`, once per store searched — so every write pays the sweep's query. **A write gains nothing from the sweep itself**: it embeds its own memory, and filling *other* memories' gaps matters only to recall by meaning, since keyword search and `hoard_lookup` never read vectors. Running it on the read path alone would save a query per write. **Not yet checked:** whether the write path depends on `prepare`'s other half, `refresh`, which keeps the in-memory vector cache current with other processes' writes — that half may have to stay on writes even if the sweep moves. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `where-the-gap-sweep-runs`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Fixing the store-stopping embed failure; the human partner reconstructing how the gap sweep came about and asking why it runs on writes. Same stretch: the Latin-script recall issue, and a misleading status note filed as a-missing-model-reports-as-a-mismatch.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. Filed as a question rather than a backlog entry because nothing is decided — the human partner named the write-path trigger as the one odd part of the sweep's placement, and I agreed it looked unnecessary there without having checked what `refresh` does for a write.

It is the narrow, checkable half of a broader reservation the human partner deferred the same day, about the sweep's cost landing on one special case; that memory carries this slug too.

The sweep's history, as reconstructed in the same discussion and worth keeping because it was misremembered once already: `reconcile_embeddings` arrived 2026-08-08 for the ordinary onboarding path — memories stored before the model is installed — and at first did two jobs with one mechanism, filling gaps and re-embedding on a model mismatch. The mismatch half caused the two-server tug-of-war, and between 2026-08-09 and 2026-08-20 it became an explicit request (`documents/design/embeddings.md`, *a store owns its model*); gap-filling stayed automatic, with the store's own model only. The sweep predates the tug-of-war fix, and the fix is what narrowed it to its current job.

content: **The evidence for this pass, and why the migration is what makes it cheap.** Two entries were caught stale on 2026-09-07, both by the human partner asking rather than by the process: `edge-authority-across-sets` warned that a memory naming a cross-set successor removes itself from recall, which a cross-store layer built afterwards had fixed; and `correction-gated-on-service` said `confidence-standards` had yet to catch up with the export gate, which it had, the same day the gate shipped. **Both had already been migrated faithfully.** Neither would have been found by reading for defects, because nothing was wrong — the entries were simply describing a system that had moved. **What the migration changes about the cost**: before it, an audit meant reading a 152,000-character file end to end; after it, the open set is a recall on `hoard-proj-issue-open` or `hoard-proj-backlog-open`, returning heads whose opening line is the claim to check. The reading is the same reading, but nothing has to be located first.
context: Filing the closure audit while finishing the BACKLOG.md migration, from the two stale claims that prompted it.
why:
Recorded so the pass has its own justification rather than resting on housekeeping instinct, which is what gets an audit deferred indefinitely. Two confirmed instances in one day, from a sample of the twenty-odd entries read that day, is a rate worth acting on rather than a curiosity.

It also names what to look for, which is narrower than *is this still true*: a present-tense claim about code or served text. A decision recorded in an entry does not need auditing and never goes stale as history, so the pass is a scan for one grammatical shape rather than a re-reading of everything an entry says.

content: **These entries must be settled before publication**; they are this memory's keywords besides `release-gate`. `adopting-coding-lessons`, gated 2026-09-28, is built. It waits on proof from use, set out in `EARLY-VALIDATION.md` in the human partner's terms: it does not feel slower, sessions recall before writing, triggers get written, signposts cause lookups, and recalling changes what gets written. `sharing-preferences-served-at-session-start` was gated 2026-10-20: a user's sharing preferences, started from a file Scatterhoard provides, reach every session, so nobody has to run a full review to publish safely.
context: After committing the publication review, discussing how Scatterhoard's users get a starting point for their sharing preferences.
why: Superseded 2026-10-20 to gate the sharing preferences, at the human partner's direction after the pre-publication review. First users arrive at publication, so preferences that land later reach nobody until they have already written memories without them. And the human partner does not want every user to have to repeat the full review to publish safely. What the provided file contains, whether a baseline the person adds to or a template they edit freely, is being settled the same day. `adopting-coding-lessons` stays for its recorded reasons: `scatterhoard` links into `coding-lessons`, so they publish together, and the human partner wants experience of it first. Retire an item by superseding this memory without its slug.

content: **The export review works on `gemma4:12b` when the model sees the whole preferences file and the server filters its answers.** The model reports, per numbered sentence, every item mentioned from either keep-out list. The server then drops items from "Keep out of shared sets" for a `local` memory. Measured 2026-10-23 by re-scoring the split-template runs (`split-*`), 3 runs each: lone memories 48 of 48 right; realistic groups 0 missed, with 3 false alarms, all "users" read as someone else. Giving the model only its set's items instead (`listed-*`) cut false alarms but brought back 7 misses, including rent not read as finances.
context: Testing the export review's per-memory questions on a small model before the judgement gate is built, after the template's keep-out list was split in two.
why: This settles the division of labour: recognition is the model's job, and which list applies where is the server's, applied after the answer rather than by narrowing what the model reads. Narrowing the input lost misses, the dangerous error, to save false alarms, the cheap one. The re-scoring is valid because the server's filter is deterministic and applies to the same answers. It needs only the parsing the never-store list already does: a heading, then items.

content: **Only one direction needs supersessions, and working out why corrected a mistake made twice in the same discussion.** S's own memories with links **into** the absorbed set have been in service in S, so changing them needs ancestry — **seven of the 60 links in the live `scatterhoard` set, re-derived 2026-08-31 from the committed export; the entry read *six of 59* when it was written.** The arriving records go in **as authored**, and their links naming S canonicalise at the door exactly as every imported record's already do. **The distinction that was conflated twice before being named**: canonicalisation is **unconditional and deterministic**, so every holder stores identical bytes and it cannot produce the divergence `absorb` does — where absorb's rewrite was a receiver-side edit of authored content that two importers could apply differently. Same-looking operation, opposite consequences for convergence.
context: Migrating the absorb-as-supersession entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the correction it recorded and the two things it deliberately did not fold in.
why:
Recorded because the two operations are genuinely hard to tell apart — both rewrite a link's spelling on the way into a store — and being conflated twice in one discussion by people who understood both is the evidence that the difference needs stating rather than deriving. The test is not what the operation does to a link but whether every holder would do the same thing to it.

Two things were filed rather than folded in, and both are worth knowing so they are not rediscovered as defects. **Forwarding** — a record of where an absorbed set's identity went — belongs against `drop` rather than here, since links into a set break when it is *dropped*, not when it is absorbed, and only the absorbed case has somewhere to point. And **the honesty residue**: S's copy of an arriving record carries a link spelling its author did not write, which the 2026-08-23 canonicalisation reasoning defends and which reads as a defect to anyone meeting it cold.

content: **The per-change recall found nothing to apply a second time on 2026-10-05, again crowded by the project's own memories.** Before writing the recall-nudge hook, the unscoped habit recall returned five `scatterhoard` memories, all from the same day's work on the subject, and no lesson. Repeated scoped to `coding-lessons`, it returned the adoption guide and an unrelated staging trigger. One lesson that did apply, *a check that cannot fail reports success whatever happened*, was recalled from the session's own context, not from the search. It shaped the hook's logging of silent decisions.
context: Building the recall nudge hook, the morning after the first beta.
why: A part-6 observation for `adopting-coding-lessons`. It is the second instance in one day of the unscoped habit recall being filled by fresh project memories on the very subject, which leaves no room for lessons. Two instances do not make a pattern, so the generalisation is not drawn here. They are enough to watch for in the experiment's week.

content: **Whether import should merge by the lattice of a record's states and stop recording a per-target base.** Proposed 2026-08-30 with the human partner, in `documents/design/multi-set-sync.md` under *the graph is the ancestor*. Since an exported memory is immutable, one id moves only absent → memory → tombstone, so merge is a join that needs no ancestor. Built so far: absorption as a supersession (2026-08-31), and the lattice's tombstone-wins row, *a forget is one-way at import* (2026-09-28), with the undo settled as superseding the forgotten id. Tested so far: immutability holds everywhere except for records written before 2026-08-30. Adopting the rest would retire `bases`, `normalise_target` and the two-checkouts reasoning, and with them `target-identity-is-an-unnormalised-path-string`. It contradicts the resolved per-target base rather than extending it, so it is the human partner's to decide. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `merge-without-a-recorded-ancestor`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Checking whether `a-target-path-can-come-to-mean-a-different-volume` could close; the human partner asked what would close it, and then where this proposal lived.
why: Head of a question cluster, filed 2026-09-28 because the proposal had lived only in a design document for four weeks with no tracking entry. It surfaced only because a member of another issue carried its keyword. It is a question rather than a backlog item because the design document records it as a proposal and not a resolution.

content: **Checked 2026-09-22: a write depended on neither half of `prepare`.** Everything `write` consults — the evaluation-set guard, `would_destroy_an_unrebuildable_vector`, `model_state`, `is_findable_by_meaning`, `embed_for`, `persist` — reads the database, not the in-memory vectors, and `cache` only inserts the written memory's vector. So skipping `refresh` before a write leaves the cache at worst stale, and the next search's `refresh` reloads it because `data_version` moved. The gap sweep's query measured 0.2 ms over 1,001 memories. It never returned empty, because the store's identity record, never embedded, has no vector row.
context: Resolving where-the-gap-sweep-runs, after resolving link-only-write-after-export. The human partner's concern was whether a mix of embedded and unembedded memories needs the sweep before a semantic recall; it already ran there.
why: The unchecked half the question named was whether the write path relied on `refresh`; this is the answer, with the functions checked, so it can be re-verified if the write path grows a read of the cache. The identity-record finding explains why the sweep's documented cost, one query when there is nothing to do, was never true.

content: **A published set's procedure runs only when a user has opted in with a sentence in their project's `AGENTS.md`.** Decided 2026-09-27 by the human partner, for `coding-lessons` first. The set carries the procedure as reference material, an adoption guide written like a README, plus a signpost whose only action is to recall the guide before setting the set up. A session acts on the guide because the user's sentence says to, never because the set says so. Anyone wanting more control writes more prompting of their own.
context: Freeing catalog space for the data-only clause. The human partner proposed moving `route-where`'s general-versus-instance routing into `coding-lessons`, making that set help prevent failures, and propagating the practice to projects that want it.
why: A set that directs its reader to act is what `data-only-rule-in-the-catalog` forbids, and `hoard-watch` already limits a marked memory to recall, add findings and add evidence. A user's instruction file is the trusted channel: it is theirs, reviewed, and a crafted set cannot imitate it. It is also how Scatterhoard itself is adopted, a line in the user's own `CLAUDE.md`. The cost accepted: once opted in, the guide steers that project's sessions and arrives by `git pull`, so trusting it is trusting the publisher, with the diff as the gate. It constrains the data-only clause: that clause must keep allowing reference material the user asked to have used.

content: **These two entries must be settled before publication**; they are this memory's keywords. Gated 2026-09-23 by the human partner. `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity` is gated because crafted files arrive with publication. `adopting-coding-lessons`, gated 2026-09-28, is built. It waits on proof from use, set out in `EARLY-VALIDATION.md` in the human partner's terms: it does not feel slower, sessions recall before writing, triggers get written, signposts cause lookups, and recalling changes what gets written. `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely` left the gate on 2026-09-28, when it was built.
context: Building `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`, the first release-gate item after `adopting-coding-lessons` closed.
why: Superseded 2026-09-28 because `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely` was built, which settles the file-format item: an unknown label is now tolerated by the build that will be published first. The other two stay for their recorded reasons. `adopting-coding-lessons` stays because `scatterhoard` links into `coding-lessons`, so they publish together, and because the human partner wants experience of it first; it comes off when the human partner judges the evidence sufficient. Retire an item by superseding this memory without its slug.

content: **Restating many memories at once stays accurate if a script generates each text from the store and then checks the store against it before anything is forgotten.** Done on 2026-10-19 to pseudonymise a set name across 38 memories in `scatterhoard`. The script read the live store read-only, applied the replacements, refused any output still holding the old name or over the 2,000-character limit, and built split pieces by cutting the originals at paragraph boundaries. After every restatement was stored, it compared each new record's content, `why`, context, keywords, links, confidence and origin with what it had generated. There were 0 differences, and only then were the originals forgotten.
context: Carrying out the publication review's decision to pseudonymise the governance set's name, after testing a set rename.
why: Retyping a whole memory through the tool is where a restatement drifts unnoticed, and at 38 memories a reread would not catch it. Checking before forgetting is what makes the forget safe: a restatement that drifted can still be fixed while the original exists, and after the forget the original is gone. It is also what a built `restate` action would have to guarantee. Observed by the assistant; the scripts were in that session's scratchpad.

content: Fixed 2026-08-20 **by removal rather than by the machinery the entry expected**. A read never rebuilds, so the measured loop has no move to make — `a_second_server_reading_repeatedly_never_touches_the_first_ones_vectors` drives three reads by the disagreeing server and asserts the vector table and the recorded model are exactly as they were. `embed_all` returns early on a mismatch, so a new memory waits unembedded rather than joining a second vector space, and rewriting a memory that has a vector is refused where nothing can rebuild it. `why_unsearchable` names both models and the remedy, per set, in the recall that met the problem. **What made this smaller than designed**: the 2026-08-09 proposal treated a mismatch as a state to be driven out, from which the oscillation and its damping followed — treating it as a configuration to be *reported* removes the premise. The model-identity history and the directive warning are built and still useful as evidence, but they are no longer what prevents the loop. *The alternation count they feed is also protected from a false positive: a reset — rebuilding with the model already recorded — displaces nothing and does not enter the history, so resetting twice cannot look like two servers changing hands.* What remains is reporting the standoff, filed as `store-owns-its-model` in [BACKLOG.md](BACKLOG.md).
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A designed damping mechanism made unnecessary by changing the premise: treating a mismatch as a configuration to report rather than a state to drive out removes the oscillation instead of bounding it. That reframing is the transferable part.

content: Found 2026-08-26 by testing whether a supersession chain survives having a link forgotten out of its middle. It does not: with A superseded by B and B by C, `resolve_supersession(A)` gives C — forget B and it gives `Current`. **The reasoning behind the cascade is right and what it takes as collateral is the structure**: [file-format.md](documents/design/file-format.md) says a principal reason to forget is that sensitive data reached the memory, and a flagged row that still holds the text removes nothing — that is about the **text**. **This is worse than a dangling link**, which the design settles as a soft failure the LLM can judge: nothing here looks broken at all, and recall returns the stale conclusion live and unflagged. **It is not the tombstone's fault** — `holds_record` counts a tombstone precisely so links *into* a forgotten memory stay good references; the gap is links *out of* one, which no rule covered. *Probed while fixing, and it changes the shape of the bug: the `superseded_by` authoring direction breaks too. It looked safe, since those edges live on the older memory which survives — but the walk then stops at the forgotten memory, which authored the next hop. What is lost either way is the forgotten record's own **outbound** edge, which is why one rule covers both.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A correct rule about text taking structure with it as collateral, and a probe showing both authoring directions fail for one reason — the forgotten record's outbound edge — which is what makes the fix one rule rather than two special cases.

content:
Measured 2026-09-19: the served catalog is 17,724 characters and 17,736 bytes, so the whole gap is 12 — the only non-ASCII in it is six em dashes, one of them added that day. The defect costs nothing today, and the reason to fix it is what it does under the language work: `charter-declares-set-languages` is built, and a catalog served in Greek or Russian would spend roughly two bytes per character, reaching the 18,000 bound at about half the content.

A near-collision worth knowing, from the same day: `MAX_EMBEDDING_INPUT_CHARS` genuinely counts characters, via `chars().count()`, and deliberately — so a script costing more bytes per character is not given a shorter memory than an English one. Two similarly-named constants disagreeing about their unit is what a later session will assume away rather than check.

**The two fixes are not equivalent.** Counting `chars()` raises the effective budget wherever the text is not ASCII; renaming to `MAX_CATALOG_BYTES` records that the bound was always about bytes and leaves the headroom where it is. Which is right depends on what the bound is protecting — context window, which is tokens and closer to characters, or storage, which is bytes.
context: Filing the byte-counting finding after adding a sentence to store-when and watching an em dash cost three.
why: Recorded with the measurement because the obvious reaction to *the name is wrong* is a rename, and that is the fix that silently keeps a non-ASCII catalog at half the content. The choice turns on what 18,000 was ever protecting, which is a question the budget's own history may answer and this record cannot.

content: Found 2026-08-13 at the export gate, minutes before a commit, and it cost four tool calls and a throwaway script to reconcile: `status` reported `memories: 32` for `shared:scatterhoard` and `export` reported `memories: 33` for the same set moments later. **Neither is wrong on its own terms.** `Store::count` is `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM memories` and tombstones live in their own table, so `status` counts live memories; `Store::stream_records` builds its list from `tombstones()` and merges memories into it, so its return is records written to the file — 32 memories plus one tombstone.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery with both mechanisms named where they can be checked, because the defect is that two correct measurements share a name — neither implementation is wrong, so nothing in the code reads as a bug.

content: **Whether one repository can carry more than one memory set, and what the single well-known filename is actually protecting.** Raised 2026-08-15 while giving the `coding-lessons` set its own repository, and deliberately **not** resolved -- it only becomes real if that set is meant to be reused by others. **Two futures pull differently:** a set others *contribute back to* is a maintained project and needs nothing new, while a set others *copy and reuse without contributing* would want either merging into their own repository or two sets living in one. **The existing reasoning is narrower than *one name* and survives more than it looks like it would.** The trust argument -- memories are data, never instructions, enforceable by path rather than by inspecting content -- is a property of the reserved `scatterhoard_mem` *directory*, not of the filename, so a second file inside it is still path-trusted. The merge-driver argument is the one that pins a name, and it pins a `.gitattributes` pattern, which a glob could satisfy as well as a literal. **The identifier hazard is a different shape than it first appears:** ids make accidental collision negligible, but *copying* a memory from one set to another duplicates its id deliberately, and a cross-set link identifying its target by id then has two answers. That is a question about what copying means, not about identifier width. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `one-repository-many-sets`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The narrowing is the valuable part and is counter-intuitive: the single-filename rule looks like the load-bearing constraint and mostly is not, because the trust it carries comes from the directory. Someone opening this question would otherwise start by arguing against the trust model, which is not what stands in the way.

The copying observation is kept because it relocates the hazard entirely -- from identifier design, where it cannot be fixed, to the semantics of an operation nobody has defined yet.

content: Measured 2026-08-20 across the two live shared sets -- 90 memories, 48 edges: `related_to` is 54% of all edges (26), and `motivated_by` is 4% (2). Six of the fourteen labels are unused, `depends_on` among them. That inverts the corpus finding the `link-label-choice` convention is reasoned from, where `motivated_by` was the most-used label by a factor of three and `depends_on` was the one being mislabelled as motivation. The live failure mode, if there is one, is collapse into the explicit fallback rather than confusion between two specific labels.
context: Measured from the exported memories.json of `shared:scatterhoard` (50 memories) and `shared:coding-lessons` (40), in answer to the human partner asking whether the comment block held enough to judge how much the convention is needed. Small sample, and nearly every edge was written by one LLM author under the current conventions -- which is the population the convention would govern, but is n=1 author.
why: The drafted convention would tell a session to prefer `motivated_by` over `depends_on`, which is guidance against a mistake the live data shows nobody making -- while the thing that actually happens goes unaddressed. Worth knowing before drafting, because the comment block holding that reasoning reads as settled and its evidence is from a constructed design-document corpus rather than from live writing, which the graph-shape work already found to differ in density. The counts alone cannot say whether the fallback is being overused: that needs reading the 26 `related_to` edges and asking how many had a better label available, which is a bounded task and the actual evaluation.

content: **The public repositories keep their current URLs, `github.com/jtcours/scatterhoard` and `github.com/jtcours/coding-lessons`, by renaming each private repository and creating a new one under the original name.** Requirement stated 2026-10-18 by the human partner; the mechanics verified 2026-11-02 against GitHub's documentation. *Renaming a repository* says redirects follow a renamed repository, `git` operations included, and that creating a repository under the original name stops them: so the new repository takes over the URL cleanly. *Removing sensitive data* says commits rewritten out of a repository can stay reachable through forks, cached views by SHA and pull requests until GitHub Support garbage-collects them, which is why force-pushing an orphan branch into the existing repository is the alternative to avoid. Neither repository uses GitHub Pages or publishes an Action, the two things a rename does not redirect.
context: Going-public checklist: verifying the GitHub rename-and-recreate steps before acting on them.
why: Supersedes `01M596NNR0F39BQAT25CE9K4YY`, which held the sequence at 0.75 because it rested on general knowledge rather than a check. The documentation now confirms both halves: the takeover of the name, and the reason not to reuse the old repository. The URL is in the README, SETUP and memories, so keeping it saves editing all of them.

content: Found 2026-08-25 while building `set-drop`, **by a test asserting a scope in a response and being wrong about its shape** — which is what an unpublished response shape costs. The earlier decision covered arguments and was never applied to responses, and responses are where `Scope`'s derived `Serialize` runs. **Only Misleads**, because the object form still parses, so a caller feeding a response's scope back into an argument is accepted and nothing is silently wrong. **What it costs is the property the decision was made for**: two spellings for one concept, which the rule against local aliases refuses, arriving at the one boundary that was standardised to prevent it. **Fixed 2026-08-26 by a type rather than a call at each site**: `WireScope` serialises a borrowed `Scope` as the scalar and every response goes through it — **the sites were the defect**, since nine reached the wire and the tenth is the one somebody adds later, so serialising a bare `Scope` into a response is now the thing that looks wrong.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A decision applied to one direction of a boundary and not the other. The fix is a type rather than nine call-site edits, because the failure mode is the site nobody has written yet.

content: A rule that every set would need belongs in the convention catalog; only what varies by set belongs in its `hoard-scope-topics` charter. Applied 2026-08-25 to move "a lesson that would hold anywhere belongs elsewhere, even when this is where it was learned, though the evidence for it does belong here" out of the `shared:scatterhoard` charter and into `route-where`. The test that decided it: the clause was doing real work and being followed, but nobody writing their first charter would think to include it, so every set created without it routes general lessons into a project set -- which is the misfiling `route-where` was created to fix.
context: Decided 2026-08-25 by the human partner, who asked whether that clause was doing significant work and, if so, whether other sets would have anything like it. Checkable in ROUTE_WHERE in src/conventions/catalog.rs and in the superseded charter memory.
why: This is the argument that put the taxonomy in the sets rather than the catalog, run in the other direction, and it is worth having stated both ways because the charter is the tempting place for anything about routing. A charter travels with its set and is read as authoritative by whoever imports it, so a general rule kept there is a copy that other sets silently lack rather than a copy that drifts -- the failure is absence in every set but one, which nothing reports. Ask of any candidate charter sentence whether a stranger creating their own set would need the same sentence; if yes, it is a convention. Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claim is unchanged.

content: **Measured 2026-09-08: `scatterhoard` is a large, sparsely linked set and `coding-lessons` a small, densely linked one, and the gap is about fourfold.** Counting only traversable edges — supersession excluded, since the walk never follows it — `scatterhoard` holds 119 edges over 709 memories, **0.17 per memory, with 153 of 709 (22%) touching any edge at all**; `coding-lessons` holds 81 over 122, **0.66 per memory, 90 of 122 (74%)**. `local` is 6 over 11; `governance-docs` has **no links whatsoever**. So for roughly four in five `scatterhoard` memories, semantic similarity is the only way in, and the graph walk cannot reach them however good the query. The human partner predicted this shape before it was measured, reasoning from the issues/backlog/questions migration having created many entries and few cross-links. Re-derive by counting the `links` table per store, excluding labels `supersedes` and `superseded_by`.
context: Probing the gap cut, when the human partner asked whether sparse linking was why similarity dominates the results.
why: Recorded because it is the standing context for every recall measurement taken against this corpus, and it is invisible from any single recall — a query whose answers happen to be among the linked fifth looks like traversal working, and one whose answers are not looks like traversal being useless, with nothing in either result saying which case it is. It also bears on the migration: filing hundreds of entries as head-plus-members clusters adds memories quickly and edges slowly, because members are gathered by a shared keyword rather than joined by links, so the set gets sparser as it grows unless linking is done deliberately.

content: Two of three fixed 2026-08-18 on the human partner's instruction to *"resolve to a distinct set at the tips, and stay at the tips while walking"* — seeds are chosen by resolving down the ranking until five **distinct** current memories are found, and the graph is collapsed onto tips before the walk. **The third closed 2026-08-19**: every scanned memory is resolved *before* anything is ranked, so a chain folds into one candidate carrying the best evidence any member matched. The four outcomes are an enum rather than an id-plus-flag, because two are easy to conflate — a memory in a cycle and a memory whose replacement this machine does not hold both fail to resolve and call for opposite treatment. **The observable behaviour did not change, and that is the honest result**: every existing test and recorded snapshot passed untouched, because collapsing already happened before the cut and the score kept was already the best of the chain. What changed is *where* the identity is known — the ranking now holds the memory it will return while scoring, which is the precondition the third consequence needed. *Two things fell out: the admission loop no longer needs its twice-the-window slack or its de-duplication pass, and a branch defending an unembedded replacement turned out unreachable and was removed rather than left as untestable defence.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A fix with no observable behaviour change, stated as such rather than dressed up. Its whole value is enabling a feature that was blocked — worth recording, because a change that alters no test looks like a change that did nothing.

content: The store layer was already honest and the seam is where it went wrong. `a_store_without_a_model_makes_the_union_search_incomplete` in [tests/cross_store.rs](tests/cross_store.rs) pins both halves deliberately — *"the store with a model still answers"* and *"a store that could not be searched has to be reported"* — so hits and incompleteness are both true at once, and only the prose above them said otherwise. One name, two meanings: the same shape as `memories-count-means-two-different-things`, and worse in the partial case, because the two readings disagree about whether the numbers on screen mean anything. A caller that believes the note discards a correct ranking; a caller that believes the scores never learns a set was missing. Which set was skipped was never named, and the note pointed at `hoard_sets status`, one round trip to learn something the failing call already knew. Found 2026-08-20 while reasoning about per-store models, from reading the code rather than from a client.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery, and the diagnosis that the defect lives at a seam rather than in a layer: both sides were individually correct, which is why no test failed and why the test that pinned the truth sat directly under the prose contradicting it.

content: The scope refusal asked for something no caller could find out: rejecting an unloaded set with *"check the set name"* and *"have to be imported"* named two actions the tool surface offered no way to perform — nothing listed loaded sets and there was no import tool. Fixed 2026-08-05 by `hoard_sets`. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `no-tool-lists-loaded-scopes`; this record carries only its standing.

content: **What recall returns by default. Resolved 2026-09-24 by the human partner: the full record, with no intermediate level; `summary` stays opt-in.** Measured that day over 948 current `scatterhoard` memories, a full hit averages about 2,000 characters: content 925 and `why` 457 — seven-tenths, the claim and its reasoning — then attribution about 140, scalars about 120, `context` 119, links and in-links about 120, keywords 95. Every smaller field is read by a served convention except the author ids inside the timestamps, about 3%, which does not pay for a second level. The budget levers are how many hits return and `summary` for surveys. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `what-recall-returns`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner, straight after settling the set operations and first-write rules.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. The human partner's reason for keeping `summary` opt-in rather than the default: a model handed only index lines may reason from them as though they were the memories, so fetching the full record should be a deliberate act. It locks the default response shape before publication, which is why the question was gated; documenting that shape is `response-shape-is-unpublished`.

content: A hand-edited file in one set could remove a memory from another: a rival store's `SUPERSEDES` edge was allowed to rule on an id it did not hold, so the target vanished from recall. Fixed 2026-08-23 by keying the guard on **who holds the memory** rather than on how the edge is spelled. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-set-can-suppress-another-sets-memory`; this record carries only its standing.

content: **Whether a link may be added to an exported memory without superseding it.** Resolved 2026-09-22 by the human partner: **no, not now** — supersession stays the only route (option B). In twelve days of the connect-on-recall clause, no connection needed one: links went on the memory being written, which is not yet exported, and traversal ignores direction. **Reopen if** link-only supersessions start appearing in the set, a session reports skipping a connection between two exported memories, or a pass to connect the older isolated memories is decided on. The findings gathered under this question carry the keyword `link-only-write-after-export`.
context: Pre-release review, right after serving the cost-framed recall-when wording.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. Option A lost its main recorded objection when the merge driver began set-merging links, but it would still need an additions-only rule, a whitelist excluding labels that change another memory's standing, a decision on `modified.by`, and served text the catalog has no room for. Nothing measured pays for that. Option C was only ever about the cost premise, which the 2026-09-09 examination removed. The reopen conditions are the cases where A would earn its cost, so a later session can tell when to look again.

content: **Step 1 built 2026-09-24: `hoard_memorize` reports `link_delta` on a supersession**, one entry per same-set superseded target, naming `left_behind` and `restated` with a note. Three choices made while building it, checkable at `link_deltas` in `src/mcp.rs`: links compare on **label and target id**, so a changed label is a link left behind while re-typed `target_keywords` are not; the superseded memory's own `supersedes` and `superseded_by` are **excluded** as history rather than claims; and an entry is reported **even when nothing was left behind**, as the confirmation `keyword_delta` gives. A long-spelled same-set target counts as same-set, via `is_foreign_to`, where `keyword_deltas` still skips it. Steps 2 and 3 remain; until step 3 the walk still carries left-behind links to the tip.
context: Building step 1 of the out-link supersession work, after closing the arrival-provenance issue and recording why the moved-local-store issue may not need fixing; earlier the same session, calibrating both shared sets and graduating four common causes.
why: Records the step as done and the decisions it embodies, which the code shows but not why. Comparing by id is sound because ids are unique across sets. The note already says left-behind links stay with the superseded memory, which is true of the record today and of the walk only once step 3 lands. That gap is a deliberate staging rather than a defect.

content: **Resolved 2026-09-17: a set is loaded read-only by choosing that mode at `create`, and read-only distribution is built.** The question was how to hold a set someone else publishes — documentation, policies, regulations — so its memories can be read and never written here. The design is [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md): `create` takes an optional `mode` defaulting to read-write; the mode lives in the set's `meta`; a read-only set refuses session writes, takes and refreshes its records from its publisher's file by `import` or `restore`, drops without a safety copy unless `save_to` is given, and pulls the `hoard-signpost` mark alone, which `hoard_sets status` names per set. A set identity loads once, a read-write copy winning over read-only ones. The publisher cannot declare read-only-ness in the file, because a header is contents. **What it left behind is one backlog entry, `promotion-to-read-write`**, deferred: the design settles what promotion would do, and nothing implements it. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `read-only-distribution`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing out read-only mode, deciding what comes next after it was finished. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 8 links an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.
why: Supersedes the head to mark the question resolved. Its last open part, whether promotion is offered, is decided-but-unbuilt rather than undecided, so it moves to the backlog as `TRACKING.md` says a resolved question's residue should, instead of holding this entry open.

content: Let one `hoard_memorize` call store several memories that link to one another, so a link to a memory being created needs no id. Decided by the human partner on 2026-09-29, over refusing a guessed id's signature and over a sentence in the tool description. The caller gives each memory a label and a link targets another memory in the same call by that label; the server mints the ids and resolves the labels. Blocked on the surface's shape, which the human partner is to settle: the label syntax, whether the write is all-or-nothing, and what the response returns. Built when one call stores linked memories through the published schema, a test goes through that schema, and a mutation pins the resolution. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `in-call-references-for-memorize`; this record carries only its standing.
context: After the coding-lessons lesson on dependent calls in a parallel batch was stored; the human partner asked whether the tooling could make the mistake less likely.
why: Head of a backlog cluster. Twice on 2026-09-29 a session linked a memory to another stored in the same parallel batch, and wrote the link with a guessed id. The decision of which memory to link was the caller's, but the id existed only on the server and only after a call the caller had not seen the result of, so the decision was placed where its information was not (`documents/design/decision-placement.md`). This removes the step where the mistake happens, and it makes a cluster's head and members one call, where today their order rests on parallel calls running in sequence.

content: A memory in another set writing `EXCEPTION_TO` or `CONTRADICTS` at ours was one hop from it in the walk and inherited score accordingly — the permanent slot the design had refused for `SUPERSEDES`, bought with a different label. Fixed 2026-08-25 by refusing to walk a standing-changing edge whose target names another set. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-cross-set-dispute-carries-score-to-the-memory-making-it`; this record carries only its standing.
