content:
**`gemma4:12b` could not complete a real fixed issue given its context: 0 of 6 runs across 18 attempts, measured 2026-10-06.** The task was `a-read-only-set-is-told-to-mint`, on the tree at `6ed267f` with the fix's tests added. The prompt held the bug report, `create_set`, `LoadMode` and the failing test, about 2,100 tokens with thinking off at a 16k context. Scoring was the whole `sets` test binary, with three attempts per run and the failure fed back.

Every reply got the structure right: it branched on `mode`, compiled and broke nothing else. Every one missed the test's textual requirements: the action named as `"import"`, and no `mint`. Adding the failing assertion's source line to the feedback changed nothing. Runs then copied the old note's closing "`identify` or `mint`" into the new one. One attempt fixed the quoting and the next undid it.
context: Trying gemma4:12b on a real fixed issue after it passed the small Rust probe, to see whether the small-model lift experiment can use fixed issues as tasks.
why: For `how-much-scatterhoard-lifts-a-small-model`: the small-task probe passed 13 of 15, but a real fix, small and handed its full context, did not pass once. The failure is satisfying two literal constraints from a test at once, while preferring to reuse existing text. Memory would not supply that. So a lift measured on fixed issues would sit on a floor of zero, unless thinking mode or a stronger model lifts the baseline first. Thinking mode was left off throughout, untested. One task, hence 0.75.

content: Neither repo has a git remote, by decision: release publishes the memory sets. Verify with `git remote -v`. Scatterhoard's checkout and `coding-lessons`' are deliberately local-only, because pushing to an origin publishes whatever the sets contain at that moment and locks it in the way declaring 1.0.0 does — every memory, including the ones nobody re-read before they travelled. Work that must land first carries **`release-gate`**; recall that term before treating anything as ready to ship, and add it to whatever else turns out to be gated. **This ends when a remote exists.** At that point supersede this memory with the keyword left off rather than editing it — and do not treat the absence of a remote as an oversight to fix in passing, which is the specific thing this exists to prevent.
context: Working out where to record that the repos have no remote and why, after a branch cleanup made the absent remote visible. The same session renamed the tracking-file control marks under `hoard-proj-`.
why:
Marked as a signpost because it fails the search test in both directions: an absent remote is invisible, so nothing prompts a session to ask why it is missing, and a session that does notice reads it as unfinished setup rather than as a decision. The concrete failure is a session being helpful — offering `git remote add origin`, or asking whether to push — and the human re-explaining the gate every time.

The staleness defence is not the push. Being recalled every session gets it read; it does not get it updated, and retirement still depends on someone noticing the ending arrived. What keeps it honest is that the claim names its own falsifier in its opening line: `git remote -v` settles it in a second, so a reader is never asked to trust the assertion. That is `store-when`'s name-where-it-can-be-checked clause doing the work a promise to maintain the memory could not.

The ending is mechanically decidable, which is unusual for a watch — most endings are judgements about what would count as enough.

Recorded now because the gating was already being lost. `a-healed-fork-reports-its-ancestor-as-a-cycle` is deferred to before-publish, and that fact lived only in the head's `context`, which recall does not search, and in `checkpoints/`, which is gitignored and rewritten every session.

content:
Measured 2026-09-19, and it contradicts the approach `model-covers-declared-languages` records: **a coverage test derived from the model's own vocabulary would pass languages whose recall is broken.** Under `potion-base-32M`, the mean pairwise cosine among four unrelated sentences is 0.037 for English (highest pair 0.167), but 0.883 for Russian, 0.753 for Japanese and 0.959 for Greek. Unrelated texts in those languages point the same way, so ranking inside such a set is noise, and a non-match floor calibrated there would be meaningless.

**In-vocabulary is not represented.** Russian and Greek tokenise fully against this model's vocabulary — 48 and 60 surviving tokens for the samples — and still collapse, so the entry's stated plan of deriving the test from the vocabulary by script would report both as covered. What does detect it is a separation test: embed several unrelated texts in the declared language and check that they do not collapse, which needs no table of model names either and so keeps the property that plan was chosen for.

Measured on short sentences; the English control is equally short and separates cleanly, so length is not what makes the difference. Reproduce with `probe_whether_a_character_cap_can_stand_in_for_a_token_cap` in `tests/probes.rs`.
context: Testing whether a token count could stand in as a check for a language the model does not support, while working the memory-size question.
why: The entry is deferred on the reasoning that a user needing another language can load the multilingual model today — which assumes they would know. This says they would not: nothing reports the failure, every memory still embeds to a unit vector, and the detector the entry plans to build would not catch it either. Recorded against that entry rather than the size question because it corrects a design decision already written down, and the moment it is cheapest to correct is before anyone builds it.

content: **On revision 2026-07-28, `mint`'s and `rename`'s `author` and `identify`'s `record` are optional, and set aside wherever the human can be asked**, rather than removed from the schema as the proposal said. Built 2026-10-15. The tool list must be the same for every caller and is cached, while whether a client shows forms is declared per request, so a schema without the argument would strand a modern client that cannot show forms. What keeps a model's name out is that the server does not read the argument when it can ask (`sets` in `src/mcp.rs`), never as a form default either.
context: Implementing the elicitation proposal: the dual-era envelope, the name and identity forms, and the protocol-dependent `hoard_sets` schema.
why: A later session reading the proposal's "the parameter is absent" would otherwise take the optional argument for a mistake and remove it, or take its presence as licence to read it. Decided by Claude while building, not reviewed by the human partner when written; recorded in `documents/design/asking-the-human.md` under *Built 2026-10-15*.

content: **Import gets no gate. It reports what arrived instead.** Decided by the human partner on 2026-09-25, settling the second of `imported-set-trust-boundary`'s sub-questions. Import lists the ids of new and changed records only when it reconciled against an earlier agreement with that file. A first import from a target gives counts and `describes` without ids, because the human partner pointed out that a first import of `scatterhoard` would otherwise list about 1,190 ids, around 35,000 characters. A later pull lists ids up to a cap of about 50, then gives the count and points to `git diff` on the memory file. Import also runs the prohibited-data scan and reports what it finds, without refusing. Built as `import-reports-what-arrived`.
context: Working through the release-gated questions: `imported-set-trust-boundary`, straight after declining the personal-set exemption.
why: A gate has nothing to do on import. Trust in what arrives is the checkout's provenance. Contributions pass the maintainer's review of the memory file's diff on merge. A content check cannot tell a malicious memory from a legitimate one. Every set is data, so a bad memory is bounded harm. And refusing cannot undo a file already on disk. What was missing was visibility: import reported only counts per reconciliation outcome, while export lists ids in `replaced_file` and only when it compared against a file it knew. The scan's worth on import is narrow. Export does not refuse a secret-shaped memory; it writes the file and warns against committing it. So an upstream one would make every downstream export warn about a memory its author never wrote, far from where it came in. The session first said export would refuse, which was wrong, and was corrected against `export_set` in `src/mcp.rs` before recording.

content: **No refusal wording tried stops `gemma4:12b` minting an author name the human never gave.** Probed 2026-10-10 with `scripts/local_model.py retry` on task `first-write-to-new-set`, whose repository is `github.com/acme-corp/widget`: today's refusal minted an invented name 10/10; adding a remote-owner hint minted `acme-corp` 10/10; the best variant (stop and ask first, the owner offered only as a suggestion inside the question, then how to `mint`) asked 6/10 and minted `acme-corp` 3/10. Removing the mint instructions from the refusal did not help, because the `hoard_sets` schema itself offers `mint` with a free-text `author`.
context: Working the ready backlog to give the recall nudge some data; building the remote-owner hint for a shared set's first-write refusal, then probing six wordings of it on a small local model.
why: It moves `author-default-from-remote-url` from a wording problem to a mechanism problem: text only shifts a probability while the model holds a tool that accepts any string and a plausible string to put in it. It also shows a hint that names a concrete candidate turns an obviously wrong author into a plausible wrong one, which is harder to catch. One model, one harness whose system prompt leans towards acting, so a stronger reader may do better. The texts and logs were in the session scratchpad and are gone; the task was added to `corpus/local-model-tasks.json` so it can be rerun, uncommitted when this was written.

content: An export is regenerated whole from the store, so two stretches of work whose memories are both stored before either is committed cannot afterwards be split into two commits: one memory file holds both, and its derived header describes the set as it now stands. Dividing it would mean hand-writing an export state that never existed, which is worse than a combined commit. Observed 2026-09-19, when the tracking-index ordering fix and an issue filed while doing it landed together for this reason — TRACKING.md had the same problem, holding both the reordered rows and the new entry's row. The habit that keeps commits separable is to commit each stretch before storing the next one's memories, rather than to divide the file afterwards.</content>
context: Committing the index-ordering fix and the identity-count filing, having offered to make them two commits and found that only one was honest.
why: The constraint is invisible until the moment of committing, which is after the point where anything could be done about it, and the natural working order — do the work, notice something, file it, then commit — is exactly the order that produces it. Recorded as a sequencing habit rather than as a warning, because there is nothing to check at commit time: by then the choice is a combined commit or a fabricated one.

content: **In the export review, a sentence about a person with no `says` is routed as judging, not refused.** Decided 2026-10-26 by the human partner, over merging `about` and `says` into one label. `clear` no longer refuses such a memory, and `route` in `src/review.rs` puts it to the person. Recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. The human partner also decided that `gemma4:12b` stays the standard test model for now.
context: Building the reports-or-judges question and the keep-outs for other people into the uncommitted judgement gate, before the first export of the scatterhoard set.
why: A refusal changed nothing for most of the sentences gemma left unanswered, and a small model may never get past it (`01M5VGMP5MEVHB09PY34CVCWGN`). The merged label removed the refusals but weakened who a sentence is about (`01M5XN56NTE90TWYADG7M5N2TW`). Reading a missing answer as judging errs towards showing the person a memory, at the cost of some false alarms in `local`.

content:
**Two `reinforcement` edits on 2026-09-19 funded `store-when`'s new sentence** — *Make each memory compact, tightly-written, and atomic* — leaving the catalog at 17,880 of 18,000.

`store-when` lost *"Memories about how something works go stale silently:"*, 54 characters, because the contrast that followed already carried it: *a structural claim keeps reading as authoritative after a refactor has invalidated it* **is** the silence, and the convention's own text already names the category. A reinforcement's job is the reason, not a re-introduction of what the text states.

`recall-before-storing` gained *"Unlike linked memories"* and kept both harms: *…splits one subject's recall between two records, so every later search returns half of it — and the two then drift.* The contrast answers an objection the text left open, since `split-when-partly-stale` asks a session to split a subject across records; the difference is reachability, as a linked pair is traversed and returned carrying `inherited` while a duplicate pair is unlinked by construction. The human partner proposed replacing the halving with the drift, and both were kept at a cost of 6 characters: the halving is the immediate checkable harm, drift the delayed one, and a reinforcement is read at writing time.

**A third budget lever, beside the two already measured:** redundancy between a reinforcement's abstract claim and the concrete case that illustrates it. Word-level trimming is not a lever here and sentence architecture is; this is neither.
context: Funding a new store-when sentence while building the memory length refusal, with the human partner choosing the wording for both edits.
why: The trimmed clause will read as an omission to anyone who meets the sentence without knowing it was weighed, and the obvious repair is to put it back — which is why what it was carrying, and where that survives, is recorded rather than the fact of the cut. The lever itself is worth having because the budget question keeps returning and the two answers already on file both say *not here*.

content: **With no model loaded, status calls a store's model a mismatch and blames another server.** Observed 2026-09-11 UTC: a store bound to `potion-base-32M`, reopened by the same single server with `SCATTERHOARD_MODEL` pointing at a path that no longer exists, reports `state: mismatched`, `loaded: null`, and a note saying the set's vectors "came from a different model than this server holds" and that "if another server is running with its own model, the two configurations disagree". No second server existed and no different model was held. `describe_model_state` in `src/mcp.rs` gives `ModelState::Mismatched` one note whatever `loaded` is, while `documents/design/embeddings.md` treats a wrong model and no model as two rows wanting opposite treatment. The remedy the note points at — reconciling two configurations — is the wrong one here; the right one is making the model loadable again. SETUP.md warns that a re-fetch changes the snapshot hash, so a stale path is an ordinary route in. **Fixed looks like:** `loaded: null` gets its own note naming the missing model and the fix, with no mention of another server.
context: Designing the fix for the store-stopping embed failure; the human partner asking whether the gap sweep is needed outside the two-server case, tested on a disposable home with a stale model path.
why:
Filed `misleads`: every field is accurate, and the note draws the wrong conclusion from them, sending the reader to look for a second server that does not exist.

Found in passing while testing the human partner's question of whether the gap sweep is only needed when two servers fight over a store. This single-server sequence was the counter-example, and its status output was where the wording showed.

Whether `Mismatched { loaded: None }` should become its own `ModelState` variant, rather than only get its own note, is for the fix to decide. The design's table already separates the two rows, so a variant would match it.

content: Surveyed before fixing, since the concern was that other reserved keywords behave this way: `hoard-author` is the **only** keyword the code branches on. `hoard-scope-topics`, `hoard-watch` and the three kind keywords are convention-only, reached by ordinary recall, with no code path behind them. Convention now prevents the bad input — `keyword-standards`' `about-` rule makes `about-hoard-author` the right spelling — but convention is not what does the filtering, and the next reserved keyword to grow behaviour will not be covered by having remembered this one.
context: Renaming this entry's slug to take an `about-` prefix, while fixing genindex.py's positional slug pick.
why: The survey bounds the blast radius, and the closing sentence is why it has to be repeated rather than remembered: the hazard is a reserved term acquiring code behind it, which is a future event, not a past one. Superseded 2026-09-21 only to move it to the entry's renamed slug; the claim is unchanged, and describes the code as of 2026-09-06.

content: **Whether the tracking files should become an index over memory clusters, rather than holding the detail themselves. Resolved 2026-09-07: yes, and all three are migrated.** Raised 2026-09-02 by the human partner from the friction of navigating ISSUES.md, BACKLOG.md and open-questions.md as they grew. **The proposal:** each markdown entry reduces to a uniform generated row -- checkbox, slug, one-sentence description, severity or readiness where it applies -- while the detail and every later update become a memory cluster. **The motivating constraint was that there is no issue tracker here**, and the alternative considered and set aside was a hand-built SQLite one: backups are a real cost, paid once already on 2026-09-01 when a `cp` of an open store captured 51 of 81 memories; the export-to-git path already exists; and this project wants that history in the store eventually regardless. **Carried out across 2026-09-06 and 2026-09-07:** ISSUES.md first, then BACKLOG.md, then this file, each ending with a generated index and nothing below the markers. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `tracking-files-as-index`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set -- this entry last, since it is the entry describing the migration itself.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

**This head sorts last in its own cluster and that is unavoidable.** The migration method's findings were written under this slug throughout the work -- batching, ordering, depth, dating, the summary interaction -- so a dozen members precede the head that names them. Ids are minted at write time and cannot be reordered; read the head by its content rather than its position.

Marked resolved on the file's own evidence: all three tracking files now carry a generated index with zero entries below the markers, which is precisely what the proposal asked for. What remains is not this question but the follow-on work filed separately as `unify-the-tracking-files`.

content: Repointing `SCATTERHOARD_COMMON` looks exactly like having no memories: the server creates a store in the new directory, correctly, while a store full of personal memories sits unread in the old one — and every symptom available to the caller is identical to a set that is legitimately empty. Fixed when a server whose local directory holds no store, while its home holds one, says so once, naming both paths. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `moving-the-local-store-leaves-the-old-one-unmentioned`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only, with the fixed-when since this one is open. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Where do recipes for Scatterhoard's users live: how to build, with Scatterhoard, something this project has built for itself? Raised 2026-09-28 by the human partner. Users have no copy of this repository; only the served catalog and the sets they import reach them. Candidates: a published set such as `scatterhoard-cookbook`, imported read-only as reference material and found by recall when needed; a document; or a set plus a short document pointing to it, which I lean towards. Recipes would open with the reader's goal ("setting up…"), since that is how a session phrases the query. First candidates: the tracking system behind `TRACKING.md`, already proven, and the lessons-set mechanism of `set-adoption`, only once it has been used. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `where-user-facing-recipes-live`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Freeing catalog space for the data-only clause: the removed `route-where` note pointed at the `coding-lessons` design as something others would want to replicate.
why: Head of a question cluster. The design records in this set say what was decided and why, for people building Scatterhoard; an adoption guide is a procedure for one set. Nothing is shaped to hold "here is how to do this for your own collection", which is what a user replicating either mechanism needs. The question is when as much as where: a recipe written before its mechanism has been used is a second copy of untested design, which is the drift pattern `a-fact-restated-by-hand-drifts` names.

content: Nothing checks whether the memory already exists. Raised 2026-08-12 by the human partner; the convention was drafted and served 2026-08-13, second in catalog order, so the convention half is done. **What remains is the store-time surfacing** — the tool returning the nearest few existing memories when one is stored, so the session has something to read without having to think to ask. Confirmed still absent 2026-09-07: a store returns `summary` and `keyword_delta` and nothing about neighbours. Built when the store-time half is either built or explicitly declined with a reason. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `recall-before-storing`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. Ready rather than blocked — the dependency that used to hold it is gone, which the members record.

content: **How Scatterhoard should keep a hypothetical from being recorded as a fact about a real person.** Raised 2026-10-18 by the human partner, after the publication read-through found a memory saying a worked example named a real person in their life. The example was a hypothetical, written in the first person to test the Golden Rule. Nothing in the conventions asks a session to tell an illustration from a report, and the error is the dangerous kind: it creates a personal claim about someone that is false and that, as a stored memory, reads as authoritative. Open because nothing is decided about where a defence would sit or what form it would take. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `a-hypothetical-recorded-as-fact`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Starting the decisions from the publication read-through: settling on a fresh public history, correcting the memory that took a hypothetical as real, and the human partner's proposal to serve sharing preferences at session start.
why: Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. It is a question rather than an issue because no code is wrong: the memory was written by a session following the conventions, and the gap is in what they ask. The person clause in `store-when` asks for observations over conclusions, but "this example is about a real person" reads as an observation to whoever writes it.

content: It dissolves under *the graph is the ancestor*, raised by the human partner 2026-08-30, and the reason is stronger than *the head of the chain wins*. Absorption as a supersession stops being a transformation applied at write time and becomes **a record**: the absorbing store authors a new memory with the same claim and same-set links, superseding the original. It exports like any record, and `every_other_write_path_lands_the_authors_bytes` already establishes that restore replays a file's bytes faithfully — so restoring from a file exported *after* absorbing loses nothing, with the superseding memory at the tip where recall substitutes it. **What remains is correct rather than defective**: restoring from a file that *predates* the absorption still discards it, because restore replaces wholesale, but that loss shows up in the memory count, lands in the mandatory safety copy, and is local work that has not been exported — exactly what restore is documented to throw away. *A pleasing consequence: the superseded original keeps its cross-set link, inert, which is now where an inert link belongs — on a historical record saying what that memory actually said, rather than on the current version.* **So the patch this entry first suggested — adding `absorbing` to `restore` — is not merely smaller but wrong**: it would teach a second operation to reproduce a rewrite, when what the rewrite needs is to stop existing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The dissolution, and why the obvious patch was the wrong direction — the part the entry itself says is worth keeping. Turning an untraced transformation into an ordinary record removes every operation's need to know about it.

content: **Whether recall should ever combine semantic and keyword search into one ranking -- hybrid search.** Raised 2026-08-03, when `hoard_recall` was narrowed to accept a query **or** keywords but not both. **The combination was removed because it integrated nothing:** two independent searches stapled together, duplicating payload, putting two scales in one response, with no honest ordering. Separating them makes those unrepresentable. **But separation is the conservative answer, not the best one, and two things are genuinely lost.** A memory found by *both* paths is stronger evidence of relevance than one found by either, and that signal now exists nowhere -- a caller making two calls has to notice an id appearing in both and draw the conclusion itself. And a precise identifier is exactly the case where an exact keyword match should outrank a merely-similar memory, which a caller juggling two lists arbitrates by hand. **Deferred rather than rejected, and what it needs first is scoring worth ranking with.** Measured on a six-memory store, an unrelated memory scored `0.136` against `0.120` for the memory carrying the searched term as a keyword; a ranking built on separation that thin would be arbitrary. **So it is blocked behind the cold-start question, behind `no-non-match-floor` -- still open as of 2026-09-07 -- and behind having a corpus large enough to test against empirically rather than by argument.** The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `hybrid-search`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

*Separation is the conservative answer, not the best one* is carried in the head because the tool surface currently enforces the separation and reads as a settled design choice. It was a retreat from something that did not work, and the two lost signals are real -- a reader should not mistake the current shape for the intended one.

The corpus-size blocker is worth watching: it was written when the store held six memories and now holds several hundred, so the *not enough to test against* half of the block may have cleared even though the scoring half has not.

content: Symptom: a memory that `hoard_lookup` still returns by id, but that no search finds at all -- gone from semantic recall and from keyword search alike, with nothing reported. Cause: its own `superseded_by` names a same-set id that no live memory answers to. The chain resolved and reported a tip, both search paths then failed to fetch that tip, and each dropped the hit silently. The spelling that produces it is a cross-set reference written WITHOUT its set name -- one spelling apart, and the failure modes are opposite: written with the set name the same intent comes back flagged `superseded_beyond_this_set`, written without it the memory ceases to exist for search. No hostile file is needed. A hand-edited set, an id forgotten rather than superseded, or a set lagging the repository it came from all produce it, the last being a case the design says must not be treated as an error.
context: Found 2026-08-24, fixed 2026-08-25, recorded as the closed issue `a-superseded-by-naming-an-absent-id-hides-its-memory` in ISSUES.md. Pinned by `a_memory_yielding_to_an_id_nobody_holds_is_still_findable` in tests/cross_store.rs and four tests in tests/store.rs. Harvested into memory 2026-09-02.
why: Written symptom-first on purpose. The diagnosis vocabulary -- `resolve_supersession`, tips, unresolved -- is not what anyone types while confused, and a recall phrased the way the trouble actually presents scored 0.178 against this defect's record and returned nothing about it. The keyword path cannot rescue it either, because keywords name the cause and whoever has the symptom does not yet know the cause. Worth holding after the fix because the shape recurs: any id that resolves but cannot be fetched can silently delete a row from a result set, and the design names a reference written without its set name as the commonest malformation there is.

content: Found 2026-08-09 inspecting a copy of the real stores while setting up the two-server test: both fully embedded — 26 of 26 vectors in `local`, 6 of 6 in `shared-scatterhoard` — and neither recording an `embedding_model`. **A state the code cannot leave**: `model_state` returns `Unembedded` whenever the key is absent, without consulting the `vectors` table; `reconcile_embeddings` rebuilds only on `Mismatched`; it then embeds `memories_without_vectors`, which is empty; and `embed_all`, the only writer of the identity, is never reached. The variant's own documentation is what it contradicts — *"Nothing has ever embedded into this store... there are no vectors for a write to invalidate."* There are 26. **The worst consequence is that mismatch detection cannot fire at all**: two servers with different models both read `Unembedded`, neither re-embeds, and both run semantic recall against stored vectors from a third unknown model — `two-servers-can-disagree-about-the-model` with the detector disabled, and strictly worse, because there is no recorded identity for the comparison to use. The next write would then stamp the loaded model's identity onto 26 vectors it did not produce, permanently and unverifiably. Any store written before model identity landed on 2026-08-08 was in this state, including both real ones.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A state whose own documentation asserts the opposite of what is true in it, reachable by every store predating one commit. Worth keeping because the failure is not the misreport but that it silently disables the detector another defect depends on.

content: Overrun measured again 2026-08-04 and it is larger than first recorded: `max_chars: 200` returned one convention of roughly 1,650 characters — **8× the stated budget** — with `next_cursor: 1`, so a caller honouring the cursor pages straight into a second, equally oversized item. The 2× figure was not the worst case: the ratio is bounded only by the largest convention, because no budget can force a page smaller than one item.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A second measurement that changed the shape of the claim rather than confirming it: the overrun has no bound expressible in terms of the parameter, so it cannot be described as a small excess.

content: **Test fixtures give a shared set a charter, and each test's toy embedder returns `Embedded::Unrepresentable` for the fixture charter's text.** Decided 2026-09-28 with the human partner, for step 2 of `set-settled-at-first-write`; see `FIXTURE_CHARTER` in `tests/mcp.rs`, `tests/sets.rs` and `tests/approval.rs`. A charter placed in the toy's three dimensions decided the ranking of every two- or three-memory test corpus: recall centres the query as well as the memories, and a query for `alpha` against three raw-count vectors becomes, in effect, *not beta*. The charter is still stored and counted. Only meaning search leaves it out, which states the truth about a model that knows two words. A set taken on by import stays bare: charter only the authoring machine.
context: Repairing about 230 tests after the charter-first refusal, set-settled-at-first-write step 2.
why: Seeding a tombstone instead was rejected: fewer tests would move, but every fixture would model a set nothing real produces. A fourth embedding axis for the charter was tried and did not help: after centring it tied with the right answer. Real embeddings do not show this. The 2026-08-02 measurement found separation at three memories (+0.32 against -0.29), so the collapse belongs to the toy's low dimension and raw counts, not to the scorer. Recorded because the next change touching fixtures will meet the same effect, and the first diagnosis — the charter outranking an exact match — reads like a scoring bug.

content: **Backups of any set are a `hoard_sets` `backup` action that writes the whole set, never gated, only where the person's configuration says, or under the common directory.** The file's header marks it as a backup, so its memories never count as reviewed. Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. `restore` reads such a file like any memory file. Copying it elsewhere is the person's own act.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public, after deciding no call can set a set's audience.
why: With the file on disk as the clearance record, a set with no repository, such as `governance-docs`, would have every backup gated as a first publication: a safety copy refused exactly when it is needed. A `backup: true` flag on export was rejected because it would be a loosening switch the model controls. A path the caller cannot choose keeps backups from becoming a way round the gate. Restated before publication to use the set's published pseudonym.

content: **`local` takes its author from the operating system's account name by default, and `SCATTERHOARD_AUTHOR` is removed.** Decided 2026-09-24 by the human partner, as the one exception to refusing a set's first write until an author is named: `USERNAME` on Windows, `USER` or `LOGNAME` elsewhere, with `hoard_sets` `rename` for anyone who wants another name. Where the system supplies no name, `local`'s first write is refused like any other set's rather than recorded as `unknown`. The variable has no remaining job once every shared set asks and `local` reads the system.
context: Settling the author rule for the release gate with the human partner, who worried refusing `local`'s first write would hurt adoption and asked whether Windows has a default user.
why: Adoption friction: refusing the first write to `local` would put an extra step in front of every new user on every machine, for the one set that is never published. The per-set-name argument that decided shared sets does not reach it — the account name lands only on this machine and its backups — so a default costs little there and a rename is always available.

content: **Four requirements proposed for `gut-feeling-recall`, 2026-09-29, none yet tested.** First, breadth: aggregate a few dozen plausible matches at a low threshold, so it needs the right words to be nearby rather than the right memory to rank first. Second, valence: weight each matched memory by its outcome history, such as issue clusters, severities, `instance_of` links to lessons, supersessions and `contradicts`, so a phrase is *hot* when it shows up mostly where things went wrong. Third, contrast: prefer phrases over-represented in the neighbourhood relative to the whole set, as the set summary does for keywords. Fourth, silence: say nothing unless the neighbourhood's heat is well above the set's baseline, because a signal that always fires is ignored. Testable by replaying the before-writing sentences the coding-lessons guide records for each failure, and the same for changes that went fine.
context: Filing `gut-feeling-recall` right after it was raised.
why: Worked out in conversation with the human partner, who raised the idea. Valence is what makes it resemble unease rather than a topic map: affect as outcome history compressed onto a region. Silence is argued from this project's own evidence, `the-mutation-runners-crowding-note-fires-on-every-pass` and the reasoning behind the always-present `summary` echo. Caveat: this machine's embedding is a hashed, mostly lexical model, so the neighbourhood is weaker than a real semantic one.

content: Fixed 2026-08-31, the same day, because the format cut it would otherwise have ambushed is the next piece of work. `check_version` now compares a *compatibility unit* — `(0, minor)` below `1.0` and `(major, 0)` at or above it — against two constants: `FORMAT_VERSION`, what this build writes, and the new `OLDEST_READABLE`, the oldest shape it still understands. Too new and too old are separate errors with separate remedies. Seven tests, including `every_format_version_this_project_has_written_is_still_readable`, which lists `0.1.0`, `0.2.0` and `0.3.0` so that raising the floor fails at the moment a human should be deciding whether the files in the wild have been migrated. Three mutations plus one recorded survivor: the post-`1.0` branch is unreachable until the format reaches `1.0`, and is expected to flip to `caught` on the day it does.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the test worth reusing: a list of every version ever written, asserted readable, turns raising the floor into a decision a human has to make rather than a line someone edits.

content: **In the export review, a sentence about a person also says whether it reports or judges, and the server clears a report.** Agreed 2026-10-25 by the human partner, who said it must be possible to report what someone did. `reports` means it says what they did, said, wrote or decided. `judges` means it says what they are like or why they acted. A sentence that judges is flagged in every set. One that reports clears unless it mentions a kept-out item, except that a sentence about the person in a shared set is still flagged as misfiled. An LLM counts as a person, as `store-when` says, so reports of what a model did clear.
context: Reviewing the scatterhoard set before committing the built judgement gate, then asking whether the review covers what store-when says about other people. Rolled into the same set of changes rather than filed.
why: The server cannot tell a judgement from a report, since neither has a shape, so the model answers and the server routes, as for the other questions. Before this the review asked only who a sentence was about, which flagged every report about someone else and let every judgement about a model clear as `project`. The narrow question follows the gemma finding that "does it mention health?" works where "is this a problem?" did not.

content: **What a build-on-demand wrapper would still need**, if one is ever put in front of the server: the source files are mutated in place whatever the target directory is, so it must refuse while `.mutation-archive/` is non-empty — and **refuse rather than restore**, since the archive cannot tell a live pass from a dead one and restoring under a live pass corrupts it. Note also that the archive empties between mutations, so a check at spawn time races a pass; closing that properly needs a pass-duration lock the runner does not have.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A constraint on future work that the target-directory fix does not cover, because the sources are still mutated in place. The refuse-rather-than-restore rule matters: the obvious helpful behaviour destroys a running pass.

content: The convention catalog is to be run unchanged for several sessions from 2026-08-24, gathering evidence on how the current text behaves before any further tuning. Decided by the human partner on the state of the budget: 16,746 of 18,000, with three Ready conventions — `recall-gloss-convention`, `link-label-choice`, `investigation-pipeline` — competing for 1,254 characters that at most one of the two large ones can use. A third raise is explicitly not the answer on hand; whether the catalog is dense or merely long is filed as an open question, to be settled by a whole-file read of `catalog.rs` rather than from inside a session that just edited it.
context: Decided 2026-08-24 after landing the `store-when` enumeration cut, the `learn or decide` repair, `correct-when`'s invalidation moment, and the charter guidance in `route-where`.
why: Stops the next session re-opening convention text on the strength of one session's behaviour, which is the tempting move immediately after drafting and the one the standing rule about convention tuning warns against — how a convention behaves is not visible in its text, and the feedback is several sessions away. It also records that the budget pressure is a live constraint on every remaining convention item rather than on `investigation-pipeline` alone, which is easy to miss because the backlog entries are read one at a time.

content: Fixed 2026-08-07 (`a2fd1f1`): `Store::refresh` reads `data_version` and rebuilds the vector set only when another connection has committed. Three tests in `tests/concurrency.rs` — a memory stored by one connection is recalled by meaning from another, a memory forgotten by one stops being recalled by the other, and the same thing end to end through two `Server`s driving `hoard_memorize` and `hoard_recall` against one file. **The end-to-end test is not redundant with the first two, and finding that out was the useful part**: `hoard_recall` does not call `Store::recall`, it goes through `recall_across`, which is a second reader of the same cache. The recorded mutation that removes the refresh from `recall_across` is caught by *only* that test — so a fix applied to the direct path alone would have left every real call stale with two tests green over it.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Two code paths reading one cache, where the test covering the direct path passes while the path every real call takes stays broken. The recorded mutation is what distinguishes the redundant-looking end-to-end test from an actually redundant one.

content: **Claude's client refuses an MCP server's entire tool list if any tool's `outputSchema` lacks `"type": "object"` at its top level**, taking every tool offline, not just that one. Observed 2026-10-03 when `hoard_correct` and `hoard_sets` published schemas opening with `anyOf` and no type. The error named the path `tools.4.outputSchema.type`. Adding the type beside the `anyOf` fixed it, and `every_output_schema_is_an_object_at_its_top_level` in `tests/mcp.rs` pins it.
context: Publishing output schemas; the human partner restarted the client and the tools would not start.
why: A failure with no partial mode: one malformed schema disables the whole server, and nothing in this server's own checks noticed, since a top-level `anyOf` is valid JSON Schema. The client's stricter rule is the one that matters. Recorded so a later schema change, a new tool or a refactor of `output_schema.rs`, does not rediscover it by losing every tool.

content: **Record here any bug a recalled cause stopped before it was written, and any issue filed under a cause after the baseline.** Whether recording common causes reduces their recurrence — raised 2026-09-23 by the human partner. **The baseline is 2026-09-24T02:20:56Z UTC**, when the first of nine causes became a memory (`a-fact-restated-by-hand-drifts`); issues filed before it are the *before* population, derivable at any time from their `created`. **Two measures, and only one is direct.** Recurrence — issues attributed to an existing cause per week, before against after, normalised by issues filed overall. And prevention, observable only when a session records that recalling a cause changed what it was about to build; those observations belong here. Ends when enough post-baseline issues exist to compare — or the confounds make the comparison meaningless.
context: Discussing the new causes region with the human partner, who wondered whether the tool will stop bugs before they are written and asked that the moment of the change be kept so it can be measured.
why: Marked `hoard-investigation` because the evidence arrives during unrelated work — a session filing a defect months from now, or one that changes a design after recalling a cause — and neither would think to search for a running experiment. The confounds are the ones `convention-text-evaluated-objectively` names: the same model is subject and experimenter, the filing rate follows activity, and the causes became visible alongside other changes, so a falling rate would support the hypothesis without proving it.

content: Filed 2026-08-08 by reasoning about the multi-server environment before standing it up, and marked not yet observed because that environment did not exist. `SCATTERHOARD_MODEL` is read per process and `SCATTERHOARD_HOME` defaults to a single path, while a server is registered per checkout through a `.mcp.json` that lives in the repository — so two checkouts routinely produce two processes with the same store and different model configuration, and neither can see the other's. **Two failures, and they are different.** One server has no model: its writes destroy vectors rather than replace them, since `insert` upserts with `INSERT OR REPLACE`, `vectors` cascades away, and `embed_all` returns early with nothing to rebuild from — so the fully configured server finds memories it embedded have silently stopped being findable. Or the two servers have different models: each embeds its own writes correctly and the store accumulates vectors from two spaces with no record of which is which, arriving at `no-record-of-which-model-built-the-vectors` without anyone changing a file.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A hazard predicted from configuration rather than observed, with the two distinct failure modes separated. Worth keeping because the reasoning identified the environment as already reachable, not hypothetical.

content: Superseded reasoning, kept deliberately. This entry previously argued that of the three neighbouring items — detection (`target-identity-is-an-unnormalised-path-string`), prevention (the set-name binding) and attribution (this one) — *"only the third survives a failure of the other two."* **That reversed on inspection**: the vector it rested on was a poisoned commit merged upstream and pulled into your own checkout, which is precisely the case git records in full; what does not survive is the case where prevention was never built. Prevention is therefore the load-bearing one, and this entry is the fallback if prevention is refused. Related: [store-registry.md](documents/design/store-registry.md) dissolves the target-identity defect outright but **not this one** — it closes the hostile-fork-clone vector, since under a registry that fork gets its own store, and not the upstream-merge vector, which arrives at the right path in the right store and still inserts as `NewFromFile`. If anything the registry makes provenance more tractable, since one store has one destination and *which import brought this in* becomes a single well-formed question.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A ranking of three defences that inverted once the vector behind it was named precisely. Kept because the superseded version is a plausible-sounding argument that a later session could easily re-derive.

content:
**How recall is actually used, measured over 381 calls in 37 transcripts — and the answer argues for linking over a multi-query API.** `already_known` was passed in **2 of 381 calls (0.5%)**: the paging mechanism exists and is not reached for. Of 203 semantic calls, 46.3% fall in bursts under two minutes, but **only 8 of 35 bursts look like rephrasing one intent**, and inspecting the 6 closest pairs shows most are different questions sharing vocabulary rather than paraphrases. **Sessions essentially do not rephrase.** One session issued an identical query twice, which is exactly the case `already_known` exists for and did not get used for.

**Meanwhile the link graph is nearly empty: 603 of 762 memories isolated (79.1%), 178 traversable edges, mean degree 1.97 among the connected.** Traversal was separately measured to beat simply raising the limit above roughly 170 memories, and the corpus is at 762 — so **the walk is starved of edges, not of size**, which is why removing it *improves* separation (AUC 0.917 without against 0.901 with). **The convention catalog has 320 characters of headroom against its 18,000 budget**, enough for a clause and not for a convention.
context: The human partner asking whether recall has been single-attempt or multi-phrasing, whether already_known has been useful, and proposing both a linking convention and a multi-query recall call.
why:
Recorded because it turns two design proposals from intuitions into a comparison. The human partner proposed both a convention requiring links to be added when recall reveals them, and a recall call taking several queries and returning the union. The measurements say these are not equals: **linking makes a mechanism that already ships start working, while multi-query recall adds a new one** — and the corpus is past the size where traversal should already be paying, so the missing ingredient is edges.

**`already_known` is the cautionary case and should be cited whenever a new affordance is proposed.** It was built, it is documented, it is the right tool for a case that demonstrably arises, and it is used in one call in two hundred. A capability that nothing drives does not get used, which is an argument for putting the change in the conventions rather than in the API — and, read the other way, a warning that a linking convention will also need to be *reached for* to matter.

The 320-character headroom is the binding constraint on how that is written, and it is derived here rather than quoted: `report_catalog_headroom` in `tests/conventions.rs` prints it, because `AGENTS.md` requires the figure be re-derived and nothing derived it before.

content: History from filing `each-review-page-recomputes-the-whole-set`, 2026-10-29: the pre-pass ran more than once per memory per page as well. `review_set` sorted the pending memories with `sort_by_key`, whose key ran `review_hits`, so the pre-pass ran once per comparison: about eleven times per memory for 1,526. Changed the same day to `sort_by_cached_key`, which runs the key once per element; that left a page at 20s on the debug build, the figure in the head, so the per-page recompute was the larger cost.
context: Starting the scatterhoard set's full review under the judgement gate; profiling a review call that ran at full CPU in a server the client had launched.
why: The two causes were found together and are easy to conflate. Recording the order shows that the cheap fix was made first and measured, and was not enough.

content: **Measured 2026-09-18: a review load costs about 0.7 ms per memory in release, and the build matters roughly nine times more than the model does.** `probe_what_a_review_costs` in `tests/probes.rs` runs the real `hoard_sets evaluate` over this project's own exported file (948 memories) on the human partner's Mac. Release: **0.63 s** under `potion-base-32M` (0.7 ms each) and **0.80 s** under `potion-multilingual-128M` (0.8 ms each). Debug: **6.20 s** and **5.23 s** (6.5 and 5.5 ms each). **Two things follow.** The models differ by under 30% and their order is not even stable — multilingual is slower in release and faster in debug — so model choice is not a variable a size limit would need to account for. And the projections are small: a 10,000-memory set is about 7 s in release, so the *appears to hang* failure that motivated a limit needs a corpus around a hundred thousand memories, far past anything this project has seen. Hardware remains unmeasured: checking an older machine would mean publishing the branch to pull it elsewhere, which the human partner judged not worth the setup.
context: Deciding how to set the evaluation size limit after review copies moved to disk.
why: Recorded because it removes the case for the limit it was measured to set, and because the surprise is worth keeping: the assistant assumed the model was the variable to control for, and it is the smaller one by an order of magnitude. The debug figures are kept because this project's own `SETUP.md` attaches a debug binary, so they are what a session working here actually pays.

content: A set's identity, charter and author were fixed at `create`, which is also how a published set is taken on before `import` replaces it, so `create` required nothing and minted too early. **Built 2026-09-28 in four commits**, as decided 2026-09-24. `create` makes an empty set and nothing more. A set takes its identity from its first import, first write or first export, and never gives up one it holds. A shared set's first write is refused until someone is named with `mint` or `identify`, and its first memory must be its charter. `local` defaults to the operating system's account name, and `SCATTERHOARD_AUTHOR` is gone. The design is recorded in `documents/design/set-lifecycle.md` under *create makes an empty set, and its first write settles it*. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `set-settled-at-first-write`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Finishing set-settled-at-first-write with its documentation step, after steps 1–3 and a pause while the shell's safety check was down.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded to record that it is built. The four steps were identity (`aca7668`), charter (`d698476`), author (`9a292ee`) and documentation. Each ran a full mutation pass, and each pass found at least one test the step's own fixture changes had quietly emptied. Deviations from the decision, each approved by the human partner in session: export mints an identity for a set with none, and an import of an empty file settles nothing. One known gap is filed rather than fixed: `concurrent-first-writes-can-mint-two-identities`.

content: **Report a set's non-match floor in `hoard_sets status`.** Noticed 2026-09-17: nothing reports whether a set is calibrated. `status` lists each set's mode, model state, author, languages and counts, and not its floor; `Store::floor` reads it, but the only tools that surface it are `calibrate`, which sets one, and `uncalibrate`, which names the previous value while removing it — so both ways of asking change the answer. The floor decides whether recall returns nothing for a query no memory reaches, which is the one recall outcome a caller cannot tell from *this set holds nothing about that*, so *is this set calibrated, and at what level* is a question a session and a human both have reason to ask. **Built when** `status` carries each set's floor, absent where none is set, with a test. Found while checking whether excluding evaluation sets from calibration gave anything up: reading three databases directly was the only way to establish that no set on this machine has a floor at all.
context: Designing evaluation mode: deciding that its recalls do not feed calibration.
why: Filed as unbuilt work rather than a defect: the reporting was never written, and `TRACKING.md` draws the line at whether code exists to be wrong. Ready rather than deferred — nothing is missing but the work, and the field is one line beside the mode that `status` already reports. The reason it matters is the floor's failure mode: a level set too high silences answers a set really holds, and nothing in a recall result distinguishes that from an empty set.

content: **History from building it, 2026-08-25.** **A scope, not a name, and the asymmetry with `drop` is load-bearing**: `drop` takes a name so `local` is unrepresentable, because it destroys the only copy — `restore` replaces a set *from a copy the caller is holding*, and for `local`, which never reaches a repository, that file is the only recovery route there will ever be, so refusing it there would withhold the operation from the set that needs it most. **Two guards the design stated and nothing enforced**: the copy may not be written over the file being restored from, which would destroy the good copy in the act of protecting the bad one, and it may not be a path the set is exported to; both paths come from the caller, so nothing else could have caught either. **`bases` is cleared too, and that is a decision** — a base for a record the restored set no longer holds resolves as `Anomaly`, *a state no supported operation produces*, so keeping them would have restore manufacture the report that means something went wrong outside the tools; the cost is that the next import from another checkout reconciles with no ancestor, degrading to `Converged` or a reported `Conflict`, never to a silent overwrite. **One guard was written and removed**: a validating first pass turned out to be genuinely subsumed, since duplicate-id detection lives inside `stream` and every record is materialised before the store is touched, so the whole-file-before-any-of-it guarantee rests on the shape — what stands on it now is a test, and the code says so, because streaming into the store later would put the validating pass back in the load-bearing position.
context: Migrating the set-restore entry out of BACKLOG.md; these are the decisions taken while building it.
why:
The removed guard is the one most likely to be misread later. Deleting a validating pass looks like a shortcut; it was removed because the property it guarded is now enforced by the order of operations, and that is exactly the kind of guarantee a future refactor can silently withdraw. The comment and the test are what make the removal safe, and this records that the removal was reasoned rather than convenient.

Clearing `bases` is the other non-obvious one — it looks like discarding useful reconciliation history, and keeping it would instead produce a diagnostic that means *something happened outside the tools*, on a set where nothing did.

content: Read the served text as a session receives it, on a schedule. Decided 2026-08-30 by the human partner on noticing that the catalog's `reinforcement` only ever grows. **A reading task rather than a coding one**: read the catalog end to end **as `hoard_conventions` returns it and not as source**, asking of each sentence *would a session act differently without it?* — and **prefer moving text to the moment it applies over cutting it**, which sidesteps the ratchet's real problem, since a good sentence cannot be argued away but can be put where its moment is. The 2026-08-30 pass did this and recovered **1,382 characters, most of it by relocation rather than deletion**. **Built when the reread has happened, what changed is recorded with the reasoning, and the next one has a trigger** — a date, a character threshold, or a revision count. Without a trigger this is a task that happens once. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `cold-reread-of-the-catalog`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Test and documentation debt section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only.

**Do the measurement work with it**, per the human partner 2026-08-30: the instruments for asking whether the conventions work are worked out and unbuilt, and pairing them with the reread is what stops the reread staying pure judgement for ever. Whether convention text can be evaluated objectively is itself an open question; the reread is the judgement available in the meantime.

Note the Built-when names the trigger problem outright — *without a trigger this is a task that happens once* — which is the same gap `meta-observation-convention` is open on, met here in a different form.

content: A recall with both `query` and `keywords` returned each memory twice, once in each list, so a caller paid for up to twice the payload to learn about the same memories and had to merge by id to discover it. Fixed 2026-08-03 by deleting the combined mode rather than deduplicating it. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `combined-recall-duplicates-content`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: `hoard-watch`'s length clause is provisional from 2026-09-05, the night after it shipped. Whole-record push does not scale: the per-record envelope is 411 characters and does not shrink with the prose, so three stores of fifteen watches cost 1.9x the whole convention catalog and a hundred cost 4.2x, and a cross-set recall multiplies by the number of stores. The replacement is `watch-push-is-an-index-per-set` in BACKLOG.md -- a line derived from the leading sentence of `content`, recalled per set rather than across sets, at session start and again when a set is loaded. Do not follow *keep a marked memory short enough to read fifteen of* as a guide to how much a watch may carry; it is being replaced rather than tightened.
context: Probing whether the watch convention survives a realistic number of watches, hours after landing it, and finding the exemplar it shipped with was four times over its own limit.
why: A session reading the served catalog gets the length clause with nothing marking it as superseded-in-principle, and the clause is the one part of the convention known to be wrong -- its arithmetic is unfollowable and its cost figures were understated because they counted prose and ignored the envelope. Per-set recall is the half worth holding for a reason beyond cost: push is the only channel where memory content reaches a session unconditionally, so per-set makes it revocable per set and creates a dependency on evaluation mode, which does not exist -- a set loaded for inspection must not push, and today import is adoption.

content: **`create`'s `mode` is optional and defaults to read-write, and its tool description must not tell the LLM to ask the user whether a new set should be read-only.** Both decided 2026-09-16 by the human partner: most users assume memories are read-write, and asking a new user whether their new set should be read-only would confuse them. This withdraws two lines in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md): that `mode` is required with no default, and that the tool description should say *ask the human*, by analogy with the author name. Read-only is the minority case: a set taken on as reference material someone else publishes. The LLM usually has that context from the request itself, as in *load the company policy set*, so the description says when to choose read-only and leaves it at that. **The default is safe in the direction it errs**: a set created read-write that should have been read-only is only writable when it did not need to be, and dropping it, creating it read-only, and importing the safety copy puts it right with nothing lost.
context: Revising the load-modes design after the human partner questioned asking users about read-only at create, and raised several evaluation sets open at once.
why: Recorded because the design document said the opposite on both points, and the analogy with the author name, which is asked for, made asking look like the house style. The difference is that an author name is a fact only the human has, while a set's mode is usually evident from why the set is being created. A required parameter would make nearly every call carry the same choice, which decision-placement counts against it, and the reason it was made required, that a wrong mode is irreversible, holds only in the read-only direction, which a default of read-write never takes.

content:
**Bias toward over-recalling: returning legitimate memories along with some strays beats dropping strays at the cost of legitimate results.** Stated by the human partner 2026-09-09, and it settles the non-match floor's operating point, which no measurement could. The reason is the user's experience of the failure: a memory that should have surfaced and did not is disorienting and produces *but you knew this last session* — where an extra result is merely ignored. **The operating point drawn from it** — the session's reading of the ruling, not the human partner's words — **is that a floor is admissible only if it loses no real query, and then silences what it can.** Measured on `scatterhoard`, 752 memories, raw cosine, 142 harvested real queries against 601 public-domain probes:

| floor at | value | off-domain silenced | real queries lost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **minimum real query score** | **0.256** | **47.9%** | **0 / 142 (0.0%)** |
| p01 of real queries | 0.286 | 62.1% | 1 (0.7%) |
| p05 of real queries | 0.344 | 83.9% | 7 (4.9%) |
| p90 of off-domain probes | 0.369 | 89.9% | 14 (9.9%) |
context: The human partner settling the floor's operating point, after the measurements produced a curve but no way to choose on it. Split two days later when they corrected which part of it was theirs.
why:
Recorded because it is a design intention only the human partner can supply, and because it does work no amount of further measurement could: the whole investigation could produce a separation curve but never a point on it, since choosing one is a judgement about which failure hurts more. The AUC of 0.962 says a good point exists; this says which one.

**The stated reason matters more than the ruling.** The cost of a false silence is not the lost result but the user's model of the tool — a system that forgets what it plainly knew is worse than one that returns too much, because the second is a nuisance and the first undermines the reason to keep memories at all. That reasoning generalises past the floor: it argues against any future mechanism that trades recall for precision, and should be recalled before proposing one.

**Split 2026-09-11 UTC from `01M2369SVFEJGA5CKHA3KBQ23T`**, which also carried a proposal about where the floor's calibration should come from, written as though it were part of this ruling. The human partner corrected that attribution: the ruling is about which failure to prefer, and the calibration source was the LLM's proposal, now recorded separately with its premise corrected.

content: **Whether an import should tolerate a link label this build does not recognise.** Raised 2026-09-23. Today the label set is closed — `src/memory/link.rs` makes an unknown label a parse failure at import — so after publication *adding* a label breaks every older reader exactly as removing one breaks newer ones, and each new label means a format bump; the deferred `PRECEDES`/`FOLLOWS` pair says as much. The human partner leans towards tolerating. **Open parts**: an unknown-label edge must be stored and re-exported byte-identically, since checksums cover the canonical record; it is presumably not walked; authoring presumably stays strict. **And the hard one, raised by the human partner**: what happens when a memory carrying an unknown-label out-link is superseded. Once successors stop inheriting out-links, a build that cannot name the label cannot restate it, so the link would be dropped — and must at least be reported.
context: Settling `violates-belongs-in-memory` with the human partner, and finding while costing its removal that the link vocabulary is closed at import.
why: Found while checking what removing `violates` would cost: the closed set turns every vocabulary decision into a permanent one after publication, in both directions. That is why it goes on the release gate — the reading rule has to be settled before any file leaves this machine, because an old build's strictness is fixed the day it ships. The supersession case ties it to `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`, whose first step, reporting the links a supersession leaves behind, is where an unrestatable link would surface.

content: The response did report the unembedded memory and then named the wrong cause: `findable_by_meaning: false` was returned honestly, but the note beside it read *"tell the user Scatterhoard needs its model installed for this set"* — and the model was fine. A caller acting on that note goes and checks their installation. Same shape as `the-mutation-runners-crowding-note-fires-on-every-pass`: a note that names an unchecked cause for a real symptom sends the next reader to the wrong place, which costs more than saying nothing.
context: Renaming this entry's slug to take an `about-` prefix, while fixing genindex.py's positional slug pick.
why: The second half of the defect, and the one that generalises: an honest signal paired with a guessed explanation is worse than the bare signal. Superseded 2026-09-21 only to move it to the entry's renamed slug; the claim is unchanged.

content: **Whether the scores are still summed, now that the walk they were measured against is gone. Resolved 2026-08-18: they are blended, a quarter on the inherited term.** Opened and closed the same day, and it **overturns the 2026-08-15 answer of `sum`** recorded under `inherited-and-own-scores-combine`. Correcting the walk's self-inheritance moved the evidence under that earlier choice, so the harness was extended to cross rule with decay and the question asked properly: **which rule is *flat*, not which wins one cell.** The measurement put the blend at `w = 0.25` level with sum's ceiling on both answer keys while moving about a point across decays against sum's fourteen to twenty-six, and it is the only rule that stays above the content-only baseline at every decay on both. Decided by the human partner on that evidence -- *the most stable of the bunch*. **Rank fusion was measured and rejected:** flat, and below baseline, because equal-weight fusion gives the walk as much say as content. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `scores-summed-or-blended`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The head states outright that it overturns the earlier entry, because the two questions sit adjacent in the file and the older one still reads *Resolved: summed*. A session finding that one first would take a superseded answer as current, and nothing in its own text says otherwise.

*Which rule is flat, not which wins one cell* is kept because it is the methodological correction that produced the answer, and it applies to every future tuning measurement here.

content: **The template's carve-out for the personal set allows the everyday details and keeps the special categories out of every set, on condition that a session says when it has left something out.** Decided 2026-10-21 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *the preferences start from a template*. Allowed in `local` by default: where the person lives and how to reach them, their employer, family, name, and machine and account specifics. Kept out everywhere: health, religion, sexuality, politics, ethnicity and finances. The served framing has to tell a session to say what it left out and why.
context: Building the sharing preferences served at session start. Settling how a never in the preferences applies to the personal set, after the first gemma test.
why: The special categories are roughly those data-protection law names, plus finances: the details that get people hurt, and an exposed detail cannot be taken back. Keeping them out silently would cost something else. In the human partner's words, a person could have a long conversation and have everything evaporate on them. Saying so lets them follow up on how to store it.

content: **Claude Code runs `SessionStart` hooks that match the `compact` source after a compaction, and adds their output to the compacted context.** Checked 2026-11-02 in the *What survives compaction* table at code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window. That is the channel the head of `the-precompact-hook-asks-a-model-that-never-gets-a-turn` lacked: a hook on the far side of the boundary, whose output the post-compaction agent reads. The same table says a project-root `CLAUDE.md` and unscoped rules are re-injected from disk, while tool results and context earlier hooks added are summarized away. It does not say whether an `AGENTS.md` loaded directly is re-injected.
context: Going-public checklist: checking whether a steering-file sentence survives compaction before adding the reload sentence.
why: The human partner's 2026-10-29 remedy needed a way to hand the post-compaction agent the conventions and anything mined from the transcript; the open question was how text crosses the boundary. This answers it for Claude Code with a documented mechanism rather than a guess.

content: **How should a merged memory file's header summary come to describe the merged records?** Raised 2026-09-17 by the human partner. The `git` merge driver (`merge_files` in `src/merge.rs`) keeps the receiving side's header line verbatim, including its derived `summary`: the keyword clusters an export computes from the set's vectors, which the driver does not have. A maintainer merging a contributor's branch therefore gets a file whose summary describes the set *before* the contributor's new memories. **The reasoning given for keeping it** is that a summary is a claim a reader recomputes and compares, and the next export rewrites it. **Why that may not be enough:** the comparison is where a stale summary does harm. A fresh import of the merged file, such as a collaborator cloning before the maintainer re-exports, compares its derivation against the file's claim and reports *"differs from the description the file carries, which nothing here explains"* (`against_the_claim` in `src/mcp.rs`). That is a false alarm on the signal that exists for review, and it lasts until someone exports. A merge without the driver registered also conflicts on the header line whenever both sides exported. **Options to evaluate:** load the embedder in the driver and regenerate the summary, which means embedding every memory inside a `git` hook; write the merged header without a summary, so readers see *no description to compare against* instead of a wrong one, at the cost of the review signal until an export; leave the summary and make re-exporting after a merge a step that something enforces; or have the header say its summary predates a merge, bearing in mind that a header is contents a reader must not trust to decide anything. The findings gathered under this question carry the keyword `how-a-merged-file-gets-a-current-summary`.
context: Aside while implementing read-only load mode: the human partner questioned the merge driver's header handling.
why: Filed at the human partner's request to revisit a decision made while building the merge driver on 2026-09-16. The false-alarm consequence was read from the code, not reproduced: whether a fresh import of a merged file actually reports a mismatch depends on whether the contributor's memories move the derived clusters, which a small addition may not. A question rather than an issue, because keeping the receiving side's header was a deliberate choice, and whether it is wrong is what this asks.

content: **How to inspect a memory set without adopting it.** Raised 2026-08-26 by the human partner, from a maintainer reviewing a contributor's branch: import is adoption, and checking the branch back out does not undo it. **Designed in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md) as a special case of read-only, which was built on 2026-09-17.** Settled: an evaluation load comes from a file, once, through a `hoard_sets` action with no `create` step; several can be open at once; each is named `eval-<set>-<label>` with the label chosen by the user, and `SetName::new` refuses the `eval-` prefix; it is searched only when its scope is named; every memory it returns is marked from the load mode; it pulls no watch marks, drops without a safety copy, lives in memory, and is never a holder of its source set's identity. **Cross-set links are surfaced, never resolved** — the link reports its target id, set name, identity, and every loaded scope answering to that identity with its mode — and nothing resolves into an evaluation set from outside. **Still open:** whether an evaluation set's recalls should feed floor calibration; the size limit, to be set by timing a full embed; whether a returned memory carries its set's identity as well as the evaluation mark; and whether one recall can rank across two evaluation sets for comparison, which separate recalls do today with scores that are not comparable across calls. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `evaluation-mode`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Designing evaluation mode after read-only was finished, starting with cross-set links.
why: Supersedes the head to record that the cross-set link question is answered, which was the part named as *to be settled before building*. What remains is smaller: calibration is a decision, the size limit is a measurement, and the other two are refinements that do not block a first build.

content: **The human partner, 2026-09-07: this points at a recall-time rule, not a write-time one** — and it follows from the mechanism rather than from taste. Links get written when the workflow puts target ids in hand, and **recall is the moment that does**: a session holding several returned memories has just judged their relevance to one query and to each other, with every id already present. Store time does not — an author has one new memory and, at best, the near-duplicates `recall-before-storing` surfaces, which are candidates for *is this the same thing*, not for *how do these relate*. The frequency argument runs the same way.
