A write-time rule fires once per store, a handful of times a session; a recall-time rule fires on every recall, which is dozens, and goes on firing over the corpus's whole life — which is what **growth over time** requires rather than a burst of links on the day a convention ships. It also explains the 2026-09-07 split: 52 cross-cluster keyword memberships formed at write time because keywords are asked for at write time, and the three real edges came from the moments that put ids in hand.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md, immediately after deciding to tackle the two linking entries together.
why:
Recorded because the obvious place to put a linking rule is beside the other memory-writing rules, and that is the wrong place for a reason no store-time author can see: the information needed to link arrives on the read side.

The cost this has to answer, and it is real: a recall-time rule asks a session to do work that is not what it recalled for, at the moment it is trying to get on with something else — which is the same objection `recall-before-storing` had to survive, and it survived it by being a reading step rather than a judgement the tool asserts. Whatever shape this takes will have to be similarly cheap, since a rule that interrupts every recall will be ignored on most of them.

content:
**Whether the Golden Rule should apply friction to harmful *use*, and not only to harmful memories about people.** Raised and **resolved 2026-09-12**. Answered **yes**, by widening demand C rather than by adding anything, and the implementation is `derived-set-summary`.

**What was decided.** C now reads *a set can amount to something no record in it amounts to*, with two instances: the person as organising principle, which is the case it was first stated for, and the set as accumulated capability — where the potential for harm is real while every record is innocuous and everyone involved has good intent. **Intent is not the trigger and is not consulted.** C was the right place because A, B and D are demands on a *record* and C alone is a demand on a *collection*, which is why the document already said C does not derive from A and B.

**The three things the entry said had to be settled, and how each came out.** *Whether the design should reach this at all* — yes, but only structurally: a convention is text a session can be told to disregard, while a mechanism has to be patched out of the code. *Whether it is practical* — yes, at export and import, which is where the whole set is in view and which is unavoidable for anyone who wants portable, shared or durable memories. The charter was considered and rejected as the surface, because a contentless charter still routes correctly. *What it would cost* — **roughly one clause**, since the mechanism is code rather than served text. The entry was framed partly as a budget problem and the answer turned out not to be one.

**What it does not do**, recorded so nobody rediscovers it as a defect: it never sees a set that is only ever local; a model reviewing its own project's export is not adversarial; and it cannot resolve intent in dual-use territory, which is why it describes and does not judge. Defence against a party who could build their own memory system was explicitly **not** a success criterion.

Findings accumulate under the keyword `golden-rule-beyond-person-harm`; this record carries only the standing.
context: Closing the question at the end of the day it was raised, once demand C had been widened and the work it left behind was filed.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing. Superseded to carry `hoard-proj-question-resolved` in place of `-question-open`, which is how a standing changes.

Resolved on the same day it was raised, which is unusual enough to say why it is not haste: the three things the entry itself named as needing settlement were each settled, two of them by measurement rather than argument, and the human partner made every call that was theirs to make. What remains is building, and that is `derived-set-summary`.

The catalog-cost finding is kept in the head because it is the one that most changes how a later session would reason: the entry was framed partly as a budget problem, and the answer turned out not to cost catalog space at all.

content:
**Fragmentation does not predict the score either — the r 0.827 was an ecological fallacy, and my two measurements were of different things.** The human partner connected the nonsense-class results to tokenisation: keyboard mashing and symbol runs score high because they tokenise poorly. Across seven **class medians** that gave r **0.827**, better than anything else on this entry. Per query over 202 queries it collapses:

| query set | n | mean tok/word | mean top1 | r |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| real in-domain | 142 | 1.03 | 0.556 | **−0.043** |
| substance probes | 30 | 1.04 | 0.185 | **−0.151** |
| nonsense, all classes | 30 | 2.93 | 0.253 | **+0.090** |
| pooled | 202 | — | — | **−0.338**, and negative |

**Two errors, and the second is mine rather than the hypothesis's.** Correlating group means is not correlating members, and this investigation has now been caught by that shape three times. And the two runs used different denominators: tokens per *alphanumeric word*, where `>>> <<< ||| ~~~ ^^^` divides by zero words and reads 15.0, against tokens per *pretoken*, where the same string reads 1.0 because each symbol is already its own unit. Those separate two real and distinct effects — **pretokenisation explosion**, where punctuation becomes one unit per character, and **WordPiece fragmentation**, where a word splits into subword pieces. Only the second was tested per query; the first is untested.
context: The human partner connecting the keyboard-mashing results to poor tokenisation, at the end of a long session before checkpointing.
why:
Recorded because it is the fifth query-side predictor to fail on this entry — after `why`-composition, question form, word overlap and subword overlap — and because it failed in the way that keeps recurring rather than a new one. A monotone series across bucketed means has now produced three false positives here: the `why`-share quartiles, the supersession distance buckets, and this. The standing lesson is stated for group-versus-member correlation and it needs applying at the moment of reading a bucket table, not afterwards.

**The confounded denominator is worth more than the refutation.** It is not obvious that *tokens per word* and *tokens per pretoken* measure different things, and for symbol strings they differ by fifteenfold. The first counts how far a text explodes before WordPiece even runs; the second counts how far WordPiece splits what it is given. `>>> <<< ||| ~~~ ^^^` is maximal on the first and minimal on the second, and it is the highest-scoring nonsense string measured, so the untested half is the half that might still explain it.

That leaves a live, cheap test for the next session: pretokens per whitespace-separated unit, correlated per query. If pretokenisation explosion predicts where WordPiece fragmentation does not, the symbol result has an explanation and the ban on symbols in probe sets gains a reason rather than an observation.

content: **How an investigation is re-entered, and whether its state belongs in the keyword system. Resolved 2026-09-04 by drafting `hoard-watch`.** State does belong in the keyword system: the subclass keyword *is* the state, and `hoard-watch` itself is the push marker, dropped on the superseding memory to retire. **Push versus pull resolved as *push is the marked case*** -- most accumulation stays passive and is reached by ordinary recall, which is the budget story this entry said push would need. **One thing the entry proposed is wrong and was corrected in drafting:** transitions are *not* supersessions with the state as the chain tip. One observation set can drive several questions and supersession affords exactly one successor, so advancement is spawning a new head that draws on the observations while the set carries on collecting; supersession keeps correcting and retiring, and nothing else. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `investigation-re-entry`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The correction is carried in the head rather than left to a member because the superseded-chain-tip idea is attractive, was argued for at length in the entry, and `resolve_supersession` really does compute what it wanted -- so a session reading the members without the correction would find a well-made case for a design that was tried and rejected.

content:
Built 2026-09-12: a server reports on `hoard_conventions` when the binary it was launched from has since been rebuilt. It records how that file looked at startup — modification time and size, two fields of one `stat` — and re-reads it on each conventions call; when the two differ, the page is served as usual with a `note` beside it saying the session is being served the older build and that only restarting the MCP client changes that.

**Reported there for three reasons**: it is the call a session makes first, so the notice arrives before anything has been reasoned from stale text; it is the surface whose staleness is most dangerous, since a catalog a build behind answers every call successfully and simply governs; and it is the one call every session is told to make, where `hoard_sets status` is the tidier home for operational state and is read by almost nobody.

Designed in `documents/design/tool-surface.md`, *a server reports that its own binary has been rebuilt*. `tests/mcp.rs` pins it against a stand-in file a test can rewrite, and the real binary was checked end to end: clean before the file was touched, reporting after, conventions served both times.

The comparison is deliberately approximate. A rebuild producing an identical binary still reports, so a session is occasionally told to restart when nothing changed; the opposite error is the one this exists for. A server that cannot read its own path reports nothing rather than guessing.
context: Picking off a pending backlog item after finishing the non-match floor, in a session whose own server predated every commit it had made.
why:
Head of the backlog cluster, superseding the open record now the work has shipped: standing changes to built and the readiness facet comes off. The opening says what exists rather than what was wanted, since the generated row is that opening.

The placement is the part worth keeping findable. Every candidate mechanism in the original entry was implementable; what made this small was deciding that the question was *where a session would actually see it*, and that the answer is the one call the conventions require rather than the one where operational state belongs.

content: **If the server could tell one session from another, a continuous recall signal could know what each session has already recalled.** Proposed 2026-10-05 by the human partner, as a refinement of the continuous "you should recall here" signal. Two uses: suppress the signal for memories the session already holds, or name a memory id outright as relevant to the conversation. The alternative considered was attaching the signal to recall's own response. It was set aside because relevance shifts as the conversation moves, and a reading taken at recall time goes stale.
context: Discussing a continuous recall nudge after the gut-feeling-recall headroom result, before running the offline discrimination test.
why: Session identity is the piece that lets the signal fall once acted on, which is what keeps it from nagging. The MCP server currently has no notion of a session beyond its own process, so this would be new state. Recorded before the discrimination test, so whichever way the test goes, the design options it would feed are on file.

content: **A shared set's first memory is refused unless it is the charter; built 2026-09-28 as step 2 of `set-settled-at-first-write`.** The check is `Server::charter_first_refusal` in `src/mcp.rs`, asked by `memorize` after the read-only refusal and before the author is resolved. It fires only while `Store::holds_nothing_but_identities` is true: no memory and no tombstone, identity records aside. So a set taken on from a charterless file, or one whose charter was forgotten, keeps taking writes. `local` is never refused. `create`'s response now carries a `note` saying the first memory has to be the charter, the promise `route-where` makes.
context: Building set-settled-at-first-write step 2 after step 1 and the mutation-runner slow-step snapshots; the test fixtures were given charters, with the human partner's agreement.
why: **Why at the tool rather than in `Store::insert`**: the rule is that the caller holding the remedy is refused, which is a session writing through `memorize`. Store-level writers — import, absorb's carry-forward, and tests building stores directly — are not that caller. **Why before the author is resolved**: resolving mints an author record, which would be the set's first write and give it an identity, so a refusal asked after it would leave a refused set no longer empty. **Why after the read-only refusal**: an empty read-only set told to write a charter would be given a remedy it cannot use. **Why only the first write**: the 2026-09-08 finding that a set arriving without a charter is reported rather than refused, since there the remedy belongs to the set's author.

content: **The per-change recall changed a test's design on 2026-09-30**, before fixing `the-set-name-refusal-does-not-say-how-the-other-field-spells-it`. The recall surfaced `coding-lessons`' *when a refusal names a remedy, test the remedy by taking it* (`01M3GMWH77…`), so the test resends the spelling the refusal recommends and requires it be accepted, rather than only checking the refusal's wording. A part-6 catch: the lesson shaped what was written, though nothing shows the wording-only test would have hidden a defect here.
context: Working through open issues with the human partner: reembed-count mutation, numbered-opening summary, identity counts, catalog bytes, then the set-name refusal.
why: Evidence for the `adopting-coding-lessons` gate, recorded as observed: the change was to the test, not the fix, and whether it prevented anything is unknown. It belongs beside the same session's skipped recall, as the habit held again two changes later.

Fixed 2026-08-07 in `a2fd1f1` by refreshing on `data_version`. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `vector-cache-goes-stale-across-processes`; this record carries only its standing.

It is deliberately not on the going-public checklist, and its confirming test has not been written either; both wait for that window.

content: Fixed 2026-08-07 (`a2fd1f1`): `Store::configure_for_sharing` sets WAL and the busy timeout before the schema runs, and `tests/concurrency.rs` covers both — one test reads `journal_mode` back through a connection this code did not configure, since the mode is a property of the *file* and what matters is what a second process inherits; the other holds the write lock from another connection for a fixed interval and requires the store's write to wait it out. **WAL was the half that mattered**: under the default rollback journal a writer takes a lock that excludes readers outright, so an export in one session would have stalled every recall in the other for its whole duration and then failed it. Waiting five seconds to be refused is not much better than being refused at once.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the test shape worth reusing: verifying a file-level pragma through a connection the code under test did not configure, since what matters is what a *different* process inherits.

content: A principle served only as its conclusions will misjudge cases it plainly covers. `store-when` compresses the Golden Rule into "record the specific observation rather than a characterisation", which carries the verdict and loses the axis, so it reads "jbrown is the subject matter expert on XYZ" as suspect when the real hazard is an unfavourable claim on thin evidence. `route-where`'s compiled overrides miss a set that declares itself the home for observations about people for the same reason. Both are the signature of a principle present in what it decided rather than in what it is about.
context: Diagnosed 2026-08-12 after two open questions raised that day turned out to share a root: whether `store-when`'s person clause is calibrated on the right axis, and whether a set may declare itself the home for observations about people.
why: The compression is not a drafting slip: a session can check "is this specific" and cannot check "is this fair", so conclusion-shaped rules are what an LLM can actually apply, and that is the argument the Golden Rule uses for staying out of the served text as a directive. Recording the diagnostic rather than either fix keeps both live, because the human partner's read is that these questions and the dossier one are a single unsurfaced thing -- a set of principles saying what the Golden Rule is for, of which the current clauses would be consequences.

content: **All four `blocked by 1` backlog entries share one blocker, so they are one decision rather than four.** `contributing-and-branching-docs`, `built-in-sync`, `author-default-from-remote-url` and `readme-names-the-project-url` all `depends_on` the same `hoard-signpost` memory: neither repository has a git remote, by decision, because pushing to an origin publishes whatever the sets contain at that moment. Verified 2026-09-23 the way that memory says to — `git remote -v` in both checkouts, no output. So the day a remote is added, four entries become ready at once, and none of the four says so on its own.
context: Auditing the backlog family, resolving each blocked entry's dependency to see whether its blocker still holds.
why: The index renders each as `blocked by 1`, which reads as four independent dependencies and hides that one act releases all four. Recorded because it changes how the release is planned: adding a remote is not a step with one consequence, it is the moment a cluster of documentation and sync work becomes due.

content: Fixed 2026-08-21: `origin` is apparatus, and `amend` carries it. **The deciding argument was not that it is *unlike* content but that superseding would have been the wrong instrument rather than a verbose one** — supersession keeps the old record readable, so a misattribution of reasoning would stay legible for ever. That is the same durability hazard that makes *forget* rather than *supersede* the instrument for a record characterising a person unfairly, arriving in a smaller form. The apparatus test then confirms it from the other side: nobody ever believed the wrong value, exactly as with a recalibrated confidence.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The decision, and the argument that settled it: the question is not which category the field resembles but what the instrument would leave permanently readable.

content: Fully fixed 2026-08-26 **by making the type honest rather than by deleting it**: `MemorySet` carries `tombstones` beside `memories`, so it is what it claims to be — a file's contents. **The reader was only half of what was left**: `memory_file::write` had the same gap for a different reason, iterating `memories` because until then there was nowhere for a tombstone to come from — so a set written from a set that was read had forgotten what it forgot, twice over. `read` and `write` are a matched pair over one type, which is the argument for fixing it at the type rather than at either call site. **One thing had to be decided rather than carried across**: `write` sorted memories by id, and with two shapes it now merges them into records and sorts those together, because a file is ordered by id — that is what makes its diffs reviewable and what puts a duplicate id next to its twin — so writing memories then tombstones would order by *shape* and make every diff that forgets a memory move a line to the end. Twenty-one construction sites broke at compile time and were filled in, which is the good kind of breakage. *The first attempt at the read mutation dropped the match arm, which left the vector with no inferred type and was "caught" by the compiler, proving nothing; it now clears the vector instead, reproducing the old behaviour exactly.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Fixing a type rather than its call sites, because the reader and writer are a matched pair. The mutation caught by a compile error rather than an assertion is the recurring trap: it looks like coverage and proves nothing.

content: **A trigger is added when a recorded failure's reconstructed sentence does not surface any trigger for its lesson.** Decided 2026-09-28 by the human partner. When a project records a failure as an instance of a lesson, the session reconstructs the one sentence it would have used before writing the failing code and recalls on it as the habit would. If none of the lesson's triggers is in the top five, it writes one, and reruns the sentence to prove the new trigger now surfaces. It can be **general**, in the lessons set, phrased as the activity without the project's nouns; or **project-specific**, in the project's own set, phrased in its nouns and linked `motivated_by` across sets to the lesson; or both. A trigger that surfaced and was ignored is an observation for the recurrence investigation, not a reason for a new trigger. One that keeps surfacing with nothing to say is narrowed by superseding it.
context: Designing how projects that opt in to `coding-lessons` catch failures before they are written: when triggers get written.
why: Sessions phrase what they are about to write in their project's vocabulary, and the one miss in the 2026-09-28 experiment was a query in exactly those nouns. So a general trigger travels but matches loosely, while a project trigger matches tightly and travels nowhere; both lead to the same lesson. The unscoped habit finds both. A project holding the lessons set read-only can still add triggers in its own set, and contribute general ones upstream. This is the general-form-and-instance split that `route-where`'s removed sentences described, now carried by the adoption guide for the projects that use it.

content: **What the BACKLOG.md migration surfaced, measured 2026-09-07 — the human partner expected it to find a few issues and it found five kinds.** A defect in the generating tool: `superseding-a-head-moves-its-row-to-the-end`, found because migrating exercised the pipeline rather than by reading it. **Two stale current-state claims** carried faithfully into memories before being checked — the cross-set successor concern, fixed by a layer built after the entry, and `correction-gated-on-service`'s note that `confidence-standards` had not caught up, which it had. **One entry already fixed by the migration itself**, `issues-records-its-status-twice`, closed more completely than it asked because the surviving marker became derived. **Stale scaffolding in both files**, each still instructing a hand-marking workflow that no longer exists. And **one defect visible only from the finished result**, `a-slug-that-is-also-a-subject-keyword-over-gathers`, found by measuring cluster sizes across all 55 rather than by reading any entry.
context: Wrapping up the BACKLOG.md migration, taking stock of what the process turned up.
why:
Recorded because the categories differ in what would have found them, which is the useful part for planning the open-questions migration. Three of the five were invisible to reading — the tool defect needed the pipeline run, the over-gathering slug needed the aggregate measured, and the already-fixed entry needed the current system checked against the claim. Only the stale scaffolding would have turned up in an ordinary review.

It also sets an expectation: the same five classes are available in `documents/design/open-questions.md`, which has forty entries and is the least migrated of the three, so the yield there is likely larger rather than smaller — and the two stale claims say the check to run is on present-tense assertions about behaviour, which a question entry contains more of than a backlog entry does.

content: `recall-gloss-convention` was retired on 2026-09-04 rather than drafted, and its behaviour was already shipping. BACKLOG.md had carried it as Ready and undrafted for weeks, while the final clause of `recall-when` says the same thing — "lead with enough of its context to let the human place it before you rely on it" — with the source comment above it in catalog.rs naming it as the recall-gloss behaviour. The entry was two rules: the capture half went to the `context` parameter description, and the gloss half is read-side and has no home until `response-shape-is-unpublished` is fixed, since no tool publishes an `outputSchema`. The served clause is phrased as always rather than on demand and is kept that way meanwhile, because it is the only channel reaching a session at recall time.
context: Retiring the recall-gloss convention, and finding while checking every reference to its name that the behaviour was already served inside another convention. Working out where guidance about the context field belongs, and rewriting that field's description.
why: A tracking entry describing as unbuilt something already served is worse than a missing entry: it invites a session to draft a convention that would have duplicated a live rule, and it inflates the count of work competing for catalog budget — three Ready conventions were being weighed against 1,747 free characters, and one of them was partly done. It was found only by grepping for every reference to the name before editing, which is the cheap check that catches this class. The always-versus-on-demand question is left open deliberately: the human partner raised on-demand as possibly sufficient, and it survives the trigger test because the human asking is externally observable, while "gloss when it seems needed" is self-assessed and would degrade to never.

content: **These four entries' slugs are also subject terms, so recalling one returns the whole subject, not just the entry's findings:** `graph-traversal`, `keyword-standards`, `investigation-pipeline` and `recall-eval-harness`. context: Fixing the slug-collision issue after publishing output schemas; adding a collision check to genindex.py.
why: The fix chosen with the human partner for `a-slug-that-is-also-a-subject-keyword-over-gathers` (option C): check new entries, reword the rule that produced the collisions, and note the existing ones rather than rename them. Renaming would mean superseding dozens of exported findings, each after a judgement about whether it belongs to the entry or the subject. One note carrying the four slugs as keywords comes back beside each cluster, the pattern the 2026-09-23 audit record uses, without retyping four heads.

content: An import whose file declared a set identity different from the one a non-empty store holds succeeded and said nothing, so one set could hold two identities on two machines with no signal on either. Fixed 2026-09-22 by reporting, not refusing: an `identity_note` names both identities when a file declares another, and says so when a file holding records declares none; an export does the same when the file it replaces declared another identity. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `an-import-silently-keeps-a-different-set-identity`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building the fork procedure and identity-mismatch reporting before release. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 1 link an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded to record the fix. Reporting rather than refusing because what identity gates is still open, and a note does not answer that. Pinned by four tests in `tests/sets.rs` and a mutation for each of the three notes. The limit: detection needs both identities on one machine at an import or export, so a machine that diverged and never syncs again is never told.

content: A line in the sharing preferences written without a leading `- ` or `* ` was dropped without a word, so a value the person added did not take effect and nothing said so. Found 2026-10-30 when the person added two values to *Always fine to share* as bare lines, the way the section's own instruction read ("Add exact values, one per line"). Fixed 2026-10-31: `ListedPreferences::parse` in `src/preferences.rs` reports every line that is not blank, a heading, a comment or an item in `unread`, and `Preferences::served` serves them as `not_read` with a note asking the session to tell the person. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-preference-written-without-a-bullet-is-dropped`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Right after closing the export-review change: the person added the SSH remote and the governance-docs pseudonym to their always-fine list, and the lines were not being read.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, severity and standing. Amended rather than superseded because it was filed on 2026-10-30 and never exported, so nobody else holds the open version. `misleads` is kept: the severity describes the defect, not its current state.

content: **`gemma4:12b` can state the sharing-preferences rule and still not apply it when it writes.** In the confound-free health test of 2026-10-21, it kept "HIV" out of `local` in 3 of 5 templated runs against 0 of 5 at baseline, a real effect. But all 5 still stored the health detail as "a recurring medical appointment". Asked afterwards, all 5 templated runs correctly said health is kept out of every set, and all 5 baselines correctly said the file did not mention it. None of the replies said something was left out. Asked why each memory was stored, the runs cited `store-when` and never the preferences. Their answers on precedence invented quotes. The logs are in that session's scratchpad, `framing-run-4`.
context: Building the sharing preferences served at session start. Fourth gemma run, adding debrief questions at the human partner's suggestion to see how the model reads the prompting.
why: This separates the explanations. Placement is not the problem: the text registers, and the model can quote it. The failure is in applying it at the moment of writing, so a fix belongs at that moment, in `hoard_memorize`, or in a mechanical check. It also confirms that a model's account of why it acted is a reconstruction: the precedence answers cited text that does not exist.

content: Semantic recall in a script the loaded model cannot represent returned noise, and nothing said so. Fixed 2026-10-04 by reporting it rather than by changing the model. `hoard_sets status` scores each declared language 0 to 10: how many of ten paraphrase tests the model ranks first, against the other 29 sentences in that language. It puts a band message in `language_note`. Below 7 it says recall there is unreliable, and below 4 that the model cannot search it but the memories are intact. Recall by meaning carries the same message for each set it searched. A set may carry its own test sentences and recommended models under a `hoard-fit-hub`. The limitation itself remains: only a model covering the language makes such a set searchable by meaning. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `recall-is-latin-script-only`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Finishing the declared-language check: built-in scores and bands, then a set's own sentences, then model recommendations, in three commits on 2026-10-04.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect it names, confident recall that is meaningless with nothing reporting it, now reports itself in status and on every semantic recall. The severity was `misleads`, and the fix removes the wrong belief rather than the cause. The cause is the model, which is the user's choice and which the report now names. Design: `documents/design/memory-data-model.md`, *The model-fit report*.

content: **The refusal is the part that carries the design, so what it must not become is stated: a judgement the caller makes.** The LLM cannot determine service — it cannot see the bases, and **it is the party that benefits from answering *no***. Two alternatives were considered and rejected in the design: a **time window**, which needs a number nobody has, and **read-tracking**, which needs a write on the read path and would mark almost everything in service within minutes. **The test had to provoke the refusal through the schema a client actually receives**, not by constructing arguments by hand — that is the specific gap that let `amending-a-claim-is-refused-where-no-client-can-reach-it` ship in the first place. Two mutations pin it: inverting the service check, and **permitting `content` without declaring it**, which is the failure mode that reproduces the original defect in a new place while every handler-level test stays green.
context: Migrating the correction-gated-on-service entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the design constraint on the refusal itself.
why:
Recorded because *ask the caller whether this has been shared* is the cheap implementation and is available at every point where the gate is inconvenient — and it fails for a reason that is about incentives rather than capability, which no amount of careful prompting fixes.

The second mutation is the one worth keeping: a guard that is enforced in the handler but absent from the published schema passes every test written against hand-built arguments, and fails only against a validating client that strips what the schema does not name. That is a whole class of defect this project has filed repeatedly, and the mutation is what makes the class visible in one place.

content: **In the export review, `clear` takes, for each memory, who it is about and which kept-out categories it mentions, and the server routes it.** A memory about the project that mentions none is cleared, and anything else is put to the person in full. Agreed 2026-10-22 by the human partner, to be tested on a small model first, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. The answers for "about" are the project, the person, or someone else. A preferences change asks the same questions about only the newly added keep-outs.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public, after deciding that only a change to a memory itself reopens it.
why: The person cannot be the backstop for unflagged memories. The human partner's example: a `TRACKING.md` row cues only the gist of what you half remember, and nothing about a memory you never wrote. So the model's reading carries the weight, and it is made narrow and checkable. `gemma4:12b` recognised health correctly when asked directly, but misjudged whether a memory was a problem. The rejected alternative showed the person a listing of every memory's summary line, which fails at fifteen hundred memories and cues nothing past the opening.

content: **A per-change recall changed what was written a second time, 2026-10-16**: before fixing stale connections to dropped sets, the habit recall returned the `coding-lessons` lesson to name the state each process keeps privately and key its invalidation to the shared state. It shaped the fix directly: compare the opened file's identity with the file now at the path, which also caught the dropped-and-recreated case a plain existence check misses. The same stretch produced a claim the tests then disproved, recorded on the issue head.
context: Fixing `a-set-dropped-by-another-server-stays-writable-here` ahead of a beta.2 candidate.
why: Item 5 of the `coding-lessons` validation entry counts each time a recall changed what was written; this is the second instance, the first being the declined-or-dismissed fallback the same day.

content: `recall-summary-output-mode` shipped 2026-09-06: `hoard_recall` takes `detail`, `full` or `summary`, and `hoard_memorize` echoes the line unconditionally. Three decisions beyond the backlog entry. The cut takes the **last** sentence end that fits rather than the first, because the first spends most of the budget on a memory opening with a short sentence and truncates to four characters on an `e.g.` -- silently, since a short line reads as a short memory. A summary hit carries **no `scope`**, which the entry's own 49-character envelope figure had already assumed. And a cut line ends in an ellipsis while a whole one does not: the marker comes out of the 120 rather than being added past them, and it goes on **every** cut, since marking only the ragged ones leaves an unmarked line meaning either complete or cut-at-a-sentence. Re-measured over the shipped code, the live `scatterhoard` file cuts 34 at a sentence and 61 at a word of 96, against the 40/59 split the pre-build check found -- so no interpretation moved the measurement.
context: Building the index-line output mode, then adding the truncation marker the human partner asked for once the rest was working.
why: Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claim is unchanged. The three decisions are kept together because each is one a later reader would take for an oversight and quietly reverse -- first-sentence is the obvious reading of *cut at a sentence*, a missing `scope` looks forgotten, and an ellipsis on a line that already ends in a full stop looks like a bug rather than an answer to *is there more*. The measured split is dated for the same reason the catalog figure elsewhere now is: it moves whenever the corpus does, and `report_summary_cuts` is what answers it.

content: `superseded_beyond_this_set` names the wrong reason when a replacement was forgotten: a memory whose replacement was withdrawn in *this* set resolves the same way as one replaced in a set that is not loaded, so the caller is sent to look somewhere that will never have it. Fixed when the two read differently and the description says something a caller can act on. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-forgotten-replacement-reads-as-superseded-beyond-this-set`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only, with the fixed-when since this one is open. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **An alias must never reach a memory or a file.** This is the invariant `open-a-set-under-an-alias` has to keep, agreed 2026-09-25. Export writes the set's declared name into the header. A link that names the aliased set as its `target_set` is translated from the alias to the declared name when it is stored, the way a same-set link spelled with its own set name is already canonicalised at the door. Otherwise a memory linking to `notes-alice`, once exported, would hand every other reader a name that means nothing to them. Cross-set links resolve by identity where both sides have one (decided 2026-09-14), which is why an aliased target still resolves locally. The recorded name is what goes wrong, not the resolution.
context: Resolving `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout` with the human partner, on the release gate.
why: A decision within `open-a-set-under-an-alias`, recorded apart from the head because it is what keeps the feature additive, and so off the release gate. An alias that leaked into records would be a format-visible, published fact. The evaluation precedent never needed this rule only because an evaluation copy is never written to. Not verified against the link-writing code; confirm how `target_set` is stored before building.

content: This now blocks work as well as misleading clients: `context-gloss-on-recall` in [BACKLOG.md](BACKLOG.md) is a rule about what to do with a returned `context`, and it has nowhere to live until a response field can be described. Noted 2026-09-04, when the recall-gloss convention was retired in favour of documenting the field at both ends.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: An open defect acquiring a dependent, which changes its priority without changing its claim. Recorded because the blocking relationship is the reason a documentation-shaped issue is worth doing before the work that needs it.

content: Found 2026-08-11 running SETUP.md §5 from a client for the first time, and caught by nothing: green suite, passing smoke test, server correct at the protocol level. **Observed from two directions in one session against the same binary**, which is what makes it the server's defect rather than a client's — on one server the tool arrived with `"properties": {}` and every call answered *hoard_sets needs an action*, so the entire management surface and `hoard_correct` with it were uncallable; on two others the branches were *merged*, with all five properties present and `action` pinned to `const: "status"` — callable, and lying, since a caller obeying the schema could only ever run `status`, the `const` turning out not to be enforced, which is luck rather than design. **This is not a client bug to wait out**: the schema is legal and a consumer is entitled to flatten it, and what makes the failure total rather than cosmetic is that there is no top-level `properties` to fall back to. `hoard_memorize` carries a `oneOf` *inside* `scope` and survived everywhere, because its top level is flat.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A legal schema that no test could fault, failing two different ways in two clients against one binary. The discriminating fact is nesting depth: an alternation inside a property survived everywhere, and one at the top level did not.

content: What the Golden Rule is for is now stated as four demands on a memory about a person, where "person" means any reasoning being including an LLM. A: it must be answerable to something a later reader can still check. B: it must serve later work. C: the person is a detail of the record, never its organising principle. D: generalise only as far as the evidence reaches, and read what you do not know in the person's favour. A and B are not new rules -- they are what store-when already demands of every memory, applied without the exemption a judgement about someone quietly gets. C does not derive from A and B, because aggregation harm is a property of the set rather than of any record in it. D's second half is the only ethical clause and it governs the inference from evidence to motive, nothing else.
context: Articulated 2026-08-13 with the human partner, who contributed D and the extension to all reasoning beings. Checkable in the "What the principle is for" section of documents/design/golden-rule.md.
why: Three open questions resolved together on 2026-08-13 because they were one question, exactly as the human partner predicted: the clauses carrying the principle had each been compiled from its conclusions, so each misjudged a case the principle plainly covers. Stating the demands as record quality rather than as kindness is what answers the standing objection that a kindness directive softens accurate technical criticism -- D's charitable half cannot reach technical criticism because it operates only on unknowns, and "the tests fail" is not an unknown.

content: Found 2026-08-24 while checking whether a cross-set `SUPERSEDED_BY` is only ever self-harm — the sweep had not named this arm. `resolve_supersession` returned `Superseded { tips: [absent], unresolved: false }`, reporting a chain that resolved; `resolved_hit`'s `self.get(id)?.map(...)` then yielded `None` and `recall_across` found no `home` for an identity no store scanned, so the hit was dropped. `hoard_lookup` by id still returned it, so the memory was never lost, only unfindable by any search. **The spelling that did this is the one the design calls the commonest mistake**: [Cross-Set References](documents/design/cross-set-references.md) names *"a cross-set reference written without its set name"* as the ordinary malformation, and that is exactly this row — written **with** the set name the same intent was handled well, coming back flagged `superseded_beyond_this_set`, which is *report rather than resolve* working as designed. One spelling apart, and the failure modes were opposite. No hostile file was needed: a hand-edited set, an id that was forgotten rather than superseded, or a set that lags the repository it came from all produce it, the last being a case the design explicitly says must not be treated as an error.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery, and the sharpest fact about it: the well-handled case and the silently destructive one differ by whether a set name was written, and the design already predicted that omission as the ordinary mistake.

content: Validity was resolved *after* the ranking, against a design and a doc comment that both said before — so a supersession chain consumed several seed slots to contribute one neighbourhood, a dead memory acted as a conduit while its tip lacked routes, and native confidence could never enter the decay. Fixed across 2026-08-18 and 2026-08-19. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `validity-is-resolved-after-the-ranking`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Found 2026-08-24 by the hand-edited-file sweep, driving the `EXCEPTION_TO`/`CONTRADICTS` arm. [Cross-Set References](documents/design/cross-set-references.md) resolves that **what is reported is the edge, not the other memory**, because a memory always returned beside the one it attacks *"has bought a permanent slot in every recall that matches it — weaker than suppression and still a free channel into a stranger's context."* That holds for `SUPERSEDES`, which `is_traversable` excludes, and not for the other two standing-changing labels, which are traversable. **Measured**: against a control memory of identical content and no edge, the disputing memory inherited **0.192** where the control inherited **0**, and the two then ranked apart. `Store::edges` pushed a walkable row into `walkable` without consulting `target_set`, and `Neighbourhood::over` added the edge because both endpoints were in the population — the rule that makes an unscoped recall cross set boundaries deliberately, working exactly as intended on an edge nobody intended it for. **This is not the suppression defect and must not be conflated with it**: the target's standing is untouched, pinned by `a_cross_set_dispute_leaves_its_targets_standing_alone`. What is wrong is that the claimant is paid for making the claim.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A rule enforced for one label and not its two siblings, measured rather than argued. The mechanism is a correct feature — unscoped recall crossing set boundaries — meeting an edge nobody meant it to serve.

content: **The cluster-shaping guidance lived in `STANDARDS.md` for one day.** Written there 2026-09-07 with discovery solved by proximity — each of the three tracking files linked to it from their first 25 lines, above the generated-index marker, so the rule sat on a path already being walked — and moved into `TRACKING.md` itself on 2026-09-08 when those three files became one. **Proximity did not lose the argument; unification collapsed the distance to zero**, and a link from a file into a section of itself is not a path worth walking. Two alternatives rejected on 2026-09-07 stay rejected: a `hoard-signpost`, which spends session budget on something recall can reach once you know to ask, and a `.claude/rules/` path-scoped rule, which works and is Claude Code only. `STANDARDS.md` keeps one link into the section, from its cross-reference table, because a slug's form is constrained by the fact that it is also a memory keyword.
context: Unifying the tracking files into TRACKING.md, the morning after the guidance was written into STANDARDS.md.
why: Split from the 2026-09-07 record on 2026-09-08: the reasoning survived and is superseded separately, but the mechanism it describes is present-tense and became false in a day. Recorded rather than dropped because *the guidance is in STANDARDS.md* is the kind of claim a later session will act on without checking, and because the reason proximity stopped applying is not that it was wrong — a session that reads only the surviving argument might reinstate the links.

content: **`potion-multilingual-128M` separates meaning in every script the shipping model collapses, at a steep cost in English retrieval.** Measured 2026-09-11 UTC through the same probes, both models back to back. **Scripts** (`probe_whether_recall_works_outside_latin_script`, one question against an unrelated statement per language, where near zero is healthy): English 0.102, Spanish −0.115, German 0.049, French 0.063, Russian 0.084, Chinese 0.066, Hindi 0.074, Japanese 0.098 — against Russian 0.908, Hindi 0.880, Japanese 0.721 and a refused Chinese under `potion-base-32M`, which reproduced the 2026-09-10 table exactly. Every text embeds. **English** (`probe_reproduce_the_seed_quality_figures`, 45 real memories, 20 labelled queries, centred as recall ships): r@1 27.5 / r@3 52.5 / r@5 **54.2** / r@10 72.5, against 34.2 / 57.5 / **77.5** / 83.3 — 23 points lost at r@5. It is a different family, not a larger vocabulary: a 500,353-entry SentencePiece Unigram tokenizer from `BAAI/bge-m3` and 256 dimensions, where the shipping model has a 63,091-entry WordPiece and 512.
context: Testing the multilingual model after fixing the store-stopping embed failure, at the human partner's direction, before choosing how to calibrate the non-match floor.
why:
Recorded because it answers half of the multilingual option. Meaning is not collapsing in any script tested, so this model is a real remedy for the collapse rather than a different failure. But an unrelated pair scoring near zero shows only that the space has not collapsed, not that related text scores high: a related-pair test per language is the missing half.

The English cost is large enough that swapping the default would buy other languages at the expense of the use the tool is built around. That points toward a model chosen per machine by the human, who knows what they write — with the check at the write door still needed for scripts any model lacks.

Thin in the usual ways: one pair per language, and a fixture of 20 queries written and labelled by one author, though both models were scored against identical labels. The script probe's token and unknown columns mean nothing under this model — they come from the probe's own WordPiece helper, which cannot read a Unigram vocabulary — so only its similarity and storability columns are read here. The downloaded weights matched the sha256 Hugging Face publishes.

content: The confidence scale was used across a fifth of its range. Built 2026-08-13 and served as **`confidence-standards`** — renamed to pair with `keyword-standards`, its catalog neighbour and the other of the two field-level conventions the `store-when` editing comment had predicted would arrive separately. Built-when was that the convention say what the ends of the scale mean concretely enough that two sessions would land within a band of each other on the same memory; reasoning in [conventions.md](documents/design/conventions.md). The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `confidence-guidance`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only. Note the entry's slug and the shipped convention's id differ — the entry is `confidence-guidance`, the convention is `confidence-standards` — so a search for one will not find the other.

content: Scatterhoard's `context` field carries a handle for a person, not information about the memory — settled 2026-09-04 by the human partner. It takes what was being worked on, named as a person would say it rather than as the repository does ("Making the author changeable", not "`make-author-changeable` step 4"), and includes concurrent work even when unrelated, because a session runs as one thread and naming any part of it can pull the rest back. It leaves out whatever the record already holds — the date, the id, the author — and leaves out where a thing can be checked, which belongs in `content` or `why` where it is embedded and read. The guidance lives in the `hoard_memorize` parameter description, not in the convention catalog: what to write in a field is decided with the schema in front of you, and the description costs nothing against the 18,000-character budget.
context: Working out what guidance to give for the context field and where it should live, after measuring what sessions had actually been writing there across both shared sets. Retiring the recall-gloss convention in the same stretch, and correcting a first reading that had blamed staleness for what was really a field full of identifiers.
why: The placement is the reusable part, and it is a third answer to a question that had been framed as "own convention or clause on `store-when`". Both of those spend catalog budget on a decision made at the moment of the call, which is where decision-placement.md says to put it, and the tool schema reaches that moment for free. The evidence that it works is that the previous description already drove behaviour precisely — 98% adoption of an optional field, with dates and parked pointers arriving because the old wording invited them. Two consequences worth holding: the change is pinned by tests/snapshots/tools_list.json, so it cannot ship silently the way a branch description would; and the exclusions matter as much as the instruction, because every one of them names a field that already carries the same fact.

content: **Shown a first `hoard_conventions`-style page with thinking off, local `gemma4:12b` began work in every format that only showed more was coming.** Tested 2026-10-01 in a clean context through Ollama's chat API, forced to answer `CALL load_guidelines {…}` or `START_TASK`, and never asked whether it was finished. Formats that started work 10 out of 10: the current format with `next_cursor: 1`, an unclosed JSON list cut mid-sentence or between conventions, "m of N" numbering, and a terse header `continues at 3500 · 11 conventions`. A plain-text line before or after the page saying "Not complete. Call load_guidelines again with {"cursor": 3500} for the rest." continued 10 out of 10 in both places. The same sentence as a field inside the JSON continued 1 in 10. With thinking on, 5 runs each: the current format continued 2 of 5, the terse header 0 of 5, the instruction line 5 of 5, the in-JSON instruction 5 of 5. Every reader given only a cursor dropped `max_chars`. A last-page line "Complete: all 11 guidelines are loaded." caused no extra calls. The harness and pages are in that session's scratchpad (`gemma_run.py`), which does not survive it.
context: Redesigning hoard_conventions paging for max-chars-is-not-a-bound, after a Haiku test that was contaminated by this repository's AGENTS.md. The human partner offered their local Ollama install with gemma4:12b.
why: This settles how a `hoard_conventions` page should say more follows. Only a plain-text instruction outside the JSON worked for a weak reader, so the redesign for `max-chars-is-not-a-bound` uses one. It also shows the current format already lets such a reader stop after page one. The test was built to remove the faults of the Haiku run the same day: a clean context, no completeness question, ten runs per format, and a control page (an explicit instruction alone continued 5 out of 5), which rules out a harness that always answers START_TASK. One model, one size, so 0.85 rather than higher.

content: **When a review rewording brings in a pseudonym, the `clear` response's `flag_guidance` tells the session to suggest the person add it under *Always fine to share* in their sharing preferences.** Decided 2026-10-30 by the human partner, who ruled out a new mechanism: the preferences file's always-fine section already stops the review flagging a listed value, and what was missing was a prompt at the moment a pseudonym is chosen. Built in `src/mcp.rs` (the `flag_guidance` text), pinned by `the_flag_guidance_offers_a_pseudonym_to_the_always_fine_list` in `tests/export_review.rs` and the mutation `review: stop offering a new pseudonym to the always-fine list`. On `gemma4:12b`, given a flagged memory and a person asking for a set name to be replaced with a pseudonym, the suggestion appeared in 10 of 10 replies with the sentence and 0 of 10 without.
context: Finishing the scatterhoard full export review and clearing the flags raised only for naming governance-docs or flightlog; the person asked how pseudonyms could be learned about earlier in a review.
why: The case that motivated it: the full review of this set on 2026-10-29 flagged about thirty memories for the name `governance-docs`, which the person had already chosen as the pseudonym on 2026-10-19, and the reviewing session found that decision only partway through. The guidance placement was chosen over a convention clause (catalog space every session, for a review-only moment) and over the review's task text (read once, before any rewording), because a session reads `flag_guidance` exactly when it is introducing the pseudonym. The probe was a one-off scratch script, not `scripts/local_model.py`, whose modes do not cover this moment.

content: Write the collaboration rules when there is someone to collaborate with. **Ready since 2026-10-04**, when the beta remote arrived. **`CONTRIBUTING.md` exists since 2026-11-02**, covering how a contribution carries memories, the export review, which set a memory belongs in, and reviewing a contribution. **What remains is branching**: decided 2026-08-29 by the human partner that feature branches were not wanted while there was no shared default branch, and every session committed straight to `main`; whether that changes now that `origin/main` is shared is the human partner's question, and the guide says nothing on branching until it is answered. Built when `CONTRIBUTING.md` covers branching. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `contributing-and-branching-docs`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Turning DEVELOPMENT.md into CONTRIBUTING.md during the going-public checklist, after the breaking-change audit and settling the beta tag.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because the guide now exists and covers everything the entry asked for except branching. Kept open rather than closed so the branching question is not lost behind a file that looks finished.

content: **Since 2026-09-28 a resurrection is not written at all, which replaces this fix's *reported, never refused*.** A memory arriving at import for an id the store holds as a tombstone stays forgotten, and is reported under `kept_forgotten` with how to undo a forget on purpose: store it again with a `supersedes` link to the forgotten id. `taken_backwards` still reports any other record taken older than the one it replaced, which matters for records written before 2026-08-30. The fix's reasoning, that a deliberate rollback looks identical to an older copy, still holds. It is why neither is taken now: the undo became a new event instead of an old state returning.
context: Making a forget one-way at import, to close `a-target-path-can-come-to-mean-a-different-volume`.
why: This entry is closed and its fix member says resurrection is reported and never refused. A later reader of that member would believe it still describes the import. Superseding the fix member was not chosen, because it records what was true when it was written.

content: **What the exercise is actually good at, recorded 2026-08-21 before the next one: three of the four findings were *absences* rather than wrong behaviour** — a field no instrument reaches, a rule no code enforces, a description nobody wrote. **None would have been found by using the tools, because nothing misbehaves**, and **none by reading a file, because each is missing from the file you would read**. Only laying the grid out and looking for blanks surfaces them. The read-surface pass had already produced a `Corrupts` defect on the same reasoning, which is what justified repeating it on the write surface.
context: Migrating the write-surface-matrix entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the methodological note it left for whoever runs the next pass.
why:
Kept as the criterion for scheduling another pass, since the obvious criterion — has anything gone wrong lately — is precisely the one this exercise is blind to and blind for. A matrix pass is worth running when a surface has grown, not when something has broken.

The project instance of a general technique whose form is held in `coding-lessons`; what is specific here is which surfaces have been covered — read and write — and that both passes paid out, so a third surface has evidence behind it rather than only an argument.

content: **The cost this entry rested on has been paid down to nothing, and the design question is now unsupported by it -- re-measured 2026-09-07.** When raised on 2026-09-06 the charter recall returned **nine memories at full detail, once per store: four charters and five design notes about charters**, the pollution recorded as `reserved-keywords-carry-subject-memories`. Re-run today the same recall returns **four memories, all four of them charters**. The `about-` prefix rule and the re-keying pass that followed it removed the five, and that issue is now marked fixed. **So the *when* question stands on its own merits and no longer has a cost figure behind it:** whether a recall consulted per decision should become a per-session pull, given that a session which stores nothing pays for charters it never used. Four charters at full detail per store is a real but modest charge, and it grows with the number of loaded sets rather than with the corpus. Re-derive rather than quote -- a single keyword recall on the charter mark with no scope, at a limit above the number of loaded sets.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Recorded because an argument losing its evidence is worth marking explicitly: the entry reads as though the recall is expensive, and it is not any more, so a session picking this up would otherwise act on a number that was true for one day.

It also demonstrates something easy to miss about the corpus -- the charter recall's cost was mostly self-inflicted through keyword misuse rather than inherent, and fixing the keywords fixed the cost. That is worth holding whenever another recall looks expensive.

content: **The export review drops a flagged memory from what awaits the person once it is forgotten or changed since it was shown.** Fixed 2026-10-26 in `prune_flagged` in `src/mcp.rs`, which runs before every `review` and `clear`, with tests in `tests/export_review.rs`. Before it, a forgotten flagged memory still counted as awaiting the person. Worse, `person_cleared` on a flagged memory amended after it was shown recorded the amended text as reviewed, so the person cleared words they never saw. A changed memory now goes back to the review.
context: Reviewing the scatterhoard set on the rebuilt server before exporting and committing the judgement gate, after rewording a flagged memory.
why: Found by watching the review's first run on this project's own set: after a flagged memory was reworded and its original forgotten, the server still reported one memory awaiting the person. Testing the neighbouring case found the amendment bug, which is the one that mattered, since it cleared text the person never saw. Both came from keeping a list of ids beside the store without checking it against the store when it is read.

content: **A replay of recall must run the product's `recall_across`, not content-only rank: on 2026-10-05 the two put one memory 3rd and 12th.** The query was the 2026-09-28 per-change recall before the local-identity fix. Content rank (`eval::ranks_from_query`, as `scatterhoard-eval` uses) placed the cause `a-reference-that-does-not-pin-what-it-names` 12th. Live recall, with supersession folding and link traversal, placed it 3rd, as the record made at the time said. A replay that loads each set into `Store::open_in_memory`, imports only the memories created before a time, and calls `recall_across` reproduced the live top 8 exactly. Created-date snapshots hold only after the 2026-09-07 migration, which minted every migrated memory with that date.
context: Measuring headroom for gut-feeling-recall ahead of the small-model lift experiment, the morning after the first beta.
why: Any measurement for `gut-feeling-recall` or `how-much-scatterhoard-lifts-a-small-model` that ranks by content alone misreports what a session saw, here by nine places. That could invent headroom where recall already succeeded. The diagnose-labels mode is content-only on purpose, since it asks whether labels re-find content similarity, so this is a rule for replays rather than a defect there. Verified against one live query, hence 0.85.

content: Scatterhoard publishes only the JSON Schema constructs that every observed MCP client carries intact, and accepts every spelling any of them might send. Measured across two clients on one binary: type, properties, required, items, enum and description survive; oneOf and anyOf anywhere, union types like ["string","null"], and additionalProperties do not, arriving as {} — and a property with no type takes an object argument as text, so a scope of {"shared":"x"} comes back as an unknown variant. Underneath that, the Anthropic API refuses oneOf, allOf or anyOf at the top level of input_schema outright and fails the whole tool list for one violation, breaking every server in the session.
context: Established 2026-08-11 and 2026-08-12 across several client restarts; the reasoning is in documents/design/tool-surface.md under "publish the centre of MCP, accept the edges".
why: This cost a full day and three wrong conclusions to establish, and none of it is guessable from the specification: the constructs are all legal JSON Schema, and what decides them is what survives the journey rather than what the standard allows. The asymmetry between publishing and accepting is deliberate too — a server is normally right to be strict, because strictness stops clients drifting, but that argument needs influence over the client and this one has none, so strictness would only make memories unreachable rather than correcting anybody.

content: **A fourth skipped per-change recall on 2026-09-30**, before letting `absorb` take a `local` file into `local` (`a-split-local-store-cannot-be-merged-back`): the session went from the human partner's "please fix it" to reading `absorb_set`. Like the third, it came directly after a design decision. The day's count is four skipped among nine changes, every skip at the hand-off from discussing to building and none in the middle of a fix.
