content: **The lattice's *the tombstone wins* conflicts with an earlier decision that a reverted forget is honoured, found 2026-09-28 and not yet settled.** On 2026-08-26, `an-older-file-silently-resurrects-a-forgotten-memory` was fixed by reporting a memory taken back over its tombstone (`taken_backwards`), never refusing it. The reason: a deliberate rollback, such as a `git revert` of the commit carrying the tombstone, looks identical at import to an older backup, and only the caller can tell them apart. `an_import_that_resurrects_a_forgotten_memory_says_so` in `tests/sets.rs` pins it. The proposal says one id moves only absent → memory → tombstone, which forbids that revert, and does not address it. So adopting the lattice, or applying its tombstone-wins row alone, first needs a decision on how a forget is undone: by reverting the file, or only by `restore` or re-storing.
context: Filing the lattice proposal as an open question, right after the human partner asked for it and for the tombstone-wins step to be built.
why: Caught before any code was written. A session proposed applying only the tombstone-wins row at import, to close `a-target-path-can-come-to-mean-a-different-volume`, and claimed it never discarded anything legitimate. Reading the closed issue's cluster first showed the claim false. Recorded because the proposal's own text reads as complete, and a later session reaching for it would repeat that mistake.

content:
**Should calibration be an explicit labelling pass the LLM runs, rather than a level read off passively accumulated labels?** Raised by the human partner 2026-09-12 as an alternative to keep in reserve while the accumulating design is tried. The shape: a session starts a calibration, issues several recalls drawn from what it has actually been doing in that session, labels the memories that come back, and then asks the server to recompute from those labels.

**What it would buy.** Label quality, which is the weak point of the accumulating design: `scope` attests only that the session knew which set to ask, and `used` sees only the uses that need a second tool call — a memory read straight out of a recall response and acted on is invisible to it. A deliberate pass replaces both proxies with a judgement. It also makes frequency a decision rather than a consequence of traffic, which is what the accumulating design cannot offer: at the measured rate of 19-20 labelled queries a week, a window filling to forty triggers about every two weeks per active set, and neither the rate nor the moment is anybody's choice.

**What it would cost, and what to watch for.** It spends session context on something that is not the session's work, and it asks the model to judge its own recall — the queries are drawn from what that session happened to do, so they inherit its topic and are not a sample of what the set will be asked. Both are reasons to measure the accumulating design first rather than to rule this out.
context: Designing the floor's recalibration with the human partner, after the min-over-everything rule turned out to be a ratchet.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing. Filed rather than carried because it is an alternative to a mechanism just built, and an alternative that lives only in a conversation is one the next session rebuilds the argument for. Recorded at 0.8 because the question is certainly live while its framing is one turn old.

Open rather than resolved deliberately: the human partner asked to try the accumulating design first and keep this in the back pocket, so what settles it is the measurement of the other one.

content: A proposed clause in `keyword-standards` forbidding a person's name as a keyword was rejected on 2026-08-12. The legitimate uses are ordinary -- "the third pull request from jbrown carrying this error", "jbrown is the subject matter expert on XYZ" -- and the dossier hazard is contained by routing rather than by spelling: a topical set returns what someone did on that project, not who they are. The keyword layer knows how a term is spelled and not what it aggregates, so a safeguard placed there sits where the information is not. `store-when`'s content rule is the right home, and it is already there.
context: Decided by the human partner while reviewing the keyword-standards draft, 2026-08-12. Checkable in the "What was left out" section of documents/design/conventions.md and the comment above KEYWORD_STANDARDS in src/conventions/catalog.rs.
why: Recorded because the clause is tempting and will be proposed again: it looks like a cheap safeguard, and what defeats it is not that the harm is unreal but that this layer cannot see it. That is decision-placement applied to a safeguard rather than to a parameter, which is the less obvious half of that principle. Two holes in the routing containment were left open rather than closed -- the personal set, which is the catch-all but never travels, and a set that declares itself for dossiers on people, which no keyword rule would stop anyway.

content: **Probed 2026-09-08, and the first finding is that `cut_at_largest_gap` is not a candidate mechanism for `no-non-match-floor`: it shipped on 2026-08-18 and recall has applied it ever since** — `src/store.rs`, the tail of `recall_across`, cutting on `traversal::combine(similarity, inherited)`. So the recorded caveat *wiring this to recall means deciding which score the cut reads* was already decided: it reads the combined score, and the precondition holds internally because `ranked` is sorted on the same value. **What survives of that caveat is a client-side hazard, now measured.** The `similarity` a caller sees is own-similarity alone, so the returned order is not monotonic in it — 5 of 9 probe queries, the worst being a hit at `0.520` ranked *fourth* behind three that inherited from the walk. Any client applying its own floor to `similarity` therefore drops top-ranked results and keeps lower ones. Re-run with `cargo test --test probes -- --ignored --nocapture`; needs `SCATTERHOARD_MODEL`.
context: Probing the gap cut against the live 844-vector corpus, the morning the tracking files were unified.
why: Recorded because the entry's own cluster reads as though the mechanism is still to be wired, and a session picking this up would set out to build what is already there — the 2026-09-07 caveat was written from the 2026-09-02 replay, which measured the harness rather than the shipped path. Naming the call site is what stops that happening twice. The non-monotonicity is kept because it is the half of the caveat that is real, and it is invisible from the payload: nothing in a result says the order was decided by a number the caller is not being shown.

content: **Left open deliberately when the non-match floor was built, 2026-09-12:** whether the window size of 100 is right, which the sweep could not settle because both stores held fewer labelled queries than that and their corpora were frozen while the real ones grew; whether the percentile and margin generalise past two stores of one project; and whether a walk-reached memory whose origin cleared the floor should survive a floor its own content similarity fails, which today it does not. `explicit-calibration-pass` holds the alternative shape the human partner asked to keep in reserve.
context: Moved 2026-09-24 out of the entry's head, which was over the length limit, in step 2 of the out-link work.
why: The built entry's deliberate stopping points, recorded because the state shows and the stopping does not: each looks like a finished choice from the code.

content: **Under `potion-multilingual-128M` the paraphrase test passes most languages that fail under the English models, so it discriminates; but three triplets per language are too few to set a threshold on.** Measured 2026-10-03, with the anchor's paraphrase ranked against seven other sentences. Multilingual scored English, Spanish, French, Russian and Hindi 3 of 3, Chinese and German 2, Japanese 1. Chinese's one miss was by 0.006. Under `potion-base-32M` the same languages scored 3, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1. A bar of all three would warn a multilingual user writing German or Japanese. More triplets per language, perhaps ten, should come before any threshold.
context: Building the declared-language check; the human partner asked about the multilingual model, which was found at SETUP.md's manual path after being wrongly reported missing.
why: It settles that the paraphrase test measures representation and not just difficulty, which the English-model runs alone could not show. It also exposes the sample size as the remaining weakness before the detector for `recall-is-latin-script-only` can be built. German and Japanese failing under a model that supports them points at the triplets, which one author wrote to share few words, rather than at the model.

content: Nothing recorded which file an imported memory came in from, so a repository claiming a set's name could contribute memories with no conflict and no warning. Closed 2026-09-24 on a report rather than the prevention its fixed-when asked for: set identity makes an import that declares another identity say so in its result (`identity_note_for_import`), and what that leaves unreported is only which repository a memory came from — records keep their authors, the committer is on the commit, and exporting to the wrong repository shows up as a noisy diff at merge. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `imported-memories-carry-no-arrival-provenance`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Settling the two issues whose prevention arrived as a report rather than a refusal, after calibrating both shared sets and graduating four common causes to coding-lessons; next is the out-link supersession work.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. Closed by the human partner after the corrected analysis showed the residue was not the local user being credited with others' memories but only the missing name of a source repository, a gap git leaves for copied code too. The human partner's reason for accepting that: a wrong-repository export will surface as a noisy diff during the merge attempt. The fixed-when's *cannot* was met by *did, and says so*, the project's usual report-not-refuse choice.

content: `absorb` internalised links to memories that did not arrive: absorbing part of a set turned working cross-set links into same-set links to ids this set lacked. Fixed 2026-09-28 in `absorb_set` in `src/mcp.rs`: a link is made internal only if its target will be a memory here, either arriving in the file or already held, and a tombstone does not count as held. The rest keep their cross-set form and are named under `not_internalised`, and a memory with nothing to internalise is not superseded. Pinned by four tests in `tests/sets.rs`, among them `absorb_internalises_a_link_whose_target_arrived_in_an_earlier_absorb` and `absorb_does_not_internalise_a_link_to_a_memory_this_set_forgot`, and by five mutations. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `absorb-internalises-links-to-memories-that-did-not-arrive`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Starting on the open issues after both code items on the release gate were closed the same day; this was the first of the three corrupts-severity issues, revised after the human partner asked about absorbing a set in steps.
why: Superseded the same day, before commit, because the first fix asked only whether the target arrived in this file. The human partner's scenario broke that: C absorbed first, B later, and a link to C written in between was left cross-set, to dangle once the absorbed set was dropped. The first fix rested on a worry that a held id might be a different memory. The human partner questioned it, and it was mistaken: ids are generated universally unique, so one id in two sets is one memory copied, and absorb refuses an arriving copy that differs. The mutation `absorb: collect every memory with any foreign link as a candidate` survives with its recorded reason. Left open: `absorb` could replace the manual steps for moving memories between sets (set-lifecycle.md).

content: **Build the non-match floor: a local query log, calibration from labelled queries, and a floor read against raw similarity.** Decided 2026-09-11 by the human partner; designed in `documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md` under *Proposed 2026-09-11: the floor is calibrated from a local query log, and reads raw similarity*. **Built so far:** the log itself, on 2026-09-11 — every semantic recall a session asks writes one row per store it was scored against, carrying the raw and centred top scores, the scope label, whether a floor silenced that store, and the ids the session received, and no query text; `tests/query_log.rs` and the *Built 2026-09-11* section of that design document. **Still missing:** the `used` label, which needs a later lookup or link to find the queries that returned that memory; the calibration action; the floor's storage per store and model; and the raw similarity the floor should read — `Stages::floor` still compares the centred score. **Built looks like:** a calibration that sets a floor only once there are about forty labelled queries, a margin below the lowest, cleared on a model change; the scan carrying raw content similarity beside the centred score so the floor reads one while ranking keeps the other; recall reporting when the floor silenced everything, with a way to ask again without it; and the floor lowering itself whenever a scope-labelled query scores below it. **To settle while building:** whether forty queries and a 0.05 margin generalise beyond two stores of one project, what bounds the log, whether a query no session ever labelled is worth keeping in it, and whether a walk-reached memory whose origin cleared the floor should survive a floor its own content similarity fails. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `calibrated-non-match-floor`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Picking the entry up from the 2026-09-12 checkpoint and building the log, the piece the checkpoint named as the next step.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. Superseded 2026-09-11 because its *Missing* list opened with "the log, since nothing records queries", which stopped being true that day — a present-tense claim in a head is the kind that reads as current for ever and sends the next session to build something that exists. Still open and still ready: the log was always the piece everything else waited on, and what remains is the calibration, the floor's storage and the raw score the floor reads.

The evidence lives in the resolved question `floor-calibration-source` and is not repeated here: two stores simulated walking forward, raw against centred, the forty-query threshold and what a floor costs the queries it does not silence.

content: **Trialled properly 2026-09-08: `potion-retrieval-32M` does not fix the non-match problem, and the six-query pilot that suggested it did was flattered by its sample.** Against 29 real queries harvested from session transcripts and 15 with no answer in the corpus, the best possible split leaves **4 errors of 44 under the shipping `potion-base-32M` and 4 of 44 under `potion-retrieval-32M`** — identical. The distributions shift together rather than apart: in-domain median 0.488 against out-of-domain max 0.444 for the base model, 0.462 against 0.388 for the tuned one, overlapping in both. On the six hard cases the tuned model had looked clean, with every in-domain query above every unanswerable one by a margin of 0.011; at 44 queries that gap is gone. **Retrieval quality is a wash and the two labelled corpora disagree about its direction**: on the 45 real memories the base model leads on P@5, 32.0% against 29.0%, while on the 429 synthetic ones the tuned model leads under both blind labellers, 51.7% and 43.3% against 47.5% and 40.0% — and MRR reverses the other way on the synthetic corpus, 0.834 against 0.757. The one consistent direction is r@10, favouring the tuned model by two to four points on all three. **No change recommended.** What the tuned model does change is *which* queries fail, not how many.
context: Trialling the retrieval-tuned model properly after its six-query pilot looked promising.
why:
Recorded because leaving this as a promising lead would cost the next session the same day: the pilot numbers are genuinely striking, the model is on disk, and the swap is a one-line configuration change, so it will be reached for again unless the trial that closed it travels with it.

The pattern underneath is the more useful record, and it is now three for three. A charter pilot on seven queries, an alignment pilot on twelve, and this one on six all showed clean separation that a properly sized trial erased. Small query sets manufacture separation, because whichever way the errors fall there is room for a threshold between them; the errors only become visible once the classes are large enough to overlap. **Anything proposed on this entry should be shown at least forty queries before it is believed**, and the best-split figures here are still optimistic, since the split is chosen after seeing the labels.

content:
**The per-change recall habit decayed from session to session, though every session recalled the guide at its start.** Measured 2026-10-04 from flightlog, against each session's behaviour-changing commits:

| Session | Habit recalls before changes | How the guide was read |
|---|---|---|
| `4268f526` (2026-09-29) | about 7 of 7, in the guide's exact form | full, limit 10 |
| `2abe4c7e` (2026-09-30 to 10-01) | about 6 of 10, `coding-lessons` scope, limit 10, no `ignore_floor` | `detail: summary` |
| `8a1c2c6d` (2026-10-01 to 10-04) | 2 of about 8 | `detail: summary`, limit 5, so parts 5 and 6 were never shown |
| `e28cf0bd` (2026-10-04) | 1 of about 8 | full, limit 3 |

**The drift was the summary read**, not a checkpoint or a compaction: part 2's summary line stops before its parameters, so the session invented its own. **The fade is not explained by it**, since today's session read part 2 in full and still lapsed. In the same sessions, rules in `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` held.
context: Preparing the first beta release. This came after a replay showed signposts would have preceded 4 of 38 failures, and the human partner proposed shipping `coding-lessons` with only the recall habit.
why: The human partner asked whether putting the habit in the opt-in language would have helped it stick. No session has run with that, so this is circumstantial. It fits a habit delivered by one recall at startup: sometimes truncated by the reader's own choice of detail, and otherwise read and then forgotten, while always-loaded text stays present. Four sessions, one author, differing in task and length: suggestive rather than settled. Re-measure the same way after any change.

content: This set holds knowledge about Scatterhoard itself: how it works, how it came to be as it is, and how the work on it is done. A memory belongs here when it would still matter to someone working on Scatterhoard in a later session and would not matter to someone working on a different project.
context: Superseded 2026-08-25 at the human partner's request, after the convention it applies was itself revised by being applied to the two live charters. `coding-lessons` is deliberately left unchanged as the control, so the two sets' intake over the next several sessions measures whether this rewrite did anything.
why: Rewritten 2026-08-25 under `route-where`'s new charter clause, and this set is the case that clause was drafted from. The previous version opened with a list — decisions, measurements, defects, constraints — every item a kind of *conclusion*, and the corpus followed it: methods and paths-to-a-decision went unrecorded here while `coding-lessons`, whose description names technique, accumulated them freely under the same `store-when`. A charter's description silently decides which kinds of thing get written, not only where they go, so the subject now leads and no list stands in its place. "How the work on it is done" is what admits a measurement procedure without naming *method* as a category, since naming categories is what rebuilt the whitelist last time. The dropped sentence about lessons that would hold anywhere was not lost: it moved into `route-where`, because it is a routing rule every set would need rather than a fact about this one.

content: **Whether, and how, the write path should stop a subject memory carrying a reserved control mark.** Raised 2026-09-11 by the human partner after the third documented round of `reserved-keywords-carry-subject-memories`: five memories on 2026-09-06, one on 09-07 by a session that had loaded the corrected `keyword-standards` that day, and two written 09-08 and found 09-11 — every one a memory *about* charters carrying `hoard-scope-topics`, all in the `scatterhoard` set, which has had a live charter since 2026-08-12. The served `about-` rule is not holding on its own. **Three candidates so far.** (1) A dedicated tool for setting a charter, the only path allowed to write the mark — exact, at the cost of another tool. (2) A block-list at `memorize`, `amend` and supersession: refuse a `hoard-` keyword that is not a known control mark, leaving `hoard-proj-` to projects, and never at import, where sets written by other versions must still load — it catches typos and invented marks, but not this case, because the misused mark is a legitimate one. (3) A shape check for marks that have a shape: a charter is one per set, so a write adding `hoard-scope-topics` while the set has a live charter, without superseding it, is refused with both remedies named — supersede the charter, or use `about-hoard-scope-topics`. That would have refused every instance on record; `hoard-author` has a shape too, since an identity record attributes itself; the watch-list marks have none. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `guarding-reserved-keywords`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Re-keying two charter-matching measurements that carried the reserved charter mark, after the human partner asked why they had been flagged and said they were watching for repercussions of the conventions update. Same stretch: the store-stopping embed fix and its commit.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. Filed as a question because nothing is decided: the human partner offered the first two as ideas with their costs, saying they had no clever answer that avoided new complexity, and the third was mine, raised in reply.

**Why software rather than more convention text.** Three rounds in six days, the second by a session that had just loaded the rule, is the evidence that served text alone does not prevent it; `01M1ZCCGZNFDRAEG6C1GEMT80W` concluded that the rule does not fire on its own and something has to look. Since the 2026-09 conventions update, the session-start charter recall does look, and it found the third round — but only after two days of delivering those memories to every session as though they were charters.

**What each candidate depends on.** The shape check turns a description into an invariant: `documents/design/memory-data-model.md` says a set's charter is a singleton, as a contrast with `hoard-author`, but nothing enforces it, so adopting (3) is a design decision rather than a fix. The block-list needs something that does not exist yet — a single list of control marks in code. Only `hoard-author` is a constant today (`AUTHOR_KEYWORD` in `src/store.rs`); the others appear as strings in the catalog and the documents, so a list would be a new source of truth that the served text must be kept in step with.

content: Reported 2026-10-29 from Claude Desktop on a different machine: auto-compaction appears to fire when a session's context is above some minimum level and the session has been idle for more than an hour. This fits the evidence already under `the-precompact-hook-asks-a-model-that-never-gets-a-turn`: session `8a53d486` was compacted at about 54% of its window after its last turn ended 05:45 UTC and the hook fired at 06:39, roughly 54 minutes idle, while idle stretches of 6 and 16 hours at about 100k tokens produced nothing. The minimum level is still unknown; it lies somewhere between about 100k tokens and about 54% of a 1M window.
context: The scatterhoard set's full review, stopped at about 410 memories to resume in a new session at 76% context; the human partner passed this on from another machine.
why: Turns "the threshold is unknown" into a two-part trigger a test can aim at: a session left idle past an hour above the level will be compacted, which bears on any long task, a review especially, that pauses for the human. Reported second-hand from one other machine rather than measured here, hence the confidence; checkable by leaving a session above roughly half full idle for an hour and reading its transcript for a compaction boundary.

content: A memory opening with a numbered heading like `1.` summarised to just `1.…` when no later sentence ended within the cap. Fixed 2026-09-30: in `summarise` in `src/memory/text.rs`, a terminator ends a sentence only if the sentence it closes is more than one word, so `1.` and `No.` are passed over and the cut falls to an earlier boundary or a word. Chosen over a length floor, which would also catch `Found 2026-08-02.` but needs a number and would have turned about ten good heading lines into word cuts. Over the live corpora the change moved no line: 278 and 64 sentence cuts before and after. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-numbered-opening-summarises-to-its-number`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through the open issues with the human partner, after fixing the reembed-count mutation and auditing every surviving mutation against the whole suite.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed as its fixed-when asked: a boundary that leaves nearly nothing is passed over for a word cut. Decided with the human partner between a structural rule and a length floor, from a measurement of every sentence cut in both shared sets: no one-word sentence cut remained, the shortest was 17 characters, and the short ones were deliberate headings. Limit: `Step 1. Do X` still cuts after `Step 1.`, since that sentence is two words. Guarded by `a_one_word_sentence_is_not_where_the_line_ends` and its after-another sibling in `tests/memory_model.rs`, and by two mutations.

content: **Measured 2026-09-07: `capture-before-ending` names *you are about to commit* as a trigger, and across ten commits that day it fired once.** `export-before-commit` fired all ten. The two are halves of one convention that was deliberately split on 2026-08-12, when the one-sentence version turned out to carry an unstated assumption that anything worth exporting had been captured — and the failure landed exactly on the seam that split created. **The mechanism looks like this: the mechanical half crowds out the judgement half.** Export has a tool call, so running it feels like the pre-commit step is done; capture has only a question, and a question that nothing refuses to answer is easy to have answered already in one's head. **A second crowding compounded it**: the day's task *was* storing memories, one cluster per entry, so the capture convention felt continuously satisfied — but *what is worth remembering from this stretch* is a different question from *what does this entry hold*, and the answers to the first kept ending up in conversation instead.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md, when the human partner proposed a say-it-then-store-it prompt and a deliberate meta-level check.
why:
Recorded because the split was right and this is not an argument to undo it. Merging them back would restore the implication that exporting produces a capture, which is what the split removed. What it says instead is that a judgement step paired with a mechanical one needs its own evidence of having run, or the mechanical one's completion stands in for both.

The task-crowding half is the more interesting one and is specific to this kind of work: any session whose object-level task is *storing memories* will feel the capture convention satisfied by the task itself. That is a hazard of memory work rather than of memory conventions, and it predicts that migration sessions in particular will under-capture at the meta level while over-capturing at the item level — which is precisely what the day's record shows.

content:
**A write that would give a set a second live charter is refused.** Built 2026-09-14. Decided 2026-09-11 by the human partner and recorded in `documents/design/conventions.md` under *Decided 2026-09-11: the write path guards the reserved namespace*: a write adding `hoard-scope-topics` while the set already has a live charter, and not superseding it, is refused, and the refusal names both ways out — supersede the charter, or give a memory about charters `about-hoard-scope-topics`.

**What shipped:** `Store::check_one_live_charter`, called from `Store::insert` beside the cycle check, so `memorize` and amendment both reach it; a charter that supersedes every live charter, and the live charter rewritten under its own id, pass. Import writes through `accept_from_file` and is never refused, so a merge carrying two charters still loads. **`absorb` carries charters forward through `Store::carry_forward`**, which keeps the cycle check and not this one: absorbing merges the other set's records by the import path, can leave two live charters, and then supersedes this set's memories that linked into the absorbed set — the charter among them if it did — and refusing that replacement would stop the absorb with the records already merged. A set left with two charters shows both in `hoard_sets status`, and the next charter written has to supersede both. Contract: seven tests and a carry-forward test in `tests/store.rs`, and an absorb test in `tests/sets.rs`; five mutations, all caught.

The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `one-live-charter-per-set`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building one-live-charter-per-set, the fourth item taken that session, right after closing charter-declares-set-languages and restarting the server.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because the entry is built. Readiness facet dropped, as built entries carry none.

The absorb exemption is recorded in the head rather than left to the design document because it is the one place the built guard departs from the letter of the backlog entry, which said the refusal goes in `Store::insert` and not in `Store::write` — absorb also reaches `insert`, and the entry did not foresee that. The departure keeps the entry's own principle: refuse on the authored path, never on the reconciling one.

content: Two keyword spellings for what looked like one idea turned out to be two opposite policies, so the split was not a defect: `refuse-not-remark` and `remark-not-refuse` name a design and the design that replaced it. Filed and withdrawn 2026-09-02, both errors found by reading the memories instead of the keyword list. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `a-split-keyword-spelling-halves-every-search-for-it`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster whose standing is withdrawn: the shapes were real and the reading was wrong, and this file keeps a withdrawn entry because the investigation is worth being able to find.

content: **Why the timing was the whole question, and why it was decided rather than deferred -- 2026-08-20.** The change is a **format-version bump touching the wire form, the store's `meta` row and the file header**, with a reader accepting both spellings for a window -- the same shape as migrations already done here, and **cheap only while one machine holds every set**. **After release it is a breaking change to every user's configuration.** So the question was never *should we ever* but **do we, before the door shuts**. It was deliberately not decided the night it was raised. **The migration itself was smaller than it looked and the real cost sat elsewhere:** no memory quotes a full id in its prose, since cross-references live in the `links` structure, so there was nothing to chase through the corpus by hand -- what existed was mechanical, roughly 219 id-bearing rows across the live stores, about 2,400 occurrences in machine-generated corpus and labelling files, and five in tests.
context: Migrating open-questions.md, recovering content a faulty deletion boundary had left orphaned after the entry's head was already stored.
why:
Recorded because *the door shuts at release* is the reasoning that made this urgent, and it applies unchanged to every other record-shape or wire-format question still open -- the window is a property of the project's stage rather than of ids.

The cost breakdown is kept because it contradicts the intuition: an identifier change sounds like it should ripple through prose everywhere, and the design's own discipline of keeping references in structure rather than in text is what made it mechanical. That is an argument for the discipline as much as a fact about this migration.

context: Preparing the first beta release, right after adding the GitHub remotes and retiring the no-remote signpost.
why: Testers' bug reports need a build they can name, and their stores will outlive the build that wrote them. A pre-release suffix says "not yet 0.1.0" and `0.x` promises no compatibility. It goes on the conventions page because that is the one call every session makes, and on the first page only, as the other asides are.

content: **Whether a memory's author is a name or a reference. Substantially built by 2026-09-07, and open only in its residue.** Proposed 2026-08-31 with the human partner: `created.by` holds the id of a `hoard-author` memory rather than the name itself, so changing a published identity supersedes one record instead of rewriting every record that names it. The motivating case is general -- the account name a machine supplies is not the identity a person publishes under, and joining the two in a public trail is a cost rather than tidiness. **What shipped, verified 2026-09-07:** `by` is a `MemoryId`, `local` gets author records too (decided rather than exempted, so the field is not a union), the set carries `hoard-author` records, and the old single `author` action became the three operations `mint`, `identify` and `rename`, split because one entry point inferring which was meant would be a decision-placement violation. **What has not shipped is the refinement that motivated part of it:** `create` still does not require an author, so the silent machine-account default it was meant to remove is still there. Also open: whether the first record attributes itself. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `author-name-or-reference`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

**Kept open rather than resolved on migration**, unlike `set-uuid` which was closed the same day. The distinction is that this entry names a specific refinement -- `create` requiring an author -- which is verifiably not built: the tool's `create` takes a name and nothing else. Marking it resolved would retire a named piece of work that nobody did. The head says what shipped so the row does not read as though none of it had.

content: **A fourth candidate source for the floor's calibration: a query log the server keeps in the store, locally, and never exports.** Reached 2026-09-11 in two steps. It began as *harvest the queries from this machine's session transcripts* — the `flightlog` MCP server the human partner had just added indexes past Claude Code sessions and filters by tool name, so every past `mcp__scatterhoard__hoard_recall` comes back with its arguments, `scope` among them. **The human partner then asked what would be distributed with the project and how anyone else would reach it, and that killed the transcript form:** it works here only because Claude Code writes JSONL under `~/.claude/projects/`, and Scatterhoard is a server behind MCP that cannot assume any client keeps such a log, or where. **Moving the log into the server keeps what mattered and travels:** the server sees the query, its `scope` argument, which sets the hits came from, and a later `hoard_lookup` of a returned id — the answerability labels the harvest was recovering — and it works for every client. Nothing data-like ships: no probe set and no calibration corpus, only the mechanism; a fresh import gets no floor until its own queries accumulate, which is the over-recalling end of the ruling. flightlog stays useful here as a one-off bootstrap for history that predates the log.
context: Returning to the floor after making the multilingual model a supported alternative; the human partner added the flightlog MCP server, saying past sessions get mined often.
why:
Recorded because it keeps the query history out of the export entirely, which removes the objection the human partner raised against carrying queries in the set — queries can hold private text and the export is what gets published. Staying local does not make that concern vanish, since a query can carry anything a memory can; it stops being a *publication*, which is the one-way door.

It also fits what the design already does with derived state: vectors never leave the machine, and a floor calibrated from local evidence is the same kind of thing.

**The correction is worth as much as the candidate.** The transcript version looked strongest until it was asked what a second user would receive, and its premise turned out to be an artifact of this machine's client. The general form — *a design that reads the client's files is not one the server can ship* — applies well beyond calibration.

Open: where the log lives and what bounds it — a table the export never streams, a cap on how much is kept, a way to clear it, and whether a query no session ever used is worth keeping at all.

content: Scatterhoard's `local` is one set, not a class of machine-bound sets, resolved 2026-08-23. The long-running question of what to call the class was answered by there being no class: once the cross-set trust gradient was withdrawn, `Local` had exactly one property left -- `exports_to` answers None -- and one property needs a boolean rather than a class word. Every other set is a symmetric `Shared` set, including ones with no repository (a set across two of your own laptops, a household set, a volunteer board's institutional memory); those are created as shared sets today and nothing further is coming to serve them better.
context: Decided by the human partner 2026-08-23 while exploring whether a simpler symmetric design could meet the Golden Rule constraint. Recorded in documents/design/set-lifecycle.md under "Resolved 2026-08-23: `local` is one set"; the scalar-discriminant question in open-questions.md was closed by it. Checkable against `Scope::exports_to` in src/memory/scope.rs, which as of that date had exactly one live caller outside tests.
why: The reason the class question was unanswerable is the part worth carrying: `local` was class-shaped only because it had a power no other set had. A scope with special powers invites a scope system -- you start asking which other scopes get which powers, and that needs a vocabulary -- so removing the power dissolved the question instead of answering it. Three recurring questions closed together this way: whether `local` is unique or a class, what to call the class, and why a binding choice had to be made when the person knew least. The binding-choice complaint dissolves too, because publishing a set later changes nothing structural, so creating a set shared and never publishing it loses nothing. What must be protected in any future change is the by-construction guarantee that the local set always exists, since `route-where`'s fallback clause points at it.

content: Forgetting a memory that other memories link to says nothing about those links, so a session restating it can strand them without noticing. Decided 2026-10-18 with the human partner: when the forgotten memory has in-links, `hoard_correct`'s `forget` response names them and says that storing the replacement with a `supersedes` link to the forgotten id carries them across. Built when that note appears on a forget with in-links and is absent on one without, both cases tested. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `forget-is-silent-about-in-links`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Carrying out the publication review's decisions: the first restate-then-forget stranded three in-links until the human partner remembered the earlier test.
why: Head of a backlog cluster. Ready: nothing is missing but the work. The mistake happens at the forget, and only a cue at that moment reaches a session that did not search beforehand. A search would not have helped either: the earlier test that proved the mechanism (`01M3NQCSQZE0G8ESQ609GB7D6D`) is worded as undoing a forget, and a session restating a memory asks in different words. Restate-then-forget will be routine once the sharing preferences reach the export review. A supersession of a forgotten id already returns nothing, which that memory records as undecided. This entry covers the forget side only.

content: **Where a memory whose subject genuinely is a person goes, in a set shared with a small known audience.** Raised 2026-08-23 while checking the publish-boundary resolution against a household set. **Most of the case is already handled and this was initially overstated.** `route-where`'s third override refuses a set *organised around* people, which a household set is not -- it is organised around a household -- and its operative half routes a memory about a person to *the work it concerns*, so a note about a contractor who helped with an installation lands in the household set correctly, because the work it concerns is the installation. The convention permits that today. **The residue is narrower and real:** a memory whose subject is a person and which concerns no work -- a household member's dietary restriction, say -- routes to the personal set, which does not reach the spouse the household set exists to share with. **Why this is not simply a drafting fix.** The obvious scoping remedy does not transfer, because under the symmetric design every non-local set can publish, so the clause would be unchanged in effect. The test has to come from the Golden Rule's demand C directly -- *the person is a detail of the record, never its organising principle* -- which is a judgement about a set's shape rather than a branch on its scope. **So: do not redraft from the conclusion again.** Compiling this principle from its conclusions rather than its derivation has already misfired twice, `route-where`'s overrides being one of the two. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `person-as-subject-in-a-shared-set`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

**The self-correction is carried in the head deliberately** -- *this was initially overstated* -- because the entry's own first reading was that the convention forbade something it permits, and a session meeting the residue without that context would re-open the wider question and redraft the override.

*Do not redraft from the conclusion again* is the operative instruction and has a track record behind it: two misfires, one of them the very override this question is about. Any change here starts from demand C's derivation, and the case to test against is a set whose charter is a shared domain in which named people recur as participants.

The illustrative examples are given generically rather than with the names the entry used, since the record does not need them and they would outlive the question.

content: Fixed 2026-08-21 **by the neighbouring question rather than by the field**, and the human partner's reading is what got there: this is not a link problem, it is that `Scope::Shared(SetName("local"))` is constructible at all, so the same ambiguity arrives through `hoard_sets create`, a file header and the `shared:local` scalar form as well. `local` is now a **reserved set name**, refused case-folded at `SetName::new`, and the link case falls out with no check of its own — unrepresentable rather than detected. **It overturns a stated intent, which is worth recording**: two tests read *"A project may legitimately be called `local`"* and asserted its store path did not collide with the local store's, and that permission was recorded nowhere else — not in a design document, only in those comments. What the tests actually protected is path derivation being injective across scopes, which does not depend on the word; they now assert that with names that are still legal, and the word itself is pinned as unconstructible in [tests/memory_model.rs](tests/memory_model.rs). Recorded in [Memory Steering](documents/design/memory-steering.md), where the permission should have been in the first place.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A fix that moved up a level and made the bad state unconstructible, and a permission that existed only in two test comments — which is where an intent goes to be overturned without anyone noticing it was ever decided.

content: Scatterhoard resolved 2026-08-23 that no edge changes the standing of a memory in another set, in either direction: a cross-set SUPERSEDES, EXCEPTION_TO or CONTRADICTS is reported, never acted on. This withdrew the earlier trust gradient (a local memory may supersede a project memory; a project memory may not suppress a local one), which had settled local-versus-project and said nothing about project-versus-project -- the case the `a-set-can-suppress-another-sets-memory` Corrupts defect rests on. An authored SUPERSEDED_BY naming a cross-set target stays legal, because it is a memory's own claim about itself rather than a reach into someone else's standing.
context: Decided by the human partner 2026-08-23, extending their 2026-08-21 argument that an LLM can hold two contradictory memories in context and software cannot. Recorded in documents/design/cross-set-references.md under "Resolved 2026-08-23"; the withdrawn reasoning is preserved there as a quotation. Implementation is unbuilt -- see `edge-authority-across-sets` in BACKLOG.md and the Corrupts entry in ISSUES.md.
why: Two things make this worth keeping beyond the document. First, the fix has two halves and only one protects anyone: refusing the write stops an honest client, but ignoring the edge at resolution is what protects the reader, because a hostile file was never written by our client -- a refusal alone would be theatre, and that is easy to invert when reading the rule later. Second, it is a security fix that shrinks the design: the gradient needed a three-case comparison of both endpoints' scopes, and the replacement asks one question, so no scope comparison enters the resolution path at all. Measured the same day: all ten SUPERSEDES edges in the three live sets are same-set, so the capability given up has no live instance.

content: **The `backup` action writes to `$SCATTERHOARD_BACKUPS/<set>/<timestamp>.json`, set by the person in the client configuration, and to `<common>/backups/` where it is unset.** Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. Each backup reports how many that set already has, and pruning is left to the person.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public, after deciding backups are their own ungated action.
why: Writing only beside the store gives a same-disk backup, which the human partner had already found protects against deletion and nothing else, so they kept their backups off the machine. Those were `file` exports, which the gate would now review as public. A location set by whoever configures the machine, never by a call, keeps the rule that a model cannot loosen the review. Automatic pruning was rejected because a safety mechanism should not delete copies on its own. Restated before publication without where the human partner keeps their backups, which is a fact about their machine.

content: For the length of a mutation pass, every client that spawned a Scatterhoard server got a deliberately broken one: each mutation rebuilt `target/debug/scatterhoard`, the absolute path every server entry names, so a session could write to the operator's real sets with whichever guard that mutation removed. Fixed 2026-08-25 by giving the pass its own `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-mutation-pass-publishes-a-broken-server-to-the-path-clients-spawn`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Measuring Scatterhoard's graph shape from the exported memory file counts only half of every relation. Export carries each edge once, written on the memory that authored it, so a per-memory count of the links array yields out-degree alone. Doing that put isolated memories at 21 of 36 when the true figure counting both directions is 11 of 36. Any measurement of graph shape must count source and target both.
context: Made and corrected 2026-08-14 while reopening the graph-traversal design; the human partner caught it by asking whether the observed asymmetry was an artifact of uncomputed reciprocal links. Checkable at Store::incoming in src/store.rs and the module note "Edges live in their own table, and that table is the reverse index".
why: The error is easy to make and hard to notice, because the exported file looks like the complete record and the resulting number is plausible. It nearly supported a wrong conclusion — that the graph was too sparse for traversal to be worth building — when the real sparsity is roughly half that. The reverse direction is not missing from the system: the links table is indexed on target as well as source, so it is a second index over the same rows rather than a derived copy.

content: A malformed tool-call close absorbed the parameters after it, so a swallowed `why` or `context` landed inside `content` and the call returned success — twenty occurrences across a month, six of them repairs for the one before. Fixed 2026-08-19 by an escape mechanism first and then a refusal keyed on a conjunction. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `malformed-tool-call-damage-is-stored-silently`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row. This is the largest entry in the file — nine dates, twenty occurrences — and its members are the clearest case for the episodic shape.

content: Putting a Scatterhoard store inside the checkout's `scatterhoard_mem/` is attractive and rejected. An in-tree store dies with an ordinary `rm -rf` of the working tree, taking unexported memories with it and bypassing the save-first rule, which exists so memories cannot be discarded without first being written somewhere the caller named. It can also be committed by accident, shipping unexported memories past the export review gate. Central storage plus a registry keeps both guarantees, and separating a UUID identity from a recorded path survives a checkout being moved or deleted better than a self-locating store does.
context: Considered and rejected 2026-08-06 while drafting documents/design/store-registry.md, where the argument is recorded under "why the stores stay central rather than in the working tree".
why: The in-tree location is the first idea anyone has once the many-to-one mapping is named, because it makes the store self-locating and needs no registry -- so it will be proposed again. The deciding argument is not the obvious one: accidental commit comes to mind first, but casual deletion of a stale checkout is both more likely and entirely unguarded, and it defeats a safety rule the design spent real effort establishing.

content: **Restate-then-forget takes a detail out of an exported memory before publication: store the corrected memory with a `supersedes` link to the original, then forget the original.** Used twice on 2026-10-18 in the publication review. The tombstone carries no content, and a search for the removed wording returns only the restatement. The `supersedes` link is what keeps the original's in-links: the tombstone's `superseded_by` names the replacement, and the walk carries links to the forgotten id across to it with their labels intact (`01M3NQCSQZE0G8ESQ609GB7D6D`). The link can be added after the forget, since a supersession of a forgotten id is accepted. **Two costs remain.** A memory written before the 2,000-character limit cannot be restated whole, so restating splits it, and each part supersedes the original. And the whole memory has to be retyped through the tool to change one phrase, which is where a restatement can drift from the original without anyone noticing.
context: Carrying out the first decisions of the publication review: removing the volunteer-role detail and correcting the memory that took a hypothetical as real.
why: Once the sharing preferences reach the export review, this becomes the instrument it uses whenever a flag is cleared by rewording rather than removal. Superseding alone cannot do the job, because the superseded version stays in the exported file. Forgetting alone strands every in-link, and that happened first time: the restatements were stored without the `supersedes` link, and the human partner remembered the earlier test that showed the link carries them. Nothing in the forget response mentions the in-links or the link that would keep them. Ids: `01M596KMRHEBS9K6A68V1RQRXB` (the split) and `01M596MJA6FCH857ZSYM0ENVA4`.

content: **Refuse a write that would give a set a second live charter.** Decided 2026-09-11 by the human partner and recorded in `documents/design/conventions.md` under *Decided 2026-09-11: the write path guards the reserved namespace*: a write that adds `hoard-scope-topics` while the set already has a live charter, and does not supersede that charter, is refused, naming both remedies — supersede the charter, or use `about-hoard-scope-topics` for a memory about charters. A set's first charter and a replacement by supersession pass. **Missing:** all of it — searching `src/` for `hoard-scope-topics` finds only documentation and served text, so no code treats the charter mark specially today. **Built looks like:** the refusal beside `check_no_cycle` in `Store::insert`, the authoring path, and *not* in `Store::write`, which import also reaches through `accept_from_file` and which must never refuse here; tests for the refused second charter, the first charter, replacement by supersession, and an import carrying two live charters; a mutation proving the guard is covered. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `one-live-charter-per-set`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Filing the guard on the reserved charter mark after the human partner decided to enforce one live charter per set. Same stretch: re-keying two measurements that carried the mark, and the store-stopping embed fix.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. Ready, because nothing is missing but the work — the one design choice with any weight, where the guard lives, follows from the supersession-cycle precedent, which refuses on the authored path and reports on the reconciled one for the same reason. The case for the check, three rounds of the misuse in six days that it would have refused, lives in the resolved question `guarding-reserved-keywords` and is not repeated here.

content: Fixed 2026-08-08: `Store::reconcile_embeddings` embeds every memory with no vector, and runs on first *use* rather than at open — embedding at open is the thing the in-memory vector cache exists to avoid. With no gap it costs one `LEFT JOIN` and never touches the model. **One mechanism, three cases, deliberately**: a store that has just gained a model, one whose model was swapped, and one holding memories written during a gap are all *memories with no vector for the model in hand*, so they are one query and one repair rather than three code paths that could disagree.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the generalisation that made it one mechanism: three defects that looked distinct share a single predicate, so they are repaired by one query rather than by three paths free to diverge.

content: Unpublished sets have no transport but a file syncer. Raised 2026-08-23 by the human partner. Every set other than `local` is a symmetric `Shared` set, including those with no repository: a set across two of your own laptops, a household set, a volunteer board's institutional memory. **What is wrong with a syncer**: it produces conflicted copies rather than merges, where `git` merges three ways against a common ancestor. Per-record base checksums make two conflicted copies reconcilable by importing both, so it is recoverable but manual, and it degrades as a set gets more use. A SQLite store in a synced folder is a different and worse matter and stays prohibited. **What this is not**: a new scope class; the scope question is settled in the negative. **Still blocked**, now on one condition: at least one unpublished shared set lived with long enough to say whether the syncer is inadequate or merely inelegant. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `built-in-sync`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Adding the first git remotes for the beta release, after rewriting the author address out of both histories.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because the first of its two conditions, the release gate's remote, was met on 2026-10-04. The second, lived experience with an unpublished set, has not started, so the entry stays blocked, now without a link to a memory, since what it waits on is experience rather than a decision.

content: A deletion that leaves no trace cannot be told from something that never existed, so every part of the system that meets the absence misreads it. In this project: forgotten memories whose vectors stayed in the scan, a file read that dropped every tombstone, an older file silently resurrecting a forgotten memory as an ordinary change, a forgotten id coming back as a memory and a tombstone at once, and forgetting a chain's middle cascading away the edge that said its end was stale. **The structural fix is to make a deletion a record** — a tombstone carrying what a later reader needs, here its ancestry and the checksum it replaced — and to treat absence as carrying no meaning at all.
context: Re-deriving the common causes of defects across all 104 issues, and moving them from a hand-written section of TRACKING.md into memories the index is generated from. Linked to its general form on 2026-09-24, alongside calibrating both shared sets.
why: Not in the original analysis; all five instances are from the tombstone work between 2026-08-07 and 2026-08-30. Its general form went to `coding-lessons` on 2026-09-24; superseded only to add the `instance_of` link to it.

content: **Read-only loading is built; evaluation is not.** As of 2026-09-17: `LoadMode` in `src/store.rs`, stored in `meta` under `load_mode`; `Store::choose_read_only`, refused once a set holds records; the write refusal on `insert`, `carry_forward` and `forget`, with early refusals in `Server::author_for`, `absorb` and the author actions; `create`'s optional `mode`, defaulting to read-write; `status` reporting it; `drop` with an optional `save_to`, skipping the safety copy for a read-only set and honouring a path given anyway; and **one copy of each identity loaded, in `Server::settle_identity`** — a lone copy loads whatever its mode, the single read-write copy wins among several, and otherwise every copy is withheld and `status` lists them. Dropping a copy settles the identity again, so a survivor loads without a restart. **Not yet built:** how a read-only set's signposts get recalled, which needs a decision between convention text and a `status` field; promotion to read-write; and evaluation mode, which also needs the cross-set link question answered first. Check the status line in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md), which is kept current as slices land.
context: Finishing the load-once slice of read-only mode.
why: Supersedes the partway record written on 2026-09-16, which named the drop and load-once slices as unbuilt and pointed at an unused `owes_a_safety_copy` and a withhold-all `add_store` as signs of it. Both are now built, so that memory would send a session looking for work that is done. What remains is listed for the same reason the old one listed it: the state shows, the deliberate stopping does not.

content: **All three ways back from an accidental adoption are wrong, and the one that looks right is the harmful one -- the analysis from when this was raised, 2026-08-26.** **`forget` is actively harmful:** it writes tombstones, tombstones propagate, and the maintainer would be telling everyone that memories which legitimately exist on the contributor's branch have been forgotten. **Declining to adopt something is not the same act as forgetting it, and only one of them has a tool.** **`restore` from the main branch's file and `drop`-then-`import` both work and both discard all local divergence**, including whatever the maintainer has written themselves since; `drop` additionally takes every other target's bases with it. **This project had already made the argument once**, in `set-drop`'s backlog entry, about an evaluation corpus: *it is test data shaped like memory, and it has no business in a store at all.* A contributor's proposed memories under review are the same shape -- not yours yet, and possibly never. **Not the same question as how memories written during a code review reach the set**, which is about the reviewer *writing* and about authority; this is about the reviewer *reading*.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the `forget` trap is the one a maintainer will actually fall into: it is the only operation whose name matches the intent, it succeeds, and its damage is invisible locally and visible to everyone else after the next export.

The distinction in the last sentence is recorded because the two questions sit near each other in the file and are easy to merge, and merging them would produce a design that gives reviewers write access in order to solve a reading problem.

content: Fixed 2026-08-26 by the cheap form, which turned out to cover both operations without distinguishing them: `import` reports `taken_backwards` naming every record whose incoming version predates the one it replaced, with guidance naming the causes a reader can act on. **Judged in `import_set`, not in `reconcile`** — `resolve` stays a pure function of three checksums, which is what keeps the clock out of the arithmetic; this reads the result and adds a sentence, changing nothing about what is written. `Record::as_of` reads `modified` on a memory and `forgotten` on a tombstone, so **a resurrection compares like any other edit** and one comparison covers `amend` and `forget` alike. **Reported, never refused**, because a deliberate rollback looks identical from here and only the caller can tell them apart — the same line the design draws for the clock: an input to judgment, never to arithmetic. *Per-record ancestry would answer this from the data instead of inferring it and remains open, but the observation that the graph already carries ancestry for inserts and supersessions makes it a much smaller question than it looked.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix keeps a timestamp out of the merge arithmetic and uses it only for a report — the project's standing rule about clocks. One accessor over two record shapes is what let a single comparison cover both operations.

content: **Two issues had their prevention half arrive as a report rather than a refusal, which their fixed-when did not anticipate.** Read 2026-09-23. `imported-memories-carry-no-arrival-provenance` is fixed when "the set-name binding lands so one store cannot serve two repositories"; set identity landed, but `identity_note_for_import` in `src/mcp.rs` names both identities and says outright that the records "were imported as usual". `moving-the-local-store-leaves-the-old-one-unmentioned` has `status` reporting a `shadowed` store present in both directories — which leaves untouched the case it was filed for, `SCATTERHOARD_COMMON` repointed somewhere new, where the old directory is no longer scanned at all. Both need the human partner's call on whether reporting closes them.
context: Auditing the open issues for closure, a day after the streaming merge driver went in.
why: Recorded together because they are one shape rather than two coincidences, and the shape is worth naming: this project keeps choosing to report a hazard instead of refusing it, so an entry whose fixed-when says *cannot* will keep being met by something that says *did, and here is what happened*. Whether that satisfies the entry is a judgement about the entry, not about the code.

content: Fixed 2026-08-20, and the guess that the answer was two fields was half right. `Recall` now carries `searched`, `complete` and `skipped` — three facts the store layer always knew and could not express. On the wire, though, **no `complete` field was added**: *every set in scope is searchable* and *the search covered every set* are the same predicate, since a set is skipped exactly when it cannot be searched, so a second field would have been a second copy of `semantic_search_available` — the drift this repository files more of than any other kind. The wire change is `skipped_sets`, each entry naming a scope and its own reason, plus a note that no longer contradicts the payload it sits on. **The remedy moved from the note to the set it applies to**: one sentence for a whole union could only ever name one remedy, and two sets can be skipped for different reasons — a set with no model needs one installed, a set with foreign vectors needs someone to decide which model wins — so `Store::why_unsearchable` answers per set, naming both models where they differ.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the correction to the entry's own prediction: the internal type wanted three fields and the wire wanted one, because two of the three were the same predicate. Worth keeping because the entry had confidently proposed the wrong shape.

content: Measured 2026-09-21 in a scratch repository with a bare remote and the real binary. With the driver registered as `/nonexistent/scatterhoard merge-file %O %A %B`, merging a branch that added three memories into a `main` that added three: `git` printed `CONFLICT (content)` and the file showed `UU`. context: Testing the merge driver end to end before documenting it in SETUP.md.
why: The evidence behind the issue and behind the fallback in the documented command. Recorded because the degradation argument in `multi-set-sync.md` had never been tested for a registered-but-absent binary, and a later edit that simplified the SETUP command would reintroduce the hazard.

content: **Building the merge driver on 2026-09-16 settled three things about merging records.** *(1)* **`modified` forces a decision that costs something.** Every edit moves it, so in exactly the case the driver exists for — ours bumped `confidence`, theirs added a link — the two sides always disagree there, and treating that as a conflict would mean nothing ever merges. The later attribution wins, so **a merged record claims an authorship neither side wrote**. *(2)* **Collections are set-merged against the base, never unioned**: a union would resurrect a keyword one side deliberately retired. *(3)* Merged records go through `memory_file::write_record`, because the reconciliation checksum is taken over exactly those bytes; a driver spelling a record its own way would make every merged record read as changed at the next import.
context: Retiring the header summary and its comparison, which left the merge driver's recorded findings partly stale.
why: Decisions a later reader would otherwise meet as unexplained code. Taking the later `modified` reads like a clock-based merge, which this project refuses elsewhere; the distinction is that it stamps a record that already merged rather than choosing between versions. The cost in (1) is stated plainly because it is what a reviewer should push back on. Split out 2026-09-21 from a memory whose fourth finding, about the header, went stale when the header stopped carrying a summary.

content: **The principle that separates push from pull is what the trigger is made of, and it is the reasoning that survived into `hoard-watch` intact** -- established when the question was raised, 2026-08-29. **Push is needed exactly when the thing to notice is something the session would not otherwise put into words.** Recall can only match what you say; if you would never think to say it, recall cannot reach it, and that is precisely what a watch exists for. A recurring bug is something you *will* describe when it recurs, so pull suffices and costs nothing until then -- which is why a sporadic bug wants rediscovery by ordinary recall rather than a monthly reminder. **What push costs was already a known quantity one layer out:** a session-start list is a standing charge against the context window that grows monotonically as investigations accumulate -- the convention catalog's budget problem in a new place, against a project that has twice argued *a budget raised whenever it binds is not a budget*. So push needs a budget story, an eviction rule, or both, and pull needs neither. **That asymmetry is the whole argument for pull as the default and push as the marked case**, and it is what the served convention now says.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because this is the reasoning behind a convention that is currently served, and the served text states the rule without the argument -- *mark only what you would never think to search for* is the conclusion, and a session wondering whether something qualifies needs the *recall can only match what you say* test to apply it.

The budget-cost half is kept separately from the marking rule because it is the reason the catalog does not simply push more: any future proposal to widen what gets pushed has to answer the monotonic-growth objection, and the objection is not visible from the convention text.

content: **A gut feeling for `gut-feeling-recall` may come from the same pattern met elsewhere, not from a memory about this code.** Stated by the human partner on 2026-10-05. Experience arrives first as a feeling, "something is wrong with that design" or "there's a good solution here", and the feeling then drives the effort to recall. The memory behind it may concern a different piece of code, or another domain entirely, so recall can transfer a lesson. A model's training already does this, which argues the effect is redundant. The human partner chose to keep it, because software projects, literature, legal documents and similar works organise around repeated patterns. So a headroom measurement counts an analogous memory from elsewhere as a hit, and needs both `scatterhoard` and `coding-lessons`.
context: Deciding to measure the headroom for gut-feeling-recall before the small-model lift experiment, the morning after the first beta.
why: This widens what counts as a governing memory when labelling cases for the headroom measurement. A same-code-only ground truth would undercount exactly the transfer the idea exists for. The redundancy-with-training argument is recorded beside the decision because it is the obvious objection and was weighed, not missed.

content: **A line of the sharing preferences the server does not read is reported, rather than read as an item or refused.** Decided 2026-10-31 by the human partner. Reading a bare line as an item would turn every sentence of prose into one and spend that syntax for good. Refusing the file would have to block storing until it was fixed, because falling back to the template drops the person's own never-store words. Reporting keeps the file loading line by line and leaves a bare line free to be given a meaning later. Recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md`, *a line the server does not read is reported, never dropped*.
context: Fixing the dropped bare-line issue in the preferences file, after restoring from the 2026-10-30 checkpoint and restarting the server.
why: The three options look equally reasonable from the issue alone. The deciding facts are not visible in the code: refusal has no safe fallback, and a lockout over a typo lands on a person who may not code. A later session tempted to "just accept bare lines" or "fail fast" would otherwise redo the weighing.

content: **Measured 2026-08-30 over the catalog's whole history: `reinforcement` grew in 15 of 17 revisions and shrank in exactly one.** That one was `2e2b11e`, the restructure pass, which cut 151 characters as a **side effect** and whose own comment says length is *not a lever worth reaching for again*. The text-to-reinforcement ratio drifted from **1.27** at the first commit to **1.42**, and the sharpest single divergence is `ac85f71`: text **+394**, reinforcement **+1,192**. **Five reasons it ratchets, none of them carelessness.** Text is shaped by being an instruction so it resists growth, while an argument that grows reads as better supported. The editing rule filters for *a sentence that only helps a reviser*, which is a real test that catches the wrong thing — nobody is asked the harder question, **would a session act differently without this?** The judge is the author, minutes after finding the argument compelling. Nothing triggers a re-read, since conventions are edited locally where a decision touches them. **And additions carry a recorded reason while removals carry none**, so cutting means overruling a written argument with a judgement backed by nothing.
context: Migrating the cold-reread-of-the-catalog entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the measurement that motivated it.
why:
The asymmetry in the last reason is what makes this a ratchet rather than a drift, and it is the one a session cannot notice from inside a single edit: every individual addition is justified, so the growth has no moment at which it looks wrong.

The measurement is irreproducible as stated — it counts a 17-revision history that has since grown — and it is the evidence that the problem is structural rather than a run of bad edits. Re-deriving it later would answer a different question about a different history.

Confirmed in passing on 2026-09-07: a 367-byte trim made that day was **entirely relocation**, moving cross-entry duplication into `//` comments beside the entries, with no argument removed. The prescribed method worked on the first unrelated occasion it was used.

content: Withdrawn 2026-08-23, the same day, and kept because the mistake is more instructive than the entry was. `memory_file::stream` has always refused a file carrying one id twice — *"line 3 repeats a memory id that already appeared in the file"* — on the production import path, with a test whose docstring says outright *"Two lines with the same id is what a bad merge produces, and it is not resolvable by picking one — the reader refuses rather than silently dropping a memory."* **How the wrong conclusion was reached**: the probe called `Store::import` with a `MemorySet` **built in memory**, bypassing the reader entirely, where `INSERT OR REPLACE` did lose a record — but no file can reach that path, because `read` and `stream` are the only ways a `MemorySet` is constructed outside a test. The probe tested a layer below the guard and reported the absence of a guard that sits above it. **The lesson, which is the reusable part: search for the behaviour before probing for its absence.** A grep for the error *type* found nothing in the tests and was read as untested — but the test names the behaviour, not the type. Probing a lower layer directly will always show the unguarded primitive; that is what the guard above it is for.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A defect invented by probing beneath the layer that holds the guard, and a grep for a type name that missed a test named for the behaviour. Both are cheap mistakes to repeat, and the second is why the first was believed.

content: **The sharing preferences reach a session at its start because a rule consulted only at export runs after the moment it governs.** Decided 2026-10-18 by the human partner, recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *the preferences reach the session at its start*. The export review stays, because aggregation (seventy memories about one association, none a problem alone) and a change of audience (exceptions lapse when a repository goes public) are invisible at writing time. The context cost is accepted because it falls only on the file's author, who controls its length, where catalog text costs everyone.
context: Starting the decisions from the publication read-through, right after settling on a fresh public history.
why: Member of the backlog cluster, history from the decision. The cost argument is the human partner's own and is the one most likely to be asked again: someone weighing a new served text against the character budget will ask why this text is exempt, and the answer is who pays for it.
