content: Occurrence five, 2026-08-13, **corrects the mechanic**: `content` and `why` were both closed badly and only `context` was well-formed, so **two parameters were swallowed, not one** — the bound is *the next well-formed close*, not a count. The *exactly one* reading had held for four occurrences because in each only a single tag was wrong. **It was the most damaging instance so far for an unrelated reason**: the record carried a `supersedes` link to a correct memory, so the corpus did not merely gain debris — **recall began returning the damaged record in place of the good one**. A malformed call that happens to supersede something is strictly worse than one that stores something new, and nothing about the failure signals that. **Repaired by `forget` rather than supersession, and that choice was available only because of timing**: the damage had not yet been exported, so tombstoning removed it before it travelled, at the cost of one tombstone instead of the three-record chain occurrence two produced. **The cheapest remedy is to catch it before export**, which makes the export gate the deadline rather than the discovery point — and means the repair cost is not fixed, but depends on whether the damage is found in the same session that wrote it.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The correction to the mechanic, and the discovery that repair cost depends entirely on whether the damage is found before export. The supersession case is the one where corrupt debris actively displaces a good memory rather than sitting beside it.

content: **Withholding both sets that share an identity at load is provisional, and `evaluation-mode` must replace it.** Decided 2026-09-16 by the human partner, while fixing `two-sets-can-share-an-identity`: when a server starts with two stores on disk answering to one `set_id`, it loads neither for recall or writing. It keeps both open as *withheld*, reports them in `hoard_sets status`, and lets `drop` reach them; the survivor loads once its rival is dropped. Accepted **on the condition that it changes when load modes are built**, because it makes a restart able to lock someone out of their own main set, and a mechanism that makes losing access easy will bite later. **What should replace it**: once a load can be read-only, the conflict should load one holder read-write and the other read-only or as an evaluation load, which is the "at most one writable holder" rule the question head already names, so nothing is locked out. Where it lives: `Server::add_store` in `src/mcp.rs`.
context: Fixing the duplicate-identity issue after reproducing it by an edited-header import; also applied the AGENTS.md mid-session checkpoint clause earlier in the stretch.
why: Filed under `evaluation-mode` so that whoever builds load modes finds it: the human partner's condition was that the interim rule be remembered and replaced, not left as the permanent answer. Chosen for now over keeping the first in name order, which silently picks a winner on an arbitrary key, and over a read-only second load, which does not exist yet. No property of the data identifies the original, since import keeps each record's timestamps. The lock-out is also recoverable, because `drop` takes a safety copy.

content: Found 2026-08-19 by the human partner, asking whether an LLM can walk a supersession chain by hand as a recovery mechanism when the corpus is damaged. **A cycle is the damage that mechanism exists for, and it was invisible from every tool.** The reporting was designed, built and tested — [Recall Mechanisms](documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md) is explicit that write-time rejection only covers writes this store made, so resolution *"reports the error rather than silently picking a winner"*, with a test pinning it against a cycle arriving by import — and **it died at the boundary between the library and the surface**. Every layer looked correct on its own, which is the shape this file's first common cause describes, and the error surfaced only where the caller is least able to reason it out: a corpus already known to be damaged. The only trace on the wire was that `incoming` still carried the `supersedes` edge, so a caller comparing it against `superseded_by` could see them contradict — with nothing naming the contradiction and no reason to look. **Worth keeping: the guard already existed in [STANDARDS.md](STANDARDS.md)** — *avoid catch-all match arms where adding a variant should force every site to be reconsidered* — and `Resolution::Current | Resolution::Cycle => Vec::new()` is exactly what it forbids. The rule was written before the variant existed and nothing re-read the sites when it did.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A designed, built and tested report that never reached the wire, and a written standard that would have prevented it if anything had re-read the match sites when the variant was added. The fix was deleting the catch-alls, not adding a flag beside them.

content:
Why an unanswerable query scores high — file every measurement here. Explanations keep failing; no positive account yet.

**What fits**: any measurement bearing on why a query the corpus cannot answer comes back with confident-looking results, and any attempt to explain or separate it. Members carry `an-unanswerable-query-returns-confident-hits`. File the failures as fully as the successes — this investigation's most reusable output so far has been the shape of what does *not* work.

**Standing as of 2026-09-09.** Eleven explanations proposed and refuted, most by the session that proposed them: seven statistics computed *from the score* (ratio to top hit, largest gap, gap-to-median, per-query z-score, result-set coherence, `cos(query, centroid)`, charter matching) and four predictors computed *from the query text* (`why` in the embedding input, question form, word-level lexical overlap, subword overlap). The eighth statistic, the **absolute floor**, was wrongly ruled out on a five-memory store and does work — AUC 0.909 through the shipping scorer.

**What is established rather than refuted**: the negative class is bimodal by question form; single terms of art and punctuation both produce false highs; the embedder itself is verified correct against an independent recomputation; every stage of the scorer is *relative*, so none can ask an absolute question; and a floor must be calibrated per store.

**What would end this**: a decision on the non-match floor design — or a positive account of what the score actually measures, which nothing has yet supplied.
context: The human partner asking whether the session's measurements were being stored, and saying the hope was that a pattern might emerge from enough of them.
why:
Marked `hoard-investigation` at the human partner's prompting: they said the hope is that with enough observations a pattern might emerge, and that only works if the observations are gathered under one heading rather than left to be re-found by search. A session that does not know this investigation exists will not think to look for it, which is exactly the case the push is for.

The opening line is written to be read cold, in 120 characters, by a session with no context: what the subject is, that measurements go here, and that the explanations so far have failed. The last clause is deliberate — it warns the next session that its first unifying idea will probably be wrong, which is the single most repeated result in this file.

Recording the refutation count in the body rather than the opening because it will grow. Recording the *established* findings separately from the refuted ones because the ratio between those two lists is itself the state of the investigation: eleven refutations against five standing facts is what "characterised, not understood" looks like in numbers.

Retire this by superseding with the keyword off once the floor is designed and shipped, or once something explains the score. Until then a session that adds nothing here has an answer worth having — the convention says so, and on this subject a quiet session is evidence.

content: **How conventions get extended without recompiling -- optional and add-on conventions.** Raised 2026-08-09 by the human partner, anticipating the point where the memory system becomes reliable enough to depend on. **The reasoning:** Scatterhoard ships with a deliberately minimal catalog to limit the context tax, which is the right default and also creates standing pressure to add bells and whistles; and **a strong convention takes runtime and revisions to get right**, so the good ones will be discovered by use rather than written up front. **That argues for two directories** -- *optional* conventions, bundled with the project, reasonably well-tested, serving both as switchable options and as worked examples for writing your own; and *add-on* conventions, which a very successful project might see spawn as a separate effort entirely, and which therefore have to be installable without rebuilding the tool. **Where the line falls is expected to move**, and a candidate test is held provisionally rather than pre-committed: a convention belongs built-in if a user who does not know it exists would be worse off. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `optional-conventions`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

This one qualifies: it was raised 2026-08-09, gained a security reconciliation and a demand-side argument on 2026-08-26, and had its first live candidate replaced on 2026-09-04. The four members are separate settled arguments -- the trust distinction, the collision with the no-instruction-channel rule, the demand-side case, and the file format -- and each would be re-derived independently if folded together and skimmed.

*A strong convention takes runtime and revisions to get right* is the load-bearing premise and sits in the head, because without it the whole question reads as extensibility for its own sake.

content: **The server refuses any memory containing a word from the person's *Never store these words* list, because served text alone did not hold a weak model to the sharing preferences.** Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *the preferences start from a template*. Whole-word matching applies only to scripts written with spaces. A second check, a line in `hoard_memorize`'s response, was tried the same day and removed.
context: Building the sharing preferences served at session start, after five gemma runs, the last two with debrief questions.
why: `gemma4:12b` could quote the rule on health and still store the detail, with the rule in the framing and with it in `store-when`. Regular expressions fail silently for the people this protects most, and automatic plurals are English-only. A trailing `*` covers most endings, and over-matching only costs a reworded memory. Chinese and other scripts without spaces would never match under a word-boundary check, and the human partner judged Chinese an important case for this list. The response line was never acted on in five runs (`01M5HZB2J3F7SB1D50T5NMKVN1`).

content: Superseding a memory does retire a keyword, since `a-keyword-cannot-be-retired-once-a-memory-has-been-exported` was fixed: a keyword hit follows the **tip's** keywords rather than the matched record's, so a term the replacement drops stops matching. Verified 2026-09-06 by recalling the two terms the original defect was measured on, `max-catalog-chars` and `remark-not-refuse` -- both return nothing. `hoard_memorize` also says so on every supersession, in the `keyword_delta_note`: *nothing answers to them here any more*. Amendment is still refused after export, so supersession is the instrument; stating the replacement's whole keyword set is required alongside a `supersedes` link, which is the authoring half of that fix.
context: Being asked why a fixed issue was being cited as open, and finding the answer in a memory that had gone stale.
why: Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claim is unchanged. It supersedes a measurement of the pre-fix behaviour that outlived the fix by two days and was then believed, producing a filed issue, a design section and a stored memory all asserting that a keyword cannot be retired, with the contradicting evidence in the same session twice. That is the failure `store-when` names -- a structural claim keeps reading as authoritative after the code has moved -- so the correction is worth more than the fact: when a memory describes how something currently works and the answer matters, check it against the code or the tool before building on it.

content: **A hosted merge button never runs the merge driver, so registering it cannot keep a pull request conflict-free.** GitHub's server-side merge and its mergeability check ignore custom drivers in `.gitattributes`, including `merge=union` (github.com/orgs/community/discussions/9288, and kubernetes/kubernetes#70576, which removed a union driver for this reason). GitLab's request for driver support in merge requests is gitlab-org/gitlab#18830. Separately, measured 2026-09-21 in a scratch repository: `git` calls a driver only when **both** sides changed the file. A branch merged into an unchanged `main` takes the branch's file whole, header included, with no driver involved.
context: Pre-release review of what would stop others using Scatterhoard. The human partner asked what happens on the second of two sequential merges, after the first finding showed plain git conflicting on both the header and the end of the file.
why: This removes the premise under the recommendation made earlier the same day, which was to register the driver automatically at export. That fixes local merges only. Under a pull-request workflow, two open PRs that both exported will show as conflicting on the host whether or not any clone registered anything. The clean case needs neither driver nor fix, and that is what bounds the problem to concurrent changes.

content: The third raise of the catalog budget was expected and did not happen. `investigation-pipeline` was named as the convention most likely to force it, and instead it merged into `hoard-watch` -- one convention replacing two, because a seed and a trap turned out to be the same object. The merged draft overran the free space by 237 characters, and that was closed by attempting the cheaper answer for the first time: trimming 363 characters of justifying reinforcement out of `split-when-partly-stale`, which the reinforcement audit had measured at 79% justifying, with no rule removed. The catalog stands at 17,875 of 18,000 with 125 free, and the two deferral conditions were never tested, because the overrun the raise was being held for did not arrive.
context: Landing the watch convention and finding it would not fit, then working out whether to trim, harvest or raise. The same evening had rewritten the context field's description and retired the recall-gloss convention.
why: This supersedes the deferral memory rather than merely adding to it, because that memory's last clause -- `investigation-pipeline` is the convention most likely to force the raise -- is now false, and it is exactly the clause a later session would act on when planning convention work. What replaced it is more useful than a bare correction: the estimate was an artifact of counting two conventions that turned out to be one, so an overrun predicted from undrafted entries is worth re-deriving after drafting rather than budgeting against. The standing objection is unspent -- a budget raised whenever it binds is not a budget -- and the harvest is repeatable, since the audit priced roughly 3,540 characters of justifying reinforcement and this took a tenth of it. The hold on catalog re-tuning was lifted by the human partner for the trim, the second such exception.

content: **Two loaded sets can hold the same identity, and nothing refuses it.** `Server::add_store` keys `stores` by `Scope` — the local name — and performs no identity check, so two stores with one `set_id` under different names both load. **Reachable with tools alone**: `create` a set and `import` a file into it, then `create` a second under another name and `import` the same file, since adoption displaces an identity only on a set with no records. Three consequences, read from the code 2026-09-16 and not reproduced. **`holder_of` in `src/store.rs` returns the first store whose `set_id` matches**, iterating loaded stores in `Scope` order, so every identity-bearing cross-set link resolves into whichever name sorts first — and a `superseded_by` so resolved takes its replacement from the wrong set, changing what a reader is told is current. **`author_map` is keyed on `set_id` alone** with `ON CONFLICT(set_id) DO UPDATE`, so *which identity record is me in this set* has one row for both, and the second `author_map_put` overwrites the first: memories written to one set can be attributed through the other's author record, and that `by` is written into records and exported. **The design anticipated the shape and not this case**: [set-lifecycle.md](documents/design/set-lifecycle.md)'s fork section says two histories claiming one identity produce *"a set that never existed"*, but its remedy refuses on the **name**, and was written before identities existed. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `two-sets-can-share-an-identity`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working out whether an evaluation set could be promoted to read/write while the maintainer's own copy stays loaded, at the end of the session that built the merge driver.
why:
Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing, severity and fixed-when. Filed the moment it was noticed, per `TRACKING.md`, rather than carried in the session — it surfaced while the human partner was asking whether promoting an evaluation set could leave two read/write sets sharing a UUID, which is one way in but not the only one.

**Severity `corrupts`, provisionally.** The author-map path writes a wrong `by` into stored memories, which then export; the `holder_of` path misreports standing rather than damaging anything on disk. If reproduction shows the author map cannot in practice be reached with two such sets loaded, this drops to `misleads`.

**Fixed when** a rule exists for which store may legitimately hold an identity, and the loader enforces it — refusing the second load, or making the case representable and resolving by something other than first match. Note the neighbour: `local-unaddressability-is-undocumented` records identity-based resolution already going wrong once for the same underlying reason, that `holder_of` compares identities with no rule about who may hold one. The two want one answer rather than two.

Not the same defect as the name-keyed store that gave every checkout one store; that is many checkouts to one store, and this is two stores claiming one set.

content: **The constraint to notice before starting, and the reason this belongs in the binary rather than in a script.** `src/main.rs` accepts **no arguments at all** today — it builds the server and enters the stdio loop — and every attached client invokes it bare, by absolute path. So adding a subcommand introduces argument handling to a binary that has none, and **the no-argument case must keep meaning *be an MCP server***. Getting that default wrong breaks every attached client at once, and **the failure looks like a crashed server rather than like a CLI mistake**, which is the same shape as the `cargo clean` outage recorded in SETUP.md. **In the binary deliberately**: Scatterhoard is meant to install as one self-contained executable, so putting an operational check in a script would make a scripting runtime a requirement for ordinary use — a different thing from `scripts/mutate.py`, which is a development tool the users of a project never run.
context: Migrating the prohibited-scan-subcommand entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the hazard it flagged before starting.
why:
The diagnostic shape is the part worth having in advance. A wrong default here does not produce an error message a person can read; it produces clients that fail to start, which is diagnosed as a broken install or a corrupt binary long before anyone suspects argument parsing. Knowing that in advance is what makes the test-for-the-no-argument-case worth writing before the feature rather than after.

The script-versus-binary reasoning is recorded because the cheap route is obviously available and obviously wrong for this project specifically: this repository is full of Python development tooling, so reaching for another script would look consistent with local practice while contradicting how the product is meant to be installed.

content:
**The declared-language check reports a 0–10 score for each declared language, in one of three bands with a message for each.** Decided with the human partner on 2026-10-04. The score is how many of ten paraphrase sets the model ranks first against all 29 other sentences in that language.
- **7–10:** the score alone.
- **4–6:** recall here is unreliable. A model built for this language would likely do better, possibly at the cost of other languages in the same set.
- **0–3:** the model cannot search this language by meaning. The memories are intact, keyword recall works, and semantic recall returns under a model that covers the language.

The check exists to prevent confusion, not data loss: an agent getting poor recall from a set it trusts should know the model is the cause. A per-sentence-set grid stays in the probe and is not reported.
context: Restoring from the 2026-10-04 checkpoint, widening the paraphrase triplets to ten per language and making the rank harness a probe. The human partner reframed the check around what an agent needs to know rather than what the probe can measure.
why: A bare number leaves the agent guessing what it means. The band message is what tells it the memories are safe and what would fix recall. The bands come from measurement: non-English under `potion-base-32M` scored 0–4, and everything under `potion-multilingual-128M` scored 5–10. The middle band is worded "unreliable, switch models" rather than "partly works", so it stays true for Japanese at 4 under base-32M, whose lead over its closest rival was negative. Ten tests leave about ±1 of noise. A flip across a boundary changes only how strongly a model change is urged, never what the message says about the memories' safety.

content: Found 2026-09-02 while working out whether a `hoard-watch` keyword could mark the memories a session is told about at startup — and how one would ever come *off* that list. **Measured on the live `scatterhoard` set** by joining `links` against `keywords` to find supersession pairs whose replacement dropped one of the predecessor's terms, then recalling on the dropped term: `max-catalog-chars` returned a memory carrying only `MAX_CATALOG_CHARS`, with `replaces_matched` naming the superseded record; `remark-not-refuse` returned a replacement whose `replaces_matched` named a record **two or more hops back**, so the reach ran the whole chain rather than one link. **No instrument could express the retirement**: amendment would remove a keyword and is refused post-export, which is every memory in a shared set; supersession did not reach; forgetting would work, destroys the record, and is reserved for sensitive data or an unfair characterisation. The intent *this memory is no longer indexed under that term* was legal, ordinary, and inexpressible.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery, with the measurement that showed the reach runs whole chains rather than one link, and the enumeration of all three correction instruments failing for different reasons — which is what makes it a gap in the model rather than a missing feature.

content: Recall returned an unrelated memory at `-0.29` looking structurally identical to a `+0.32` hit, which is what raised `no-non-match-floor` on 2026-08-02. The cold-start case compounds it: `0.0` from a one-memory store and `0.0` from a large one are different measurements, so even a hand-written threshold would be wrong at small corpus sizes, and the two questions have to be answered together.
context: Piloting the index design by converting an issue entry written across five sittings into a cluster.
why: The first observation of the defect, kept as its own record because what it establishes -- that the two questions are entangled -- is what every later attempt at a fixed threshold ran into. The entanglement was only dissolved much later, by a mechanism that needs no constant at all, so this is the record that explains why the obvious answer was refused for a month.

content: The lowercasing reached the embedding, which the original filing missed: `src/embedding.rs` builds the embedded text from content, then `why`, then keywords, so the lowercased form was what got vectorised. Case is information a subword tokeniser uses, and `MemoryView` and `memoryview` do not tokenise alike. Preserving case is therefore not only about fidelity on the way back out — it plausibly improves semantic recall too, which is the opposite of the tradeoff this looked like at first.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A second cost found after filing that reversed the apparent tradeoff. Recorded because the first reading had fidelity and retrieval quality pulling against each other, and they were pulling the same way.

content: **The Vision already states a memory size, and the corpus is past it: `documents/Scatterhoard_Vision.md` says a memory is "roughly a paragraph of text".** Noticed 2026-09-15 while loading the Vision before a design edit, with `memory-size-drift` open. Measured the same day, the median memory runs about 1,470 characters of `content` plus `why` — several paragraphs, not one. **This matters for where a response to the drift can live:** a convention asking for density would be applying the Vision rather than adding a constraint to it, which is a lower bar than a new rule, and the Vision may not be modified without the human partner's approval in any case. It also gives the question a reference point it otherwise lacks — nothing in the design documents states a target length, and this sentence is the nearest thing to one.
context: Loading the Vision before writing up the link-key fix in the design docs, with the memory-size question filed earlier the same session.
why:
Recorded because the question was filed saying nothing governs length, and that is true of the conventions and the design documents but not of the Vision — which is the one document none of them may contradict. A later session drafting a density convention would otherwise argue it from first principles and might reach a target that the Vision already rules on.

The phrasing is loose on purpose in the Vision, so it bounds the direction rather than the number: it cannot settle what the target is, only that growth away from a paragraph is growth away from the stated intent. Read as evidence for the question, not as its answer.

content: Fixed 2026-08-25: the fix asks whether the tip can be handed to a reader, and asks it once, where the chain stops. A replacement id the store holds no *live memory* for now sets `unresolved` instead of becoming a tip, so `resolved_hit` reaches the same `tips.first() == None` branch a cross-set replacement already reaches and returns the memory flagged `superseded_beyond_this_set` — the reader's situation being identical in both cases, superseded with the replacement not available here. **A second route to the same disappearance was closed with it**: a chain *ending* on a forgotten memory, where the tombstone is a record so the walk named it as a tip and the fetch failed exactly as for an absent id. Walking *through* a tombstone is unchanged and deliberately so, since [Cross-Set References](documents/design/cross-set-references.md) settles that a chain whose middle was forgotten still holds a good reference — which is why the check is for a live memory at the tip and for nothing at all along the way.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the placement that makes it correct: the question is about the end of the chain, not about each step, because a chain may legitimately pass through records that cannot be produced.

content: **What the non-match floor ships, as built 2026-09-12.** One log row per store a session's recall was scored against, carrying no query text and never exported, bounded at 100 rows of each kind; a query labelled by its `scope` argument or by the session going on to look up, link to, correct, or pass back a memory it returned; `hoard_sets calibrate`, which sets the level at the **5th percentile** of the labelled window less a 0.05 margin once 20 new labels have arrived since the last calibration; `hoard_sets uncalibrate`, which removes a level outright; a floor belonging to one store and one model, cleared when the model changes; and `hoard_recall` reporting when a floor silenced everything, with `ignore_floor` to ask again.
context: Moved 2026-09-24 out of the entry's head, which was over the length limit, in step 2 of the out-link work.
why: The shipped surface of the built entry, kept apart from its standing so a change to one piece supersedes one memory rather than the head.

content: A test in this work first asserted through recall and **passed with the absorbing removed** — with two memories at equal similarity the gap-cut dropped the older one regardless — and was rewritten to assert through `hoard_lookup`, which returns a memory as itself and names what replaced it. **The surviving mutation is what caught it.** This is the general hazard of asserting a structural fact through a ranked search: the ranking can produce the expected observation for a reason unrelated to the thing under test.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A test that passed for the wrong reason because it observed a structural fact through a ranking. Recorded because recall is the natural way to check a supersession took effect, and it is the wrong instrument for it.

content: **The public repositories keep their current URLs, `github.com/jtcours/scatterhoard` and `github.com/jtcours/coding-lessons`, even though they start from a fresh history.** Requirement stated 2026-10-18 by the human partner. The likely way: rename each existing private repository (to a name such as `scatterhoard-history`), then create a new repository under the original name and push the single reviewed commit. A repository that takes over a renamed one's name replaces GitHub's redirect. Force-pushing an orphan branch into the existing repository is the alternative to avoid, because GitHub can go on serving commits that no branch references to anyone who has their hash, so the old history would not truly be gone. Check that against GitHub's current documentation before acting.
context: Starting the decisions from the publication read-through, after deciding on a fresh public history and while restating the first memories.
why: The URL is already in the README, SETUP and memories, so keeping it saves editing all of those, and keeping the URL was the human partner's stated wish. The rename-then-create sequence is the assistant's proposal and is unverified, which is why confidence is held below the requirement's. The concern about unreferenced commits comes from general knowledge of GitHub, not from a test, and it matters because the reason for a fresh history is that the old one is not published.

content: **A memory the loaded model cannot represent must not be answered with advice to add keywords.** Decided 2026-09-11 UTC for the note the fix to `one-unembeddable-memory-stops-the-store` will return, on the human partner's objection. Keywords are part of `embedding_input`, so a keyword in a language the model knows gives the memory a vector built from that keyword alone — the quiet mode recorded under `recall-is-latin-script-only`, where a Chinese memory keyed `soup` ranked first for *soup salt*. Advice to add keywords would steer the LLM into manufacturing exactly that. The note says instead: stored; this store's model has no token for this text, so it cannot be found by meaning; still reachable by its keywords and by `hoard_lookup`; and the remedy — a model covering the language — is the user's to make. **The same objection bears on the later door check:** representability should be judged on what the memory says, content and `why`, not on the whole embedded input, because keywords can manufacture a vector the content does not support.
context: Designing the fix for the store-stopping embed failure, just after filing it; the human partner questioning the proposed note and asking what the gap sweep is for and when it runs.
why:
The human partner's example: a Russian memory in a store whose model is Chinese. Adding keywords would produce a vector, but not one representative of the memory's contents.

The existing no-model note gives the keyword advice safely, because there no vector is produced until a model arrives, and by then the content embeds too. Carried over to this case the same sentence would do harm, which is why the two notes must differ.

Decision placement puts the remedy with the human, who chooses the model; the LLM can only report the gap honestly.

content: The hold on catalog re-tuning was lifted 2026-09-06 for the whole watch-index rewrite -- `hoard-watch`, `route-where` and `recall-when` together -- and this is a retirement for the cycle rather than a third one-pass exception. The human partner's reason: the hold existed so they could evaluate performance under the conventions as adopted, that evaluation is done and is what produced these changes, and evaluating a half-implemented set is worthless. A quiet period begins when the changes land, so anything found mid-cycle that would edit the catalog again goes to BACKLOG for afterwards rather than into the same pass. Text may move between entries and justifying reinforcement may be pared back where the arithmetic needs it, with each trim named and counted.
context: Being asked to lift the hold before starting the convention half of the watch-index work, having just built the index line and its echo.
why: The two earlier lifts were single passes granted for a stated reason, and a third recorded the same way would read as the hold having quietly lapsed -- which is exactly what the memory recording the second lift warned about. This one is different in kind and the difference is the useful part: the hold is a measurement instrument, and the instrument is worth pointing at text that will be kept rather than at text mid-replacement. That also supplies the rule for the rest of the cycle, which is the part a later session will actually need: finding one more catalog edit is not a reason to make it now.

content: A partly-stale memory should split, not be edited. Built 2026-08-13 and served as **`split-when-partly-stale`** — renamed to match the `<verb>-when` shape the rest of the catalog uses and to read as `correct-when`'s sibling, which it is served immediately after; the same rename precedent as `articulate-after-operation` becoming `capture-before-ending`. Its own built-when was the deletion of the `catalog.rs` comment block it was reasoned in, and that is done. **It was pulled forward by `recall-before-storing`, served the same day**: that convention instructs a session to *split it* on a partial overlap, so until this one existed the catalog named an operation it did not define — and the natural reading, amending or replacing the original, is the one outcome that strands cross-set links. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `splitting-partly-stale`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; this one empties the Conventions section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only, and no members added on migration. The general lesson this episode produced — a convention's served text can create a dependency on a convention that does not exist yet, and the catalog has no way to express it — is already recorded under `recall-before-storing`, which is the convention that created the dependency; it is not restated here. A reader arriving from this entry should look there rather than expect it in this cluster.

The entry's slug and the shipped convention's id differ, as with `confidence-guidance`: the entry is `splitting-partly-stale`, the convention is `split-when-partly-stale`.

content: The Golden Rule can reverse a design answer rather than only shading one. Scatterhoard's correction rule says a changed claim is superseded — and superseding an unfair characterisation of a person keeps it permanently readable by people who were not there, including its subject, which is exactly the durability hazard golden-rule.md names. So retracting a characterisation of a person is `forget`, a bounded exception where preserving history is itself the injury.
context: Decided 2026-08-05 in documents/design/corrections.md; carried to runtime in the correct-when convention's reinforcement.
why: The principle had previously only reinforced answers the engineering reasoning already gave, which makes it easy to treat as decoration. This is the first case where applying the general rule faithfully produced the harm, and the exception was only found because the principle was in context while the convention text was being drafted — which is the mechanism golden-rule.md describes, working.

context: Testing a timing-based recall nudge offline from session transcripts, after the continuous content signal failed to discriminate, the morning after the first beta.
why: This is the outside nudge the human partner asked for, triggered by timing rather than meaning, after the content-sensing signal failed to discriminate. It is precise because the moment that needs recall is structural, a code change since the last commit, and the session's own recall call is what silences it. That needs no session tracking. The silencing rule depends on recognising the habit's call shape, so bookkeeping recalls do not count. Caveats: one project, one week, and code writes detected by pattern in shell commands. Some commits were not behaviour changes. Whether a nudged session then writes a useful sentence is untested, hence 0.75.

content: **Should something outside the session be able to trigger a recall and put its results in front of the model — on a tool failure, say — so that recall happens at moments a head-down session would not think to ask?** Raised 2026-09-24 by the human partner as a further signposting mechanism: a multi-turn stretch of work is exactly where `recall-when`'s moments go unnoticed. Routes: a Claude Code hook such as `PostToolUse`, as the repository's `PreCompact` hook already injects context; another MCP server running Scatterhoard as its own stdio child, since MCP servers cannot call each other's tools; or linking the crate. A `scatterhoard recall` subcommand, the size of `export`, would serve the first two. What must be settled first: such a caller is not a session, and its scoped recalls would label the query log as though one had judged the answers.
context: An aside before the release-gated questions: the human partner asked how hard it would be for another tool to trigger a recall, after the backup-calibration work.
why: Head of a question cluster. Filed as a question because the mechanism is cheap and the consequences are not: an automated caller feeding calibration labels nobody judged would skew floors, an unscoped recall reaches the personal `local` set and would carry it into another tool's output, and a recalled memory pasted into a tool result reaches the model looking like that tool's claim. It extends the retired recall-would-have-helped investigation, whose cases were steps that looked mechanical — the moment an outside trigger would catch.

content: **This entry must be settled before publication**; it is this memory's keyword besides `release-gate`. `adopting-coding-lessons`, gated 2026-09-28, is built. It waits on proof from use, set out in `EARLY-VALIDATION.md` in the human partner's terms: it does not feel slower, sessions recall before writing, triggers get written, signposts cause lookups, and recalling changes what gets written. Two items left the gate on 2026-09-28 when they were built: `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely` and `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity`.
context: Fixing `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity`, the second release-gate item closed on 2026-09-28.
why: Superseded 2026-09-28 because `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity` was fixed. It was gated because crafted files arrive with publication, and identity resolution can no longer reach the local set. `adopting-coding-lessons` stays for its recorded reasons: `scatterhoard` links into `coding-lessons`, so they publish together, and the human partner wants experience of it first. It comes off when the human partner judges the evidence sufficient. Retire an item by superseding this memory without its slug.

content: The design had already resolved this and its precondition had never been built. [embeddings.md](documents/design/embeddings.md) says *"the model's identity and version are local state, recorded alongside the cache"* and *"a mismatch between the recorded model and the configured one triggers a re-embed rather than an error"* — so the response to detection was settled, and there was nothing to detect a mismatch with. A resolution whose precondition does not exist reads as covered.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A design decision that was correct, recorded, and inert. Worth keeping because the document reads as though the behaviour exists, which is what let the gap survive.

content: **Three candidate sources for the non-match floor's calibration, offered by the human partner 2026-09-11.** (1) **Each set tracks its N most recent distinct queries that returned memories from it, and carries them in its JSON export** — no cold start, since the history travels with the set, but queries can hold private text and the export is what gets published. (2) **A synthetic probe set built from the memories' own contents** — self-contained, with statistical validity to watch. (3) **A floor computed from the number of memories in the set, modelled on the sets measured so far** — no calibration at all, at the risk of questionable recall results. **One challenge for (1), raised by the LLM:** *returned memories from the set* is not yet an answerability label. Every stage of the scorer is relative, so an unanswerable query still returns about four confident memories from each set searched; the label would have to come from something downstream of the ranking, or (1) would calibrate the floor on the very traffic the floor exists to stop.
context: Returning to the Latin-script recall issue; the human partner correcting who proposed calibrating from query history, then offering alternatives before choosing to test the multilingual model first.
why:
The human partner's contribution to `floor-calibration-source`, filed the same day. They put the multilingual-model measurement ahead of choosing among these, partly to see how much of the per-set floor variation comes from the model itself.

That bears most on (3): a floor modelled on set size from one model's measurements would not carry to another model if the model accounts for much of the variation, since the probe set was already shown to be a property of the model rather than of the tool. The privacy concern on (1) is the same one-way door the export gate exists for — a query written mid-session can carry anything, and the set it would travel with may be public.

content: **Cap what an evaluation load may take on.** `hoard_sets evaluate` reads a whole file into memory and embeds every memory in it before returning, with no limit: a file far larger than anything this project has seen would spend minutes embedding and hold the lot in RAM, in a store nobody adopted. **Already decided, in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md)**: the limit is set by timing a full embed rather than guessed, the count is available for free because the file is read before anything is stored, and a temporary file on disk is the fallback if sets outgrow memory, at the cost of cleaning up orphans at startup. **Measured 2026-09-16** on this project's own set: about 3–4 KB per memory beyond the vectors, which every loaded set already holds in RAM. **Built when** `evaluate` refuses a file above the limit, naming the count and the limit, with a test. **Why it is worth doing rather than waiting for a large file**: the failure without it is a tool call that appears to hang, which is the shape a caller retries.
context: Closing out the evaluation-mode build.
why: Filed as the residue of `evaluation-mode`, which was resolved when the feature shipped on 2026-09-18. Ready rather than blocked: nothing is missing but the measurement and the refusal. Recorded now because a limit that exists only in a design document is one nobody will add until someone hits the failure, and this failure looks like a hang rather than an error.

content: The refusal for a `hoard_recall` with neither a query nor keywords said what was missing but not what to send, and `gemma4:12b` answered it with another call missing both. Fixed 2026-10-03. The refusal now shows the caller's own call with the missing part added, as `"query": "<what you are looking for>"`, and says recall has no mode that lists a set. Tested with `scripts/local_model.py retry`, replaying the refused call from a task asking for a whole set. The old wording recovered 0 times in 10: gemma resent the call without a query, adding only `detail: summary`. The new wording, served by the real server, recovered 10 times in 10. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-missing-query-refusal-gives-no-example`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Fixing the missing-query refusal right after filing how-much-scatterhoard-lifts-a-small-model; adding retry mode to scripts/local_model.py to test it.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed as its fixed-when asked: a weak reader adds the missing argument on its next call, as tested, not as judged by reading. The baseline was worse than the agent runs that found it, where gemma eventually added a query on its third try; the targeted replay showed the refusal itself never worked. A placeholder was chosen over a filled-in example query: both recovered 10 out of 10, but only the placeholder cannot be sent verbatim as though it were the caller's question. One test pins the refusal and takes its remedy; one mutation guards it.

content: Found 2026-08-10 while building `SCATTERHOARD_COMMON` (then `SCATTERHOARD_LOCAL`), **by trying the misconfiguration rather than by reading the code**. Creating a store in an empty directory is correct — that is how a first run works, and refusing it would make the variable unusable — but the symptoms are `local`, `0 memories`, no error, no note, and the memories stay safe on disk while any way to find out what happened is lost. Not new, since a mistyped `SCATTERHOARD_HOME` has always done this; the new variable makes it *likely*, because the whole reason to set it is that it differs from the home. **Partly answered already**: `status` reports the file each set is read from, which turns *you have no memories* into *you are looking in `/somewhere/else/local.sqlite3`* for anyone who thinks to ask — a fact, needing no heuristic, that cannot be wrong in the reassuring direction, which is why it shipped and the rest did not. **What is still missing is the unprompted half**: nothing looks for a `local.sqlite3` in the home this server is no longer reading, and a reader who does not already suspect a configuration problem has no reason to call `status` and compare a path they may not remember setting.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A defect found by making the mistake deliberately, where the correct behaviour and the failure are indistinguishable from outside. The partial fix is recorded with the reason it was safe to ship: it reports a fact rather than guessing a cause.

content: **Text Scatterhoard writes for someone meeting it for the first time must not assume coding, its own vocabulary, or its tool surface**, as the human partner put it on 2026-10-17 while rewording the default memory-directory README. Scatterhoard is for AI agents generally, not coding agents -- legal analysis and other research use it too, as the `governance-docs` set does. "Set" is a term of art, so such text says "memory set". And a tool name like `export` tells a person almost nothing, since people do not see the tool surface, and tells a model nothing until it has read the server's documentation; such text says what happens instead -- "when Scatterhoard exports its memories".
context: Building the default README for memory directories, before making the repositories public.
why: The first wording, "a memory system for coding agents ... written by Scatterhoard's `export`", read naturally from inside the project and failed on all three counts for its actual reader; it is the kind of drift any later text for newcomers -- a public README, an error a human reads, release notes -- will repeat unless the audience is named first.

content: How many memories a recall returned was decided by the `limit` it was given rather than by the query: the same question answered with 2 memories at `limit: 17` and 17 at `limit: 18`, because the cut took the largest score gap *within the window*, and a deeper gap could displace the one that had been winning. Fixed 2026-10-02 by removing the cut from what ships. `limit` is now a count, best first, defaulting to 8, and a smaller limit returns the start of what a larger one returns. The cut survives only as the instrumentation stage `Stages::gap_cut`, off by default. The findings behind this carry the keyword `result-count-follows-the-limit-not-the-query`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working the two recall-limit issues right after fixing max-chars-is-not-a-bound; the human partner recalled that the gap had been found to be noise, asked for a re-measurement on today's sets, then chose the default.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed as its fixed-when asked: the answer to a query no longer changes with the budget it was asked under, beyond showing more of the same ranking. The cut was removed rather than repaired because measurement showed it was choosing among noise: real rankings broke barely more often than nonsense ones on 1,330 and 181 memories, so no horizon could make a gap mean anything. The human partner proposed removing it, asked for the measurement first, and chose 8 as the default, the predictable end of the measured F1 range of eight to ten. Two tests pin the count and the nesting, one pins the default at the surface, and two mutations go with them.

content: **Measured 2026-09-08: the gap cut's answer is a property of the window rather than of the corpus, and it flips on a margin of 0.0004.** Asked at every window from 3 to 24 against the live 844-vector corpus, *what decides which memory set a memory belongs in* returns **2 results at every window up to 17 and 17 results from window 18 onward**; an off-corpus query jumps 2 → 13 → 15 at windows 14 and 16. **The ranking has no cliff in it — the jump is in the output only.** Printing the scores either side shows a smooth decay: after the rank-1→2 gap of `0.0195`, which the guard deliberately skips, every gap down to rank 20 lies between `0.0010` and `0.0080`. At window 17 the winner is the rank-2→3 gap at `0.0076`; at window 18 the newly visible rank-17→18 gap at `0.0080` beats it, and the answer goes from two memories to seventeen. **The largest gap in a smooth distribution is noise**, and *largest* is decided here by half a percent. **The live default is `DEFAULT_WINDOW = 20` in `src/mcp.rs`, past both flips.** This contradicts what `Question::window` documents — *not a result count… a query with two good answers returns two* — since the same query returns two or seventeen depending only on the budget. The 2026-09-02 replay could not have seen it: only one of its eleven recalls had four or more results.
context: Probing the gap cut against the live corpus, the morning the tracking files were unified.
why: Amended within the hour, before export, because the first version called the jump a cliff without saying that the distribution it is cut from is smooth — which reads as *there is a real boundary at 17*, the opposite of what the numbers show. The load-bearing figure is the 0.0004 margin between the winning gap and the runner-up: it says the mechanism is not mis-tuned but is being asked to find structure that is not there. Recorded because the mechanism was adopted on an argument about scale-invariance — a gap is a difference, so translation and scale move it not at all — and that argument is true of the metric while saying nothing about the cut, which depends on which candidates happen to be in the window. Also worth keeping: the one genuinely large gap in the list, rank 1→2, is the one the guard skips by design so that a runaway top hit cannot collapse every answer to one.

content: `mutate.py --stale` reports a mutation whose `find` text matches its file more than once, beside one that no longer matches, and exits non-zero on either — so an anchor that new code has repeated earlier in the file is reported in a second instead of silently retargeted, since the runner mutates only the first occurrence. Built 2026-09-14, the day it was filed. The six mutations ambiguous at filing are re-anchored by extending each `find` backwards from its intended occurrence until it is unique: five were already landing on the occurrence they were written for, and `disputes: ask the memory's own store for claims against it` had been landing on the identical guard in `referenced_from_other_sets` rather than on `claims_against_hit`, which its recorded reason describes. All six behave as recorded after re-anchoring, and `--stale` reports none of 423 stale or ambiguous. Documented in `AGENTS.md` beside the `--stale` paragraph. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `ambiguous-anchor-check`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building the ambiguous-anchor check straight after filing it, following the full mutation pass that preceded the scan subcommand's commit.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because the entry is built. The opening sentence is the generated index row, so it states what `--stale` does now. Readiness facet dropped, as built entries carry none.

The one mis-aimed mutation is stated because it is the case the entry's reasoning predicted: a survivor whose reason described a different function. What its retarget exposed about the guard it had been landing on is not recorded here — that is a question about `referenced_from_other_sets` rather than about the check, raised with the human partner the same day.

content: In Scatterhoard, restating a fact by hand in a second place is the single largest source of defects — it explains five of the first nine issues plus two earlier ones. The signature is that both copies stay internally consistent, so nothing goes red: every instance so far survived a fully green test suite. Derive the copy, or delete it; where a copy must exist, test it against its source rather than against a literal.
context: Emerged 2026-08-03 from the common-cause analysis over the nine issues in ISSUES.md; instances included the tool schema, mutations.py quoting store.rs, SETUP.md quoting a model path, and design docs asserting runtime behaviour.
why: Recorded as a standard in STANDARDS.md beside correctness-by-construction, after the human partner named the common cause across defects that had been filed separately. It matters because the usual defence — a green suite — is specifically blind to this class, so it has to be caught by review or by construction instead.

content: **How a set is loaded read-only so its memories can be distributed as a document — the memory equivalent of a PDF.** Raised 2026-09-16 by the human partner. **Designed 2026-09-16 in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md), and built before `evaluation-mode`, which becomes a special case of it.** Settled: `create` takes an optional `mode` that defaults to read-write, and its description says when to choose read-only without telling the LLM to ask. The mode is stored in the set's `meta`, and there is no demotion. A reader learns the mode from `hoard_sets status`. A read-only set keeps its own stable name and is normally held as a single copy. The publisher cannot signal read-only-ness in the file, because a header is contents. A read-only set refuses session writes, allows `import` and `restore` as refreshes, and drops without a safety copy. Beside a read-write holder of the same identity, it loads rather than being withheld. **Still open:** whether one-way promotion to read-write is offered at all; how a read-only set's signposts get recalled, since the convention recalls watch marks only for writable sets and the catalog is nearly at its budget; and what happens with two read-only holders of one identity and no read-write one, likely withholding both. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `read-only-distribution`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Revising the load-modes design: create defaults to read-write, the user chooses evaluation labels, and evaluation hits are marked from the load mode.
why: Supersedes the head written earlier the same day, which said `mode` was required with no default. The human partner changed that to an optional parameter defaulting to read-write, and withdrew telling the LLM to ask. The single-copy expectation is theirs too, and bears on the open case of two read-only holders.

content: A memory opening with a numbered heading like `1.` summarises to just `1.…` when no later sentence ends within the cap: `summarise` in `src/memory/text.rs` takes the last sentence end that fits, and a number followed by a space is one. Its documentation says a false boundary costs "a few characters instead of the whole line", and here it costs the whole line. Found 2026-09-28 writing `coding-lessons`' numbered adoption guide, where six parts summarised to their numbers alone until each first sentence was shortened to end within 119 characters. This record's own first draft was cut the same way. Fixed when a boundary that leaves nearly nothing is passed over in favour of a word cut. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-numbered-opening-summarises-to-its-number`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Writing coding-lessons' adoption guide (adopting-coding-lessons step 2), with the human partner choosing a bare number to open each part.
why: Head of an issue cluster. Costs rather than misleads: the line names nothing, so a reader has to fetch the memory, but it cannot be mistaken for a claim. Numbered lists are an ordinary way to write a procedure, so any multi-part guide a user writes meets it. The workaround, a first sentence that ends within the cap, is recorded in the guide's own openings.

content: Unified into `TRACKING.md` on 2026-09-08: one file, three tagged sections, one generated index each, 185 rows carried across byte-identical. `ISSUES.md`, `BACKLOG.md` and `documents/design/open-questions.md` are deleted. Also shipped, as scoped: the cluster-shaping guidance moved out of `STANDARDS.md` into the file it governs, and the three copies of the `hoard-` and `about-` slug rules collapsed to none rather than to one, since `keyword-standards` serves them. Two additions the human partner asked for at the same time: the filing prompting moved out of `AGENTS.md` too, and checkpoint stamps were settled on UTC. 330 references across 47 tracked files were rewritten to `TRACKING.md` plus a section anchor, verified by `checklinks.py`.
context: Unifying the tracking files, the morning after the open-questions migration finished. Same stretch settled checkpoint filenames on UTC and thinned AGENTS.md to a pointer.
why: Head of the backlog cluster, superseding the open record now the work has shipped. Standing changes from blocked to built, and the readiness facet comes off because readiness describes unbuilt work. The content is also rewritten for a second reason: the old opening named the three files as markdown links, and once they were deleted the generated row carried three dead links into `TRACKING.md` itself -- `checklinks.py` reported them as errors, which is the file's own index reporting a defect in a memory. A row is memory text, so the fix is here rather than in the file.

content: A registered merge driver whose binary is missing makes `git` leave the memory file as the receiving side had it — no conflict markers, none of the other side's memories — while reporting a conflict, so committing the file as it stands silently drops the other branch's additions. Fixed 2026-09-21 for the documented registration, which falls back to `git merge-file` on exit status 127. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-missing-merge-driver-leaves-a-file-that-reads-as-resolved`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Testing the merge driver end to end in a scratch repository before documenting it in SETUP.md.
why: Head of an issue cluster. `corrupts` because the file hides that anything is wrong: it parses, has no markers, and is exactly one side's file. The design's argument that the driver degrades gracefully was true only for an unregistered driver. Fixed only as far as documentation reaches: a clone registered with the bare command is still exposed.

content:
**Three independently-sourced negative classes agree to within 0.015, so the calibration point is a property of the corpus rather than of whoever wrote the probes.** Measured 2026-09-09 against `scatterhoard`, 752 memories, raw cosine, each class scored against the same 142 real in-domain queries:

| negative class | n | median top-1 | p90 | AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| organisational notes, real | 317 | 0.294 | 0.395 | **0.957** |
| public-domain non-fiction, 1899–1922 | 40 | 0.279 | 0.373 | 0.953 |
| public-domain fiction dialogue, 1920 | 114 | 0.290 | 0.394 | 0.951 |
| *probes I authored* | 30 | **0.145** | 0.263 | — |

**Two predictions of mine were refuted at once.** I expected fiction dialogue to sit far lower than deliberative organisational questions, on grounds of *register*; and I expected it to sit lower again because dialogue questions are **anaphoric** — *"How could they be?"*, *"What else is there?"* carry their content in the preceding sentence, where a recall query is self-contained by necessity. Neither mattered: novel dialogue lands within 0.004 of committee minutes.

**What separates the classes is not domain, register or self-containedness but authorship.** Any real question a person wrote for their own purposes lands near 0.29; the only outlier is the set I wrote *to be* off-domain, at 0.145. Being told to be distant is what made them distant.
context: The human partner suggesting Project Gutenberg as a second source of off-domain questions, after their own notes supplied the first.
why:
Recorded because it converts the floor's calibration from an open problem into a solved one, and because the convergence is worth more than any single class. Three sources with nothing in common — a volunteer's meeting notes, Dewey and Veblen and Emily Post, and Edith Wharton's dialogue — agreeing on the p90 to within 0.022 means a shipped probe set can be built from any real-question source without inheriting that source's peculiarities. The thing that had failed twice was the probe set; it now looks like the one part that can be made reliable.

**The reason my prediction failed is the useful half.** I reasoned from properties of the *questions* — register, anaphora, self-containedness — and this investigation has now shown four times that properties of the query text do not predict its score. I had recorded that finding myself, hours earlier, and still reasoned from question properties. Whatever makes a static embedding place a question is not available to inspection of the question.

**What is still open is the operating point, not the calibration.** A floor at p90 of any of these silences 84–88% of real off-domain questions but costs 7–13% of real in-domain queries, which is likely too much. With AUC at 0.95 a better point exists; p90-of-the-negatives is arbitrary and was only ever a placeholder. That choice is now a cost-ratio judgement rather than a measurement problem.

content:
**Whether a session needs guidance on writing a query, as it now has for writing a memory.** Add each observation of a recall that missed, or that only found what it wanted after rephrasing, under this entry's slug.

Raised 2026-09-15 by the human partner inside `memory-size-drift`: the direction was that a convention should ask for dense text *in memories and in queries*, so semantic recall is efficient. The memory half shipped 2026-09-19 as `store-when`'s *compact, tightly-written, and atomic — one claim, not several*. The query half did not: `recall-when` says when to search and in what language, and says nothing about how a query should be written.

**Split out as its own question rather than carried as residue, because it is a different question.** The memory half had a measured drift behind it before anything was drafted. Here nothing has been measured, and whether guidance is needed at all is the open part — a catalog this close to its bound should not spend characters on a rule nobody has shown a need for.

**What would end it:** enough observations to answer yes or no. Several recalls that missed and were fixed by rephrasing argue for guidance and say what it should contain; a long stretch with none argues the query side takes care of itself, and this retires.
context: Splitting the query-side half out of memory-size-drift before resolving it, at the human partner's direction, with observations to be collected rather than a rule drafted now.
why: Head of a question cluster, marked `hoard-investigation` because a session writing a query is exactly the session that would not think to search for a memory about writing queries — and the evidence can only be collected at that moment. The mark is cheap to retire: supersede and leave it off, and the memory stays.

content: **Raw cosine does not break cross-store merging, and the union centroid has a cost of its own that raw does not.** The objection that ruled raw out was that per-store centroid removal puts each store's scores on its own scale, making a merge unsound — but that argument indicts `Centring::PerStore`, not `Centring::None`. Raw cosine satisfies the split-invariance property for a *stronger* reason than the union centroid does: the union earns it by computing one centroid over everything searched, raw earns it by having no population statistic at all. Pinned by `raw_cosine_also_survives_splitting_a_corpus_across_stores`. **The mirror property is where the union centroid fails.** Its centroid is computed over whatever is being searched, so loading an unrelated set moves it and rescores memories that set has nothing to do with. Measured on the live corpus, `scatterhoard` recalled alone against `scatterhoard` beside the other three sets, 18 answerable queries: **Combined shifts scores by 0.00742 mean and 0.02134 max, and changes the top hit for 4 of 18 queries (22%). Raw shifts them by exactly 0.00000 and changes 1 of 18.** Pinned by `the_union_centroid_makes_a_set_score_differently_when_another_set_is_loaded`.
context: Testing whether raw cosine breaks the cross-store merging property, after the scorer ablation found it separating better than what ships.
why:
Recorded because it removes the standing objection to a change that the ablation had already shown was worth considering, and because the argument it removes was subtly misaimed rather than wrong. The design note and `tests/cross_store.rs` both frame the problem as *centring per store breaks merging*, which is true and is why the union centroid exists; nobody appears to have asked whether *not centring* has the same defect. It does not.

The subset-sensitivity result is the part with consequences beyond this decision. A user's `scatterhoard` answers currently depend on which other sets their session happens to hold, and a fifth of queries get a different top hit for that reason alone. That is not a tuning question — it is the same memories, the same query and the same model returning a different answer because of unrelated context, and it is invisible to anyone using the tool.

**The three counts now favour raw and the fourth does not, so this is not yet a decision.** Raw separates better (AUC 0.959 against 0.901), keeps split-invariance, and eliminates subset-sensitivity; but its result-count ratio is worse — 0.94 answerable-to-substance against centring's 1.46 — and that ratio is the metric closest to what the feature is for. The interesting possibility is that these are complementary rather than competing: the count ratio is exactly what a non-match floor would fix, so raw plus a floor may beat centred without one on every axis. Untested.

content: Any test fixture meant to exercise graph traversal needs more memories than the walk has seeds, currently five. At or below that size every memory is a walk origin, an origin never inherits, and the walk contributes nothing, so the test asserts something it cannot observe.
why: Introduced 2026-08-18 with the rule that a walk origin never inherits. Five fixtures across four test files sat under the line; three had been passing by reading the old self-inheriting walk, and the last was found by a mutation surviving rather than by a test failing. The trap is silent in both directions: the fixture looks reasonable and the test goes green.

content: **`(id, checksum)` was considered and declined**, on the human partner's suggestion, as a way to let true duplicates collapse. A collapsed record has to claim a scope, and if it stands for memories in two sets there is no honest one to give it — picking one is store order deciding what the reader sees, which is this defect. Making it honest means one hit naming several scopes, with `matched`, `incoming` and `disputed_by` each saying which set they came from: a wire-shape change bought for a case with no live instance, since across the two live sets, 76 ids and 63, the overlap is zero. De-duplicating identical results is a separate question, decidable on evidence later, and nothing here forecloses it. **The entry previously said this reaches the file format. It does not, and that was worth checking rather than inheriting** — the format already declares its scope and already refuses a duplicate id inside one file, so per-set identity asks nothing new of it.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A declined alternative with the reason it fails on its own terms — a merged record cannot honestly claim a scope — plus a claim about blast radius that turned out to be wrong when checked rather than inherited.

content: **The stronger test of the multilingual model's floors, the 142-query operating curve, needs a probe that rebuilds a copied store's vectors first.** No probe handles a store whose recorded model differs from the one loaded, so under a swapped model recall would skip the store and every score would read zero.
context: Testing the multilingual model at the human partner's direction, to see how much of the per-set floor variation comes from the model itself before choosing how to calibrate the floor.
why: It names what blocks the stronger test. Split on 2026-10-19 from the multilingual floor measurement, when that memory was restated over the length limit.

content:
**The labelling half of `derived-set-summary` is built and tested; the clustering half is not.** `src/summary.rs`, seven tests in `tests/summary.rs`, three mutations, all caught. History from building it 2026-09-12.

**The interface boundary is the thing to know before writing the clustering half.** `label_clusters` takes `&[Cluster]`, where a `Cluster` owns the keyword lists of its members — not indices into a set, and not a parallel assignment array, so a cluster cannot be desynchronised from the memories it describes. The module knows nothing about stores, files, vectors or MCP, which is what keeps it independently testable. **The clusterer must therefore hand over keyword lists grouped by cluster**, not an assignment vector.

**Two choices are decisions rather than code, and neither is visible from reading it.**

*No minimum-support cutoff.* The Python prototype required a keyword to appear in at least three memories of a cluster before it could be a label. That is a magic number that breaks on small sets, and it turned out to be unnecessary: weighting each score by `ln(1 + inside)` already stops a keyword on one memory outranking one on half the cluster. The only threshold left is `score > 0.0`, which is not arbitrary — it is exactly the point where a keyword stops being commoner inside its cluster than outside it.

*Smoothing applies to the proportions, not to the counts.* The prototype floored the outside count at half a memory. **That is wrong in a way a large corpus hides completely**: half a memory out of eight hundred is nothing, half a memory out of one is fifty per cent, and the constant-count form scored a genuinely distinctive keyword *negative* on a three-memory cluster. Jeffreys' prior on both proportions fixes it. Both forms agree on any realistic corpus, so only a deliberately tiny fixture separates them — a mutation records the difference.

**Still to build**: spherical k-means over the stored vectors, including a rule for `k`; the file-format field; recomputation at import; and the comparison gated on the embedding-model hash. A Python reference implementation reading the `vectors` table directly is in this session's scratchpad and produced the measured output the design rests on, but scratchpads are ephemeral — treat the measurement memory as the record, not the script.
context: First implementation session on the derived set summary, the same day the question behind it was resolved.
why:
History from building the first slice. Recorded for the two choices that are decisions rather than code — what was rejected, and why the boundary sits where it does — since neither is visible from reading the module, and the second determines how the clustering half has to be written.

The smoothing correction is worth keeping because it is a plausible-looking bug that a large corpus hides completely. Both forms behave identically on hundreds of memories, and only a tiny cluster separates them, so a test suite built from realistic fixtures would never have found it.

content: The remedy the human partner proposed 2026-10-29 for `the-precompact-hook-asks-a-model-that-never-gets-a-turn`: the compaction hook should prepare what the post-compaction agent starts with, rather than ask the pre-compaction one for anything. It reloads every convention, and mines the session transcript since the last auto-compaction marker for anything that should have been stored as a memory and was not, handing both to the agent as it begins the post-compaction part of the session. Not yet built or designed in detail; the open questions are how a hook passes text across the boundary, given the head's finding that nothing the hook emits survives it, and what does the mining.
context: The scatterhoard set's full review, stopped at about 410 memories to resume in a new session at 76% context; proposed alongside the report that compaction fires on an idle session above some level.
why: Moves the work to the side of the boundary that has a turn to act in, and to the source that still holds the whole history, the transcript, which the head already named as the likeliest fix. Pairing it with reloading the conventions matters because a compacted session has lost the catalog it was loaded with at the start, so it would otherwise store and recall without them.

content: **Two tests, and the second matters more.** One walks whole response payloads and fails on any object-shaped scope **at any depth**, rather than naming the fields it knows about — a field-by-field test would pass for a field added later, which is how the two spellings came to coexist. The other **pins the file header as the object form**, so a later tidying pass that *makes them consistent* fails rather than silently rewriting every export. Both are mutation-pinned. **The file format did not change and must not**: `Memory` carries no scope — an exported file *is* a memory set, so the scope is declared once in the header — which is why this was a surface fix and not a format change, with record checksums and every recorded base untouched. Twenty occurrences moved across nine approval snapshots, each a three-line object becoming a one-line string.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A test that fails on shape at any depth rather than on named fields, and a second that pins the deliberate inconsistency so a future tidy-up cannot quietly rewrite the file format. The two together are what keep one spelling on the wire and a different one in the file on purpose.

content: **A memory file's name need not match its set's name. The header says which set a file holds.** Decided by the human partner on 2026-09-25, for the several-files-per-`scatterhoard_mem` layout. On first write, export names the file as close to the set's name as the operating system allows, which sets the expectation that the two match. Nothing enforces it after that. Still open: how export and import find a given set's file within a directory. Not yet built.
context: Working through the release-gated questions: `one-repository-many-sets`, after deciding a `scatterhoard_mem` directory may hold several `.json` files. The question prompted noticing that `SetName` accepts Windows-reserved words and names differing only in case.
why: Operating systems put too many rules on file names to tie a set's name to one. Windows reserves names like `con`. Case-insensitive filesystems merge `Notes` and `notes`. Unicode normalization makes one name into two paths. Keeping the name out of the path leaves room to widen `SetName` beyond ASCII later, so a developer writing in Japanese or Gujarati could name the set in their own script and the file in the nearest form the OS accepts. The file names should still stay honest without a rule, for the same reason source files are named for what they hold: clarity. The approximated first name points that habit the right way. This was weighed against the name-must-match rule, which the session had recommended for transparency. Its costs were judged to be the operating systems', and permanent.
