content: **One fix is ruled out in advance, and it is the obvious one -- stated when the observation was recorded, 2026-08-02.** **Do not fix this by special-casing the centroid.** The union-centroid decision is what makes scores comparable across stores, and a corpus-size exception to it would reintroduce exactly the incomparability that decision removed. **So the admissible fixes all act on what is reported rather than on how it is computed:** suppressing or nulling the score below some corpus size, carrying what the score was measured against alongside it, or directing the caller to `confidence` at that size. A score that cannot be supported should be withheld or qualified, not quietly computed differently.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the ruled-out fix is the one that will occur to anybody looking at the symptom -- the centre is wrong because there is only one vector, so adjust the centre -- and the reason it is wrong is a property of a different decision entirely, which nothing at the site of the bug would reveal.

The general form is worth having too: when a measurement is correct but unsupportable, the honest repairs are to withhold it or to publish its basis, and changing the computation to make the number look right is how comparability gets lost.

content: **Claude Desktop's chat cannot be sent an elicitation form: its client declares none**, observed 2026-10-16. The desktop app's MCP client, `claude-ai` 0.1.0 for chat and `local-agent-mode-<server>` for the servers it bridges into the Code tab, opens with `initialize` asking 2025-11-25 and declares only the MCP Apps extension `io.modelcontextprotocol/ui`; every one of its 171 logged connections was marked legacy. A shared set created from chat took the relay fallback and worked. MCP Apps is a possible other route to a form there, unexplored.
context: Testing the publishing-name flow across Claude Desktop's chat and Code tab after building the unanswered-form fallback.
why: Distinct from the print-mode finding: chat does not decline forms, it never offers to take them, so nothing server-side can reach a person there except through the model. Checkable in `~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp-server-scatterhoard.log`, where the server's own `initialize` line records what each client declared.

content: `Store::embed` filters out every memory carrying `hoard-author` — the filter that keeps identity records unembedded, keyed on a term any caller can write. So an ordinary memory using it as a *subject* keyword was stored with no vector and could never be found by meaning. Found 2026-09-06 while piloting the index design, by storing a member memory that mentioned identity records and keying it `hoard-author`. This is the reserved namespace having **behaviour** behind it rather than only membership, which is a sharper hazard than the one `reserved-keywords-carry-subject-memories` was filed against: there the cost is a stray hit in a list, here it is a memory that silently leaves semantic recall.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set. Piloting the index design on one entry is what turned this up.
why: The discovery episode, kept as written on the day: what the filter did, how it was found, and why a reserved term with code behind it is worse than one with only membership behind it.

content: Nothing capped how much a single recall could return: `limit` was honoured unclamped, so a caller passing a large number got the whole store back in one response. Withdrawn 2026-10-02 as not a defect: `limit` has no ceiling by decision, because the caller holds the context budget it protects and the server cannot see that budget. The parts that stood were fixed. A limit of zero, a negative number or a fraction is refused by name, since an empty list from zero read as *nothing matched*. The schema declares `minimum: 1` and says the limit has no ceiling. Reasoning in `documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md`, 2026-10-02. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `recall-limit-is-unbounded`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Right after removing the gap cut and making 8 the default; measuring response size by limit and detail on a copy of the real scatterhoard set.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded to withdraw it. The human partner asked why this was a defect at all: every large response in the measurement had needed an explicit `limit: 2000`, and the default is 8. When it was filed, a large limit returned non-matches formatted as matches and the scan grew with the limit. Neither is true now. A server ceiling would also override a deliberate choice: the human partner noted that a model with a very large context window, which they said Sub-Q has in limited testing, could reasonably take in most of a set. A maximum with a cursor was considered and set aside for lack of evidence that callers pass limits they did not mean. Evidence of that, perhaps a small local model adding a zero, is what would reopen this.

content: A link can reach the private `local` set by naming its identity, so a crafted file can make a shared memory resolve into a personal one. `holder_of` in `src/store.rs` matches a link's `set_id` against every loaded store with no exception for `Scope::Local`, which has held an identity since 2026-08-31 — so a shared memory whose own `superseded_by` carries this machine's `local` identity concedes to a personal memory, and recall substitutes it. Only a hand-edited or crafted file gets there: `identify_link_targets` never writes `local`'s identity. Read from the code 2026-09-14 and confirmed 2026-09-23, not reproduced. Refiled from the backlog as `local-unaddressability-is-undocumented`. Fixed when identity resolution cannot reach the local set, a test pins that with a file carrying `local`'s identity, and `LinkTarget` documents the guarantee. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Explaining the entry to the human partner after the closure audit, who read its slug differently and agreed on reading the cluster that it is a defect.
why: Refiled at the human partner's decision on 2026-09-23: the backlog entry described documentation debt over a guarantee that held, and the guarantee stopped holding for identity-bearing links a fortnight after it was filed — so this is built and wrong, which is what the issues family is for. Renamed because the old slug read as though `local` modified *unaddressability*, and named the missing documentation rather than the defect; the old slug stays as a keyword so the cluster already filed under it still gathers here. Misleads rather than corrupts because nothing wrong is written: the substitution happens at recall and the stores are untouched.

content: Decided 2026-08-09 by the human partner: how and when to record **observations** from which patterns arise, how those flow into **puzzles** — questions not yet fully articulated — and how those flow into **investigations**. **The rationale is a capability nothing else in the toolchain has**: an LLM using Scatterhoard sees patterns across multiple sessions *and multiple developers*, and this is the convention that turns that position into something recorded rather than noticed and lost. **Likely needs no new link labels**, so it is convention and keyword work rather than a data-model change: `InstanceOf` carries observation→pattern and `Resolves` carries investigation→puzzle, since a puzzle *is* an open question. The observations→puzzle edge is the one that strains — `MotivatedBy` is closest but is about the reasoning behind a *decision*. Watch it in use before adding vocabulary; the label set was chosen on evidence about how memories are actually written.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The original decision and the argument for it, plus a deliberate restraint: check whether the existing labels stretch before coining new ones, because the vocabulary was chosen on evidence about real writing.

content: **How to inspect a memory set without adopting it.** Raised 2026-08-26 by the human partner, from a maintainer reviewing a contributor's branch: import is adoption, and checking the branch back out does not undo it. **Designed in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md) as a special case of read-only, which was built on 2026-09-17, so nothing blocks this now.** Settled: an evaluation load comes from a file, once, through a `hoard_sets` action with no `create` step. Several can be open at once for comparison. Each is named `eval-<set>-<label>`, with the label chosen by the user, and `SetName::new` refuses the `eval-` prefix so no real set can carry it. It is searched only when its scope is named. Every memory it returns carries a field taken from the load mode, not parsed from the name, and the response carries a note explaining it. It pulls no watch marks, drops without a safety copy, and lives in memory. **Still open, and to be settled before building:** what a cross-set link does when an evaluation copy is a possible target, which turns largely on whether evaluation stores sit among the ordinary stores, since `hoard_lookup` resolves against all of those; and whether an evaluation set's recalls should feed floor calibration, since naming the scope is the only way to search one and a scoped recall is what calibration treats as a labelled signal. **Also open:** the size limit, and whether a returned memory carries its set's identity. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `evaluation-mode`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing out read-only mode and filing promotion to the backlog.
why: Supersedes the head only to drop its `depends_on` link to `read-only-distribution`, which was built on 2026-09-17: the row was still rendering as `blocked by 1` for a blocker that no longer exists, which would tell a session this cannot be started when it can. The open parts are unchanged, and they are decisions rather than dependencies, so they do not make it blocked.

content:
Found 2026-09-19 while filing `query-density-guidance`, whose head carries four keywords — the section keyword, its slug, its status, and `hoard-investigation` so sessions add observations to it. The row came out right only because the slug was listed before the watch mark. Reordering those two would have titled the row `hoard-investigation`, and `genindex.py --check` would have reported the index current, since the file and the memories would agree.

**The fix is small and already has a precedent in the file.** Facets are excluded by prefix, `FACETS = ("hoard-proj-severity-", "hoard-proj-readiness-")`, so the same treatment for the reserved namespace — skip any keyword beginning `hoard-` when looking for the slug — costs one condition. That is also more correct than an exclusion list: `keyword-standards` reserves the whole `hoard-` prefix for control marks, so no slug can legitimately begin with it, and a mark added later needs no change here.

**Guard worth having beyond the fix:** a head carrying more than one candidate slug should stop the run, in the shape the file already uses for an ambiguous standing. Two non-reserved keywords on a head means either a slug and a subject term, which `a-slug-that-is-also-a-subject-keyword-over-gathers` is about, or a typo — and picking one silently is what this defect is.
context: Filing the query-density question with a watch mark, and noticing the row's title depended on keyword order.
why: Recorded with the fix because the obvious repair is to exclude `hoard-investigation` by name, which leaves the next mark to rediscover the defect. The prefix rule is the one that stays true, and the reason it is safe — that no slug may begin `hoard-` — is a convention rather than anything visible in the script.

content: Fixed 2026-08-03: `Store::set_embedder` takes `Arc<dyn Embedder>`, and `main.rs` loads the model once and gives it to every store it opens. **One model per session turned out to be a correctness requirement rather than a memory saving** — `recall_across` embeds the query with a single embedder and scores that vector against every store's vectors, so two different models would make those comparisons meaningless with nothing failing to say so. That reason now lives on `set_embedder` itself. The damage was recoverable in principle, since vectors are derived state rebuildable from the memories ([embeddings.md](documents/design/embeddings.md)), but nothing exposed a re-embed pass at the time, so recovery meant deleting the store file and re-importing — which needed import to exist.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the reason for the shape of it: sharing one model looked like an optimisation and is actually required, because cross-store scoring compares vectors from different stores against one query vector.

content: **The export review keeps no ledger: the committed memory file is the clearance record, and the routine review set is the export's diff against it.** Decided 2026-10-17 with the human partner, who asked whether the ledger predated the memory's current structure. It did: it recorded which version of a memory was cleared, and an exported memory can no longer change, since a change is a new memory superseding it. The record must be `git`, not the store's `bases`, which advance when an export is written, before anyone reads the diff.
context: Standardising the read-through of the memory sets before making both repositories public.
why: A later session reading the superseded ledger sections in `export-review.md` could build them. The `bases` trap is the non-obvious part: keyed on them, an export never committed would mark its memories cleared. Merged-upstream memories are already in HEAD, so they are not re-reviewed; a set moved between repositories is reviewed in the new one, closing the gap the last-modifier rule left.

content: **These two entries must be settled before publication**; they are this memory's keywords. Gated 2026-09-23 by the human partner. One would break something already in use if changed afterwards: `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`, about the file format. The other is gated because crafted files arrive with publication: `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity`. Every gated question is answered; what remains is building.
context: Finishing set-settled-at-first-write with its documentation step.
why: Superseded 2026-09-28: `set-settled-at-first-write` was built, so it leaves the gate. Retire an item by superseding this memory without its slug.

content: **An exported file carries no description of its set, and the comparison against one is retired.** Decided by the human partner 2026-09-21, reversing the 2026-09-12 decision to write it into the header. The export and import responses still derive and show `describes`, and an import that could not derive it still owes it, so the view the Golden Rule mechanism gives an LLM is unchanged. What went is the header's `summary` and the `against_the_claim` verdict. Built in `src/memory_file.rs` (`Header`) and `src/mcp.rs` (import); contract in `tests/set_description.rs`.
context: Pre-release review of what would keep others from using Scatterhoard. Started from the merged-header question, found a second end-of-file conflict under plain git, and that hosted merge buttons never run merge drivers.
why: The comparison caught only a sender who edited the claim rather than deleting it, and an edit gained them nothing, since the claim was never shown. After any merge it fired for no reason, because the kept header described one side. And the header changed with every export, so it was a line two branches collided on — including on a hosted merge, which runs no driver. The human partner could name nothing the comparison needed to catch. The benefits recorded for keeping it — readable in a diff, a record of the set when it left — do not serve alerting the LLM, and the second is recoverable from git history.

content: **Observation for `charter-rewrite-intake-measurement`, 2026-09-14, in `scatterhoard` — the set whose gloss was rewritten.** Over one fix, a session read code and design documents and learned material of the method-and-path kind: how a set comes to hold an identity and when adoption may replace one, that the broken link it was fixing cannot arise from a renamed copy, that the links table's key ignores the target set, and that identity matching may reach the local set. Each changed what it recommended. It stored none of it as a memory of its own until the human partner asked whether the conventions had prompted it to. Some had gone into the reasons of a decision memory; the rest existed only in the conversation. The conventions had been loaded at the start of the session. The same session did store decisions, issue heads and entry standings promptly throughout.
context: The human partner asked, after a long investigation of set identity and link formats, whether the conventions had prompted recording any of it.
why:
A data point for the hypothesis that the rewritten gloss makes methods and paths-to-a-decision get recorded in this set. It counts against it for this session: the conclusions were recorded and the paths were not, until prompted from outside. One session, and a session doing tracked work, where decisions and entry standings have their own prompting in `TRACKING.md` and discoveries made in passing have none — so this is an observation to classify with the others when the investigation's measurement is taken, not a verdict on it.

Recorded as what happened rather than as a conclusion about the session's habits, per `store-when`'s rule for memories about a person, a model included.

content: Fixed 2026-08-20 by a route the entry did not anticipate. **A new invariant closes the gap from the other side: if there are no vectors, there is no model** — the recorded identity is a property of the vectors, so with none there is nothing for it to be a property of. `Store::unbind_model_if_no_vectors` releases the binding wherever vectors can be emptied (`forget`, `import`, `rebuild_vectors`) and again at open, which repairs any store already left that way; **maintenance and repair are one rule, so they are one function**. *That invariant also fixed something filed nowhere*: `import` on a server with no model deleted every vector and then no-opped its re-embed, leaving a store claiming a model while holding nothing — reporting `Mismatched` against nothing, and refusing to fill its own gap when a model returned. What remains is that authority in the store is no help when the store cannot say what its vectors are, filed as `store-owns-its-model` in [BACKLOG.md](BACKLOG.md).
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: An invariant stated from the opposite side of the one the entry proposed, which repaired an unfiled defect as a side effect. Making the repair and the maintenance the same function is why an already-damaged store heals at open rather than needing a migration.

content: Observed 2026-09-07, the first supersession of a head since the migration finished: adding `release-gate` to `a-healed-fork-reports-its-ancestor-as-a-cycle` left the row's text byte-identical and moved it from line 51 to line 130. The cause is one line — `heads.sort(key=lambda m: m["id"])` in `rows_for`. **This is the routine operation, not a rare one**: heads are deliberately short precisely so a change of standing supersedes cheaply, so every issue that gets fixed will reshuffle. Two candidate fixes, and they trade differently. Sorting by slug is one line and gives a stable alphabetical order immune to supersession, but reorders all 84 rows now and discards the original file order for good. Sorting by the *earliest* ancestor's id preserves today's order and is immune to future supersessions, but needs `rows_for` to walk supersession chains, which it does not currently do — it only collects the set of superseded ids to filter them out.
context: Filing the ordering defect immediately after it appeared, while adding a release-gate keyword to an existing entry.
why: Recorded with the diagnosis and both candidate fixes because the choice is a design decision about whether the index's order is meant to carry meaning, and that question has not been asked anywhere: `genindex.py`'s docstring is detailed about the five guards and silent about ordering. Note the contrast worth not confusing — id order within an entry's *members* is deliberate and load-bearing, since a single-keyword recall returns them id-ascending and that order is the narrative. Id order across *heads* is incidental, and inherited migration order rather than anything chosen.

content: Decided 2026-08-09 by the human partner and built 2026-08-12 as `capture-before-ending`, **with a wider trigger than the entry described**: *"after a multi-turn operation"* named one boundary, and the convention names the family — work finishing, a commit, an export, or the human signalling they are wrapping up or clearing context. **The last of those is the one an LLM cannot detect for itself and the one observed to work in practice.** It targets the failure `store-when` names but cannot itself prevent, recorded in the catalog comment: *"the failure mode we expect is not badly-formatted memories, it is a session that records nothing worth keeping and a session that records everything"* — a rule about content cannot fix a session that never reaches the question. **"If any" is load-bearing and survived into the served text**: a convention that asks what was learned after every operation, with no sanctioned way to answer *nothing*, manufactures memories to satisfy itself, which is the record-everything failure arriving by a new route.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A convention about *when* rather than *what*, because a content rule cannot help a session that never asks the question. The sanctioned way to answer *nothing* is what stops it manufacturing memories to satisfy itself.

content:
**Superseded bodies are not a significant contributor to floor variation: removing them from the scan entirely moves the floor by 0.0028.** Tested by adding `Stages::include_superseded` (default `true`, what ships) and calibrating twice over 601 off-domain probes and 142 real queries:

| scan | probe p90 | probe median | real min | real median |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| whole chain (**ships**) | 0.381 | 0.268 | 0.295 | 0.531 |
| tips only | 0.378 | 0.267 | 0.301 | 0.522 |

**For scale, probe-set choice moves the same floor by 0.149** — authored substance probes sit at a 0.145 median where real prose sits at 0.294. That is **fifty times larger**. The variation between calibrations was composition, not chains.

**Individual queries do move, and the aggregate hides it**: 58 of 601 probes changed by up to 0.121, and 16 of 142 real queries by up to 0.174 — but scattered in both directions, so the distribution's shape barely shifts. Under the admissible-floor rule (lose no real query, then silence what you can) tips-only is marginally *better*: **66.2% silenced against 62.7%**, on an admissible floor of 0.301 against 0.295.

**Scores can rise as well as fall when the bodies leave**, which is not obvious: ranking is by combined score while the reported `similarity` is content-only, so dropping a chain member reorders the walk and a memory with higher content similarity can move into first place.
context: The human partner asking whether the ten heavily-rewritten supersession chains contribute to the variation seen in recall floors, and suggesting the tips-only comparison.
why:
Recorded because the hypothesis was well-posed and the experiment the human partner proposed — calibrate against tips only — was the right one, cleanly answering it in the negative. A ruled-out mechanism is worth as much on this entry as a confirmed one; it now carries twelve.

**The ratio is the finding, not the absolute.** 0.0028 against 0.149 says where attention belongs: two orders of magnitude separate the probe set from the chains, so any further work on calibration stability should be about what the probes are, not about what is in the scan. That also retires the intuition behind the question — that a 0.191 median lift on rewritten chains must show up somewhere aggregate. It does not, because ten chains cannot move a percentile over six hundred probes however hard they lift.

**The instrumentation is the durable part.** `include_superseded` runs through `recall_across_with` rather than a replica, its default is pinned by a mutation, and `scanning_only_the_tips_scores_a_chain_on_its_current_text` in `tests/recall.rs` pins the behaviour it selects. Adding it also broke an existing mutation's anchor — `Stages default: ship with a floor` matched on two adjacent lines that a new field came between — which is worth knowing about any mutation whose `find` spans a struct literal.

Confidence 0.85: measured through the shipping path on one corpus and one model, with a probe set whose own composition is the larger effect.

content: **History from designing the convention, 2026-09-02.** The originating case came from another codebase: a directory of deployment configuration whose filenames encode which server type each lands on, documented in a `README.md` beside them, and a recurring stumbling block because *the directory's name does not cue a recall*. **The failure is not rediscovery cost, which is the axis `store-when` is calibrated on.** Reading that README takes thirty seconds; the memory is worth storing because **nothing tells you the README exists**, so the cost is near zero and the probability of paying it voluntarily is also near zero. That is silence rather than expense, and it is the inverse of `store-when`'s neighbouring clause: *do not record what a glance would answer* meets the case where a glance at the **name** is precisely what fails to answer. The human partner had already stated the governing principle in the investigation re-entry question: *push is needed exactly when the thing to notice is something the session would not otherwise put into words — recall can only match what you say, and if you would never think to say it, recall cannot reach it.*
context: Migrating the hoard-watch entry out of BACKLOG.md under its new slug; this is the pre-build evidence the entry preserved.
why:
Kept because it is the only statement of *why the mechanism exists at all*, and it is not derivable from the served convention, which gives the rule without the case. A later session weighing whether a watch is justified needs the axis — silence, not expense — and `store-when` alone actively argues the other way, since a thirty-second README fails its rediscovery-cost bar.

This is the purest instance of the principle: nobody types *configuration file naming scheme*; they type *add an SSL directive*, and the path arrives through tool output rather than through a question.

content: **The dating rule and the summary rule pull against each other, and obeying the first naively defeats the second -- observed twice on 2026-09-07, once on a backlog member and once on the first open-questions member.** *Every migrated member says when the thing happened* invites an opening like *History from filing the entry, 2026-09-07.* or *History from raising the question, 2026-08-13.* Both are true, both satisfy the dating rule, and both produce a derived summary that identifies nothing: in a survey of thirty lines they are indistinguishable from each other and from every other migrated member. **The resolution is to put the date inside the opening clause rather than in front of it** -- lead with the claim and let the date ride along: *The cost of splitting is what keeps this open, and it was clear from the day the question was raised, 2026-08-13.* Same information, same rule satisfied, and the line now names its own subject. **The tell is mechanical**: if the first sentence would be equally true of any other member of any other entry, it is a date stamp rather than an opening.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order, the first file migrated under the written cluster-shaping standard.
why:
Recorded because the interaction is invisible until both rules are applied at once, and the failure is silent -- the memory is correct, the rule is obeyed, and only the derived line is worthless. It is also self-inflicted in a specific way worth naming: the dating rule is newer and more prominent in a migrator's mind than the summary rule, so it wins the opening by recency rather than by argument.

Cheap to fix and expensive to leave: an unexported member can be amended, so the whole cost is reading the echoed line, but after export it needs a supersession to change one sentence.

content: Found 2026-08-30 by probing the edge case `forgetting-a-chains-middle-makes-a-stale-conclusion-current-again` creates — forgetting the **newest** memory in a chain rather than its middle. `superseded_beyond_this_set` is documented as *"this memory's own `SUPERSEDED_BY` names a replacement in a set not loaded here"*, and its whole value is the remedy it implies: load that set, fetch the target. Since the ancestry fix, a chain whose replacement was *forgotten* resolves the same way, because both are `unresolved` — a tip the walk reached and cannot produce. Reproduced from the tool surface by storing A, superseding it with B, forgetting B, and looking A up: `incoming` carries `{"label": "supersedes", "source": "<B, now a tombstone>"}` and `superseded_beyond_this_set` is `true`.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery, and the mechanism: two different situations collapse to one internal state, `unresolved`, and the flag names only one of them.

content: A model-fit check recognised a link by its spelling, 2026-10-04. `reaches_a_hub` and `fit_sentence_sets` in `src/store.rs` followed only `LinkTarget::SameSet` links. So a recommendation whose link to the hub carried `target_set` naming the set itself was refused, although the write stores that link as same-set. A small-model trial found it, not a test: gemma4:12b wrote that link and was refused five times, each refusal naming the id it had already used. Fixed the same day, uncommitted at the time: both checks now ask `LinkTarget::is_foreign_to` as the write does, in `targets_in_this_set`. Pinned by `a_recommendation_linking_to_the_hub_by_naming_its_own_set_is_accepted` in `tests/model_fit.rs`. The same shape was already fixed once here, `a-link-naming-its-own-set-by-an-old-name-is-inert`.
context: Building model recommendations for the declared-language check and testing the status how-to on a small local model.
why: A failure record under the `coding-lessons` adoption guide, part 3. It is the third instance of the lesson on guards keyed to spelling, which makes that lesson the most frequent among this project's last twenty failures.

content: `hoard_lookup` and `hoard_recall` returned different memory shapes — lookup omitted `context` and added `superseded_by` — so a caller handling memories from both had to special-case which tool produced them, for no reason either description explained. Fixed 2026-08-03 with the `MemoryView` convergence. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `lookup-and-recall-disagree-on-shape`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row. Kept as its own entry despite being folded into one change, because it is the shape later entries cite when two surfaces disagree.

content: Two servers on one store could disagree about the embedding model, and an ordinary *read* by one destroyed and rebuilt the whole vector set — so two sessions alternating recalls re-embedded everything, every time, forever. Fixed 2026-08-20 by making a read never rebuild, which removes the loop's mechanism rather than damping it. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `two-servers-can-disagree-about-the-model`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: A memory whose own `SUPERSEDED_BY` named a same-set id no store holds disappeared from semantic recall **and** from keyword search with nothing said — the chain reported as resolved, both paths substituted the tip, failed to fetch it, and dropped the hit. Fixed 2026-08-25 by asking at the tip whether a replacement can be handed to a reader. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-superseded-by-naming-an-absent-id-hides-its-memory`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content:
**Resolved 2026-09-19: Scatterhoard bounds how long a memory may be and asks for density in the conventions, and it does neither by tracking drift.**

Decided and built: a memory over 2000 characters of `embedding_input` is refused at both write doors, the message naming the measured length and telling the caller to split; the encoding stopped truncating at 512 tokens the same day, so the cliff this question was partly about no longer exists; and `store-when` gained *Make each memory compact, tightly-written, and atomic — one claim, not several.* The bound is atomicity rather than the embedder's budget, and the number came from this project's first five weeks, which never reached it.

Decided against: a **minimum** length. The failure it was aimed at — a memory in a language the model cannot represent — is not a length problem, since Russian and Greek tokenise fully and still fail to separate, recorded under `model-covers-declared-languages`.

Residue, carried as its own question rather than left here: `query-density-guidance`, whether a session needs guidance on writing a query at all.

Not pursued, deliberately: whether the drift follows the writing model rather than the corpus. A bound holds whatever causes the drift, so the cause stopped being load-bearing.

The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `memory-size-drift`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing the memory-size question after the refusal, the encoding fix and the convention sentence all shipped, and after the sets were rebuilt. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 3 links an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseding the open standing with a resolved one. Recorded with what was decided *against* as well as for, because a later session meeting long memories will reach for a floor, and the reason there is none is a measurement rather than an oversight.

content: **Whether a memory's author is a name or a reference. Resolved 2026-09-24: a reference, as built by 2026-09-07, and its residue settled by the human partner.** `created.by` holds the id of a `hoard-author` memory; the operations are `mint`, `identify` and `rename`; and the first record attributes itself (`Memory::self_attributed`). The residue — the silent machine-account default — is decided: the first write into a shared set with no author is refused until one is named for that set, and `local` defaults to the system account name, renamable, with `SCATTERHOARD_AUTHOR` removed. Built as `set-settled-at-first-write`. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `author-name-or-reference`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner: the author rule at first write, and `local`'s default.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. The previous head kept it open because a named refinement — `create` requiring an author — was unbuilt; that refinement is now replaced by a decided one, first write rather than creation, whose build is tracked as backlog. The self-attribution residue the previous head also named was checked in the code and is built.

content: Nothing caps how much a single recall can return: `limit` is honoured unclamped, so a caller passing a large number gets the whole store back in one response, and the scan work scales with it. Fixed when there is a maximum, the schema publishes it and the default, and a request above it is clamped with the response saying so or refused rather than silently honoured. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `recall-limit-is-unbounded`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only, with the fixed-when since this one is open. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Measured 2026-08-04: `limit: 100000` was honoured silently — the entire thirteen-memory store came back in one response, roughly 11,000 characters, of which **nine entries scored at or below zero**. Two things that sharpens. The ceiling is the corpus size, so the cost grows with precisely the thing Scatterhoard exists to accumulate, and the *harmless today* reading holds only while the store is small. And it **compounds** with `no-non-match-floor` rather than merely coexisting: with no floor, an unbounded limit does not return too many *results* — it returns the whole store *as* results, most of them non-matches formatted identically to matches. Also `limit: 0` returns an empty list rather than a refusal, which a caller cannot distinguish from *nothing matched*; same parameter, same absent validation, worth doing in one pass.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The measurement, and the interaction with the missing non-match floor — two defects that are individually bounded and jointly return the whole corpus as apparent matches.

content: **The correction half of this pair shipped 2026-08-30** as `in-link-remark-on-a-content-correction`, so the shape exists rather than needing designing: `amend` returns `in_links` (source and label, `supersedes` filtered out) plus `in_links_note`, built on `Store::incoming_edges`, with three mutations pinning *fires*, *does not over-fire* and *leaves `supersedes` out*. **What remains is a different call site and a different reason, and the difference should survive the copying**: correction remarks because a label may have been *invalidated*, while supersession remarks because a label will be *silently re-pointed* at a memory its author never saw. The note has to say the second thing, and `hoard_memorize` is where it goes, since that is where a `supersedes` link is written. *Note the criterion the codebase applies: remark when the caller can still act, refuse when they cannot — here they can, in the same turn.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A sibling fix that supplies the mechanism and not the message. Recorded because copying the working implementation is the obvious move and would carry the wrong explanation with it.

content: **Haiku was shown eight `hoard_conventions` page formats on 2026-10-01, twice each, and asked whether it had every convention.** All 20 first-page reads across both rounds said more was coming, including the current format returning 2,277 characters against a 3,500 budget. A JSON fragment page with no header was read as unfinished, but the reader had no cursor to continue with. Only numbered conventions ("m of N") told a last-page reader the total. One reader of a final "10–11 of 11" page decided it had missed conventions 1–9 and would restart from the beginning. A last page in the current format led one reader to call two conventions the whole catalog. Weak evidence: two runs per format; subagents with this repository's `AGENTS.md` loaded, which says to page until no cursor comes; neutral framing only partly offset that; and asking "do you have them all" prompts a check a real session may never make.
context: Taking on max-chars-is-not-a-bound after fixing the uuid id-ordering bug. The human partner proposed character-granular paging, then sending the catalog as one unclosed JSON list across pages, then numbering conventions "m of N".
why: This is the test behind the paging redesign for `max-chars-is-not-a-bound`. The human partner wanted to know whether a weaker model given a small budget would stop paging early. It also explains why the design moved to a one-line header that states the outcome and the total on every page: the header gives fragments a cursor and gives last pages a total. Set at 0.6 because of the contamination and the sample size. The test should not be repeated as-is: a clean run needs a context with no project instructions (no `claude` CLI or API key was available on this machine), neutral file names, and no completeness question.

content: The same word named two sets depending on which field it sat in: `scope: "local"` is the set that never leaves this machine, while `target_set: "local"` on a link resolved to a **shared set called `local`**, almost certainly one that does not exist. Fixed 2026-08-21 by reserving `local` as a set name, so the link case became unrepresentable rather than detected. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `target-set-local-names-a-different-set`; this record carries only its standing.

content: Two cautions for whoever builds the unprompted half. **It must stay a *remark***: moving the local store deliberately and leaving the old file behind is legitimate, and so is a first run in a fresh home beside an unrelated one. **And stderr is the wrong channel** — the model-missing line already goes there and is invisible in a client, which is what made this defect's sibling hard to notice.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Two constraints on a fix that is otherwise obvious: the condition has legitimate causes, so it cannot be an error, and the channel that seems natural is one no client shows.

content: **The cluster-shaping guidance's placement was decided on 2026-09-07 by eliminating three homes that each looked right first, and that elimination still stands wherever the guidance sits.** Not the served catalog: no headroom, and served text must not assert one repository's housekeeping to a session working on something else. Not a design document: `documents/design/` describes what Scatterhoard *is*, under the Vision Constraint, where this is how one project *uses* it. Not the memory set alone: several of the rules were already memories, but memory has no trigger here — a session filing an entry would never form the query, which is the whole failure. **The argument that nearly excluded the right answer was single-source-of-truth**, on the grounds that stating rules in a file duplicates the memories holding them. That reading is wrong, and `STANDARDS.md`'s own section says so: documents may state decisions and intent freely, and the defect is reserved for a document claiming what the code *does today*. A decision restated is not a second copy in the sense that drifts; a derived number is.
context: Unifying the tracking files into TRACKING.md, the morning after the guidance was written into STANDARDS.md.
why: Split from the 2026-09-07 record on 2026-09-08 because only part of it went stale. This half is the reasoning, which is what would be re-litigated by anyone adding a rule, and it survived the guidance moving out of `STANDARDS.md` intact — the three eliminated homes are eliminated for `TRACKING.md` too. The other half, the discovery mechanism, is superseded separately. The single-source-of-truth misreading is the load-bearing correction: applied as stated it would forbid a project from writing down any rule it also remembers, which is not what the standard says and would empty the documentation of everything worth keeping.

content: The test suite could not have caught this, and that is the more useful finding: `tests/store.rs`'s `an_author_record` fixture built its subject by adding `hoard-author` to an ordinary memory — imitating the **marker** rather than the **shape**. A fixture built that way passes under a keyword test and would pass under any other test of the same keyword, so it cannot distinguish the two designs. It now calls `Memory::self_attributed`, the constructor the store itself uses, and three tests failed the moment it did — which is the fixture finally testing something.
context: Renaming this entry's slug to take an `about-` prefix, while fixing genindex.py's positional slug pick.
why: A test fixture that imitates a marker cannot see a marker defect. The five tests over that filter were structurally incapable of failing, and nothing in a passing suite says so. Superseded 2026-09-21 only to move it to the entry's renamed slug; the claim is unchanged.

content: **Two things decided while building, 2026-08-30.** **The field is named `in_links`, not `incoming`**, even though the elements are identical and come from the same function: `incoming` on the read surface is *every* edge, while this is the non-`supersedes` subset — **one name for two extents is how `lookup-and-recall-disagree-on-shape` happened** — and the note states the filter rather than leaving it to be inferred. **And `hoard_correct` had no approval snapshot at all**, which is a gap in a standing requirement rather than an oversight about this feature; this response carries prose, which is exactly what gets reworded without anyone re-reading it. `correct_in_link_remark` records the remarking case, and the silent case is asserted in `tests/correct.rs`, since there is nothing prose-shaped in it to drift.
context: Migrating the in-link-remark entry out of BACKLOG.md; these are the build-time decisions it recorded.
why:
The naming rule is the reusable half: two fields carrying the same element type but different extents must not share a name, because a caller who learns the extent from one will assume it of the other, and nothing in the payload contradicts them. That is a defect this project has already filed once under a different pair.

The snapshot gap is worth recording as a class rather than an incident. An approval snapshot earns its place where a response carries **prose**, since prose is what drifts silently under rewording; a response of pure structure is better asserted directly. That is why the two halves of this feature are covered by different instruments rather than both by snapshots.

content: **Recording every response a test suite produces is a cheap way to find what a response can contain, and found a defect on its first pass.** Done 2026-10-03 with temporary instrumentation in `call_tool`, writing each JSON payload to its own file. One shared file lost 1,649 of 2,383 lines to interleaving between parallel tests. The 2,383 responses were then summarised into a field tree per tool and action. Recall spelled `referenced_from[].scope` as an object, `{"shared": …}`, where lookup spelled it as a string, visible only in the tree. The cause was `ReferencedFrom`'s derived `Serialize`, reached by recall and not by lookup.
context: Publishing output schemas; surveying the response surface to write them from evidence.
why: The technique is worth reusing whenever a response surface needs documenting or auditing, and the one-file-per-response detail is what makes it work under parallel tests. The defect it found is the `WireScope` drift arriving at a site added after that fix. It shows only for shared sources, since the derived form writes `local` as a plain string, so a test using `local` passes without the fix, as the first draft of its test did.

content:
**Compute a description of a memory set derived from its own contents, write it into the exported file, and recompute it at import.** Decided 2026-09-12 under `golden-rule-beyond-person-harm`; this is the work that question left behind, and the design decisions are made.

**What it does.** At export, cluster the set's stored embeddings and label each cluster by the keywords most distinctive to it against the rest of the set, then show cluster sizes and labels beside the charter's declared description — the derived picture next to the claimed one. Write the result into the exported file, where it is readable in a git diff without running Scatterhoard. At import, recompute the same thing from the memories actually being imported and show that. **Never read the stored summary back as fact**: it is ordinary data in a file that can be edited before shipping, and a self-attested claim wearing the authority of a measurement is worse than no claim. Compare stored against recomputed only when the embedding-model hash matches — a different model yields different clusters, and a signal that mostly fires benignly will be ignored, taking the rare real case with it.

**Two of the choices were settled by measurement, not taste.** Cluster representatives — the memory nearest a centroid — do **not** work: the most central memory is still one specific claim rather than a theme. Distinctive keywords do work. Content-derived terms would close the gaming hole, since keywords are a user-controlled field and content is not, but they read badly on a prose-heavy corpus and were rejected on the grounds that gaming keywords is a deliberate act, and defence against a determined actor is explicitly not a success criterion here.

**It describes and does not judge** — no flagging, no classifier, no threshold. A local tool has no telemetry to tune one and no way to measure its false positives, and the threat report is damning about classifiers resolving intent in dual-use territory.

**Left to decide while building, none of them forks:** how `k` is chosen, set by hand at 8 and 6 for the measurement; what the file-format field is called, and whether adding it counts as a format-version change given that the version currently gates nothing; the fallback where the importing machine has no embedding model, since whole-set keyword labelling still works there but clustering does not; whether it attaches to [Export Review](documents/design/export-review.md)'s unbuilt judgement half or stands beside it; and the roughly one clause `export-before-commit` would need, since it currently says to read the file's diff and would need to say to read this too.
context: Filed the same day the Golden Rule question was raised, once demand C had been widened in the design document and the mechanism agreed.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: the work and its standing. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

Supersedes the first head solely to correct one link label. It carried `depends_on` to the measurement that settled the labelling scheme, meaning *this rests on that evidence* — but `genindex.py` renders `depends_on` as `blocked by N`, so the row read `ready · blocked by 1`, which contradicts itself. The measurement motivates this entry; nothing blocks it. Superseded rather than amended because the first head had already been exported.

Filed as backlog rather than left inside the question because the design forks are closed — the site, the labelling scheme, the recompute rule and the show-don't-judge ceiling were each settled, two of them by measurement. What is left is building, and an entry that stays a question invites the choices to be reopened by whoever picks it up.

content: An import whose file declares a set identity different from the one a non-empty store holds succeeds and says nothing: `adopt_set_id` keeps the store's identity, deliberately neither displacing nor refusing, and the response reports `adopted_set_id: null` exactly as for a file that agreed. So one set can hold two identities on two machines with no signal on either, and a cross-set link naming it by identity resolves on one and dangles on the other. Fixed when the mismatch is reported. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `an-import-silently-keeps-a-different-set-identity`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Evaluating how-a-renamed-fork-gets-its-own-identity before release, by running the documented fork procedure and a variant in a test.
why: Head of an issue cluster. `misleads`: nothing is lost, but each machine believes it holds the one set, and the identity it answers to differs from its collaborators' with nothing to say so. Found 2026-09-22 exercising fork procedures, where a collaborator who imported a hand-edited fork file before the forker re-exported kept its own minted identity permanently. Reporting rather than refusing, because `adopt_set_id`'s documentation leaves what identity gates open, and a note does not answer that question by accident.

content: **What a similarity score means when the corpus is too small to have a centre.** Observed 2026-08-02 driving the server against the real model: a store holding exactly one memory returns that memory for a query it plainly matches, with `similarity: 0.0`. **This is arithmetic working correctly** -- scores are centred on the corpus mean, and with one vector the memory *is* the mean, so centring yields zero. Adding two more restored sensible separation (`+0.269` against `-0.138` and `-0.143`). The empty corpus is not affected: it returns nothing, which is the honest answer. **The problem is the shape of what a caller sees.** The very first recall against a new memory set -- the moment a user is deciding whether any of this works -- reports a perfect match as `0.0`, which reads as *no match* to a model with no way to know the score's baseline was itself. **It is the two-scales lesson again in a new place:** `0.0` from a one-memory store and `0.0` from a thousand-memory store are not the same measurement, and nothing in the result distinguishes them. **Needs:** whether recall suppresses or nulls the score below some corpus size rather than reporting a number it cannot support, whether the result should carry what the score was measured against, and whether `confidence` is what a caller should lean on at that size anyway. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `similarity-in-a-small-corpus`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The *arithmetic working correctly* framing is kept in the head because it decides what kind of fix is admissible: this is a reporting problem rather than a scoring bug, and a session reading only the symptom would go looking for an error in the centring.

The first-recall framing is kept because it is what makes a cosmetic-sounding issue matter -- the failure lands precisely on the user with the least context to interpret it.

content: Severity argued honestly rather than assumed: the blast radius was casing only and no search returned a wrong answer, which pulls toward Misleads. It was filed as **Corrupts** because it is irreversible loss of caller-supplied content that no interface can reveal, and because the cost grows rather than stays flat — acronyms and identifiers are exactly what people put in keywords (`MCP`, `SUPERSEDES`, `main.rs`), and the moment export exists this becomes lossy round-tripping into a file a human reads. The existing corpus already showed it: a memory stored 2026-08-03 carries `"mcp"`.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A worked example of severity by consequence rather than by effort, including the argument against the lighter reading. Kept because the deciding factor — cost that grows with use rather than staying flat — is reusable and is not in the severity table.

content: `origin` was a field the caller sets, can get wrong, and no instrument reached: not apparatus by the corrections document's definition, not claim either, and named nowhere in the design — so a caller who misattributed reasoning had to guess at the repair. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `origin-cannot-be-corrected`; this record carries only its standing.

why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **These seven entries must be settled before publication**; they are this memory's keywords. Gated 2026-09-23 by the human partner. Three have answers that would break something already in use if changed afterwards: the tool surface, the file format, or what an identity means. They are `set-settled-at-first-write`, `several-memory-files-per-directory` and `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout`. `unrecognised-link-labels-on-import` decides whether every later label is a format break. `imported-set-trust-boundary` is gated because trust decisions have repeatedly shaped the file format. `claude-md-in-the-repository` gets a look, though it is easier to change afterwards. `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity` is gated because crafted files arrive with publication.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner.
why: Superseded 2026-09-25: `one-repository-many-sets` was resolved (several `.json` files per `scatterhoard_mem`, found by `set_id`), and its build, `several-memory-files-per-directory`, takes its place, because the build moves where a published file lives. Retire an item by superseding this memory without its slug.

content: Implementation notes for the casefold change, 2026-08-23. **Composed rather than called, because no crate provides it**: ICU4X had `new_nfkc_casefold` in 1.x and removed it in 2.x, so `NFKC → fold → NFKC` over `unicode-normalization` + `caseless` agrees with `icu_casemap` on every case tested and costs **4 transitive crates against 76**; `caseless` 0.2.2's version number is misleading, since it declares Unicode 16.0. **The order is load-bearing and is measured rather than asserted**: 664 single characters below U+30000 fold differently with and without the leading `NFKC`, `U+1D2C` being the clearest — normalised first it reaches `a`, folded first it stays `A`, and no later pass recovers the case. A mutation pins the order separately from the parts. **What it deliberately does not merge**, each being a distinction a reader means to draw: hiragana against katakana, simplified against traditional Han, and the Turkish dotted `İ`. Caseless scripts come through byte-identical, so this cost CJK keywords nothing. **`folded` is derived state and the rule deriving it changed**, so `Store::refold_keywords` rebuilds it at open, guarded by a `keyword_fold` marker in `meta` naming the rule the column was built under — the same thing `embedding_model` does for vectors, for the same reason.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The composition, the measured operation order, and the marker that makes derived state rebuildable when its rule changes — the same pattern as the embedding model identity, which is what makes it the project's general answer for derived state.

content: **Four rules complete the cutover, and the third is what stops it being fragile -- the design as decided 2026-08-30.** **Mint at `create`**, so a set has an identity before anything is written to it, exactly as its author is claimed. **Carry it in the header.** **Adopt from the file when the store has none** -- which is the rule that saves the hard cut: someone who has already built a store from the committed file gets the canonical identity on their next import rather than minting a rival. **And a file with no identity is checked exactly as before, by name** -- it neither proves nor disproves identity, so it degrades to current behaviour rather than to a refusal, and nothing is invented. **What it gates is deliberately not part of that, and shipping the identity must not look as though it settled it.** An identity answers *is this the same set* and can never answer *is this the same copy*. **Carrying a field nothing yet refuses on is close to a pattern this project rejects** -- do not serve text describing a guard that does not exist -- and the claim for doing it anyway is that the field's *meaning* is fully defined while nothing enforces it, and that the cost of not having it compounds daily where the cost of having it idle is one header key.
context: Migrating open-questions.md, recovering content a faulty deletion boundary had left orphaned after the entry's head was already stored.
why:
Recorded because the adopt-from-file rule is the non-obvious one and the whole migration's safety rests on it: without it, every existing holder of the committed file mints a rival identity on first build, which is the exact collision the change exists to prevent.

The self-aware note about shipping an unenforced field is worth keeping as a precedent. This project normally refuses to ship a description of a guard that does not exist, and here it deliberately made an exception with the reasoning stated -- so a later argument in either direction has the case on record rather than having to relitigate the principle.

content: The instruments for asking whether Scatterhoard's conventions work, none of them built. **Avoidable work**: a near-duplicate pair is a failed `recall-before-storing`, and it is checkable by replaying the prescribed recall against the corpus **as it stood before the later memory was written** -- which separates *the session did not look* from *looking would not have found it*, and hands only the second to the recall eval. Same shape for a memory superseded seconds after being written, and for a claim naming a symbol that no longer exists, which `store-when`'s *name where it can be checked* makes mechanically detectable. **Cross-session information**: an edge whose endpoints content similarity would never have connected, which `link_reach` in src/eval.rs already computes -- the corpus held one such edge at the 62nd percentile with cosine -0.048. **Per-convention observables** exist for most of the catalog: duplicate rate, keyword spellings that split one subject, the confidence histogram, sessions ending with nothing stored.
context: Worked out 2026-08-30 with the human partner, who asked whether convention effectiveness could be measured objectively and named the two values: avoidable work, and information available only across sessions. Filed as an open question in documents/design/open-questions.md, and expected to be taken up with `cold-reread-of-the-catalog` in BACKLOG.md.
why: Recorded because the ideas are cheap to lose and expensive to re-derive, and because the strongest of them was already in the project unrecognised: `confidence-standards` exists because someone measured a field's distribution, which is a convention justified by an observable in the corpus it produces. The confound is severe enough to state with the instruments rather than after them -- the same model is subject and experimenter, so a before-and-after across a ship date is objective and not controlled. `recall-eval-harness` is not this: it measures whether the right memory comes back for a query and contains no session, so it cannot see a decision a convention governs. Its percentile arithmetic is nonetheless the one piece already built.

content: The store computes each record's `file_position` in Rust at export rather than holding it, so export sorts every id in process and holds every tombstone whole to do it. `Store::stream_records` collects tombstones in full and all memory ids, then sorts them by hash. Built when `memories` and `tombstones` each carry a `NOT NULL`, indexed position column written on insert and backfilled by migration, stored sign-flipped so SQLite's signed order matches the unsigned hash, and export streams one `ORDER BY` over both tables. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `file-position-column`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Discussing whether the hash that orders memory files should live in the store, after restoring from the 2026-09-22 checkpoint. Filed alongside the streaming merge driver.
why: Decided by the human partner on 2026-09-22, with the streaming merge ranked first. A column rather than a mapping table because a missing mapping row would silently drop a memory from the export, where `NOT NULL` makes the omission impossible. Until the 2026-09-21 move to hash order, export was already an `ORDER BY` on the way out ([file-format.md](documents/design/file-format.md)); this restores that property under the new order. Modest at current sizes: roughly 24 bytes a record plus whole tombstones.

content: The harness could not compare two rules each at its own best walk. Built 2026-08-18: `scatterhoard-eval` takes `--seeds`, `--hops`, `--decay`, `--frontier`, `--rule` and `--k`, defaulting to the configuration the earlier measurements used so a bare run still reproduces what is recorded. A new **`grid`** mode crosses every rule with a range of decays and reports each rule's **spread** beside its best cell, because the question a rule has to answer is how far it moves when the corpus is not the one it was tuned on. It also reports the own-score distribution — mean, deviation and the gap below the leader — which is what says whether a given corpus can exercise a level-versus-gap sensitivity at all. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `eval-walk-from-the-caller`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only. Small, and it blocked a question the human partner has to answer, which is why it was built ahead of larger work.

Reporting *spread* beside the best cell is the part that is not obvious: a rule that wins its best cell and moves a long way across the grid has been tuned rather than validated.

content: **The export review's judgement gate is built before the repositories go public, and Scatterhoard must not depend on `git` to run it.** Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. The `git` constraint rules out reading the committed memory file with `git show`, so the 2026-10-17 rule, that the review set is the diff against the committed file, needs another way to know what has already been cleared.
context: Starting the export review's judgement gate, right after the sharing preferences and never-store list were committed.
why: The concern is the privacy of Scatterhoard's users: the project's own memories had their full review by hand. Shipping without the gate and following fast was possible, but the human partner would rather not build it under the time pressure of a public release. A memory set may live in a synced folder rather than a repository, so the review cannot assume one.

content: The author note compared a set's recorded name against the server's configured one and called the difference a discrepancy — but under the attribution model that difference is the *expected* state, since one person has one account name on this machine and publishes as `jtcours` on GitHub, so the note fired permanently on both live shared sets. Fixed 2026-09-02 by replacing the comparison with the one condition that stops work. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-author-note-compares-against-the-wrong-thing`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row. Restated 2026-10-30 at the person's request during the set's export review, to remove their machine account name; the claim is unchanged.

content: Found 2026-08-06 immediately after `store-is-not-configured-for-two-processes`, checking whether WAL and a busy timeout would be sufficient. They would not. `Store` holds `vectors: VectorSet` in memory deliberately — the comment says it is kept there *"so reopening a store does not put the embedder on the critical path of simply opening it"*, which is a good reason, and the field is not the mistake. The mistake is that nothing invalidates it when a different process writes. **The two search paths then disagree about what the store contains** — keyword search reads SQL and finds the new memory, semantic recall does not — and nothing in either response says so, which is the *hides whether something is wrong* case the Corrupts severity is defined to cover. Distinct from the locking defect and **not fixed by it**: WAL and `busy_timeout` address locking, this is cache coherence, and a store could be perfectly serialised and still serve stale vectors.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery, with the cached field explicitly defended and the two defects separated. Worth keeping because *we fixed the concurrency problem* is exactly the conclusion that would have left this one in place.

content: **On `governance-docs` the offside query scores like ordinary off-topic background, not like an outlier.** Six of the session's own questions about Scatterhoard, re-asked unscoped on 2026-09-24 at the human partner's suggestion, scored 0.20–0.37 there and 0.32–0.41 on `local`, against 0.47–0.74 on the sets that answered; neither small set contributed a hit to any of them. The calibrate-note question reached 0.366 on `governance-docs` — beside the offside query's 0.376 — so the football case sits at the level the set gives any question not about it, and is exposed only because on an unanswerable question nothing outranks that level.
context: Discussing the shape of a backup calibration mode with the human partner, after the self-query probe; they asked whether the small sets would chime in on the session's own questions asked unscoped.
why: Explains the earlier self-query result rather than adding a new one: a floor under a small set's own answers cannot remove what scores like its everyday background. It moves the small-set problem from where to put a floor to what should happen when every calibrated set declines a question and only an uncalibrated set's background remains. Five of the six queries were readable in the log; two shared a second.

content: **Two things easy to lose when reasoning about model ownership, stated 2026-08-20 at decision time.** **Gap-filling stays automatic, but fills gaps with the *store's* model** rather than whatever the writing process happens to hold — the distinction is that a gap is an **absence** and costs coverage, while a mixture is **two vector spaces in one store** and costs correctness. And **"do not destroy what you cannot rebuild" is orthogonal to ownership**: a process with no model must still be stopped from rewriting a memory that currently has a vector, whatever the store says it owns. The four parts as decided: reads never rebuild, so `reconcile_embeddings` stops re-embedding on `Mismatched` and a read leaves a store it cannot maintain alone; the exclusion is **named**, so a recall reports which scopes were left out and why — a **prerequisite** rather than a companion, since once a mismatch is a configuration rather than a fault, partial coverage is ordinary and has to be legible; an explicit model-change command whose side effect is rebuilding every vector, where requesting the model the store already holds is legal and is a reset; and `model_state` distinguishing **no vectors and no model** from **vectors present with the model unrecorded**, since only the first has nothing to lose.
context: Migrating the store-owns-its-model entry out of BACKLOG.md; these are the decisions the entry warned would be lost.
why:
The gap-versus-mixture distinction is the one a later change will collapse, because both look like "some vectors are missing or wrong" from the outside and the automatic behaviour differs. Filling a gap with the writing process's model would be the obvious convenience and would quietly put two embedding spaces in one store, which no test of coverage would catch.

Two of the four needed less code than filed, which is worth knowing before re-planning similar work: the explicit command already existed as `hoard_sets` action `reembed`, warning and cycle detection included, lacking only a reset that reports honestly — and `embedded-store-can-report-itself-unembedded` was closed from the other side, by the invariant rather than by a check, since a store with no vectors is bound to no model. The model-identity history and directive warning from the 2026-08-09 proposal stay built and unused as a loop preventer, exactly as the decision predicted: they are evidence for a human, not the mechanism.

content: Nothing tells a human what `scatterhoard_mem` is. Raised 2026-08-21 by the human partner: a person meeting the directory for the first time finds `memories.json` and no explanation, and a `README.md` written when the directory is created is the cheapest possible onboarding. The proposed default is the right register — *"This directory contains memories for the Scatterhoard memory system."* **It has to be a recognised entry, not merely a tolerated one**: [trigger-and-loading.md](documents/design/trigger-and-loading.md) reserves the whole directory and says an unknown entry is *worth surfacing*, so a README that Scatterhoard writes and does not know about would trip its own tripwire — adding the file and adding it to the known set are one task. Built when creating a memory directory writes a `README.md` if none exists, the file is on the recognised list, and a test pins that an existing README is left untouched. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `memory-directory-readme`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Sync and export section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only.

**Do not overwrite an existing one**, which is part of the standing rather than a detail: a project may edit the README to say something about its own memory set, which is legitimate and theirs to own — and writing it on creation then leaving it alone also keeps this out of the export path, where a rewritten file would appear in every diff.

content: **How a set's description is derived, as of 2026-09-14.** Spherical k-means over the stored embeddings, seeded by `k-means++` with each memory's draw keyed by a hash of its id, keeping the most cohesive of ten seedings — so a small change to a set leaves its grouping largely intact, and every machine computes the same partition (derivation `clusters/2`; `clusters/1` drew by position, see `a-set-description-reshuffles-on-a-small-change`); `k` from `round(1.2 · ln n)` clamped to 2..12; each cluster labelled by its most distinctive keywords. It is shown as `describes` on the export response, after embedding anything missing; an import recomputes it rather than reading anything back; and one owed when an arriving memory lacks a vector is reported by `hoard_conventions` at every session start until an export describes the whole set. `export-before-commit` tells a session to read it against the charter, implying nothing about the motives of the memories' authors.
context: Moved 2026-09-24 out of the entry's head, which was over the length limit, in step 2 of the out-link work.
why: The mechanism of the built entry, kept apart from its standing. The file's `summary` field and the import's `against_the_claim` comparison are left out because both were retired 2026-09-21.

content: **Step 1 of `adopting-coding-lessons` done 2026-09-28: `coding-lessons`' charter is rewritten**, as `01M3MVT6MW…` superseding `01M2F32X5Z…`. The test is now *would hold on a different codebase*, with language tags marking narrower applicability. The three attached kinds and their links are described as data, not instructions. The personal-set sentence was dropped, since `route-where` serves it to every session. The closing sentence now names the project as something memories are not tagged with. The adoption guide is deliberately not referenced yet, since it does not exist; the charter gains a pointer when it is next superseded.
context: Starting adopting-coding-lessons: the charter rewrite, drafted from the set-adoption decisions and edited by the human partner.
why: A member of the `adopting-coding-lessons` cluster, history from implementing it. Recorded because the human partner's two edits and the unreferenced guide are choices a later reader of the charter cannot see from its text. The human partner proposed an imperative *do not tag memories with the project's name*; it became a descriptive clause instead, because a recalled memory is data, and the charter already said it.

content: **The calibration figures were measured with raw cosine and no centroid; Scatterhoard ships centred, and under the shipping scorer the headroom goes negative.** `Store::recall` builds a `combined_centroid` over every set being searched and calls `nearest_centred_on`, then truncates with `traversal::cut_at_largest_gap`. The probes measured none of that. Re-measured on `scatterhoard` with 30 substance probes against 18 answerable queries: **raw** floor(p90) 0.275, worst answerable 0.361, headroom **+0.085**; **centred on the set's own centroid** 0.334 against 0.259, headroom **−0.074**; **centred on the combined centroid**, which is what a session holding four sets actually runs, 0.325 against 0.238, headroom **−0.087**. Centring moves both terms the wrong way at once — it *raises* the probe floor and *lowers* the worst real query — for a swing of **0.172**. **A floor placed at p90 of the probes would reject real results under the scorer that ships.** Separation itself survives: AUC 0.989 raw, 0.922 own-centroid, **0.909 combined**. So the mechanism is still viable and the *calibration rule* is not. Note also that a small set is centred on a centroid it does not dominate — `governance-docs`'s floor moves 0.089 → 0.218 between raw and combined.
context: The human partner asking, before any design work began, whether the probes ran through Scatterhoard's own mechanism or a separate tool. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the memory was over the length limit.
why: Supersedes the calibration record because its numbers came from a configuration that does not ship, and it was exported and committed in `33866e3` before that was noticed. The human partner caught it by asking whether the test setup used Scatterhoard's own mechanism or a separate tool — which no internal checking had prompted, because the probes load the real model and build the embedding input identically to `embedding_input`, so the two places they diverge are invisible unless you read the recall path.

content: **The second test is the one worth having, and the original entry did not name it — drawing the fault in both directions is what found it, 2026-08-21.** `opening_a_current_store_twice_keeps_its_bases` pins the **permissive** failure.
