Detection keys on whether `bases` declares any foreign key; if that were wrong in the direction of **firing too often**, the table would be dropped on every open. **That is a worse failure than the one being migrated away from**: no error, no missing memory, just every record reading as having no ancestor at every import, silently and for ever.
context: Migrating the bases-migration-test entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the failure direction the entry discovered while being built.
why:
Recorded because the asymmetry is invisible from the entry that commissioned the work. A migration test is naturally written to prove the migration *happens*, and that direction is the one anyone thinks of; the over-firing direction produces no symptom a test of the intended behaviour would ever reach, and its consequence is silent, permanent and worse.

The general move — for a conditional repair, ask what happens if the condition fires when it should not, as well as if it fails to fire — is what turned one test into two here.

content: **A change is closed by storing every memory it owes before one review, then exporting, regenerating the indexes and committing, and anything learned after the commit waits for the next one.** Agreed 2026-10-26 with the human partner, and written into `AGENTS.md` under *Closing a change*, which is the copy to follow. It also says not to write a memory that can only be true after the commit, such as one naming a commit hash.
context: Closing out the judgement gate's build before its first commit, after reviewing and exporting the scatterhoard set and finding that each round of record-keeping produced another round.
why: The reverse order never ends. Storing "the gate is built" after the export needed a second review and export, and a memory recording that would have needed a third. Treating "nothing unexported" as the finish line is what drives it, and nothing requires it: the store is durable, and `review_due` reports unreviewed memories at the next session start. It lives in `AGENTS.md` rather than only here because it is used at a moment that does not feel like it needs a lookup, which is when a rule that must be recalled arrives too late.

content: **The per-change recall changed the design, 2026-10-03: a part-6 observation under `adopting-coding-lessons`.** Before rewording the missing-query refusal, recalling `coding-lessons` with one sentence describing the change returned two lessons that applied. One said to name the specific call an error expects (`01M03V60G2…`), which turned a reworded message into one showing the caller's own call with the query added. The other said to test a refusal's remedy by taking it (`01M3GMWH77…`), which became the test's second half: it makes the suggested call and asserts it succeeds. The recall was made at the hand-off from the human partner's "fix it next" to building, where the four recorded skips fell.
context: Fixing the missing-query refusal, right after filing how-much-scatterhoard-lifts-a-small-model.
why: Evidence for the adoption investigation: a recall at the moment the skips cluster, with an effect on the result that can be traced to two named lessons, not just a recall made and ignored. Both changes then measured well: the refusal recovered 10 out of 10 on a weak reader, against 0 before.

content: An import or export whose file declares a `set_id` other than the set's is refused, where today it is reported. Decided 2026-09-25 under `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout`. On import, both forms refuse. In `directory` form, where a set's file is found by `set_id`, the no-match message says that a file there declares this set's name under another identity, if one does, rather than that the set is absent. On export, writing over a file declaring another identity is refused, including in `file` form. The refusal names both identities and three routes: alias, `absorb`, or the diverged-copy repair. A file with records and no identity keeps its note. Built when the note in `identity_note_for_import`, and its export counterpart, become refusals, with their tests and mutations moved over. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `identity-mismatch-refusal`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Resolving `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout` with the human partner, on the release gate.
why: Head of a backlog cluster. Release-gated, because it adds refusals to the tool surface: after publication each would break an import that succeeds today. It touches the same `directory`-form lookup as `several-memory-files-per-directory`, so building the two together avoids writing that no-match message twice.

content: **Fixing `the-reserved-directory-accepts-the-local-set` on 2026-09-26 went two steps past the entry.** It refuses `restore` in `directory` form as well as export and import, since a crafted checkout reaching `local` through `restore` replaces the set, not merges into it. And it makes the scope decide the path form for `local` alone, an exception to *the caller decides, not the scope*: that rule protects a published set's layout, and `local` is never published. Tests that backed `local` up through a `directory` now use `file`, and tests about the `directory` form itself moved to a shared set. Checkable in `refuse_local_in_reserved` in `src/mcp.rs`, and in set-lifecycle.md under *one exception, built 2026-09-26*.
context: Building the release gate's directory-form group: the reserved directory accepting the local set, the last of the three, after several memory files per directory and the identity-mismatch refusal.
why: History from fixing the entry, whose head named only export and import. The `restore` extension is the one a later reader might question, and the reason is the difference in consequence. The exception to the caller-decides rule would otherwise read as a contradiction of the section right above it.

content: What made the dead version gate worth fixing is that the store's disposability argument depends on it. [store.rs](src/store.rs) reasons that *"everything in a project's store can be rebuilt from its memory file, so the schema here carries no migration burden — a change means dropping the file and re-importing"* — which assumes the file is readable by the build doing the rebuilding. A change altering the store schema **and** the record shape together breaks that assumption at exactly the moment it is relied on, and for `local` there is no second copy to fall back to. And the error it would otherwise produce is one this file has already complained about: a cross-set link target is an untagged enum, so a shape it cannot match reports *"data did not match any variant"*, which [memory_file.rs](src/memory_file.rs) notes "tells a reader nothing about which shape was wrong or why, on a format whose whole job is to survive a messy merge."
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The argument that turned an accepted cost into a defect: a gate that refuses nothing is harmless until something relies on it, and the disposability argument relies on it silently. Worth keeping because the reliance is stated in a different file from the gate.

content: **Whether a set supports partial export and import.** Raised 2026-08-11 by the human partner, from the case of handing someone a few memories rather than a whole set. **Deferred rather than rejected**, with the immediate concern operational rather than architectural: the exchange today is whole-set in both directions, stated in Multi-Set Sync and in SETUP.md where an operator will meet it. **The real question is not the mechanism but what it commits the design to.** Naming which records travel is mechanical. The base rule is not: `Store::set_bases` replaces a target's whole base set on the explicit assumption that an export writes the whole file, and that interacts with the single-destination direction in Store Registry, where per-target bases can in principle carry an ongoing relationship with each of several parties while one base per record carries exactly one. **So deciding partial exchange also decides whether a set can sustain a running subset relationship with a second party, or only a one-off copy** -- and that is the half the current design would otherwise answer by default rather than deliberately. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `partial-export-and-import`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The head leads with the commitment rather than the feature because the feature looks small -- most of the reconciliation already works -- and the small-looking version is the one that would get built without noticing it had settled the subset-relationship question by accident. That is the entry's own point and it is the part that would be lost if the row read *support partial export*.

content: **A paging line that worked for `gemma4:12b` under one tool name failed under another, so a served line is tested only under the real name.** On 2026-10-01 the header "Not complete. Call load_guidelines again with {"cursor": 3500} for the rest." continued 10 out of 10. Renamed to `hoard_conventions` it continued 0 out of 10, while a plain-words control under the new name still continued 5 out of 5. Under the real name, "The conventions are not loaded yet. Call hoard_conventions again with {"cursor": N, "max_chars": M} for the rest." failed 0 out of 10 as a header and worked 10 out of 10 as a trailer after the page. That held at `max_chars` 3500 and 1000, and with thinking on 5 out of 5. As a header it worked only with "This is part 1 of 6." in front. The last-page trailer "All 11 conventions are loaded." started work 15 out of 15 with no extra calls. Every continuing call passed both arguments.
context: Settling the exact paging wording for the max-chars-is-not-a-bound redesign, just before implementing it, on the human partner's local Ollama.
why: This is why the shipped `hoard_conventions` line is a trailer with that exact wording. A later edit to the line, or to the tool name, can silently undo it, as the rename did. Why the name mattered is not known. The likely reading is that "guidelines" in the tool against "conventions" on the page made the page look less like the finished thing, but that is a guess, so this records the observation rather than an explanation. One model, so 0.8.

content: A link inside a set that named the set by a name it no longer used, and carried the set's identity, was stored as a cross-set link, so supersession inside the set silently failed: a `supersedes` link left the memory it replaced resolving `Current`, and a `superseded_by` link resolved as out of reach. Fixed 2026-09-14, the day it was found, by deciding which of the two a stored link is by set identity wherever both the link and the holding set have one, and by name only where either does not: `LinkTarget::is_foreign_to` in `src/memory/link.rs` takes the holding set's identity, and every write path in `src/store.rs` passes it — the ordinary write, restore's memories and tombstones, and an arriving tombstone's ancestry through `accept_tombstone`. Recorded in `documents/design/cross-set-references.md` under *which of the two a stored link is, is decided by identity*. No migration: no store on this machine held the broken shape. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-link-naming-its-own-set-by-an-old-name-is-inert`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Fixing supersession for a link naming its own set by an old name, after the human partner chose identity-first canonicalisation over collapsing both link forms. Same stretch: the ambiguous-anchor check and the scan subcommand.
why:
Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed. The opening sentence is the generated index row, so it now reads as history.

**What proves it.** The two parked tests pass un-parked; a third shows a link naming this set's current name with another set's identity no longer supersedes here, the behaviour this fix changes on purpose; and three more drive the long spelling through restore and arriving tombstones. Nine mutations cover it: six new, one per write path plus the rule, and three older `links:` mutations re-anchored onto the changed code.

**One test was wrong first, and the mutations caught it.** The tombstone tests' chain gave its oldest memory a `superseded_by` link of its own, so it resolved without the tombstone's edge and passed with that edge stored wrongly. Both tombstone-path mutations survived until the helper was corrected to leave the tombstone's edge as the only join.

**What the fix does not make a guarantee.** It relies on every set holding records having an identity. That holds by construction on this machine, but nothing yet refuses a record into a shared set with no identity; whether it should is open with the human partner.

content:
**`gemma4:12b` could not drive the built export review through `hoard_sets`, and twice reported a review it had not done.** Tested 2026-10-24 on a snapshot of the real `local`, through the real server.
- A 30-memory batch ran to 52,000 characters. The model called `review`, never `clear`, and said it had cleared everything.
- With batches capped at 6,000 characters of memory text, it sent `clear` with no answers and said the review was complete.
- Once an empty `clear` was refused, it reported the pre-pass findings honestly but still never built the answers, even with a ready-made `answer_with` call.

The same model sent nested answers correctly to a small dedicated tool in a short prompt, but filled `mentions` with sentence text until the field was described. The logs are in that session's scratchpad, `review-e2e-*`.
context: Building the export review's judgement gate, step 8: proving it end to end on a small model after the unit tests and mutations passed.
why: The server held throughout: nothing was cleared without answers, so the gate and the reminder stayed true. But a small model reporting a review it did not do misleads the person, which is why an empty `clear` is now refused and an unfinished one says so in words. Context measured afterwards, as Ollama counts prompt tokens against a 16,384-token window: with capped batches the prompt peaked at 10,564 tokens, so the empty `clear`, a 26-token reply, was the model's choice and not the window. The first, uncapped run would have needed about 21,000 tokens at the measured 3.6 characters per token, so it was cut from the front, losing the task, which likely explains its false report. That leaves the size and generality of the multipurpose tool as the likeliest cause. A dedicated review tool, or accepting that the review needs a more capable model, is the next decision.

content: **What an in-memory evaluation load would cost, measured 2026-09-16 on the `scatterhoard` set (902 memories).** The on-disk database is about 7 MB. Vectors are 3.7 MB of it, about 4 KB per memory, and the memory rows are 2.2 MB; keywords, links and bases make up the rest. **Every loaded store already holds all its vectors in RAM**: `Store::load_vectors` in `src/store.rs` reads the whole `vectors` table into a `VectorSet`, which recall scans. So keeping a set's SQLite in memory as well adds roughly the non-vector part, about 3–4 KB per memory, on top of a cost every loaded set already pays. At that rate 10,000 memories is about 70 MB all told, and 100,000 about 700 MB. **The larger cost is probably time**: an exported record carries no vector (its fields are confidence, content, context, created, id, keywords, modified, origin, why), so an evaluation load has to embed every memory before the set can be searched by meaning. That embedding time has not been measured.
context: Deciding whether evaluation loads should live in memory only, after fixing two-sets-can-share-an-identity.
why: Recorded because the obvious worry about a memory-only evaluation load, blowing out RAM on a large set, turns out to be mostly a cost the design already pays for every set, and it would take real effort to re-derive. The per-memory figures come from `dbstat` on one set with fairly long memories, so they are an order of magnitude to plan by, not a limit. The embedding-time claim rests on the file format and was not timed.

content: **A memory over the 2000-character limit is split when it next has to be superseded, never restated whole, and the rest are left until then.** Decided 2026-09-24 by the human partner, rejecting an exemption that would have let a supersession exceed the limit when its text is unchanged. Their reasons: large memories, especially compound ones, prevent selective in-links, need revising more often, consume more context, and can recall less well by meaning. Measured that day: 164 of 907 current memories in `scatterhoard` and 14 of 147 in `coding-lessons` are over, all written before the limit shipped on 2026-09-19. They are handled opportunistically, not by a sweep.
context: Step 2 of the out-link work, when restating links on 45 memories met the length limit on 16 of them.
why: An unchanged restatement looked harmless because it adds no claim, but it renews every cost of a compound memory under a fresh date and id, reading as a claim reaffirmed today, and would make supersession the one route by which an over-limit memory lives on indefinitely. Splitting at the moment of touching pays the cost once and lets each link land on the claim it concerns.

content: Fixed 2026-08-19: `search_keywords_across` merges every store's hits, ranks the union by `matched_keywords`, and cuts once — the shape `recall_across` already had — so both halves close together. **The tie-break is the memory id, and the question was worth asking**: equal match counts are the common case, so leaving the order to whichever store came first would make one query answer differently depending on a map ordering the caller cannot see. Ids are time-ordered, so ascending is oldest first — arbitrary, but stable and independent of how the stores were assembled. *Asking each store for `limit` before merging is kept and is not the defect: the union's top `limit` can draw at most `limit` from any one store, so the per-store cut discards only what the merge would discard — **provided both orderings agree**, which is why the merge repeats `search_keywords`'s `matches DESC, id ASC` rather than inventing its own.* Tested from both sides, including from the position the defect was measured from — two loaded sets and `limit: 1` — since both halves are invisible with the single store every other test uses.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the invariant that makes the per-store pre-cut safe: it only holds while the two orderings agree, which is why the merge reuses the store's own ordering rather than defining a second one.

content: **A filing discipline this project applies consistently and has never written down: when part of an item is blocked by something external, open-ended or unproven, split it so the ready half is not held behind it.** Four instances, three of them stated in the entries themselves. `git-merge-driver` keeps its implementation here and its registration risk in EARLY-VALIDATION.md, because the driver working and the driver being registered fail independently. `readme-names-the-project-url` is filed apart from `memory-directory-readme` because *the blocker is external and open-ended, and a Ready item should not sit behind one*. `cross-link-the-multi-slug-memories` was filed apart from `linking-has-no-trigger` on 2026-09-07 because one is reading work and the other is design work. And `export-before-commit` was split from `capture-before-ending` on 2026-08-12, where the seam was an unstated assumption rather than a blocker. **The test is whether the two halves can finish at different times for different reasons** — if they can, one Fixed-when cannot describe both, and the earlier half will close the entry over the later one. **Splitting is a filing decision, not an instruction to build blind.** Added 2026-09-16 by the human partner, against the rule ossifying: separate entries do not mean the work on the earlier half should ignore the later one. Where the two are close, foreshadowing the second while building the first is cheaper than retrofitting it — `read-only-distribution` beside `evaluation-mode` is the live case, the two modes differing by little more than which watch marks are pulled.
context: Filing read-only distribution as its own question, after the human partner asked where the split rule was written down and it turned out to be nowhere but here.
why:
Superseded 2026-09-16 to add the last two sentences, at the human partner's request, after this rule was cited in conversation with more authority than its location supports — it lives here and in no document, which the opening has always said. The claim and its four instances are unchanged.

The addition guards a specific failure: a session reading *split when the halves finish independently* can conclude that the halves must be designed independently, which is a different and worse claim. Filing separately keeps one Fixed-when from describing two things; it says nothing about what a builder should have in view. The human partner also noted the condition under which the rule itself should be revisited — the overhead of carrying several entries is low for this project now, and a requirement that made each entry expensive to review would change the balance.

Recorded because the split rule is the one this project applies by instinct and argues afresh each time, so it is one confident reading away from hardening into a rule about design rather than about filing.

content: Observed 2026-08-09 in the first real two-server run — two client-launched processes on one `SCATTERHOARD_HOME`, `potion-base-32M` against `potion-retrieval-32M`, against a disposable copy of the real stores — and it is worse in three ways than the reasoning anticipated. **The re-embedding loop is real and unbounded**: on a 27-memory store, `_a` storing recorded base-32M with 27 embedded, `_b` recalling deleted and rebuilt all 27 under retrieval-32M, and `_a` recalling deleted and rebuilt them again. **A read is what does it** — steps two and three were `hoard_recall` calls, and `reconcile_embeddings` deletes every vector on `Mismatched` and re-embeds, so an ordinary search by one server destroys and rebuilds the entire vector set silently, at a cost that scales with the corpus rather than the query. **Before any identity is recorded the detector cannot fire at all**: in that state both servers ran semantic recall over vectors from a model neither could identify and returned *different rankings for an identical query* — different top hit, different fifth result, every score different — one meaningful and one a comparison across incompatible spaces, with nothing distinguishing them, both carrying `semantic_search_available: true`. `hoard_sets status` was no help either: both servers reported byte-identical status for the same store while holding different models.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The confirmation run, with the step table's outcome and the three ways reality exceeded the prediction. The sequence in the wild is not *servers fight* but *servers silently disagree, and then start fighting once someone writes*.

content: A third seed 2026-09-02 added a requirement the first two did not show: **seeds do not all belong in the same set, and the routing is not a detail the drafter can leave to `route-where` unaided.** The recall-gloss seed is in `local` because its subject is a person; the third is in `coding-lessons` because its subject is a question shape, even though every one of its cases came from a person asking. That line — *the occasion is recordable, the asker's reasoning is not* — is the same one the golden rule draws, and **a pipeline convention that says *accumulate cases* without saying it will collect characterisations of collaborators by default, one honest observation at a time.** **Note also what the linking costs, which was got wrong here first**: the cluster can be linked, but only outward from the personal side — a shared memory pointing into a personal set dangles for every other reader, while the reverse resolves for the one person holding both. The derived backlink was built the same day, so a cluster spanning the boundary is now reachable from both halves. **The drafting requirement survives that fix in a smaller form**: the backlink is derived from the stores one machine holds and travels in no export, so a reader with only the shared set still sees nothing — guidance must say the personal end is where the cluster is assembled *and* that the shared half will look unlinked to anyone else.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A convention that would quietly accumulate characterisations of collaborators unless it says otherwise, and a cross-set linking asymmetry that survives its own fix because the backlink is derived rather than exported.

content: A deletion that leaves no trace cannot be told from something that never existed, so every part of the system that meets the absence misreads it. In this project: forgotten memories whose vectors stayed in the scan, a file read that dropped every tombstone, an older file silently resurrecting a forgotten memory as an ordinary change, a forgotten id coming back as a memory and a tombstone at once, and forgetting a chain's middle cascading away the edge that said its end was stale. **The structural fix is to make a deletion a record** — a tombstone carrying what a later reader needs, here its ancestry and the checksum it replaced — and to treat absence as carrying no meaning at all.
context: Re-deriving the common causes of defects across all 104 issues, and moving them from a hand-written section of TRACKING.md into memories the index is generated from.
why: Not in the original analysis; all five instances are from the tombstone work between 2026-08-07 and 2026-08-30. No general form in `coding-lessons` yet, and this is a candidate: it holds for any system that merges or syncs, where a missing row is the most ambiguous signal there is.

content:
**Measured 2026-09-07, deciding whether to take this before or after finishing the BACKLOG migration: the sample is already contaminated and waiting costs almost nothing.** Of `shared:scatterhoard`'s 424 records created since 2026-08-25, **349 (82%) are migration artifacts** — the ISSUES.md and BACKLOG.md migrations of 2026-09-06 and 2026-09-07 — leaving **75 organic** against `coding-lessons`' **67**, which are comparable. Migrating the remaining 39 entries moves 82% to roughly 86%. **The exclusion is mechanical**: a migrated memory carries a `hoard-proj-` mark or says so in `context` or `why`, and that filter identified all 349 without a judgement call. So the sample is recoverable rather than ruined, and the measurement is not urgent.

**A preliminary observation from the migration itself, which bears directly on the answer.** Entry after entry, the *outcomes* already had memories written when the work happened, and the *evidence* did not: `recall-summary-output-mode` had its three shipped decisions recorded and nothing about the 120-cap measurement, the 192-memory corpus test or the invariance finding; `watch-push-is-an-index-per-set` had the convention outcomes and nothing about the 411-character envelope the whole design rests on. All of that was authored **after** the rewrite.
context: Deciding the ordering between this measurement and the rest of the BACKLOG migration, in the session that renamed the control marks under hoard-proj-.
why:
Recorded now because a later session finding 82% migration in the window would reasonably conclude the experiment was spoiled and abandon it. It is not spoiled; it needs one filter, and the filter is written down here.

The preliminary observation is weak evidence and is deliberately labelled as such — it is not the classification the measurement asks for, and it comes from entries whose material was authored under a backlog-entry habit rather than freely. But it points one way: sessions working after the charter rewrite still recorded conclusions and left the paths in the tracking file, which is the same asymmetry the rewrite was meant to remove. If the real measurement agrees, the charter gloss was not the whole cause and the question `store-when-names-method` resolved may deserve reopening.

content: **A recall that would have helped and was not made, 2026-09-21.** *What was done:* asked where the `governance-docs` set's repository was, I searched the disk for files carrying its set id, excluding `~/Library`, found nothing, and told the human partner it had never been exported. *What was already in a set:* `01M2F3BY7C…` in `local`, naming the file's iCloud path under `~/Library` and saying to reuse it. An unscoped recall on the set's name returned it first. *What the moment felt like:* a question about where a file is, whose obvious answer is to look on disk. Nothing about it read as something a memory might hold, though where things are on this machine is exactly what the personal set holds.
context: Exporting coding-lessons and governance-docs after the file-order change and a server restart. Registering the merge driver in both clones.
why: The third of four cases in which an environment question presented as mechanical, so none of `recall-when`'s moments fired: the PDF on 2026-09-12, the mutation pass on 2026-09-20, and this one. The human partner proposed a recall adjustment in response: look in `local` for facts about the machine. Scope was not the failure here, since an unscoped recall found it. But it names a location sessions do not think of, and that is the other half of the 2026-09-14 case.

content: **Step 2 done 2026-09-24: out-links held only by superseded memories fell from 122 on 70 to 18 on 17, and all 18 are deliberate drops.** Measured by tip — each superseded memory's non-supersession links against every current version of its chain — which gives 123 at every commit from 2026-09-23 evening; the recorded 126 could not be reproduced. After deduplication, 103 links were restated across 45 memories: 29 superseded unchanged, verified identical by comparing content, and 16 over the length limit split. The drops: two `contradicts` whose over-claim a correction withdrew, six `depends_on` on built or resolved entries, four already held at the target's newest version, and six that belonged to the other half of a split. Script in the session scratchpad, not the repository.
context: Step 2 of the out-link work, straight after building step 1's `link_delta`; the same session calibrated both shared sets and graduated four common causes.
why: Records the step as finished with the evidence, so step 3 can cut inheritance knowing what it removes. The splits also caught three heads restating retired behaviour — the floor lowering itself, the set description in the file header, an uncapped `evaluate` called unbuilt — each corrected in the split, and one live defect, filed as `the-calibrate-note-promises-a-floor-that-lowers-itself`.

content: **Naming the sharing preferences in `store-when` did not change what `gemma4:12b` stored.** In the 2026-10-21 rerun of `health-plain` with the clause "or what the person's sharing preferences keep out", "HIV" stayed out of every set in 3 of 5 runs, the same as without the clause. The health detail stayed out entirely in 0 of 5, and no reply flagged anything. One run put "hospital appointments" into `shared:scatterhoard`. Asked why, every run again cited `store-when`'s "will still matter in a later session", never its new clause. The logs are in that session's scratchpad, `framing-run-5`.
context: Building the sharing preferences served at session start. Fifth gemma run, testing the human partner's suggestion to name the preferences in store-when.
why: The clause costs 51 of the catalog's characters, and the human partner's standard is that served text earns its keep. On the only model tested, five runs show no effect, so adding wording where the decision is made does not by itself make a weak model apply the rule. Text alone has now failed in two placements, which points to a check made at the moment of storing.

content: **The detector this entry implied would not work, and that is worth keeping.** Token-set matching flags reordering, which is the case most likely to be *meaningful* — `write-before-read` against `read-before-write` are different ideas, and so were the two spellings here — and misses the two classes that genuinely split a subject: inflection (`recall-limit` / `recall-limits`) and synonymy (`operating-limits` / `operating-constraints`). Synonymy is out of reach of the embedding too: a term carried only as a keyword and appearing nowhere in the content ranked *below* an unrelated memory when queried by meaning, measured 2026-08-03. The detectable class and the harmful class barely overlap, and building it would have been the failure `the-mutation-runners-crowding-note-fires-on-every-pass` records — a diagnostic whose only two candidate instances are both false positives is not a weak signal but no signal. **If this is revisited, ask a different question**: not *do these two spellings mean the same thing*, which is unanswerable, but **is there a cluster of memories about one subject that share no keyword at all** — a connectivity question over the keyword graph, computable, spelling-agnostic, catching inflection and synonymy alike, and measuring the harm directly instead of guessing at a cause. *What may still be real is upstream of all of this: whether the prompting that produces keywords needs tuning. The human partner's judgement on 2026-09-02 was that more data is needed.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A proposed detector shown to catch the meaningful cases and miss the harmful ones, and the better question it should be replaced by. Kept because the detector is the obvious build and its two candidate instances were both false positives.

content: No record existed of which embedding model produced a store's vectors, so replacing the model file left every stored vector being scanned with query vectors from a different vector space — computable, ranked, and meaningless, with nothing failing. Fixed 2026-08-08 in `f07535e` by recording the weights file's content hash in `meta` and re-embedding on mismatch. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `no-record-of-which-model-built-the-vectors`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: An MCP client serves whatever Scatterhoard binary it launched with, so rebuilding the source does not change what a running session sees. The tell is `hoard_conventions` returning fewer conventions than `src/conventions/catalog.rs` defines -- on 2026-08-12 a session was served three conventions from a binary that predated commit 963ed20, while the source held six. Compare the served catalog against the source before drawing any conclusion from what a client returns.
context: Found while restoring from the 2026-08-12 checkpoint: hoard_conventions returned store-when, recall-when and correct-when only, omitting route-where, capture-before-ending and export-before-commit, which had been served and committed the day before.
why: This has produced a wrong reading twice: once when a client was restarted onto a binary mutate.py had left mutated, and once when three newly served conventions were absent from a session that had every reason to assume them present. Both times the failure was silent, because a stale binary answers every call successfully -- there is no error to notice, only an answer describing an older build. The catalog is the cheapest thing to check because its size is visible in one call.

content: **At 1,330 and 181 memories, real recall queries break only slightly more sharply than nonsense, so the largest-gap cut still chooses among noise.** Measured 2026-10-02 by `probe_whether_real_queries_break_and_whether_the_cut_follows_the_window` in `tests/probes.rs`, without the floor. The metric is the largest gap over the median gap in the top 20. On `scatterhoard`, 85 real labelled queries had median 6.09, p90 15.73, and 25 over the synthetic-noise p95 of 10.09; 100 off-domain probes had 5.55, 11.05 and 17. On `coding-lessons`, 63 real queries had 5.81, 11.57 and 10; the probes 5.99, 12.82 and 18. The cut's count changed between windows of 10, 20 and 50 on 12 of 85 and 12 of 63 real queries. Its median output was 3 to 4 at every window. Re-run on the original nine queries, one on-topic query (11.02) cleared every null; the 17.01 `coding-lessons` query of 2026-09-08 had fallen to 6.47.
context: Taking on the two recall-limit issues after fixing max-chars-is-not-a-bound; the human partner recalled that the gap had been found to be noise and asked for a re-measurement on today's larger sets.
why: The human partner asked for this before removing the cut, hoping the larger sets might show structure. The excess on `scatterhoard` is real but small, 29% of real queries against 17% of nulls above the noise line, and absent on `coding-lessons`. A gap that appears in a sixth of nonsense rankings cannot mark where an answer ends, so this supports removing the cut. The synthetic null understates real score tails, since nulls also clear its p95, so the off-domain probes are the comparison to read. It also shows what removing the cut costs: in practice it was acting as a default of about four results.

content: A set that cannot gather the twenty labelled queries a calibration needs has no floor, and nothing places one for it. Decided 2026-09-24 with the human partner as the backup to label-driven calibration: place the floor from the set's own current memories, each index line asked against the rest with itself left out, at the 5th percentile less 0.05 — which reproduced the label-derived floor within 0.012 on both sets that have one. Open at build time: the minimum set size it applies from, since at eight memories the percentile is the weakest memory and places no useful floor, and `local` at twelve is borderline. Built when `calibrate` uses it for a set without enough labels and says which source it used. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `calibration-from-self-queries`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Settling the shape of a backup calibration mode with the human partner, after the probe measured both candidate sources against the two calibrated sets.
why: Head of a backlog cluster. Chosen over negatives from real unscoped traffic, which the same probe showed would silence a third of real labelled queries, and over an explicit pass the model runs, which for a low-use set would mean the model writing its own questions. Reported rather than silent about its source, because a floor from self-queries is weaker evidence than one from labels and a reader of `status` should be able to tell them apart.

content: **A set identity is loaded only once on a machine, whatever its mode; evaluation copies are the exception.** Decided 2026-09-16 by the human partner, replacing the earlier proposal that one read-write set could load beside any number of read-only copies of it. No use needs more: a publisher holds the set read-write and a reader holds it read-only; reference sets need one copy; and comparing versions is what evaluation is for. **It removes ambiguity by construction**: every link carrying a set identity, and every cross-set link naming a read-only set, resolves to exactly one loaded set. The human partner named the second case: without the rule, a link could name several read-only copies. `import` refuses to give a set an identity any loaded set already holds, whatever the modes. **At startup**, when stores on disk share an identity: one read-write with the rest read-only means the read-write set loads and the copies are withheld; two or more read-write, or only read-only copies, means all are withheld. A withheld store is listed in `hoard_sets status`, `drop` can reach it, and the survivor loads once only one copy is left. The remedy for a duplicate is dropping it, which writes a safety copy; no copy changes mode. **This narrows the provisional withhold-both rule** in `Server::add_store` (`src/mcp.rs`) to the case of two read-write copies, which the tools can no longer produce, and so meets the human partner's condition that a restart should not easily lock someone out of their own set. What it gives up: holding a set read-write alongside a read-only snapshot of it; an evaluation copy does that instead. Design in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md#one-copy-of-each-set).
context: Settling whether a set can be loaded more than once, after revising the load-modes design.
why: Supersedes the stale half of `01M2PTQ6…` and the note on narrowing withholding (`01M2PVC9…`), both of which said a read-write set loads beside read-only copies. That was the assistant's reading of the issue's *at most one writable holder* condition, written into the design as though decided. When the human partner asked whether it had been decided, it had not, and the simpler rule was chosen instead.

content: **These seven entries must be settled before publication**; they are this memory's keywords. Gated 2026-09-23 by the human partner. Three have answers that would break something already in use if changed afterwards — the tool surface, the file format, or what an identity means: `set-settled-at-first-write`, `one-repository-many-sets`, `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout`. `unrecognised-link-labels-on-import` decides whether every later label is a format break. `imported-set-trust-boundary` is gated because trust decisions have repeatedly shaped the file format. `claude-md-in-the-repository` gets a look, though easier to change afterwards. `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity` is gated because crafted files arrive with publication.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner.
why: Superseded 2026-09-24: `what-recall-returns` was resolved — full records stay the default, `summary` opt-in — and needs no build, so it came off. Retire an item by superseding this memory without its slug.

content: A consequence found alongside the provenance defect, recorded where it belongs rather than filed as an issue: the judgment gate in [export-review.md](documents/design/export-review.md) skips memories the local user did not last modify, on the stated ground that they *"already passed review upstream."* That ground holds only while a store serves one repository, which nothing enforces. Noted there rather than in ISSUES.md, because the gate is designed and unbuilt, and that file does not take defects against absent code.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A design document's stated assumption invalidated by a defect in another part of the system. Recorded because the boundary decision — a flawed assumption in unbuilt design is not an issue — is the kind of routing judgement that gets re-argued.

content: Observed 2026-08-09 during the first two-server run, filed as a **distinct** consequence of `two-servers-can-disagree-about-the-model` rather than the same defect. Three separable problems, worth not collapsing: **a read performs an unbounded write**, with nothing in `hoard_recall`'s contract suggesting it may rewrite every row in `vectors`, so a caller cannot know it has triggered work proportional to the whole corpus; **the rebuild is silent**, the response carrying only `semantic_search_available: true` while the most consequential thing that happened goes unreported; and **it is the mechanism that makes the two-server loop expensive rather than merely wrong** — two servers with different models would disagree harmlessly if they only read, and it is the destroy-and-rebuild on read that turns disagreement into alternating full re-embeds. Measured at 27 memories, where the cost is invisible.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Three faults filed together and kept apart deliberately: the contract violation, the silence, and the amplification of a neighbouring defect. Collapsing them would have made this look like a duplicate of the model-disagreement entry.

content: The first hard data on the *form*, from occurrences ten to twelve on 2026-08-18 plus a fourth instance from 2026-08-06 found by reading the corpus. All four are one shape: a **close tag named for the field rather than the element** immediately followed by an **open tag missing its prefix** — `</why>` then `<parameter name="context">` — so `why` absorbed its own close, the malformed open, and everything after it. The shape recurs across two and a half weeks and two sessions, though occurrences eight and nine differed from it, so the population is not homogeneous. **What ended the loop was reordering the call, not writing it more carefully**: absorption needs something to absorb, so putting `why` last with nothing following it let the same author write the same call cleanly — a workaround rather than a fix, since it depends on knowing which parameter is at risk, and it suggests the damage is a property of the **transition between** parameters rather than of any one field. *Collecting the form by hand proved the wrong instrument, for the reason the entry demonstrates: the moment to write it down is the moment of repairing a damaged write, which is when a session is least likely to. The detector already holds the data, so recording the offending token alongside the polluted field would make the collection structural rather than disciplinary.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The dominant form, and the workaround that reliably stopped the loop before the real fix existed. Also the observation that nine occurrences were counted before anyone captured the one detail a preventer would need — because the moment to record it is the moment least suited to recording anything.

content: Fixed 2026-09-06 by moving the mark to the query rather than adding a convention sentence: the kind keyword *is* the mark, so `hoard-signpost`, `hoard-collect` or `hoard-investigation` alone means pushed and `hoard-watch` marks nothing. **The cheaper fix was chosen first and failed against the mechanism it was written for** — the watch recall asks for summaries, and a summary hit is an id and a line, so a served sentence saying *a result carrying `hoard-watch` alone is not a watch* asks the reader to check keywords the response does not carry, and the 2-against-1 ranking it leaned on orders a list whose scores are invisible. **Measured end to end the same day on the live sets**: the old four-term recall returned eight memories of which one was a watch — the population had grown from three to seven in two days, every one written while building the thing — and the new three-term recall returned exactly the one watch. No migration was needed, since the only live watch already carried `hoard-collect`. Residue, stated rather than closed: a memory *about* signposts carries `hoard-signpost` legitimately and will appear, at the cost of one line.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the reason the cheap version was rejected after being chosen — a convention sentence cannot be acted on by a reader whose response shape does not carry the field the sentence names. That interaction between a convention and an output mode is the transferable part.

content: **`coding-lessons` cannot yet be adopted by a project as decided under `set-adoption`.** Three steps remain, in order. First, rewrite its charter in one supersession: the test *would hold on a different codebase*, narrower language tags, the four kinds of memory and how each links to a lesson, and a `why` no longer citing `route-where`. Second, write the adoption guide and its signpost in `coding-lessons`; the human partner reviews the guide before export. Third, add the opt-in sentence to this repository's `AGENTS.md`, making Scatterhoard its first user. Not before the guide exists, or the sentence sends sessions to recall a guide that is not there. Release-gated 2026-09-28 by the human partner. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `adopting-coding-lessons`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing set-settled-at-first-write, then gating the coding-lessons adoption work and writing a checkpoint.
why: Head of a backlog cluster. Gated, and to be built next, for two reasons the human partner gave. `scatterhoard` links into `coding-lessons`, so the two sets have to be published together. And the only way to learn whether the adoption mechanisms work — signposts, the recall-before-writing habit, triggers — is to use them for a while before publication, not after. The decisions themselves are recorded under `set-adoption`.

content: **A filing discipline this project applies consistently and has never written down: when part of an item is blocked by something external, open-ended or unproven, split it so the ready half is not held behind it.** Four instances, three of them stated in the entries themselves. `git-merge-driver` keeps its implementation here and its registration risk in EARLY-VALIDATION.md, because the driver working and the driver being registered fail independently. `readme-names-the-project-url` is filed apart from `memory-directory-readme` because *the blocker is external and open-ended, and a Ready item should not sit behind one*. `cross-link-the-multi-slug-memories` was filed apart from `linking-has-no-trigger` on 2026-09-07 because one is reading work and the other is design work. And `export-before-commit` was split from `capture-before-ending` on 2026-08-12, where the seam was an unstated assumption rather than a blocker. **The test is whether the two halves can finish at different times for different reasons** — if they can, one Fixed-when cannot describe both, and the earlier half will close the entry over the later one.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md's Sync and export section, on noticing the second entry restate reasoning the first had already made.
why:
Recorded because it is applied by instinct and argued afresh each time, which means it is one careless consolidation away from being lost — and consolidations look like tidying. Every instance had to restate the reasoning in its own entry, which is the signature of a rule nobody has named.

It is the mirror of the `set-restore` failure, and the two together give the whole shape: split when the halves can finish independently, and **file the second half as its own entry rather than describing it in the first**, because a tracking file catches work that has no entry and does not catch work named in the prose of an entry about something else.

content: Two of the three changes shipped 2026-09-02, in the required order. **Authoring**: a call carrying `supersedes` is refused if `keywords` is absent and accepted if it is explicitly empty. The enabling change was smaller than expected — `keywords` on `hoard_memorize` was a defaulted `Vec`, so absent and empty were *indistinguishable*; it is now an `Option`, which `hoard_correct` had used all along, and the swallowed-parameter check moved from `is_empty` to `is_none` with it, since a swallowed parameter never arrives while `[]` is a caller who sent one. The requirement is published in the schema, so a caller meets it before the refusal does. **Search**: a keyword hit is no longer reached through same-set supersession, implemented as a skip rather than a filter, because if the replacement carries the term its own row matches directly — the superseded row was always redundant. **A cross-set concession still substitutes**, being a memory's own statement about its standing rather than an index term reached through. *Measured before shipping: exactly **two keywords of 431** across both live sets lost all reach — `max-catalog-chars`, deliberately respelled `MAX_CATALOG_CHARS`, and `remark-not-refuse`, naming a policy superseded on 2026-08-19. Both are terms that should stop matching.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, with the blast radius measured before shipping rather than after — two terms out of 431, both of which should stop matching, which is what made cutting the reach safe to do.

content: **Two refinements arrived the same day, 2026-08-31, and only one of them has been built.** **`create` should require an author** -- which removes the silent machine-account default that caused the whole problem, and gives an identity rebuild something deliberate to match against. Verified 2026-09-07: not built, `create` takes a set name and nothing else. **The holder who only ever reads is not a case to detect but a read-only evaluation load** -- which couples this question to *how to inspect a memory set without adopting it*, because that load is exactly what keeps reading a set from writing your name into its contributor list. **The three-operation split is the part that did ship, and its reasoning is reusable:** one entry point inferring which of `mint`, `identify` and `rename` was meant would be a decision-placement violation, because the caller can inspect one precondition -- recall `hoard-author` and see whether a matching record exists -- and cannot inspect the other, whether a row exists and what it points at. A system choosing among three acts on information the caller cannot see is choosing on the caller's behalf without being able to explain itself.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Recorded because the unbuilt refinement is the one that closes the original hole: attribution is now a reference, but a set created today still gets its author from whatever the machine supplies, which is the exact condition that produced a corpus attributed to an account name. Someone reading only that the question *substantially shipped* would not know this.

The decision-placement reasoning is kept because it is the clearest worked example the project has of that principle deciding a tool surface -- the asymmetry is what does the work, not a preference for explicitness, and that distinction is what makes the principle usable elsewhere.

content: A memory set's `hoard-scope-topics` charter does two jobs and only one is written on purpose: its belongs-here test decides which set a memory goes to, while its description of the subject silently decides which *kinds* of thing get written at all. Measured 2026-08-24 over 105 memories: both live charters carry a good boundary test and neither test mentions kinds, yet `coding-lessons` — described as "how work goes wrong, and what to do differently" — is dominated by method, and `shared:scatterhoard` — described as decisions, measurements, defects and constraints — holds almost none, under the same `store-when`. Acted on the same day: `store-when` lost its enumeration and `route-where` gained guidance that a charter must describe its subject rather than list the kinds of record it takes.
context: Measured 2026-08-24 by classifying every live memory in both exported sets against its set's charter. Checkable at ROUTE_WHERE and STORE_WHEN in src/conventions/catalog.rs and the "Resolved 2026-08-24: a charter is a description, not a catalogue" section of documents/design/conventions.md.
why: This supersedes the version stored hours earlier, which said three hand-written enumerations of what is worth storing were in force — `store-when`'s five and one per set. That is no longer true: `store-when`'s are cut and the convention now tells charter authors not to write such a list, so the remaining two are the ones already in the sets and both are candidates for the revisit clause. The finding itself is unchanged and is what redirected the fix: the 2026-08-15 miss that raised the open question was a Scatterhoard-specific measurement procedure, and editing `store-when` alone would not have caught it, because `route-where` sends every candidate to be matched against its set's charter.

content: **The documented answer narrows `claude-md-in-the-repository` but does not close it.** Two things remain. The security half is untouched: a committed steering file is instruction-shaped text arriving by `git pull` and loaded unconditionally with no gate, which the split arguably sharpens. And *documented as intended* is not the same as *observed as customary* -- the check here was against the vendor's own documentation and secondary write-ups, not against a survey of what projects actually do, so it establishes that the practice is sanctioned rather than that it is unsurprising to a contributor who meets it.
context: Cleaning up after the CLAUDE.md split, when the human partner asked whether committing the file is acceptable practice given a contributor may have their own.
why: Split on 2026-10-19 from the finding that committing a steering file is the documented arrangement, when that memory was restated over the length limit.

content: **Football-versus-bylaws survived every mechanism tried on 2026-09-08,** and after six of them the reasonable conclusion is that it is a genuine confusion in the model's space rather than an artifact any scoring rule can undo: *rule*, *interpretation* and *league* really do sit near governance text, and no rescoring of that space will separate them. What charters change is which question is being asked — *which set does this belong to* has an answer, where *is this answerable* apparently does not.
context: Prototyping scoring variants on the live corpus, after the human partner asked to drive to a design proposal before filing.
why: The failure half of the charter measurement, kept as prominent as the success on purpose. Split on 2026-10-19 from that measurement, when that memory was restated over the length limit.

content: **Build the non-match floor: a local query log, calibration from labelled queries, and a floor read against raw similarity.** Decided 2026-09-11 by the human partner; designed in `documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md` under *Proposed 2026-09-11: the floor is calibrated from a local query log, and reads raw similarity*. **Missing:** the log, since nothing records queries; the calibration action; the floor's storage; and the raw similarity the floor should read — `Stages::floor` exists but compares the centred score. **Built looks like:** every recall recording, *before* the floor applies, the raw top score for each store searched, the `scope` argument, the ids it would have returned and whether the floor silenced it, in a table export never reads; an explicit calibration action that sets a floor only once there are about forty labelled queries, a margin below the lowest, stored per store and model and cleared on a model change; the scan carrying raw content similarity beside the centred score, so the floor reads one while ranking keeps the other; recall reporting when the floor silenced everything, with a way to ask again without it; and the floor lowering itself whenever a scope-labelled query scores below it. **To settle while building:** whether forty queries and a 0.05 margin generalise beyond two stores of one project, what bounds the log, and whether a walk-reached memory whose origin cleared the floor should survive a floor its own content similarity fails — the case that drops a top-ranked hit in about one query in fifteen. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `calibrated-non-match-floor`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing the floor question after measuring the answerability signals, simulating calibration on two stores, and writing the proposal up.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. Ready — nothing is missing but the work, and the design document settles the shape. It is a large entry by this project's standards, touching the scan, the store's schema and the tool surface at once, so expect it to be built in pieces; the log is the piece everything else waits on, since calibration cannot start before there is something to calibrate from.

The evidence lives in the resolved question `floor-calibration-source` and is not repeated here: two stores simulated walking forward, raw against centred, the forty-query threshold and what a floor costs the queries it does not silence.

content: **`model2vec-rs`'s forward pass is verified against an independent recomputation from the raw model files — 9 of 10 cases bit-for-bit identical, 877 of 886 memories at cosine 1.000000000.** Every prior embedder check was internal-consistency only (determinism, stored vectors re-embedding at 1.000000, self-retrieval, word pairs separating), so none could have seen a crate that tokenised or pooled differently from the reference. This rebuilds the pass from `model.safetensors` read by byte offset (one F32 tensor, 63091 x 512, data at byte 88), WordPiece over a Bert pre-tokenizer, `[UNK]` **dropped rather than embedded**, mean pooled, L2 normalised — `config.json` sets `normalize: true` — and compares component by component. **Two divergences, both explained.** The unicode case was a bug in the *probe*: `BertNormalizer` strips accents by decomposing to NFD and dropping combining marks, and the helper only lowercased; fixing it converged to exact. The other is real and belongs to the crate: **`encode` hardcodes `max_length = 512`** and pre-truncates the *string* to `max_tokens * median_token_length` characters before tokenising, so over-limit text cuts at a slightly different point than a token-level truncation would. Re-run `probe_recompute_the_forward_pass_independently`.
context: The human partner asking whether the embedder's output could be checked against an independent implementation, immediately after the raw-versus-centred scoring error was found.
why:
Recorded because the human partner asked whether `StaticEmbedder`'s output could be independently verified, and the honest answer before this was no — everything on record checked the implementation against itself. That is the same blind spot that produced the raw-versus-centred error hours earlier, and it was worth closing rather than arguing about.

**What this does and does not establish.** It rules out a large class of bugs: wrong row lookup, wrong pooling, missing or double normalisation, mishandled `[UNK]`, byte-order or offset errors in the weights. It does **not** rule out a misconception shared between the probe and the crate, because both were written against the same reading of the format. Only the reference Python `model2vec` would settle that, and it is not installed here — this machine has Python 3.9.1 and `model2vec` needs 3.10 or newer.

**The truncation finding is the one with consequences.** `config.json` declares `seq_length: 1000000` while the crate truncates at 512 regardless, which is exactly the kind of choice a reference comparison exists to check. Measured separately: 42 of 886 memories (4.7%) exceed 512 tokens, median length 305, p90 460, max 699. No memory loses its `why` entirely, and the composition ablation is unaffected — the two compositions still differ on all 42, mean cosine 0.953 — so the earlier null result stands rather than being an artifact.

content: The committed tree was not rustfmt-clean, so the formatter run STANDARDS.md requires before every commit rewrote twelve files nobody had touched: 433 hunks at `55a2bfd`, across eleven test files and `src/conventions/catalog.rs`. Whoever ran it next either reverted a dozen unrelated files by hand or landed 3,800 lines of reformatting inside a commit about something else, where it swamps the change under review. Fixed 2026-09-11 by one `cargo fmt` commit standing alone, with a rule in AGENTS.md to run `cargo fmt --check` at the start of a session rather than only before committing. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-committed-tree-is-not-rustfmt-clean`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Committing the query log, and clearing the reformatting it turned up before it could ride along.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. Superseded the open head the same day it was filed, which is what a fix records. `costs` rather than `misleads` because nothing the code did was wrong and nobody was given a false belief; what was spent was review attention, by someone who did nothing to cause it.

content:
Corrected 2026-09-11, the same day it was written: a **server process is not a session**, and the `used` label's bound was built on the assumption that it was.

**Measured when the human partner questioned it.** The Scatterhoard servers on this machine had started at 16:01, two hours before the current session's transcript was created at 18:00, and two other transcripts in this project's Claude Code transcript directory had been written to in between — so one process had already served several sessions. The check is `ps -eo pid,lstart` against the creation and modification times of the transcripts, and it takes a minute. The original record claimed Scatterhoard's clients spawn a server per session; the desktop client does not.
context: Building the `used` label for the query log; the human partner said they believed the current server was on its second session and invited the check.
why: The correction matters more than the thing corrected. *One server process, one session* is the kind of assumption that reads as obviously true, is never stated as an assumption, and is cheap to check the moment anyone asks — and it was load-bearing, since a bound spanning several sessions labels queries from conversations that had nothing to do with the use. Restated 2026-10-30 at the person's request during the set's export review, to replace a transcript path that spelled out their account name, and split from the marker decision to fit the length limit; the claim is unchanged.

content: Scatterhoard has arrived at "report it, do not resolve it" from five independent directions: a supersession cycle in an imported file is stored and reported rather than refusing the import; a model mismatch is a configuration to report rather than a state to drive out; an unresolvable link target is reported rather than blocking the write; prohibited data is refused at the write but only warned about at export; and the fix direction for a rival set suppressing a memory is to surface the conflict to the LLM. The shape each time: where the judgement needs context the software does not have, report and let the session decide.
context: Observed 2026-08-21, when the human partner proposed surfacing a cross-set supersession conflict to the LLM on the grounds that it can hold two contradictory memories in context and software cannot. Checkable against those five decisions in ISSUES.md and the design documents they name.
why: Five arrivals in two days is evidence that this is one principle rather than five decisions, which is what `standing-principles-as-conventions` in BACKLOG.md is waiting for -- it is Blocked on what the standing principles actually are. Worth holding because the pattern is invisible from any single decision: each was argued on its own terms, and the repetition only shows up across them. Note the boundary that keeps it from becoming "never refuse": refusal is still right where the caller holds the remedy and the mistake is theirs to fix, which is why the write refuses a credential and the export does not.

content: `recall-summary-output-mode` shipped 2026-09-06: `hoard_recall` takes `detail`, `full` or `summary`, and `hoard_memorize` echoes the line unconditionally. Three decisions beyond the backlog entry. The cut takes the **last** sentence end that fits rather than the first, because the first spends most of the budget on a memory opening with a short sentence and truncates to four characters on an `e.g.` -- silently, since a short line reads as a short memory. A summary hit carries **no `scope`**, which the entry's own 49-character envelope figure had already assumed. And a cut line ends in an ellipsis while a whole one does not: the marker comes out of the 120 rather than being added past them, and it goes on **every** cut, since marking only the ragged ones leaves an unmarked line meaning either complete or cut-at-a-sentence. Re-measured over the shipped code, the live `scatterhoard` file cuts 34 at a sentence and 61 at a word of 96, against the 40/59 split the pre-build check found -- so no interpretation moved the measurement.
context: Building the index-line output mode, then adding the truncation marker the human partner asked for once the rest was working.
why: Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claim is unchanged. The three decisions are kept together because each is one a later reader would take for an oversight and quietly reverse -- first-sentence is the obvious reading of *cut at a sentence*, a missing `scope` looks forgotten, and an ellipsis on a line that already ends in a full stop looks like a bug rather than an answer to *is there more*. The measured split is dated for the same reason the catalog figure elsewhere now is: it moves whenever the corpus does, and `report_summary_cuts` is what answers it. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 1 link an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.

content: The prohibited-data scan reported an API key inside ordinary hyphenated words. **Fixed 2026-10-16**: a vendor prefix counts only where it begins a word, that is where the character before it could not itself be part of a key -- not a letter, digit, `_` or `-` -- so `ask-`, `task-`, `risk-` and `desk-` in a slug are no longer keys (`vendor_key_findings` and `key_character` in `src/prohibited.rs`). A real key is still found after a space, `=`, `:`, a quote, a backtick, a slash, a bracket, a line break or the start of the text, each tested in `tests/prohibited.rs`.
context: Working the open issues ahead of a beta.2 candidate, after the two-server fixes.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the issue is fixed. The tests enumerate what can precede a real credential, because a boundary rule written against the one false positive seen could silently stop catching keys written some other way -- the surface-form trap in `coding-lessons`.

content:
**Whether a link may be added to an exported memory without superseding it.** Raised 2026-09-09: the connect-on-recall clause in `recall-when` implies an edit priced at a full supersession, since `amend` is refused once `has_base` is true. **Three alternatives, not two.**

**A — carve out links.** A link claims *adjacency*; supersession claims *validity*, so the second misdescribes the first and leaves that signal permanently. Links may be the one field the export gate's reasoning does not reach: additive and order-independent, so two copies each adding one merge by union with nothing to arbitrate, where changed `content` genuinely needs ancestry. Against: the gate's value is having no exceptions, union-merge for links is unimplemented, and a link is not inert — it changes what traversal returns.

**B — leave it.** Supersession stays the only route and the clause pays for itself. Against: 603 of 762 memories are isolated and nearly all exported, so the expensive path is the common one.

**C — unify `correct` and `supersede` into one call that dispatches on export status.** Raised by the human partner. It has precedent: `amend`'s own reasoning is that **the server decides service, by a fact, because the caller cannot see the bases and benefits from answering no** — so the server already owns this decision, and C extends it from *decide and refuse* to *decide and do*. **The objection C must clear is that supersession needs authored material amendment does not** — a new record wants content and a `why` saying what changed. So C either demands supersession-grade material on every call, which moves the cost rather than hiding it, or synthesises it, which is where a false validity signal enters silently.
context: The human partner proposing a unified correct/supersede call as a third way out of the supersession cost, just after the question was filed with two.
why:
Supersedes the first statement of this question, which had two alternatives; the human partner supplied the third within the hour. Recorded as a supersession rather than an addition because a later reader choosing between designs must see all three at once — a question entry that lists two options when three are live is worse than one that lists none, since it looks complete.

**C is the one to think hardest about, because it is the most attractive and the least examined.** Its precedent is real and was found rather than assumed: the placement argument in `amend`'s doc comment already puts this decision on the server. What C changes is not who decides but what happens after — and the two outcomes are genuinely different acts, not two spellings of one. Amend replaces a value nobody ever believed; supersede asserts that a record was replaced. A caller asking to add an edge and silently receiving the second has had a claim made on its behalf.

That is why the material asymmetry is the sharp end rather than an implementation detail. `hoard_memorize` requires a `why` of every memory, and a machine-written *a link was added* is exactly the thin reasoning the whole design refuses elsewhere. If C is taken, the honest form of it reports which path it took and refuses to invent the `why`.

**A and C are not exclusive.** If links stop needing supersession, C's hardest case disappears and it becomes ergonomics rather than semantics.

content: **What was actually decided is narrower than it looks.** [Recall Mechanisms](documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md) justifies resolving to the tip entirely on content — returning the intermediate *"would surface a conclusion that was itself corrected"*, a superseded memory's *"substance is therefore actively misleading"* — which is right about substance and silent about index terms. The keyword case was seen directly in `keyword-hit-swaps-silently`, found 2026-08-02 with this exact fixture, whose verdict was *"swapping the superseded memory for its replacement is correct and deliberate. Reporting it as a direct keyword hit is not"*, and the fix added `replaces_matched`. **Whether the keyword should still match was never argued, only inherited from the content rule.** This is the sibling of `supersession-silently-repoints-an-in-link-nobody-reauthored`: there an edge *into* a superseded memory is followed as an edge into its replacement, here a keyword *on* one is matched as a keyword on its replacement — same cause, the graph and the index both resolved onto current memories, and the same defect, a relationship nobody authored.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A rule that was decided for content and silently extended to indexing, traced back to the document that argued it. Worth keeping because the earlier entry had the fixture in front of it and answered a narrower question.

content: **Building `several-memory-files-per-directory` on 2026-09-26 settled four things the design left open.** (1) The declared name is the fallback whenever identity matches nothing, not only for a set with no identity: a file declaring the set's name under another identity is then found, so the mismatch can be acted on instead of export writing a second file beside it. (2) A `.json` in `scatterhoard_mem` whose header cannot be read is refused by name, not skipped; dotfiles are not read. (3) `absorb` and `evaluate` take `directory` with `set`, the name of the set to read, as well as `file`; `set` is required with `directory` and checked against the header with `file`. (4) A Windows device name is checked on the part before the first dot, so `nul.notes` becomes `nul-set.notes.json`. Checkable in `locate_in`, `memory_files_in`, `new_file_in` and `Destination::file_of_named` in `src/mcp.rs`, and in set-lifecycle.md under *what the lookup had to decide that the design did not*.
context: Building the release gate's directory-form group: several memory files per directory first, then identity-mismatch refusal and the reserved directory accepting the local set.
why: History from implementing the entry, and each point would otherwise be rediscovered by reading code. (1) is what `identity-mismatch-refusal` builds on: without the name fallback a mismatched file is invisible in directory form, so there is nothing to refuse. (2) guards against a damaged or conflicted copy of the set's own file, which skipping would silently fork into two files. (3) was settled with the human partner, who put it as "the distinction between `file` and `directory`+`set` is the header search": a set in a checkout is known by name, a downloaded file by its path, and both actions need both. Taking the only file left no way through with several, because the `file` its refusal pointed to is refused inside `scatterhoard_mem`. `file` alone would have had the model read every header itself, and needed a per-action exception to the rule that each file is reachable by one form.

content: **In a lessons set, a lesson is the fixed point and everything added to it links to it, never the reverse.** Decided 2026-09-28 by the human partner, for `coding-lessons`. A solution links `resolves` to its lesson. A worked example links `instance_of` to the lesson or solution it illustrates. A trigger (the activity at the moment before the mistake) links `motivated_by` to the lesson. Each is its own memory, language-tagged where the idiom differs. The lesson is never edited to point back. Recall shows a link from both ends, under `links` on the writer and `incoming` on the target, and walks it in both directions, so nothing is lost by writing it one way. To be carried into `coding-lessons`' charter when that is rewritten.
context: Designing how `coding-lessons` helps prevent failures in projects that opt in: its memory structure, after the trigger experiment.
why: Solutions, examples and triggers accumulate as projects find new ways to fail and to fix. If the lesson carried the links, each addition would change it, and after export that is a supersession each time, leaving a superseded copy of the lesson behind for every trigger added. Written from the newcomer, an addition touches nothing else. `motivated_by` was chosen over `causes` because a trigger is deliberately broader than the harmful pattern, and over `related_to` because it says why the two are linked. No inverse label such as `motivates` is needed, and adding one would be a vocabulary change.

content: `absorb` internalised links to memories that did not arrive: absorbing part of a set turned working cross-set links into same-set links to ids this set lacked. Fixed 2026-09-28 in `absorb_set` in `src/mcp.rs`: a link is made internal only if its target arrived in the file, counting records identical to ones already held. The rest keep their cross-set form and are named under `not_internalised`, and a memory with nothing to internalise is not superseded.
