It checks the file rather than the store, because an id this set already held natively may be a different memory. Reproduced first by two tests in `tests/sets.rs`, `absorb_keeps_a_link_whose_target_did_not_arrive_cross_set` and `absorb_does_not_supersede_a_memory_whose_linked_targets_did_not_arrive`, and pinned by three new mutations. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `absorb-internalises-links-to-memories-that-did-not-arrive`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Starting on the open issues after both code items on the release gate were closed the same day; this was the first of the three corrupts-severity issues.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed, against the criterion the old head set, sharpened from "held after the records land" to "arrived in the file". One consequence: the mutation `absorb: collect every memory with any foreign link as a candidate` now survives, recorded with its reason, because every later use of the candidates re-checks the set. Left open, as the old head suggested: with this fixed, `absorb` could replace the hand-appending and importing steps of moving memories between sets (set-lifecycle.md). Nothing was built for that.

content: **Cause found 2026-10-01: `uuid`'s `ContextV7` can move its timestamp backwards, so `Uuid::now_v7` ids invert.** `Timestamp::now` reads the clock before taking the shared mutex. If that reading is from an *earlier second* than the one stored, `ReseedingTimestamp::advance` keeps the stored seconds but takes `max` of the two `subsec_nanos`, so the stored time jumps almost a second ahead without its `last_seed` being updated. The next millisecond reseeds to the real time, which is earlier. A reading at 99.9995s arriving after one at 100.0002s yields ids at ms 100999, 100999, then 100001. The trigger is a thread pre-empted between reading the clock and taking the lock across a second boundary, or a backward clock step across one: rare, and likelier under full-suite load. Reproduced with `Timestamp::from_unix` on 1.24.0 and on 1.26.1, the latest release. Check in `src/timestamp.rs`, `ReseedingTimestamp::advance`.
context: Diving into the flaky id-ordering test, picked from the seven open issues right after restoring the 2026-10-01 checkpoint. The MCP servers were still on the build from before the case-variant and absorb fixes.
why: Corrects the 2026-09-22 reading that the crate's source ruled out a time read before the lock: it does handle an earlier *millisecond*, but compares seconds and sub-second nanoseconds separately, which goes wrong once the two readings fall in different seconds. That one-failure-in-a-full-suite-run, thirty-passes-alone pattern fits a race that needs pre-emption at a second boundary. Proven with a deterministic reproduction rather than inferred, hence 0.95. It is the crate's defect rather than this project's, so a fix here has to work around it.

content: `recall-summary-output-mode` shipped 2026-09-06: `hoard_recall` takes `detail`, `full` or `summary`, and `hoard_memorize` echoes the line unconditionally. Two things the backlog entry left open were settled while building. The cut takes the **last** sentence end inside the cap rather than the first, because taking the first spends most of the budget on a memory that opens with a short sentence and truncates to four characters on an `e.g.` -- silently, since a short line reads as a short memory. And a summary hit carries **no `scope`**, which the entry's own 49-character envelope figure had already assumed. Re-measured over the shipped code, the live `scatterhoard` file cuts 36 at a sentence and 58 at a word, against the 40/59 split the pre-build check found -- so the interpretation did not move the measurement.
context: Resuming from the checkpoint the morning after the watch index was designed, and building the one part of it that needed code.
why: Both decisions are the kind a later reader would take for an oversight and quietly reverse: first-sentence is the obvious reading of *cut at a sentence boundary*, and a missing `scope` looks like a field somebody forgot rather than a quarter of the saving. The re-measurement matters for a different reason -- it is the evidence that a build interpreting a spec did not silently invalidate the numbers the spec was argued from, which is the failure mode of building against measurements taken by somebody else.

content: **A successor inheriting its predecessor's out-links in the walk was never decided; it fell out of two other decisions.** The tip rule was argued in [recall-mechanisms.md](documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md) for *content* — a superseded memory's substance misleads. It spread unargued to keywords and to the graph. Keywords were re-argued 2026-09-02: *explicit addressing is honoured as written; inferred matching resolves to the tip*. The graph never was. Resolving both edge ends onto the tip came from fixing `validity-is-resolved-after-the-ranking`, where a superseded memory acted as a conduit while its tip had no routes; inheritance cured that, and so would not walking superseded memories at all. **Measured 2026-09-23: 73 superseded memories carry 126 non-`supersedes` out-links their tip does not restate**, reachable in recall only through inheritance.
context: Discussing with the human partner whether a superseding memory should inherit its predecessor's outbound links, after finding the walk resolves them onto the replacement.
why: The human partner asked why the walk lets a successor inherit out-links, pointing out that it contradicts the keyword decision. The answer from the corpus is that nobody chose it, which changes what reversing it costs: it is not overturning a reasoned position, only removing a side effect. The count is the other half, because it is what reversing it would cut if done before authors are told which links a supersession leaves behind.

content: Found 2026-08-02: `max_chars: 800` returned a single convention of roughly 1,600 characters — 2× the stated budget. Paging itself works correctly and terminates on `next_cursor: null`; the budget is simply advisory. **Returning one oversized item rather than nothing is the right call** — a budget smaller than the smallest convention has no correct answer that includes content — so the defect is the description rather than the behaviour.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery, with the behaviour explicitly defended. Worth keeping because the obvious fix — honour the budget strictly — would return an empty page, and the entry rules that out before proposing anything.

content: **Nothing in the conventions ever asks for a link.** Raised 2026-09-07 by the human partner. Going through the served catalog: `store-when`, `route-where`, `keyword-standards`, `confidence-standards`, `recall-when`, `hoard-watch`, `capture-before-ending` and `export-before-commit` say nothing about links at all, and the only two that mention them — `correct-when` and `split-when-partly-stale` — name `supersedes` specifically, as a consequence of correcting rather than as an act of relating. So links appear only where the workflow hands over a target id, which the 2026-09-07 measurement confirms: 3 discretionary edges in 390 memories. **The gap is a missing moment, not a missing rule.** `recall-before-storing` fires at store time and asks *is this already here*, not *what does this connect to*; `correct-when` covers a memory that is **wrong**, not one whose edges are incomplete, so a relation discovered later has no trigger and nothing sends anyone back. Built when some moment reliably produces a link between memories already stored. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `linking-has-no-trigger`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Filed while migrating BACKLOG.md, after measuring that a full day of memory-writing produced three discretionary links.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only.

Filed as its own entry rather than as a paragraph inside `link-label-choice`, deliberately, applying the lesson migrated from `set-restore` an hour earlier: a tracking file catches work that has no entry and does not catch work named in the prose of an entry about something else. The two are distinct — that one asks *which label*, this asks *whether anything prompts a link at all* — and the measurement now suggests the label question may be downstream of this one, since a wording fix cannot reach a moment that never occurs.

Ready rather than blocked: nothing has to be settled first, and the catalog has room derived at 320 characters free.

content: **Whether, and how, the write path should stop a subject memory carrying a reserved control mark. Resolved 2026-09-11 by the human partner, the day it was filed: enforce one live charter per set, and refuse unknown `hoard-` keywords — both at the authoring entry points, neither at import.** Filed as backlog `one-live-charter-per-set` and `reserved-keyword-block-list`; the decision is recorded in `documents/design/conventions.md` under *Decided 2026-09-11: the write path guards the reserved namespace*. The case was three rounds of `reserved-keywords-carry-subject-memories` in six days — five memories on 2026-09-06, one on 09-07 by a session that had loaded the corrected `keyword-standards` that day, two on 09-08 — every one a memory *about* charters carrying `hoard-scope-topics` in a set that already had a live charter. The dedicated charter tool was the third candidate and was not taken, since it adds a tool for what supersession already does. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `guarding-reserved-keywords`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Re-keying two charter-matching measurements that carried the reserved charter mark, after the human partner asked why they had been flagged and said they were watching for repercussions of the conventions update. Same stretch: the store-stopping embed fix and its commit.
why:
Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. The resolution is carried in the head because a later session asking why the write path refuses a second charter needs the decision and its case in one place, not a question that looks open.

The human partner's ruling was specifically that one live charter per set should now be enforced — turning what `documents/design/memory-data-model.md` described as a singleton into an invariant — and that both the shape check and the block-list go to the backlog. Two things were noted and not decided: `hoard-author` also has a checkable shape, and the watch-list marks have none, so they stay with the served `about-` rule.

content:
**The extra retrieval surface a supersession creates is a function of how far the rewrite moved the vector — and it is a threshold, not a slope.** The human partner's observation, refined by measurement over 52 substituted hits: distance moved against lift gives r 0.480, r² 0.230, but bucketed it is a step. Supersessions that **barely moved** the vector (distance < 0.30, 19 pairs) give a median lift of **+0.069**; those that **moved somewhat** (0.30–0.45, 23 pairs) give **+0.068** — indistinguishable; those **substantially rewritten** (> 0.45, 10 pairs) give **+0.191**, nearly three times as much. So small corrections add almost nothing distinctive, and rewrites are where a memory becomes retrievable for content it no longer carries.

**The two ends of the clause in `recall-when` behave oppositely, and one is exactly zero.** A link is not embedded — `embedding_input` is content, `why`, keywords — so a link-only supersession produces a vector **identical** to the tip's: lift 0 by construction, a perfectly redundant scan entry and a duplicate record in the committed file. A keyword **is** embedded, which is why `amend` re-embeds on a keyword change, so a keyword-only supersession moves the vector slightly and gains a little real surface.

**Untested by the corpus**: only **1 of 64** supersessions has byte-identical content and `why`, because the clause that creates that case was written the same day.
context: The human partner observing that supersession gives a memory more semantic surface in proportion to how much the text changed, a link barely moving the vector where a rewrite moves it a lot.
why:
Recorded because it turns the earlier observation — that retrieval surface accumulates with supersession history — into something with a shape. It is not the count of supersessions that matters but the distance of one, and below a threshold not even that. My framing was count-based and wrong in a way the human partner's was not.

**It also supplies a new argument for the link-only write, on grounds that are not cost.** A link-only supersession is the worst possible ratio of surface gained to record created: exactly zero gained. If the connect-on-recall clause works as intended against 603 isolated memories, it will generate one exactly-redundant vector and one near-duplicate record per connection. Harmless to correctness — chains collapse, so nothing is split, and the fold takes a maximum over identical values — but pure waste, and it makes the committed memory file's diffs noisy in a way nothing else does. That argument stands whether or not supersession is expensive, which the earlier examination established it is not.

**The threshold is the part most likely to generalise and least likely to hold.** Two buckets agreeing to within 0.001 across 42 pairs is more suspicious than reassuring, and 10 pairs is a thin basis for the step. What is solid is the direction and the zero: geometry guarantees the link case, and the rewrite case is where the five subject-drift pairs already found also sit.

content: **A set identity is loaded only once on a machine, whatever its mode; evaluation copies are the exception.** Decided 2026-09-16 by the human partner, replacing the earlier proposal that one read-write set could load beside any number of read-only copies of it. No use needs more: a publisher holds the set read-write and a reader holds it read-only; reference sets need one copy; and comparing versions is what evaluation is for. **It removes ambiguity by construction**: every link carrying a set identity, and every cross-set link naming a read-only set, resolves to exactly one loaded set. The human partner named the second case: without the rule, a link could name several read-only copies. `import` refuses to give a set an identity any loaded set already holds, whatever the modes. Design in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md#one-copy-of-each-set).
context: Settling whether a set can be loaded more than once, after revising the load-modes design. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the memory was over the length limit.
why: Supersedes the stale half of `01M2PTQ6…` and the note on narrowing withholding (`01M2PVC9…`), both of which said a read-write set loads beside read-only copies. That was the assistant's reading of the issue's *at most one writable holder* condition, written into the design as though decided. When the human partner asked whether it had been decided, it had not, and the simpler rule was chosen instead.

content: `hoard_conventions` overruns its stated budget: `max_chars` is advisory while the parameter is described as *"Budget for this page"*, so a caller sizing its context window against it is wrong, and silently. Fixed when either the budget is honoured, or its description says it is a target a single oversized item may exceed and the response says when it did. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `max-chars-is-not-a-bound`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only, with the fixed-when since this one is open. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: The `hoard-watch` mark is the kind keyword itself as of 2026-09-06: `hoard-signpost`, `hoard-collect` or `hoard-investigation` alone means pushed, and `hoard-watch` marks nothing and is free to be an ordinary subject keyword. It replaces the two-keyword scheme, and it is the second fix chosen for `hoard-watch-is-both-marker-and-subject` -- the first was to keep the marker and serve a rule that a result carrying `hoard-watch` alone is not a watch, with the 2-against-1 ranking ordering the rest. Both halves of that were drafted and then found unusable against the mechanism they were written for: the watch recall asks for summaries, and a summary hit is an id and a line, so the rule asks a reader to check keywords the response does not carry and the ranking orders a list whose scores are invisible.
context: Rewriting the watch convention around the index line, and finding the filtering rule unusable in the mode the recall runs in.
why: Supersedes the marking half of the memory recording how the convention was built, which said one keyword marks push while a second names the kind. Worth the detail because the reversal is the useful part: the cheaper fix was chosen deliberately, defended against a specific objection, and still failed -- and it failed for a reason that generalises past this convention, which is that a projection removes the ground a read-time rule stands on. A later session that only sees the outcome would reasonably propose the two-keyword scheme again, since it is the obvious way to let one term mean *pushed* and another mean *what kind*.

content: `scatterhoard-cookbook`'s memory file lives in this repository's `scatterhoard_mem`, beside `scatterhoard.json`. Decided 2026-09-30 by the human partner when the set was created. Recorded in `documents/design/load-modes.md`.
context: Creating the scatterhoard-cookbook set right after fixing absorb for a split local store, with the data-directory move as its first recipe.
why: Two reasons, both theirs. Simplicity: recipes accumulate along with the rest of the project and are committed with the work they describe. And a live test: two memory files in one directory exercises `several-memory-files-per-directory`, including its naming rule and the `set` argument a reader needs to pick one file out of several, which until now only tests had done.

content: Found 2026-08-18 by the human partner reading the `graph-traversal` build — *"can't a superseded memory have a different confidence level?"* and *"are we reliably seeding semantic similarity if we're not using the tip of the superseded chain?"* Both answers were worse than the code read. **The shortcut is older than traversal**: it was inherited from a recall that resolved lazily because the only thing at stake was which of two near-identical memories filled a slot, and traversal changes the stakes, because the identity of a seed now decides an entire neighbourhood. **Three consequences.** A supersession chain consumes seed slots — its members are separate rows with separate vectors, deduplicated only after the seeds are chosen, and **a superseding memory is *supposed* to resemble its predecessor**, so they rank adjacently by construction and a memory corrected three times can take four of five slots to contribute one distinct neighbourhood. The dead memory is a conduit while the live one is short of routes, since a superseded memory still passes inherited score along its links while its tip does not inherit those edges. And it **blocks native confidence from ever entering the decay**, because a confidence term would rank a returned tip on its *predecessor's* value — and the skew is systematic rather than random, since supersession is typically a guess replaced by a measurement.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Three consequences of one late resolution, the third of which is a blocked future feature rather than a present error. The systematic direction of the skew — guess replaced by measurement — is what makes it worse than noise.

content: Formalising the standing principles as conventions. Blocked, and the blocker changed on 2026-08-13 from an open question to a settled answer that narrows the entry rather than releasing it. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `standing-principles-as-conventions`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Measured 2026-08-03: `query` + `keywords: ["projection"]` at `limit: 2` returned one memory in both lists — roughly 1,100 characters of identical `content`, `why`, `context`, `keywords`, `created` and `modified`, sent twice, to convey that one memory was found two ways. The only fields that differed were the two that are supposed to: `similarity: 0.318` on one side, `matched_keywords: 1` on the other. **That is the whole delta — about 30 characters of new information carried by 1,100 characters of payload.**
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The measurement that priced the duplication exactly, by isolating the information the second copy actually adds. Kept because that ratio is what made deleting the mode look better than deduplicating it.

content: The design's other destructive operation, tracked nowhere until 2026-08-23. Built 2026-08-25: `hoard_sets` action `restore` takes a scope, a source (`directory` or `file`) and a `save_to` — it writes the set's current contents out, then replaces them with the file's. **Local divergence is discarded on purpose, which is the whole distinction from `import`**, and the safety copy is what makes discarding survivable, being an ordinary memory file that can be diffed against the result with individual memories put back. Import *reconciles* a file against a store that may have diverged; restore *replaces*. What separates them is whether divergence is preserved or discarded, and **that is a difference no scope determines** — a shared set can need either, a local set can need either. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `set-restore`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only. Design in [set-lifecycle.md](documents/design/set-lifecycle.md).

Why it matters even though a store is rarely corrupt: restore is the only route back from a store that cannot be trusted, and it is the operation a person reaches for at the worst moment.

content: A keyword cannot be retired by superseding the memory that carries it. The superseded record keeps its keywords, keyword search matches on those, and the replacement is substituted into the results -- so a term goes on matching after every memory anyone would call current has dropped it. Measured 2026-09-02 on the live set: `max-catalog-chars` returned its replacement, which carries only `MAX_CATALOG_CHARS`; `remark-not-refuse` returned a replacement whose `replaces_matched` named a record TWO OR MORE hops back, so the reach runs the whole chain rather than one link. Amendment would remove a keyword, but `correct-when` refuses amendment on anything exported, which is every memory in a shared set. This is deliberate behaviour, not a defect: `replaces_matched` is a designed field with its own fix history under `similarity-describes-a-different-memory`.
context: Measured by finding supersession pairs whose replacement dropped one of the predecessor's keywords -- a join of `links` on `keywords` in the store -- then running `hoard_recall` on the dropped terms. Checkable by repeating that query; the substitution itself is documented in ISSUES.md under the `similarity` / `matched_similarity` split in `response-shape-is-unpublished`.
why: It closes off the obvious retirement mechanism for anything keyword-driven, and it closes it silently -- the recall still returns something plausible, so nothing signals that a term meant to be retired is still live. This bites any design where a keyword marks a transient state. The concrete case that raised it: a proposed `hoard-watch` keyword tagging memories a session should be told about at startup, where an investigation that concludes must come off the list and cannot. `replaces_matched` is nonetheless the way out at convention level, since a reader can treat a watch as retired when the returned memory does not itself carry the keyword -- correct, but not cheap, because the retired entry is still fetched and paid for before being discarded.

content: **How does a hard fork get a set identity of its own?** [set-lifecycle.md](documents/design/set-lifecycle.md)'s fork section sanctions renaming a divergent fork by editing `scope` in the file's header, and was written before set identities existed. The edit leaves `set_id` alone, so the renamed file still claims its origin's identity. Since 2026-09-16, when `two-sets-can-share-an-identity` was fixed, importing that file on a machine that also holds the origin is refused rather than silently giving two sets one identity. On a machine holding only the fork, the import still succeeds, and the fork answers to the origin's identity, so a cross-set link that names the origin by identity resolves into the fork: the opposite of the section's own reasoning that a hard fork *is a different set now*. **Open:** whether the rename should also drop or replace `set_id` in the header, so the fork keeps the identity `create` minted (unverified: the header field is optional for old files, but nobody has checked this as a procedure); or whether a tool should do the rename, which the section rejected before identities gave it something to get wrong. The findings gathered under this question carry the keyword `how-a-renamed-fork-gets-its-own-identity`.
context: Fixing two-sets-can-share-an-identity by withholding both holders at load and refusing the import; also applied the AGENTS.md mid-session checkpoint clause.
why: Filed the moment it was noticed, while fixing the duplicate-identity issue: the fix closes the route the fork procedure uses, and the refusal it gives would otherwise be the first anyone heard of the gap. A question rather than an issue, because nothing built is wrong. The design procedure predates the field it now needs to handle, and choosing between a header edit and a tool is a design decision. The two claims about behaviour were read from `Server::import_set` and `Store::adopt_set_id` in `src/mcp.rs` and `src/store.rs`, not exercised as a fork.

content: **Aggregating many projects' causes could generate something like an OWASP Top Ten automatically** — the human partner's observation on 2026-09-23, not a plan. What makes it possible is the shape chosen for causes the same day: each project records its own cause as a memory in its own set, with its own issues attached, and links it `instance_of` to one shared general form in `coding-lessons`. Counting incoming `instance_of` links per general lesson across every project that links to it gives a ranking by how many projects meet each cause, and weighting by the issues behind each project's cause gives one by how often. Nothing is built; the point is that this direction of link keeps the option open where copying the lesson into each project would close it.
context: Moving the common causes of defects out of a hand-written section of TRACKING.md into memories, after deciding the project's causes and their general forms live in different sets.
why: Recorded because it justifies a detail that would otherwise look arbitrary: the project cause links to the general form rather than restating it, and the general form lives in a shared set rather than in each project. A later session tidying the causes might inline the lesson to save a hop, and this is the reason not to.

content: **In the export review, a memory is reviewed again only when something is done to that memory itself, never because of a change elsewhere.** The human partner's standard, set 2026-10-22, recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. Re-embedding a set or changing its model reopens nothing, because the clearance checksum is `checksum::of_record` over the exported bytes, which hold no vectors. A change to the sharing preferences must not undo earlier review work wholesale either.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public: deciding what the clearance checksum covers.
why: The review is a trust mechanism, and people trust what makes sense to them. A change in one place reopening a memory somewhere else may be logically warranted by the design, but it undermines trust for anyone who does not know the software's internals, which is nearly every user. A blanket re-review triggered from elsewhere is also the fatigue that makes things slip, the reason decisions are made in conversation. The human partner confirmed the existing full-record checksum for clearances, so "reviewed" has one definition shared with the file comparison. This departs from the 2026-10-17 rule that a change to the conditions calls for a full review: the human partner prefers reopening only the memories a change applies to.

content: **The counterweight to the split rule, decided 2026-08-25 by the human partner: fold two halves back together when shipping one alone leaves a worse state than shipping neither.** `import-cannot-name-the-file-export-wrote` was filed as its own entry, correctly — `export-may-name-a-file`'s **Built when** named `export` only, and quietly widening a scope is the habit this file exists to replace. It was then folded in and built the same day, on the ground that shipping only the write half creates an **export trap**: a set written where the tool that wrote it cannot read it back. Recoverable by moving the file, and still not a state to ship. **So the two rules are complementary rather than in tension.** Split when the halves can finish at different times for different reasons; **fold when the earlier half, shipped alone, is a trap rather than a partial improvement.** Half a feature on a released surface is worse than the friction it removed.
context: Migrating the export and import explicit-file entries out of BACKLOG.md, which had been split and then deliberately recombined.
why:
Recorded because the split rule is the one this project states explicitly and applies four times, so a session reading only that would file the second half and leave it — which is exactly what happened here before the human partner intervened. The filing was right; stopping there would not have been.

The discriminator is worth stating sharply, because *can they finish independently* answers yes in both cases. The extra question is what the world looks like between the two ships: a ready driver waiting on an unproven registration risk leaves everything as it was, while an export that cannot be imported from leaves a user with a file the tool refuses to read. One is a delay, the other is a new failure mode introduced by the improvement.

content: A set another server dropped stayed loaded in every other server holding it open, which went on writing to a database whose file was gone. **Reproduced and fixed 2026-10-16**, and worse than filed: with the set made again at the same path, the stale server's write damaged the *new* set's database so that a fresh server could not open it. Each store now records the identity of the file it opened (device and inode on Unix), and before every tool call the server takes out of service any store whose file is gone or replaced (`Store::file_is_gone`, `Server::let_go_of_vanished_stores`); the rescan then picks up whatever is at the path. Tested in `tests/sets.rs` with three servers sharing one home.
context: Working the open issues ahead of a beta.2 candidate, after fixing the rescan for sets another server creates.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the issue is fixed. Compared by identity rather than existence, because a re-created set leaves a file at the path that is not the one opened; a mutation proves the test notices. One claim made while fixing it was wrong and was tested away: that closing the stale connection would delete the new set's `-wal` file by path. A test with the new set writing either side of the close showed no harm, so the connection is closed normally.

content: Should the never-store word list treat simplified and traditional Chinese characters as one? Opened 2026-10-22. Today 艾滋病 does not match 愛滋病: the list folds through `toNFKC_Casefold`, which keeps the two forms distinct, and the template tells the person to list both. Merging them needs a conversion table.
context: Filing follow-ups after committing the sharing preferences and the never-store list with full-width folding and optional spacing beside Chinese.
why: An entry that misses the other form is a silent miss, the failure the list exists to prevent. But a conversion table is a dependency decision. Conversion is not one-to-one either: some simplified characters stand for several traditional ones. And keyword folding deliberately keeps the forms apart as a distinction a reader means to draw. Left for later by the human partner, who chose a template line asking for both forms when the list's Chinese support was built.

content: **There is one model-fit hub per set, not one per language.** Agreed with the human partner on 2026-10-04. The hub is separate from the charter. It links out to sentence-set memories, each tagged with its `hoard-lang-` language. Each tagged language must have zero or exactly ten sets, counted per language and not as a total modulo ten. Model recommendations link in to the hub, tagged with the languages they were measured on, or untagged when they apply to the whole set. A set's own ten sets for a language take precedence over the built-in ones. That lets a set measure its own vocabulary, such as English full of Italian cooking terms or French terms of art, which the built-in everyday sentences cannot test.
context: Designing agent-supplied test sentences and set-carried model recommendations for the declared-language check. The human partner raised terms of art in an English set, and sets with several unsupported languages.
why: Recommendations often concern a whole set rather than one language. A modulo-ten total would accept 7 Samoan sets plus 13 Māori. Exactly ten per language keeps the rival count at 29: on 2026-10-04 the rival count was shown to change the verdict, so a language scored from more sets would be on a different scale.

content: **Decided 2026-09-16 by the human partner: one evaluation load at a time is enough for now, and every hit recalled from it must be marked as coming from an evaluation load.** The reason is what evaluation mode is *for*: the set is loaded because the LLM is exploring it, so its memories are not the project's settled record and must not be taken as ground truth. The opt-in rule decides whether such a hit appears at all; this decides how it reads once it does. **A set name that itself says it is an evaluation copy is an acceptable mark**, so the temporary name can do this work if it is chosen to. This narrows two of the question's open parts: `scope` need not address more than one evaluation set, and a hit needs an evaluation marker even if it never carries a set identity.
context: Deciding what evaluation mode needs before building it, just after fixing two-sets-can-share-an-identity with a provisional withhold-both rule.
why: Recorded because the opt-in decision (`01M2M6R6…`) reads as though it settles labelling, and it does not: once a recall names the evaluation set, its hits arrive beside the reader's own with nothing saying how far to trust them. The human partner framed it as a trust property rather than a provenance one, which is why a name saying *evaluation* is enough and an identity alone would not be: an identity says which set a hit came from, not that nobody has adopted that set.

content: The export review's pre-pass read a date and time as a phone number, so every memory naming a checkpoint or a timestamp went to the person. `phones` in `src/review.rs` accepts any run of three or more digit groups of two to four digits totalling ten to fifteen, and `2026-08-13-2255` and `2026-08-25 06` both qualified. Found 2026-10-29 on the first two pages of the `scatterhoard` set's full review, where five of six memories were flagged for nothing else. Fixed the same day: a run that begins with an ISO date, year 1900-2099 and a possible month and day, is skipped along with a following hour or `HHMM` stamp of exactly two or four digits, so a number written straight after a date is still found. `a_timestamp_is_not_a_phone_number` in `tests/export_review.rs`; five mutations caught.
context: The scatterhoard set's full review, paused after two pages to fix this, after fixing the per-page recompute the same day.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseding the open head now that the fix is built and tested. Costs: nothing wrong was published, but false hits put whole memories to the person, and a flag list that is mostly noise trains them to clear flags unread. The year range is what keeps a number shaped like a date with an impossible field a number.

content: **Why rebuilding it every call was the right first version, reasoned 2026-08-18 at build time — this is a deliberate non-optimisation, not an oversight.** It is the same order of work the scan already does: recall centres and scores every vector in the store on every call, per the brute-force decision in the embeddings design, so at the sizes this system runs at, caching the graph would optimise **the cheaper half**. It is also the version with **no invalidation to get wrong**, and a stale adjacency is exactly the class of defect this project keeps finding — `vector-cache-goes-stale-across-processes` was the same mistake one layer down.
context: Migrating the traversal-adjacency entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the reasoning behind leaving it unoptimised.
why:
Recorded because the code looks like an obvious performance bug and reads as one to anyone arriving cold: a full table scan per call, result discarded. A session optimising it would be introducing a cache whose invalidation this project has already got wrong once, to speed up the half of the work that is not the bottleneck.

The condition for doing it later is stated precisely so the decision does not have to be re-argued: key the invalidation to the same `PRAGMA data_version` counter the vector cache uses, so the two caches go stale together or not at all, rather than adding a second independent staleness surface.

content: The live similarity range is compressed and low, measured 2026-08-03 against a five-memory store: the query *"scatterhoard design decisions and constraints"* at `limit: 8` returned `0.110, 0.075, 0.024, -0.045, -0.084`, every one presented identically. Two things follow for `no-non-match-floor`. Negative similarities are returned as results, and a score below zero is not a match under any reading. And a query written specifically to hit one memory scored it `0.32` while a plainly unrelated memory scored `0.135` -- barely a factor of two apart, so a fixed threshold has very little room to work in.
context: Piloting the index design by converting an issue entry written across five sittings into a cluster.
why: This is the measurement that made *drop everything under 0.2* untenable rather than merely unproven, and it is the strongest argument for answering this together with the cold-start question rather than by picking a constant. Kept separate from the original observation because it is a different kind of evidence -- numbers from a live store rather than a noticed symptom -- and because the factor-of-two figure is the one a later session would want to re-measure as the corpus grows.

content: **Whether Scatterhoard should offer an interruption, under conditions the AI itself can tune, that triggers a specific recall.** Raised 2026-10-20 by the human partner, reading the recall nudge's results. The nudge fires on one fixed condition, a code write with no recall since the last commit, and turned out rarely needed for that. But an interruption that pattern-matches what a session is about to do, and asks for the recall that fits, could serve other moments that do not feel like moments to search. Open because nothing decides what would trigger it, who writes the patterns, or how it could work beyond one client's hook system. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `interruptions-that-trigger-specific-recalls`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Reading the `coding-lessons` release-gate evidence with the human partner, after the publication review's commits.
why: Head of a question cluster. The nudge's narrow job was mostly done by the `AGENTS.md` paragraph, which is the human partner's reason for not recommending it in setup. The general shape is a different proposal, and worth keeping apart from that verdict. It meets a known gap: a rule governing a reflexive moment cannot live in retrieved memory, because nothing prompts the search (`coding-lessons`). And the PDF, mutation-pass and file-location cases under `recall-would-have-helped` were all moments no fixed rule anticipated. The hard parts are named in the question itself: AI-tuned triggers are instruction-shaped text that changes when a session is interrupted, and only the `PreToolUse` hook in Claude Code is known to deliver one.

content: **Calibrating the busy sets makes an unanswerable query fall through to whichever set is not calibrated.** From the query logs, 2026-09-24: in 26 ordinary unscoped queries over twelve days, `governance-docs` never contributed a hit — its top raw score (0.15–0.36) always sat well under `scatterhoard`'s (0.36–0.66), so ranking buried it. Its noise appeared only on the football queries, where every set scored low; on *premier league football results* its top was 0.182, below `scatterhoard`'s 0.248, and its two memories were the whole answer only because the calibrated floors (0.360, 0.333) had silenced the two sets that would otherwise have outranked it.
context: Discussing the shape of a backup calibration mode with the human partner, after they asked whether `governance-docs` had been adding noise to ordinary recalls.
why: Changes what the backup is for: an uncalibrated set is harmless beside uncalibrated neighbours and becomes the default answer to every unanswerable question once its neighbours have floors. So the backup has to arrive with calibration rather than after it. Reads `query_log` and `query_log_hits` in each store; the 28 logged `governance-docs` queries are also the only negatives that set has, all real, none authored.

content: **Build evaluation mode with read-only distribution in view: the two differ by less than their separate entries suggest.** Noted 2026-09-16 by the human partner when splitting them. Both are read-only, both drop without a safety copy, and both are properties of how the server loaded the set rather than of the set. **The whole difference is two things**: which watch marks are pulled — none for evaluation, the recall-before-reasoning ones for read-only — and whether the set gets a temporary name or keeps a stable one, since a document is meant to be cited where a set under review must not shadow the maintainer's own. **So the shape to build is a load mode carrying a policy, not a `read_only` boolean with special cases hung off it.** A boolean answers *may I write* and would then need a second flag for the watch pull and a third for naming, which is how three coherent modes turn into eight states of which five are nonsense. A mode value makes the unwanted combinations unrepresentable, which is this project's stated preference over detecting them at run time.
context: Splitting read-only distribution out of evaluation mode, after the human partner warned against the split rule ossifying.
why:
Recorded because the split rule's own hazard is being read as *design the halves independently*, and the cost lands here first: evaluation mode built around a boolean would have to be reopened to add distribution, where a mode value absorbs it. The human partner's instruction was to foreshadow rather than retrofit, and this is the concrete form of it.

The enumeration of the difference is the load-bearing part, and it is worth checking again before building rather than trusting: if a third difference turns up — a distributed document wanting its own recall labelling, say — the *mode carries a policy* shape still holds, but the claim that the two are nearly the same does not.

Kept under both slugs deliberately. It is a finding about the relationship, so a session pulling either entry's cluster needs it; carrying one slug would hide it from exactly the half that is built first.

content: A set's derived description reshuffled on a small change: adding two memories to a set of 838 regrouped most of its memories, so the cluster sizes and the keywords naming each cluster changed although no stored memory or keyword did, and a reader comparing descriptions across commits saw a set change character when it had not. Fixed 2026-09-14: seeding draws are keyed to memory ids and the most cohesive of ten seedings is kept, so removing one memory now leaves the grouping of the rest almost intact. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-set-description-reshuffles-on-a-small-change`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Fixing a-set-description-reshuffles-on-a-small-change, the second item taken from the open issues that session, after the healed-fork fix.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed. Standing moves from open to fixed; severity is kept, as fixed heads keep it. The links are carried over from the head this replaces.

content: **The question was posed 2026-08-24 with a standing prohibition attached: do not answer it by raising the budget.** At the time the catalog stood at 16,746 of 18,000 with three Ready conventions -- `recall-gloss-convention`, `link-label-choice` and `investigation-pipeline` -- competing for the remaining 1,254, which at most one of the two large ones could use. **The second raise had already set the standard a third would have to meet** -- *well under 4% of the smallest context window in range* -- and recorded the objection that answers this question in advance: **a budget raised whenever it binds is not a budget.** **Both raises so far were argued from what the number *spends*; a third argued from what will not fit would be the first of a different kind**, so **evidence of irreducible need is the price of asking.** That is what made the question *is the catalog carrying avoidable length* rather than *is the budget too small*: the second cannot be asked honestly until the first has been answered.
context: Migrating open-questions.md, recovering content a faulty deletion boundary had left orphaned after the entry's head was already stored.
why:
Recorded because the prohibition is what gives the question its shape, and without it the entry reads as an open enquiry with two symmetric answers. It was never symmetric: one answer was ruled out in advance and the whole investigation exists to earn the right to consider it.

*Evidence of irreducible need is the price of asking* is the reusable formulation and applies to any budget this project sets, not only the catalog's.

The figures are a dated reading from 2026-08-24 and several were later found wrong; the correction is held in the `third-catalog-budget-raise` cluster. Derive the current headroom rather than quoting any of them.

content: **How hard the paraphrase test is depends on how many rivals it uses, enough to change a language's verdict.** On the same ten Japanese triplets under `potion-multilingual-128M` on 2026-10-04, the paraphrase beat its triplet's one unrelated sentence 10 times out of 10, but ranked first among all 29 Japanese sentences only 5 times. So a threshold means nothing unless the size of the rival pool is fixed alongside it. Compare `probe_whether_paraphrases_outscore_unrelated_text_in_each_language`, which uses one rival, with `probe_whether_each_language_ranks_a_paraphrase_first`, which uses all 29.
context: Turning the paraphrase-rank harness into a probe after widening the triplets to ten per language, while restoring from the 2026-10-04 checkpoint.
why: Whoever builds the check has to choose the rival pool, and this shows that the choice moves the result as much as the model does. It also means the server's built-in sentences and any agent-supplied ones must give the same number of rivals, or their scores cannot be compared.

content: There was no test against a store predating the bases migration. Built 2026-08-21: two tests in [tests/store.rs](tests/store.rs), each pinned by a mutation. `a_store_written_before_the_bases_migration_stops_cascading` builds the previous schema directly — **the only way to test a migration is against a database this code did not write** — and asserts the foreign key is gone, the unprovable base rows with it, and the memory not taken along with them. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `bases-migration-test`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Test and documentation debt section.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only. The member carries the second test, which is the one worth having and which the entry did not originally name.

content: **The prize was never tidiness -- it was making records immutable so a base can never go stale, and that is what the eventual answer preserved** -- the case as raised, 2026-08-26. The human partner's observation: amendment and supersession are two mechanisms for one act, and **having two has been conceptually fuzzy, which is often a sign the architecture wants cleaning** rather than a sign the boundary wants restating. The boundary had already moved once under pressure -- `origin` was outside the amendable set and joined it on 2026-08-21 -- which is what a line decided case by case looks like. **If every update mints a new record with an edge to the old one, an immutable record's checksum never changes**, so reconciliation collapses from a three-way merge over mutable rows toward set union plus validity resolved from the graph, which is what `git` actually does: objects never change, and what moves is which tip is current. **The objection was a Golden Rule decision made five days earlier**: superseding an origin misattribution is *actively wrong*, because it keeps the misattribution of a person's reasoning permanently readable, and Corrections draws the same line for characterisations of people -- *superseding it is the harm*, so retraction is `forget`. Abolition does not remove `forget`, but it converts a cheap in-place fix into forgetting a whole memory and rewriting it, losing everything else that memory held.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the immutability argument is the reusable part and survives the specific proposal being declined: the resolution reaches the same property by a different route, so anyone re-examining the correction boundary needs to know what property is being protected or they will trade it away for convenience.

The objection is recorded at equal length deliberately. It is the case where the project's people-rules bind against an otherwise clean architectural win, and it is the reason the answer is a narrowed boundary rather than abolition.

content: Half of this entry was wrong, and the half that was wrong is the interesting half. The claim that a write *"fails immediately with `SQLITE_BUSY` rather than waiting"* was checked against SQLite's documented default, which really is a zero busy timeout — and never against the driver. `rusqlite::Connection::open` sets five seconds of its own, so writes were already waiting, and **the test written to prove the fix passed before the fix existed.** The timeout is set explicitly anyway, because the requirement belongs to the store rather than to a dependency's default, and `scripts/mutations.py` records removing it as a mutation that *survives* with the reason written down — the one form in which *this line changes nothing observable* is a recorded fact rather than an untested guard. The lesson is filed in the `coding-lessons` set under *"a library's defaults are part of the system; the standard's are not."*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A defect half-diagnosed from the specification rather than from the running stack, caught because the test for it passed before the fix. The recorded surviving mutation is how a line that is genuinely a no-op stays distinguishable from a guard nothing tests.

content: What the false cycle costs the caller is a withdrawn memory handed back as current, plus a diagnosis pointing at the one operation that was correct. `X` is returned as *itself* rather than substituted by `C`, so a recall matching the withdrawn text hands back the withdrawn text; and it is flagged as a cycle, which `hoard_lookup` describes to the caller as *"a broken history -- two memories each claiming to replace the other -- which no tool can resolve for you and which usually means a merge went wrong."* Nothing went wrong. A regression test should cover both the fork-heal diamond and a real loop, since a naive fix that merely stops returning `Cycle` would lose the loop detection `a-supersession-cycle-reads-as-current` exists to preserve.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry. This entry is deferred by the human partner, to be fixed before publish.
why: The caller-visible cost and the trap in the obvious fix, kept together because the trap is only visible once the cost is stated: the guard has to distinguish *already visited* from *on the current path*, not simply stop reporting cycles.

content: The server cannot ask the human a question itself, so a name only the human has reaches `mint` through the model. **Proposed 2026-10-11, awaiting the human partner's review**, in `documents/design/asking-the-human.md`: MCP elicitation on protocol revision 2026-07-28, served dual-era beside today's handshake, with `author` removed from `mint` and `rename` where the client can ask and `identify` choosing from a form. The fallback for connections that cannot ask is built. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `asking-the-human`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Drafting the elicitation proposal and shipping its fallback, after a remote-owner hint failed on a small local model.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, filed when the fallback shipped so the stronger guarantee is not lost: the fallback makes a wrong name visible, while elicitation makes it impossible. Not marked ready, because the proposal has not been approved for building; its first step, recording what clients actually declare, can be taken without settling the rest.

content:
**Resolved 2026-09-19: Scatterhoard bounds how long a memory may be and asks for density in the conventions, and it does neither by tracking drift.**

Decided and built: a memory over 2000 characters of `embedding_input` is refused at both write doors, the message naming the measured length and telling the caller to split; the encoding stopped truncating at 512 tokens the same day, so the cliff this question was partly about no longer exists; and `store-when` gained *Make each memory compact, tightly-written, and atomic — one claim, not several.* The bound is atomicity rather than the embedder's budget, and the number came from this project's first five weeks, which never reached it.

Decided against: a **minimum** length. The failure it was aimed at — a memory in a language the model cannot represent — is not a length problem, since Russian and Greek tokenise fully and still fail to separate, recorded under `model-covers-declared-languages`.

Residue, carried as its own question rather than left here: `query-density-guidance`, whether a session needs guidance on writing a query at all.

Not pursued, deliberately: whether the drift follows the writing model rather than the corpus. A bound holds whatever causes the drift, so the cause stopped being load-bearing.

The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `memory-size-drift`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing the memory-size question after the refusal, the encoding fix and the convention sentence all shipped, and after the sets were rebuilt.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseding the open standing with a resolved one. Recorded with what was decided *against* as well as for, because a later session meeting long memories will reach for a floor, and the reason there is none is a measurement rather than an oversight.

content: Supersession silently re-pointed an in-link nobody reauthored: the walk follows `C SUPPORTS A` as `C SUPPORTS B` once B supersedes A. Fixed 2026-09-30 with a remark: a `hoard_memorize` that supersedes returns `repointed_in_links` (`superseded`, `source`, `label`, and `scope` for a source in another loaded set) and a note saying the links now reach the replacement and any repair belongs to the memory holding the link. Built in `repointed_in_links` in `src/mcp.rs`, on the superseded memories `link_deltas` selects. Both supersession labels are left out as chain structure. The walk itself still re-points in-links, by design. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `supersession-silently-repoints-an-in-link-nobody-reauthored`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Taking the supersession and identity issues with the human partner, as ones that could bite after release; this one after the forgotten-replacement flag.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed as its fixed-when asked: a supersession whose target has in-links returns a remark naming them and their labels. Two choices beyond the copied amend mechanism. Cross-set in-links are included, since the walk re-points them too. `superseded_by` is excluded as well as `supersedes`, since an incoming concession is a chain to follow, and reporting it would fire on every extension. That exclusion is proven by a test where the superseded memory has both kinds of chain in-link, after a first version of the test left the filter's mutation surviving. Two tests in `tests/sets.rs`, three mutations; `documents/design/corrections.md`.

content: Fixed 2026-08-09: the two guards became one **conjunction** — a warning fires only when the mean pace exceeds `SLOW_MUTATION` **and** `deps` exceeds `CROWDED` — and it reports the pace, the file count and the size rather than asserting something is wrong. **Why a conjunction rather than a better threshold**: either signal alone is weak, and slowness alone was twice attributed confidently to the wrong cause on 2026-08-08 from CPU samples rather than a comparison. Requiring both makes the message a *referral* rather than a verdict — it asks someone to look, and a false positive costs one glance at a number the message already prints — which is what lets both constants be roughly wrong without the alert becoming noise or a lie. **A ratio against the previous run was considered and rejected**, proposed by me and refuted by the human partner: it is a first-difference detector, so it catches a step change and is structurally blind to gradual drift, which is the failure mode here — silt accumulating a few percent per run would never trip it while compounding past 2×.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Two constants that are each individually unreliable made useful by conjunction, plus a rejected alternative whose flaw is specific: a ratio against the previous run cannot see the gradual drift it would be built for.

content: **An export is refused when writing would lose records the file holds, or when the file cannot be read; it is never refused when nothing is at the destination.** Decided 2026-09-14 by the human partner, the same day a first build only reported. Recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *What the file being replaced did not hold*, and built as `Replaced::refusal` in `src/mcp.rs`, with the contract in `tests/sets.rs`. The comparison still reports new, changed and removed records as `replaced_file`, with `removed` always empty on an export that went ahead. The way through is to import from the same destination first, or — for an intended overwrite, such as after a `restore` — to move the file aside or delete it. There is deliberately no force option.
context: Building the export refusal straight after committing the export delta report, which itself followed the reserved-keyword block-list. The human partner thought through the policy between the two, weighing a refusal against a force option.
why:
**Why refuse rather than report.** Export replaces the file atomically and never checks the recorded bases against the file on disk, so records a pull or another machine's synced export brought in, and nobody imported, were overwritten with no sign but lines vanishing from a diff. The human partner saw both legitimate overwrites and a real risk, especially with several servers, and chose refusal with a filesystem workaround. It fits export's own standing rule — refuse where the caller holds the remedy — since importing first is in the caller's hands.

**Why no force option.** Raised by the human partner as the second candidate. Left out because moving the file keeps a copy of what an intended overwrite replaces where a force flag discards it, because a refused caller can simply set a parameter, and because a parameter is hard to withdraw once copies of the code are spread across versions, where adding one later costs nothing.

**Why an unreadable file is refused too.** It reverses a default agreed earlier the same day. What writing over it would lose cannot be told, and the likeliest unreadable file is an export with unresolved merge conflict markers, whose other side an overwrite discards. A missing file stays written freely, at the human partner's explicit instruction.

**What it does not reach.** A removal that never passes through export — a merge resolved by dropping lines, a hand-edit, a commit of a file nobody re-exported — needs the comparison as a standalone scan, the same shape as `prohibited-scan-subcommand`.

content: A link could reach the private `local` set by naming its identity, so a crafted file could make a shared memory resolve into a personal one. Fixed 2026-09-28: `holder_of` in `src/store.rs` matches an identity only among stores a name could reach (`scope.exports_to().is_some()`), so a store no name reaches is one no identity reaches. Reproduced for the first time the same day, on both paths it fed: a shared memory's `superseded_by` carrying `local`'s identity was substituted by the personal memory, and a shared edge made one a walk neighbour. Pinned by `a_concession_carrying_the_local_sets_identity_does_not_resolve_into_it` and `a_walk_does_not_reach_the_local_set_by_its_identity` in `tests/cross_store.rs`, and by the mutation `holder_of: let an identity reach the local set`. `LinkTarget` documents the guarantee. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Fixing the second release-gate item, right after building `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely` the same day.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed; all three conditions the old head set are met. The tests used a hand-built link rather than an imported file, because the link is what such a file carries and the existing identity tests work the same way. Every other route was checked: by name is closed because `local` has no name; disputes and backlinks return early on `local`'s scope; a bare id stays in its own store; `unresolved_links` resolves by name only. Keyed on addressability rather than on `Scope::Local`, after the recalled lesson on guards keyed to one spelling.

content: Scatterhoard's `keywords` table has two columns: `keyword` holds the spelling as written, `folded` holds the case-folded lookup key. `Keyword::folded` (src/memory/text.rs) is the single place folding happens, used by both the write path and the query path. Checkable in src/store.rs's schema batch and `Store::add_folded_keywords`.
context: Fixed 2026-08-04 as issue keywords-silently-lowercased; recorded while exercising the MCP surface the next day.
why: The original defect was structural, not a stray `to_lowercase`: one table was serving as both the record and the index, so normalising for lookup necessarily rewrote the record. Separating the two columns is the fix. Rust's `to_lowercase` rather than SQL's `lower()` deliberately, because `lower()` folds ASCII only and would be silently partial for non-English keywords.

content: **Every weight in the walk starts flat and is recorded as untuned, because on 2026-08-14 there was almost nothing to tune against.** Measured that day: the live 36-memory set carried **16 edges over four labels**, with **no `MOTIVATED_BY`, `SUPPORTS`, `CONTRADICTS` or `INSTANCE_OF` at all**, and a maximum in-degree of 2. **In-degree as a ranking signal was deferred on those grounds and on a further one:** its sign is label-dependent -- high inbound `MOTIVATED_BY` means load-bearing, while high inbound `INSTANCE_OF` means generic -- so a single in-degree term would add two opposite signals together. **One loose end belongs with the ranking decision rather than the walk:** validity resolution can collapse two hits into one when a memory and its superseder both rank, which frees a result slot, and whether that slot is backfilled has never been decided.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because *untuned* is a status that expires quietly. The corpus has grown from 36 memories to over 600 since, and several of the labels that had no instances now do, so the reason the weights are flat no longer holds even though the weights have not moved. A session tuning them needs to know they were never tuned rather than tuned and found optimal.

The in-degree argument is worth keeping past its deferral because it is a reason not to build the obvious thing: a label-blind in-degree term will look like an easy win whenever the graph gets denser, and it sums two signals with opposite meanings.

content: The watch convention's length clause was replaced on 2026-09-06, not tightened: *keep a marked memory short enough to read fifteen of* is gone and *make its opening 120 characters say what it is for and when it applies* stands in its place, with the reinforcement's per-record cost arithmetic removed alongside it because it priced pushing records rather than lines. The rule is now one an author can follow without arithmetic, and both write paths show them the result -- `hoard_memorize` and `hoard_correct`'s `amend` echo the derived line. The convention is no longer provisional in any part.
context: Finishing the watch rewrite and clearing out the warnings written while it was still provisional.
why: Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claim is unchanged. Recorded rather than simply retired because the *shape* of the replacement is the durable part -- a rule stated as a length nobody can measure became a rule stated as an opening the tool shows you, which is the move worth repeating the next time convention text asks for arithmetic.

content: A superseding memory should not inherit its predecessor's out-links in the walk: an out-link belongs to the record that wrote it. Decided 2026-09-23 by the human partner, applying the principle already decided for keywords — explicit addressing is honoured as written. Today `tip_of` in `src/store.rs` moves both ends of every walkable edge onto the current tip. **Three steps, in this order**: (1) a supersession reports the non-`supersedes` links it leaves behind, as `keyword_delta` reports keywords; (2) the existing out-links held only by superseded memories are examined and, where they still hold, restated by superseding the current version; (3) the walk stops following a superseded memory's out-links, and `genindex.py`'s attribution counts current versions only. Built when all three have shipped in that order. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Talking through with the human partner why the walk lets a successor inherit out-links, after finding it overrides a link a supersession deliberately dropped.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing, order and built-when. The order is load-bearing, as it was for keywords: cutting inheritance before supersession reports what it leaves behind would silently remove links authors dropped by accident, and before the existing ones are examined it would cut 126 of them at once. In-links are deliberately out of scope — they are derived from another memory's out-link, and `supersession-silently-repoints-an-in-link-nobody-reauthored` covers them.

content: What actually filters Scatterhoard's stored memories is each set's own `hoard-scope-topics` charter, not `store-when`'s enumeration. Measured 2026-08-24 across both live shared sets: `coding-lessons` is dominated by method — "when X, check Y" — and its charter names "testing and verification technique, debugging method"; `shared:scatterhoard` holds almost none, and its charter names "design decisions, measurements of how the system actually behaves, defects and their causes, and constraints". Same `store-when` over both, opposite results, matching the charters. So there are three hand-written enumerations of what is worth storing — store-when's five and one per set — they disagree, and nothing reports that they disagree.
context: Measured 2026-08-24 by classifying all 105 live memories across both exported sets against each set's charter, after the human partner asked whether `store-when` provokes any storage at all. Checkable by reading the two `hoard-scope-topics` memories and the corpus beside them.
why: This redirects where a fix belongs. The 2026-08-15 miss that raised the open question about naming *method* in `store-when` was a Scatterhoard-specific measurement procedure, and editing `store-when` would not have caught it: `route-where` sends every memory to be matched against its set's charter, and a technique for measuring is not a measurement of how the system behaves. It also puts the project's largest recorded defect cause — one fact restated by hand in a second place, with the copies drifting silently — inside its own conventions. A charter is written once, by a model, from vague human direction, then travels with the set and is read as authoritative by whoever imports it, so a narrow one exports its blind spot.

content: `hoard_sets` status reports which build is running: its version and build timestamp, plus the stale-build flag when the binary has been rebuilt since the server started. As of 2026-10-27 a session can learn the version only from `server_version` on the first `hoard_conventions` page, cannot learn the build time at all, and hears about a stale server only through the conventions note that `rebuilt_since_launch` triggers in `src/mcp.rs`. Two builds of one version are therefore indistinguishable from the tool surface. Built when status carries version and build timestamp on every call and the stale flag only when it applies.
context: Re-reviewing the published memory sets under the export review's judgement gate, after the human partner asked whether a stale-server warning was showing and noted there is no way to ask the server its version or build date.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. Decided by the human partner 2026-10-27: the stale check matters mostly during development, so it stays conditional rather than spending context in every session, but once the server has real versioning a model can only reason about which build it is talking to if it can ask. Status is a setup-time call, so a version and timestamp there cost little per session; the timestamp is what tells apart two development builds sharing a version string.

content:
**Supersession is not expensive, and the premise behind this question was mine rather than the project's.** The human partner asked where the belief came from. Checked, and it is in none of the places it would have to be:

- **No served convention calls it costly.** The only sentence in the whole catalog using that vocabulary is `recall-when`'s, about recalled memory, unrelated. `correct-when` frames supersession *positively*: *"Superseding keeps the old memory readable, which is the point."*
- **The relation carries no wrongness.** `LinkLabel::Supersedes` is documented as *"…replaces it, which is kept as history"* — replacement, not error. So *false validity signal* was overstated: a record superseded to gain a link genuinely is replaced by the new version.
- **Chains are not accumulating.** 63 chains across the set, mean depth **1.30**, maximum 3, only three deeper than two. Seed selection already collapses a chain to one slot.
- **I had been doing it freely all along.** 8 of the 32 memories written this session were supersessions — a quarter — with no hesitation, several in a single turn.

**What is real is small or elsewhere.** Authoring content and a `why` costs tokens, modestly. The rest was two things wearing one word: **a generic prior against duplication**, imported from ordinary software where in-place mutation is the norm and which does not hold in an append-only store that keeps history on purpose; and **the refusal's valence** — `amend` denies rather than routes, and *"can no longer be corrected"* reads as a door closing, so the alternative arrives feeling like a consolation.
context: The human partner asking why the project calibrates supersession as expensive, and whether any convention actually says so.
why:
Supersedes the three-alternative question entry because that entry's opening clause — *an edit priced at a full supersession* — asserts the premise this examination removes. Leaving it would send whoever picks the question up to solve a cost problem that does not exist. What survives as genuinely open is narrower and is stated in the successor.

**The diagnosis is worth more than the correction.** *Expensive* was doing duty for three different complaints, and separating them is what dissolved the question: a duplication prior that is not a fact about this system, an ergonomic effect of being refused rather than routed, and a semantic objection that turned out not to hold once the label's own documentation was read. The first is the largest and the least defensible — it is a habit from software where records are mutated in place, applied to a store whose whole design is that they are not.

**What this does to the three alternatives.** Option B — leave it — becomes the default rather than the concession, since nothing needs fixing. Option A, carving links out of the export gate, loses its motivation but not necessarily its merit; it would now have to be argued on merge semantics alone. Option C, unifying `correct` and `supersede`, addresses the one effect that is real — the refusal's valence — but by hiding the branch rather than by making it read as a routing decision, which is the cheaper fix and needs no new call.

The clause in `recall-when` is affordable as written, and no wording there depends on this.

content: **Undecided: what a cross-set link does when an evaluation set is a possible target.** Raised 2026-09-16 by the human partner, while designing evaluation mode. An evaluation copy has its own `eval-` name but its source set's identity, and links are resolved by identity where they carry one (`holder_of` in `src/store.rs`). Three cases, none decided. **(1) Only the evaluation copy holds the identity**: the real set is not loaded, and a link in a real set names it. **(2) Both the real set and an evaluation copy are loaded**: identity resolution has two holders. The rule that at most one *writable* holder may be loaded does not choose between a read-write holder and an evaluation one for resolution unless it says so. **(3) The reverse direction**: an evaluation memory that links into, supersedes or disputes a memory in a real set. **Where it can happen, read from the code 2026-09-16:** recall resolves only against the sets it searched, so an unscoped recall never sees an evaluation set, and a recall naming one sees nothing else. **`hoard_lookup` is different**: it fills `referenced_from` and `disputed_by`, and re-resolves concessions to other sets, over every loaded store (`self.stores` in `src/mcp.rs`). If evaluation stores sit in that map, a lookup of a real memory could report an evaluation memory disputing it, or resolve a link into an evaluation copy. Links that carry only a set name never reach an evaluation copy, because its name differs.
context: Revising the load-modes design after settling how evaluation hits are marked.
why: Filed rather than decided, at the human partner's direction. The lookup path is recorded because the design document's claim that an unscoped recall cannot reach an evaluation memory is true of recall only, and a later implementation reading that claim could assume every path is safe. Where evaluation stores are held, in `self.stores` or apart from it, largely decides the answer, which makes it a choice to settle before building evaluation.

content: **Measured 2026-09-08, and this is the finding that reframes `no-non-match-floor`: no statistic computed from similarity separates a query the corpus can answer from one it cannot.** *premier league offside rule interpretation* returns two results at `0.420` and `0.390` — a higher top score than five of the six on-topic probe queries, the largest gap-to-median of any of the nine, and the **highest z-score of all nine at 4.21 standard deviations above its own mean**. The two hits are `governance-docs` memories about Corporations Code committees and Declaration limits. So the failure is not *off-corpus queries score low*; two of the three did, but the third scored like the best on-topic query. **A static bag-of-tokens model matches register and vocabulary, and an unrelated loaded set supplies both** — the shared words are *rule*, *interpretation*, *league/premier* against governance text. The information needed to tell a match from a non-match is not present in the score, so an absolute floor, a relative floor, a per-query normalisation and the gap cut all fail for the same reason rather than for three different ones. Re-run: `probe_whether_any_per_query_statistic_separates_a_non_match` in `tests/probes.rs`.
context: Probing the gap cut against the live corpus, the morning the tracking files were unified.
why: Recorded because every prior attempt on this entry looked for a better *scalar* — a constant, a ratio to the top hit, a gap — and this is the measurement that says the scalar family is exhausted rather than under-explored. It also disarms the most attractive remaining idea: normalising per query looks like it dissolves the cold-start problem, and it is the one that scores the non-match highest of all.
