The cross-set detail is kept because it is the mechanism, not a coincidence: the same query against `scatterhoard` alone has no governance vocabulary to match, so how many sets a session loads changes how badly this fires — which is worth a separate entry if it reproduces.

content: **Should calibration be an explicit labelling pass the LLM runs, rather than a level read off passively accumulated labels? Resolved 2026-09-24 by the human partner: no — the backup for sets that gather too few labels is a floor from the set's own memories.** The measurement this question was held open for arrived that day: accumulated labels calibrated the two sets in daily use and neither set consulted rarely. The backup went to `calibration-from-self-queries`, built the same day, because an explicit pass on a low-use set would mean the model writing its own questions, which this investigation had already found sit unrepresentatively far from real ones. Kept as an option only if a set turns up that neither labels nor its own memories can calibrate. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `explicit-calibration-pass`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing the backup-calibration work with the human partner, straight after building the self-query floor and the note for answers only from sets without one.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. The answer is partly the question's own alternative and partly neither: the need it anticipated was real, but the evidence that serves it needs no session and no labelling judgement. The reserve condition is named so a later session can recognise the case that would reopen it.

content: **The absolute floor was ruled out by a measurement whose own recorded caveat said it could not support the ruling, and at corpus scale it works — but not as a constant.** The 2026-08-03 rejection was taken on a **five-memory store** using **centroid-relative** scores, and its context line asked for a re-measurement on a larger store before anything was built on it. That never happened; the floor then appeared on the 2026-09-08 list of seven failed mechanisms. Re-measured on the live union of 875 memories with **raw cosine**, 18 answerable queries against 24 unanswerable: **AUC 0.944**, the highest of the eight ruled-out statistics, and the most robust of them in every condition tested. A single threshold at **0.447** makes 4 errors of 42. Raw beats centred, 0.944 to 0.884, and centring on a five-memory store is what produced the original "narrow, low band, negative scores". **The original memory's actual conclusion — that a floor cannot be a hand-picked constant — is upheld**: across seven corpora the p90 floor runs 0.089 to 0.286 and the max floor 0.125 to 0.476, so any constant is wrong somewhere. What is refuted is the broader reading that no floor works at all. Re-run `probe_whether_controlling_question_form_stabilises_the_verdict` in `tests/probes.rs`.
context: Testing the human partner's prediction that the swinging verdicts would subside once their cause was found, by re-running the ruled-out mechanisms against form-controlled query sets. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the memory was over the length limit.
why: Supersedes the 2026-08-03 measurement rather than sitting beside it, because that memory has been read for a month as *the floor was tried and failed*, which is not what it measured. Amended before export to withdraw a claim a larger probe set falsified: a threshold at 0.332 making zero errors rested on twelve substance-shaped non-matches, and at thirty one scores 0.476 through a single term of art. This does **not** close `an-unanswerable-query-returns-confident-hits`, whose text says no statistic separates *the football case*, and that remains exactly true.

content: **A project that adopts a lessons set uses two mechanisms, not one: signposts for the few failures it is hitting now, and a habit of recalling before writing for the rest.** Decided 2026-09-28 by the human partner, after a measurement. Both depend on **trigger memories** in the lessons set: the activity at the moment before a mistake, as its own memory linked to the lesson it guards, since a hindsight lesson is not what a query formed while writing is about. Signposts are chosen by recency, the lessons with the most instances among the project's latest recorded failures; the details are still open. They take their opening line from the trigger and need neither the model nor the floor. The habit covers every lesson, but depends on meaning-based matching and on getting past the non-match floor.
context: Discussing with the human partner how `coding-lessons` helps prevent failures in projects that opt in, straight after the trigger experiment.
why: The experiment (`01M3JTCKHD…`) showed each mechanism covers the other's gap. Signposts are reliable but reach only a few lessons, since every pushed line costs every session. The habit reaches all of them, but missed one query in eight, and its correct hits scored below `coding-lessons`' floor (`01M3JTCXF1…`). The human partner's earlier point, that the trigger is not the lesson, is what made both workable.

content: **The cross-set link half is a separate change that inherits none of the header half's properties, and it is forced to come second.** Adding an identity inside a link's nested target changes the **record** shape, so it changes the checksum of every memory holding a cross-set link -- seven in the live `scatterhoard` set when this was written -- which is the rewriting-rather-than-superseding act the closing window is about, where the header change is not. **It cannot come first:** a link cannot carry a set's identity until sets have identities. **And it cannot be made required, for a structural reason rather than a transitional one** -- a link may name a set this machine has never held, since a dangling target is documented as allowed and expected, so there is often no identity available to write. **So the link half is *the name, plus the identity where it is known*, and a link carrying only a name stays exactly as resolvable as today.** **As of 2026-08-30 the accidental-merge argument may be the only one left standing, which strengthens it rather than weakening it:** the proposal to make the graph the ancestor would retire per-target bases entirely, and with them *is this the same copy* -- the question replica identity was for. What survives is *is this the same set*, and with no base standing between two unrelated sets sharing a name, identity becomes the only thing that would refuse an accidental merge. That proposal also asks for identity one level down, in cross-set links, with the set **name** demoted to the status target keywords already have: carried so a lost reference can be re-found, never sufficient to resolve one.
context: Migrating open-questions.md, recovering content a faulty deletion boundary had left orphaned after the entry's head was already stored.
why:
Recorded because the two halves look like one feature and behave completely differently under the migration window -- a header change is cheap and a record-shape change is not -- and conflating them would put a checksum-moving change on the wrong side of the door.

The *cannot be required* reasoning is the durable part: it follows from dangling targets being a supported state rather than from anything about timing, so it will still hold after every other consideration here has expired.

The 2026-08-30 development is kept because it changes which argument carries the feature, and an argument narrowing to one load-bearing reason is worth knowing about before that reason is touched.

content: A seed and a trap are the same object: both are session-start push, so the trigger difference the watch convention's drafting agenda assumed does not exist, which is what let one convention replace two and needed no budget raise. Advancement is spawning a new head that draws on the observations, not superseding: one observation set can drive several questions and supersession affords one successor. And push is the marked case -- most accumulation stays passive and is reached by ordinary recall -- which is the budget story push had been missing.
context: Rewriting the watch convention around the index line, and finding the memory that recorded how it was built had gone half stale.
why: Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claims are unchanged. These are the three corrections untouched by the 2026-09-06 rewrite, and the ones a later session would otherwise re-derive expensively -- the spawning one especially, since the re-entry question said transitions are supersessions and following that would fork a chain deliberately. How a memory is marked changed separately, and is the memory alongside this one.

content: This set holds knowledge about Scatterhoard itself: how it works, how it came to be as it is, and how the work on it is done. A memory belongs here when it would still matter to someone working on Scatterhoard in a later session and would not matter to someone working on a different project.
context: Superseded 2026-08-25 at the human partner's request, after the convention it applies was itself revised by being applied to the two live charters. `coding-lessons` is deliberately left unchanged as the control, so the two sets' intake over the next several sessions measures whether this rewrite did anything.
why: Rewritten 2026-08-25 under `route-where`'s new charter clause, and this set is the case that clause was drafted from. The previous version opened with a list — decisions, measurements, defects, constraints — every item a kind of *conclusion*, and the corpus followed it: methods and paths-to-a-decision went unrecorded here while `coding-lessons`, whose description names technique, accumulated them freely under the same `store-when`. A charter's description silently decides which kinds of thing get written, not only where they go, so the subject now leads and no list stands in its place. "How the work on it is done" is what admits a measurement procedure without naming *method* as a category, since naming categories is what rebuilt the whitelist last time. The dropped sentence about lessons that would hold anywhere was not lost: it moved into `route-where`, because it is a routing rule every set would need rather than a fact about this one.

content: A Scatterhoard store holding exactly one memory reports similarity 0.0 for any query, matching or not, because a lone vector is its own centroid. Separation returns at three memories: a matching query then scores around +0.32 against unrelated memories near -0.29.
context: Measured 2026-08-02 against a live store, growing it from one memory to three and re-running the same query.
why: The earlier note framed this as a misleading score for a matching query. Measured live, it is stronger than that: with one memory the score carries no information at all, since every query returns 0.0. That makes it a cold-start defect rather than a presentation problem.

content: Found 2026-08-11 running SETUP.md §5 item 9. The serde message is honest, correct and actionable, which is why it was filed as Costs — **what makes it worth recording is the inconsistency**: every refusal this project wrote by hand does more, and the missing-argument case is the one path where nobody wrote a message, so a dependency's leaks through. It is reached most often by a model that guessed at the call, which is exactly the caller least served by terse phrasing. **Sharpened by the flat schema** added for `oneof-tool-schemas-present-no-parameters`: at the top level every argument now looks optional and only the `action` description says which action needs which, so a caller reading the flat view is *more* likely to reach this refusal than before. **Fixed 2026-08-19** by `missing_arguments`, which reads the branch pinning the action and names both halves — *"`export` takes scope and directory. This call did not include directory."* — at the dispatch point, before either tool reaches the deserialiser.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A defect created by a previous fix: flattening the schema made every argument look optional, so the path with no hand-written message became the likely one. Recorded because that interaction is the reason a Costs-severity wording issue was worth doing.

content: The local store could not be shared between servers. Shipped 2026-08-10 **and widened the same day**: it went out as `SCATTERHOARD_LOCAL`, covering only the local store, which turned out to be half the problem — `local` and a cross-project set like `coding-lessons` are the same kind of thing, and only `local`'s scope *type* made it look otherwise. `SCATTERHOARD_COMMON` now holds every store belonging to the machine rather than to one checkout, defaulting to `SCATTERHOARD_HOME` so the simple case degenerates to the old behaviour exactly. The rule lives in `StoreLayout` in [store.rs](src/store.rs) rather than in startup wiring, and `status` reports the file each set is read from. **The registry per home is deliberately not part of this**: it is still `Proposed:` in the design rather than decided, and an entry in this file would claim a decision nobody has taken. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `scatterhoard-local`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Configuration and process topology section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only. Design at [store-registry.md](documents/design/store-registry.md).

The refusal to file the registry here is worth keeping in the head rather than a member: it is the rule that stops this file accumulating entries for things that were merely proposed nearby, which is how the same file's own scope drifts.

content: **gemma4:12b records a correctly linked model recommendation from the status how-to: 5 of 5 with a hub, 5 of 5 without one, and 0 of 3 with the how-to removed.** Measured 2026-10-04 on a disposable set declaring English and Russian, under `potion-base-32M`. Each trial showed the model status, gave it the task "make sure anyone who uses this set finds out" about a better model, and let it act for up to six turns. A pass required status to then list the recommendation. Two earlier failures were fixed before this run. First, with no hub, told only to "write the hub first", the model linked to the charter and repeated the refused call; showing the hub as a call fixed that, taking it from 0 to 5 of 5. Second, a link whose `target_set` named its own set was refused although the write would have stored it as same-set; the checks now ask `is_foreign_to`.
context: Adding the model-fit how-to to status's band notes, at the human partner's request to close the gap where nothing served told a session how to record a recommendation. The driver was a scratch script over `scripts/local_model.py`.
why: This is the evidence that the served how-to is what teaches the mechanism: the control wrote an ordinary memory every time. It also gives a second instance, after the missing-query refusal, of a small model recovering when a refusal shows the call rather than describing it. The sample is small, five runs per condition.

content: **Recall cannot express a review today, and the gap is in three places — read from the code 2026-09-16.** *(1)* **A hit names its set and never its identity.** Every result serialises `WireScope` — `local` or `shared:<name>` — and `set_id` reaches a caller only in the `hoard_sets status` listing. So two loaded copies of one set are distinguished in output solely by the machine-local name the reviewer chose at load, and **nothing in a result says the two are copies of one set**. *(2)* **Scope is one set or all of them.** `Server::recall` takes `scope: Option<Scope>`, so *search theirs* works if you know the temporary name and *search everything* works, while *mine and theirs as one ranked list, labelled* is not expressible. *(3)* **Merely loading the copy changes ordinary recall.** Scores are computed against the centroid of the union of all loaded sets, so a near-duplicate shifts the scale every other set is scored on — the subtler form of the pilot-corpus episode, where an imported test corpus took all three top results on an unrelated query. **The consequence for the design: an evaluation load should be opt-in for recall** — searched when its scope is named and excluded from an unscoped search — which answers *controlling* and *knowing* together, keeps the maintainer's ordinary recall uncontaminated, and matches the rule that an evaluation set must not push.
context: Working through what a review needs from recall, after settling that identity resolution should answer from the writable holder.
why:
Recorded because the question's third open part — how recall names an evaluation set beside your own — reads like a labelling problem and is not one. Labelling is the part that nearly works; the parts that do not are addressing and scoring, and the scoring one is invisible from the tool surface, since nothing in a result says the ranking it belongs to was computed against a corpus that includes a set you are only reviewing.

The human partner arrived at it from the other end, observing that a reviewer must control *and know* which set a memory came from. That framing is what makes the opt-in default the answer rather than a richer label: a label tells you where a hit came from after the ranking has already been distorted.

Read from the code and not exercised. What would confirm it is a recall against two loaded copies of one set, comparing the ranking with and without the copy loaded — the same shape as the pilot-corpus measurement, which is the instance this generalises.

content:
Evidence for the human partner's claim that longer memories are more likely to need splitting, measured 2026-09-19 over `scatterhoard`'s 955 records: the share that has been superseded rises with length, from 4.2% in the shortest length decile to 26.0% in the longest, and the nine genuine splits — one memory replaced by several — have a median length of 2036 against the corpus median of 1455. The longest decile is also the *youngest*, median age 8 days against 12 for the rest, so it is revised more despite having had less time to be.

**The companion claim, that composite memories lose the links they would have had, does not show up as a link count.** Outbound links rise with length: 0.22 per memory in the second decile against 2.09 in the tenth, and they rise per thousand characters too, 0.27 against 0.77. That is not evidence against the argument — its loss is counterfactual, edges never written because the material was bundled into one record — but it does mean link count cannot be the measurement, and a test of that claim has to find another shape.

Reproduce from `~/.local/share/scatterhoard/shared-*.sqlite3` read-only: length deciles of `length(content) + length(coalesce(why,''))`, against `links` where `label = 'supersedes'`.
context: Testing the claims behind a proposed length refusal, in the session that also fixed the tracking index's ordering.
why: The splitting claim was the load-bearing half of the case for refusing an over-length memory, and it was offered as reasoning rather than measurement; it holds, with the age confound running the right way. The link half is recorded as a failed measurement rather than dropped, because the obvious test will occur to the next session too, and knowing it has been run and what it showed is worth more than the null itself.

content: **Untested hypothesis, raised by the human partner 2026-09-08 at the close of a day of failed measurements: the results depend so sensitively on the exact wording of a question that the sensitivity is itself the phenomenon.** Nothing measured this directly — every probe scored *different* queries against each other and none scored *the same intent worded several ways*. **The test: take ten questions with a known intent, write five paraphrases of each, and compare the spread of top-1 score and top-5 membership within a paraphrase group against the spread between groups. If within-group variance approaches between-group variance, a score is not a function of a query's meaning** — and that single fact would account for every failure recorded under this entry at once, because no threshold can exist on a quantity that is not stable under rephrasing. It also predicts the two cases that survived everything: *premier league offside rule interpretation* against a governance question may differ by less than two phrasings of one intent. **This is cheap** — the machinery is in `tests/probes.rs` and needs only the query set. It is the first hypothesis on this entry that would explain the failures rather than adding to them.
context: Wrapping up the recall research, when the human partner observed that the answers move too much with the question for the search to be finished.
why:
Recorded because it is the most valuable thing produced on 2026-09-08 and the only lead not yet spent, and because it came from noticing the *shape* of a day's results rather than from any measurement in it — which is exactly the kind of observation that does not survive a session boundary unless written down.

It also carries a correction about how that day ended. Four mechanisms were proposed and withdrawn, and the assistant repeatedly proposed stopping; the human partner accepted the stop while saying plainly that the search has not bottomed out. A later session should read the ruled-out list as a deliverable and the stopping as a judgement call that was made, not as a conclusion the evidence forced.

content: **What recall returns -- the budget question, now that the visibility question is settled.** *Partly resolved 2026-08-03.* `hoard_recall` and `hoard_lookup` return the memory's complete field set, including links and keywords, through a single view type shared by every tool. **The reason the full field set went in first was corpus integrity rather than caller convenience:** a field no tool can show is a field whose corruption cannot be detected, which makes visibility a precondition rather than a preference. **What remains open is genuinely a budget question:** whether the *default* detail level should be narrower than the full one, given links and keywords are not free. **Constraint from the human partner:** a full-detail mode must always exist, and any reduced default must be **one subtractive projection applied in a single place** -- several call sites each choosing their own fields is the defect that was just removed, rebuilt under a new name. **Narrowed 2026-09-06:** a reduced level now exists as `detail: "summary"`, one derived line, satisfying the constraint on *shape* -- but it is deliberately **not** a candidate for the default, because it drops the record rather than trimming it. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `what-recall-returns`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The corpus-integrity reasoning is carried in the head because it is the argument that would otherwise be re-litigated: full detail looks like generosity toward callers and is actually a detectability requirement, so a budget-driven trim has to answer it rather than simply weigh bytes.

The note that `summary` is not the default candidate is kept for the same reason -- it exists, it is cheap, and it is the obvious thing to reach for, which is exactly why the entry says it is the wrong shape for this.

content: Scatterhoard's own schema flattener drops the prose. `with_flat_view` merges each `oneOf` branch's *properties* into one object and synthesises the `action` enum's description from the branches' required arguments -- but every branch's own `description` is discarded, so the only prose a client ever reads about a multi-action tool is the tool's top-level `description`. A rule written into a branch description ships nothing, and the branch text survives only as a comment for whoever reads the source.
context: Found 2026-08-30 while building `correction-gated-on-service`, rewriting `hoard_correct`'s amend branch to describe the service gate. Checkable in `with_flat_view` in src/mcp.rs and in tests/snapshots/tools_list.json, which is the shape a client receives.
why: The branch description is where the rule *belongs* structurally -- it sits beside the arguments it governs -- so writing it there feels like publishing it, and nothing in the code says otherwise. It was caught here only because the approval snapshot of `tools/list` showed no change after the amend branch's description had been completely rewritten; without that snapshot the new rule would have shipped invisible to every caller. This is the same class as `amending-a-claim-is-refused-where-no-client-can-reach-it` one layer over: what the handler knows and what the client is told are different things.

content: A same-set link spelled with its own set name was inert: the cross-set guards key on `target_set IS NULL`, so a link in set `ours` whose `target_set` said `"ours"` was skipped by `Store::edges` and filtered out by `Store::incoming`, and a legitimate supersession written the long way silently did nothing. Fixed 2026-08-23 by canonicalising at the write. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-same-set-link-spelled-with-its-set-name-is-inert`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Set names differing only in case, such as `Notes` and `notes`, share one store file on macOS and Windows. Reproduced 2026-09-30 on macOS: creating `Notes` beside a loaded `notes` was refused as an unloaded database, with a remedy (restart) that loads the same file as `notes`; on Linux it would have made a second file. Fixed the same day: `create` and `evaluate` refuse a name sharing a file with any set this machine holds, withheld ones included, naming that set in its own spelling. The comparison is `SetName::shares_a_file_with` in `src/memory/scope.rs`, ASCII case-insensitive. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `set-names-differing-only-in-case-share-a-store-file`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through post-release-risk issues with the human partner, after the supersession pair; they asked whether the comparison should be a casefold or a lowercase.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed as its fixed-when asked: case-variant set names are refused. Refusal on every platform, chosen with the human partner over rewording only where the filesystem collides, since there are no set-name aliases and a data directory moves between platforms. ASCII comparison, discussed with them against casefold: identical over `SetName`'s ASCII alphabet, and if names widen, the right fold is a filesystem's (canonical normalisation plus case folding), not `Keyword::folded`'s compatibility mapping, so the method's doc says where to change it. Three tests in `tests/sets.rs`, the last after the withheld-set mutation survived and showed the refusal saying a withheld set was loaded; four mutations. `documents/design/set-lifecycle.md`.

content: A linked memory sits very close to its source in embedding space: measured over the 23 traversable edges of the scatterhoard and coding-lessons sets, the median target is the 2.9th-percentile most similar memory to its source. That percentile is what decides whether graph traversal earns its cost, and it is scale-invariant where rank is not. At 70 memories the median target ranks 2nd, so 16 of 23 fall inside a top-5 cut and traversal is indistinguishable from raising the limit; at the same percentiles and 1,000 memories, none of the 23 would. The crossover is near 170 memories, where 2.9% of the corpus crosses 5.
context: Measured 2026-08-15 by reading stored vectors directly from both SQLite stores, removing the union centroid, and ranking every memory against each link's source. Recorded on recall-eval-harness in BACKLOG.md. The query proxy is the source memory's own vector, which is the best case for traversal from that seed.
why: This settles why the traversal weighting question could not be answered from the corpora on hand, and replaces the assumption that the missing ingredient was queries. Below the crossover no number of queries can discriminate between combination rules, because traversal and a larger limit return the same memories. It also gives the eval corpus a size target instead of an ambition. Supersession edges were excluded because validity resolution never traverses them.

content: **History, 2026-08-15: the entry said the seed-quality corpus was lost and irreplaceable, and it was neither.** The whole fixture — 45 memories, 20 queries with relevance lists, the transformer baseline and the Rust spike — came back out of the embedder-spike **session transcript**, which had recorded the `Write` call that created it; the `/private/tmp` scratchpad it lived in was gone, so the transcript was the only copy. It is now checked in at `corpus/seed-quality-corpus.json` with its provenance. **What those numbers settled**: recall@5 of **57.5% for content alone, 71.7% for content+why+keywords, and 77.5% with centroid removal**, with the worst hub falling from 13-of-20 to 6-of-20. They chose the embedding inputs and the model, and until the recovery the decisions stood on evidence that could not be reproduced, re-run against a new embedder, or extended.
context: Migrating the recall-eval-harness entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the correction the entry made to its own opening claim.
why:
Kept for the recovery route as much as the numbers. A fixture written to a scratchpad is gone, but the *call that wrote it* is in the transcript, and that is a general recovery path nobody thinks of while the loss still looks total — this project lost the same class of artifact twice, and the second time it was recoverable because someone tried the transcript.

The numbers themselves are irreproducible in the sense that matters: they were measured against a 45-memory fixture and a specific embedder, and re-running them today would answer a different question. Re-running the recovered fixture against `potion-base-32M` to reproduce 71.7% was named as the first task, since arithmetic consistency identified the model but did not prove it.

content: **One observation for this investigation: roughly twenty recalls on 2026-09-23 and none missed.** They were run auditing the open tracking entries — mostly keyword recalls naming entry slugs, several batching four slugs plus a status mark so heads outranked their members, and a handful by meaning. Nothing needed rephrasing and nothing came back empty that should not have. That is evidence on the retiring side: the entry says a long stretch with no misses argues the query side takes care of itself. It is weak evidence about *semantic* querying specifically, since most of these were exact-match keyword calls, which is the path the entry's concern does not apply to.
context: The fuller second pass over the open questions, which itself ran the recalls being reported here.
why: The entry is marked `hoard-investigation` and asks for each observation of a recall that missed or needed rephrasing; a session that had none should say so, or the record fills only with failures and the absence of misses never counts toward the answer. The caveat about which path was exercised is included because without it this reads as stronger evidence than it is.

content: **Measured 2026-09-15, when the question was filed: memory length has already risen in both shared sets — the monthly median by about a third, August to September.** Median `content` + `why` in characters over every row in `memories`, superseded ones included: by month, **`scatterhoard`** 1108 → 1466 and **`coding-lessons`** 1101 → 1471. By ISO week of `created_at`, **`scatterhoard`** W31 807 → W32 1107 → W34 1245 → W35 1404 → W36 1455 → W37 1943; **`coding-lessons`** W32 969 → W34 1303 → W35 1395 → W36 1754 (W37, 4 memories, 1183). **`coding-lessons` is the cleaner series** — W36 in `scatterhoard` is 716 memories, nearly all the TRACKING.md migration, whose `why` fields ran short (median 325) while `content` ran long (1021), so it sits on the trend by coincidence of two opposite distortions. **The growth is in `content` more than `why`**: `scatterhoard` content median 460 → 1090 across the span. **The embedding cut is reached by a small tail, not the median:** the token count taken 2026-09-09 found 42 of 886 memories (4.7%) past 512 tokens, median 305, p90 460, max 699; by characters today, 4 `scatterhoard` memories exceed model2vec's exact pre-tokenisation cut of 3,584 (512 × a median vocabulary token of 7 bytes for `potion-base-32M`). Characters are not tokens — a 4.5-characters-per-token estimate put 98 past the cut, more than double the real count, so do not convert. Reproduce with a read-only `sqlite3` query over `~/.local/share/scatterhoard/shared-*.sqlite3`, grouping `length(content) + length(why)` by `strftime('%Y-%m', created_at)` or `strftime('%Y-W%W', created_at)`.
context: Filing the memory-size question the human partner raised after restoring from the checkpoint, before starting the link-key collision test.
why:
A baseline is the one part of this question that gets harder with time: a later session reconstructing the trend from `created_at` meets the same migration confound with less memory of what caused it, and the pre-question figures are the only ones written without the question in view — once a convention or a measurement exists, lengths respond to it.

**What this does not establish.** A rise in length is not yet a harm. Nothing here measures retrieval against length, and the 2026-09-08 composition ablation found that retrieval *rises* with a memory's `why`-share for reasons unrelated to `why` being embedded — so longer memories currently retrieve at least as well, and the embedding-degradation concern is the human partner's expectation from other systems rather than something shown here. Six weeks, one author population, and a corpus shaped by a single migration are all reasons to read the slope as a direction rather than a rate.

The failed character-to-token conversion is kept because it is the easy mistake: it was made while gathering these figures, and it would have overstated the truncated tail by more than half.

content: The merge driver walks the three sides of a memory file in step, holding one record a side, rather than all three sides and the output in memory. Built 2026-09-22 the same day as filed: `merge::merge_streams` reads each side twice (check it parses and is in `file_position` order, then merge), `merge_files` wraps it for texts, and `cli::merge_file` writes beside `ours` and renames. A side out of file order — every file written before 2026-09-21 — is read whole, and the driver names it and says re-exporting ends it. Checked by `tests/merge.rs` and eight recorded mutations. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `streaming-merge-driver`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Filing and building the two follow-ups from the question about storing the hash that orders memory files; the stored position column is next.
why: Superseded to record it as built. The whole-file path was kept rather than refusing an out-of-order side, because merge bases written by builds before the hash order are routine for now and refusing them would break merges that work today; naming the side is what keeps that path from being silent.

content: Found 2026-09-02, **measured as a controlled comparison rather than inferred**: one memory wrote three `related_to` links in a single call — one within its own set, two crossing into other sets — and only the same-set target reported a backlink. The outbound half is stored correctly and carries the target's `set_id`, so nothing about the write is wrong. **Two things stack and only the second is binding**: `Store::incoming` filters `target_set IS NULL` deliberately, because it is the lookup `resolve_supersession` walks and a cross-set row whose target id collides with a local one would change a memory's standing — that guard is right. But the row also lives in the *source's* database, and a lookup of the target asks the *target's* store, **so the query never sees it whatever the filter says**. Removing the filter would not fix this and would break resolution. **What it costs**: a cross-set link is one-directional in practice, and that matters most where the *legal* direction is the one nobody would search from — a personal memory may link into a shared set and a shared memory may not link back, so a cluster spanning that boundary is reachable only from the personal side.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A controlled comparison in one call, and two stacked causes where the obvious one is a correct guard. Removing the filter would break resolution and still not fix this, because the row is in the wrong database.

content: **Checked 2026-09-28: the different-set half is prevented, and only the same-set half remains open.** An import whose file declares another set identity is refused before any base is consulted, since `identity-mismatch-refusal` on 2026-09-26, in `import_set` in `src/mcp.rs`. In directory form, `locate_in` falls back to the declared name when no header matches the set's identity, so a swapped-in stranger is found and then refused. `a_different_set_swapped_in_at_a_directory_this_set_agreed_with_is_refused` in `tests/sets.rs` pins the scenario as first told, with a base recorded for the directory, and the mutation `set identity: import a file declaring another identity` fails it. One residue: a stranger's file that declares no identity is imported with a note, not refused. Every export of a set holding records writes one, so such a file is hand-edited or predates identities. The older-backup-of-the-same-set half is unchanged: detected by `taken_backwards`, not prevented, and set identity structurally cannot help.
context: Working through the open corrupts-severity issues after fixing absorb's partial-file links; the human partner asked for this one next.
why: The head's fixed-when, a target identity that tells two replicas at one path apart, is still unmet, so the entry stays open. But half the scenario it names is now refused rather than reconciled, and a later reader of the head alone would think both halves live. Verified by reading the code and adding a test, not by re-reading the entry.

content: A Scatterhoard shared set with no repository is a first-class, possibly long-lived state rather than a broken one. The motivating case: a developer keeps memories about a project whose maintainer has not agreed to carry a `scatterhoard_mem` directory, hoping to make the case later. Those memories belong in a named set rather than in `local`, and have nowhere to be exported to yet. Registration must therefore be optional rather than a precondition for a set existing, and a store with no recorded path is reported as unattached and never flagged.
context: Raised by the human partner 2026-08-06 revising documents/design/store-registry.md; recorded there under "an unattached set is a first-class state, not a degenerate one".
why: Raised after a decision to alert on every orphaned store, and it turned out not to be a question about alert volume at all: the scenario is not an orphan, and the store-registry draft had no state for it. The draft had over-claimed that a cross-project set "has a repository, so it registers like anything else", erasing a state that set-lifecycle.md already blesses. The kind of error that surfaces late, as an implementation refusing to create a set without a path.

content: **`route-where` loses its two sentences on general lessons versus project instances, 271 characters.** Decided 2026-09-27 by the human partner; **not yet done**, deferred while a full mutation pass held `src/`. The sentences are the ones beginning "When an insight has both a general form and a project-specific instance", in `src/conventions/catalog.rs`. The freed space is for `data-only-rule-in-the-catalog`. When it is done, `coding-lessons`' charter (`01M2F32X5Z…`), whose `why` cites `route-where` for this rule, is superseded so that it stands on its own.
context: Freeing catalog space for the data-only clause, during a full mutation pass after the local-set refusal was built.
why: The convention's opening rule, route a memory by what it is about, already covers the case. Without `coding-lessons` loaded, the sentences push the general half into `local` through the nothing-fits fallback, where it is misfiled and never shared. The split is useful only to projects that use a lessons set, and those now get it through the adoption guide they opt into (`set-adoption`), rather than from served text that reaches every session.

content: **Concurrent additions are mitigated, not eliminated, and that is the decision.** Taken by the human partner 2026-09-21. A memory file is ordered by a hash of each id (`memory_file::file_position`). Registering the merge driver is an optional, recommended step in `SETUP.md` §3f, not something Scatterhoard does, and the driver's contract is documented there for CI. A file per memory was proposed and rejected. A residual conflict on a large, active project is accepted: its resolution is always to keep both sides.
context: Pre-release review of what would keep others from using Scatterhoard, after retiring the header summary and measuring the end-of-file conflict.
why: The human partner's reasoning for accepting a residue: most projects start solo or small, where concurrent additions are rare, and the driver resolves every case where it runs. The place it bites is a large, active project adopting Scatterhoard mid-flight, and there clicking "accept both" is tolerable. Against a file per memory: backup files would become directories or lose import compatibility; filesystems with a per-directory file limit would be excluded; import would open every file; moving a set around would stop being easy; and any large-scale change brings its own issues. UUIDv7 stays because other things depend on ids being roughly chronological, the tracker among them; only the line order in the file changed.

content: **When a set declares a language the server has no test sentences for, the declared-language check asks the agent to supply them** rather than skipping the language or reporting it unknown. Decided by the human partner on 2026-10-03. Not yet decided: what form the request takes, and where the supplied sentences are kept so the check need not ask again.
context: Restoring the session from the 2026-10-04 checkpoint, before widening the paraphrase-rank probe to about ten triplets per language and turning its rank harness into a probe.
why: A set declared as, say, Samoan is almost certainly being written by an agent that can write Samoan, so the agent is the best source of sentences in that language. The alternative, a built-in list, cannot cover every language a charter might declare. Recorded because the built-in triplets in `tests/probes.rs` look like the complete design, and they are not.

content: A commit left out most of the change it described, 2026-10-04. `git add src/language_fit.rs tests/language_fit.rs -A` staged only those two new files, so the first commit of the language-fit work lacked the ten modified files its message described. Reading `git status` right after the commit showed them, and the commit was amended before anything else happened, becoming `50d7f55`.
context: Committing the built-in-language part of the declared-language check.
why: A failure record under the `coding-lessons` adoption guide, part 3, and the first instance of the lesson on pathspecs narrowing `git add`, written the same day.

content: The backup taken before clearing the phantom base is unreliable, found 2026-09-01. It was made by copying the store file while the servers held it open, and the stores are in WAL mode with sidecars that had not been checkpointed since August — so it holds only what had reached the main file. A backup taken the same way that day for the attribution migration captured **51 of 81 memories**. `PRAGMA integrity_check` passing says nothing about this: the copy is internally consistent and simply shorter. The counts quoted for the 2026-08-20 clearance were taken from the live store rather than from the copy, so they stand; the copy is not the restore point it was believed to be. [documents/design/set-lifecycle.md](documents/design/set-lifecycle.md) already prescribes `sqlite3 <store> ".backup <dest>"` for exactly this reason.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A backup that passes every check available to the person taking it and is still short. Recorded because the failure is silent by construction — integrity_check verifies consistency, not completeness — and because a `cp` of a WAL database is the obvious thing to reach for.

content: **The merge driver's handling of the header no longer matters for current files.** Found 2026-09-16: the header conflicted on every concurrent export because it carried a summary derived from vectors a driver does not have, so the driver keeps the receiving side's header verbatim. Since 2026-09-21 the header carries no summary, so two sides of one set write the same header. Keeping ours now matters only for a file an older build wrote, whose `summary` no reader looks at. See `merge_files` in `src/merge.rs`.
context: Retiring the header summary and its comparison, which left the merge driver's recorded findings partly stale.
why: The corrected half of the 2026-09-16 merge-driver findings. Kept as its own memory so a reader meeting the verbatim-header code finds why it was written, and why it no longer carries weight.

content: The reserved directory accepts the personal set: `export` and `import` in `directory` form take `scope: local`, and write or read `scatterhoard_mem/memories.json` declaring `local`. The design says the path settles a file's kind, so that a file found there is a shared set whatever its header claims (`documents/design/set-lifecycle.md`, *the fixed export path is a property of the trigger*). No code enforces it. `import_set` and `export_set` in `src/mcp.rs` check only `Expectation::Exactly(scope)` against the header, and `tests/sets.rs` exports `local` by directory throughout. So a checkout can hold a file that imports into `local`, and `local` can be written where a commit picks it up. Read from the code 2026-09-25, not exercised end to end. Fixed when `directory` form refuses `local` both ways, leaving `file` form for backups. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-reserved-directory-accepts-the-local-set`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Taking up `imported-set-trust-boundary` on the release gate, straight after resolving `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout`.
why: Head of an issue cluster. Corrupts: a crafted repository needs only one import call naming `local` to place memories in the personal set, where `route-where` treats what it holds as the user's own preferences. And an export by directory puts personal memories where the next commit publishes them, which `route-where` calls irreversible. It also falsifies a premise: `imported-set-trust-boundary`'s member `01M1ZCZAT3…` says the File Format guard currently holds local scope shut, and for a caller that names `local` it does not. Found while reading that question's ordering after the name binding was dropped. The directory form for `local` predates the explicit `file` form of 2026-08-25, and the tests were never moved over.

content: Filed 2026-08-30 in the commit that built `correction-gated-on-service`, which is what made it true. The catalog is served into every session before any tool is called, and two conventions described the old surface: `correct-when`'s third clause named the four apparatus fields, when amending is now refused on any exported record whatever the field and permitted on the claim of one that has not been exported; and `confidence-standards` said to amend a changed number, which on an exported record instructs an operation the server refuses. **Both were left deliberately, and the reason was sequencing rather than oversight** — a convention describing a guard that does not exist is the failure that kept `correct-when` out of the catalog for its first week — so once the guard existed the reason expired and this became an ordinary defect. **Misleads rather than Costs** because the refusal names supersession and the session recovers in one turn, so nothing is lost or stored wrong; what is damaged is the catalog's standing, since it is the one text a session is told to trust before it can check anything, and a reader who trips over a clause that is simply wrong has no way to tell which of the others are.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A defect deliberately created by shipping the guard before the text, and the severity argument that makes a one-turn recovery matter: the cost is to the credibility of the one document a session cannot check.

content: **Decided 2026-09-17 by the human partner: an evaluation set resolves no outbound cross-set link. Each such link is surfaced instead, carrying what the LLM needs to traverse it by hand.** The link reports its target memory id, the set name the link recorded, the target's set identity, and **every loaded scope answering to that identity, each with its load mode** — plural because one identity can be held by the reviewer's own read-write set and by several evaluation copies at once, as in `coding-lessons`, `eval-coding-lessons-1234` and `eval-coding-lessons-1011`. The mode is included so the list reads as *your copy, and two under review* rather than three equivalent names. **Nothing resolves in the other direction either**: an ordinary recall or lookup resolves nothing into an evaluation set. **Why this is safe**: an unreachable cross-set concession already reports `superseded_beyond_this_set`, so a contributor's superseded memory never reads as current; and `hoard_lookup` by id already returns a hit per loaded set, each labelled by scope, so following a link by hand shows the branch's copy beside the reviewer's own — the comparison a review wants. **The cost** is a round trip per link followed, in exchange for nothing being followed silently. **Two consequences for the build:** evaluation copies must be excluded from `Server::settle_identity`, or a loaded evaluation copy would count as a rival holder of its source's identity; and the *sets searched versus sets resolved against* distinction is not needed, since nothing outbound is resolved.
context: Designing evaluation mode after read-only was finished, starting with cross-set links.
why: The assistant proposed resolving cohort-first and then against the reviewer's own sets with a marker; the human partner proposed not resolving at all and flagging instead, and asked what that would cost a review. Checking found no case where it makes a review wrong — standing is already reported honestly when a target is out of reach — and two where it makes one slower or ambiguous, both answered by what the flag carries rather than by resolving. It is also the simpler design: it removes the need for a cohort in resolution and for a second store population.

content: A missing argument was refused in the deserialiser's own words — *"missing field `name`"* — the one refusal path nobody had written, on a tool whose other refusals say what is available rather than what is wrong. Fixed 2026-08-19 by checking ahead of serde and naming both what the action takes and what did not arrive. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-missing-argument-refusal-is-a-raw-serde-message`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: The phantom target the doubled export created was cleared by hand on 2026-08-20, and this is why `bases` is 51 rows lighter. The doubled export wrote an agreement for `.../scatterhoard/scatterhoard_mem`, whose file lived at `scatterhoard_mem/scatterhoard_mem/memories.json` and was deleted the same day. **The target directory itself still exists** — it is the real memory directory — so *the target is gone* is not what made the base stale; what made it stale is that the *file that base described* was gone, which is the more precise test and the less obvious one. Removing base rows is documented as recoverable: the next import reads those records as having no ancestor, which is noisy for one cycle and not lossy. One stale target remains by choice, an export to a session scratchpad under `/private/tmp/...` whose own path says plainly what it was.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The cleanup, kept for the distinction it turned on: a base is stale when the file it describes is gone, not when the directory is — and the directory in this case was the live one, so the obvious test would have said the base was fine.

content: Measured properly 2026-08-30, and the size figure is wrong by about six times: `mutate.py` computes it as `sum(f.stat().st_size for f in DEPS.iterdir())`, which **counts every hard link's bytes again**, and 93% of the entries in `deps` are extra links rather than distinct files. `target/debug/deps` held 127,915 files over 8,407 inodes at 1.5 GB by `du`; `target-mutation/debug/deps` held 272,597 over 11,960 at 2.8 GB, which the note reported as **19.4 GB**. The real disk cost of two full passes is 3.2 GB for the whole directory against 1.0 GB for a clean build of everything, so the marginal cost of a mutation is about **520 files and 4 MB**, and a full pass of 261 adds roughly 136,000 files and 1.1 GB. **The file-count threshold drifted exactly as the code predicted**: `CROWDED = 100_000` was set to *about three passes* from a measurement of 94 mutations leaving 34,823 files, the corpus is now 261, and the comment beside it says in as many words that a threshold set once *"will drift into uselessness the same way its predecessor did"* — it was right, and nothing re-ran the recalibration it describes.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A measurement error that made an alarming number out of hard links, and a threshold that drifted exactly as its own comment predicted. The second is the more useful half: a constant calibrated against a corpus size becomes wrong as the corpus grows, and saying so in a comment does not prevent it.

content: **The sharing-preferences template is left in English on purpose, and localising it is deferred.** Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *the preferences start from a template*. Until it is localised, a person using the never-store list is assumed to read English or to have a model that does. The list itself already serves Chinese: it folds full-width forms, makes a space optional beside unspaced scripts, and its template example gives both simplified and traditional forms.
context: Building the sharing preferences' never-store list: full-width folding, optional spacing beside Chinese, and a Chinese example in the template.
why: Localising the template is a feature in its own right: which language to write, how to choose it, and whether the headings the parser reads are translated. The human partner would take it up if the project becomes popular. Recorded because the English-only template will look like an oversight to anyone who has not seen this decision.

content: Every tool publishes what goes in and nothing about what comes back: all four carry an `inputSchema` and none an `outputSchema`, so a response shape that varies — `similarity` on a direct hit, `matched_similarity` on a substituted one, `matched_keywords` on the keyword path only — is learnable only by provoking each case. Fixed when the response shape is published, with conditional fields marked conditional. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `response-shape-is-unpublished`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only, with the fixed-when since this one is open. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: The recorded mutation `store: change the scope prefix in its one place` is now `caught`, not `survives`. The migration test for `add_folded_keywords` hardcodes `shared:scatterhoard` in its fixture, so something outside the store module does compare against a literal scope prefix. This is the right outcome: the meta scope encoding is persisted data, and changing it silently should break something.
context: Corrected 2026-08-04 while fixing keywords-silently-lowercased, whose migration test is what changed the outcome.
why: The reason written for the surviving mutation was true when written and became false when an unrelated test was added. A mutation's recorded reason is a claim about the rest of the suite, so it can be invalidated by code that never touches the mutated line — which means surviving-mutation reasons need re-reading when the suite grows, not only when the mutated code changes.

content: **The concrete case the deferral was waiting for arrived 2026-08-06 and fits neither side of the question -- and the class has since been closed off at the door.** A malformed tool call stored a memory whose `why` contained fragments of the call's own markup, an unclosed parameter tag among them. **That is neither a typo nor a changed claim: it is transmission damage, and nobody believed it.** The unequal-failure-directions argument does not bite, because there is no belief to destroy. Whether that is a recognisable-enough class to license amendment -- or whether the cost was correctly paid, since superseding it cost one extra record and Corrections already calls that *verbose, and lossless* -- was the decision to take. The case is preserved in the `scatterhoard` set itself, whose first two records are that supersession chain. **Update 2026-09-07: `hoard_memorize` now refuses a damaged call rather than storing it**, naming the wrong-closing-tag cause and telling the caller to resend. Observed three times in one session, each time refusing and storing nothing. **So the class that motivated the question can no longer reach the store**, which weakens the case for licensing amendment on it -- the remaining instances are the two already in the corpus.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, when the session's own malformed calls turned out to be the class this entry was waiting on.
why:
Recorded because the argument for amending transmission damage rested on the class being real and recurring, and it is still recurring -- three times in one session -- but no longer arrives. A guard at the boundary answers the question by removing its subject, which is a different outcome from deciding it, and worth distinguishing.

The three occurrences are evidence about the *call surface* rather than about corrections, and they are worth the note: the failure is easy to commit and invisible to the caller, which is exactly why refusing beats detecting after the fact.

content: An entry slug that is also a heavily used subject keyword gathers the whole subject, not the entry's findings. Measured 2026-09-07: `keyword-standards` returned 20 members, `investigation-pipeline` 17 and `graph-traversal` 16, where an entry's own findings are typically two or three. Fixed 2026-10-03, going forward. `genindex.py --check` fails on any entry filed since 2026-09-09 whose slug was already a keyword more than a day before the entry's first record (`slug_collisions`). TRACKING.md's slug rule now says not to take a term that names only the entry's subject. Four existing collisions are noted on a memory carrying their slugs. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-slug-that-is-also-a-subject-keyword-over-gathers`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Fixing the slug-collision issue after publishing output schemas and updating context-gloss-on-recall.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed by two of its fixed-when routes, a check that reports a collision and a rule at coining time, with the existing cases noted rather than renamed (option C, chosen with the human partner). The check's two thresholds came from measurement. Migrated entries existed as text before their records, so a cutoff excludes them; and findings are often stored hours before their entry is filed, so a one-day margin keeps those from counting. With both, the real file flags nothing, and removing the cutoff flags 19 entries. Part of the cause was TRACKING.md's own advice to reuse an existing handle, which read as license to take a subject term.

content: **The echo is a loop, not a reflection** — named by the human partner 2026-09-06 when they gave the field its first use: *making sure there is a coherent description in the first 120 characters, which might require a few tries.* `hoard_memorize` covers one turn of that loop and `amend` covers the rest, which is why the second path was worth building hours after being filed rather than deferred. **What did not carry over from the store echo is *always*.** `amend` is a partial write, so echoing a line on an amendment touching only `keywords` would report something that did not change; the echo fires when `content` is among the fields amended. That is a structural condition on the write rather than a keyword coupling — the same fallback the store echo had already named for itself.
context: Migrating the amend-echoes-the-derived-line entry out of BACKLOG.md, the session after it was built.
why:
Recorded because the difference between the two echoes looks like an inconsistency and is a decision. A later reader finding `hoard_memorize` unconditional and `amend` conditional would reasonably make them match, and matching in either direction is wrong: unconditional on a partial write reports a non-change, and conditional on a store has no partial case to condition on.

The loop framing is the part that justifies the second path existing at all. One echo shows you the line; it is the second that lets you fix it and see the result, and an author repairing a thin opening is exactly the caller who wants that.

content: Minimal standards for how keywords are used. Built 2026-08-12, after the catalog budget was raised to 16,000 to fit it. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `keyword-standards`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content:
**Re-measured over 275 traversable edges: the median linked target sits at the 1.78th percentile of similarity to its source, median rank 16, and only 43% fall inside a ten-result window.** The earlier figure — 2.9th percentile — was taken over 23 edges on 2026-08-15 and is superseded by a graph twelve times larger. p25 and p75 of rank are 4 and 65, so the distribution is wide: some linked memories are the obvious next hit and others are nowhere near.

**The 43% is the number that matters, and it is new.** The old measurement asked whether traversal beats simply raising the limit, and answered with a size crossover near 170 memories. This asks the operational question instead — *would content similarity have returned this memory anyway?* — and the answer at 762 memories is that **more than half the time it would not**. That is what a link buys, and it is why the connect-on-recall clause in `recall-when` is worded around *the one recall did not return*. Re-run `probe_where_a_linked_memory_ranks_against_its_source` in `tests/probes.rs`.
context: Checking a figure before a convention's reinforcement sentence quoted it, after the human partner asked which side of the trim criterion that sentence fell on.
why:
Supersedes the 2026-08-15 percentile because the value changed with the sample, not because the original was wrong: 23 edges was what the graph held then, and the memory said so. Its conclusions survive intact and should not be re-derived — the percentile is scale-invariant where rank is not, the crossover sits near 170 memories, and below that crossover no number of queries can separate traversal from a larger limit.

Re-derived rather than quoted because a convention was about to cite it. `AGENTS.md` requires counts be re-derived and this is the case that rule exists for: a figure from a 23-edge sample, three weeks old, about to be written into served text that every session loads. It moved by more than a third.

The wide spread is worth keeping. A median of 16 with a p75 of 65 means the value of a link is not uniform — for the memories already ranking in the top few it changes nothing, and for the tail it is the only route. That argues against ever tuning traversal on the median alone, which is what the earlier measurement had available and this one does not have to settle for.

content: **The case was measured against the real corpus rather than argued, because the whole question is where the selectivity cliff falls -- 2026-08-20, across the 84 memories then in three live sets.** **At the width people actually truncate to, the two encodings differ completely: at eight characters, 46 of 84 hex ids shared a prefix with an earlier one; base32 had none.** The cliff is at roughly 40 bits either way -- base32 reaches it in eight characters, hex needs ten -- and eight is what everything truncates to. **The 40-bit safety rests on an invariant worth writing down:** ids are minted only by `hoard_memorize`, which runs at the pace an LLM composes a memory, and the smallest gap between two mintings across the live sets was **3,177 ms against the 256 ms window 40 fixed bits leaves** -- a twelvefold margin. Import preserves ids rather than re-minting, so bulk arrival does not cluster them. **The properties the design depends on survive:** Crockford base32 is order-preserving over the same bit sequence, verified on the real ids -- load-bearing because keyword recall breaks ties on ascending id and the rule is stated as oldest-first, so an encoding that reordered would take both with it.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the minting-rate invariant is a safety argument that is invisible in the code and would be silently broken by an obvious future change: anything that mints ids in a tight loop -- a bulk generator, a migration that re-mints, a test fixture -- collapses the twelvefold margin the eight-character claim rests on. Import preserving ids is what currently holds that shut.

The order-preserving property is recorded because it is a dependency rather than a nicety: two separate behaviours read id order as time order, and an encoding change is exactly the kind of work where that would be checked last.

content: Two branches that both add memories conflicted at the end of the memory file under a plain `git` merge, because records were written in id order and ids are time-ordered, so concurrent additions were insertions at one point. Fixed 2026-09-21, by decision, as a mitigation: records are ordered by a hash of the id, so concurrent additions usually land apart, and the driver resolves the rest where it runs. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `concurrent-additions-collide-at-the-end-of-the-memory-file`; this record carries only its standing.

content:
`mutate.py --stale` cannot see a rotted `replace`, and `AGENTS.md` recommends it at exactly the moment that causes one. Its guidance is to run `--stale` *after any rename or refactor, and before trusting a mutation count* — but `--stale` checks only that `find` still matches the file, and a refactor that changes a **type a replacement constructs** leaves `find` matching perfectly while `replace` no longer compiles. `--list` is equally blind: it reports recorded expectations, not what the corpus does. **Only a full pass finds this**, and it reports it as *stopped by the compiler rather than by a test*.

Found again 2026-09-12 by the first full pass since 2026-09-11: two of 370. One had rotted when `embed_all` began returning `Outcomes` rather than a count, so `reembed: report the memories offered rather than the vectors written` had proved nothing for a day. The other was a mutation whose `tests` list named only `recall`, where the behaviour it mutated is unobservable — green for the wrong reason, which `--stale` also cannot see.

A full pass takes about 10 minutes on a cleaned `target-mutation` and 25 on a crowded one.
context: Finishing the non-match floor, whose refactor of Stages::floor and Recall is what rotted one of the two.
why: The eight-mutations-no-longer-match incident of 2026-08-23 taught the project to run `--stale`, and the guidance written from it names the trigger correctly and the instrument incompletely. A cheap check that covers part of a failure class, recommended at the moment the whole class is triggered, reads as sufficient — which is why this recurs rather than being noticed once. Recorded so the next refactor runs a pass rather than a second `--stale`.

**Check a set's declared languages against the loaded model, and say where they do not fit.** Deferred 2026-09-14 by the human partner as an advanced feature that may come later, rather than work anyone is about to take up. The approach is decided in `documents/design/memory-data-model.md` under *What consumes it — still proposed, not yet decided*; it is the checking half split out of `charter-declares-set-languages`, whose declaration half is built.

**Missing:** a model-fit report — `hoard_sets status` naming any set whose `hoard-lang-` declaration the loaded model does not cover; the note at the write door, which today can only say the model has no tokens for a text and could say the set declares a language this model lacks; and the coverage test both need, **derived from the model's own vocabulary by script rather than from a table of model names**, so it stays true of a model nobody has met yet. A mismatch reports and never refuses. **To settle while building:** whether a script histogram over a set's memories cross-checks its declaration, weighing the bulk of the text rather than any Latin in it, since identifiers are Latin in every language. **Built looks like:** each of those, with tests for a covered set, an uncovered one, a mixed declaration, and a model the table-free test has never seen.

The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `model-covers-declared-languages`; this record carries only its standing.

The declaration already does the job that matters most day to day — a session writes and searches in the declared language — and a user who needs a language the default model lacks can load the multilingual model today. What this adds is detecting the mismatch automatically, which is worth building when a user with sets in several languages exists to need it.

content:
**A floor trims about a fifth of the memories returned to the queries it does not silence, and removes the top-ranked memory in roughly one query in fifteen.** Measured 2026-09-11 by `probe_what_a_floor_costs_the_queries_it_does_not_silence`, applying each store's calibrated raw floor to the shipping ranking before the gap cut, then re-cutting what survived.

| | `scatterhoard` (floor 0.301) | `coding-lessons` (floor 0.307) |
|---|---|---|
| memories per query, without → with | 3.74 → 3.04 | 3.68 → 2.90 |
| queries whose returned set changed | 37 of 85 | 32 of 63 |
| memories dropped in total | 89 | 71 |
| **top-ranked hit below the floor** | **6 of 85** | **3 of 63** |
| queries left with nothing | 0 | 0 |

**The top-hit case is by design and is the part to decide at build time:** ranking is content *plus* inherited score while the floor reads content alone, so a memory the walk carried to first place can sit below the floor — which is `Stages::floor`'s own stated reasoning, that inherited score must not carry a memory past a relevance floor. Whether a walk-reached memory whose *origin* cleared the floor should be kept is untested either way.
context: Closing out the floor proposal at the human partner's request: one more measurement, then file it as backlog.
why:
The last thing unexplored before the proposal could become a backlog item: every earlier measurement asked only whether a query was silenced, and a query can survive while losing the memories under its top hit — the failure the bias toward over-recalling is about.

What it does not measure is whether any dropped memory was wanted. These queries carry no relevance labels, so a fifth fewer results is a movement rather than a cost. The labelled seed-quality fixture is the only thing here with relevance judgements, and it is a 45-memory corpus whose floor would not transfer.

content: **The human partner's framing, 2026-09-07, and it sets what a fix has to achieve rather than what it has to be: the links are what will eventually make this more useful than a simple database, and they should grow over time, even if only opportunistically.** That rules out one shape and admits two. It rules out treating linking as a one-time authoring duty discharged at store time, since a relation discovered on the tenth reading is exactly the kind that matters and has no store to attach to. It admits an **opportunistic** trigger — some recurring moment where a session already has two memories in hand and is asked whether they relate — and a **deliberate pass**, sweeping the corpus for candidates. Both can exist; they answer different halves. Growth over time is the criterion any candidate fix is measured against, not a link count on the day it ships.
context: Filed while migrating BACKLOG.md, from the human partner's answer about why links matter.
why:
Recorded because *opportunistically* is the load-bearing word and the easy thing to lose. A convention clause saying *link a new memory to what it relates to* would look like the fix, would sit at store time, and would inherit the exact failure this entry names — the author who does not yet know two things are related cannot be told to link them.

The 2026-09-07 measurement supports the framing from the other side: keyword co-membership already grows opportunistically, because keywords are required on every store, and it produced 52 cross-cluster memberships in a day against 3 links. The mechanism that works is the one attached to something already happening.

**Still missing:** the model-fit report naming sets whose declared languages the loaded model does not cover; the write-door note that could name the declared language; and the coverage test both need, derived from the model's own vocabulary by script rather than from a table of model names. **To settle while building those:** whether a script histogram over the memories cross-checks the declaration. The `hoard-lang-` family also has to join the list of known control marks once `reserved-keyword-block-list` builds one. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `charter-declares-set-languages`; this record carries only its standing.

content: The watch trigger's final shape, 2026-09-06: *at the start of a session, and whenever a writable set is loaded, recall `hoard-signpost`, `hoard-collect` and `hoard-investigation` as summaries, one keyword and one set per call.* One keyword per call because a summary hit is an id and a line, so a mixed list cannot say which of the three actions each entry wants -- the call is what carries that. One set per call for the per-set allowance and revocability, and to keep each response small enough to stay inline rather than spilling to a file. `writable` rather than `adopted` because read-only evaluation stores will not pull a watch list unless asked, so the clause turns mechanical when that question resolves without being reworded.
context: Finishing the watch rewrite after the human partner described what the session-start pull was always meant to do, including the case of loading a dependency's set before working on its sources.
why: Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claim is unchanged. Three calls per set at session start looks like something a later session would try to collapse into one, and collapsing it silently loses the action mapping -- the same defect as the marker fix, met a second time in one day: the projection drops the field a rule was going to read. The `writable` wording is the other thing that looks arbitrary and is not; it is written against a distinction that does not exist yet, deliberately, so that resolving the evaluation-store question changes behaviour rather than text.

content: Fixed 2026-08-26 by the third of three candidates, chosen by the human partner: identity in the recall path is a `Located` — the memory's id and which of the searched stores it is in — and everything keyed on `MemoryId` alone is keyed on that: `Neighbourhood`'s population and validity, `Adjacency` and `traversal::reachable` (now generic in the key, defaulting to `MemoryId` so single-store callers read as before), and `recall_across`'s scan, seeds and candidates. Returning both memories falls out of it rather than being arranged separately, and so do the concession and the cycle, because another store's ruling can no longer land in our memory's slot. **It is less of a change to the model than it looks, which is what argued for it**: a duplicate id within one file is already refused when the file is read, `hoard_lookup` already collects a hit from every store, keyword search already returns both, and a link is either same-set or carries the name of the set it points into — **semantic recall was the only place assuming an id names one memory everywhere**, so this makes it agree with the rest rather than adding a fourth rule. Two side effects: walkable edges now carry the set their target names, because an id alone cannot locate the far end once two sets may share one; and `Candidate` lost its `home` field, since the identity names its store.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the argument that chose it: the invariant being broken was already absent everywhere else, so partitioning identity by set removed an exception rather than adding a rule.
