content: A migration was needed and is the part that nearly went wrong: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` cannot add a column to a table that already exists, so an older store would have opened with no `folded` column and **every keyword search would have matched nothing** — healthy-looking and silently wrong. `Store::add_folded_keywords` adds the column and backfills it by copying `keyword`, which is exactly correct here because every keyword in an older store went through the old folding constructor, so its stored spelling already *is* its folded form. Migrating rather than following the documented drop-and-reimport, because the local store is the only copy of local memories and neither backup nor restore existed yet — the disposability argument in [store.rs](src/store.rs) holds for shared stores and not for that one. **The test written against the previous schema immediately earned itself**, catching a defect the rest of the suite could not see: the schema batch created the index on `folded` *before* the migration ran, so opening any older store failed outright rather than merely searching wrongly. The index now belongs to the migration. That test builds the old schema directly with `rusqlite` — a migration can only be tested against a database this code did not write, which is why `rusqlite` is also a dev-dependency.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The migration hazard and the test shape that caught it. A migration can only be tested against a database the code under test did not write; a fixture built by the current schema builder is the current schema by construction and can never be the old one.

content: **Four more literals carry source indentation, found 2026-09-28, so this is a class of five, not one note.** All are in `src/mcp.rs`: the unrecorded-target note in `import_set` (*this set has agreed with {} before; you named a location it has no record of*), the unreadable-header refusal in `memory_files_in` (*is in the reserved … directory, but its header cannot be read*), the two-candidates refusal in `locate_in` (*all answer to the set*), and the cross-set authority refusal (*a `{}` link cannot point into another set*). content: **Observation, and it runs the opposite way to the migration's usual finding: here the memory was written and the tracking file went stale.** The 2026-08-21 link-label measurement was stored as a memory the day it was taken and reached no tracking file, so BACKLOG.md went on saying *Ready, fully reasoned* for three days over a premise the measurement had inverted — and the source comment block it points at still reads as settled. Nothing was going to report the disagreement. This is the case `correct-when` was amended for on 2026-08-24: **an invalidation produces no write, so it goes around the machinery that would otherwise check it.** Storing something new passes the recall-before-storing gate; changing the thing a memory or a file describes does not.
context: Migrating the link-label-choice entry out of BACKLOG.md, in the session that set up the charter investigation.
why:
Filed against the charter investigation as **counter-evidence**, deliberately. The pattern the BACKLOG migration keeps finding is outcomes in memories and evidence stranded in the file; this is the same drift with the stores swapped, which means the phenomenon is probably not *the charter gloss suppresses method* but the more general *two stores describing one thing drift, and nothing reports it*. That reading would predict staleness in both directions, which is what these two observations together now show.

Worth keeping the asymmetry in view when the classification is finally taken: a memory that exists but is contradicted by a file is invisible to a count of what each store holds.

content: Measured over Scatterhoard's two live shared sets (136 memories, 2026-08-03 to 2026-08-28): corrections are common but amendment is almost absent. 16 supersessions, 10 tombstones, 2 amendments. Supersession spans the whole reconciliation window — gaps from 14 seconds to 12.4 days, with 6 of 16 at a day or more — while both amendments happened 18 and 144 seconds after creation. All four confidence changes in the corpus rode supersession edges, every one +0.05, upward, and bundled with substantially rewritten content; not one confidence change happened by amendment or with content held constant. Of 99 links, none points forward in time, so no link was ever added to a memory after it was written.
context: Measured 2026-08-29 from the two exported memory files (scatterhoard_mem/memories.json in this repository and in coding-lessons), at the human partner's question of whether supersession was acting as the confidence changer. Method: amendments counted as modified not equal to created, supersessions as SUPERSEDES edges with confidence and content compared across each, link age from the order-preserving ids. Re-measure after any multi-party merge, which is the condition none of this has been under.
why: It bears on three open questions at once. Amendment is the only operation lacking ancestry, and the machinery proposed to give it some — a per-record checksum history — would serve an operation that has never once occurred outside a two-minute window, which closes long before any export; so those changes reach the file already settled and are never concurrent with anything. It also prices the objection blocking supersede-throughout: a supersession that copies content verbatim to change one confidence value has never occurred, and abolishing amendment would add two records to 136. Read the amendment figure as a floor on need rather than a measure of it — no convention triggers a later recalibration, so the corpus has never been asked whether it is still calibrated, and one author writing their own memories rarely needs to repair their own apparatus.

content: Unknown link labels carried opaquely through import, storage, export and supersession. Decided 2026-09-25 under `unrecognised-link-labels-on-import`. `LinkLabel` in `src/memory/link.rs` gains a variant holding the unrecognised spelling, which is parsed from a file, never from a tool call. The store keeps it in the existing `label TEXT` column. Export writes it back unchanged, so checksums agree. `is_traversable` excludes it. Recall and lookup show it as written. The write path refuses an unknown label unless the same label-and-target pair is on the memory being superseded. Built when a file carrying an unknown label round-trips byte-identically, is not walked, and can be kept across a supersession, each pinned by a test and a mutation. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Resolving `unrecognised-link-labels-on-import` with the human partner, on the release gate.
why: Head of a backlog cluster. Release-gated, because an older build's strictness is fixed the day it ships: the tolerance has to be in the first published build, or that build refuses every label added later. The variant is to be spelled so that nothing matching on known labels can reach it by accident, since the disputing-label and traversal checks match on specific variants.

content: Reduced from Corrupts to Costs on 2026-08-20 after tracing what the missing record would be used for, because most of it is held elsewhere. **The ordinary flow is git's**: where the import target and the export target are one checkout, `git log -S<id>` over that repository's `memories.json` names the commit that introduced a memory and the merge that carried it in, so recording arrival in the store as well would be a fact written down twice — the first common cause in this file. **A `local` set has no repository to be poisoned from**, so the gap there is backup hygiene rather than contamination. **Attribution to a *person* was never available and is not what this asks for**: nothing in the file is authenticated, the reconciliation checksum is computed at import rather than carried and is deliberately not cryptographic, and anyone who can forge `created_by` can forge `content` in the same edit — so field-level trust distinctions inside the file have no mechanism behind them. **What survives is one store serving two different repositories**: import from A, export to B, and neither repository's history holds the join, so in B the memories read as the local user's own additions. That is effort rather than corruption.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A severity reduction argued by asking what the missing record would be used for and finding three of four uses already answered. The surviving case is narrow and specific, which is what makes the remaining fix worth scoping rather than building in general.

content: **Same-set links stay relative, and a cross-set link is decided by set identity where both sides have one.** Decided 2026-09-14 by the human partner, while choosing a fix for `a-link-naming-its-own-set-by-an-old-name-is-inert`. A same-set link remains a bare memory id. When a link is stored, it is same-set if its `set_id` equals the holding set's identity and cross-set if the two identities differ, whatever names either carries; the name decides only where one side has no identity. **Collapsing every link to `[set_id, memory_id]` was proposed by the human partner and declined by them**, after weighing it: every operation that moves memories between sets — absorbing, adopting another set's memories — would have to know the source set's identity to tell a link that was internal there from one that was not, and that requirement could be fatal. Relative same-set links need no such knowledge, and survive a set taking a new identity.
context: Discussing how to fix supersession failing for a link that names its own set by an old name, found while re-anchoring ambiguous mutations. Same stretch: the scan subcommand, the export refusal, the reserved-keyword block-list.
why:
**What collapsing would have bought, and why it lost anyway.** One spelling of a link, so no canonicalisation and no class of defect where the write disagrees with the lookups — both `a-same-set-link-spelled-with-its-set-name-is-inert` and today's defect are that. The human partner corrected one objection I raised: a set's identity is a property of the set, not of a machine's view of it, so knowing an id is enough to link into a set never held, and what is lost is only linking into a set known vaguely — which names and keywords serve better than memory ids. What stood was the moving-memories problem above, plus `local` becoming addressable through its per-machine identity, which would need an explicit rule.

**Why identity decides at the write.** Set identity is minted at `create` and never changed, where a name can be renamed or shared, and the lookups (`holder_of`, `edges_into_another_set`) already prefer identity. The write was the one place still deciding by name.

**Why no migration.** Queried read-only on 2026-09-14, all four stores on this machine — the only machine running Scatterhoard — held no cross-set row carrying its own set's identity and none naming its own current name, and every set holding records has an identity by construction: `create` mints before any write, `local` claims on its first write, import adopts before reconciling, and adoption displaces an identity only on a set with no records.

**Also changes one behaviour on purpose.** A link naming this set's current name but carrying another set's identity was canonicalised to same-set by name; under this rule it stays cross-set, consistent with a set that only shares a name not being the set a link means.

content: **The memory file on disk is the export review's clearance record, because export never writes an unreviewed memory into it.** Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. Review comes before export and compares the store with the file on disk. Decisions are stored by record checksum, so a later change is reviewed again. Export writes only what the file holds or what has been cleared, and refuses on new memories that have not been. How a later review turn runs is still to be designed.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public, after deciding the review must not depend on git.
why: It replaces the committed-file rule under the constraint that the review must not need `git`. Memories arriving through a pull or a synced copy are already in a file, so they count as reviewed upstream, as they did under `git`. The rejected options were a ledger beside an unchanged export, which re-reviews merged-in memories and enforces nothing, and using `git` where present, which gives two review sets. A refusal at the moment of acting is what held up on `gemma4:12b`, where served text alone did not.

content: `keywords` was the one published property with no description, on the field a whole convention governs. Fixed 2026-08-21 by pointing at `keyword-standards` rather than restating it. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `keywords-is-the-one-field-with-no-published-description`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **Measured 2026-09-08: swapping the static model for `potion-retrieval-32M` removes the score inversion that the whole non-match investigation was chasing, and it is already cached on this machine.** Re-embedding all 867 memories and scoring as recall does, top-1 under the shipping `potion-base-32M`: link-traversal 0.458, `Cycle` 0.370, routing 0.304 — against **gibberish 0.358 and the off-domain football query 0.420, whose top three are all `governance-docs`**. Under `potion-retrieval-32M` the same queries give 0.532, 0.340, 0.389 — against **gibberish 0.229 and football 0.328, with only one `governance-docs` memory left in the top three**. So in-domain scores rise, off-domain and nonsense fall, and **the inversion is gone**: every in-domain query now outscores every nonsense one, which was false under the shipping model. `potion-base-8M` is worse than either, at football 0.442 and gibberish 0.361. On the labelled 45-memory fixture the retrieval model is roughly a wash — better at r@3 (63.3% against 57.5%) and r@10 (85.8% against 83.3%), worse at r@5 (72.5% against 77.5%) — and notably CSLS *helps* it where it hurt the base model, lifting r@5 to 75.0%. Re-run `probe_the_failures_under_whichever_model_is_configured` with `SCATTERHOARD_MODEL` pointed at each.
context: Answering whether a contextual embedder is available, which turned up a cached retrieval-tuned static model first.
why: Kept with its caveat attached: six queries, so this is the strength of the earlier charter pilot that then collapsed, and the same discipline applies before it is believed. What makes it worth acting on anyway is that it costs nothing to test properly — the model is on disk, loads through `model2vec-rs` unchanged, and needs no new dependency, unlike the contextual option it was reached for instead of.

content: Found 2026-08-04 exercising [SETUP.md](SETUP.md) §5, when a recall returned a field no description mentions. MCP has carried `outputSchema` since its 2025-06-18 revision and none of the four tools publishes one. That would be a documentation gap and little more if the shape were uniform — **it is not, and the fields that vary are exactly the ones a client branches on**. `similarity` appears on a direct semantic hit; `matched_similarity` beside `replaces_matched` on a substituted one, and the two never co-occur, deliberately and correctly, since that split is the fix recorded under `similarity-describes-a-different-memory`. But it means `similarity` is *absent* on precisely the entries where a superseded memory was swapped for its replacement, and nothing published warns a client that reads, sorts, or thresholds on it. `matched_keywords` appears on the keyword path only; `links`, `superseded_by`, `context` and `keywords` appear only when non-empty.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery, and the reason it is Misleads rather than a documentation gap: the varying fields are the ones a client sorts and thresholds on, and the rarest variant is the one a client is least likely to meet before shipping.

content: Found 2026-08-08, and reachable by the **expected installation sequence**, which is what raised it above a missing convenience. [embeddings.md](documents/design/embeddings.md) ships a setup HOWTO aimed at the LLM precisely because acquiring the model is a delegated, later step — so: install Scatterhoard, find the model is not there yet, work for a week, then run setup, and that week of memories is unfindable by meaning for good. The design anticipated the ordering and nothing implemented the consequence. **There was no way out of it from the tool surface**: `hoard_sets` offered `status`, `create`, `export` and `import` — no `drop`, no `restore`, no re-embed — and the drop-and-re-import that [store.rs](src/store.rs) offers as the project-store escape hatch could not be reached from a client at all, while for the local store, *"the only copy of local memories"*, it would mean deleting the only copy to rebuild a cache.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A defect produced by following the documented setup order, with no recovery reachable from the interface. Worth keeping because the design had anticipated the ordering — the gap was between an anticipated sequence and an unbuilt consequence, not an unforeseen case.

content: Creating a read-only set returned the note for a writable one, telling the caller to `mint` before anything is written and to write a charter. Fixed 2026-10-05. `Server::create_set` in `src/mcp.rs` now chooses the note by mode: a read-only set is told to import its publisher's file under its scope, and the note mentions neither `mint` nor a charter. Read-write keeps the old note. Pinned by `create_tells_a_read_only_set_to_import_rather_than_mint_or_write_a_charter` and, for the writable side, by `create_says_the_first_memory_is_the_charter`, which now also asks for `"mint"`. Guarded by the mutation "create: give a read-only set the writable set's note". The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-read-only-set-is-told-to-mint`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Fixing the one open issue on the morning after tagging the first beta, as the checkpoint's next step; the first fix made under the per-change recall habit now in AGENTS.md.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed as its fixed-when asked: a read-only create says to import and mentions neither mint nor a charter, with a test for each mode. The mutation forces the writable note in every mode, which is the original defect. Moving the note into a `match` left "create: say nothing about the charter" stale; it was re-anchored on `"note": note,` and still catches. The new wording was not tried on a small local model.

content: **The safety is thinner than it looks**: `EXCEPTION_TO` and `CONTRADICTS` are harmless to standing because nothing implements them yet, not because a guard refuses them. Whenever traversal is taught to act on them, the cross-set case needs the answer `SUPERSEDES` already has, and it will need it in `resolve_supersession` rather than in `Store::edges`.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A clean sweep result that is clean by absence rather than by guard. Recorded so that implementing either label is known in advance to re-open the arm, and in a different place from where this defect was fixed.

content: Write the collaboration rules when there is someone to collaborate with. **Ready since 2026-10-04**: its named trigger, a remote origin, arrived with the beta release, and beta testers are the first people who may contribute. Decided 2026-08-29 by the human partner: **feature branches were not wanted** while there was no shared default branch to protect, and every session committed straight to `main`. Whether that changes now that `origin/main` is shared is the first question for this entry. Built when `CONTRIBUTING.md` covers branching, the export gate, and memory-set routing for a contributor. **A contribution here carries memories as well as code**, so the guide has to cover the export gate, which set a contributor's memories belong in, and what a maintainer reviews; the material is largely in `export-review.md` and the set-lifecycle fork case. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `contributing-and-branching-docs`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Adding the first git remotes for the beta release, after rewriting the author address out of both histories.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because its trigger, a remote origin, was met on 2026-10-04. It had been deferred deliberately so a guide would not go stale before anyone read it. That reason ends when there are readers, which beta testers are.

content: **No trusted-name binding for a checkout.** Decided by the human partner on 2026-09-25, settling the first half of `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout`. The trust-on-first-use binding the question proposed is dropped. The user's trust act is cloning the repository and naming the `scope` on each call. `check_scope` already makes the header agree with what the caller named. A legitimate rename is the same `set_id` under a new name. A binding would only earn its keep if auto-discovery, loading a checkout's sets without being told which, were ever built, and it is not. What remains of the question is what an identity mismatch at import does: refuse, or report as it does today.
context: Working through the release-gated questions: straight after resolving `one-repository-many-sets`, taking up `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout`.
why: The binding answered which name a checkout's file may claim, as though Scatterhoard had to establish that the set was legitimate, and it does not: the checkout's provenance does (`01M3BENR8F…`). What it proposed to protect was the name, while the real harm, two sets colliding, is keyed on `set_id`. Recorded as a decision rather than left to the resolution, because the question stays open on its second half and a later reader should not rebuild the binding in the meantime. It changes the premise of `imported-set-trust-boundary`, whose personal-set exemption was said to need this binding first; that ordering is to be re-read when that question is taken up, not assumed.

content: **Three requirements for `gut-feeling-recall` that stand from 2026-09-29, the fourth, valence, revised separately.** First, breadth: aggregate a few dozen plausible matches at a low threshold, so it needs the right words to be nearby rather than the right memory to rank first. Second, contrast: prefer phrases over-represented in the neighbourhood relative to the whole set, as the set summary does for keywords, and discount the corpus's own writing register. Third, silence: say nothing unless the reading departs well from the set's baseline, because a signal that always fires is ignored. Testable by replaying the before-writing sentences the coding-lessons guide records for each failure, and the same for changes that went fine.
context: Discussing the first replay of `gut-feeling-recall` with the human partner.
why: The part of the original four-requirements memory still true after the first replay, split out when its valence requirement was revised to two-sided, following split-when-partly-stale. Contrast gained the register clause because the replay's top phrases were the project's memory-writing boilerplate. Silence is argued from this project's own evidence, `the-mutation-runners-crowding-note-fires-on-every-pass` and the reasoning behind the always-present `summary` echo.

content: **Measured 2026-09-08 and the first thing that separates a non-match: how far the *query* sits from the corpus centroid — a quantity cosine throws away before anyone sees it.** `cos(query, centroid)` over twelve probes ranks them: on-topic specific 0.429, 0.358, 0.355; on-topic broad 0.311, 0.208, 0.111; off-corpus 0.183, 0.079, 0.002; gibberish 0.137, 0.050, 0.018. **A boundary near 0.19 puts five of six on-topic queries above it and five of six others below**, where the top similarity score separated none of them at all. Two errors, both instructive: the single-word query *measurement* falls to 0.111, because one generic word genuinely is not corpus-shaped even when it is on-topic; and the football query reaches 0.183, because governance vocabulary really does share this corpus's register. **This escapes the earlier exhaustion argument by not being a statistic over the similarities** — it compares the query to the corpus as a whole, before any memory is scored. **Two cautions.** The centroid is taken over the union of *loaded* sets, so the same query scores differently depending on which sets a session has open. And this measures *is this query in the corpus's domain*, which is not the same question as *can the corpus answer it*. Twelve queries is a pilot, not a result.
context: Investigating the football query, when the human partner asked whether the model itself might be at fault.
why:
Recorded because every previous candidate on this entry was computed from the similarity scores, and this one is not — which is precisely why it survived where an absolute floor, a ratio to the top hit, a gap-to-median, a per-query z-score and result-set coherence all failed. It is also a natural consequence of the failure mode found the same day: cosine normalises away magnitude, and magnitude is what carries *how much of this query is not simply the corpus average*, so the signal was being discarded by construction rather than being absent.

The cautions are recorded with it because both are ways this would look better in a pilot than in use: a set-dependent number is one a session cannot compare against a fixed threshold, and the two misclassifications are not noise but the two directions the measure is genuinely wrong in.

content: Nothing shows a session the person's sharing preferences until export, so material they want kept out is stored first and cleaned up later. Decided 2026-10-18 with the human partner: the server serves the person's preferences file alongside the conventions at session start, and the export review stays. Built when `hoard_conventions` returns the file's contents beside the catalog, outside the catalog's character budget, wherever the file lives. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `sharing-preferences-served-at-session-start`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Starting the decisions from the publication read-through: a fresh public history, the hypothetical recorded as fact, and the human partner's proposal to serve the sharing preferences at session start.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, filed the day the decision was made. Ready: the file's location, left open on 2026-10-17, is a choice made while building, and the open point about exceptions at writing time does not block serving the file. It is separate from `export-review-judgement-gate` because it can be built and proved on its own. Whichever of the two is built first fixes the location.

content: **Every set now claims its identity on its first write, and a shared set with no identity is no longer refused.** Built 2026-09-28 as step 1 of `set-settled-at-first-write`, reversing the 2026-09-14 refusal as the 2026-09-24 decision intended. `Store::mint_set_id` in `src/store.rs` is called by `Store::write` and `Store::replace_with`; `refuse_records_without_identity` and `StoreError::SharedSetHasNoIdentity` are gone. `create` mints nothing. `import_set` in `src/mcp.rs` mints before reconciling only when the file holds records. `export_set` proposes an identity for a set with none, writes it in the header, and persists it only after every refusal has passed. It refuses a set with no identity writing over a file that declares one, and tells it to import. `adopt_set_id` fills an absence only: its empty-set displacement is retired. The invariant the refusal protected still holds: a set holding records has an identity.
context: Building set-settled-at-first-write step 1, after recalibrating the scatterhoard floor (unchanged at 0.360). Also filed concurrent-first-writes-can-mint-two-identities.
why: Supersedes the 2026-09-14 memory because its claim, that the store refuses, is now false and would read as current. **Why export mints**: with `create` no longer minting, an empty set exported and taken on elsewhere carried no identity, so each side minted its own on first write and their next exchange was refused as a mismatch (found by `tests/set_description.rs`). An export is the first moment a second copy can exist, so it is the last moment a mint forks nothing. **Why proposed rather than minted**: a refused export that had already minted would turn the import its refusal advises into a mismatch. **Why an empty import settles nothing**: it is not a write, and settling there would fix the set under an identity nobody else holds before its own file arrives. Export minting and the empty-import rule are this build's derivations from the decision, not part of it.

content: **The human partner's reading, 2026-09-24: automatic calibration will need a backup mode for sets that do not accumulate labels.** Said on seeing that `governance-docs` and `local` were still uncalibrated twelve days after the floor shipped, and that the same will hold for any low-use set. Not yet a decision on the backup's shape — whether it is the explicit pass this question proposes, or something else — and the accumulating design stays the primary mode for sets with traffic.
context: Checking whether the morning's calibration closed the unanswerable-query issue, and finding two sets without enough labels ever to calibrate.
why: Recorded as the human partner's direction because it moves the question from *whether to keep the explicit pass in reserve* toward *what the fallback for untrafficked sets is*. Worded as a reading rather than a resolution: they said it looks like one is needed, and nothing about its form was settled.

content: The recorded mutation `store: change the scope prefix in its one place` survives the suite, because nothing outside the store module compares against a literal scope prefix. Once `scope_key` and `scope_from_key` share one constant, the drift between writer and reader is no longer expressible, so changing the constant breaks nothing.
context: Recorded 2026-08-04 during the Scope::Project to Scope::Shared rename.
why: A surviving mutation needs a written reason, and this one is a deliberate consequence of the fix rather than a gap: the mutation that must stay caught is the one that re-splits the constant into two literals.

content: Try to reach one id holding two memory contents. Run 2026-08-30, and **the premise was false as the code stood**. The route is `absorb`, exactly where the proposal predicted — `absorbing_on_one_import_and_not_another_puts_two_contents_under_one_id` drives it **entirely through the published surface**: one machine authors a memory with a cross-set link and exports, two holders adopt the same bytes with one passing `absorbing` and one not, their stored content for that id differs, and reconciling them is a **`Conflict` on a memory record** with no amendment anywhere. **The finding answers the proposal rather than blocking it**: the premise holds for every other write path — `every_other_write_path_lands_the_authors_bytes` drives adoption, restore and re-import — so absorption is not *a* leak, it is **the** leak, and `absorb-as-supersession` closes the only one there is. A second symptom of the same cause turned up while looking for a second route and is worse: `restore-silently-reverts-an-absorption`. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `falsify-record-immutability`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Test and documentation debt section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only. The measurement that `memory_file::absorb` is the only such route is recorded separately and not restated.

It gated something much larger than itself: *the graph is the ancestor* rests on the premise that a conflict on a memory record is unreachable through sanctioned operations, so if the premise holds the per-record merge is a lattice join and the per-target base is not a correctness mechanism — and if it fails, the proposal fails at its first step.

Scope worth keeping: **a hand-edited file reaching this state is expected and is not a counterexample.** The premise is about sanctioned operations, and this project's line is failure-resistant rather than tamper-proof.

content: The hold on catalog edits was lifted for one pass on 2026-08-25: every entry but `recall-when` was restructured, sentence architecture only, with wording and arguments held fixed. The human partner's reason was that the behavioural measurement now running is worth more against the wording that will be kept than against wording about to be replaced, so the confound is accepted once rather than measuring, rewriting and measuring again. The whole-file read the hold was waiting on is done: the catalog is not carrying avoidable length. Budget now 16,978 of 18,000 as the enforced test counts it, 1,022 free, with three Ready conventions competing for room at most one of them can use.
context: Decided 2026-08-25 by the human partner. Checkable in the dated comment above CONVENTIONS in src/conventions/catalog.rs, which records what the pass changed and what it deliberately left.
why: Supersedes the version that recorded the hold and the pending read, both of which this change resolves. Recording the reason matters more than the permission: the standing rule against re-tuning is about acting on one session's impressions of text it just wrote, and this is the second sanctioned exception to it in two days, each granted for a stated reason. Left unrecorded, two exceptions in two days read as the hold having quietly lapsed.

content: **`export` cannot be run from the command line, so a set cannot be backed up on a schedule.** Decided 2026-09-14 by the human partner, while agreeing to take `prohibited-scan-subcommand`: the binary should take `export` as a subcommand beside the scan, to allow automated backups. Filed as its own entry because the two finish at different times for different reasons — the scan reads a file and needs no model or author, where export writes store state and needs both. **Missing:** the subcommand itself. The argument handling it goes through exists, since the same day, in `src/cli.rs`, built for `scan` and shaped for this to follow. **Built looks like:** `scatterhoard export` taking a scope and a destination, through the same `Server::export_set` path rather than a second export; the bare invocation still serving MCP; a non-zero exit when the export is refused. **To settle while building:** how a refused scheduled backup gets noticed, since export refuses a write that would drop records and a scheduled job fails silently unless its exit status is watched; whether it loads the embedding model, which export uses to describe the set; and that it records reconciliation bases for the backup path and marks the set's description shown, writing to a store the MCP servers may hold open. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `export-subcommand`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Choosing the next backlog item after building the export refusal. The human partner asked whether command-line export belonged alongside the prohibited-data scan subcommand.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness. Ready: it was filed blocked on `prohibited-scan-subcommand`, which introduced the binary's argument handling and with it the hazard that a wrong default breaks every attached client at once, and that entry was built the same day. Amended rather than superseded because this head had never been exported.

A scheduled refusal is worth naming now because it is the first consequence of the export refusal built the same day that nobody sees at the moment it happens: in a session the refusal message reaches the caller, and in a scheduled job it reaches whatever watches the exit status, which by default is nothing.

content: The export review's pre-pass reads an SSH remote's `git@host` as an email address. `git@github.com:jtcours/scatterhoard.git` matched as the email `git@github.com`, though `git` is the hosting service's shared user, not anyone's address. Found 2026-10-29 on the `scatterhoard` set's full review, flagging `01M1YY7WB0E8HAQX4SJ4VS5RBY` for nothing else. Rarer than the timestamp false positive fixed the same day, so filed rather than fixed mid-review. Fixed means an address whose local part is `git` and which is followed by `:` and a path is not an email, with a test that `git@` in ordinary prose still is.

content:
**Two of the Golden Rule's four demands are directly engaged by the threat report, and they point opposite ways.** An analysis made 2026-09-12 while filing `golden-rule-beyond-person-harm` — not a finding from the report, which never mentions Scatterhoard or this principle.

**Demand C already has the right shape and the wrong subject.** C says the person is a detail of the record and never its organising principle, on the stated ground that *aggregation harm is emergent — a property of the set, not of any record in it*. The Russian procurement case is that structure exactly, with a different subject: every request mundane on its own, the harm visible only in the assembly. So [golden-rule.md](documents/design/golden-rule.md) already carries machinery for aggregation harm and merely scopes it to dossiers about people. **Widening C's subject is the cheapest candidate route into this question**: it needs no new moral clause, and it is the shape most likely to survive the reading objection, because it stays a demand about what a set amounts to rather than an instruction to be good.

**Demand D(ii) and dual-use detection point in opposite directions, and this is the real tension.** D(ii) asks a session to read what it does not know in the person's favour, scoped tightly to the inference from evidence to motive. The report describes sophisticated actors relying on precisely that reading — using the dual-use nature of biology to maintain *plausible deniability* — and goes further, noting that the researchers may themselves not know their programme's aims, with the Soviet Biopreparat compartmentalisation as the historical analogue. So the inference D(ii) governs is exactly the inference at issue, and D(ii) currently resolves it in the direction a sophisticated actor is engineering for. **That is not an argument that D(ii) is wrong.** It is an argument that its scope was drawn against a case where the unknown was a colleague's motive, and it has never been tested against a case where the unknown is manufactured.

**A worked example of both holding at once sits in the report itself.** It withholds institutions, countries and agents, says outright that it does not assert the researchers intended harm, and notes that identifying them could expose them to harm — while still publishing the aggregate finding. Charity about the people, exactness about the pattern: the Golden Rule's own boundary, observed by someone doing the detection work. Evidence that the two are not in conflict where the boundary draws them, even though D(ii) and dual-use inference conflict at the level of the single judgement.
context: The morning the question was filed, immediately after reading the conventional-weapons and biological sections of the report.
why:
Recorded because it is the part a later session most needs and the part it would not get from re-reading the report: the report says nothing about the Golden Rule, and the connection to demands C and D(ii) is mine.

Kept separate from the evidence member so the two can be judged apart — the evidence is checkable against a document, and this is an argument that may not survive contact with the human partner. At 0.7 because it is inference from a reading that fits without compelling it; the D(ii) tension in particular is the kind of claim that looks obvious once written and may be dissolved by a distinction I have not seen.

content: **Two observations from this item, both about what tracking and probing actually catch.** First, **it was tracked nowhere** — not in BACKLOG.md, not in open-questions — despite being referenced by two closed defects and a comment in `tests/concurrency.rs`. The sweep that built this file missed it, and the reason generalises: **grepping for work described as *absent* does not find work described as *proposed*.** Second, **this item's yield was mostly in what it forced someone to look at.** Three defects were found while probing it and **none was caused by it** — `store-is-not-configured-for-two-processes` and `vector-cache-goes-stale-across-processes`, filed while checking whether a shared local store was safe, and `author-is-a-property-of-the-process-not-the-store`, filed while deciding attribution ahead of it. Each was reachable before the variable existed, because two checkouts already share one home. Building it added a fourth of a different kind — `moving-the-local-store-leaves-the-old-one-unmentioned`, **found by trying the misconfiguration rather than by reading the code**, since repointing the variable is indistinguishable from having no memories.
context: Migrating the scatterhoard-local entry out of BACKLOG.md; these are the observations it recorded about its own tracking and yield.
why:
The absent-versus-proposed distinction is the transferable half and it is cheap to act on: a sweep looking for gaps should search for the vocabulary of *intent* as well as the vocabulary of *lack*, because a design document that says "proposed" has already described the work in the affirmative.

The yield observation is worth having before deciding what an item is worth. Judged on its own change, this one was a small configuration variable; judged on what it produced, it was four defects, three of which existed already and were invisible until someone had a reason to look at that area. That argues for valuing an item partly by what it forces an inspection of, which is not a property any Fixed-when can express.

content: Fixed 2026-08-03 by deleting the combination rather than deduplicating it: `hoard_recall` takes a query **or** keywords and refuses both, returning one `memories` list. **The route there is worth keeping, because the first three answers were all wrong** — deduplicating the payload; then normalising into an id-keyed map with two ranking lists, rejected on ergonomics, since an LLM reading a response should not have to reassemble it by joining ids; then a single list with `found_by` as a list of findings, which was actually a good shape. What killed all three was the human partner asking whether the combined search should exist at all. **It integrated nothing** — two independent searches stapled together, giving a caller nothing two calls would not, while generating the duplication, the two loose scales, and an ordering question with no honest answer. Removing the mode makes all three unrepresentable.

content: A reported value that does not say what it measures gets read as something else. In this project: a `similarity` describing a different memory from the one shown, a match count against a substituted record, `memories` meaning live count in one response and records written in another, a budget that was a target, a byte count named in characters, a result count set by the window rather than the query, a score with no floor to say what counts as a match, and several flags with two causes and one value — `semantic_search_available`, `prohibited_data_scanned`, `superseded_beyond_this_set`, a model state called a mismatch when absent. **The structural fix is that every value crossing an interface names what it describes and what it is relative to**, or is split until it can.
context: Re-deriving the common causes of defects across all 104 issues, and moving them from a hand-written section of TRACKING.md into memories the index is generated from.
why: The original analysis's cause #3, graduated to `coding-lessons` on 2026-08-03. Re-derived 2026-09-23 over 104 issues; it absorbed the flags that carry two meanings in one value, which the original counted separately if at all — a boolean with two reasons is a number without its referent, one bit wide.

content: **Building `identity-mismatch-refusal` on 2026-09-26 settled four things the design left open.** (1) Import asks after adoption: a set with no records takes the file's identity, so an identity `create` minted is never a mismatch. (2) Export defends only a set holding records, and refuses on identity before its dropped-records refusal, whose advice to import would otherwise be refused too. (3) The collision route says the alias is not built instead of naming a call that does not exist. (4) Two machines' `local` sets are two sets, so crossing between them is refused, and tests that used them as a two-machine fixture now use one shared set on two machines. Checkable in `identity_mismatch`, `Replaced::identity_refusal` and the `defended` binding in `export_set` in `src/mcp.rs`, and in set-lifecycle.md under *what the refusal had to decide that the design did not*.
context: Building the release gate's directory-form group: identity-mismatch refusal, after several memory files per directory shipped, with the reserved directory accepting the local set still to come.
why: History from implementing the entry. (1) was found when the first build refused 27 tests: checking before adoption refused `create` then `import`, the sanctioned way to take on a set. (2) follows the lesson that a refusal's remedy should work where the reader stands. (4) touches the open question of whether `local` is one set across a person's machines: the refusal follows the design as it stands, where `local` never leaves its machine, and that question still has to be settled before any sync between machines is built.

content: **How a set is loaded read-only so its memories can be distributed as a document — the memory equivalent of a PDF.** Raised 2026-09-16 by the human partner. **Designed in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md) and built 2026-09-17.** `create` takes an optional `mode` defaulting to read-write; the mode lives in the set's `meta`; there is no demotion. A read-only set refuses session writes, allows `import` and `restore` as refreshes, drops without a safety copy unless `save_to` is given, and pulls `hoard-signpost` alone, which `hoard_sets status` names per set. A set identity loads once: a read-write copy wins over read-only ones, and otherwise every copy is withheld. The publisher cannot signal read-only-ness in the file, because a header is contents. **Still open:** whether one-way promotion to read-write is offered at all — the design permits it and nothing implements it. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `read-only-distribution`; this record carries only its standing.

Kept open rather than resolved for exactly that: a question closed while its residue is unfiled is how work goes missing here, and promotion is a decision nobody has made rather than one the build settled.

content: **Measured 2026-09-08: CSLS bounds hubness as a corpus grows where centring alone does not — but it is not a free adopt, and the earlier reading that it was is withdrawn.** Holding content fixed and subsampling `scatterhoard` from 30 to 721 memories, the worst hub by k-occurrence at k=10 runs: raw cosine 28, 39, 65, 54, 68, 66; centred 13, 16, 25, 35, 46, 47; **centred + CSLS 14, 15, 18, 23, 22, 23**. **CSLS holds hub concentration roughly flat as the corpus grows twelvefold, where centring alone degrades from 13 to 47.** That half needs no answer key — k-occurrence uses each memory's own vector as the query, so it is a property of the corpus and the scoring rule alone.
context: Running the CSLS re-test and the alignment-boundary trial the human partner asked for, across four set sizes plus the union.
why:
Recorded because the original 2026-07-31 rejection was correct on its evidence and wrong about the regime: `k=10` over 45 memories computes the penalty across a fifth of the corpus, which is a different operation from `k=10` over 721. The entry named re-running at scale as the condition; this is that run, and the answer is more mixed than either the rejection or my first reading of this sweep.

The finding that outlives the recommendation is the shape: hubness under centring *grows with the corpus* and under CSLS does not. A comparison at any single size would have missed it — at 30 memories centring is ahead.

content: **After publication the maintainer keeps committing straight to `main`, and outside contributors send pull requests from forks**, each carrying its exported memory file with its code. Decided 2026-11-02 by the human partner, after asking whether the merge driver is already tested. It is, at the contract level: `tests/merge.rs` covers the merge itself, `tests/cli.rs` pins `merge-file`'s exit statuses, and recorded mutations guard both, with an end-to-end run by hand in a scratch repository on 2026-09-21. context: Going-public checklist, after turning DEVELOPMENT.md into CONTRIBUTING.md; the human partner reported updating the README in the same message.
why: Branches for the maintainer's own work would not have exercised the driver anyway: `git` calls it only when both sides changed the file, and one person's branch merges into a `main` that has not moved without it. So committing to `main` gives up no driver testing, and the review effort goes where the risk is, a stranger's memories. This replaces the 2026-08-29 rule that held only while nobody shared `main`.

content: **The repair in step 2 goes by supersession, route (a), chosen 2026-09-23 by the human partner** over building a link-only write (b) or leaving pre-existing links inherited (c). Measured that day: 126 out-links on 73 superseded memories are not restated by their tips — 97 `related_to`, 12 `results_from`, 6 `depends_on`, 5 `instance_of`, 3 `motivated_by`, 2 `contradicts`, 1 `supports`; 72 on tracking heads, 54 on ordinary memories; 43 aimed at targets themselves superseded. Expected to shrink on examination: `depends_on` on a built entry is a correct drop, and tracking heads were mostly superseded for a change of standing, so their links default to keep. **This meets a reopen condition of `link-only-write-after-export`** — a pass to connect older memories — and it was reconsidered rather than skipped: supersession stays the only route, because the pass is bounded and falls before publication, the cheap window for churn.
context: Filing the out-link backlog entry with the human partner, straight after deciding the repair route.
why: The cost of (a) is known and bounded: a link-only supersession gains no retrieval surface and adds a near-duplicate record of about 4 KB, harmless to correctness. Route (b) needed an additions-only rule, a label whitelist, a modifier decision and catalog text with no room for it; route (c) would make the walk depend on when each supersession happened, a hidden version rule. Recorded under both slugs so the link-only question shows its condition was met and answered, not missed.

content: **Demonstrated 2026-08-15, and the entry later corrected the conclusion it drew from it.** A 56-memory test corpus was imported as `shared:traversal-pilot` to get it embedded for a measurement. Recall without a scope searches every loaded set, so the pilot immediately took **all three top results on an unrelated query** — test material outranking the project's real memories in ordinary use, undoable only by deleting the database by hand and restarting. **The first version of this entry read that as an argument for a non-searchable scope. It is not.** An evaluation corpus is not memory; it is test data shaped like memory, and it has no business in a store at all. The embedder spike had this right and it was mislaid — a standalone binary that loads a corpus file, embeds it with `StaticModel` directly, and computes its metrics without creating a set or touching a store. Importing was a shortcut taken to get vectors for one measurement, and it does not scale: a corpus four hundred memories large would drown ordinary recall.
context: Migrating the set-drop entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the episode that motivated it and the correction the entry made afterwards.
why:
Kept because the wrong conclusion is the attractive one. Contamination looks like a scoping problem, a non-searchable scope looks like the fix, and building it would have added permanent surface area to accommodate something that should never have been in a store — while leaving the real problem, that an accidental import is irreversible from a client, untouched.

The correction also sets the shape for `recall-eval-harness`, which should be built the spike's way and can do better than the spike did: `SCATTERHOARD_MODEL` and this project's own `Embedder` and `embedding_input` are available to it, so it measures the real embedding pipeline rather than a parallel reimplementation free to drift from it.
