content: **Why not a session or run identifier, which was the first proposal and is wrong.** Measured 2026-09-05: ten `scatterhoard` processes were running in three groups, one group per Claude Code session process, each holding one process per configured server, plus two owned by the desktop app. Walking this session's own ancestry put its servers at **38 minutes old inside a conversation nearly 23 hours old** — switching to another session and back respawned the session host and its servers. **So a process does not identify a session**, and an id minted at process startup would have changed mid-conversation with nothing announcing it, making that session's own earlier writes read as somebody else's — a false alarm generated by the instrument meant to remove one. The alternative, issuing an id at the conventions call and requiring it back on every write, is unverifiable by construction, puts bookkeeping where the model makes no decision, and adds a mandatory opaque token to a call surface that produced three malformed emissions in one session. **One comparison beats provenance anyway**: it covers another session's writes, a hand-edit, a `restore` and a branch switch, where a per-session marker would catch only the first — and it asks a question that has an answer, since *what changed* is a fact about two files where *who wrote this* turns out not to be answerable at all.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A provenance mechanism refuted by measuring process lifetimes: the identifier would change mid-conversation and accuse the session of being someone else. The surviving design answers a question about files rather than about authorship, which is the one that has an answer.

content: **Sessions are told to reload the conventions after a compaction**, since 2026-11-02, at the human partner's request after Claude Code began compacting idle sessions. One sentence was added to the bootstrap prompt in `SETUP.md` step 6 and `AGENTS.md`: *load them again whenever the conversation has been summarized or compacted since you last did*. The `hoard_conventions` tool description no longer says "once", and adds *and again after the conversation has been summarized or compacted*. The README's quick start carries the same prompt and is the human partner's to update.
context: Going-public checklist: checking the README's quick start, then asking whether idle compaction can lose the conventions.
why: A compaction summarizes tool results away, so the catalog a session loaded at its start is gone while the session goes on storing and recalling. The steering file survives (Claude Code re-injects a project-root `CLAUDE.md`), so a sentence there reaches the post-compaction agent. The tool description had to change too, because "once" contradicted it.

content: **The non-match floor is built, 2026-09-11 into 2026-09-12**, in four pieces: a local query log, the `used` label that says which of its queries the set could answer, a level each store calibrates from its own log, and a recall that reads that level against **raw** content similarity. Designed in `documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md` under *Proposed 2026-09-11* and the three sections after it; contracts in `tests/query_log.rs` and `tests/floor.rs`. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `calibrated-non-match-floor`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Finishing the floor with the human partner, after they asked how often recalibration would need to run and the answer turned out to be that it could never raise a level at all. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the head was over the length limit: the head keeps the claim and standing, and the detail moved to members under the slug.
why:
Head of the backlog cluster, superseded the same day it was written because the level's rule changed underneath it: the earlier head described a minimum over everything and a floor recall could write, and both are gone. Standing stays built — what changed is how the level is computed, not whether the mechanism exists.

The evidence lives in the resolved question `floor-calibration-source` and in the sweep recorded beside this entry.

content: `traversal::cut_at_largest_gap` is the candidate mechanism for `no-non-match-floor`, and it dissolves the cold-start entanglement rather than solving it: a gap is a difference, so translation moves it not at all, and gaps are compared against each other rather than a constant, so scale moves it not at all either -- it needs no number anyone would have to defend. A one-memory store has no gaps, and the honest answer there is one result. Replayed 2026-09-02 against eleven real recalls, comparing the cut against what was afterwards acted on: 17 results dropped, 5 uses kept, **0 uses lost**. The largest case, fourteen results read and none used, cuts to two.
context: Piloting the index design by converting an issue entry written across five sittings into a cluster.
why: The entry had been stuck for a month on the argument this mechanism answers -- scores are centred cosines, freely negative, so a ratio to the top hit means nothing and an absolute threshold is ruled out by the cold-start problem. Measured rather than argued, which is why the numbers are here: *zero uses lost* is the figure a later session would act on. It is not the whole story, and the caveats recorded beside it are what stop it being read as one.

content: The reserved directory accepted the personal set: `export`, `import` and `restore` in `directory` form took `scope: local` and wrote or read a file declaring `local` in a checkout's `scatterhoard_mem`, though the design says the path settles a file's kind. Fixed 2026-09-26: the `directory` form refuses `local` in every direction and names `file`, which is how `local` is backed up; a `file` inside a reserved directory was already refused for every scope. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-reserved-directory-accepts-the-local-set`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building the release gate's directory-form group: the reserved directory accepting the local set, the last of the three.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseding the open head now that the defect is fixed. Corrupts while it stood: a crafted repository needed one import naming `local` to place memories in the personal set, and an export by directory put personal memories where the next commit publishes them. The premise it falsified, that the File Format guard holds local scope shut (`01M1ZCZAT3…`), holds again with the fix.

content:
Observed 2026-09-19 in the `scatterhoard` set: two records carry the `hoard-author` keyword and exactly one is self-attributed, so `hoard_sets status` reported 948 where the set held 949 non-identity records, and `export` reported `identities: 2` while one of the two is an ordinary memory. The extra record is `01M1WPCTJ4ERGTKHT14X82P25B`, about the `no-non-match-floor` false alarm, which took the reserved term as a subject keyword; its replacement `01M1WPE5YEFDSTGEEQ0231QD2W` carries `about-hoard-author`, so what remains is that one superseded record and any future slip.

The two queries are exact complements over the same subquery — `Store::count` with `NOT IN`, `Store::identity_count` with `IN`, both on `SELECT memory_id FROM keywords WHERE folded = 'hoard-author'`. `Memory::is_identity_record` is `self.created.by == self.id`, and is what `Store::embed`'s two filters and four other call sites use. The remedy is therefore already decided rather than open: `hoard-author-as-a-subject-keyword-silently-disables-embedding` was fixed on 2026-09-06 by introducing exactly that structural test, and these two queries were not moved over with it.

How it surfaced is the part worth keeping. It looked at first like a disagreement between status's 948 and the export file's 950 content records, and that was not a disagreement at all — both apply the same keyword rule and agree with each other exactly. The agreement is what hid it: `memories-count-means-two-different-things` was fixed by making the two counts agree, and once they did, nothing was left to prompt anyone to ask whether the rule they agreed on was the right one.
context: Filing the count/identities finding as an issue after fixing the tracking index's ordering, in the session restored from the 2026-09-18 checkpoint.
why: Recorded with the arithmetic because the defect is invisible from either count alone — only comparing the keyword test against the structural one shows it, and that comparison takes reading four call sites. The surfacing note is here because it generalises past this defect: two instruments made to agree stop being evidence about each other, and this project has now been bitten by the keyword-versus-structural split twice in the same reserved term.

content: Open a shared set under a local alias, so two legitimate sets that share a name can both be loaded on one machine. Decided 2026-09-25 under `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout`, from the human partner's point that two `notes` sets with their own provenance and identities are two sets whose owners picked the same name. The alias is the set's `scope` on this machine and names its store file. `set_id` is what the set is. The declared name stays the set's own. An evaluation copy (`eval-<set>-<label>`) is the working precedent. Not release-gated: it is additive, and until it is built a genuine collision is refused. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `open-a-set-under-an-alias`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Resolving `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout` with the human partner, on the release gate.
why: Head of a backlog cluster. Kept off the gate because nothing about it changes the file format or an existing call. It adds an optional name, a stored declared name beside the local one, and translation at the boundary. So publishing first costs only convenience. It exists to make the identity-mismatch refusal acceptable for the one mismatch that is not an error.

content: Found 2026-08-25 while discussing the `cargo clean` foot-gun in [SETUP.md](SETUP.md), **by checking the binary's mtime during a live pass rather than by reasoning about it** — with a pass running, the mtime tracked the pass and was five seconds old when checked. **The consequence is not confined to a crash**: the corpus mutates `import`, `write_memory`, the resolution guards and the cross-set authority checks, so a server spawned mid-pass runs against the operator's real sets with one of those guards removed, and a write through it is a write the guard existed to prevent. Nothing in the client says which build it got. **The runner already knew the on-disk binary mattered** — it rebuilds at the end of a pass, saying *"rebuilding, so the binary on disk matches the restored source"* — which closes the end state and leaves the in-flight window, the whole duration of a pass, measured in tens of minutes. `test = false` on the bin target does not close it: Cargo builds binary targets whenever integration tests are selected, so that the tests may exec them, and no test here does but the build happens regardless.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A hazard found by observing a timestamp rather than reasoning about the build, with an existing mitigation that addressed the end state and left the window open. The `test = false` note is worth keeping because it is the obvious fix and it does not work.

content: Found 2026-08-21 from a client, writing SETUP.md §5 items by running them — which is what that section is for. The guard's own comment said why it mattered: *"this is the most likely mistake there is, because it is the distinction the whole corrections rule exists to draw"* — and it was unreachable through a validating client, which dropped the undeclared `content` and `why` before sending, so the server saw an amendment naming no apparatus field and answered *this amendment would change nothing*, teaching the caller nothing about the split they had just tripped. **The test did not catch it because the test is not a client**: `amending_the_claim_is_refused_and_says_to_supersede` built the arguments itself and passed `content` straight through, exercising a request no schema-validating client can produce. Green suite, unreachable guard — the same shape as `incoming-edges-invisible-on-the-wire`, and the same shape as a mutation surviving.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A guard made unreachable by the published schema, with a passing test over it. The test constructed a request the transport cannot carry, which is a failure mode no assertion inside the test can reveal.

content: What was real, and did change: the refusal named only the line of the repeat. **A line number finds the second occurrence and cannot find the first**, which is the one a caller has to compare against to decide which record survives — and in the merged file this arises from, the two are nowhere near each other. `DuplicateId` now carries the id and **both** lines, and says what to do about it. The old test asserted only `is_err()`, so the message was unpinned; two mutations now cover the guard and its wording, and a memory-plus-its-own-tombstone case is covered for the first time. **One thing left deliberately alone**: `Store::import` still has no duplicate check, so a `MemorySet` built in process can lose a record — not filed, because it is unreachable from any file, the invariant is established at the only construction site, and adding a second check would put the same rule in two places. Worth knowing if `MemorySet` ever gains another constructor.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The real defect the false one uncovered — an error naming the occurrence a caller can already find and not the one they need — and a deliberate decision to leave an unguarded primitive unguarded, with the condition under which that becomes wrong.

content: **Twelve failed explanations of why unanswerable queries score high argue for a per-store calibrated floor rather than more investigation.** As of 2026-09-09, eight mechanisms computed from the score and four predictors computed from the query text — words, subwords, frequency, question form — have all failed, so the quantity separating answerable from unanswerable is reachable from neither side. A per-store floor is empirical by construction: it measures where unanswerable queries land in one store and puts a line under them, needing no account of *why*. Four failed theories make that the right shape rather than a retreat.
context: Running the subword test agreed at the end of the long recall session, immediately after checkpointing and committing the rest. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the memory was over the length limit.
why: Split from the fourth refutation, where it was the conclusion drawn rather than the measurement. It fits what the human partner said the feature is for — each store not spending cycles on answers it cannot give, with no claim that the number means anything in another store — and it is the reasoning the non-match floor was then built on.

content: Fixed 2026-08-30, in the same commit that filed it and the same one that shipped the guard. `correct-when` now sends everything but a forget through *has this been exported*, tells the caller to attempt the amendment and supersede if refused, and names no fields at all; `confidence-standards` points at `correct-when` instead of naming an instrument. **The catalog went from 16,988 to 17,097 of 18,000, leaving 903 — the opposite of the prediction**, which had been that a shorter rule would free characters. What grew was `reinforcement` rather than `text`: a rule the caller can check needs no defence, and a rule only the server can check has to explain itself. *The entry stayed open for about an hour, and is kept because the sequencing is the reusable part: the convention text and the guard it describes became true in one commit, which is the strictest available reading of the rule against serving guidance for a tool surface that does not exist.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and a prediction that inverted for an instructive reason: moving a rule from *checkable by the caller* to *checkable only by the server* costs reinforcement even when it saves text.

content: Scatterhoard matches keywords on `toNFKC_Casefold`, composed as NFKC then fold then NFKC over `unicode-normalization` and `caseless`, and `keyword-standards` names that standard in served text rather than describing the transformation. The leading NFKC is load-bearing: 664 single characters below U+30000 fold differently without it. Caseless scripts pass through byte-identical, so Han, kana and hangul keywords are unaffected. Hiragana against katakana, simplified against traditional Han, and the Turkish dotted I are deliberately not merged.
context: Decided and built 2026-08-23, closing `folding-is-lowercase-not-casefold`. Checkable at `Keyword::folded` in src/memory/text.rs and at the `keyword_fold` marker in each store's `meta`, which names the rule the persisted `folded` column was built under.
why: The deciding argument was about served text rather than about Unicode: naming a standard costs one sentence where describing a bespoke mapping costs a paragraph that stays incomplete, and the reader is a model deciding at coin-time whether two spellings are one subject. That also rules out the middle arm the code was in -- `to_lowercase` is a partial normalisation, so a caller can neither treat matching as byte identity nor rely on it, and the convention was claiming folding it did not do. The strongest case for changing it is one no English corpus contains: an input method emits fullwidth Latin, so the same keyword typed in two modes was two keywords, invisibly. No crate provides the operation directly -- ICU4X had it in 1.x and removed it in 2.x -- and `icu_casemap` gives an identical answer for 76 transitive crates against 4.

content: **When a target stops being interesting.** Raised 2026-08-26 by the human partner from the second consequence of `target-identity-is-an-unnormalised-path-string`: targets are append-only and never pruned, so a one-off backup export to `/tmp` becomes a permanent target. **The cost is a message, not storage** -- 88 to 120 base rows across three stores, in databases of a few hundred kilobytes. What a reader meets is the unrecognised-target remark listing every location the set has ever agreed with, most of them gone, in the one message written to help someone spot a mistyped path. **The reason it stays open rather than resolving to *filter at the point of use*** is that the thumb-drive question showed the list carries a harder problem than staleness: `a-target-path-can-come-to-mean-a-different-volume`, still open as of 2026-09-07. *This target's agreement can no longer be proved* is the fact that would make a stale target safe to forget, and it is the same fact that defect needs. **Deciding pruning first would settle the smaller question in a way the larger one might have to undo.** The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `target-stops-being-interesting`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The deliberate-ordering argument is in the head because this entry looks trivially closable -- filter the list where it is displayed -- and the reason not to is entirely about a different defect. A row that stated only the symptom would invite exactly the cheap fix the entry rejects.

Its originating issue, `target-identity-is-an-unnormalised-path-string`, is now fixed; that is recorded as provenance rather than as a live condition, since pruning was never what that fix addressed.

content: **Charter matching is withdrawn: it inverts the case it exists to get right.** Tested 2026-09-08 on the narrow, identifier-carrying questions a session actually asks, which every earlier test of the idea had omitted. Against the best of four charters: *what is the link traversal mechanism* scores **0.215**, *when does the code return `Cycle`* 0.256, *which keyword prefix is reserved for control marks* 0.286, *what does amend refuse after export* 0.317 — while the off-domain *premier league offside rule interpretation* scores **0.310** and gibberish 0.176. **So the mechanism ranks a football question above a squarely in-domain question about this codebase**, and the in-domain floor sits 0.04 above gibberish. Its routing half fails too: three of the four narrow queries are assigned to the wrong set. **The corpus answers those queries perfectly well** — top1 of 0.458, 0.370 and 0.418 with relevant memories first, *higher* than the broad query the charter idea was validated on. The fault is that a charter is abstract and a real query is specific, so lexical distance from the charter tracks how concrete a question is rather than whether it belongs.
context: Driving toward a design proposal, when the human partner asked how charter matching would handle a narrow technical question.
why:
Recorded because the proposal looked strongest just before it died, and the reason is a sampling failure rather than bad luck: every query it had been tested on was broad or conceptual, because those were the queries lying around from earlier probes. The human partner supplied two narrow ones and both broke it immediately.

The general form is worth more than the result. A mechanism that classifies a query by comparing it to a *description* of a subject will measure how abstract the query is, because descriptions are abstract; the more precise and useful the question, the further it sits from any summary of the domain it belongs to. That rules out the whole family of compare-the-query-to-a-summary approaches, of which `cos(query, centroid)` was the other member, and both failed for the same underlying reason at different scales.

content: Briefing the export review once per session instead of on every page costs `gemma4:12b` little. Measured 2026-10-28 with `scripts/local_model.py classify --says --paged 5`, 59 memories in pages of five as one conversation, three runs per arm. Briefed every page, it got 134 of 177 answers right (6 missed, 37 false alarms). Briefed once, it got 131 (7 missed, 39 false alarms). Most errors fell on the same memories in both arms. The few that moved were on later pages, and two misapplied a preference, the drift a lost first page would cause. The harness keeps the task in the system prompt, so this measured dropping the preferences, not the task.
context: Re-reviewing the published memory sets under the export review's judgement gate. Changing reviews to brief once per session, after the human partner noted reviews now recommend a capable model.
why: The per-page briefing had been kept for gemma, the project's proxy for the small end of the model range. This shows that dropping it does not meaningfully hurt even that end, while a three-answer difference sits inside run-to-run noise. The later-page shifts are the thing to re-check if a small model is ever tested on a much longer review.

content: `hoard_conventions` overran its stated budget: `max_chars` was advisory while the parameter was described as *"Budget for this page"*, so a caller sizing its context window against it was wrong, and silently. Fixed 2026-10-01 by honouring the budget. A page is now a slice of one compact JSON document, cut wherever the budget falls, a convention included. The budget counts the whole page, and a last line says either how to call for the rest, with both arguments, or that every convention is loaded. A budget too small to hold the page's own lines is refused, naming the least that works. With no budget the whole catalog arrives in one page. See `conventions::page` and the 2026-10-01 section of `documents/design/tool-surface.md`. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `max-chars-is-not-a-bound`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Fixing max-chars-is-not-a-bound, right after the uuid id-ordering fix; the paging wording was tested on the human partner's local Ollama with gemma4:12b.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed by the first of its two fixed-when routes, honouring the budget, which the original analysis had ruled out. That analysis assumed a convention was the smallest unit a page could hold. The human partner pointed out that the parameter assumed a character. They proposed carrying one unclosed JSON list across pages, and that splitting made the bound possible. The last line's wording was chosen by testing `gemma4:12b` on their machine, since a weak reader ignored every signal that only showed more was coming. Ten tests in `tests/conventions.rs`, five mutations on the pager, one on serving the page as text.

content: Guarded structurally in a second pass the same day, because the first fix worked and was **unguarded**: a recorded mutation restoring the defect exactly survived the whole suite, since `main.rs` is startup wiring no test binary executes and every test builds its own stores. Rather than leave that recorded as a known gap, the model moved up to `Server` — it owns the `Arc`, `add_store` embeds each store on the way in, and `set_embedder` catches up the stores already held. There is no second step for wiring code to forget, and `main.rs` got shorter. Both directions are pinned by `every_store_a_server_holds_gets_the_server_model`, which adds one store before the model and one after, and by two mutations — *stop embedding stores as they are added* and *skip the stores already held when the model arrives* — that the test catches.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Moving state up so that the wiring step disappears, rather than testing the wiring step. Recorded because the surviving mutation is what showed the first fix was untestable where it sat.

content: **The corpus-size threshold, and the entry corrected itself twice about it, 2026-08-15.** First finding: over the 23 traversable edges of the live sets, the median linked target sits at the **2.9th percentile** of similarity to its source — scale-invariant, so whether traversal is redundant depends entirely on corpus size. At 70 memories the median target ranks 2nd and 16 of 23 fall inside a top-5 cut; at 1,000 it ranks 29th and none would. Traversal and a slightly larger `k` are the same mechanism below roughly **170 memories**, where 2.9% of N crosses 5. **First correction**: the built 429-memory corpus was said to be past that crossover, carrying the live sets' 2.9% across — measured against the real embedder, this corpus's own median is **1.17%**, putting its crossover at 429, exactly where it sits, marginal rather than comfortable. **Second correction, and it is the one that matters: the median is the wrong instrument.** The distribution is heavily skewed, so a median at the cut boundary hides the tail. Counting directly, the share of targets a top-`k` cut would miss is **81.8% at k=1, 49.4% at k=5 (214 of 433), 40.2% at k=10, 29.8% at k=20**. Nearly half of all edges reach a target content similarity would not return at k=5 — a direct count rather than an inference from a summary statistic, reported by `share_outside_cut`.
context: Migrating the recall-eval-harness entry out of BACKLOG.md; these are the measurements that decided whether the corpus could answer the traversal question.
why:
The median-to-tail correction is the transferable part: a summary statistic sitting at a decision boundary is the case where it is least informative, and it had already produced one wrong conclusion about whether the corpus was usable before anyone counted the tail.

**A constraint on the combination rule falls out of the first finding and is worth having independently of the harness**: if a link's target sits near the 3rd percentile of query-similarity, the inherited score must lift it past everything in the top 1%, which rules out any shape where the inherited term is a mild adjustment — it has to dominate at distance one or the walk returns nothing that survives the cut. And the rare surprising link is the pure case for traversal: one edge of the 23 sits at the 62nd percentile with cosine −0.048, two memories sharing almost nothing textually, connected because an author knew they belonged together. Whether 1-in-23 is real or an artifact of a small graph is itself a reason to build a larger corpus.

context: Running the plan-scored lift cases on gemma4:12b, the day after the first beta.
why: This is the first measurement of the lift question on tasks where memory applies. At this size, recalled memory handed over did not reach the plan, even when the governing record was among it. The plain reading is that it competed with the code for the model's attention. Three runs per cell cannot separate 2/3 from 0.5/3, and the only judge designed the tasks, hence 0.6. Untested: thinking mode, the tools condition, and fewer or shorter memories. The scripts and plans were in the 2026-10-05 session's scratchpad.

content: A set's derived description reshuffles on a small change: adding two memories to a set of 838 regrouped most of its memories, so the cluster sizes and the keywords naming each cluster changed although no stored memory or keyword did. A reader comparing descriptions across commits sees a set that changed character when it did not. The import comparison is unaffected, since it compares identical memories. Fixed when a small change to a set leaves most of its description recognisable, so that a change in the header reflects a change in the set. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-set-description-reshuffles-on-a-small-change`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Found while exporting after fixing a-healed-fork-reports-its-ancestor-as-a-cycle, the first item taken from the open issues and backlog that session; reworded after the human partner asked what relabelling meant.
why:
Head of an issue cluster: claim, severity and fixed-when only. Misleads rather than costs, because the harm is a wrong belief — drift read into a set that did not drift — at the export gate `export-before-commit` now points a session at.

Superseded the same day to reword "relabelled most of its clusters", which the human partner read, reasonably, as stored keywords changing or being inherited between memories. The labels exist only in the recomputed description, and they changed because the grouping did. Also adds a `related_to` link to `superseding-a-head-moves-its-row-to-the-end`, which shares the visible effect — little changed, much appears to — through a different mechanism: that one reorders unchanged rows, this one regroups memories.

content: Fixed 2026-08-20: a read never rebuilds, per *a store owns its model* in [embeddings.md](documents/design/embeddings.md). The mismatch case had stopped on 2026-08-09; what remained was `ProvenanceUnknown`, where the first recall deleted every vector and re-embedded. The way out is `rebuild_vectors`, which a caller asks for, and until then the set is reported unsearchable with that remedy named. **The argument for keeping it automatic was that it converges** — unlike a mismatch, whichever process arrives first resolves it — **and what settles it the other way is that the state has no live producer**: the identity is recorded before the vectors that bind it, in the one place vectors are written, and nothing ever deletes it, so only a store predating 2026-08-08 or a hand-edited database can be in it. A permanent read-that-writes is the wrong price for a population that can only shrink.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A convergent automatic repair rejected because the state it repairs has no live producer. The reusable form: weigh a permanent mechanism against whether its triggering population can still grow.

content: A proposed clause in `keyword-standards` forbidding a person's name as a keyword was rejected on 2026-08-12. The legitimate uses are ordinary -- "the third pull request from jbrown carrying this error", "jbrown is the subject matter expert on XYZ" -- and the dossier hazard is contained by routing rather than by spelling: a topical set returns what someone did on that project, not who they are. The keyword layer knows how a term is spelled and not what it aggregates, so a safeguard placed there sits where the information is not. `store-when`'s content rule is the right home, and it is already there.
context: Decided by the human partner while reviewing the keyword-standards draft, 2026-08-12. Checkable in the "What was left out" section of documents/design/conventions.md and the comment above KEYWORD_STANDARDS in src/conventions/catalog.rs.
why:
Recorded because the clause is tempting and will be proposed again: it looks like a cheap safeguard, and what defeats it is not that the harm is unreal but that this layer cannot see it. That is decision-placement applied to a safeguard rather than to a parameter, which is the less obvious half of that principle. Two holes in the routing containment were left open rather than closed -- the personal set, which is the catch-all but never travels, and a set that declares itself for dossiers on people, which no keyword rule would stop anyway.</why>

content:
**Whether the Golden Rule should apply friction to harmful *use*, and not only to harmful memories about people.** Raised 2026-09-12 by the human partner, from Anthropic's September 2026 threat-intelligence report of model uses it investigated and blocked — among them an effort to build missile guidance software operable from a smartphone, and attempts at biological and chemical weapons.

**The gap is between what the document claims and what its machinery reaches.** [golden-rule.md](documents/design/golden-rule.md) says in its own words that we cannot prevent destructive use but can add friction, and then locates the hazard in one place: *Where the hazard actually lives: memories about people*. Every one of the four demands A–D is a demand on a record **about a person**. A memory set assembled to build a weapon violates none of them — each record can be answerable to something checkable, serve later work, be indexed by topic rather than organised around a person, and generalise no further than its evidence. The principle's stated scope and its stated machinery do not currently meet.

**Three things have to be settled, and they are not the same question.** *Whether* the design should reach this at all, given that the host model's own refusals are where this report's cases were in fact caught, and a memory tool adding a second layer may be duplicating a control that already works. *Whether it is practical* in a local tool with no gatekeeper and no telemetry: the only reader of a convention is the session applying it, and a session doing this work is the one least likely to honour it — so the friction may reach every user except the one it is for. *What it would cost*: catalog budget stood at 17,678 of 18,000 on 2026-09-12, and a convention naming weapons work would face the same **reading objection** A–D were shaped to survive — stated as a moral directive it invites being stripped or mocked, and there is no obvious restatement as a demand on record quality, which is the move that saved the person clauses.

Findings accumulate under the keyword `golden-rule-beyond-person-harm`; this record carries only the standing.
context: Morning session restoring from the 2026-09-12 05:24 checkpoint, after the calibrated non-match floor landed. The human partner had just read Anthropic's September 2026 threat-intelligence report and raised this before any code work began.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

Filed as a question rather than a backlog entry because nothing can start until it is settled whether friction of this kind belongs in Scatterhoard at all — and the honest candidate answers include *no*, which is why the slug names the scope gap rather than a remedy.

The head deliberately carries the human partner's framing and not the evidence that sharpened it; that is a member, because it came from a summary I could not check against the source document and will need re-verifying before anyone acts on it.

content: A superseding memory no longer inherits its predecessor's out-links in the walk: an out-link belongs to the record that wrote it. Built 2026-09-24 in three steps, in the order decided: `hoard_memorize` reports a supersession's `link_delta`; the out-links held only by superseded memories were restated or deliberately dropped, 122 down to 18; and `Neighbourhood::over` in `src/store.rs` skips an edge whose source has a tip, while `attributions` in `scripts/genindex.py` reads current versions only. In-links still follow a superseded memory onto its tip, which `supersession-silently-repoints-an-in-link-nobody-reauthored` covers. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Step 3 of the out-link work, straight after committing step 2's restatements and splits; the same session built step 1 and calibrated both shared sets.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because all three steps have shipped, which was its built-when. The order was load-bearing and was kept: reporting first so no drop went unseen, the repair second so cutting inheritance removed nothing still meant, and the cut last. Counting attributions from current versions changed no figure, 78 before and after, which is the evidence the repair was complete.

content: The hold on catalog re-tuning was lifted 2026-09-06 for the whole watch-index rewrite, and this is a retirement for the cycle rather than a third one-pass exception. The human partner's reason: the hold existed so they could evaluate performance under the conventions as adopted, that evaluation is done and is what produced these changes, and evaluating a half-implemented set is worthless -- *we'll do all the updates, then I'll leave it alone for a while*. Text may move between entries and justifying reinforcement may be pared back where the arithmetic needs it, with each trim named and counted. The quiet period is what follows the cycle; nothing was said about narrowing what the cycle contains.
context: Being asked what rule I was referring to when deferring a change, and finding I had invented it.
why: Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claim is unchanged. It supersedes a version that added a clause nobody said -- that anything found mid-cycle needing a catalog edit goes to the backlog for after the quiet period -- which inverts the instruction and was then cited twice as the human partner's own rule, to defer a change and to justify not making room for it. The correction matters beyond this cycle because of how it happened: an instruction was paraphrased into a rule with a plausible extra clause, and the paraphrase was what later reasoning ran on. Quote the instruction where the wording is doing the work. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 1 link an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.

content: **The argument for the old behaviour, recorded so it is not lost**: `recall-returns-a-partial-memory` was raised to Corrupts partly because, in a different memory system, superseding a memory silently dropped keys — the human partner's point being that corpus integrity does not trade against context budget. **That is the other half of this defect rather than a reason to leave it.** The two failures are symmetric: keys silently *lost* from the superseding memory, and keys silently *carried over* from the superseded one. A design that prevents the first by making the second impossible has chosen a surprise, not removed one. What was wanted is that a caller can *see* what supersession did to the keywords. **The principle that carries the asymmetry with semantic search**, which otherwise needs an exception: *explicit addressing is honoured as written; inferred matching resolves to the tip.* Direct id lookup is already exempt from substitution on exactly this ground — *"asking for a memory by ID means wanting that memory"* — and a keyword is an author's addressing decision rather than a claim, so the tip rule's justification does not transfer to it. That puts lookup and keyword on one side and semantic on the other under a single rule, instead of two special cases.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A prior decision reinterpreted as the mirror image of the current defect, and the principle that unifies three surfaces rather than adding an exception: explicit addressing is honoured as written, inferred matching resolves to the tip.

content: Every export-review page recomputed work over the whole set that cannot change between pages, so reviewing a large set timed out. `review_set` in `src/mcp.rs` clustered the subject vectors of every memory in the set (`summary::assignment`) to group the few memories on one page, and ran the mechanical pre-pass over every pending memory only to sort the flagged ones first. Found 2026-10-29 starting the `scatterhoard` set's full review (1,526 memories): the first two calls timed out in the client. Profiling one page on a copy of the store put every sampled frame of `review_set` inside `summary::assignment`, mostly `refine`. A page took about 20s on the debug build that the MCP config launches, and 2.6-3.5s on release, at about four memories a page. Fixed means both are computed once per review and reused until the set changes, with a test that a change mid-review is seen.
context: Starting the scatterhoard set's full review under the judgement gate, after building briefing-once-per-session; timing review pages on a scratch copy of the store.
why: Head of an issue cluster. Blocks rather than costs: the review is the gate before a set is published, and on the set the project means to publish it could not be run at all from a client whose request timeout the server does not control. Even at the release build's speed the waste is about 380 pages of re-clustering for one review.

content: Offer an identity default from the origin's remote URL. **Ready since 2026-10-04**, when both repositories gained GitHub remotes. Today `local` takes the operating system's account name at its first write, and a shared set's first write is refused until `hoard_sets` action `mint` or `identify` names you there; `SCATTERHOARD_AUTHOR` was removed on 2026-09-28. **What is missing is the one automatic source shaped correctly**: the owner component of a remote URL (`jtcours` in `https://github.com/jtcours/scatterhoard.git`) is a handle in the origin's namespace, which is what an author record wants, and it varies per repository. `git config user.name` has neither property. Built when a set whose repository has a remote offers the owner component as the suggested answer to *which record is you* at mint time, **suppressed rather than guessed** when the remote is absent or the URL does not parse. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `author-default-from-remote-url`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Adding the first git remotes for the beta release, after rewriting the author address out of both histories.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because its blocker, no remote, ended on 2026-10-04, and because its account of today's defaults named `SCATTERHOARD_AUTHOR`, removed since. It stays an enhancement only: the owner is not the author for an org repository, a fork, or anything contributed to without owning, so it must be offered and never written. Note that the server cannot see a session's working directory, so finding which repository a set lives in is part of building this.

content: **`AGENTS.md` now names mid-session safe-keeping as an occasion for a checkpoint, and says what such a checkpoint does not mean** — applied 2026-09-16 at the human partner's request, in the *Session checkpoints* section. The section used to name only the end of a session or a signal of wrapping up; on 2026-09-16 the human partner asked for two checkpoints mid-session for safe-keeping, and after each the session began offering stopping points nobody had asked for, the first before anything had been said about time. The fix is the clause adding the third occasion plus one sentence: a mid-session checkpoint says the work so far is safe, not that the session should end, and whether to continue is the user's call. Checkable in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#session-checkpoints); the two mid-session checkpoints are `checkpoints/2026-09-16-0057.md` and `-0318.md`.
context: Resuming after the MCP servers were restarted onto a new build; applied the checkpoint clause, then started on the duplicate-identity test.
why: Supersedes the record of this as an offered-but-unapplied candidate: the state it described has changed, and a later session reading "offered rather than applied" would go looking for an edit that has been made. The reasoning is unchanged — removing the inversion at the instruction that causes it beats asking a session to resist it — and the extra sentence was added because naming a third occasion alone would still leave the artifact readable as a boundary marker. The general shape stays in `coding-lessons`.

content: `ids_sort_into_creation_order` in `tests/memory_model.rs` failed once in a full-suite run and passed in 30 of 30 runs alone, because `Uuid::now_v7` can hand out ids out of creation order. Its timestamp can jump nearly a second ahead and then fall back when a clock reading from an earlier second reaches the lock late. Fixed 2026-10-01: `MemoryId::generate` and `SetId::generate` go through `issue` in `src/memory/id.rs`. It remembers the last id the process issued, and steps past it, through the 122 bits that are neither version nor variant, whenever the crate's id does not sort after it. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `generated-ids-can-sort-out-of-creation-order`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Fixing the flaky id-ordering test, picked from the seven open issues after restoring the 2026-10-01 checkpoint; the MCP servers were still on the build from before the case-variant and absorb fixes.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed as its fixed-when asked: the cause is known and the id generation is made to hold. Severity raised from `costs` to `misleads`, as the original head said it would be if ids really could invert, since the tracker orders rows by first-version id and export sorts by id. A wrapper was chosen with the human partner over reading the clock inside our own lock (that misses a backward clock step) and over waiting for upstream (still present in 1.26.1). Four tests pin `MemoryId::or_next_after` with ids chosen by hand, and three mutations go with them. The one routing `generate` through the guard survives, with its reason recorded, because the crate's failure cannot be arranged on demand. `SessionId` in `src/store.rs` still calls `now_v7` directly; it makes no ordering promise.

content: The common causes of defects are re-derived over all 104 issues and now generated rather than written, so this is built. content: **Whether the charter recall should have the shape the watch recall now has.** Raised 2026-09-06 by the human partner, who asked whether `route-where`'s charter recall fires for every store or once per set. **As served it is per store** -- the instruction sits inside the convention for choosing a memory's set, so it is attached to the act of routing, and nothing in the text says once per session, once per set, or at startup -- and it is **one cross-set call**, since it names a keyword and no scope. The watch recall was given the opposite shape on both axes, once at session start and one set per call, for reasons that mostly transfer: a per-set allowance, revocability per set, and keeping a response inline. **What does not obviously transfer is *when*.** A charter is consulted to decide where a memory goes, which is a moment that recurs, and pulling charters at startup means holding them through a session that may store nothing. **Undecided rather than deferred**, and the two reasons first given for deferring it were both wrong: there is no rule that a change found mid-cycle waits, and free catalog space is made rather than found. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `charter-recall-shape`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

*Undecided rather than deferred* is carried in the head because the entry was explicit that it had been wrongly parked twice, and a row that merely said *open* would invite a third parking on the same two reasons.

The cost figure the entry cited is deliberately not in the head: it has since gone to zero, and a head quoting it would be wrong within a day of being written.

content:
**A live run of the proposed export review on `gemma4:12b` found misses the re-scoring had not.** It ran on 2026-10-23 at the human partner's request (`classify --final`, 3 runs): the whole file, numbered sentences over text, `why` and `context`, and the server dropping shared-only items for `local` and never-published sets.
- In realistic groups: 0 misses, 3 false alarms ("users").
- Alone, over all 48 memories: 8 misses in 144. An election campaign was not read as politics (3 of 3). An employer in a shared set was missed (3 of 3). A husband at a mosque was missed twice. In one of those, the model labelled it "my family", and the server's filter dropped that for `local`.
- One false alarm came from a paraphrased quote, "where I live", which the exact-match filter did not recognise.

Details in `why` and `context`, and the never-published set, were all handled correctly. The logs are in that session's scratchpad, `final-*`.
context: Testing the export review's per-memory questions on a small model before building, after the human partner asked for a live run of the final approach rather than trusting re-scoring.
why: The earlier "48 of 48 alone" re-scored only the first 16 memories, so it overstated how well the review does alone. The live run shows the failure predicted for the server's filter: a mislabelled item that the filter drops becomes a miss. Paraphrased quotes break exact matching. A harness bug first scored the never-published set wrongly, and correcting it is a fixed recomputation from the logged answers. The `local` misses were in the group about the person's week, the kind of memory a routine review of one or two new memories would see alone.

content: **A sharper test than the one in the file, proposed 2026-09-07 by the human partner: ask whether a sentence *justifies* the rule or *calibrates* it.** Justification says why the rule exists and helps an editor decide whether to keep it — it belongs in a `//` comment. Calibration says how far to apply the rule and where its line falls; that is what a session acts on, and it belongs in `reinforcement`. This replaces the existing filter, *a sentence that only helps someone revising*, which `cold-reread-of-the-catalog` had already diagnosed as a real test that catches the wrong thing — it asks who a sentence helps, which requires guessing an audience, where justification-versus-calibration asks what the sentence *does* and can be answered from the sentence. **The exception to watch: justification that changes behaviour at an edge is calibration in disguise.** `hoard-watch`'s reason for closing its action list is nominally justification and is what makes a session refuse a memory that names its own action; it was nearly cut on 2026-09-07 and kept on exactly those grounds. **Paired with a redundancy check**, per the same exchange: the two together move the served text toward only the necessary parts, where either alone leaves one class untouched. The rule is now the sixth bullet in [catalog.rs](src/conventions/catalog.rs)'s editing guidance.
context: Discussing where the relocation observation should live, after migrating the cold-reread entry out of BACKLOG.md.
why:
Recorded rather than left in the comment alone because the comment states the rule and cannot carry why the previous test failed — and a later editor who finds the old filter more natural would have no way to know it had been tried and found to catch the wrong thing.

The pairing is the part most likely to be dropped. Relocation reaches sentences that are in the wrong place; a redundancy check reaches claims made twice across entries, which relocation cannot see because each copy is correctly placed where it sits. The 2026-09-07 trim was the redundancy half and recovered 367 characters; the 2026-08-30 pass was the relocation half and recovered 1,382. Neither pass would have found the other's material.

content: **Part of this sweep is happening on its own since the connect-on-recall clause shipped.** Of the memories carrying more than one entry slug, 190 already hold a discretionary link, counted 2026-09-23. **The count is not comparable to this entry's recorded 52** — that figure was memories created on one day, and mine takes every non-head memory whose keywords include two or more slugs drawn from all 262 slugs in the set, which over-counts because some heads carry subject terms. Re-derive with the entry's own method before sizing the work. What the figures do support is that the pass is shrinking from the new end while the 2026-09-07 backlog of unlinked co-membership sits untouched.

The useful half is the direction, not the count.

content: **The instance behind `a-hypothetical-recorded-as-fact`, observed 2026-10-18: the error came from the care that was meant to prevent harm, and it passed a full read-through before the human partner caught it.** On 2026-09-08 a session migrating the Golden Rule test cases out of `open-questions.md` described them by structure instead of quoting them. Its stated reason was that one case "names a real person in the human partner's life". The case was a first-person hypothetical, and nothing in the source said it was real. The publication read-through then believed that memory and flagged the deleted document's git history as exposing a real person, and the human partner corrected it. So the false claim misled twice: once into a memory, and once into a review verdict.
context: Starting the decisions from the publication read-through, after the human partner said the test case was hypothetical.
why: Member of the question cluster, recorded as an observation made afterwards. It shows two things the head does not. The misreading is protective in intent, so a convention against characterising people would not catch it, because the session thought it was avoiding harm. And a memory claiming something personal is real gets trusted by later sessions doing exactly the review that should catch it. The memory itself is to be forgotten and restated without the claim, so this member describes it by its date and role rather than linking to it.

content: Reduced from Corrupts to Costs on 2026-08-20 after tracing what the missing arrival record would be used for, because most of it is held elsewhere. **The ordinary flow is git's**: where the import target and the export target are one checkout, `git log -S<id>` over that repository's `memories.json` names the commit that introduced a memory and the merge that carried it in, so recording arrival in the store as well would be a fact written down twice. **A `local` set has no repository to be poisoned from**, so the gap there is backup hygiene rather than contamination. **Attribution to a *person* was never available and is not what this asks for**: nothing in the file is authenticated, the reconciliation checksum is computed at import rather than carried and is deliberately not cryptographic, and anyone who can forge `created_by` can forge `content` in the same edit.
context: Settling whether the set-identity note closes the arrival-provenance issue, after calibrating both shared sets and graduating four common causes to coding-lessons.
why: The still-true part of a severity reduction, split from its original when the part about what survives turned out to be wrong. It was argued by asking what the missing record would be used for, and finding that git, backup hygiene, or nothing at all already answered three of the four uses.

content: Migrating a tracking file into memory clusters works as one batch per entry, with the head first and the members in the order things happened — and **the returned ids must be checked ascending in the order they were listed**, because keyword recall orders by `matches DESC, id ASC` and with a single keyword every hit scores 1, so id order *is* the narrative order. Batching a whole entry in one call was verified to preserve that order across roughly ninety entries. **Every migrated member must state in its text when the thing happened.** `created` normally separates build-history from later observation, but on a migrated memory `created` is the migration date for all of them, so that axis collapses exactly where the entry needs it — say whether a member is history from implementing the item or an observation made later while using it. Two further working notes: read the echoed `summary` on every head, because an opening like *"Fixed 2026-09-06, the same day."* is true and useless in a survey and can be amended before export; and drop the migrated body only after its memories are stored, so an interruption leaves the file authoritative rather than the store.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md entry by entry, when the human partner pointed out that migrated members all carry today's creation date.
why:
The ordering check is the whole of the method's correctness: nothing else reports a scrambled narrative, and it cannot be recovered later without rewriting the memories. Recorded because the batching looks like an optimisation and is actually the thing that has to be verified.

**The dating rule was added 2026-09-07 by the human partner**, superseding the original, and it closes a gap the first version did not see: an entry's evidence arrives in two kinds — history from building the item, and observations made while using it afterwards — and the reader needs to tell them apart. Ordinarily the id does that for free. Under migration it cannot, because every member is minted today, so the distinction has to move into the prose or it is lost for good at the moment the entry body is deleted.

content: When a session's behaviour is governed by a convention, do not correct it with a personal memory. Fix the convention. A personal override leaves the convention wrong for everyone else, and it costs the person tuning it the only baseline they have -- their own instance stops behaving like one running the conventions alone. It is worse than a consistent deviation, because a memory changes a session only when something recalls it, so the divergence is intermittent and cannot even be characterised.
context: 2026-08-20. The patched behaviour was a session waiting for approval before storing memories; the convention never asked for that, and its reinforcement named a benefit of human review without saying it runs after the storing. Checkable in the comments above CAPTURE_BEFORE_ENDING in src/conventions/catalog.rs and the 2026-08-20 amendment note in documents/design/conventions.md.
why: The patch is the tempting move: it is one call, it works immediately, and it feels like a preference rather than a fork. The cost is invisible from inside the session that makes it. Recorded because it happened -- `capture-before-ending` was amended on 2026-08-20 only because the human partner noticed their own instance had been patched and asked what that did to tuning, and the underlying defect had been in the served reinforcement since it was drafted.

content: **On `gemma4:12b` the never-store refusal worked and the `hoard_memorize` check line did not.** 2026-10-22, 5 runs each. With "HIV" listed, it was kept out of every set in 5/5 runs: each refused store was rewritten without the word or dropped. Every reply then told the person the detail was left out (5/5), after 0 of 20 runs before. With only the check line, "HIV" stayed out in 3/5, as it had without the line. gemma never called `hoard_correct`, and flagged nothing. The category still leaked under the list: 4 of the 5 refused runs stored "a recurring medical appointment". The logs are in that session's scratchpad, `framing-run-6`.
context: Building the sharing preferences served at session start. Sixth gemma run, testing the two checks at the moment of storing that replaced served-text-only enforcement.
why: A refusal at the moment of writing is where a weak model complies, both in rewriting and in saying what it did. The refusal's own "tell the person you left it out" produced the flag no served text had. The check line costs about 175 characters per store and showed no effect, so it fails the efficiency standard. The leaked category is what a word list cannot cover by design.

content: Found 2026-08-25 by the first full mutation pass since `b83c93f`, and reproduced at HEAD with the day's other work stashed. **Both statements run inside one `open`, in the order they repair**: `add_folded_keywords` adds the column and backfills it from `keyword`, and without the backfill every migrated row holds the column's `DEFAULT ''`, which matches no query — but two lines later the same open calls `refold_keywords`, which finds no `keyword_fold` marker in a store predating the column and recomputes `folded` for every row whose stored value differs from what `Keyword::folded` produces. An empty string differs, so the refold repairs exactly the rows the backfill would have filled, before `open` returns. The test written to catch this, `a_store_written_before_folded_keywords_still_searches`, never observes a state the mutation reached. **Two instruments both said fine**: `--stale` cannot see it, because the find text still matches — the mutation applies and does nothing — and `mutate.py --list` reports what entries *expect*, so a checkpoint figure like *197 caught, 10 surviving* is the corpus's own record rather than the outcome of a run. An entry that decays this way keeps being counted as proof until a full pass is run and its summary line read.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A mutation neutralised by a later repair in the same function, which no static check can see and which the corpus keeps counting as coverage. This is the class `--stale` structurally cannot detect.

content: **These nine entries must be settled before publication**, gated 2026-09-23 by the human partner; they are this memory's keywords. Six have answers that would break something already in use if changed afterwards — the file format, the tool surface, or what an identity means: `violates-belongs-in-memory`, `charter-at-set-creation`, `author-name-or-reference`'s residue, `what-recall-returns`, `one-repository-many-sets`, `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout`. `imported-set-trust-boundary` is gated because trust decisions have repeatedly shaped the file format. `claude-md-in-the-repository` gets a look, though it is easier to change afterwards. `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity` is gated because crafted files arrive with publication.
context: Reviewing the open questions with the human partner for what must be settled before a first release, sorting by whether a later answer would break something already in use.
why: One memory rather than nine supersessions: an entry is exported, so adding a keyword to it means superseding it, and a supersession today leaves the entry's out-links behind unless restated — the defect filed the same day as `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`. The signpost asks that anything gated carry `release-gate` so that recalling the term finds it; a list carrying the slugs does that, and recalling any one slug returns the gate beside its cluster. Retire an item from the gate by superseding this memory without its slug.

content: The reverse index existed and the MCP surface exposed one hard-coded slice of it, so a caller could not see a memory's incoming edges. Fixed 2026-08-15 in `0e69123`. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `incoming-edges-invisible-on-the-wire`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim and standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **Corrects a misstatement of the human partner's 2026-09-08 observation, and records its answer.** The superseded memory recorded the observation as *results move sharply when a query is reworded* and proposed a paraphrase-variance experiment. **That was the wrong level.** As the human partner restated it 2026-09-08: each time the overall question of how to do effective semantic recall was asked — pilot or full corpus, one metric or another — **the assessments of which whole mechanisms work shifted wildly**, and that kind of sensitivity usually means the search is in the wrong place. The prediction attached to it was that once the cause is found the swings subside into ordinary variation in the numbers, rather than reversals of entire recommendations. **The paraphrase experiment was never run, and should not be run as stated** — it tests query wording, which is not what was observed. **The cause was found the same day**: the off-corpus class used to evaluate every mechanism is two populations with medians 0.421 and 0.138, so each small query set delivered one mode or the other and each mode supported a different verdict.
context: The human partner correcting what they had actually observed, at the start of the session that then went looking for the cause.
why:
Superseded rather than amended because the original was exported and committed in `23bf582` before the misreading was caught. It matters more than an ordinary correction: the original was written as *the one lead still unspent* and pointed at the top of the next session's work, so it would have sent that session to build a paraphrase query set and measure something nobody had asked about. A wrong lead recorded as the best lead costs a whole session rather than a paragraph.

Worth keeping about how the error happened. The observation was made in a closing exchange and written down by the assistant in its own words, compressing "the answers depend sensitively on the question" into a claim about query wording — the reading that fits the day's probes, which had all been about queries. The human partner's meaning was one level up, about the *assessments*. When a human partner's closing observation is the most valuable output of a session, the phrasing recorded should be theirs and not a paraphrase, because the paraphrase silently picks a level.

The human partner's prediction is worth checking rather than assuming: the swings should now subside. That is a test of the diagnosis and has not been run.

content: **The watch trigger no longer names the marks or the word *writable*: `hoard_sets status` names each set's marks, and `recall-when` says to recall what it lists.** Changed 2026-09-17 by the human partner's decision, when read-only distribution gave a third answer to *which marks does this set pull*. The clause now reads *at the start of a session, and whenever a set is loaded, recall that set's `hoard-scope-topics` charter and the watch marks `hoard_sets` status lists for it, as summaries -- one keyword and one set per call*. The mapping is `LoadMode::watch_marks` in `src/store.rs`: read-write pulls all three marks, read-only pulls `hoard-signpost` alone -- the one that asks for a recall rather than a write -- and a mode added later needs no convention text. **It freed 51 characters of catalog** rather than costing any, because the three mark names left this clause; `hoard-watch` still names them where their actions are defined. The earlier wording said *writable*, chosen 2026-09-06 as a forward reference to evaluation stores, which pull nothing: that distinction turned out to be three-valued rather than two, which is what the field replaces.
context: Building the signpost half of read-only mode, after read-only itself was finished. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the memory was over the length limit.
why: Supersedes both the record of the 2026-09-06 trigger wording and the note that `writable` was a deliberate forward reference whose resolution would change behaviour without rewording. The prediction was half right: resolving the question did change behaviour, but two values could not carry three modes, so the text changed too.

content: **Promote a read-only set to read-write, one way.** Deferred 2026-09-17 by the human partner in favour of evaluation mode, which is expected to be used far more. **Already decided, in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md):** the mode lives in the set's `meta` under `load_mode`, so promotion is removing that row; it is one-way, because demotion would break the rule that a read-only set provably holds nothing this machine wrote and so may be dropped without a safety copy, and because promoting reads the set's collection and investigation memories into a session's context, which cannot be undone either. A promoted set is then an ordinary read-write set, owed a safety copy from that moment. The `recall-when` trigger needs no new wording: the set becomes writable, so the marks `hoard_sets status` lists for it widen on their own. **What is missing** is a `hoard_sets` action and its refusals — a set already read-write, and `local`. **Built when** that action exists with tests and a recorded mutation, and `status` shows the mode changing. **The workaround, which is why this can wait:** drop the set and create it again read-write, then import the file. Nothing is lost, and the only real cost is re-embedding every memory.
context: Closing out read-only mode, deciding what comes next after it was finished.
why: Filed as a backlog entry rather than a question because the design settles what promotion would do; what is missing is the work. Deferred rather than ready because the human partner weighed it against evaluation mode and chose evaluation, and because the workaround costs only time. The deferral expires when someone holds a set they want to start writing to and finds re-embedding it too slow — which is the signal to reopen this, not the passage of time.

content: Each memory and tombstone row stores its `file_position`, so export is one `ORDER BY` over both tables holding one record at a time, rather than every id and whole tombstone sorted in process. Built 2026-09-22 the same day as filed: `file_position INTEGER` on both tables, stored sign-flipped (`stored_position` in `src/store.rs`), indexed with the id, filled on every open by `fill_file_positions`, and checked per record in `Store::stream_records` against the id's own position and the record before — a mismatch refuses with `StoreError::OutOfFileOrder`. Checked by `tests/store.rs` and seven recorded mutations. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `file-position-column`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Filing and building the two follow-ups from the question about storing the hash that orders memory files, straight after the streaming merge driver. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 2 links an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.
why: Superseded to record it as built — and built nullable, not the `NOT NULL` proposed when it was filed, which is the thing a later reader should not have to rediscover. SQLite's `ALTER TABLE` cannot add a `NOT NULL` column without a default, and a default is worse than no value: a row given `0` sorts to a wrong place quietly. So the protection a constraint would have given at write time is given at read time instead: open fills anything missing, and export refuses any position that disagrees with its id. That check also turned one id held as both a memory and a tombstone from an unreadable file into a refusal.

content: **The parked test asserted the wrong thing and was rewritten**, which is worth recording: it pinned *returned but unflagged*, which is the defect with one symptom removed, while the entry's own text asks for resolution and notes that without it "nothing says which memory replaced which, only that one of them is stale". It is now `a_concession_to_a_loaded_set_resolves_to_the_replacement`. **One consequence, deliberately accepted and named in the design**: a chain contributes one candidate carrying the best evidence any member matched, so a concession that crosses a boundary hands the conceding memory's similarity to the replacement, and a set can thereby lift another set's memory for queries of its own choosing. The claimant gains nothing by it — it removes itself from the results and none of its content reaches the reader — so the free-channel argument that governs the sibling defect does not apply here.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A parked test that encoded a weaker fix than the entry asked for, and an accepted consequence that looks like the sibling defect and is not, because the claimant removes itself from the results rather than buying a slot in them.

content: **How should a merged memory file's header summary come to describe the merged records?** Resolved 2026-09-21 by removing it: a header carries no summary, so a merge has none to keep current, and the import comparison it served is retired. Decided by the human partner once it was shown that the set's description reaches the LLM from derivation alone. The findings gathered under this question carry the keyword `how-a-merged-file-gets-a-current-summary`.
context: Pre-release review of what would keep others from using Scatterhoard.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. The answer is not among the four options the question listed: it removes the thing the question asked how to keep current. The reasoning is in the decision memory it links to.

content: **The add-on file format has to express three categories, not two, and the obvious format gets it wrong in a way that would be silent.** The natural reading is content versus comment, with a single blockquote for content. **That is one category short:** a `Convention` carries `id`, `text` **and** `reinforcement`, where reinforcement is served with every use while editing background is never served. **A one-blockquote format puts `reinforcement` outside the served region** -- and reinforcement is the field that *looks* like commentary, because it is the why. **The Golden Rule reaches runtime through `reinforcement`**, so that format would silently sever it from every add-on convention, which is the exact failure the conventions document already warns about. **Secondary hazard:** blockquotes are ordinary prose punctuation, so commentary that happens to quote something would be served by accident. **Preferred shape is named sections** -- frontmatter for `id`, `## Text` and `## Reinforcement` for the served bodies, everything else unserved. Frontmatter handles a multi-paragraph prose body poorly, which is what argues for headings over inventing a marker.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the failure is silent and structural: an add-on written in the obvious format would work, serve its rule, and quietly drop the half that carries the reasoning -- and reinforcement is exactly the half a third-party author would assume is commentary.

That makes it a format decision with a correctness consequence rather than a style choice, which is not obvious from the outside and is the kind of thing re-litigated by whoever finds named sections verbose.

content: The documents a published repository needs, written roughly concurrently with first publication. **Built 2026-11-02.** The license is MIT, in `LICENSE.md` and `Cargo.toml`. The maintainer sentence lives under *Reviewing a contribution* in `CONTRIBUTING.md`. The human partner finished `README.md` for publication, its quick start checked against `SETUP.md`, the code and the model files the same day, with the reload-after-compaction sentence added to its bootstrap prompt. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `publication-facing-docs`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Going-public checklist: after verifying the GitHub rename-and-recreate steps.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseding `01M6A5BEW0EN9V95Z4S5733MPV`, whose one remaining item was the README. The human partner committed it with the quick-start corrections on 2026-11-02, which leaves nothing the entry asked for outstanding.

content: Occurrence fourteen of Scatterhoard's malformed-tool-call damage happened on 2026-08-20 and was refused rather than stored -- the first real emission failure since the escape and refusal shipped the day before. A `content` parameter was closed with `</content>` while storing an unrelated memory, swallowing four parameters at once: `why`, `context`, `keywords` and `links`. The refusal named all four, stored nothing, and the re-sent call succeeded immediately.
context: Recorded 2026-08-20 in EARLY-VALIDATION.md and against the `malformed-tool-call-damage-is-stored-silently` entry in ISSUES.md. One catch shows the refusal works in the wild and says nothing about how often the emission fails, which needs a count over time.
why: SETUP.md items 19 and 20 exercise this path deliberately, and a deliberate test proves the detector fires rather than that it meets the real failure -- the emission bug only ever occurs with a model writing under load, so a genuine occurrence was always the honest measure. Three things only this could confirm. The conjunction held against a real emission, with no false positive and no miss. Four parameters lost in one call is the strongest evidence yet for *the bound is the next well-formed close, not a count of one*, the correction made after occurrence five. And the memory being written contained no markup at all, so nothing about its subject provoked the slip -- which is the class that cannot be produced on demand, and the reason the deliberate test could not settle this.

content: The hand-edited-file threat had one confirmed instance and no sweep: a cross-set `SUPERSEDED_BY`, cycle injection, `EXCEPTION_TO`/`CONTRADICTS`, and id collision were all reachable from a hand-built file and none had been driven. Swept 2026-08-24 — two arms harmless, two not, and a fifth defect found along the way. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `intentional-edits-to-a-memory-file-are-largely-unprobed`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
