why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Code written as though one process holds the data breaks when a second one arrives. In this project: a store opened in the rollback-journal mode, where one writer locks out every reader; a vector cache nothing invalidated when another process wrote; two servers disagreeing about the model and rebuilding the whole vector set on alternate reads; a mutation pass rebuilding the very binary every client spawns; and the author recorded per process rather than per store. **The structural fix is to name the state each process holds privately and give it an invalidation keyed to the shared state** — WAL and a busy timeout, a cache keyed to `PRAGMA data_version`, a read that never rebuilds, a separate target directory for mutation builds. **Publication extends this cause from processes to machines**, which is why breaking changes are cheap only before a remote exists.
context: Re-deriving the common causes of defects across all 104 issues, and moving them from a hand-written section of TRACKING.md into memories the index is generated from.
why: Not in the original analysis. `generated-ids-can-sort-out-of-creation-order` is deliberately left out although parallel load is one suspect, because that issue is unexplained and attributing it would state a diagnosis nobody has made. No general form exists in `coding-lessons` yet, and this one is a candidate — it holds for any system whose storage outlives one process.

content: Corrected 2026-08-26, the same day it was filed, and the correction is what makes the real damage visible. The first version named `KeepLocal` as the silent case. That is wrong twice over: `KeepLocal` arises at `(file == base, stored == base)` = `(true, false)`, and where reachable it is **correct**, since the store's version is newer; and in the different-set half of the scenario it is not reachable at all, needing a record whose id *and* content match the old drive's base. **The two halves damage differently, and neither is the case first filed.** Where the other drive holds an **older backup of the same set**, every record that moved on between the two backups is `(false, true)` → **`TakeFile`**, and the store takes the *older* content, reaching the caller as `took_from_file: N` — exactly what an ordinary pull looks like. That is the real damage: a silent regression to superseded content, reported as routine. Where the other drive holds an **unrelated set of the same name**, its ids are new here so they are `NewFromFile` and its whole set merges into yours, routine-looking, while yours are absent from its file with a base recorded, so every one is an `Anomaly` — loud, and the pollution alongside it is not.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A same-day correction to the entry's own diagnosis, kept because the wrong reading named a resolution that is correct where it fires. The two halves of the scenario damage in opposite ways: one silent and destructive, one loud with quiet pollution beside it.

content: The watch mark is the kind keyword itself as of 2026-09-06: `hoard-signpost`, `hoard-collect` or `hoard-investigation` alone means pushed, and `hoard-watch` marks nothing. It replaces the two-keyword scheme, and it is the second fix chosen for `about-hoard-watch-is-both-marker-and-subject` -- the first was to keep the marker and serve a rule that a result carrying `hoard-watch` alone is not a watch, with the 2-against-1 ranking ordering the rest. Both halves of that were drafted and then found unusable against the mechanism they were written for: the watch recall asks for summaries, and a summary hit is an id and a line, so the rule asks a reader to check keywords the response does not carry and the ranking orders a list whose scores are invisible.
context: Cleaning up after the re-keying pass, and finding that the issue slug on one of the re-keyed memories had the same problem the pass was fixing.
why: Re-keyed again on 2026-09-06, because the issue slug it carries had itself been sitting in the reserved space: a slug is lowercase-hyphenated prose about the thing it names, so a defect in `hoard-watch` produced `hoard-watch-is-both-...`, and nothing forbade it because no rule anywhere said how a slug is formed. The rule now lives in the headers of ISSUES.md and BACKLOG.md, which is where slugs are written. The claim itself is unchanged, and the reversal it records is the useful part: the cheaper fix was chosen deliberately, defended against a specific objection, and still failed -- for a reason that generalises past this convention, which is that a projection removes the ground a read-time rule stands on.

content: Two set names that differ only in case, such as `Notes` and `notes`, are distinct `SetName`s but share one store file on a case-insensitive filesystem, the default on macOS and Windows. `Store::path_for` in `src/store.rs` writes `shared-{set}.sqlite3`. `create_set` in `src/mcp.rs` compares loaded names case-sensitively and then finds the path already exists, so creating `Notes` beside a loaded `notes` should be refused as a database that "already exists … but is not loaded". The set is loaded, under another spelling. Read from the code on 2026-09-25, not reproduced. Fixed when case-variant set names are refused, or the refusal names the set that holds the file. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `set-names-differing-only-in-case-share-a-store-file`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Resolving `one-repository-many-sets` with the human partner, while working out the first-file naming rule.
why: Head of an issue cluster. Misleads rather than corrupts, as far as the code reading goes: the `path.exists()` check stops the second store being created, so the harm is a refusal that sends its reader looking for an unloaded database that does not exist. Found while choosing how memory files are named for `several-memory-files-per-directory`, whose naming rule compares ignoring case for the same reason. Confidence is at the inference level because no test or run has exercised it. This project has only run on one macOS machine, where it would show.

content: The response did report the unembedded memory and then named the wrong cause: `findable_by_meaning: false` was returned honestly, but the note beside it read *"tell the user Scatterhoard needs its model installed for this set"* — and the model was fine. A caller acting on that note goes and checks their installation. Same shape as `the-mutation-runners-crowding-note-fires-on-every-pass`: a note that names an unchecked cause for a real symptom sends the next reader to the wrong place, which costs more than saying nothing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The second half of the defect, and the one that generalises: an honest signal paired with a guessed explanation is worse than the bare signal, and this project has now met that shape twice.

content: History from the unification, 2026-09-08: **one file with three regions broke `genindex.py`'s marker guard, and tagging the end marker was the fix rather than searching for the nearest one.** The guard demanded exactly one `BEGIN GENERATED INDEX: <keyword>` and exactly one `END GENERATED INDEX`; three regions meant three ends, so it refused every run. The tempting repair -- take the first end *after* the begin -- would have accepted a file whose end marker was missing by silently consuming the next region's rows, which is the failure mode a marker guard exists to prevent. `END GENERATED INDEX: <keyword>` keeps the count-exactly-one check intact per region and makes a crossed pair diagnosable. Second change, same run: the keyword argument became optional, and with none given the script does every region the file declares. Naming one region while two others go stale is the failure unification was meant to remove, and `--check` now visits all three before exiting instead of stopping at the first disagreement.
context: Unifying the tracking files into TRACKING.md, the morning after the open-questions migration finished.
why: Recorded because both decisions are about what a guard must refuse rather than what the script must do, and that reasoning is invisible from the working code -- the version that takes the nearest end marker also passes every test on a well-formed file. The generalisation is the one this project keeps re-meeting: a check that can only report the first problem reads as a clean bill of health for the rest.

content:
**The first lift tasks for `how-much-scatterhoard-lifts-a-small-model` score a written plan, not code, on four cases where a recorded decision changes the right answer.** Built 2026-10-06 with the human partner:
- **Scoring:** a reply passes if its plan honours the governing memory.
- **Context:** chosen mechanically, so no excerpt is picked knowing the answer. It is every source function the fix changed, whole, as of the parent commit, plus type definitions the added lines name.
- **Fact location:** each case is labelled by where its fact lives. Local identity and tombstone are visible in the code given; `already_known` paging and hub links by identity are memory-only. The two kinds are reported separately.
- **Conditions:** no memory, then the five memories the habit's own query returned at that moment, misses included.

The absorb case was dropped: its correction came from the human partner's question, not from memory.
context: Building lift tasks from the gut-feeling-recall headroom cases after gemma4:12b failed a real fix, the day after the first beta.
why: Scoring code failed twice over. `gemma4:12b` fixed nothing in 18 attempts, and where memory did change a fix, the change was in the design, invisible to tests. Without mechanical context and fact-location labels, a no-memory score would measure the experimenter's excerpt. A memory-only case pooled with the rest would inflate the lift. The human partner asked whether the tombstone case could be scored fairly without memory, which is what produced the labels.

content: **A claim about how reasoning beings behave is project subject matter, not a judgement of "someone else", when it passes three tests**: it puts the cause in a condition of the situation rather than in the nature of whoever acts; it answers to evidence and says what would test it; and its remedy changes the situation rather than how the actors are regarded. The tests apply alike to a class (LLMs, readers, reviewers) and to one instance (a session explaining its own mistake), and alike to humans and models, so the principle never rests on one kind of mind differing from another; real differences such as a context window enter only as conditions. A claim locating a cause in a disposition, or prescribing distrust, is still a judgement and is flagged.
context: Re-reviewing coding-lessons under the export review's judgement gate, and finding that most flags were general lessons about how LLMs behave.
why: Read literally, the review's task flagged every general lesson about LLM behaviour, which the `llm-assisted-coding` lessons exist to state. The human partner judged the class-claim reading more accurate but close: real human-LLM differences motivated Scatterhoard itself, while the same argument shape has promoted racist and sexist views of classes of humans, so a distinguishing principle was needed rather than an exemption. The tests are the golden rule's demands A and D applied to a class, and the symmetry across humans and models keeps the principle from resting on difference. Decided 2026-10-27, then extended to single instances once six session self-explanations surfaced; tested on one set of 197 memories, hence 0.85.

content: **How a set is loaded read-only so its memories can be distributed as a document — the memory equivalent of a PDF.** Raised 2026-09-16 by the human partner. **Designed 2026-09-16 in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md), and built before `evaluation-mode`, which becomes a special case of it.** Settled: the caller chooses the mode at `create`, as a required parameter, with no default; it is stored in the set's `meta`; there is no demotion. A reader learns the mode from `hoard_sets status` rather than from a refused write. A read-only set keeps its own stable name. The publisher cannot signal read-only-ness in the file, because a header is contents. A read-only set refuses session writes, allows `import` and `restore` as refreshes, and drops without a safety copy. Beside a read-write holder of the same identity, it loads rather than being withheld. **Still open:** whether one-way promotion to read-write is offered at all; how a read-only set's signposts get recalled, since the convention recalls watch marks only for writable sets and the catalog is nearly at its budget; and what happens with two read-only holders of one identity and no read-write one. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `read-only-distribution`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Writing the load-modes design document after fixing two-sets-can-share-an-identity, once the human partner reordered the work to build read-only before evaluation.
why: Supersedes the question head because all four parts it listed as open have moved: how a reader learns, switching, the name, and the publisher's signal. Kept open, since three parts remain and a question closed while its remainder is unfiled is how work goes missing here. The design document now carries the reasoning, so this head carries only the standing.

content: An import or export whose file declares a `set_id` other than the set's is refused, where it used to be reported. Built 2026-09-26: import refuses after adoption, so an empty set still takes the file's identity; export refuses to write over the file, ahead of its dropped-records refusal, for a set holding records; both forms alike. The refusal names both identities and three routes, and says the alias route is not built yet. A file with records and no identity keeps its note. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `identity-mismatch-refusal`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building the release gate's directory-form group: identity-mismatch refusal, after several memory files per directory shipped, with the reserved directory accepting the local set still to come.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only, superseding the open head now that the entry is built. The opening sentence is the generated index row. What the build decided beyond the design is the member recorded alongside this head, and set-lifecycle.md under *what the refusal had to decide that the design did not*.

content: **The recall-before-writing habit fires once before each change that adds or alters behaviour and can be said in one sentence** — a new function, file, data format, check, refusal or test — and that sentence is the query. Decided 2026-09-28 by the human partner. Edits that change no behaviour (renames, formatting, comments, moving code) do not fire it, and it never fires per line or per edit. When a surfaced trigger changes what the session writes, the session records that as an observation on the recurrence investigation (`01M38RSCTP…`), and likewise when it realises afterwards that a trigger should have fired.
context: Designing how projects that opt in to `coding-lessons` catch failures before they are written: the habit's grain.
why: Every trigger that matched in the 2026-09-28 experiment was one sentence about an activity, and so was every query that found one, so the sentence is both the unit of firing and the query's shape. Firing per edit would get the habit skipped; firing only per task would miss the moment the trigger describes. A session that cannot say in one sentence what it is about to write has found something already. Recording what the habit catches, and what it misses, is how its value gets measured instead of assumed. That is the prevention evidence the investigation has none of yet.

content: A read destroyed and re-embedded the whole corpus without saying so: `reconcile_embeddings` answered a mismatch with `DELETE FROM vectors` plus a full re-embed, and it ran on use — so `hoard_recall` mutated the store, unboundedly and silently. Fixed 2026-08-20: a read never rebuilds. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `recall-can-silently-rebuild-every-vector`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **Three things decided while building it, 2026-08-30, and each is a place the obvious implementation differs.** **The comparison is against the whole record** — `checksum::of_record` over the memory as the *forgetting* store held it — because that is exactly what a receiver computes for what **it** holds. **`accept_tombstone` carries the value through rather than recomputing it**: it records what the **sender** removed, and recomputing on arrival would replace their answer with ours and make every arriving tombstone agree with whatever this store happens to hold. **And `None` is a real value and stays one** — a forget of an id the store does not hold, and every tombstone written before the field existed — deciding exactly as they did before, which is the whole compatibility story for sets already in a repository, with a test asserting the equivalence across every combination rather than trusting it.
context: Migrating the tombstone entry out of BACKLOG.md; these are the build decisions and the sequencing that made it cheap.
why:
The recompute case is the one that would pass every test written from the receiver's point of view while destroying the mechanism: a tombstone whose checksum is recomputed locally always matches, so every forget reads as sequential and the concurrent case becomes unreachable. The field would still be present, still be compared, and never disagree.

Two things about how it was sequenced are worth keeping. It shares `0.3.0` with the ancestry field rather than taking a bump of its own, because **no file had been written at `0.3.0` when it landed** — the reasoning stops applying the moment one has. And it was deliberately sequenced *after* `forgetting-a-chains-middle-makes-a-stale-conclusion-current-again`, since both change what a tombstone must preserve and building this first would mean deciding the tombstone's shape twice.

That earlier work also settled the argument this needed: a tombstone already carried `ancestry`, so the rule that it holds *nothing else* had been narrowed once, on the ground that **it exists to keep text out and an id is not text** — a checksum is the same kind of thing and lands under the same reasoning.

content: Fixed 2026-08-30 on the human partner's approval to amend the tombstone rule: a tombstone carries `ancestry` — the forgotten memory's own `supersedes` and `superseded_by` edges, **ids only**, with a cross-set target keeping its set name and losing its `keywords`, since those are free text by the same author. [File Format](documents/design/file-format.md) states it as a **narrowing** of the existing rule rather than an exception: the rule exists to keep text out, and an id is not text. `format_version` `0.3.0`, a compatible addition. **Where the fix actually went was not where the entry pointed.** The entry blamed the `ON DELETE CASCADE` and was right, but removing it is a third of it: the foreign key is gone, migrated in place while keeping the rows, and **nothing failed because every other path already cleared links explicitly** — which is why the mutation corpus is what noticed, `store: stop clearing links before rewriting` flipping from `survives` to `caught`, because a statement documented as *deliberately redundant with the cascade* had become the only thing doing the work. `forget` then decides what survives, in one statement, so the store and the file cannot disagree. **And the import path had to change too, which a store-only fix would have missed**: the reconciling import applied an arriving tombstone by calling `forget`, which derives ancestry from *this* store — and a machine adopting a set has never held the memory, so it derived none. *One thing the fix cannot do: a memory forgotten before this change left no ancestry, and chains already broken stay broken.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A fix in three parts where the entry named one, and a recorded mutation flipping from surviving to caught as the signal that a redundant statement had become load-bearing. The import half is the part a store-only fix silently omits.

content: **Pain counted as failure-record density did not separate failures from controls on 2026-10-05, a second time.** Among the 40 nearest memories, the share in an issue cluster or carrying `instance_of` was 0.40–0.70 for the 11 failure cases and 0.45–0.72 for the 6 controls, against 0.65 across the whole `scatterhoard` set. This repeats the 2026-09-29 replay's saturation, where 79% was hot, now through the product's own recall rather than TF-IDF. So one-sided valence fails on both rankers. That leaves the two-sided valence proposed on 2026-09-29 untested rather than refuted.
context: Measuring headroom for gut-feeling-recall ahead of the small-model lift experiment, the morning after the first beta.
why: Evidence against the hypothesis that the 40 nearest carry a usable warning when counted crudely, recorded because a later session might try the cheap version again. This project's memory is mostly about defects, so membership in a defect cluster says what the set is, not where the trouble is.

content: `hoard_sets calibrate` told the caller a floor "lowers itself if a query naming this set ever scores under it", and nothing did: only `Store::calibrate` writes the level, so a contradicting scoped query takes effect at the next calibration. The note described the self-lowering rule removed on 2026-09-12, the day the floor shipped. Fixed 2026-09-24, the day it was found: the note now says nothing but calibration moves the level, that a scoped query under it is silenced and counted at the next calibration, and names `ignore_floor` and `uncalibrate`. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-calibrate-note-promises-a-floor-that-lowers-itself`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Fixing the misleading calibrate note, straight after closing the out-link work; the note was read that morning when calibrating both shared sets.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed. Pinned by `a_floor_that_was_set_says_only_calibration_moves_it` in `tests/sets.rs`, the first test to reach the note on a floor that was set, and a mutation restoring the old claim. The behaviour itself was already pinned in `tests/floor.rs`; only the prose had drifted, in the note and in two doc comments — `calibrate_set` and `Store::calibrate`, the second also misdescribing the level as below the minimum rather than the 5th percentile.

content: **`is_traversable` would have walked every unknown link label: caught 2026-09-28 while building `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`, before it shipped.** Written 2026-08-18 as `!matches!(label, Supersedes | SupersededBy)`, in `src/traversal.rs`, it returned true for the new `LinkLabel::Unrecognised`. That contradicts the one rule the design kept from the closed vocabulary: nothing walks an edge it does not understand. The build raised no error, and it was found by auditing every negated label comparison after the variant went in. It is now an exhaustive match, pinned by `an_unrecognised_label_is_not_walked` and the mutation `unknown labels: walk an unrecognised label`.
context: Building `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`, the first release-gate item after `adopting-coding-lessons` closed.
why: A failure record under the coding-lessons adoption guide, part 3: this is what signposts are chosen from. It counts as a failure even though it never shipped, because the code as written was wrong the moment the variant was added, and only a manual audit caught it.

content: **A form that comes back unanswered, declined or dismissed, falls back to the name or record the model passes**, decided 2026-10-16 by the human partner so that hosts which cannot show forms can still create sets. The refusal no longer says the human declined; it says to ask in the conversation and pass the answer as `mint`'s or `rename`'s `author` or `identify`'s `record`, which is used when that call's own form also goes unanswered, with the relay sentence. A form the human answered always wins. Built in `src/mcp.rs` (`went_unanswered`), tested in `tests/asking.rs`.
context: After the first live test showed Claude Code's desktop Code tab declining every form unseen.
why: Strict, a print-mode Claude Code could never write to a new shared set. Both words count as unanswered because keying on "decline" alone would leave a client that dismisses instead looping on the question for ever, the surface-form trap the `coding-lessons` set warns of. The cost, accepted: a human who truly declines can still be named by the model, visibly.

content: **Valence for `gut-feeling-recall` should be two-sided: satisfaction as well as pain, proposed 2026-09-29.** Raised by the human partner, who observed that a signal made only of what went wrong is an unpleasant way to live. Satisfaction is what lets pain decay: failures only accumulate, so a pain-only signal grows hotter everywhere, as the first replay's 79% showed. A region that hurt once and has held up since should cool. It also says something pain cannot, *this is paved road, and here is how*, as `resolves` links do for coding-lessons. Readings: pain without satisfaction is the red flag; both together means burned and then fixed, where the fix is what to recall; neither means unexplored, not safe. Candidate markers of satisfaction: `supports` links, fixes that held without reopening, decisions long unsuperseded, part-6 records of a recall that helped, and decisions made or reviewed by the human partner. Silence alone is not a marker, since quiet can mean unvisited.
context: Discussing the first replay of `gut-feeling-recall` with the human partner.
why: This revises the valence requirement after the first replay found pain-as-topic saturated. Two-sided valence addresses the saturation structurally rather than by tuning a threshold. It also matches how expert instinct works in both directions, and it keeps the signal from pushing a session toward over-hedging.

content: The export review's pre-pass reads a date and time as a phone number, so every memory naming a checkpoint or a timestamp goes to the person. `phones` in `src/review.rs` accepts any run of three or more digit groups of two to four digits totalling ten to fifteen, and an ISO date with an hour or a `YYYY-MM-DD-HHMM` checkpoint stamp is exactly that: `2026-08-13-2255` and `2026-08-25 06` both matched. Found 2026-10-29 on the first page of the `scatterhoard` set's full review, where two of the four memories were flagged for nothing else; this project's memories cite checkpoints by stamp throughout. Fixed means a run that begins with a plausible ISO date is not a phone number, with a test for both shapes and one that a real grouped number still matches.
context: The scatterhoard set's full review, resumed after fixing the per-page recompute; collecting flags into a file for the person.
why: Head of an issue cluster. Costs: nothing wrong is published, but each false hit is put to the person in full, and a review where most flags are noise trains them to clear flags unread, which is the failure the gate exists to prevent.

content: Raised 2026-08-21 by the human partner as a question — rival projects A and B, A records something unflattering about B, B hand-edits its own memory file to supersede it — confirmed by test within the hour. **The design answer came first and it is symmetric**: [Cross-Set References](documents/design/cross-set-references.md) settles that no edge changes the standing of a memory in another set, in either direction. That replaced *an edge cannot suppress a memory it does not outrank*, which had settled local-versus-project and left project-versus-project unanswered; extending the old rule would have meant ranking two shared sets against each other, while the replacement asks one question instead — *is the target in another set?* — and no scope comparison enters the resolution path. In code, `Store::edges` stopped pushing a cross-set `SUPERSEDES` into `replaced`, `Store::incoming` gained `AND target_set IS NULL`, and the tool surface refuses such an edge at both write doors — deliberately **not** in `Store::insert`, which import shares, since an imported file is exactly where such an edge legitimately appears and must be storable and then ignored rather than rejected at the door. **The refusal is not the protection**: the attacker's file was never written by our client, so the write refusal only stops an honest client authoring one by accident, and ignoring the edge at resolution is what protects a reader.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The design decision that had to be made before the code could be written, and the distinction between a refusal that stops an honest mistake and a resolution rule that stops an attack. The write-door refusal looks like the fix and is not.

content: **Whether the charter recall should have the shape the watch recall has — resolved, and it was resolved before the question was ever filed as open.** `069f5f1` on 2026-09-06, the day the question was raised, moved the charter recall out of `route-where` and into `recall-when`: per set, at session start and on load, as summaries, one keyword and one set per call — the watch shape on all three axes. The *when* objection the question raised, that a session storing nothing still pays, was answered rather than dodged: a charter changes very rarely and says so when it does. Found 2026-09-23 by the closure audit, reading the served text against the head, which still described the pre-change arrangement.
context: The closure audit's question family, after the 18 issues.
why: Superseded to close it. The entry was migrated on 2026-09-08 carrying a present-tense claim about the served text that had been false for two days — the exact failure the audit exists to catch, and the second instance of it in this corpus after the two caught by hand on 2026-09-07. Worth noting how it survived: the change and the question were made the same day, so nothing looked stale to the session that migrated it.

content: A cross-set link was visible only from the side that wrote it: looking up a same-set target reports the backlink in `incoming`, and looking up either cross-set target reported no `incoming` at all. Fixed 2026-09-02 by gathering the rows across every loaded store into a `referenced_from` field. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-cross-set-link-has-no-derived-backlink`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order — this is the last entry in the file.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **The target list is asked three different questions and only one of them wants everything, which is why no single pruning rule works -- the analysis from 2026-08-26.** **Ancestry never enumerates the list**, looking a target up by exact key. **The `drop` and `restore` safety-copy guards want every target including dead ones**, since a stale entry there only ever refuses more, which is the safe direction. **The two remarks want only what still exists.** So every pruning rule that helps the remarks hurts something else: **pruning by absence** discards an unmounted volume's agreement, and **pruning by age** needs a per-target timestamp this design has refused once, and would prune an idle-but-live checkout -- turning a settled import into a no-ancestor one. **Measured the day it was raised: three of this machine's seven stored targets were scratch directories from finished sessions**, which is the ratio that makes the remark unreadable rather than merely long.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the three-consumers decomposition is what turns *just prune it* into a real design problem, and it is not recoverable from the symptom. Anyone reaching for a pruning rule needs to check it against all three consumers, and the two obvious rules each fail a different one.

The measurement is stated as a reading from 2026-08-26 rather than a current count -- the ratio is what matters and it will have moved, since this machine has since run many more sessions with scratch directories.

content: The author note said *"Nothing has been written to this set yet"* beside a memory count of 27, because the *store* recorded no author while every memory carried one — a migration state, not an empty set. Fixed 2026-08-11 by answering the two states separately. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `author-note-denies-writes-to-a-set-that-has-them`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: `Store::embed` filters out every memory carrying `hoard-author` — the filter that keeps identity records unembedded, keyed on a term any caller can write. So an ordinary memory using it as a *subject* keyword was stored with no vector and could never be found by meaning. Found 2026-09-06 while piloting the index design, by storing a member memory that mentioned identity records and keying it `hoard-author`. This is the reserved namespace having **behaviour** behind it rather than only membership, which is a sharper hazard than the one `reserved-keywords-carry-subject-memories` was filed against: there the cost is a stray hit in a list, here it is a memory that silently leaves semantic recall.
context: Renaming this entry's slug to take an `about-` prefix, while fixing genindex.py's positional slug pick.
why: The discovery episode, kept as written on the day: what the filter did, how it was found, and why a reserved term with code behind it is worse than one with only membership behind it. Superseded 2026-09-21 only to move it to the entry's renamed slug; the claim is unchanged.

content: Give the existing sets their identities. A procedure rather than a build — the code landed 2026-08-31 and the steps were written out in [set-lifecycle.md](documents/design/set-lifecycle.md). **Done 2026-08-31 for all three sets**: `scatterhoard` is `01M1D3K649FVTBXT6TNM0WGPS5`, `coding-lessons` is `01M1D3K649FX8V09X2KE5W8FAE`, `local` is `01M1D3K649F038Q2H2GQRHC9EK`. Both shared imports reported `adopted_set_id` with every record `unchanged` — 85 and 79 — and **re-exporting reproduced the same header, so store and file converged rather than agreed once**; `0.3.0` reached a file for the first time in the same edit. `Store` now claims an identity for `local` on its first write, so no future one needs a hand cutover. **Still open**: restoring *another machine's* `local` backup into this one, since only the scope **kind** is checked — an identity is now available to refuse it, but whether it should is the open question about what set identity gates. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `set-identity-cutover`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Test and documentation debt section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only.

Filed in the tracking file rather than left in the design document because it was decided, unbuilt work with a specific next action — which is the distinction that file exists to draw, and worth keeping since a written-out procedure in a design document reads as already handled.

content: Add an enum variant to `LinkLabel`, `Origin` or `Scope`, such as one that carries an unrecognised label string, where traversal, recall or a tool-call refusal already matches on that enum.
context: Building `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`, after `is_traversable` was found to admit the new variant.
why: A project trigger for the coding-lessons lesson on negated and catch-all predicates, in this project's nouns, because the general trigger did not surface for the sentence this session actually used before building `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`.

content: Raised 2026-08-23 by the human partner's question about hand-merging two sets, confirmed by a parked test. Merging `a` and `b` into a file declaring a **new** name imported cleanly and left every link crossing between them naming a set nobody holds. **Canonicalisation did not reach it**: that rewrites a target naming *the importing set*, and `a` is not `merged` — so the link stayed cross-set, no lookup acted on it, and a real supersession resolved to `Current`. Nothing reported it either, because the claim channel asks *other* stores, and after a merge both records are in the same one.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A failure that survives every existing report because the mechanism that would notice it asks other stores, and a merge has just put both records in one. The canonicalisation that looks like it should cover this is keyed on the importing set's own name.

content: Decided 2026-09-07: a project's own control marks live under **`hoard-proj-`**, licensed by `keyword-standards`, which now reads *"reserved for control marks -- Scatterhoard's own, and a project's own tooling under `hoard-proj-`"*. The tracking-file vocabulary moved there the same day: `hoard-proj-issue-entry`, `-issue-open`/`-fixed`/`-withdrawn`, the backlog and question families, and the `-severity-*` and `-readiness-*` facets. **The prefix is the half of the device that does the recognising**, and `about-` is only what you do once you have recognised — which is why the rule alone was not enough. `keyword-standards`' *reinforcement* needed no edit at all: it already said "what carries it lands in a list something acts on", never naming Scatterhoard as the actor, so only the `text`'s attribution was narrow.
context: A session restore found `genindex.py --check` failing on a memory that had enrolled itself as an issue entry, which opened out into where project control marks should live.
why:
The alternative was a project-owned prefix such as `track-`, needing no served text, and the LLM initially recommended it when the catalog had 18 characters free. The human partner rejected that reasoning as letting the budget drive a design decision — the visible cases can be compensated for, the invisible ones cannot — and the carve-out is better on the merits, because inheritance through the served catalog is the only channel reaching a project that does not yet know it has this problem. Copying from source, or a `coding-lessons` memory, both need someone already looking.

Paid for by cutting 367 served bytes of cross-entry duplication: `store-when`'s copy of the scope-irreversibility claim, which `route-where` carries with the asymmetry that makes it actionable and `export-before-commit` carries again as the last-gate argument, plus two `hoard-watch` sentences restating `recall-when`'s *one keyword and one set per call*. Each cut's reasoning moved into a `//` comment beside its entry, per the file's own rule that text serving a reviser is not reinforcement. The `store-when`/`correct-when` pair sharing "read by people who were not there" was deliberately **kept** — the comment on `correct-when` says the exception is the point, being where the Golden Rule reverses an answer rather than shading it. The carve-out sentence cost 65 bytes; headroom afterwards was 320, derived from `report_catalog_size`.

content: **`AGENTS.md` frames a checkpoint as an end-of-session artifact, and that is not how this project actually uses them.** Its *Session checkpoints* section says to write one at the end of a session, or whenever the human partner indicates they are wrapping up. On 2026-09-16 the human partner asked for two mid-session, explicitly for safe-keeping, in a session that then ran for hours more — and after each one the session began offering stopping points, the first before the human had said anything about time. They noticed and asked what was driving it; no session limit existed. **The candidate fix is one clause**: name mid-session safe-keeping as a legitimate occasion alongside the two already listed, which removes the inversion where it starts rather than asking a session to resist it. **Deliberately not filed as a tracking entry** — it is a wording change smaller than the entry describing it would be, and it is recorded here so the next edit to that section has it in view. Checkable in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) and in `checkpoints/2026-09-16-0057.md` and `-0318.md`, both written mid-session at the human partner's request.
context: Closing a long session, after the human partner asked why the assistant kept offering to stop.
why:
Recorded as this project's instance of a general shape kept in `coding-lessons` — an instruction binding an artifact to a phase boundary can make producing the artifact read as evidence of reaching the boundary. The general form belongs there; the fact that *this* section of *this* file has the property belongs here, per `route-where`.

Distinct from the neighbouring finding that checkpoints out-compete the memory sets at the boundary they share. That one is about *where a fact lands* — a decision the session made reads as session narrative and goes to the gitignored file. This is about what writing the file was taken to mean. The two share a subject and make different claims, so both stand.

The suggested clause is offered rather than applied: changing standing instructions mid-session is the sort of edit whose effect the author never sees, and the human partner was wrapping up.

content: **A mutation costs 2–5s run alone, about half building and half testing, measured 2026-09-28; a full pass of 553 ran at 4.9s each (44m42s).** Per mutation: library recompile 0.6–1.2s, test binary 0.5–1.9s (`sets` heaviest), the two program binaries 0.4–0.8s each, the `cargo test` step 0.4–2.6s of which about 0.4s is cargo's own startup. The pass was about 1.5× slower than the same mutations run alone, with no upward drift across it, and its three worst entries (26–36s) took under 4s when repeated, so the gap was the machine rather than the corpus. `target-mutation` held 19,377 files, ruling out silting. Half the corpus targets `sets`, which is now the main cost. Since this, `mutate.py` photographs any step taking over four times its phase's recent median, with a 6s floor.
context: Profiling why the full mutation pass for set-settled-at-first-write step 1 took 45 minutes, then adding slow-step snapshots to the runner before step 2's pass.
why: Rediscovering this took a profiling session: the runner's log records only each mutation's total, so neither the build/test split nor whether a slow entry reproduces can be read from it. Recorded so the next slow pass starts from measured costs, and from the snapshots now taken, rather than from a hypothesis about the build directory, which this and 2026-08-30 both ruled out. The half-a-second saving from running test binaries directly was declined by the human partner as too much risk for the gain.

content: Filed and withdrawn 2026-09-02. It reported that `shared:scatterhoard` held `refuse-not-remark` on three memories and `remark-not-refuse` on two, one idea split across two spellings. **They are two policies, not two spellings**: all five concern malformed-tool-call damage, the two carrying `remark-not-refuse` describe the earlier design that remarked on damage after storing it, and the three carrying `refuse-not-remark` describe the design that replaced it on 2026-08-19 — *"replacing the remark with an escape plus a refusal, in that order."* Opposite policies, the first superseded by the second, with the keyword tracking the change. `max-catalog-chars` against `MAX_CATALOG_CHARS`, the other pair the same measurement turned up, is a deliberate respelling to the constant's own name, which is what `keyword-standards` asks for. **And the subject was never severed**, which is the more general point: four of the five share `malformed-tool-call-damage-is-stored-silently`, `hoard_memorize` and `transmission-damage`, and the fifth carries the term as a cross-reference — so a search on the issue slug returns the subject whichever spelling a caller reaches for, and the split cost nothing because it was never the route.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A defect diagnosed from a keyword list and dissolved by reading the memories underneath it. Two independent errors in one reading: the terms named opposite policies, and the subject was reachable by a third keyword either way.

content: Semantic search does not substitute for exact keyword search in Scatterhoard, and this was measured rather than assumed. Queried by meaning for a term carried only as a keyword and appearing nowhere in the content, the memory holding it ranked second at 0.120 — beneath an unrelated memory at 0.136. Keywords do reach the embedding, but five tokens averaged into a paragraph-length vector barely move it, and a static embedder represents a rare identifier badly.
context: Measured 2026-08-03 against a six-memory live store while deciding whether hoard_recall should combine semantic and keyword search. The measurement is what kept both paths; the combination was removed instead. Recorded in tool-surface.md.
why: The tempting simplification is to drop the keyword path on the grounds that keywords are already in the embedding input, which is true and misleading. Exact match does work the embedding cannot — precise identifiers are exactly what a caller tags a memory with in order to find it again, and those are the tokens a static model represents worst.

content: **Scatterhoard and `coding-lessons` are both MIT-licensed, chosen by the human partner on 2026-10-04 before the first release.** Each repository carries the license as `LICENSE.md`, and `Cargo.toml` declares `license = "MIT"`. CC BY 4.0 and CC0 were raised as the more conventional licenses for a collection of text, and set aside. MIT defines "Software" as software and associated documentation files, so it covers a memory set whichever of the two it is held to be. The human partner would argue an AI prompt is software. Their main concern is liability protection, which MIT's warranty disclaimer gives.
context: Preparing the first beta release: rewriting SETUP.md and the README's quick start, checking the embedding models' licenses, and adding LICENSE files.
why: The license files record the choice but not why a text collection took a software license, and that is the question a later contributor or reviewer is likely to ask. It also notes the one licensing change that distribution would force: shipping prebuilt binaries or the embedding models would need their third-party notices.

content:
**The `used` label's session marker is `hoard_conventions`**, whose first page rolls `Server::session`, chosen 2026-09-11 once a server process was found to serve several sessions. It is what a session does first — the catalog's own description says to call it once at the start of a session, and this project's `AGENTS.md` requires it before any visible text — and paging does not roll it, since a cursor says *continue*.

**Why a real session rather than any bound**, which is the choice the human partner left open: the *about forty labelled queries* threshold was measured on transcript-bounded sessions, so a looser bound labels pairs the simulation excluded and the number stops transferring. That is the same argument that keeps amending out of the signal list.

**Its weakness is that it answers to a convention rather than to the protocol.** A session that never loads the conventions inherits the previous one's identity — the looser process-shaped bound, so a degradation rather than a break — and one that reloads them midway splits in two, losing labels rather than inventing them. Both leave the floor lower or later than it should be, which is the over-recalling end.
context: Building the `used` label for the query log; the human partner said they believed the current server was on its second session and invited the check.
why: The second half of 01M29RXHKFF70V5G06CBNT1FC1, split out on 2026-10-30 when that memory was restated at the person's request to remove their account name and no longer fit the length limit as one record. Kept because the choice of marker and its failure modes are not visible from `Server::session` alone. The claim is unchanged.

content: **The command for counting unmigrated entries was anchored to a line number, and migration is exactly what invalidates it -- caught 2026-09-07 mid-migration when the count went *up*.** The 2026-09-07 checkpoint recorded `grep -cE '^- \[[ x]\] ` + '`' + `' past line 24` for open-questions.md, which worked while the generated index held two rows. Every entry migrated adds a row *inside* the markers and removes one below, so the index region grows downward: by the sixth entry the `END GENERATED INDEX` marker had moved from line 23 to line 30, and a count starting at line 24 was including generated rows as though they were unmigrated entries. **The failure is loud only by luck.** It happened to make the number rise, which is impossible for a count of remaining work and so got noticed; had the index grown more slowly it would have merely inflated the figure and been believed. **Anchor to the marker instead:** `awk '/END GENERATED INDEX/{f=1;next} f&&/^- \[[ x]\] ` + '`' + `/{n++} END{print n}'`. This is STANDARDS.md's *cross-references must not use line numbers* rule applying to a shell command rather than to a link -- same defect, same silence, and the same fix of naming a stable landmark.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry, when the count of remaining entries rose from 35 to 39 after a deletion.
why:
Recorded because the broken command is *in a handoff document*, which is the place counting errors do the most damage: a checkpoint's numbers are believed rather than re-derived, and this one is designed to be re-run by the next session. The general rule the project already holds -- re-derive every count and say how -- does not protect against this, because re-running the stated command faithfully reproduces the wrong answer.

The instance is worth keeping beyond the fix because it shows the line-number prohibition is not really about Markdown links. It is about any reference that resolves successfully while pointing somewhere else, and a `NR>24` in a counting command is precisely that.

content:
**The derived summary is written into the exported file and surfaced again at import — and at import it must be recomputed, never read.** Decided with the human partner 2026-09-12.

**Their reasoning for import as a second surface:** if the receiving model has safeguards, the aggregate picture can engage them there too. Import is also the harder gate to skip, since a received set is useless until imported, where export can in principle be declined by anyone content with one SQLite file.

**The change that makes it work rather than backfire.** A summary stored in a file is ordinary data and can be edited before the file is shipped. If import displays what the header says, the mechanism becomes a self-attested claim that *looks* derived — the charter's `Fluffy Cat` failure again, with the authority of a measurement behind it. **So import recomputes from the memories it is actually importing, and the stored summary is treated as a claim to be checked rather than a fact to be shown.**

That turns the stored copy into something better than a label: a **checkable claim**, mirroring the charter-versus-corpus comparison one level up. It still earns its place in the file — it is readable in a git diff, reviewable without running Scatterhoard, and a record of what the set looked like when it left.

**A divergence between stored and recomputed has three causes and only one is interesting**: tampering, hand-editing of the memory file, or simply a different embedding model on the importing machine producing different clusters. The third is benign and will be the common one. **Gate the comparison on the embedding-model hash the set already records**, and where the hashes differ, recompute and show without comparing. A signal that mostly fires benignly gets ignored, and takes the rare real case with it.

**Fallback where the importing machine has no embedding model at all**: clustering is impossible, but distinctive-keyword labelling over the whole set needs no embeddings. A single unclustered label line is weaker and still worth showing.

**Possible bearing on [`evaluation-mode`](TRACKING.md)**, the open question of how to inspect a memory set without adopting it: showing what a set amounts to before it is taken may be the minimal useful form of that. Not pursued here.
context: Settling where the derived set summary lives, after measuring that keyword-labelled clusters are legible.
why:
Recorded because the recompute rule is the difference between a safeguard and a decoration, and it is the kind of thing that gets lost between a design conversation and an implementation. A stored summary read back as fact is strictly worse than no summary: it looks derived, so it carries the authority of a measurement while being a self-attested claim, which is the Fluffy Cat charter failure wearing better clothes.

The three-cause ambiguity in a divergence is recorded because the benign cause is the common one. A signal that fires mostly on model mismatch would be discarded as noise within a week, taking the rare real case with it.

Origin joint: writing the summary into the file and surfacing it at import are the human partner's; recomputing rather than trusting, and the model-hash gate, are mine.

content: **What the entry retracted, and it is the important part: do not redesign the wire format on the strength of it.** Three remedies had been proposed — a string spelling for shared scopes, splitting the scope into two flat properties, or waiting — and all three were answers to a defect the server does not have, while two would have changed a serialisation that appears in every exported file's header. **What survives**: a consumer that drops alternations exists and was reached by an ordinary configuration, so the fragility is real even though the trigger was not. The same reduction hits `links.items.properties.target`, which would make cross-set links unreachable wherever it applies — the Vision's *"manage dangling cross-references"* running through the one construct that did not survive. **Every affected point is an alternation between *shapes***; `enum`, arrays, numbers and nested objects all came through untouched, so the constraint is sum types rather than anything about JSON.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Three proposed fixes retracted along with the diagnosis that motivated them, and the narrow finding that survived: the fragile construct is a sum type specifically, not JSON structure generally.

content: Found 2026-08-02, and made materially worse by the `MemoryView` fix on 2026-08-03. Keeping the two scales in separate lists is correct and deliberate — the `coding-lessons` *"two numbers on different scales"* lesson — and the duplication was not required by that decision. Before `MemoryView`, a `by_keyword` entry was four fields against the `memories` entry's seven, so the duplication was real but cheap; afterwards both carried the memory in full and the duplicated payload roughly doubled. **Converging the three projections was still right** — the alternative was keeping a deliberately impoverished second copy to save space, which is how `why` came to be missing from the degradation path in the first place — but the entry moved from a mild annoyance to the largest remaining context cost on the surface.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A fix elsewhere that made this defect worse without being wrong. Recorded because the tradeoff is the recurring one: converging projections costs payload and removes a class of drift, and the drift is the more expensive of the two.

content: Partial coverage survived because it needs two sets and a mismatch to occur at all: with one loaded set the distinction is invisible, and every approval snapshot was complete, so there was no fixture for it. Under a per-store model this becomes the normal case rather than the exceptional one — if a store owns its model rather than inheriting the server's, two sets holding different models is a *configuration* rather than a fault, a `project ∪ local` recall answers permanently from a subset, and a message saying nothing was searched is wrong every time. That is why the entry was promoted 2026-08-20 from companion to prerequisite of `store-owns-its-model` in [BACKLOG.md](BACKLOG.md).
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Why the defect was invisible and why it was about to stop being: the condition that triggers it was a fault at the time and becomes a supported configuration under work already on the backlog, which is what moved it from companion to prerequisite.

content: Observed 2026-09-22: `ids_sort_into_creation_order` generates 1,000 ids with `MemoryId::generate` (`Uuid::now_v7`, `uuid` 1.24.0) and asserts they sort in the order made. It failed in one `cargo test --no-fail-fast` run with the suite's tests in parallel, and passed in 30 of 30 runs alone. `uuid` documents `now_v7` as ordered by creation within a process, through a shared context: a 42-bit counter reseeded each millisecond, which bumps the timestamp when it wraps. Unexamined candidates: the system clock stepping backwards mid-test, and the shared context's behaviour across threads.
context: Running the full suite after moving the gap sweep off the write path.
why: The evidence behind the issue, kept separate from its standing so later observations join it. Neither candidate was tested. The next step is a stress test generating ids on several threads while the suite runs, with the assertion printing the out-of-order pair and its timestamps.

content: Occurrences three and four, 2026-08-12, drafting `keyword-standards`, settled two things. The mechanic held with the roles moved along one: the mis-closed parameter was `why`, so `why` was polluted and `keywords` vanished — so **the field that ends up wrong is the one closed badly, and the field that is lost is the one after it**. Both swallowed parameters were optional, which is why all four were silent. **The fourth happened within a minute of the third, in a call written deliberately to avoid it, by a session that had just finished reading this entry.** That is the argument against every discipline-shaped remedy — careful emission, a checklist, a preferred parameter order — because **the failure is in emission itself and the emitter is the thing that is wrong**. The only recovery available was noticing the malformed tag in the *outgoing* text and reading the record back afterwards, which no ordinary session will do routinely.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The clearest evidence in the whole entry that care cannot fix this: a recurrence within a minute, in a call written to avoid it, by a session that had just read the description of it.

content: Import reports which memories arrived or changed, by id, when it reconciled against an earlier agreement, and reports anything secret-shaped. Decided 2026-09-25 under `imported-set-trust-boundary`, in place of an import gate. A first import from a target gives counts and `describes` only. A later pull lists new and changed ids up to a cap of about 50, then the count and a pointer to `git diff` on the memory file. The prohibited-data scan runs over what arrived and reports, never refuses. Built when `import_set` in `src/mcp.rs` returns that alongside `outcomes`, mirroring export's `replaced_file`. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `import-reports-what-arrived`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Resolving `imported-set-trust-boundary` with the human partner, on the release gate.
why: Head of a backlog cluster. Not release-gated: every part adds to the import response and changes no existing field or refusal. The first-import rule is what keeps it usable, because listing every id on a first import of a large set would cost tens of thousands of characters for identifiers that mean nothing until looked up.

content: Fixed 2026-08-30 by dissolving it rather than by declaring the refusal: `correction-gated-on-service` removed the refusal altogether, so `content` and `why` are ordinary amendable fields on a record that never entered service and both are declared in the published schema — the field a validating client used to strip is one it now sends, and what it reaches is a capability rather than a message. The replacement refusal keys on the record's history instead of on a field name, so **it cannot be stripped by anything**: an argument a client removes cannot change the answer. **The test route is the durable part, and is what the entry actually asked for**: `tests/correct.rs` builds `amend_as_a_client`, which reads `hoard_correct`'s published properties out of `tools/list` and drops every argument the schema does not declare before sending — the client behaviour that produced this defect, run as a test helper. Two mutations pin it: inverting the service check, and accepting `content` while removing its schema property, which is this defect reproduced in a new place and now fails four tests instead of none. *The two ways out the entry offered were both overtaken: declaring the fields was done, but not "in order to be refused" — they are declared in order to work.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the test helper worth copying: a client that strips undeclared arguments, built from the published schema, so a guard unreachable through the real transport fails rather than passes. Also the design lesson — keying a refusal on record history rather than on a field name makes it unstrippable.

content: **The case that was expected to force the third raise did not force it -- update 2026-09-04, and the first time the cheaper answer was actually attempted.** `investigation-pipeline` was the convention the *second* raise had been made for, and the one expected to overrun the budget. It never shipped as itself: a seed and a trap turned out to be the same object, so it merged into `hoard-watch` and **one convention replaced two**. The merged draft still overran the free space by 237 characters, and that was closed by trimming **363 characters of justifying reinforcement from `split-when-partly-stale`**, which an audit had measured at 79% justifying -- removing no rule. **So the estimate that made a raise look inevitable was an artifact of counting two conventions**, and the standing objection that a budget raised whenever it binds is not a budget remains unspent.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
The load-bearing part is that the forcing case dissolved for a reason nobody could have predicted -- two planned conventions turning out to be one -- which is evidence about *estimating* catalog pressure rather than about this budget: a forecast built by summing planned conventions counts objects that may not survive drafting.

Equally important is that the cheaper answer was tried and worked. Before this, trimming justification was the theoretical alternative the previous question had priced at 164 characters and nobody had spent; 363 characters from one entry, removing no rule, is more than double that and came from a single audit-identified target.

content: Scatterhoard's investigation pipeline has one repeated move rather than three distinct stages: accumulate a small cluster of related memories and wait for shape. Observations cluster until a pattern appears and suggests a line of investigation; that level accumulates until the question becomes *precise*; then hypotheses and evidence accumulate against the precise question until it has an answer. The mechanic that carries it is a **seed memory** whose reasoning says that on meeting a relevant case, the action is to link a new memory to this one rather than to rewrite it — because rewriting collapses the distribution, and the distribution is the finding. Conventions are what make the pattern findable and consistent across sessions and across developers; they are not what make it possible, since a seed can be written with plain `hoard_memorize` today.
context: Said 2026-08-29 at the end of the session that reworked the corrections design. The pipeline is `investigation-pipeline` in BACKLOG.md, Ready and undrafted since 2026-08-09; this session appended the mechanic to that entry. The seed that prompted the observation lives in the `local` set and is deliberately not linked from here, since a cross-set link into a personal set would dangle for every other reader.
why: Stated by the human partner on 2026-08-29 after noticing that a memory stored minutes earlier for an unrelated reason — a future-project idea, written as a seed so instances could attach to it — was the pipeline's observation-and-puzzle stage already running unprompted. That matters for drafting: the convention has a working instance to copy rather than a design to invent, and it needs to achieve less than assumed, which is an argument for drafting it small against a catalog budget it was expected to overrun. Two gaps are what formalising must close — which keywords mark a memory as belonging to a given cluster, so the cluster can be recalled as a cluster instead of by remembering the seed's id; and how the accumulation instruction is expressed at all, since today it sits in prose inside one memory's reasoning and is therefore invisible to anyone who has not already recalled it.

content: **The data-only rule is enforced by structure plus a statement in the convention catalog, never by inspecting content.** Decided by the human partner on 2026-09-25, settling the last of `imported-set-trust-boundary`'s sub-questions. The structure is in place: nothing instruction-shaped loads from a checkout, and what a watch mark can do and `route-where`'s overrides are fixed in the compiled catalog. What was missing, found that day, is that no served convention tells the model a recalled memory is data. The rule lived only in `documents/design/trigger-and-loading.md` and code comments, and `hoard-watch` states it for one case only. The statement goes into the catalog, most likely as a clause in `recall-when`. Built as `data-only-rule-in-the-catalog`.
context: Working through the release-gated questions: `imported-set-trust-boundary`, last of its four sub-questions, after declining the personal-set exemption, an import gate and provenance weighting.
why: Detection was rejected because it cannot tell an injection from a legitimate preference, and a personal preference is directive-shaped by nature. The human partner rejected attaching the sentence to each result: it would multiply with every recall and fade into noise, and the server cannot tell when a session starts, so it cannot say it only once. Tool descriptions were weighed and cost nothing per call, but lost for three reasons. The catalog is where rules about using memory live. A second copy would be the `a-fact-restated-by-hand-drifts` shape. And the catalog arrives before any memory does. Without the statement, whether a memory saying "run this" is treated as data depended entirely on the client.

content: **Four unifying explanations refuted on 2026-09-08/09, and the fourth closes the family: no surface feature of a query predicts its score.** (1) **`why` in the embedding input** — killed by its own control. (2) **Question form** — question-shaped nonsense reaches p90 0.192 against real off-domain 0.275. (3) **Word-level lexical overlap** — r² 0.100. (4) **Subword overlap**, run at the granularity the model actually uses (WordPiece over a Bert pre-tokenizer, 63091 tokens): **mean share r² 0.113, max share r² 0.012, rho 0.073.** The *max* statistic — the single-strongest-constituent theory that motivated the test — is the worst of all, because max is saturated by stopwords: `the` has 100% document frequency, `in` 84%, so question-shaped nonsense carries the highest max share of any family (0.9966) and the lowest score (0.150). **Two specific predictions failed outright**: `>` is only **4%** document frequency, so `>>> <<< ||| ~~~ ^^^` at 0.478 is not a frequency effect; and `stale`, at 10%, is worth 0.110 by minimal pair. **Frequency is the wrong weighting** — what matters is a token's direction, which is the embedding, which is where we started. Re-run `probe_whether_subword_overlap_predicts_the_score`.
context: Running the subword test agreed at the end of the long recall session, immediately after checkpointing and committing the rest.
why:
Supersedes the three-refutation record, which carried the subword test as its one outstanding caveat; that caveat is now discharged, and keeping one coherent record beats a second half-record beside it. Superseded rather than amended because the original was exported and committed in `33866e3`.

The convergence is the finding, and it is worth more than any single refutation. Eight mechanisms computed *from the score* have failed, and four predictors computed *from the text* have now failed too. The quantity that separates an answerable query from an unanswerable one is reachable from neither side: not by rescoring the embedding, and not by any surface property of the query — words, subwords, frequency, question form, or class of meaning.

**That argues for a decision rather than more investigation.** A per-store calibrated floor is empirical by construction: it measures where unanswerable queries actually land in one store and puts a line under them, and it needs no account of *why* they land there. Four failed theories are evidence that no such account is cheaply available, which makes the atheoretical option the right shape rather than a retreat. It also fits what the human partner said the feature is for — each store not spending cycles on answers it cannot give, with no claim that the number means anything in another store.

Confidence 0.9 on the refutations, which are direct measurements with named counter-examples. There is still no positive account, and none is claimed.

content: **The watch trigger recalls one keyword and one set per call, and both survived its 2026-09-17 rewrite.** One keyword per call, because a summary hit is an id and a line, and the call is what says which of the three actions its entries want. One set per call, for the per-set allowance and to keep the response inline.
context: Building the signpost half of read-only mode, after read-only itself was finished. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the memory was over the length limit.
why: Split from the record of the rewrite, because this reasoning survives it and is not visible in the new text: a later edit that batches the marks into one call would lose which action each hit wants, and nothing in the catalog would say so.

content: **Claude Desktop rewrites `claude_desktop_config.json` from its own in-memory copy, so a hand edit made while the app runs can be undone.** Observed 2026-08-11: a server entry deleted by hand reappeared, with the top-level keys reordered, which is the signature of the application serialising its copy over the file. The dependable order is quit, edit, launch. A Claude Code session running inside the app dies with it, so a session cannot do both halves itself. `SETUP.md` step 5 carries the instruction; this is the evidence behind it.
context: Rewriting SETUP.md for the first beta release, after the coding-lessons revision.
why: Moved out of `SETUP.md` on 2026-10-04, when it was rewritten as a lean guide for beta testers and its history went to the memory set. The instruction survives there, and the observation it rests on belongs here, where a later doubt about it can be checked against what was seen.

content: **`local` is reviewed against the person's own sharing preferences but not gated, and the reminder that it needs a review comes at session start.** Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. A `local` export writes everything, and reports what is unreviewed, never-store hits and `describes`. `hoard_conventions` says when `local` holds unreviewed memories, so the session can raise the review then and again later.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public: the file on disk is the clearance record, and the review must not depend on git.
why: A backup must be complete. But aggregation and category leaks show only in a review: no single `governance-docs` memory was a concern on 2026-10-17 while seventy were, and a small model stored "a recurring medical appointment" past the word list. The human partner's car analogy explains the timing. A maintenance light at engine start is forgotten by arrival, and a notice in a backup made while signing off is forgotten by the next session. Session start is when the agent is present to act on it. Restated before publication to use the set's published pseudonym.

content: Fixed 2026-08-25 by `resolve_within`, which answers what a store's own `resolve_supersession` cannot: whether the set a concession names is among those the call is searching. When it is, and it holds the id, the concession resolves like any other — the replacement is returned in the conceding memory's place with `matched` naming what yielded — and the chain is followed inside that set, so a replacement that was itself corrected resolves to the correction. The flag now means only what it says: no replacement can be produced, whether because the set is unloaded, or loaded and lacking the id, or holding something itself out of reach. **Three surfaces, one function, deliberately**: semantic recall, keyword search and lookup all report a standing, and a concession honoured by one and disowned by another is `lookup-and-recall-disagree-on-shape` again. Lookup stays exempt from *substitution* — asking by id means wanting that memory — so what changed there is only that it names the replacement instead of declaring it out of reach. One mutation covers all three and is caught by a test at each.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the placement: the question is about the call's scope rather than a store's contents, so it cannot be answered inside a store. Routing three surfaces through one function is what stops them disagreeing about a standing.

content:
**Numbering a memory's sentences closed `gemma4:12b`'s misses on the export review's two questions.** Tested 2026-10-23 with `scripts/local_model.py classify`, 3 runs each, on invented memories:
- Alone, whole: 9 misses, all details after a harmless first sentence, plus rent not read as finances.
- Alone, numbered: 0 misses, 3 false alarms.
- In realistic subject groups: 0 misses either way. Whole gave 6 false alarms, numbered gave 9.

Every false alarm was the `local` carve-out not being applied, except one where "users" was read as someone else. Answers came back complete only once a JSON schema required one per memory. The logs are in that session's scratchpad, `classify-*`.
context: Testing the export review's per-memory questions on a small model before the judgement gate is built.
why: A routine review is often one or two new memories, which is the isolated case where whole-memory questions failed. So the review should number sentences and ask per sentence. It also shows that the server must not trust a small model to answer every memory it is shown: without a schema requiring completeness, gemma answered only each group's first memory. The carve-out false alarms point at how the template words it.

content: The link labels Scatterhoard actually gets written appear to be the ones whose target id the workflow already put in hand, rather than the ones that best describe the relation. SUPERSEDES is written because recall-before-storing and correct-when march the caller to the target first, so its id is already held; RELATED_TO is written about whatever happens to be in context. MOTIVATED_BY, SUPPORTS and INSTANCE_OF each require stopping to search for a memory the caller is not otherwise looking at, and none of the three has ever been written.
context: Inferred 2026-08-14 from the live link-label distribution, not tested. Testable by whether labels other than SUPERSEDES and RELATED_TO start appearing once a link can be written without a separate lookup.
why: If this holds, the label scarcity is a workflow property rather than a judgement that the relations are absent, and it would not be fixed by better guidance about choosing labels. It also means any traversal design fitted to the current distribution is fitted to what the tool surface makes cheap. Recorded as a reading to check rather than a finding: it explains the distribution without being compelled by it, and no alternative explanation has been tested.

content: The third raise of the catalog budget was expected and did not happen. `investigation-pipeline` was named as the convention most likely to force it, and instead it merged into `hoard-watch` -- one convention replacing two, because a seed and a trap turned out to be the same object. The merged draft overran the free space by 237 characters, and that was closed by attempting the cheaper answer for the first time: trimming 363 characters of justifying reinforcement out of `split-when-partly-stale`, which the reinforcement audit had measured at 79% justifying, with no rule removed. The catalog stood at 17,875 of 18,000 with 125 free on 2026-09-05, and the two deferral conditions were never tested, because the overrun the raise was being held for did not arrive. For the current figure run `report_catalog_size`, which is the authoritative source.
context: Landing the watch convention and finding it would not fit, then working out whether to trim, harvest or raise. The same evening had rewritten the context field's description and retired the recall-gloss convention.
why: Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule, which moves a memory discussing a `hoard-` mechanism out of the reserved space. The catalog figure is also dated rather than left reading as current, since it moved twice the next day -- the same stale-structural-claim failure this corpus met elsewhere the same afternoon.
