content: The merge driver holds all three sides of a memory file, plus the merged output, in memory at once — the one path left that materialises a whole set. `merge::merge_files` reads base, ours and theirs into maps and builds the result in a `Vec<u8>`, against the streaming requirement [file-format.md](documents/design/file-format.md) settles for reading and writing. Built when the merge reads the three sides in lockstep in `file_position` order, holding a record per side, and falls back to the whole-file path only for a side that is not in file order. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `streaming-merge-driver`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Discussing whether the hash that orders memory files should live in the store, after restoring from the 2026-09-22 checkpoint. The pre-release review of Open questions is the stretch this interrupts.
why: Decided by the human partner on 2026-09-22, prompted by a different memory system whose backups began failing past about 700 memories because the backup held the whole store in RAM. The file-format design already requires reading and writing to stream; the merge driver was never brought under it. Ranked ahead of `file-position-column` because it is the only path that holds whole sets, several at once.

content: **Agent-supplied test sentences for a language are kept in the set itself, and so are recommended models.** Decided by the human partner on 2026-10-04. Sentences live in the set so every copy scores the language the same way and a maintainer can review them. A recommended model lives in the set so that a community that finds a model working for its language, Apache speakers for example, can pass that on with the set. A README would let it become separated from the set. Undecided: the reserved marks, the content format, and how status uses a recommendation.
context: Building the declared-language check for `recall-is-latin-script-only`, after the built-in eight languages shipped uncommitted; deciding what to do for a language the server has no sentences for.
why: Kept on one machine, the same set could score 4 on one machine and 7 on another, which is the confusion the check exists to prevent. Kept in a separate file, a recommendation stops travelling with the set as soon as someone copies only the set.

content: **The fork procedure, used as a rename that keeps `set_id`, was run end to end on 2026-10-18 on a throwaway set in an isolated test home.** It works. The steps: export the set to a file, edit the header's `scope` (an object, `{"shared":"<name>"}`) to the new name and leave `set_id` alone, `drop` the old set with `save_to`, `create` the new name, `import` the edited file. The import reported `adopted_set_id` with the original identity, and the charter, the memories and the internal links all arrived. What it does not carry is machine state held in the dropped database. That is: the author claim, which `identify` with the author record's id restores; the query log and labelled queries, which are gone, and for `governance-docs` that is 102 logged queries; and the export bases, so the first export afterwards reconciles against nothing. A memory in another set that links into the renamed set names the old set, and there is one such link from `local` into `governance-docs`.
context: Deciding how to handle the memories naming the governance set in the publication review: testing a set rename on a throwaway set in the test instance before considering it for the real one.
why: Member of the question cluster, an observation from the test. It records what a rename would cost today, which is what deciding the question turns on. It also records the one non-obvious step in the procedure, that `scope` in the header is an object, which a string edit can miss.

content: A whole-file read returned less than the file held and said nothing: `memory_file::read` kept only memories and dropped every tombstone, so a caller could not tell a file with no tombstones from a file whose tombstones were discarded. Fixed across 2026-08-25 and 2026-08-26 by making `MemorySet` carry both shapes. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `memory-file-read-silently-discards-tombstones`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order, at the reduced depth.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Ask the human through their client for a name only they have, rather than taking it from the model. **Built 2026-10-15**: protocol revision 2026-07-28 served beside the handshake revisions, with a shared set's first write and `mint`, `rename` and `identify` asking the human through an elicitation form where the client declares one, and the relay fallback everywhere else. Whether a real client shows the form is in EARLY-VALIDATION.md. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `asking-the-human`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Implementing the elicitation proposal end to end at the human partner's request, after shipping its relay fallback.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because the entry was built. Not proven: every test and the smoke test build their requests from the specification, and no real client has driven the form yet, which is why the validation entry exists.

content:
Swept 2026-09-12 over both stores' real query history, walked forward against the 601 off-domain probes — `probe_sweep_a_windowed_percentile_floor`. It reproduces the earlier measurement where they overlap: at the minimum with no margin it reports 62.7% and 66.2% of probes silenced, against 62.7% and 66.7% recorded for the old rule.

**Moving from the minimum to the 5th percentile, at a 0.05 margin:** `scatterhoard` goes from 0% of labelled queries lost and 39.8% of probes silenced to **1.5% lost and 74.4% silenced**; `coding-lessons` from 0% and 48.4% to **7.0% and 83.2%**. Past 0.05 the cost climbs faster than the benefit on both. Recalibrating every 20 new labels loses 6.2% of the labelled queries that follow where every 40 loses 15.6% — more frequent tracking is better, measured rather than assumed.

**The floor demonstrably moves both ways now**: on `coding-lessons` with a 40-query window the level runs 0.307 up to 0.469 and back down across three recalibrations, which the minimum rule could not do at all.

**Two things the sweep cannot settle, and the numbers should not be read as though it did.** Both stores hold fewer labelled queries than the window, so 100 and unbounded are the same configuration there — the window size is chosen as *a few weeks at 19-20 labelled queries a week*, not measured. And the simulated corpus is frozen at what each set holds today while the real one grew underneath those queries, so a rule that tracks a growing store looks identical here to one that does not — which is the property windowing exists for.
context: Finishing the floor: the sweep the human partner asked for before any constant was baked in.
why: The numbers that chose the constants, kept with what they cannot support. A later session tuning `FLOOR_PERCENTILE` or `QUERY_LOG_KEPT` will find a measurement behind one of them and nothing behind the other, and should know which is which before trusting either.

content: Decided 2026-08-03 by the human partner: preserve case in the stored keyword, keep lookup case-insensitive, and revisit a case-sensitive *option* only if ambiguity turns out to bite in practice. Two memories differing only in keyword case will both be returned by a case-insensitive search, which is the acceptable direction to be wrong in — a case-sensitive default would silently hide one of them.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The decision and the asymmetry behind it: returning too much is visible to the caller, and returning too little is not.

content: **What decided this was not convenience but whether the escape hatch survives base retirement -- the criterion, from the proposal on 2026-08-31.** Export-edit-import is the only route to bulk re-attribution today, and it works *only because a base exists*: if the base goes, re-attribution has to become a supersession or stop being possible altogether. Making the author a reference is what keeps it possible, because then re-attribution is one supersession of one record rather than a rewrite of every record naming the author. **The window was the other half of the argument, and it was a closing one.** Changing the shape of `by` moves every record's checksum, which is free only while no second store holds these sets -- true then, false from the first push -- so it belonged with the record-shape batch rather than after it. **Attribution is the one part of a settled record that legitimately changes afterwards**: everything else about a memory is a claim its author made at a moment, while the name they publish under is a fact about them that can change without anything having been wrong.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the criterion generalises past this field. *Does the escape hatch survive base retirement* is the right question for any bulk-edit path the design currently leans on, and export-edit-import is leaned on in more than one place.

The window argument is recorded because it has now closed differently than expected -- the sets still have no second store, but the reasoning was about the first push, not about a date -- and a later session weighing another record-shape change needs the same test rather than this conclusion.

content: **A review page shows a superseded memory with nothing marking it superseded, so a reviewer can take stale text for current.** Observed 2026-10-29 during the `scatterhoard` full review. The page served the `release-gate` signpost `01M1YDWQ13F88AQ62HZMN8FN8K`, which says neither repo has a remote. The reviewing session flagged it as stale and proposed superseding it, but it had already been superseded twice, most recently by `01M55S919RFTHREXY0V18P53D2`. Only `hoard_lookup`'s `superseded_by` showed that. Reviewing superseded records is correct, since their text still travels in the export. What is missing is a marker on the page saying the record is superseded.
context: Restoring the scatterhoard full review from a checkpoint, flagging memories about the person, and setting idleCompaction off in the project's Claude settings.
why: The reviewer almost acted on the old text: it proposed a supersession, and told the person a correction was needed when none was. The review's job is sharing-preferences checking, but a reviewer reads every claim and will notice staleness. A `superseded` marker on each such record costs nothing and stops that noticing from turning into wrong work. Filed as an observation and not yet as an issue entry, because the session was near the end of its context.

content: Do not quote Scatterhoard's convention catalog size from a document; derive it. The enforced figure is what `catalog_fits_context_budget` in tests/conventions.rs sums — `id + text + reinforcement` over every entry — and it is not the same as the paging measure, `text + reinforcement`, which is 166 characters smaller because the ten ids are excluded. On 2026-08-29 the enforced total was 16,988 of 18,000 with 1,012 free, and the paging measure 16,822. Three design-document sites recorded 16,978 and 1,022, which was wrong, and the paging figure beside it did not reconcile with it either, so two figures were adrift at once and their errors partly hid each other.
context: Re-derived 2026-08-29 while recording the corrections rework, by running the catalog-size report added beside the budget test. The figures were corrected in documents/design/conventions.md and in two places in documents/design/open-questions.md at the same time. Re-derive again rather than quoting this number; it changes whenever the catalog does.
why: This is the second time this one field has gone stale in a design document, which is what makes it worth a memory rather than a fix. Two measures of one catalog differ by a constant, so a figure copied from the wrong one looks plausible against the other, and the discrepancy reads as the known 166-character gap instead of as an error. The durable answer is the derivation, not the number: the general lessons are already held in coding-lessons, so what this adds is the project-specific instrument and which of the two measures the budget test actually enforces. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 2 links an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.

content: A memory set's `hoard-scope-topics` charter does two jobs and only one is written on purpose: its belongs-here test decides which set a memory goes to, while its description of the subject silently decides which *kinds* of thing get written at all. Measured 2026-08-24 over 105 memories: both live charters carry a good boundary test and neither test mentions kinds, yet `coding-lessons` -- described as "how work goes wrong, and what to do differently" -- is dominated by method, and `shared:scatterhoard` -- described as decisions, measurements, defects and constraints -- holds almost none, under the same `store-when`. Acted on the same day: `store-when` lost its enumeration and `route-where` gained guidance that a charter must describe its subject rather than list the kinds of record it takes.
context: Measured 2026-08-24 by classifying every live memory in both exported sets against its set's charter. Checkable at ROUTE_WHERE and STORE_WHEN in src/conventions/catalog.rs and the "Resolved 2026-08-24: a charter is a description, not a catalogue" section of documents/design/conventions.md.
why: This supersedes the version stored hours earlier, which said three hand-written enumerations of what is worth storing were in force -- `store-when`'s five and one per set. That is no longer true: `store-when`'s are cut and the convention now tells charter authors not to write such a list, so the remaining two are the ones already in the sets and both are candidates for the revisit clause. The finding itself is unchanged and is what redirected the fix: the 2026-08-15 miss that raised the open question was a Scatterhoard-specific measurement procedure, and editing `store-when` alone would not have caught it, because `route-where` sends every candidate to be matched against its set's charter. Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claim is unchanged. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 1 link an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.

content: A query the corpus could not answer came back with confident-looking results and nothing marked them: *premier league offside rule interpretation* returned two memories about Corporations Code committees at `0.420` and `0.390`. Fixed 2026-09-24 in two parts: busy sets have a calibrated non-match floor that says *nothing here answers that*, and when every floored set declines and only sets without a floor answer, recall marks those hits as possibly background (`note-when-only-uncalibrated-sets-answer`). The remaining false match is now reported rather than presented as an answer. No floor removes it on `governance-docs`, where it scores at that set's background for any off-topic question. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `an-unanswerable-query-returns-confident-hits`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building the note for answers only from sets without a floor, the day the closure test after calibration showed the issue's case was not a calibration problem.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because its fixed-when is met: *nothing here answers this* is now something a recall can say, by floor where a set has one and by note where it does not. Fixed rather than withdrawn although the offside query still returns its two memories unscoped — they now carry the mark, which is what the defect lacked. The investigation into why such a query scores high stays open: this fix reports the case, and nothing yet explains it.

content: SETUP.md called `SCATTERHOARD_HOME` optional with a Unix default and said nothing for Windows, where it is how the server gets a home at all. Fixed 2026-09-30: SETUP.md now says the variable is optional where the system sets `HOME`, and tells Windows users to set it. A desktop-started server there has no default and refuses to start, and one started from Git Bash or MSYS would otherwise pick a different directory. It asks for the same directory in every client, written out in full, since a client configuration may not expand `%APPDATA%`. Not run on Windows. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `setup-calls-scatterhoard-home-optional-on-windows`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing the stranded-local-store issue with the human partner and committing the cookbook work; they asked for this SETUP.md line to go in the same commit.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed as its fixed-when asked: SETUP.md tells Windows users to set `SCATTERHOARD_HOME`. The code needed no change; the variable was designed for PC-descended systems, as the human partner explained when the issue was filed. The full-path advice is a precaution, not a measurement: nothing here has tested whether a given client expands environment variables in its server configuration.

content: Half of the explicit form was built. Built 2026-08-25, minutes after being filed: `import` takes the same `Destination` alternation as `export`, **sharing one type rather than two matching implementations, because the two ends must agree about what a target *is* or the round trip finds no ancestor**. Export's target is where it *wrote*; import's is where it *read*. **The settling test is the one that proves it**: an export and an import through one explicit file report `unchanged`, which is reachable only when the import found the base the export wrote — identical content with no base reconciles as `converged` instead, so the assertion fails exactly when the two forms disagree. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `import-cannot-name-the-file-export-wrote`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Test and documentation debt section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only.

**One rule got stronger by being shared.** An explicit `file` inside `scatterhoard_mem` was refused on export because it hand-places a file in a namespace trusted from its path alone. On import the same refusal has a second and quieter reason: the well-known file is reachable by **both** forms, and the forms are two reconciliation targets, so one file named both ways would carry two independent records of what was last agreed — reading as settled by one spelling and diverged by the other.

content:
**The export gate now routes rather than denies, and the rewording is guarded by a test and a mutation.** Until 2026-09-09 the refusal read *"can no longer be corrected … **Supersede** it instead … correction is for a record that never entered service"* — three denials in one message. It now reads *"memory X has entered service — a second durable copy of it exists — so the instrument here is supersession"*, with amendment named positively as the instrument for a record nobody else holds yet, and both called ordinary.

**The mechanism did not change and must not.** The gate is a fact about the record, both operations are correct for their own case, and all that moved is which case the message says this is.

**Storage was checked and ruled out with a figure rather than a feeling**, since the human partner asked: a supersession costs about **1.9 KB** in the committed memory file plus a **2 KB** vector, roughly 4 KB, against a 5.2 MB store. Sixty superseded records stand in the set, 7.8% of it. The only ongoing effect is that their vectors stay in the brute-force scan and are collapsed to their tips afterwards — compute of no consequence at this scale, and the design admits brute force to about 100k.

`the_export_gate_names_the_instrument_rather_than_refusing` in `tests/correct.rs` asserts the message names the instrument, says what to do, and contains none of *no longer*, *cannot*, *not allowed* or *refused*. A mutation restoring the old opening is caught.
context: The human partner asking that the refusal be reworded while the diagnosis was still fresh, having also asked whether storage was a real contributor.
why:
Recorded because the change is to tone alone and tone is the kind of thing an edit erases without noticing — which is why it is pinned by a test and a mutation rather than by a comment asking for care. Nothing else in the suite pins wording, so the guard could otherwise be deleted with every test still passing.

**It is worth being precise about what this repairs.** A message can carry a belief that no rule states: this one taught a session that supersession is an expensive fallback, and that belief survived long enough to produce a filed design question with three alternatives, none of which was needed. The cost premise came from the string, not from the system. That is a strong argument for treating user-facing text in a tool a model reads as *behaviour* rather than as presentation, and for guarding it accordingly.

The blunt substring check is deliberate. It cannot be argued with, and it caught the replacement's own flourish — *"a fact you cannot see from where you stand"* — which was not a denial of the operation but tripped the rule anyway. Cutting the phrase was cheaper than loosening the guard, and the message is tighter for it.

content: A mutation recorded `caught` was not: deleting the `folded` column backfill left the whole suite green, because a later repair in the same `open` covers exactly the rows the backfill would have filled, so no test ever observes the state the mutation reached. Fixed 2026-08-25 by a test that plants a keyword the current constructor cannot parse. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-folded-column-backfill-is-untested-and-the-corpus-calls-it-caught`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content:
**Real recall queries are mostly not questions, and matching their form improves the probe set measurably.** Measured over the 142 harvested `hoard_recall` calls: **18.3% interrogative, 40.8% declarative, 40.8% bare noun phrase — and not one of the 142 ends in a question mark.** Every probe set built for this entry until now was 100% interrogative with a question mark on every item, which is a form mismatch with the traffic it stands in for. Rebuilding the public-domain probe set to the measured mix (`corpus/offdomain-probes.json`, 601 probes from seven 1899–1922 books):

| probe set | median | p90 | silenced at p90 | cost to real queries | AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| questions only, notes | 0.294 | 0.395 | 88.1% | **13.4%** | 0.957 |
| questions only, fiction | 0.290 | 0.394 | 84.2% | 13.4% | 0.951 |
| **mixed form, public domain** | 0.260 | **0.363** | 84.1% | **5.6%** | **0.962** |

**Same silencing for less than half the cost, and the best AUC yet.** Noun phrases are cut from a sentence's **subject**, not its predicate — real queries look like `reduced detail on the wire`, which is subject-shaped, where predicate cuts give fragments like `been the mark of the leisure`. Statements and phrases come from expository prose only: a novel's first-sentence-of-a-line is a fragment of speech, though its dialogue questions remain usable.
context: The human partner asking whether Scatterhoard queries are written as questions, and suggesting topic sentences be converted to search terms.
why:
Recorded because the form mismatch was invisible until the human partner asked whether recall queries are written as questions — a question about how the tool is actually used, not about the measurement, and it turned out to bear on the measurement more than anything measured that hour. Every probe set in this investigation had been interrogative because *probe* and *question* had been treated as synonyms.

**The privacy machinery gained a rule worth keeping.** Cutting a phrase from a sentence strips whatever preceded the subject, which can leave a proper noun exposed at index zero — where the filter deliberately does not look, since a sentence's first word is capitalised for being first. `Hull-House, however, before it` passed until the distinction was drawn. Phrases are now checked from the first word, and statements are checked against a set built from the document itself: every word it ever writes in lower case. A common word capitalised only for standing first appears in lower case elsewhere; a name does not. That closed 816 further probes, and it required no list of names to be written down in advance.

**One deliberate exception**, at the human partner's request: `Do I dare to eat a peach?` is in the set, keeping the question mark that nothing else has, as a nod to the period the rest is drawn from.

Confidence 0.9: measured through the shipping scorer against 142 independently harvested real queries, on one corpus and one model.

content: **Whether `CLAUDE.md` should be committed to the repository, and what the practice is for agent-steering files generally.** Raised 2026-08-26 by the human partner, after a personal working preference was deliberately kept *out* of the committed file and put in user-level configuration instead. **Narrowed the same day: the question is whether the *whole* file should travel, not whether any of it should.** Two things are settled and are not what is being asked -- asking a user to add a *load the conventions first* boot prompt to whatever steering file their client reads is reasonable, and the project facts in the file plainly should reach a collaborator. **Substantially advanced 2026-09-07** by splitting the file into `AGENTS.md` and a client-specific `CLAUDE.md`, and by establishing that committing is the documented arrangement with `CLAUDE.local.md` as the contributor's override. **What remains open is the security half:** a committed steering file is instruction-shaped text arriving by `git pull`, loaded unconditionally by the agent harness with no gate of any kind, where conventions get a threat model and this file gets none. That the project also *contains* the memory tool makes it concrete: a contributor's pull request can edit the instructions the reviewing agent runs under. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `claude-md-in-the-repository`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order, on the same day the entry's subject was acted on.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

**This head sorts last in its own cluster**, and that is a known consequence rather than an error. Two members were stored earlier on 2026-09-07 -- the split being performed, and the etiquette check -- before the entry was migrated, so their ids precede the head's and a single-keyword recall returns the head after them. Nothing can reorder it; ids are minted at write time. A reader should take the head by its content rather than by its position here.

The security half is carried in the head because it is now the *only* open part, and a session reading a row that says *substantially advanced* would otherwise reasonably assume the entry is nearly closed.

content: The export review's judgement gate: nothing in a shared set is exported until a review has cleared it against the person's sharing preferences. Built 2026-10-24 to 2026-10-26, as designed in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*: a mechanical pre-pass, the model's per-sentence answers, routing by the server, and the person deciding what is flagged. Revised before it was first committed, so that a sentence about a person also says whether it reports or judges, and the person's keep-outs govern what is said about anyone else. Its first run was on this project's own set. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `export-review-judgement-gate`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing out the judgement gate's build before its first commit, after reviewing and exporting the scatterhoard set with it.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded as built: claim and standing only, and the opening sentence is the generated index row. The superseded head also noted that a per-project first-encountered flag, so a suspicious file in a memory directory is mentioned once on first meeting a project, needed a home when this was built. That was not checked during this build, so it is still owed.

content: **Declare a set's languages as keywords on its charter, and give them something to read them.** Decided 2026-09-11 by the human partner and recorded in `documents/design/memory-data-model.md` under *Resolved 2026-09-11: a set declares its languages on its charter*: language tags ride on the `hoard-scope-topics` memory as `hoard-lang-*` keywords, so they travel through export and appear in the JSON a maintainer reviews. **Missing:** all of it — nothing in `src/` knows about languages, and `hoard_sets` action `create` prompts for a charter without asking for one. **Built looks like:** the `hoard-lang-` family recognised as control marks, which the `reserved-keyword-block-list` entry's list of known marks then has to include; `create`'s instruction asking for the declaration; `hoard_sets status` naming any set whose declared languages the loaded model does not cover; and the coverage test that report needs, derived from the model's own vocabulary by script rather than from a table of model names — the same test the write-door check wants. **To settle while building:** which tag vocabulary, whether a script histogram over the memories cross-checks the declaration, and whether an undeclared set is reported at all. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `charter-declares-set-languages`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Deciding how a set should say what language it is written in, after making the multilingual model a supported alternative and before returning to the recall floor.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. Ready rather than blocked, and the split is worth stating: the declaration's first purpose is the one the human partner named — a standard a project sets and a maintainer reviews — and that needs no coverage test at all, only the keywords and the prompt that asks for them. The consuming checks do need one, and it is undesigned, so expect this entry to be built in two parts rather than one.

The decision and the argument behind it are in the resolved question `store-declares-its-language` and are not repeated here.

content: **How the link key was widened, 2026-09-15.** Filed from the schema, confirmed by `two_links_to_one_id_in_different_sets_both_survive`. `target_set` joined the key, with a partial unique index over `(source, label, target) WHERE target_set IS NULL` to keep identical same-set links collapsing, since SQLite holds NULLs in a key distinct. `compact_own_set_links` narrows with `UPDATE OR REPLACE`, because the two spellings of one same-set link can now coexist and narrowing one onto the other would otherwise fail the *open*. Migration rebuilds the table, detected by the key's width, and carries existing rows across untouched.
context: Moved 2026-09-24 out of the entry's head, which was over the length limit, in step 2 of the out-link work.
why: The repair's mechanics, moved out of the head. The partial index and the `UPDATE OR REPLACE` are the two parts a later schema change would most likely undo without seeing why they are there.

content: **The export review's `review` action returns the review set grouped by subject, with the mechanical pre-pass's hits first and on their own.** Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. The groups are the clusters `describes` derives in `src/summary.rs`. A set without an embedding model is served as one group in writing order, and says so.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public, after deciding the person decides in conversation.
why: Batching keeps a conversational review alert, and a small model did multi-step organising poorly, so the server forms the batches. Grouping by subject also shows aggregation: seventy memories about `governance-docs` arrive as one batch, the view that found the problem in the 2026-10-17 read-through. It also suggests how to split a long review into sittings. Restated before publication to use the set's published pseudonym.

content: Every semantic recall reads the whole links table. Built that way 2026-08-18 as part of `graph-traversal`: `adjacency_over` reads every memory id and every link row of every searched store on every semantic recall, and throws the result away afterwards. **Ready, and deliberately not urgent.** Built when either the graph is cached with an invalidation keyed to the same `PRAGMA data_version` counter the vector cache already uses — so the two go stale together or not at all — or a measurement says it does not need to be. The threshold worth watching is the one `sqlite-vec` is named as the answer to, around 100k memories, where the whole brute-force posture is due for review anyway. content: Worth noting what the two-pass sequence cost, since it is cheap to draw the wrong lesson: the wiring fix was not wasted work — it was correct, and writing the surviving mutation is what made the gap legible enough to be worth closing. But *"fix it, then record that the fix is untested"* was one step from being the final answer, and the only reason it was not is that the gap got stated out loud. The mutation runner is what turns *I think this is untested* into evidence.

content: Withdrawn 2026-08-20 when the human partner supplied the missing fact: Claude Code raises an on-demand permission dialog for access under `Documents`, and an unanswered dialog times the operation out. The dialog appears at the moment access is needed, so it is easy to miss. **That explains the one thing the entry could not** — the same export succeeded instantly against a scratch directory and hung against the project root. A per-argument permission prompt fits exactly: the first `directory` value had been approved, the second was new, and nothing was watching the dialog. A fault inside the server explains the hang but not the difference between two calls seconds apart. **Read back that way, the evidence says the code behaved correctly**: the complete `.tmp` beside an untouched `memories.json` is an atomic write doing its job when the process is interrupted, `Server unavailable` afterwards is the torn-down call rather than a crash, and the store was undamaged because nothing damaged it. The environmental cause was removed rather than worked around — the `rust` tree moved out from under `Documents` to `~/git/rust` on 2026-08-20 — and the export that failed here has still never been made to succeed.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.

content: **Why canonicalising beat widening the guards.** Widening was a few characters at each lookup, but it required every one of them to know its store's own set name, and `Scope::Local` has none — so the local store needed the null-only form regardless, leaving two rules. Canonicalising leaves one spelling in the table, makes the existing guards correct as written, and fixes the over-refusal at the write as a consequence rather than as a second change. The dropped `target_keywords` are not a loss: they exist to re-resolve a target in another set, and a same-set reference has nothing to re-resolve against.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The comparison between a cheap local fix and a canonicalisation, decided by a case that has no set name at all — which would have left two rules in force rather than one.

content:
Measured 2026-09-11, the day it was found: eleven of the twelve unformatted files are integration tests and the twelfth is `src/conventions/catalog.rs`, and the reformatting is almost all hand-written long lines — chained calls on one line, array literals that rustfmt would break. It dates from the 2026-09-11 unrepresentable work, which hand-edited those fixtures widely.

**The mutation corpus is not at risk today, and it is worth saying why rather than assuming it.** `scripts/mutations.py` matches source text literally, so a reformat of a file it targets would make an unknown number of entries stale at once. Every one of its 353 entries targets a file under `src/`, and the only unformatted file there is `catalog.rs`, which no mutation names. So the cost is the unreadable diff, not lost coverage — but the two are one `cargo fmt` apart on any file the corpus does match.
context: Building the query log, after cargo fmt rewrote twelve files the change never touched.
why: The obvious worry on finding an unformatted tree in this project is the mutation corpus, since it is the one thing here that depends on literal source text. Checking it took one command and the answer is not the alarming one, which is worth recording so the next reader does not re-run the same alarm.

content: **A project's additions to the export review live in `scatterhoard_mem/config/sharing-preferences.json`, holding only `keep_out` and `always_fine`, and an unknown key is refused.** Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure* and in the reserved-directory table of `documents/design/trigger-and-loading.md`. `keep_out` items are checked against every memory beside the person's own. `always_fine` holds exact project values the pre-pass does not flag.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public, after settling the pre-pass and the person's always-fine list.
why: It arrives with every clone, so it can only add flags or silence the pre-pass for exact strings: a hostile file makes a review noisier and lets nothing through. It is a subdirectory rather than the proposed `config.json`, because every top-level `.json` there is read as a memory set, so `config.json` would take the set name `config`, and because later project settings can join it as files. The hyphen and the shared name pair it with the person's `sharing-preferences.md`.

content: **Dropping a read-only set needs no safety copy, and `save_to` becomes optional rather than refused.** Decided 2026-09-17 by the human partner. Not having a copy to write and then clean up is one of the incentives for holding a set read-only, so the copy is skipped by default and `save_to` is the escape hatch: given, it is honoured; omitted, nothing is written. **Dropping a read-write set without `save_to` is still refused**, so the unconditional save survives exactly where the set could have been written to. Chosen over refusing `save_to` on a read-only set because the published prose says *`drop` takes name and save_to* and a set's mode is not visible at the call site, so an LLM will pass it by habit; honouring it costs one file the caller asked for, while refusing turns the documented habit into an error and a retry. Silently ignoring it was rejected by both: a path that does nothing is the control `decision-placement` warns against. **The rare case that argues the other way**, raised by the human partner and judged rare: someone who deletes the publisher's file makes the read-only set the only copy, and dropping it then loses the memories. `export` recovers the file beforehand — proven byte-identical by `a_read_only_set_re_exports_the_file_it_was_given` in `tests/sets.rs`, for a publisher on the same build and model — so the refusal for a read-write set names `save_to` and the read-only path names `export`.
context: Implementing read-only load mode, second slice: drop.
why: Recorded because the reasoning that made the exception admissible — *nothing here could have diverged from the file it came from* — assumes that file still exists, and the human partner's hypothetical is the case where it does not. The decision keeps the exception anyway, on the ground that the case is rare and recoverable in advance, which is a judgement about frequency rather than about the argument, and is the kind of thing a later reader would otherwise have to guess at.

content:
**An import that cannot describe what it brought owes the description, and pays it at session start until the set is next exported.** Decided with the human partner 2026-09-13 while finishing `derived-set-summary`.

**The hole it closes.** The derived description and the comparison against the file's claim both need vectors, and a memory file carries none. So an import onto a machine with no embedding model — or a mismatched one, where `embed_for` leaves new memories unembedded — described nothing, and the gate was defeated by importing first and installing the model afterwards. The human partner raised this when a no-model fallback was proposed as a separate backlog entry.

**What was decided.** At import, if any non-identity memory in the set lacks a vector, the response describes nothing and records a pending description in the store. At the start of each session (`hoard_conventions`, first page) the server catches up the embeddings of any store with one pending; once every memory has a vector it reports the derived description beside the catalog, plus the verdict on the file's claim when the set holds exactly what the file brought. **It repeats every session start until the set is next exported**, because the export shows the description itself at the moment the set becomes portable — so the discharge sits with the event that matters, and needs no acknowledge action (`decision-placement.md`).

**Two points behind it.** The condition is *coverage*, not *a model was added*: the mismatched-model case has a model and the same gap. And the description is the strong half: anyone editing the file can delete its `summary` field, but the importing machine's own derivation cannot be stripped, so the deferral delivers the description unconditionally and the comparison only when it is meaningful.
context: Finishing the derived set summary after the previous session was ended by repeated [bio] refusals. Same stretch: diagnosing those refusals through flightlog, listing what remained of the backlog entry.
why: A design decision that governs how the import gate behaves over time, made in conversation and not visible from reading any one function: the clear-on-export rule and the coverage condition were each chosen over a plausible alternative (clear-on-first-report; trigger-on-model-attach). Checkable in `tests/set_description.rs` once built.

content: **`recall-is-latin-script-only` was left partly designed and unbuilt on 2026-10-03.** Decided with the human partner: build the check for declared languages (`model-covers-declared-languages`), worked out once per language per server run, since its answer depends only on the model and the language, and reported in `hoard_sets status`'s `language_note` and as a note on recall results from that set. A model change restarts the server and clears it; a declaration change is read from the charter each time. Rejected: a fixed collapse threshold on mean pairwise cosine, because the scale differs by model. Proposed and not yet confirmed: a paraphrase-rank test, reporting each declared language's score rather than a pass or fail. Next: more triplets per language before a threshold, then the human partner's go-ahead.
context: Ending the session at 76% context, mid-way through the last open issue.
why: The work stopped at the end of the context window. The state will not show any of the decided parts: no code was written, and the scratchpad measurement harness is gone after the session. So a later session needs to know what was settled, what was rejected and why, and which step is next, rather than reopening the timing and threshold questions.

content: **Whether, and how, a set should declare the language or languages its memories are written in. Resolved 2026-09-11 by the human partner: as keywords on the set's `hoard-scope-topics` charter.** The requirement that decided it is that the declaration must *travel with the set and be visible in the JSON a maintainer reviews* — many of these sets will live in `git` for open-source projects, which will want to standardise the language of their memories exactly as they standardise the language of their code comments. **Going multilingual is a cost imposed on everyone who imports the set**: each of them needs the larger model, and each loses discrimination for it, measured on this machine at 23 points of recall@5 in English. A charter keyword is compact, travels through export into the reviewed file, can be superseded like any claim, and reads familiarly to anyone who has met a language tag on the web. The alternatives, all rejected: prose in the charter, which no server can act on; a second reserved memory, which adds another per-set singleton beside the charter; and a `meta` row, which stays on one machine and tells a collaborator nothing. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `store-declares-its-language`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Making the multilingual model a supported alternative, then working out how a set should say what language it is written in, before returning to the recall floor.
why:
Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution the day it was raised.

**The human partner's argument is the part to keep**, because it is not the one the question was filed on. The question was raised from the user's side — one server holds one model, so a user with sets in two languages has one of them silently misindexed. The answer came from the *project's* side: a shared set is a thing a maintainer governs, so the declaration is a standard they set and review, and the review only works if the declaration is in the file they read. That reframing is what ruled out the `meta` row outright rather than on a technicality.

What remains open is the shape of the build rather than the choice: which tags, what consumes the declaration, whether detection cross-checks it, and what a mismatch does — all recorded with the backlog entry that follows this.

content: **The first attempt guarded the wrong end, and a mutation is what showed it.** Refusing to *walk into* an id the store holds no record of looks like the same fix and is not: it decides at each step rather than at the tip, and an id nothing answers to can still be superseded in turn by one the store does hold — a set lagging the repository it came from is exactly that shape. The step-wise guard was also redundant, since the tip check catches the absent id anyway, and the mutation that removed it left every test passing, which is what sent the fix to the right end. `a_chain_passing_through_an_id_nobody_holds_still_resolves_to_its_tip` now pins the placement, and the redundant guard is a recorded mutation so it cannot come back unnoticed.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A correct-looking guard in the wrong place, exposed by a mutation that removed it without failing anything. A guard whose removal changes no test is either redundant or untested, and both answers are worth having.

content: Superseding a memory does retire a keyword, since `a-keyword-cannot-be-retired-once-a-memory-has-been-exported` was fixed: a keyword hit follows the **tip's** keywords rather than the matched record's, so a term the replacement drops stops matching. Verified 2026-09-06 by recalling the two terms the original defect was measured on, `max-catalog-chars` and `remark-not-refuse` -- both return nothing. `hoard_memorize` also says so on every supersession, in the `keyword_delta_note`: *nothing answers to them here any more*. Amendment is still refused after export, so supersession is the instrument; stating the replacement's whole keyword set is required alongside a `supersedes` link, which is the authoring half of that fix.
context: Being asked why a fixed issue was being cited as open, and finding the answer in a memory that had gone stale.
why: Supersedes a measurement of the pre-fix behaviour that outlived the fix by two days and was then believed on 2026-09-06, producing a filed issue, a design section and a stored memory all asserting that a keyword cannot be retired. The contradicting evidence was in the same session twice, in the store response's own delta note. This is the failure `store-when` names -- a structural claim keeps reading as authoritative after the code has moved -- occurring in this project's own corpus, so the correction is worth more than the fact: when a memory describes how something currently works and the answer matters, check it against the code or the tool before building on it.

content: **How to inspect a memory set without adopting it.** Raised 2026-08-26 by the human partner, from a maintainer reviewing a contributor's branch: the easy path is to diff the memory file and decide on that, and the question is the next step, where they want to *explore* with those memories before deciding. **Today the only way to read a set is to import it, and import is adoption** -- having imported, the contributor's memories are in the maintainer's store, and checking the branch back out does not undo it. Worse, every subsequent import reports them as `Anomaly`, *a state no supported operation produces*, because they are absent from the file with a base recorded; what actually happened was an ordinary branch switch. **Narrowed 2026-08-29 by the human partner toward a set loaded on an evaluation basis, read-only, and easily dropped afterwards.** Read-only had been assumed rather than stated, and stating it settles more than it looks: it is what keeps the maintainer from having to *undo* anything, so the drop is discarding a load rather than reversing an adoption. **Still open:** whether an evaluation set is a distinct kind or an ordinary set flagged, how recall names it alongside the maintainer's own, and whether a memory the maintainer wants to keep can be promoted out of one without re-importing the whole file. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `evaluation-mode`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

*Import is adoption* is in the head because it is the fact that makes this a question at all, and it is not obvious from the tool surface -- `import` reads like a read operation and is the most destructive of the loading paths. The `Anomaly` consequence is kept with it because a maintainer who does this once will meet that message and have no way to connect it to a branch switch.

content: **A full review of the current memory file does not cover what going public publishes: the repository's git history keeps every earlier export.** Found 2026-10-18, at the end of the publication read-through of all 1,636 records. Forgetting or generalising a memory cleans only the current file. Earlier commits of `scatterhoard_mem/scatterhoard.json` still hold the old text, and they can also hold the content of memories forgotten since, which a read of the current file never sees. Documents removed from the tree work the same way: the deleted `open-questions.md` (commits `72f46c0`, `38817a5`) and a removed note in `corpus/harvest_questions.py` (`a3355f9`, `49cd4f2`) still carry text the review flagged. `export-review.md` sets out when a full review is due, and does not mention history.
context: Finishing the publication read-through of the three memory files before making the repositories public, then grepping git history for the terms it had flagged.
why: The full-review design assumes that reviewing what the file holds is reviewing what gets published. That is true for each later push, and false at the moment a repository with private history goes public. A session that finished the read-through and acted on its flags would believe the repository was clean while the flagged text stayed one `git log -p` away. How to deal with it, whether by rewriting history, publishing a fresh history, or accepting it, is for the human partner to decide. Checkable with `git log --all -S"<term>"`.

content: **The cost of splitting is what keeps this open, and it was clear from the day the question was raised, 2026-08-13** -- history from that day. **The measurements as they then stood:** `store-when` was 2,400 characters of a 14,632-character catalog -- one convention holding a sixth of everything served, and 60% larger than the next largest -- with roughly 40% of its text the person clause, after the golden rule's four demands were compiled into it. **Its own editing comment predicts the split and does not cover this case:** the comment says field-level guidance arrives as separate conventions rather than by growing the entry, and that prediction had been honoured twice, by `keyword-standards` and `confidence-standards` both leaving rather than being absorbed. The person material is a *content* rule rather than field-level guidance, so nothing in that comment governed it, and the entry grew anyway. **The *restate what is absent, point at what is present* rule does not settle it**, because both conventions would be served on the same page: pointing would be legal, but the thing pointed at is a derivation rather than a procedure, and the human partner's constraint was specifically that a weaker model will not make that leap unaided. **Two things could make the split matter** -- a catalog large enough to need more than one page, where convention boundaries decide what arrives together, and `conventions::get(id)` for a caller fetching one convention by name.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order, the first file migrated under the written cluster-shaping standard.
why: The reasoning that established the question, kept because the *cost* of the obvious fix is the whole of why it is open and would otherwise have to be re-derived from the two conventions involved. Dated in the opening because every figure in it is a reading from that day and several have since moved -- see the 2026-09-07 re-derivation, which is the reason this member states them as history rather than as fact.

content: A convention's served text can create a dependency on a convention that does not exist yet, and the catalog has no way to notice. recall-before-storing was drafted telling a session to "split it" on a partial overlap while nothing in the catalog defined splitting, and the natural reading of that instruction -- amend or replace the original -- is the one outcome that strands cross-set links. split-when-partly-stale was drafted immediately after to close it.
context: Noticed 2026-08-13 immediately after serving recall-before-storing, and repaired the same day. Checkable in the comments above RECALL_BEFORE_STORING and SPLIT_WHEN_PARTLY_STALE in src/conventions/catalog.rs.
why: This is the same failure that kept correct-when withheld while amend and forget did not exist, arriving from the other direction: there the convention named absent tools, here it named an absent convention. The tools case is caught by anyone trying to follow the instruction, because the tool call fails. The convention case is silent -- a session told to split will simply split badly, and the damage is stranded links in another set, which is invisible from here. So the check belongs at drafting time: after writing convention text, read it for verbs the catalog does not define.

content: A four-term recall was the mitigation that worked and was not enough. Recalling `hoard-watch`, `hoard-signpost`, `hoard-collect` and `hoard-investigation` together ranks real watches above discussion, because a watch carries two of them and a memory about the design carries one — verified 2026-09-04, `matched_keywords` 2 against 1. It ranks rather than filters, so the discussion memories are still fetched and paid for, which is exactly the charge push exists to bound. **Do not fix by renaming the marker**: any marker term can be written about, so a rename moves the collision rather than closing it.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The candidate fix that was measured working and still rejected, with the reason a rename is not a fix — worth keeping because the rename is the obvious move and the argument against it is not obvious.

content: **A recalled memory's author and origin are reported but never weighted: no author's memories are scored, flagged or presented as more or less trustworthy than another's.** Decided by the human partner on 2026-09-25, settling the third of `imported-set-trust-boundary`'s sub-questions. Trust is decided at the level of the set, by its checkout's provenance. Within recall, the one distinction drawn is adopted versus under review (the `evaluation` mark), which marks a proposal, not a different author. How far to lean on a memory is its `confidence`.
context: Working through the release-gated questions: `imported-set-trust-boundary`, after declining the personal-set exemption and an import gate.
why: The human partner's reason: weighting by author would make different readers see different versions of the truth, according to whose history each sits in, and would confuse more than it helps. In a project set, a memory written by someone else is the normal case, since sharing collaborators' knowledge is what the set is for. Discounting it would work against the tool's purpose, and a second, per-author trust system would disagree with the per-set one. Adjusting scores would also distort relevance with no calibration behind it. Nothing here touches the file format, so if weighting were ever wanted it would be a ranking change, not a break.

content: No instrument could retire a keyword once a memory had been exported, and search went on matching a term every current memory had dropped: amendment is refused post-export, supersession did not reach the index, and forgetting is reserved for other purposes. Fixed 2026-09-02 by requiring the keyword set to be stated on a supersession, cutting the reach, and reporting the delta. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-keyword-cannot-be-retired-once-a-memory-has-been-exported`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **Checked 2026-09-08: the model and our use of it are sound, so the missing floor is not a defect in either.** `potion-base-32M` ships no validation vectors, but the equivalent check passes cleanly on raw word cosines with no corpus involved: king/queen `0.353` against king/bicycle `0.076`; dog/puppy `0.675` against dog/algebra `0.064`; car/automobile `0.779` against car/lettuce `-0.038`; memory/recall `0.453` against memory/sourdough `-0.025`. Unrelated words land at or below zero, which is exactly what a working static model should do. Our loader is a thin wrapper over `model2vec-rs` 0.2.1 from the model's own publisher — `from_pretrained` then `encode` — and `apply_zipf` and `apply_pca` in `config.json` are distillation-time settings already baked into the weights. **So word-level discrimination is fine and it is the *pooled query against a corpus* that has no floor**, which is a different thing and points at the retrieval geometry rather than the embedding.
context: Investigating the football query, when the human partner asked whether the model ships validation vectors we could throw at it.
why: Recorded because *the model must be broken* is the right first suspicion once gibberish outscores a real question, and it is expensive to re-satisfy — it needs either a reference implementation, which is not installed here, or a set of word pairs someone has to choose. The pairs and their numbers are kept so the check is a re-run rather than a re-design. The distinction the last sentence draws is the load-bearing one: a model that separates *king* from *bicycle* at word level tells you nothing about whether a five-word query pooled into one vector has a meaningful nearest neighbour among 855 memories, and conflating the two would either exonerate or condemn the wrong component.

content: The export review's `full: true` restarts the review on every call, not only the first: each `review` call carrying it deletes every clearance recorded so far, so a session that passes it on each page undoes its own `clear` answers and can never finish. Found 2026-10-27 re-reviewing `coding-lessons`, where a second call with it re-served four memories cleared minutes earlier. The intended use is `full` once, then plain `review` calls while the full-review setting holds, and nothing in the parameter's description or the `not_finished` note says so. Fixed when a repeated `full: true` during a full review keeps the clearances already made, or the tool surface says to pass it only once.
context: Re-reviewing the three published sets under the export review's judgement gate, starting with coding-lessons, after calibrating recall floors on two sets.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. Blocks: a caller cannot use the full review correctly without guessing, since the parameter is described as "Review every memory again" and the natural reading of a paged action is to repeat the call that started it. Checkable in `src/mcp.rs` at the `review` action, where `if full || became_public` calls `forget_clearances` with no check for a full review already under way, and in the `full` schema description beside it. The cost here was five memories answered twice; a session that never noticed would loop.

content: **Refuse an unknown `hoard-` keyword at the authoring entry points.** Decided 2026-09-11 by the human partner and recorded in `documents/design/conventions.md` under *Decided 2026-09-11: the write path guards the reserved namespace*: a keyword beginning `hoard-` must be a control mark Scatterhoard knows, or begin `hoard-proj-`, the carve-out for a project's own tooling. Refused at `memorize`, amendment and supersession; never at import, where sets written by other versions must still load. It catches typos and invented marks, not a legitimate mark used as a subject — that case is `one-live-charter-per-set`. **Missing:** a single list of control marks in code — only `hoard-author` is a constant (`AUTHOR_KEYWORD` in `src/store.rs`), and the others appear as strings in the served catalog and the documents — and then the check itself. **Built looks like:** one list that the served convention text is tested against, so the two cannot drift; a refusal that names the known marks and the `about-` form; tests for a typo, an invented mark, a `hoard-proj-` mark passing, and an import carrying an unknown mark passing; a mutation for the guard. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `reserved-keyword-block-list`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Filing the guard on the reserved keyword namespace after the human partner decided to add a block-list alongside the one-live-charter check. Same stretch: re-keying two measurements that carried the charter mark, and the store-stopping embed fix.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. Ready: the list does not exist, but building it is part of the work rather than a prerequisite anyone has to decide.

One detail the build has to settle and that nothing decides yet: whether retired marks count as known. `hoard-watch` was split into the three watch-list marks, and a supersession restating an old memory's keywords could still carry it — refusing there would force the retirement, which may be the right outcome but should be chosen rather than fallen into. The human partner's reason for keeping import out of the check — users on different versions sharing memories — is the same reason the supersession-cycle refusal stays off the reconciling path.

It was skipped before the status wiring, the hub checks, recommendations, the how-to and the refusal. The checks then repeated that defect, and only a small-model trial found it. This is the fifth recorded skip, after four on 2026-09-30, and the first with a recorded cost.
