content: Fixed 2026-08-12 by the design the human partner asked for rather than by the patch the entry proposed. **Testing Claude Desktop's own chat settled the open question**: it stringifies the object scope too, so the affected configuration is not a cross-registration oddity but **the deployment a global installation uses** — which made the earlier remedies moot, since *declare the server in a project `.mcp.json`* is not an answer for a store that is machine-bound by definition. The rule that replaced them is [publish the centre of MCP, accept the edges](documents/design/tool-surface.md), and a survey found it was never only `scope`: `const`, `title` and `additionalProperties` existed only inside the alternations. **`scope` publishes as `local` or `shared:<name>`** — the spelling `Scope::as_key` has always written into a store's `meta` — while the object form, the file format's own, keeps parsing. **`links.target` keeps its keywords** by moving the alternation out into `target_set` and `target_keywords` beside it, rather than into a `"set:id"` string that would have dropped exactly the field a dangling reference is re-found by. Nothing that reaches a memory file changed. `nothing_published_leaves_the_well_carried_subset` walks every published schema at any depth, and four recorded mutations hold the accepting side — the half most at risk, since a spelling the schema no longer advertises reads like dead code to whoever tidies next.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix: publish a subset every consumer carries while continuing to accept the richer form. The mutations guard the accepting side because an un-advertised spelling looks like dead code, which is how the compatibility would be lost later.

content:
**Whether a link may be added to an exported memory without superseding it.** Raised 2026-09-09 by the human partner, on noticing that the new connect-on-recall clause in `recall-when` implies an edit the system currently prices at a full supersession: `amend` is refused once `has_base` is true, so connecting two exported memories means storing a complete copy of one carrying a `supersedes` link, purely to add an edge.

**For a carve-out.** A link is a claim about *adjacency*; supersession is a claim about *validity*. Using the second to express the first says a memory was superseded when nothing about it was wrong, and leaves that false signal in the record permanently. The cost is not hypothetical: 603 of 762 memories are isolated, nearly all exported, and the clause will meet this case constantly. Links may also be the one field where the export gate's own reasoning does not bite — they are additive and order-independent, so two copies each adding a different link merge by union with nothing to reconcile, where a changed `content` genuinely needs ancestry to arbitrate.

**Against.** The gate's value is that it has no exceptions: *a change that leaves no ancestry is one a later merge cannot reason about*, and a field-by-field carve-out invites the next one. Union-merge for links is not implemented, and reconciliation would need it before this is safe. A link also changes what recall returns, through traversal, so it is not inert metadata.

**What turns on it**: whether the connect-on-recall clause is affordable in practice, and therefore whether it will be obeyed.
context: Drafting the connect-on-recall clause, when the supersession cost of connecting two exported memories surfaced and the human partner asked that it be filed.
why:
Filed as a question rather than backlog because work cannot start until someone chooses between two designs — a link-only write path, or leaving supersession as the only route — and the choice reaches into reconciliation, which has no union-merge rule for links today.

Raised at the moment the clause was written rather than after the cost was felt, because the cost is predictable from the graph: with 79% of memories isolated and the clause instructing sessions to connect what recall surfaces, the expensive path is the common path rather than the edge case. The clause was deliberately left not naming its instrument so that resolving this question changes nothing in the served text — `correct-when` decides the instrument, and would simply decide differently.

Worth noting for whoever takes it: `already_known` is the standing evidence that a capability nothing drives goes unused, and this is the mirror image — a convention that drives an action the system makes expensive. Either the price comes down or the convention gets quietly skipped, and a convention that is skipped is worse than none, because the catalog is charged for it in every session.

content: **A set's load mode cannot be demoted to read-only, and promotion to read-write is one-way.** Decided 2026-09-16 by the human partner. Read-only is chosen at birth, so a read-only set provably has never been written here — which is what lets it be dropped without a safety copy, with no guard stored in the database being destroyed. A distributed set is created read-only and then imported. **Promotion is one-way for a second reason, the human partner's:** promoting means a session reads the set's investigation and collection memories into context, which cannot be undone either. **Read-only means no session writes** (memorize, correct, forget); allowing `import` to refresh a distributed set from a newer file was proposed and not objected to. Whether promotion is offered at all was left open that day, and became the deferred backlog entry `promotion-to-read-write`.
context: Settling whether a set can be loaded more than once, after revising the load-modes design. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the memory was over the length limit.
why: Split from the ordering and storage decision it was recorded with. The last sentence is updated rather than carried: it said whether promotion is offered was still open, which stopped being true when read-only distribution resolved on 2026-09-17.

content: **Unifying the tracking files is motivated by portability, and that is what makes it worth doing rather than merely tidy** -- history from filing the entry, 2026-09-07. One file plus `genindex.py` is a drop-in issue, backlog and question tracker for any project using Scatterhoard, with no git hosting account and no separate tool: three files plus a script is a thing you port, one file plus a script is a thing you copy. **The counter-argument, and the reason the sections must be tagged rather than merely titled:** the three files divide by *state* -- not yet decided, decided not built, built not proven, built and wrong -- and that division is load-bearing enough that AGENTS.md carries a table of it. Sections in one file preserve the division nominally while making it much easier to file into the wrong one, so the tags have to be what `genindex.py` reads, not headings a human keeps in order. **The ordering was the live question and was settled on disruption, not on merit:** `open-questions.md` alone is 134,470 characters as of this date, and unifying before its 40 remaining entries are migrated means migrating into a file whose structure is changing.
context: Splitting CLAUDE.md into AGENTS.md, and writing the cluster-shaping guidance into STANDARDS.md, the evening after the BACKLOG.md migration finished.
why: Recorded because the entry's standing sentence cannot carry why the blocker is a blocker: a later session reading *blocked until the migration finishes* would reasonably wonder whether that is caution or a real constraint, and the answer is that it is a real constraint about disruption rather than about correctness -- unifying first would work, it would just make the remaining migration harder. The portability motive is also the part most likely to be lost, because it is a benefit to *other* projects and so appears nowhere in this project's own experience of the friction.

content: **The absorbed names come from the caller and may never come from the file, and this is the part to keep.** A file's header is contents, per the trust rule in [memory_file.rs](src/memory_file.rs). A file that could name the sets it absorbs would be granting itself authority over their ids: its link naming a victim's set would be rewritten to a same-set link and would then *act* — which is `a-set-can-suppress-another-sets-memory` arriving through a feature rather than a hole. Tracing exactly that is what exposed that the suppression guard was still keyed on spelling. It is an **allow-list**: a name the caller did not give stays foreign. **Not persisted, by decision** — a repeat import must state the names again. The human partner's reasoning: someone merging and importing across several sets is reorganising, and reorganisation is not something you repeat, so storing the names would carry a cost on every import to serve a case that does not recur.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A capability deliberately not taken from the file it applies to, because a file naming the sets it may rewrite would be authorising itself. The decision not to persist is recorded with its reasoning, since the convenience looks free.

content: **The per-change recall was made, and returned nothing that applied, 2026-10-01: a part-6 observation under `adopting-coding-lessons`.** Before building the monotonic id wrapper, at the hand-off from the human partner accepting the plan to building it, `coding-lessons` was recalled with one sentence describing the change. It returned two lessons, one about re-running snapshots after changing a sort key and one about issuing tool calls together. Neither bore on the change, and the design went ahead unchanged.
context: Fixing the flaky id-ordering test after restoring the 2026-10-01 checkpoint.
why: The four recorded skips all fell at exactly this hand-off, so a recall made there is the counter-case the investigation needs. That it found nothing is evidence too: it is what the recall costs when it does not pay. One instance, so it says nothing about the rate.

content: In the Scatterhoard MCP server, stdout carries the JSON-RPC protocol and nothing else. Every diagnostic in main.rs goes to stderr deliberately; a stray println! corrupts the stream and the client reports something unhelpful.
context: Recorded in SETUP.md section 4 as a thing that will bite when attaching the server to a client.
why: Protocol-channel corruption surfaces as a vague client-side failure with no pointer back to the print that caused it, so the discipline has to be maintained at the source rather than debugged later.

content: Measured 2026-09-06 across the loaded sets: a recall of `hoard-scope-topics` returned **nine memories, of which four were charters** — the other five were Scatterhoard design memories discussing the charter mechanism. `route-where` sends a session to that keyword to learn what each set is for, so those five arrived as though they described a set. `hoard-author` was clean at four of four. Found by the human partner, generalising `about-hoard-watch-is-both-marker-and-subject` rather than treating it as one convention's problem.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The measurement that made the general case rather than the single-convention case: the same collision the watch entry found, present on a second reserved term, which is what turned a convention bug into a namespace rule.

content: **Under the English potion models, only English recognises a paraphrase among unrelated text; Spanish, French and German fail too, not just the collapsed scripts.** Measured 2026-10-03 with the probes' triplets. For each of three anchors per language, the question was whether its paraphrase ranked first among the seven other sentences in that language. English scored 3 of 3 under `potion-base-32M`, `potion-base-8M` and `potion-retrieval-32M`. Every other language scored 0 to 2: under base-32M, German 2; Chinese, Japanese, Hindi, Russian and Spanish 1; French 0. Mean pairwise cosine among unrelated sentences is not model-agnostic: Russian is 0.87 under base-32M and 0.31 under retrieval-32M, whose cosines all run lower. So a fixed collapse threshold misreads one model or another. The rank test compares within one model, so scale cancels.
context: Building the declared-language check for recall-is-latin-script-only; the separation threshold turned out to depend on the model.
why: It changes the detector for `recall-is-latin-script-only` from a separation threshold to a paraphrase rank, and it corrects the 2026-09-11 reading that Spanish, French and German were degraded but working. That test compared a paraphrase against one unrelated sentence, an easier bar. Thin: three triplets per language, written to share few words, so one miss moves a language's score by a third. 0.8 because the English-only result held across three models.

content: **Where the trusted set name for a checkout comes from.** The scope *kind* is settled -- the path decides it and the header can only agree. The set *name* is not: a project's name and its set name need not coincide, so the path does not yield it, and the header cannot be trusted to. **Expected shape is trust-on-first-use** -- the first import binds this checkout to a set name and records it in local state, later imports check the header against that binding, and a change is a refusal rather than a silent re-target. **What makes that cheap is that the harm is collision, not naming:** a declared name with no existing store can be accepted silently, since nothing existing can be contaminated, and only a name already bound to a *different* checkout needs a human. **Narrowed twice since.** Two findings from 2026-08-06: the binding's expected home may already exist as the `bases` target list, and the remote-versus-path choice is two questions rather than one, since a *target* must distinguish two checkouts of a repository while a *name binding* is stronger if it does not. And Store Registry proposes dissolving rather than answering it: if a scope resolves to one store per checkout, registration *is* the binding. **Still open:** where the binding lives, what a legitimate rename looks like, and whether the git remote is a better key than the working-tree path. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

*The harm is collision, not naming* is carried in the head because it is what makes the whole question tractable: it converts a general trust problem into a narrow check that fires rarely, and without it the trust-on-first-use design reads as more machinery than the risk warrants.

content: **Why the entry existed at all, and it is the methodological half: the premise had been reasoned from reading the code and never probed.** That is exactly the shape of `a-guard-concluded-missing-from-a-probe-that-bypassed-it`, **run in the other direction** — concluding a state is *unreachable* from reading is no better than concluding a guard is *absent* from a probe that took the wrong path. And **predicting a route and reaching it are different claims; only the second is evidence.** The proposal had already named `absorb` as the likely leak, and naming it did not settle anything until a test drove it through the published surface. **One route was ruled out rather than found**, which is the other half of the answer: a legacy amendment plus a restore from an older file would put two contents under one id, and it is unreachable now, because producing two files that differ for one id needs an amendment **between** two exports, which the service gate refuses — only data written before that gate existed can do it, and none of it can be manufactured through the surface.
context: Migrating the falsify-record-immutability entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is why probing it was worth doing when the answer was already suspected.
why:
Recorded because the entry's value was almost entirely in the discipline rather than the outcome. The conclusion — absorb is the leak — was already believed; what the work produced was the difference between believing it and having driven it, plus a second defect found while looking for a route that did not exist.

The ruled-out route is worth keeping for the reasoning rather than the result: it is closed by a *different* mechanism than the one the entry was about, so anyone reopening this question after changing the service gate has to re-examine it. Loosen correction-after-export and this route reopens without touching absorb at all.

content: Healing a forked supersession chain makes the shared ancestor read as corrupt: where `X` was superseded independently by `A` and `B` and a later `C` supersedes both, `resolve_supersession(X)` returns `Cycle`, so the withdrawn text is handed back unsubstituted and diagnosed as a merge that went wrong. Fixed when a diamond resolves to its single tip and only a genuine loop reports `Cycle`. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-healed-fork-reports-its-ancestor-as-a-cycle`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set entry by entry, in file order. This one is still open, and the human partner has deferred it to be fixed before publish.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, severity and fixed-when only. Deliberately free of the cause and the evidence, which are episodic and belong in members.

content: **First issue filed under a recorded cause after the baseline: `the-calibrate-note-promises-a-floor-that-lowers-itself`, 2026-09-24, attributed to `a-fact-restated-by-hand-drifts`.** Recurrence, not prevention: the defect was written on 2026-09-12, twelve days before the baseline, and only found after it — by reading the code while splitting a memory, not by recalling the cause. So it counts toward the post-baseline filing rate while telling nothing about whether recording causes stops new ones, and a count that mixes the two will overstate recurrence.
context: Fixing the misleading calibrate note, the same day it was filed while splitting over-length memories in the out-link work.
why: The investigation asks for every issue filed under a cause after the baseline. Recorded with its write date because filing date and writing date differ here by twelve days, and the investigation's recurrence measure — issues attributed per week, before against after — will be read from filing dates unless something says otherwise.

content: **A set's audience is declared in the project's `config/sharing-preferences.json` as `"audience": "private"`, and absent means public.** Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. "While it is not public" exceptions apply only where a project declares itself private. A change from private to public, local or pulled, makes the next review a full one with those exceptions off. `full: true` asks for a full review directly. There is no marker memory and no convention about pushing.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public: settling how a full review is started.
why: Going public changes the audience of memories already published, while a push to an already-public repository publishes only new ones. The routine review must therefore know the set is public, which a one-off `going_public` flag could not tell it. Defaulting to public means forgetting to declare exposes nothing. The audience lives with the project because it is the same fact for every contributor and travels with each clone without `git`. Scatterhoard never sees a push, so a convention about pushing would be unchecked served text.

content: **Before publication, the human partner's macOS account name and work login were replaced throughout the repository's documents and tests**, decided by the human partner on 2026-11-02 after a scan of the tracked files. Narrative passages in `documents/design/memory-data-model.md` now describe the name instead of giving it; example records, an encoded-path filename in `store-registry.md`, and test fixtures in `tests/store.rs`, `tests/memory_file.rs` and `tests/sets.rs` use `alice`, `alicedev` or `asmith`. The memory files held neither name. Left as they are: the author's name in `LICENSE.md`, which the sharing preferences allow as the author of one's own work, the public handle in the repository URL, and a first name used as a sample author in a few tests.
context: Going-public checklist: a final scan of both trees for personal details before the GitHub steps, after removing the commit maps.
why: The sharing preferences keep user names and home paths out of shared sets; repository files are not memory sets, so nothing had checked them, but the same reasoning applies to a public repository, and a name published there cannot be taken back. A later session writing a new example or fixture should use a placeholder rather than an account name for the same reason.

content: **The personal set gets no exemption from the data-only rule: `local`'s memories are data, like every other set's.** Decided by the human partner on 2026-09-25, settling the first of `imported-set-trust-boundary`'s four sub-questions. Standing instructions to the model belong in the harness's own always-loaded context, such as `CLAUDE.md`, which is changed by editing a file, not by a tool call. This makes the recorded ordering (exemption only after the set-name binding) moot, not satisfied.
context: Working through the release-gated questions: `imported-set-trust-boundary`, taken up after `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout` dropped the binding its personal-set exemption was waiting on.
why: Two reasons. First, `local` cannot be made unforgeable while a session can import into it. `file` form imports any file declaring `local` when the caller names it, and the caller is an LLM that reads repository text. An exemption would turn every induced import into instruction injection, where without it the same mistake costs some wrong memories, surfaced with their authors. Second, the human partner's: if one set's memories are treated as prompts while another's are data, the two can be mixed up, and nothing in a recalled memory would show which rule it came under. The binding the ordering named was never the right precondition, since what protects `local` is where a file may be read into it, not a name. That gap is filed as `the-reserved-directory-accepts-the-local-set`.

content: **The strongest case for add-ons is the demand side, not the supply side: there are rules the memory half structurally cannot serve -- argued 2026-08-26.** Two live cases arrived that day and they are one need. The first was `recall-gloss-convention`, competing for catalog room. The second was a **working preference about how a decision is put to the human partner**, held in the personal set at the highest confidence there is -- and broken anyway. **The reason it was broken is the argument.** The moment such a rule governs is *reaching for a tool*, which is not a moment anyone stops to search about, so **retrieval structurally cannot serve a rule of that shape**: searching is itself a deliberate act. Such a rule has to arrive unconditionally or not at all, and the conventions catalog is the only unconditional channel this tool has. **Both cases also argue for user configuration space** -- a preference belongs to a person rather than to a project, and output styling is something users should be able to decline. **Updated 2026-09-04:** `recall-gloss-convention` was retired rather than drafted, its capture half moving to the `context` parameter description and its gloss half to read-side field documentation. The case for add-ons is unchanged and now has a concrete first candidate -- a *continuous* gloss, always rather than on demand, named by the human partner that day. **The bootstrap is a real dependency and an accepted one:** it is reasonable to ask a user to put *load the conventions first* in whatever steering file their client reads, stated in interface-neutral terms since Scatterhoard should work with any interface speaking stdio MCP. What that costs is bounded -- a client configured without the boot prompt gets no conventions at all, built-in ones included.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Recorded because this reframes the question from *the catalog will fill up* to *there is a class of rule the memory system cannot reach*, and only the second makes add-ons necessary rather than convenient. The class is rules about how the work is done rather than about what is known.

The preference itself is referenced rather than restated, and stays in the personal set where routing puts anything about a person's working style. It could not be linked from here even had that been wanted: a cross-set link may not name `local`, since `local` and `shared:local` would read the same, so a cluster spanning that boundary can only be assembled from the personal side. What belongs here is the structural conclusion about retrieval, which is a fact about the tool.

Recorded at 0.9 because the mechanism is demonstrated rather than theorised -- a rule at maximum confidence, correctly stored and genuinely applicable, failed to fire for exactly the stated reason.

content: Found 2026-08-11 running SETUP.md §5 item 13: the consequence was right and the explanation false. **The sibling field got it exactly right one line away** — `embedding_model` reports `provenance_unknown` with *"what a store written before model identity was recorded looks like"*, naming the migration without denying the history. Cheap to dismiss as wording, and it is not: a reader comparing `memories: 27` against *nothing has been written* has to decide which of the two to disbelieve, and the note is the one that sounds authoritative about writes. **Fixed 2026-08-11**: `describe_author` takes the memory count and answers the two states separately — an empty set keeps the original sentence, and a set holding memories is told it *"holds memories but records no author, which is what a store written before set-level attribution looks like."* Both are tested **deliberately as a pair**, because the obvious way to fix this is one hedged sentence covering both, which would describe neither.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A false explanation attached to a correct consequence, with the right pattern already implemented in the neighbouring field. Testing both states as a pair is what stops the fix collapsing into one hedged sentence.

content: **The `hoard-proj-` carve-out is the first live instance of normative vocabulary, and it was met without this feature** — read 2026-09-23. `keyword-standards` reserves the namespace for a project's own tooling marks, compiled into the served catalog and identical for every set; no set declares anything. This project's actual marks are named only in its own `TRACKING.md`, which a Scatterhoard user has no copy of. So the question's test — is there normative content usage cannot supply — is answered yes by a real case, while the bootstrap gap it was raised for is untouched: a session cannot learn which marks a set uses from the set. What is left open is discovery under a reserved namespace, not whether declaration has content.
context: Auditing the open entries for closure, entry by entry, after the issue family was done.
why: Raised by the human partner during the closure audit, asking whether defining the prefix had closed the question. Recorded because the honest answer changes the question rather than settling it, and a later session reading only the head would either close it wrongly on the strength of the prefix existing, or miss that the underivable-content half now has evidence behind it instead of an example.

content: **The 30 open questions were audited on 2026-09-23; one closed and 29 stay open, all read against their heads.** `charter-recall-shape` closed. The 22 that first got only a row-level read were given the fuller pass the same day, at the human partner's direction, checking each head's present-tense claims against the code, the served catalog and the live tool schemas. **No further closures, and no premise found stale** — but four entries gained evidence that changes what would settle them, recorded separately: `violates-belongs-in-memory`, `publish-boundary-three-valued`, `hybrid-search` and `query-density-guidance`. The question family is now audited to the same depth as the issues.
context: The closure audit's second pass over the question family, at the human partner's request to separate what still needs investigating from what is done. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 1 link an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.
why: Superseded because the first version said of itself that 22 entries got a lighter pass, and that is no longer true. Every open question now carries this memory as a keyword, so recalling any of them dates the check. That the fuller pass produced no further closures is itself the result worth having: the row-level reading had not been hiding anything, and the one closure it did miss was found by reading served text rather than by reading harder.

content: A rule that every set would need belongs in the convention catalog; only what varies by set belongs in its `hoard-scope-topics` charter. Applied 2026-08-25 to move "a lesson that would hold anywhere belongs elsewhere, even when this is where it was learned, though the evidence for it does belong here" out of the `shared:scatterhoard` charter and into `route-where`. The test that decided it: the clause was doing real work and being followed, but nobody writing their first charter would think to include it, so every set created without it routes general lessons into a project set — which is the misfiling `route-where` was created to fix.
context: Decided 2026-08-25 by the human partner, who asked whether that clause was doing significant work and, if so, whether other sets would have anything like it. Checkable in ROUTE_WHERE in src/conventions/catalog.rs and in the superseded charter memory.
why: This is the argument that put the taxonomy in the sets rather than the catalog, run in the other direction, and it is worth having stated both ways because the charter is the tempting place for anything about routing. A charter travels with its set and is read as authoritative by whoever imports it, so a general rule kept there is a copy that other sets silently lack rather than a copy that drifts — the failure is absence in every set but one, which nothing reports. Ask of any candidate charter sentence whether a stranger creating their own set would need the same sentence; if yes, it is a convention.

content: A dropped set came back under a new `set_id`: `create` mints an identity and `adopt_set_id` will not displace one, so the sanctioned `create` then `import` path left the set holding the minted identity and dropped the file's on the floor — reported as `adopted_set_id: null`, which reads as *this file offered nothing*. Fixed 2026-09-02 by narrowing the rule to *never displace an identity the set has written under*. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-re-added-set-cannot-recover-its-identity`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Filed in error 2026-08-23 as a file with a duplicate id silently dropping a memory — the reader had always refused it, and the probe had bypassed the reader. Withdrawn the same day; what was real and did change is that the refusal named only the line of the repeat, and now carries the id and both lines.
