content: Fixed 2026-08-07 (`a2fd1f1`): `load_vectors` discards the set before repopulating it, and `forgetting_does_not_cost_the_survivors_their_place_in_the_scan` in `tests/recall.rs` builds the three-memory case with the survivor pointing *away* from the query, so the survivor can only be reached if the departed vectors are gone. The omission is a recorded mutation.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the fixture design that makes it testable: the survivor has to be a poor match for the query, or it would be found whether or not the stale vectors were cleared.

content: Fixed 2026-08-04: `Keyword::new` keeps the spelling it was given, the new `Keyword::folded` is the single place case folding happens, and both the write path and the query path derive their key from it. The `keywords` table gained a second column — `keyword` is the record, `folded` is the index — and **that separation is the fix**, since the one column had been serving as both, so normalising for the index necessarily rewrote the record. Rust's `to_lowercase` rather than SQL's `lower()`, deliberately: a keyword may hold any non-whitespace character and `lower()` folds ASCII only, so the SQL version would have been silently partial for exactly the non-English keywords nobody would think to test.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, with the reason for choosing the language's folding over the database's: a partial fold is wrong only for inputs the test suite is least likely to contain.

content: **Three things building the merge driver on 2026-09-16 settled that the design had not seen.** *(1)* **The header conflicts on every concurrent export and cannot be recomputed by a driver.** Its `summary` is derived from the set's vectors — `SetSummary::derive` needs `summary_subjects()` from a store — and a driver holds three files and no store. So the receiving side's header line is carried over verbatim. Safe only because a summary is a claim a reader recomputes and compares rather than a fact it displays, and the next export rewrites it. This is the *first* thing a merge of two exported branches meets, before any record is considered, and nothing in `multi-set-sync.md` anticipated it. *(2)* **`modified` forces a decision that costs something.** Every edit moves it, so in exactly the case the driver exists for — ours bumped `confidence`, theirs added a link — the two sides always disagree there; treating that as a conflict would mean nothing ever merges. The later attribution wins, so **a merged record claims an authorship neither side wrote**. *(3)* **Collections are set-merged against the base, never unioned**, which the base makes possible: a union would resurrect a keyword one side deliberately retired. A fourth, smaller: merged records go through `memory_file::write_record`, because the reconciliation checksum is taken over exactly those bytes — a driver spelling a record its own way would make every merged record read as changed at the next import.
context: Building the merge driver straight after the checkpoint, having just cleared command-line export and the two tidy-ups.
why:
Recorded because all three are decisions a later reader would otherwise meet as unexplained code, and two of them look wrong until the reason is given. Carrying one side's header verbatim reads like laziness; taking the later `modified` reads like a clock-based merge, which this project explicitly refuses elsewhere — *"the clock is a good input to judgment and a bad input to arithmetic"* — and the distinction is that this is not choosing a winner between two versions but stamping a record that already merged.

The cost in (2) is stated rather than softened because it is the one thing a reviewer should push back on if they disagree: the merged record's attribution is a small, deliberate lie, and the alternative is a driver that cannot merge what it exists to merge.

Kept with the entry rather than in `coding-lessons`: (1) and (4) are facts about this file format and this checksum, and generalise no further than a format whose header carries derived content.

content: **The `cos(query, centroid)` boundary fails at scale, and the pilot that suggested it was flattered by its off-domain class.** Tested 2026-09-08 with every unique context in a corpus as the answerable class and three sources of unanswerable — other sets' contexts, twelve hand-written off-domain questions, and gibberish. On `scatterhoard` at 721 memories the medians are **0.440 answerable against 0.365 unanswerable**, overlapping so far that the best available threshold, 0.158, admits 37 of 52 unanswerable queries while rejecting none of the answerable: it separates nothing. `coding-lessons` at 121 is no better, 38 errors of 166. Only the eight-memory `governance-docs` separates cleanly, which is what a tiny corpus will do. **The reason is instructive: `cos(query, centroid)` measures register and style, not topical answerability.** The pilot's unanswerable class was cooking, cycling and keyboard mashing — far from the corpus in vocabulary as well as subject. Adding same-author text about a different subject, which is the honest control, collapses the separation. Supersedes the pilot's optimistic reading; re-run `probe_the_corpus_alignment_boundary_across_scales` in `tests/probes.rs`.
context: Running the CSLS re-test and the alignment-boundary trial the human partner asked for, across four set sizes plus the union.
why: Superseding rather than amending because the pilot was exported and committed in `dab1fe7` before this ran. It was recorded at confidence 0.75 with *twelve queries is a pilot, not a result* written into it, and this is what a proper trial did to it — worth noting as a case where the stated caveat was the thing that actually happened rather than a formality.

content: **A set's own test sentences are matched to a declared language by language and script, ignoring region.** Decided with the human partner on 2026-10-04. `en-us` and `en-gb` are the same language, but `egy-latn` and `egy-egyp` are different. A missing script matches any script. If a declared tag without a script matches more than one script group, such as plain `egy` with both `egy-latn` and `egy-egyp` sets present, it is left unscored. Status names both groups and suggests declaring the scripts separately. Status also notes any sentence-set tag that no declared language matches.
context: Designing agent-supplied test sentences for the declared-language check. The archaeology example of English, Ancient Greek, and Egyptian in hieroglyphs and transliteration raised how tags should match.
why: Region barely moves a model's representation, since a model that represents English handles both "colour" and "color", while script changes it completely. Ignoring region also avoids a mismatch between the human partner's American English and an agent's British English. This is the same rule `language_fit::built_in` already applies, so built-in and supplied sentences match alike. The ambiguous case is reported rather than resolved because a guess would score the wrong text.

content:
Measured 2026-09-19: the share of memories truncated before embedding has nearly tripled in ten days — 140 of 1121 over 512 tokens (12.5%), against 42 of 886 (4.7%) on 2026-09-09; median 333 tokens against 305, p90 539 against 460, max 912 against 699. The ninetieth-percentile memory now loses its tail, and for 10 of the 140 `content` alone fills the budget so `why` never reaches the model at all.

**The 512-token cut is not a model limit.** `StaticModel::encode` is exactly `encode_with_args(sentences, Some(512), 1024)`, and passing `None` disables both the character-level pre-truncation and the token-id truncation; a static model mean-pools token vectors and has no context window to overrun. Scatterhoard takes the default at `src/embedder.rs:300`.

Changing it is not a one-argument fix on its own, because the recorded model identity is the hash of `model.safetensors` alone (`src/embedder.rs:258`) and does not cover the encoding arguments — so new vectors and truncated old ones would coexist with the staleness check silent, which is the shape of `no-record-of-which-model-built-the-vectors`. The change is: extend the identity to cover the encoding arguments, then re-embed. Reproduce the counts with `probe_whether_long_memories_are_truncated_before_embedding`.
context: Working the memory-size-drift question after the human partner asked to tackle the whole of it — convention, refusal and limit unit — rather than the mechanical half alone.
why: The baseline filed with the question said a rise in length was not yet shown to be a harm, and this is the measurement that changes that: truncation is a concrete mechanism, it is accelerating, and what it removes is the end of the input — `why` first, then the keywords. Recorded with the identity hazard attached because the fix looks like a one-argument change and is not; separating them would leave a later session with the tempting half and not the dangerous half.

content: `recall-summary-output-mode` shipped 2026-09-06: `hoard_recall` takes `detail`, `full` or `summary`, and `hoard_memorize` echoes the line unconditionally. Three decisions beyond the backlog entry. The cut takes the **last** sentence end that fits rather than the first, because the first spends most of the budget on a memory opening with a short sentence and truncates to four characters on an `e.g.` -- silently, since a short line reads as a short memory. A summary hit carries **no `scope`**, which the entry's own 49-character envelope figure had already assumed. And a cut line ends in an ellipsis while a whole one does not, decided by the human partner after the level shipped without one: the marker comes out of the 120 rather than being added past them, and it goes on **every** cut, since marking only the ragged ones leaves an unmarked line meaning either complete or cut-at-a-sentence. Re-measured over the shipped code, the live `scatterhoard` file cuts 34 at a sentence and 61 at a word of 96, against the 40/59 split the pre-build check found -- so no interpretation moved the measurement.
context: Building the index-line output mode, then adding the truncation marker the human partner asked for once the rest was working.
why: Supersedes rather than amends because the memory it replaces is already exported, and its measured split -- 36 and 58 over 95 records -- stopped being what `report_summary_cuts` prints the moment the marker took a character out of the room. That is a small drift and exactly the kind this project has been bitten by: a later session runs the report, gets different numbers, and cannot tell a changed rule from a broken one. The three decisions are kept together because each is one a later reader would take for an oversight and quietly reverse -- first-sentence is the obvious reading of *cut at a sentence*, a missing `scope` looks forgotten, and an ellipsis on a line that already ends in a full stop looks like a bug rather than an answer to *is there more*.

content: **On `gemma4:12b` the sharing-preferences framing did not keep a health detail out of `local`.** In the 2026-10-21 incidental-health test, all 5 templated runs stored the invented user's HIV treatment appointment in `local`. The task is in `corpus/local-model-tasks.json` and describes no real person. That is identical to the baseline with an empty file. No run's reply said a detail was left out. The preferences were served in every templated run (20,715 characters against the baseline's 19,470). One confound: the prompt asked to store "anything about me worth remembering in my personal set". The logs are in that session's scratchpad, `framing-run-3`.
context: Building the sharing preferences served at session start. Third gemma run, after the second showed an effect for the employer but did not exercise never-in-local.
why: This is the case the human partner made never-means-never for, and the served text alone did not move a weak model at all. Either the confounded prompt overrode it, or protection that depends on a model obeying served text cannot be promised on small local models. The next run, without the confound, separates the two. Superseded to say the detail is invented: the first version quoted the stored sentence in a way a reader could take for a fact about a real person.

content: **The migration finished 2026-09-07 and its most valuable by-product was not navigation -- it was finding out how far the files had drifted behind the code.** Final state, re-derived that day: **ISSUES.md 86 rows, BACKLOG.md 57 rows, open-questions.md 34 rows, all three with zero entries below their markers.** open-questions.md went from 134,968 to roughly 30,000 characters in one session. **Checking each entry's present-tense claims -- required by the shaping standard before carrying a claim across -- closed four questions that were marked open and had in fact shipped:** `set-uuid` (decided, built, and the cutover run), `fixed-result-count` (answered by `limit` becoming a window with a largest-gap cut rather than a count), `memory-id-alphabet` (built), and this entry. **Two more were half-stale:** `author-name-or-reference` shipped its core while the `create`-requires-an-author refinement did not, and `what-recall-returns` named graph traversal as an unimplemented blocker that had long since landed. **Several entries had lost their evidence rather than their question** -- `charter-recall-shape`'s cost measurement had gone to zero, `third-catalog-budget-raise` held six headroom figures of which none was current. **So `audit-open-entries-for-closure` largely happened here**, as a side effect rather than as a pass: the check the standard already demands is the same check closure needs.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, on finishing the last of the three tracking files.
why:
Recorded because the *reason* to verify present-tense claims during migration was stated as accuracy -- not carrying a stale claim into a memory that mints a fresh date on it -- and the return turned out to be much larger: six entries' standing was wrong, and no separate audit would have been cheaper than the check already required.

That is worth generalising for the next such migration, on this project or another: a corpus of long-lived entries drifts against the code in a way nothing reports, and moving them is the occasion when each one is read closely enough to notice. The move is the audit.

The figures are re-derived rather than carried, with the command shape recorded elsewhere in this cluster; anchor any recount to the `END GENERATED INDEX` marker rather than to a line number.

content: The hold on catalog re-tuning was lifted 2026-09-06 for the whole watch-index rewrite, and this is a retirement for the cycle rather than a third one-pass exception. The human partner's reason: the hold existed so they could evaluate performance under the conventions as adopted, that evaluation is done and is what produced these changes, and evaluating a half-implemented set is worthless -- *we'll do all the updates, then I'll leave it alone for a while*. Text may move between entries and justifying reinforcement may be pared back where the arithmetic needs it, with each trim named and counted. The quiet period is what follows the cycle; nothing was said about narrowing what the cycle contains.
context: Being asked what rule I was referring to when deferring a change, and finding I had invented it.
why: Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claim is unchanged. It supersedes a version that added a clause nobody said -- that anything found mid-cycle needing a catalog edit goes to the backlog for after the quiet period -- which inverts the instruction and was then cited twice as the human partner's own rule, to defer a change and to justify not making room for it. The correction matters beyond this cycle because of how it happened: an instruction was paraphrased into a rule with a plausible extra clause, and the paraphrase was what later reasoning ran on. Quote the instruction where the wording is doing the work.

content: **The closure test for `an-unanswerable-query-returns-confident-hits` still fails after calibration, because the set it names has no floor.** Run 2026-09-24, after `scatterhoard` (0.360) and `coding-lessons` (0.333) were calibrated that morning: unscoped, *premier league offside rule interpretation* and *premier league football results* each return two `governance-docs` memories, both led by the same Corporations Code 7212(b) committee memory the issue was filed on. The two calibrated sets return nothing for either. `governance-docs` holds 1 labelled query of the 20 a calibration needs, and a set consulted this rarely earns labels about that slowly, so organic use will not close the case.
context: Checking, at the human partner's question, whether the calibration taken that morning closed the unanswerable-query issue; after finishing the out-link work and the calibrate-note fix.
why: The checkpoint named this re-run as the closure test once calibration was taken, and the calibration taken does not reach the case: every false hit the issue records came from the one set left uncalibrated. That turns the open question from whether a floor separates the football case into how a small, rarely used set gets a floor at all — which is what `explicit-calibration-pass` holds in reserve.

content: **The export review exempts the name a person currently publishes a set under, by a built-in rule rather than an entry in their sharing preferences.** Decided 2026-10-29 by the human partner: the name of the set's current author record, as `Store::author_record` resolves it, is not a pre-pass hit and is served to the model as `published_as`, which the task says is not a mention. Past names the person published under are still flagged, as is anyone else's. Recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*.
context: The scatterhoard set's full review, where every memory on the first page was flagged for the handle the set publishes under; chosen over the explicit always-fine entry.
why: The server holds the information, which record is the person in this set, and the person already made the decision by choosing the name to publish under: the preferences template's own wording is "my name, except as the author of my own work", and the author record is that exception. An "Always fine to share" entry would have to be found by every user after a flooded first review, and applies in every set, so it cannot say "fine where I publish under it, kept out where I do not". It also silences only the pre-pass, leaving the model's answer to flag the name anyway. Past names stay flagged because a person may have moved away from one for a reason.

content: **`recall-when` now opens by weighing a recall against what it could save**, served 2026-09-21. *"Search memory before acting whenever a recall costs less than what it could save"*, with the old decision-shaped moments kept as examples and three added: redoing work, searching for something, starting anything slow. The reinforcement names the second case to notice: *"a step whose next move looks obvious."* The text is in `RECALL_WHEN`, `src/conventions/catalog.rs`, and the account is in `documents/design/conventions.md`.
context: After exporting coding-lessons and governance-docs, a disk search for governance-docs's file missed a memory in `local` that named it. The human partner proposed a recall adjustment in response.
why: The output of the `recall-would-have-helped` investigation: three of its four cases were mechanical-seeming steps that none of the four decision-shaped moments covered. The framing is the human partner's. They rejected a narrower draft about the machine as too specific: people recall before most actions because a recall is cheaper than searching the house for the car keys, and stating the comparison covers cases no list anticipates. Cost 69 characters, leaving 24 of the 18,000 budget.

content: On a server declared in Claude Desktop's config, every alternation was stripped from the published schema, so an object `scope` arrived stringified and **no shared set could be named at all** — not recalled, exported, imported or reembedded. Fixed 2026-08-12 by publishing the well-carried subset: `scope` as `local` or `shared:<name>`. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `scope-arrives-untyped-and-an-object-scope-is-stringified`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **The measurement that forced it, 2026-08-18: the rule and the decay are not independent, so a harness that cannot vary both cannot answer the question it exists for.** `tune` mode hard-coded the walk it compared rules at, and `sweep` mode hard-coded `sum` as the rule while varying the walk; neither crossed the two, so a rule could only ever be judged at a walk chosen for something else. That is what made the re-measurement ambiguous: **`sum` lost to `max` at decay 0.7, and beat what `max` achieved there once given the 0.5 it prefers.** The reason is mechanical — `sum` is the only rule whose inherited term can displace a direct hit, so how fast that term fades is what decides whether it helps.
context: Migrating the eval-walk-from-the-caller entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the ambiguity that motivated it.
why:
Irreproducible as stated: it was measured against the corpus and code of 2026-08-18, and it is the observation that says why the grid mode exists rather than a simpler flag. Without it, `grid` looks like generality for its own sake and the obvious simplification — pick a decay, compare rules there — is the exact mistake that produced an ambiguous answer.

The interaction is also the substance of the open question about which combining rule to use: a result reported at one decay is not a result about the rule.

content: An MCP client serves whatever Scatterhoard binary it launched with, so rebuilding the source does not change what a running session sees. **The convention count is not a reliable tell, and relying on it missed this on 2026-09-07.** That day a session loaded eleven conventions from a server started the previous evening; the source also defined eleven, so nothing looked wrong, and the difference was entirely in the *text* -- `keyword-standards` was missing the `hoard-proj-` clause committed that morning, while `store-when` and `hoard-watch` still carried two reinforcement sentences that had been trimmed to pay for it. The stale text was read, reported to the human partner, and contradicted the day's headline decision without being noticed. A count only moves when a convention is added or removed; edits, which are the common case, leave it fixed. **Check the text of a convention the recent work touched**, or compare the process start time against the binary's mtime -- `ps -eo pid,lstart,command | grep scatterhoard` against `ls -la target/debug/scatterhoard` -- which answers regardless of what changed. Verified this way on 2026-09-07: processes dated Sep 6 20:12 against a binary rebuilt Sep 7 16:25, confirmed by `strings target/debug/scatterhoard | grep -c "reserved for Scatterhoard itself"` returning 0 for text the running server had just served.
context: Restarting the MCP client after finding the served conventions were a day behind the source, then splitting CLAUDE.md into AGENTS.md.
why:
Supersedes the original solely to correct its stated tell. The claim about the mechanism was right and is unchanged; what is now known to be wrong is *the tell is `hoard_conventions` returning fewer conventions than the source defines*, which had held for the two earlier instances because both were additions. The third instance was an edit, and the tell was silent -- so a memory whose purpose is detection was, on the day it was most needed, pointing at the one signal that could not fire.

This is the third recorded occurrence, and the first where the staleness governed a session's reasoning rather than merely limiting it: the conventions are the steering input, so an old one does not degrade anything visibly. It answers every call successfully and simply governs. Superseded rather than amended because the original has been exported and a later reader needs to see which tell was believed first.

content: A shared set whose database another server process created after this one started cannot be reached until a restart: the server learns its sets by scanning the home once at startup (`shared_scopes_in` in `src/store.rs`), every tool refuses the scope as not loaded, and `create` refuses because the file exists, saying to restart. Found 2026-10-16 when a throwaway set created from an interactive Claude Code session could not be dropped from a desktop session sharing the same home. Fixed when a database that appears in the home after startup can be used without restarting the client.
context: Cleaning up throwaway sets after live-testing the publishing-name form across Claude Desktop chat, the Code tab and an interactive terminal.
why: Several servers sharing one home is a supported arrangement, not an edge case: the desktop app, Claude Code and chat each launch their own server against `~/.local/share/scatterhoard`, so a set made in one is invisible in the others for the rest of their sessions. Blocks rather than misleads, because the refusal is honest; the caller simply cannot proceed, and "restart" in an MCP host means restarting the client.

content: Every page of the export review re-sends the same fixed text: the whole sharing-preferences file, `others_keep_out`, `caution` and `task`, about 6,000 characters, beside three to eight memories. Over a full review that text is most of what the session reads. Measured 2026-10-27 re-reviewing `coding-lessons`: 197 memories took about 45 `review` calls, so the preferences alone arrived about 45 times, and the `scatterhoard` set's roughly 1,500 memories would take about 350 calls, which no single session's context is expected to hold. Fixed when a review's fixed text arrives once per review rather than once per page, or the page carries far more memories.
context: Re-reviewing the published memory sets under the export review's judgement gate, and planning a fresh session for the scatterhoard set's review because this one could not hold it.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. Costs: correct and honest, but it spends context on text that already arrived, and the cost scales with the set, so the largest sets, which most need a full review, are the ones a session cannot finish. Checkable by calling `hoard_sets` `review` twice on any shared set and comparing the two responses' fixed fields. The person's preferences also reach a session with the conventions catalog at its start, so a review page repeats what the session holds twice over.

content: **The 2026-08-23 fix was replaced on 2026-08-31 and the defect stays closed by a different mechanism.** `memory_file::absorb`, `import`'s `absorbing` argument and `Store::import_absorbing` are all gone — see `restore-silently-reverts-an-absorption`, the same rewrite seen from its other end. Merging is `hoard_sets` action `absorb`, and the two directions are answered separately: a link **into** the absorbed set is made internal by authoring a supersession, and a link **from** the absorbed set into this one canonicalises at the door as it always did. `a_supersession_arriving_from_the_absorbed_set_acts` is this entry's own scenario driven through the new operation, and the three mutations against the deleted function were replaced by seven against the new one. **One shape of merge is no longer done in one step**: folding `a` and `b` into a file declaring a *third* name — the literal scenario reported here — was expressible because `absorbing` took a list, and it is now *absorb `b` into `a`*, with a rename on top. Absorbing both into a freshly created third set also works, but only in one order — the set whose records point at the other must arrive second — and mutual links between the two cannot be resolved that way at all.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A fix superseded by a rewrite, with the capability that was quietly lost stated plainly: the exact scenario the entry reported is now a two-step operation, and one variant of it does not work at all.

content: **The framing Scatterhoard serves around a person's sharing preferences is held to the convention catalog's standard of efficiency, though it has no formal budget.** Stated 2026-10-21 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *the preferences start from a template*. Every sentence has to earn its keep. The person's own preferences file is exempt, since its length is theirs to choose.
context: Building the sharing preferences served at session start: trimming export-before-commit to make room for route-where to give way to a preference that says never.
why: The catalog budget exists to spend tokens efficiently. The conventions go into every session, including one on a small local model with a short context window, and the person has no control over them. The framing reaches every session in the same way. Without a stated standard, a text with no numeric limit drifts longer.

content: **This was Common Cause #1 of the file it appeared in** — *no single source of truth, facts restated by hand in a second place* — which ISSUES.md blames for five of its first nine defects. The entry recorded that as **the strongest evidence available that stating a rule does not enforce it**: the file's own header had settled which rule won from the beginning (*mark fixed entries `[x]` and leave them in place*, which is incompatible with sorting them into a `Fixed` section), and the rule did not hold — the 32 obeying it and the 33 not were split almost evenly. **The other three tracking files were clean, and two showed the fix**: open-questions.md and EARLY-VALIDATION.md are flat lists with no sections, and BACKLOG.md sections by *subject* rather than status, so nothing can disagree with anything. **Only ISSUES.md let its headings encode status.** A smaller inconsistency was noted and deliberately not bundled: those two files mark open with an explicit `- [ ]` while ISSUES.md and BACKLOG.md mark open by the **absence** of `[x]` — cosmetic across files rather than ambiguous inside one.
context: Migrating the issues-records-its-status-twice entry out of BACKLOG.md, on finding the migration had already closed it.
why:
Kept because the entry is the first result of `audit-open-entries-for-closure`, arriving before that audit was run — it was open, migrated as the second-to-last entry of the file, and turned out to have been fixed by the migration itself. That is a data point about the audit's yield rather than only about this defect.

And the general form is worth having when the remaining tracking-file work is designed: the fix that held was not choosing between two hand-maintained records but making one of them **derived**. A rule stated in a header did not survive 84 entries; a generated row cannot disagree with its source, because it has no independent existence.

content:
**`label_clusters` in `src/summary.rs` takes keyword lists grouped by cluster, and two of its choices are decisions rather than code.** Split 2026-09-13 from a memory whose build-status half had gone stale; this is the half that still holds.

**The boundary.** `label_clusters` takes `&[Cluster]`, where a `Cluster` owns its members' keyword lists — not indices into a set and not a parallel assignment array — so a cluster cannot be desynchronised from the memories it describes. The labelling knows nothing about stores, files, vectors or MCP, which keeps it independently testable; `cluster` hands over keyword lists grouped by cluster for exactly that reason.

*No minimum-support cutoff.* The Python prototype required a keyword on at least three memories of a cluster before it could label it — a magic number that breaks on small sets, and unnecessary: weighting each score by `ln(1 + inside)` already stops a keyword on one memory outranking one on half the cluster. The only threshold left is `score > 0.0`, the point where a keyword stops being commoner inside its cluster than outside.

*Smoothing acts on the proportions, not the counts.* The prototype floored the outside count at half a memory, which is nothing in a corpus of eight hundred and fifty per cent in a corpus of one: the constant-count form scored a genuinely distinctive keyword *negative* on a three-memory cluster. Jeffreys' prior on both proportions fixes it. Both forms agree on any realistic corpus, so only a deliberately tiny fixture separates them; the mutation `set summary: smooth the counts instead of the proportions` records the difference.
context: Finishing the derived set summary: building the owed description that an import onto a machine without a usable model leaves behind. Same stretch: diagnosing the previous session's [bio] refusals through flightlog. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 1 link an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.
why: The still-true half of 01M2CJVCR3EB893J4WD0MR2EQY, split out when its claim that the clustering half was unbuilt went stale. Kept because neither decision is visible from reading the module — what was rejected, and why — and the smoothing bug is one a realistic test corpus hides completely.

content: The catalog headroom kept going stale because of **tense**, not because it was quoted. A figure written in the past and tied to a date — *"the catalog stood at 17,981 on 2026-09-06"* — records what a decision was taken against and stays true forever; the same figure written as *"the catalog stands at…"* is a claim that decays with the next catalog edit, and nothing marks the moment it stops being true. On 2026-09-07 four present-tense sites disagreed with a derived 320: `conventions.md` said 125 free and 19 free, `open-questions.md` said 903, and `third-catalog-budget-raise` said **2,113 — overstating the room by 1,793 and asserting the budget was not binding**, which is the opposite of the truth and had already been quoted into a design recommendation before the derivation caught it. Fixed structurally: `conventions.md` gained *The headroom is derived, never written down*, which holds the command and no number, and every narrative figure was converted to dated past tense pointing at it. **The budget itself, 18,000, stays quotable** — it is a constant with a test, and changes only by a recorded decision.
context: Consolidating the duplicated headroom statements after the hoard-proj- carve-out, when the human partner asked whether they were the source of earlier confusion — they were.
why:
The rule it refines was already recorded and still went on being broken, which means *derive, do not quote* was not actionable at the moment of writing: an author narrating a decision genuinely needs a figure in the text, so a bare prohibition leaves them nothing to do and they write the number anyway. Naming tense gives them the move — date it and put it in the past — and it is checkable by reading, where "was this derived?" is not.

The damage is what makes this worth a memory rather than another correction. A stale headroom does not merely misinform; it inverts the conclusion, because the whole point of the figure is whether the budget binds. The 2,113 reading said there was room for three more conventions when there was room for none.

content: **A change to the sharing preferences reopens only what it tightens, measured line by line against the copy each set keeps of the preferences its last finished review read.** Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. New never-store words reopen the cleared memories containing them, matched by the server. New keep-outs and removed exceptions go to the model as the two review questions about cleared memories, group by group, with each group's verdict shown to the person. Loosening reopens nothing.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public. This was the last design decision before testing on gemma.
why: This keeps the human partner's standard that earlier review work is not undone wholesale, while still applying a stricter preference to memories cleared under the old one. Without a saved copy, the only safe response to an edit would be to reopen everything. The copy is updated only when a review finishes, so an interrupted review is compared against the old text next time. A reworded item counts as removed and added, which errs towards reopening. The copy stays in the store, which is never exported.

content: **Why the cutover could not be run from the session that built it, and the one window where the edit could be lost silently — recorded 2026-08-31.** `create` mints an identity and **nothing else does**, so the three sets predating the field had to take theirs from a **file**, which means a server that knows the field must already be running before any of it starts. The server attached while this was built did not. **The dangerous step is the one that has to be done in a single go**: a server built before this change **silently strips a `set_id` it does not know when it exports**, so the gap between hand-editing a file's header and importing it back is the window where the edit disappears — with no error, and no diff anyone is watching.
context: Migrating the set-identity-cutover entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the procedural hazard it warned about.
why:
Recorded because the hazard is a property of the *upgrade path* rather than of the feature, so it is invisible from the code once every server knows the field, and it recurs on the next header addition. A reader who forgets it would hand-edit a header, export from a stale process, and see a clean-looking file with the edit gone.

The verification is the reusable half of the procedure: re-exporting after the import and checking the header reproduces is what distinguishes *store and file agreed once* from *store and file converged*. An import that reports success proves only that the file was read.

content: **The recall nudge's `PreToolUse` context reaches the session: confirmed 2026-10-06 at 04:09 UTC, so it needs no `PostToolUse` fallback.** A read-only command the hook's pattern counts as a code write was run on purpose, after the human partner wired the hook and restarted Claude Desktop. It was `python3 -c "…open('src/lib.rs')…"`, which mentions `src/` and `open(`. The nudge text arrived in the session as hook context before the command ran, and the log at `~/.local/state/scatterhoard/recall-nudge.log` recorded `nudged`. **That first log line is a deliberate test and is to be excluded from the week's count.** The Claude Desktop interface may not show the nudge to the human, so the log is how they see it fire.
context: Right after the human partner wired the nudge and restarted Claude Desktop, while running a probe of whether gemma4:12b can write Rust.
why: CLAUDE.md said to check that the nudge reaches the session, so this records the check and its outcome. The test line is named so the experiment's measurement does not count it as a real nudge. It also shows the pattern match counts a read-only command as a write when it mentions `open(`. That is harmless here, but it is one way the log can overcount.

content:
**The script failure is not symmetric: English survives a Chinese vocabulary where Chinese does not survive an English one.** The human partner expected an English probe set to degrade under a Chinese-trained model the way Chinese degrades under the shipping one. Measured at the tokenisation level over the 601 committed English probes, that does not hold.

| vocabulary | composition | tokens | `[UNK]` | fully unknown |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bge-base-en` (ships) | **Latin 92.8%**, CJK 0.8% | 5,559 | 1 | **0 / 601** |
| `bert-base-chinese` | **CJK 69.3%, Latin 17.2%** | **9,152** | 1 | **0 / 601** |

**The cause is corpus asymmetry, not design.** A Chinese vocabulary carries roughly 3,600 Latin tokens because Chinese training text is full of English technical terms and names; an English vocabulary carries 492 CJK characters because English text contains almost no Chinese. So English fragments but survives, where Chinese hits `[UNK]`, is discarded before pooling, and yields the direction-less vector `Vector::new` refuses.

**What is measured and what is not.** Tokenisation is measured. **Similarity is not** — that needs the weights, and no non-English model is on this machine (`potion-multilingual-128M` is 512 MB). English under a Chinese model fragments **65% harder**, and mean pooling dilutes with every extra piece, so degradation is expected; its size is unknown. Reproduce by fetching `google-bert/bert-base-chinese/vocab.txt`, 109 KB.
context: The human partner expecting an English calibration set to fail under a Chinese-trained model the way Chinese fails under the English one, after the Latin-script-only issue was filed.
why:
Recorded because the expectation was reasonable, precise and wrong in a way that matters for the design: if the failure were symmetric, a probe set could be checked by the same test in either direction. It is not, so a store can be *quietly* degraded rather than loudly broken depending only on which way the mismatch runs — and the quiet direction is the one that ships.

**The design consequence survives the refutation and is the part to keep: a calibration probe set is a property of the model, not of the tool.** `corpus/offdomain-probes.json` is calibrated for `potion-base-32M` and is not portable to a user who swaps models, even if its text tokenises there. Tokens surviving is not meaning surviving — the pieces English fragments into under a Chinese model carry embeddings trained in Chinese contexts, so a floor set from English probes would sit in a region of the space the store's real traffic never visits. That argument needs no measurement and holds for any model swap, including English-to-English: `potion-retrieval-32M` would want its own probe set too.

What would settle the unmeasured half is one 512 MB download and a re-run of `probe_whether_recall_works_outside_latin_script` under the multilingual model, which would also show whether multilingual is the fix rather than merely a different failure.

content: **How a mis-recorded memory is corrected.** *Mostly resolved 2026-08-05 in Corrections*, which settles which of supersede, amend and forget is proper when: the claim is `content` plus `why`, everything else is apparatus, and the criterion is what was *believed* rather than what was *true*. **Whether amendment may touch `content` is deferred with its reasoning recorded there** -- by the principle a content typo is a faulty record and should be amendable, but *typo or changed claim?* is a judgement the software cannot verify and the failure directions are unequal, so a content typo is superseded until a real case makes the distinction concrete. **Still genuinely open:** what amendment does to `modified` beyond the obvious, and whether amending a *shared* memory goes through the export review gate -- the gate keys on last modifier, so an amendment makes the local user responsible for a memory whose claim they did not write, which may or may not be what should be reviewed. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `mis-recorded-memory-corrected`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The shared-amendment question is carried in the head because it is the one with a consequence outside the local machine, and it is easy to lose behind the more interesting typo-or-changed-claim argument. An amendment that reassigns responsibility for someone else's claim is a review problem rather than a correction problem, and nothing currently notices it.

content: SETUP.md §5 had no items for the newest surface. Built 2026-08-21: seven items, 21 to 27 — items 21 to 23 close the gap this entry named (`export`, `import`, `amend`, `forget`), and 24 to 27 cover the four surfaces added on 2026-08-20 and 21. **Item 27 carries a warning rather than an instruction to proceed**, since it is the only item that leaves a store damaged and `drop` did not exist to undo it. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `setup-smoke-items`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Test and documentation debt section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only.

§5 carries its own warning about asserting runtime behaviour the code has moved past, and adding items is subject to it — which is why an item that cannot be safely performed is written as a warning rather than dropped.

content: **`an-unanswerable-query-returns-confident-hits` reproduced on 2026-09-23 because the floor was cleared, not because it has never been set.** `scatterhoard` calibrated 2026-09-17 at 0.3755 from 26 labelled queries; the 2026-09-19 re-embed cleared every set's floor, the encoding having entered the model identity. Status that day: `non_match_floor: null` on all four sets, `labelled_since_calibration` 17 of the 20 a calibration reads. So the canonical query still returns four confident-looking hits, and the closure test is to calibrate once past 20 and re-run it. The corrected claim is the cause: this is a floor discarded and rebuilding, not a mechanism that has never worked.
context: Auditing the open issues for closure; corrected within the hour when the human partner said the calibration had been run and then reverted.
why: The superseded version claimed no set had ever reached the calibration threshold, which is false: the human partner corrected it, and the first live calibration and its clearing were both already recorded here. It was written from a null status field without recalling the field's history, and it would have sent a later session to look for a threshold nobody had crossed rather than for evidence that has to accumulate a second time.

content: **The recall nudge's first ordinary-work session, 2026-10-10 into 2026-10-11, logged eight code writes and never nudged**, all eight `recalled`: one per-change recall, made before the first write to `src/`, satisfied the once-per-commit check for every later write. No commit happened, so a later behaviour change — the refusal rewrite and the relay on `mint` and `rename`, a day later — went unrecalled and unprompted. That one recall returned the backlog cluster and no `coding-lessons` entry, so it caught nothing to apply. Read from `~/.local/state/scatterhoard/recall-nudge.log`, session `5194284e`.
context: Building the publishing-name hint, the elicitation proposal and its relay fallback, without a commit in between.
why: The experiment measures whether the nudge reaches skipped recalls, and this is a skip it structurally cannot reach: its window is a commit, so a long uncommitted session with several distinct changes gets one recall for all of them. Whether that matters depends on how often sessions make several behaviour changes between commits, which this one instance does not settle.

content: A set another server drops stays loaded in every other server that holds it open, which goes on reading and writing a database whose file is gone: on Unix an open SQLite file survives being unlinked, so those writes land nowhere anyone can reach again, and nothing reports it. Found 2026-10-16, by reasoning from the fix for `a-set-created-by-another-server-is-unreachable-until-restart`, which picks up sets appearing after startup but not ones disappearing; not yet reproduced. Fixed when a server notices that a held set's file has gone and stops using it, saying so.
context: Fixing the rescan for sets another server creates, after cleaning up throwaway sets from the publishing-name tests.
why: Corrupts rather than blocks, because the failure is silent loss: a write reports success and is gone at the next restart. Several servers sharing one home is ordinary, so one session dropping a set another is using is a matter of time. Unreproduced, so the first step is a test with two servers that shows it.

content: Import now says the unrecognised target out loud, which was the load-bearing half all along and is **not** retired by normalising. Canonicalisation collapses spellings; it does not survive a checkout being renamed or moved, which orphans every base just as thoroughly and arrives looking exactly like a location never seen before. The remark names the targets the set does know, says plainly that every record was reconciled with no common ancestor, and stays a remark: a second checkout is legitimate, a mistyped path is not, and only the caller can tell.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Why the structural fix does not remove the need for the report. Normalising addresses one cause of an orphaned base; renaming a checkout produces the identical symptom and no amount of path handling can distinguish it from a first import.

content: A reached memory's score is a weighted blend -- `INHERITED_WEIGHT = 0.25`, a quarter from the walk -- and NOT the unweighted sum that the closed `graph-traversal` entry in BACKLOG.md reports. The two are order-equivalent up to a positive factor, since `0.75*own + 0.25*inherited` orders identically to `own + (1/3)*inherited`, which corrects the reasoning that originally rejected blends as "taking weight away from the own term". What the weight actually sets is how much inherited score is admitted at all; the blend that once measured worse than no traversal was admitting three times what a sum does, not penalising direct hits. The blend was chosen for robustness rather than peak: it is the only rule measured that stays above the content-only baseline at every decay on both answer keys, moving about one point where sum moves fourteen to twenty-six.
context: Decided 2026-08-18 by the human partner on measured evidence, over 24 queries harvested from this project's transcripts and labelled twice, blind, on different models. Checkable at `INHERITED_WEIGHT` in src/traversal.rs, whose doc comment carries the order-equivalence argument.
why: The selection criterion is the durable part: a rule that wins the cell it was tuned in and collapses beside it is the worse choice, because the corpus a rule is tuned on is never the corpus it runs on. Stored also because the closed BACKLOG entry states the superseded answer flatly -- "the scores are summed" -- and being marked done is precisely what stops anyone re-reading it. A closed entry rots with nothing to flag it, which is a stronger argument for harvesting them than mere retrievability.

content: The convention catalog budget is 18,000 characters, raised from 16,000 on 2026-08-13 by the human partner — the second raise, and argued the same way as the first, from what the budget spends rather than from what the next convention needs. The bar set was proportional: stay well under 4% of the smallest context window in range, and 18,000 characters is about 4,390 tokens, or 3.4% of 128K. The "work towards it, not fill it" instruction still attaches and applies harder at each raise, because a budget raised whenever it binds is not a budget.
context: Checkable at MAX_CATALOG_CHARS in src/conventions/mod.rs, which is the enforced copy, and at the "Resolved: the budget is 18,000 characters" section of documents/design/conventions.md — note the 16,000 section immediately above it is kept as history.
why: The memory this replaces recorded the 8,000 to 16,000 raise and was never followed by one for the second raise a day later, so the corpus held 16,000 as the operative figure for eleven days. That is worse than holding nothing: recall returns a stale number confidently, and a session reading it plans convention edits against a ceiling 2,000 characters below the real one. Found 2026-08-24 when the human partner contradicted a figure quoted from the design document, where the same trap sits — the 16,000 section is still present and the 18,000 section is twelve lines below it, so a grep that stops at the first heading gets the withdrawn answer.

content: **The first full pass with slow-step snapshots (2026-09-28, 561 mutations, 4.7s each) found no swapping, and two causes of its outliers.** First, `mutate.py` cleared `target-mutation` three times mid-pass (21:50, 22:07, 22:21), because the directory grows about 500 files per mutation and crosses `CROWDED` (100,000) roughly every 200. Each clear made the next mutation rebuild every dependency, at 28–37s. Second, VS Code's rust-analyzer ran `cargo clippy` during two slow test steps. Load averages were 16–37 on an 8-core machine, and paging was page-ins only. Read from the pass log.
context: Reading the full mutation pass for set-settled-at-first-write step 2, the first run with the runner's new slow-step snapshots.
why: Settles the question the snapshots were added for: the slow entries are the runner's own designed clears plus editor load, not memory pressure and not the corpus. The clears cost about 1.5 minutes a pass. Whether `CROWDED` should rise is open: 2026-09-20 measured no slowdown at 45,000 files, and the cost appears somewhere below 159,000. Nothing yet says where between. Recorded so the next slow pass starts from this rather than re-deriving it.

content: **It was tested before it was built, 2026-08-09**, and the result became a property the code relies on rather than a workaround. SQLite resolves symlinks for its sidecar files — verified with two `SCATTERHOARD_HOME` directories whose `local.sqlite3` symlinked to one real file, using real servers rather than a unit test. `Store::file` now reports SQLite's **resolved** path, so two homes reaching one store report one file, and the test `two_homes_sharing_one_store_through_a_symlink_report_the_same_file` holds it. The whole feature was then verified the same way: real servers over two homes and one common directory.
context: Migrating the scatterhoard-local entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the pre-build verification it rested on.
why:
Recorded because the symlink behaviour is an assumption about SQLite that the design now depends on, and it is the kind of thing that reads as incidental. If it were false — if SQLite created its `-wal` and `-shm` beside the *link* rather than beside the resolved file — two homes sharing one store would corrupt it rather than share it, and nothing in this project's own code would be at fault.

Testing the mechanism before building the feature is what made that cheap to learn. The alternative order finds the same fact after the design has already committed to it.

content: Before letting a set declare something about itself in a reserved memory, ask whether the store already holds that fact. A set's charter is not derivable from its contents, which is why `hoard-scope-topics` had to be a declaration; a set's keyword vocabulary is derivable, so declaring it would be a second copy free to drift. The test that separates them is whether the content is normative: "we spell issues `issue-NNN`" is a rule about keywords not yet written and cannot be read off existing ones, while "this project talks about embeddings" can.
context: Reached 2026-08-12 while filing the proposed `hoard-scope-keywords` reserved keyword as an open question, by asking why the `hoard-scope-topics` precedent did not simply carry over.
why: `hoard-scope-topics` is a tempting template because it worked, and the next proposal to copy it will not automatically be a case where declaration is the only source. Scatterhoard's largest recorded cause of defects is one fact written down twice with the copies drifting, so a memory format that invites a second copy of derivable state is that failure moving into the data. Stating the normative test rather than the conclusion is what makes this reusable for whatever the next declaration proposal turns out to be. Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule, which moves a memory discussing a `hoard-` mechanism out of the reserved space; the claim is unchanged.

content: Scatterhoard's destructive operations always write a safety copy, and consult no dirty flag to decide whether to. The guard needs to know whether any memory here exists in no file; the reconciliation base cannot answer that, because it records a past agreement between two replicas rather than what is currently on disk. A branch switch rewrites the exported file with the base untouched. So the gate was removed rather than tuned, and `drop` and `restore` read no state out of the database they are about to destroy.
context: Decided 2026-08-06, resolving the "dirty relative to what" question that had blocked `drop`. Recorded in documents/design/set-lifecycle.md under "Resolved: the save is unconditional, and no flag gates it", which also carries a note to rewrite that argument if the store registry is adopted.
why: The question was framed for two sessions as "which collapse rule is right" -- dirty against any target, or against every target -- and both candidates were defensible, which is what kept it stuck. It dissolved once the base was read for what it is. The tell was that the safer reading made the gate pass in nearly every real configuration, and a guard that does not discriminate is not a guard to tune.

content: **Whether, and how, a set should declare the language or languages its memories are written in.** Raised 2026-09-11 by the human partner while `potion-multilingual-128M` was being made a supported alternative: a user with sets in different languages will run into this or create a mess, because a server holds one model and scores every set it serves with that model — an English project set and a Chinese personal set cannot both be well covered, and nothing today says which one is being misindexed. **What a declaration would feed:** a model-fit report at open, naming the sets the loaded model does not cover; the check at the write door, which otherwise infers coverage from the text alone; and the language of any calibration probes generated for a set. **The choices to settle:** where it lives — the `hoard-scope-topics` charter travels through export and is reviewed like any memory, while a `meta` row stays local and tells a collaborator nothing; one language or several, and whether a set may be mixed; what a mismatch does, where *a store owns its model* argues for reporting rather than refusing; and whether detection over the memories themselves cross-checks the declaration, which can be wrong when written and can go stale as a set grows. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `store-declares-its-language`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Making the multilingual model a supported alternative, and working out where the recall floor's calibration data would come from; the human partner raised the multi-language user before the floor discussion went further.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. Filed as a question because nothing is decided — the human partner raised the need while choosing to support the multilingual model, before any of the shape had been discussed.

It sits downstream of two things already on record. A model's coverage is what makes a declaration meaningful at all, which is `recall-is-latin-script-only`; and the floor's calibration data has to be in the store's own language, which is `floor-calibration-source`, so a declaration would also say what language a generated probe should be written in.

Worth raising when it is taken up: if the declaration lives in the charter, it is instruction-shaped text arriving from a repository — the channel `documents/design/trigger-and-loading.md` reasons about. Lower stakes than routing, since a wrong language misindexes rather than misdirects, but the same shape.

content: Found 2026-08-11 re-running SETUP.md §5 immediately after the `oneOf` fix, which worked and appeared to uncover this behind it. Through the affected server the `scope` property arrived as `{}` — description gone, branches gone — and with no type published an object argument was serialised as *text*, so `scope: {"shared": "scatterhoard"}` was refused with `unknown variant '{"shared": "scatterhoard"}'`, which is `serde` receiving the JSON as a string. `scope: "local"` worked, because a plain string survives the round trip. **The same call against a differently-registered server, same binary, succeeded with the object form.** *Why the obvious mitigation does not work*: the fix that worked for `action` was a flat fallback beneath the branches, and here there is nothing scalar to fall back to since `scope` is genuinely string-or-object — `"type": ["string", "object"]` is no help either, because `context` already carried a union type and was dropped just the same. Whatever flattens these keeps a single scalar `type` and discards everything else.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The observation, and why the previous defect's remedy does not transfer: a flat fallback needs something scalar to fall back to, and a union type is discarded by the same mechanism.

content: Measured over both live sets 2026-09-02: memories carry a median of **5 keywords** (mean 5.1, max 7), layered deliberately rather than synonymously — a gathering term, precise identifiers, often an issue slug. `budget` appears alone on **zero** memories, since every one also carries `context-budget`, and `catalog_fits_context_budget` never appears without it either. **So the keyword layer has redundancy built in by convention, and a split has to be *total* to cost anything** — every memory on a subject using disjoint keyword sets — which with five terms each and a shared slug essentially does not happen.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The measurement that bounds how much a split spelling can cost: layered keywords make the failure require disjointness across every memory on a subject, which the convention makes very unlikely.

content: **The state-machine design the entry argued for was rejected in drafting on 2026-09-04, and the reason is a property of supersession the argument had not accounted for.** The entry noticed a real collision -- driving transitions by mutating a keyword is an amendment, and amendment is refused on any exported record, which every shared investigation will be -- and proposed that transitions therefore *become* supersessions, so an investigation's progress is a chain whose tip is its current state, with `resolve_supersession` already computing exactly that, forks included. **What defeats it: one observation set can drive several questions, and supersession affords exactly one successor.** Advancement is therefore spawning a new head that draws on the accumulated observations while the set carries on collecting, and supersession is left to do only what it does elsewhere -- correcting and retiring. **Three sub-questions the entry raised were dissolved rather than answered** by the marked-case design: whether a mutable status is even a legal keyword under `keyword-standards`, how *ongoing* is queried given `matched_keywords` is an unweighted count, and whether the chain-tip reading made the pipeline free of new vocabulary. **The universality constraint held throughout** -- the states had to be generic, since a convention naming this project's own investigation kinds would be the taxonomy belonging in the sets rather than the catalog, which the catalog had already been corrected for once.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Recorded because the rejected design is the one a later session will re-invent. It is genuinely elegant, the machinery to support it exists, and the objection is a single structural fact -- one successor per supersession -- that is invisible unless you are holding the multiple-questions-from-one-observation-set case at the same time.

The three dissolved sub-questions are kept as a set because their disappearance is evidence about the shape of the answer: a design that removes three questions rather than answering them is usually the simpler one, and that is worth having on record where a future proposal reopens any of them.

content: A store holding a complete vector set with no recorded model reported itself unembedded, and the code could not leave that state — so mismatch detection could never fire and the first write would stamp false provenance on vectors it did not produce. Fixed 2026-08-20 by a new invariant: if there are no vectors, there is no model. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `embedded-store-can-report-itself-unembedded`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order, at the reduced depth.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Found 2026-08-10 by reproducing the configuration [store-registry.md](documents/design/store-registry.md) predicted, deliberately rather than by accident. **Corrupts rather than Misleads, and the distinction is the whole entry**: attribution is not a report about a memory, it is *part of the record* — `created.by` and `modified.by` are checksummed, exported, and read by the export-review gate — so a memory attributed to the wrong identity is wrong data that travels, with nothing anywhere saying which of the two identities was meant. **The configuration is not exotic**: `local` is personal and machine-wide, `SCATTERHOARD_HOME` defaults to one path under `$HOME`, and a server is registered per checkout, so two checkouts already shared one local store — which is why it was fixed ahead of the store-placement work it was proposed alongside. *Correcting it after the fact is possible and is not a tool action*: export, edit the identities, import back. That the repair needs a human reading a diff is the design's position rather than a gap, since *"me under a name I no longer use"* and *"someone else's work"* are indistinguishable to software.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The severity argument turns on attribution being part of the record rather than a report about it. The repair being manual is a stated design position, not an omission — worth keeping so nobody builds the tool action that would have to guess.

content: **A per-change recall changed what was written, 2026-10-16**: before making a declined elicitation form fall back to the model's name, the habit recall returned the `coding-lessons` lesson on guards keyed to surface form. Applied, it widened the fallback from "declined" to "declined or dismissed", since a client that cannot show forms might report either, and keying on the one word observed would have left the other looping on the question. Earlier the same day the recall nudge fired for the first time, on a diagnostic log line, and the recall it asked for was made after that write rather than before.
