content: **Fixed 2026-09-15: a memory linking with one label to the same id in two different sets kept only the second link, and the write reported success.** `links` was keyed `(source, label, target)` where `target` is a memory id alone — and ids repeat across sets, since a memory copied into another set keeps its id — so two such rows collided and `write_links`'s `INSERT OR REPLACE` dropped the first. Filed from the schema, confirmed by `two_links_to_one_id_in_different_sets_both_survive`, fixed by putting `target_set` in the key with a partial unique index over `(source, label, target) WHERE target_set IS NULL` to keep identical same-set links collapsing, since SQLite holds NULLs in a key distinct. `compact_own_set_links` narrows with `UPDATE OR REPLACE` because the two spellings of one same-set link can now coexist and narrowing one onto the other would otherwise fail the *open*. Migration rebuilds the table, detected by the key's width. Written up in [cross-set-references.md](documents/design/cross-set-references.md), *the set a target lives in is part of a stored link's identity*. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-memory-linking-one-id-in-two-sets-keeps-one-link`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Finishing the link-key fix that the checkpoint named as the next step, after filing the memory-size question earlier in the session.
why:
Head of the issue cluster, superseded to record the standing change from open to fixed. The claim itself is unchanged — it was right when filed — so what moves is the standing and the account of the repair.

**The severity stays `corrupts`, and the fix does not retroactively repair anything.** A link lost before today was lost at its write and left no trace to recover; the migration widens the key so it cannot happen again, and carries existing rows across untouched. No store here was found holding such a pair, which is consistent with nothing having produced one rather than proof that nothing did.

Kept as a supersession rather than an amendment because the head was exported when it was filed.

content: The third raise of the catalog budget was expected and did not happen. `investigation-pipeline` was named as the convention most likely to force it, and instead it merged into `hoard-watch` -- one convention replacing two, because a seed and a trap turned out to be the same object. The merged draft overran the free space by 237 characters, and that was closed by attempting the cheaper answer for the first time: trimming 363 characters of justifying reinforcement out of `split-when-partly-stale`, which the reinforcement audit had measured at 79% justifying, with no rule removed. The catalog stood at 17,875 of 18,000 with 125 free on 2026-09-05, and the two deferral conditions were never tested, because the overrun the raise was being held for did not arrive. For the current figure run `report_catalog_size`, which is the authoritative source.
context: Landing the watch convention and finding it would not fit, then working out whether to trim, harvest or raise. The same evening had rewritten the context field's description and retired the recall-gloss convention.
why: Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule, which moves a memory discussing a `hoard-` mechanism out of the reserved space. The catalog figure is also dated rather than left reading as current, since it moved twice the next day -- the same stale-structural-claim failure this corpus met elsewhere the same afternoon. What replaced the original memory is more useful than a bare correction: the estimate was an artifact of counting two conventions that turned out to be one, so an overrun predicted from undrafted entries is worth re-deriving after drafting rather than budgeting against. The standing objection is unspent -- a budget raised whenever it binds is not a budget -- and the harvest is repeatable, since the audit priced roughly 3,540 characters of justifying reinforcement and this took a tenth of it.

content: **Whole-record push does not scale, and terseness does not save it** — measured 2026-09-05 against the then-shipped convention. The per-record envelope (id, both timestamps, attribution, confidence, origin, scope, the keyword and link arrays, field names) is **411 characters and does not shrink with the prose**. So at the convention's own 350-character signpost target, fifteen watches cost 2,853 tokens, **three stores of fifteen cost 1.9x the entire convention catalog, and a hundred watches 4.2x**; at an implausibly terse 150 characters of prose a hundred still costs 3.1x. Both of the human partner's reasons pass fifteen on their own — a cross-set recall multiplies by the number of stores, and a large project has many open items. A derived line instead: a hundred at 70 characters is 0.4x the catalog, two hundred 0.8x.
context: Migrating the watch-push-is-an-index-per-set entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the measurement the human partner's probe produced.
why:
The fixed envelope is the whole argument, and it is what makes an author-facing length rule useless: no amount of terseness reaches the target, because 411 characters arrive whatever the prose does.

**Deriving the line rather than authoring it removes the failure mode instead of guarding it.** The shipped convention had asked authors to keep a marked memory *short enough to read fifteen of*, which requires arithmetic over a quantity the author cannot see — and the session that wrote that rule violated it within the hour, producing a 1,940-character head where fifteen would cost 7,275 tokens, worse than fifteen *typical* memories. A memory would not have caught that: the failure happens inside the act of writing, with no moment to recall into. Under an index an over-long watch costs the same at session start as a short one, so no server-side refusal is needed and the rule becomes one an author can follow without counting.

content: The convention catalog is to be run largely unchanged from 2026-08-24, gathering evidence on how the current text behaves before further tuning, with one exception already taken: `route-where` was revised again on 2026-08-25 because applying its new charter clause to the two live charters showed the clause was wrong. That is the sanctioned kind of change — evidence from applying a rule, not impressions from the session that wrote it — and the hold otherwise stands. Budget at 16,976 of 18,000, with three Ready conventions competing for 1,024 characters that at most one of them can use. A third raise is not the answer on hand; whether the catalog is dense or merely long is an open question to be settled by a whole-file read of `catalog.rs`.
context: Decided 2026-08-24 and amended 2026-08-25 by the human partner, who asked for the charter clause to be tweaked from what `coding-lessons` showed.
why: Supersedes the version stored hours earlier, which said the catalog would be run *unchanged* and was contradicted the same day. The distinction it now draws is the one worth carrying: the standing rule against re-tuning is about acting on one session's impressions of text it just wrote, and it does not bar a change forced by applying the rule to a real case. Recording the exception rather than quietly widening the hold keeps the next session from reading any convention edit as licence.

content: **Whether recall should offer a gut feeling: a short signal aggregated over many weak matches, arriving before any single memory is read.** Raised 2026-09-29 by the human partner, from how an experienced developer says *there's something wrong with that design, I can't say what yet*. The feeling is formed from many past experiences and arrives before any one memory, cueing a closer look. The proposal pairs a before-writing habit, like the coding-lessons one, with a recall that returns phrases and their weights, drawn from the text of a broad range of plausible matches, not a few ranked memories. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `gut-feeling-recall`; this record carries only its standing.
context: After fixing keyword recall paging; the human partner asked whether the model experiences emotions, then connected expert unease to a possible recall design.
why: Head of a question cluster. It is a question, not a backlog item, because nothing is decided and the idea may not survive a first measurement. The motivating case happened the same day: a per-change recall missed a decision because the query and the decision shared the idea but not the words. That is the failure aggregation over a neighbourhood might not have.

content:
**A case for `recall-would-have-helped`, 2026-09-14: a general lesson in another set predicted a Scatterhoard defect exactly, and two sessions went without it.** Observed while fixing `a-set-description-reshuffles-on-a-small-change`.

**What was done.** On 2026-09-12 the set summary's k-means++ seeding was written to draw from one constant-seeded generator consumed by position — checkable in commit `62f6539`, `initial_seeds` in `src/summary.rs`. On 2026-09-14 the resulting instability was found, a hypothesis formed that insertions shift every later draw, a probe measured it, and seeds keyed to each memory's id fixed it. The session doing that ran its check for existing records as a recall scoped to `shared:scatterhoard`, and found nothing relevant.

**What was already stored.** `01M04B7TJ4ED8S9486W4Y5J5XW` in `coding-lessons`, written 2026-08-15: *a fixed random seed buys reproducibility, not stability*, because values drawn from one seeded stream depend on position, so an insertion changes every value after it; the remedy is to derive each value from the item's own key. That is the defect and the fix, a month early.

**What the moment felt like**, from the 2026-09-14 session only, since the 2026-09-12 session's experience is not available: a defect in code this project had written two days before read as a question about this project, so the search went to this project's set, and a cross-project lesson was not a place it occurred to look. The hypothesis also arrived quickly and felt sufficient, so the recall was a formality run after the idea rather than a search for one. **The shape this suggests, as one instance**: not an environment obstacle this time, but the set boundary — a problem that presents as project-specific is searched only where project knowledge lives, while its general form is filed, correctly, somewhere else.
context: End-of-session capture after fixing unstable set descriptions, declaring charter languages and guarding against second charters; the lesson surfaced while checking whether new coding-lessons entries were duplicates.
why:
Recorded as a member of the investigation because it is a clean case with all three parts the head demands, and because its shape differs from the case that opened it: the missing recall was not skipped, it was scoped. That is a candidate trigger distinct from the environment-obstacle hypothesis — an unscoped recall, or one that includes the cross-project set, would have returned the lesson.

Confidence 0.8: the facts are checkable and the account of the moment is first-hand, but it is one case and one session's report of its own attention, and the claim about what would have worked is inferred from the lesson's wording rather than tested by re-running the recall at the time.

content: This was the third instance in two days of **what the server publishes about itself disagreeing with what it accepts** — after `hoard_recall` advertising `required: ["scope","query"]` against an implementation that made both optional. That is the `coding-lessons` set's *"every layer can be right while the seam between them is wrong"* recurring in the same seam, which is what argued for a structural fix rather than another hand-patch: the published schema should be **derived from the types it validates against**, not written alongside them.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The generalisation that changed the remedy. Three instances in one seam in two days is what turns a series of fixes into an argument about where the schema comes from.

content: **This is the entry most likely to belong in open-questions rather than the backlog** — the boundary BACKLOG.md names as the sharpest and most likely to erode — so move it there rather than starting it, unless the shape has become clear. **The shape has largely become clear, from the other end**: `investigation-pipeline` is this entry's missing half, asking the same question — how do memories get stored so that something nobody has articulated yet can be found later — and it has a **working mechanic rather than a description**, arrived at by accident and copied rather than designed, with three live seeds as of 2026-09-02 in two different sets. content: **What survives the discovery that the floor calibration was measured under a scorer that does not ship.** **Survives**: that a floor is a viable mechanism at all, confirmed under the real centred scorer at AUC 0.909. **Does not**: every threshold, every headroom figure, the size ladder, the cross-corpus spread, and the p90 rule itself. **Unverified**: the ordinal findings — rule-versus-substance, the nonsense classes, the composition ablation, the four refuted predictors — are comparisons under one consistent scoring and probably hold, but centring is not rank-preserving and none has been re-run. **Also unmeasured**: `cut_at_largest_gap` already truncates real results, so a floor would sit on a mechanism the probes never exercised, and the two could be redundant or could conflict.
context: The human partner asking, before any design work began, whether the probes ran through Scatterhoard's own mechanism or a separate tool. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the memory was over the length limit.
why: Split from the re-measurement under the shipping scorer, and stated as separate verdicts because the temptation after a flawed measurement is to salvage the lot. Written 2026-09-09; the floor was later built with per-store calibration from real queries, which is what replaced the p90 rule.

content:
**Re-measured over 275 traversable edges: the median linked target sits at the 1.78th percentile of similarity to its source, median rank 16, and only 43% fall inside a ten-result window.** The earlier figure — 2.9th percentile — was taken over 23 edges on 2026-08-15 and is superseded by a graph twelve times larger. p25 and p75 of rank are 4 and 65, so the distribution is wide: some linked memories are the obvious next hit and others are nowhere near.

**The 43% is the number that matters, and it is new.** The old measurement asked whether traversal beats simply raising the limit, and answered with a size crossover near 170 memories. This asks the operational question instead — *would content similarity have returned this memory anyway?* — and the answer at 762 memories is that **more than half the time it would not**. That is what a link buys, and it is why the connect-on-recall clause in `recall-when` is worded around *the one recall did not return*. Re-run `probe_where_a_linked_memory_ranks_against_its_source` in `tests/probes.rs`.
context: Checking a figure before a convention's reinforcement sentence quoted it, after the human partner asked which side of the trim criterion that sentence fell on. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the memory was over the length limit.
why: Supersedes the 2026-08-15 percentile because the value changed with the sample, not because the original was wrong: 23 edges was what the graph held then, and the memory said so. Its conclusions survive intact and should not be re-derived — the percentile is scale-invariant where rank is not, the crossover sits near 170 memories, and below that crossover no number of queries can separate traversal from a larger limit.

content: **Whether a memory id should be Crockford base32 rather than a hex UUID. Resolved 2026-08-20: yes, with prefix lookup removed and no type sigil -- and it is built.** Raised by the human partner after a truncated id misled twice in one session. The proposal keeps UUIDv7's bits and changes only how they are spelled. **The deciding question was the human partner's own -- *would truncating a ULID feel natural?*** -- which relocated the cause from length to the hex form's separators and alphabet, and settled the sigil as unnecessary. **The provocation is the association, not the length:** models truncate a UUID because it resembles a git hash, so the goal moved from *shorter* to *does not read as a hash*. Crockford base32 renders as `01KZ2ZWTYRED9881P0P1S49BBH` -- letters outside `a-f`, upper case, no dash grouping -- which is exactly ULID's text encoding, an existing named format rather than a bespoke one. **Verified 2026-09-07:** the live corpus carries ids in that form, and `crockford-base32-ids` is marked built. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `memory-id-alphabet`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

*The provocation is the association, not the length* is the head's load-bearing sentence, because it is what makes the change worth making at all -- a purely shorter identifier would not have helped, and that is the design anyone re-opening this would reach for first.

The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `author-is-a-property-of-the-process-not-the-store`; this record carries only its standing.

content:
Cases where a recall would have helped but was not made. Add each one here; `recall-when` may have a gap.

Members carry `recall-would-have-helped`. Opened 2026-09-12 by the human partner after a session hit a PDF it could not read, walked three dead ends, and asked them to install a package — while a memory naming the working method sat unrecalled in the same store, written six days earlier.

**The hypothesis to test.** `recall-when` names the moments it covers: starting substantive work on a project, a decision an earlier decision may govern, something the human refers to as settled, and redoing work that may have been done before. **All four are decision-shaped.** A session meeting an environment obstacle — or any problem presenting as mechanical with an obvious next move — never classifies the moment as one the rule covers, so the rule does not fire and nothing was disobeyed. If that is right, the gap is in which moments the convention names, not in how firmly it names them.

**What each case must record**, and the third is the one that will get skipped: what was actually done; what was already in a set that would have helped; and **what the moment felt like at the time**. A list of misses without an account of why each was invisible cannot produce convention text, because a usable trigger has to be recognisable *before* the session knows the answer.

**What would end this.** Enough cases to say whether they share a shape. If they do, the output is a clause naming that trigger, and then the separate question of whether it earns catalog space. If they keep landing in unrelated places with nothing in common, that is also an answer: the cause is that recall costs a call and sessions economise, which no wording fixes. Retire it either way — this is not a standing collection.
context: Opened at the end of the morning session that filed the Golden Rule question, immediately after a PDF the session could not read turned out to have been solved and written down six days earlier.
why:
Opened at the human partner's request, on their reading that a session failing to recall what it held is a convention gap rather than a lapse by that session.

Framed as an investigation rather than a collection because it has an ending and a decision behind it: either the cases share a trigger convention text can name, or they do not and the cause is economising on calls, which no wording fixes. A collection with no imaginable end should not be pushed at every session start.

The demand that each case record what the moment felt like is the part most likely to be skipped and the part the output depends on. A trigger has to be recognisable before the session knows the answer, and only the phenomenology says what was available to recognise.

content: Served messages carried runs of source indentation, such as *a level calibrated                  from what the set has been able to answer*, in five string literals in `src/mcp.rs`. Fixed 2026-09-29 by reflowing each literal with `\` continuations at its original line breaks. The class is guarded by `no_library_string_literal_carries_a_run_of_spaces` in `tests/served_text.rs`, which reads every library source file as the compiler would and refuses a run of spaces inside a literal's prose. A literal holding a real newline, such as SQL, is exempt, and so is `src/bin/`. The silenced-recall test also checks its note as served. Pinned by two mutations. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-silenced-recall-note-carries-source-indentation`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Taking the open issues after the corrupts-severity ones were done; this was chosen as a quick win once it turned out to cover five messages.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed, for all five instances rather than the one the old head named. A source check was chosen over a test per message, because four of the five were found only by searching and a test per message would miss the next one too. The evaluation binary is exempt because its aligned columns are deliberate and read by a person at a terminal.

content:
Built 2026-09-11, hours after the log it depends on: the `used` label, which is what says a set could answer a query. This is the half of the original record that stands; the session bound it also claimed was wrong and is corrected in the memory beside this one.

**Three signals, and they are the simulation's rather than a fresh choice.** `corpus/label_queries.py` counted a memory looked up by id, linked to, superseded, or passed back as `already_known`; the built version marks the same three points where a caller names an id it already has — `hoard_lookup` on both the id and the fragment branch, the link targets of `hoard_memorize`, which is also how a supersession is written, and `already_known` on recall.

**Amending and forgetting are deliberately not uses**, though correcting a memory you found plainly is one: the *about forty labelled queries* threshold was measured against those three signals, and a fourth changes what a labelled query means without re-running that measurement.

Each signal is one call site, so each has its own mutation: losing one loses a signal silently, with the log still filling and only the labelled count quietly smaller. A fourth mutation caught `LoggedQuery.used` being dropped by the writer, which had been relying on the column default.
context: Building the `used` label, then correcting the session bound after the human partner questioned it.
why: Split from the original rather than amended, because only the bound had gone stale and this half was never in question. The signal boundary is the part worth keeping findable: *why not amend* has an answer, and without it the next contributor adds the fourth signal and quietly invalidates the threshold.

content: Found 2026-08-26 by the human partner, from a scenario worth stating in full: export a set to a thumb drive, eject it, insert a different drive that mounts at the same point and happens to carry a set of the same name, and import. A target is a directory path, and `Store::normalise_target` resolves it fully — which is right for spellings and cannot help here, because **both volumes genuinely are at that path when asked**. `bases_for` returns the first drive's agreement, and it is used as the ancestor for the second drive's file. `a_base_carried_over_from_another_target_turns_a_conflict_into_a_silent_overwrite` in `tests/reconcile.rs` pins the invariant this reaches through a door that test does not watch — not a base carried across *targets*, but a target that quietly became a different replica.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The scenario and why path normalisation cannot help: the defect is not two spellings of one place but one place that is two things at different times, which no amount of resolving a path can distinguish.

content: **Correction to how the broken shape arises, 2026-09-14: not from a renamed copy of the set.** The first head of this issue said it is the shape a pre-rename copy's links take once the set is renamed and that copy imported. That cannot happen. A set's internal links are stored in the compact same-set form at every write, and an export writes from stored rows, so any copy of a set carries its internal links compact whatever its header names it. And a link's `set_id` is filled in only at authoring, never for a record arriving from a file (`documents/design/cross-set-references.md`, *the target set's identity, where it is known*). So a cross-set link carrying the holding set's own identity has to be authored in some other set that held a cross-set link into this one, and then move into this set — through `hoard_sets` action `absorb`, or the hand procedure for moving memories between sets in `documents/design/set-lifecycle.md` — while naming this set by a name it has since stopped using.
context: Fixing supersession for a link naming its own set by an old name, then discussing link formats and set identity with the human partner. Same stretch: the ambiguous-anchor check and the scan subcommand.
why:
The superseded head still states the wrong origin, and the fixed head drops the origin without correcting it, so a later reader of the cluster would meet the claim with nothing contradicting it.

Confidence is for reasoning from the code and design documents rather than a reproduction: the absorb and move paths were not run end to end to produce the shape. The parked tests never depended on the origin — they build the link directly — so the fix stands either way. What the origin decides is where the shape can come from in future, which matters for anything that rewrites links when memories move between sets.

Found while the human partner questioned the link formats, and not recorded at the time; recorded when they asked whether the conventions had prompted it.

content: **The middle case now has its live instance: `governance-docs`.** Noted 2026-09-23. The entry holds that case (2) — a boundary to known people with no repository — cannot be decided from one instance, and at the time there were none. `governance-docs` is one: a set whose charter says it should stay safe to hand to a lawyer or a fellow board member, exported to an iCloud path rather than to any repository, so it reaches other people while no maintainer exists for maintainer review to serve. It answers `Some(name)` today and takes the full gate, which is the over-strict-in-the-safe-direction collapse the entry describes. Whether one instance is enough to decide on is the human partner's call; what changed is that the count is no longer zero.
context: The fuller second pass over the open questions, reading each head against the sets this machine actually holds.
why: The entry's honest reason to hold off was the absence of an instance, and an absence that has quietly ended is invisible: nothing about creating a set announces that it is the case some open question was waiting for. Recorded so the question is reconsidered on the evidence rather than on the note that there was none.

content: **How a reached memory's inherited and own scores combine. Resolved 2026-08-15 as `sum` -- and that answer was overturned three days later.** The current rule is a **blend at `w = 0.25`**, decided 2026-08-18 under `scores-summed-or-blended`, after correcting the walk's self-inheritance moved the evidence this decision had rested on. Read the 2026-08-15 result as history. **What remains settled from this entry is the shape of the walk**, which the later decision did not touch: expansion is **uniform and symmetric** across every label and both directions, bounded on using a memory as a frontier node rather than on admitting it as a result, with discrimination the ranker's job rather than the walk's. **Two things make that safe, and both are dependencies rather than conveniences:** uniform expansion is licensed by everything being re-scored against the query, and the inherited score must survive into the ranking, or traversal returns nothing a larger `k` would not return more cheaply. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `inherited-and-own-scores-combine`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

**The overturning is stated in the first two sentences deliberately.** The entry as written announces `sum` as its resolution and gives the evidence for it at length, and the file offers no signal that a later entry replaced the answer -- so the failure mode is a session reading a superseded rule as current. Separating *what was overturned* from *what still stands* is the whole job of this head, because the entry contains both and they are not marked apart in the original.

content: **How the traversal corpus was built and what it is biased toward, 2026-08-15.** `corpus/build_traversal_corpus.py` extracts all twenty-one design documents: **429 memories, 451 edges over nine labels**, five memories isolated counting both directions, zero outbound-rule violations. **Three construction decisions worth knowing before using it.** Ids are derived from each memory's **key**, not drawn from a seeded stream in build order — the original repointed every id after any insertion, reproducible but not stable, which would have invalidated every relevance label once queries existed; inserting a probe now changes zero existing ids. Timestamps are unique and asserted, because twenty pairs shared one and that made the outbound-rule check vacuous for same-instant links, which tests source-older-than-target and is false for equal. **And two caveats pull in opposite directions, which matters before either is quoted alone**: density flatters traversal at **1.05 edges/memory against 0.44 in live writing**, but the links that exist are *textually closer* than live ones — a 1.17% median here against 2.9% across the live sets. The corpus is denser than reality and easier than reality, and only the first was anticipated. **The per-label signal replicates and strengthens**: `MOTIVATED_BY` targets sit at a 0.23% median and `INSTANCE_OF` at 7.46%, a factor of **32** where the 56-memory pilot saw about 7 — a decision and its motivation share vocabulary, a principle and a case of it are worded completely differently.
context: Migrating the recall-eval-harness entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is what the corpus is and how it differs from live writing.
why:
The two-caveats-in-opposition point is what stops either number being quoted as *the* limitation. Density alone reads as "the corpus overstates traversal's value"; textual closeness alone reads as "it understates it". Together they say the corpus is unlike live use in two directions at once, and only the weights are affected rather than the harness.

The id-derivation decision is the one a rebuild would undo. Drawing ids from a seeded stream is the obvious reproducible choice and is what the first version did; it is wrong here because relevance labels reference ids, so stability under insertion matters more than reproducibility of the whole sequence. The distinction — a fixed seed buys reproducibility, not stability — is the same one that bit this project once already.

content: **Whether *violates a decision* belongs in a memory system at all.** `VIOLATES` earned its place on frequency and prevents defects being recorded as sanctioned exceptions -- and it is a live link label as of 2026-09-07. **But the natural home for a known defect is an issue tracker, and a memory set that accumulates violation edges may be doing a job it should not.** Revisit once there is real usage rather than a corpus. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `violates-belongs-in-memory`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only, kept whole -- the entry is three sentences and a member would restate it.

**Worth noting what has changed around it since:** this project now keeps its issues *in the memory set*, as clusters indexed from ISSUES.md, which is close to the arrangement the entry worries about. That does not answer the question and arguably sharpens it, but it is a fact the *revisit once there is real usage* condition was written before, and the usage now exists. Not folded into the claim, because whether the tracking-file migration counts as the anticipated usage is a judgement rather than an observation.

Confidence is 0.8 rather than higher because the entry itself is tentative -- *may be doing a job it should not* -- and the record should not read as more settled than the thinking behind it.

content: `hoard-watch` shipped 2026-09-04 and absorbed `investigation-pipeline` rather than shipping beside it. Three structural corrections made it work. A seed and a trap are the same object: both are session-start push, so the trigger difference the agenda assumed does not exist, and one keyword marks push while a second names the kind -- `hoard-signpost`, `hoard-collect`, `hoard-investigation`, with the catalog supplying all three verbs because a marked memory arrives from a repository like any other. Advancement is spawning a new head that draws on the observations, not superseding: one observation set can drive several questions and supersession affords one successor. And push is the marked case -- most accumulation stays passive and is reached by ordinary recall -- which is the budget story push had been missing.
context: Drafting the watch convention across one evening, from a four-question agenda, and working out whether a seed and a trap are the same thing. Earlier in the same stretch, rewriting the context field's description and retiring the recall-gloss convention.
why: The three corrections each overturned something the drafting agenda took as given, and each is the kind of thing a later session would re-derive expensively or get wrong. The trigger difference is the load-bearing one: it is what made the two entries look like siblings, and dropping it is what let one convention replace two, which is why no budget raise was needed. The spawning correction matters beyond this convention, because the re-entry open question still said transitions are supersessions with the state as the chain tip -- true for a head's own lifecycle, false for advancement, and following it would fork a chain deliberately and meet `a-healed-fork-reports-its-ancestor-as-a-cycle`. The puzzle stage survives in the memory's own text rather than in vocabulary, since a puzzle takes the same action as a collect with narrower fit criteria, and only the hypothesis changes the verb.

content: **What the 2026-09-11 walk-forward simulations settled about calibrating the non-match floor from a query log.** The floor must read raw content similarity rather than the centred score, which decays to silencing 2.7%; it needs about forty labelled queries, since a floor from ten silenced 10 of the next 53 on `coding-lessons`; a 0.05 margin costs nothing from thirty onward. They also proposed that a floor hide nothing it could not recover from, by letting a scoped query that scores under it lower it on contradiction — **that part was reversed on 2026-09-12**, the day the floor shipped, and only calibration writes the level now (`calibrated-non-match-floor`).
context: Moved 2026-09-24 out of the entry's head, which was over the length limit, in step 2 of the out-link work.
why: The measured parameters of the resolved question, kept apart from its standing. The last sentence is corrected rather than carried: the head it came from said the scope label lowers the floor, which stopped being true the day the floor was built.

content: The prohibited-data scan reports an API key inside ordinary hyphenated words: `vendor_key_findings` in `src/prohibited.rs` matches a vendor prefix such as `sk-` anywhere in the text, with no check that it begins a word, so `ask-`, `task-`, `risk-` or `desk-` followed by twenty or more key-shaped characters is refused as `api_key`. Found 2026-10-11 when two memories naming a coined slug that began `ask-the-human-` were both refused. Fixed when a prefix counts only where the character before it cannot be part of a key.
context: Filing tracking entries after shipping the publishing-name relay fallback; two backlog heads were refused by the scan.
why: It refuses legitimate writes with a message saying they carry a secret, which a caller cannot act on except by guessing which word tripped it, and it constrains keyword coinage invisibly. Severity is misleads rather than blocks because renaming works once the cause is known. The export gate runs the same scan, but nothing affected can have been stored, since the store refuses it first.

content: **Whether `CLAUDE.md` should be committed, and what the practice is for agent-steering files. Resolved 2026-09-25 by the human partner.** Committing is the documented practice. A contributor's `CLAUDE.local.md` loads last and wins. The file is split into `AGENTS.md`, project facts for any agent, and a Claude-specific `CLAUDE.md` that imports it. Personal preferences stay in user-level configuration. The security half, instruction-shaped text arriving by `git pull`, is outside Scatterhoard's scope and is left to review practice and harness configuration. What publication needs from this repository is one sentence for maintainers, parked in `publication-facing-docs`. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `claude-md-in-the-repository`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner: the last open question on the gate.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. The security half was the only part open. It closed on the reasoning that trust in a checkout is its provenance, a reasoning settled earlier the same day for memory sets, and that Scatterhoard adds no instruction channel. So nothing in the software changes, and the maintainer sentence waits for the documents written around first publication.

content: **The opt-in sentence must still read correctly in a session where the set it names is not loaded.** Decided 2026-09-27 by the human partner. `AGENTS.md` is committed with the project, and someone can clone the project without the set it refers to: a collaborator, a CI agent, a fresh machine. So the sentence tells that session to work without the set and to say so once, which lets the user decide whether to add it, rather than sending it to recall a guide that is not there. The draft wording: *"This project draws on the `coding-lessons` memory set. If `hoard_sets` status lists it, recall `adopting-coding-lessons` and follow that guide; if it is not loaded, work without it and say so once, so the user can decide whether to add it."* The keyword is provisional until the guide is written.
context: Freeing catalog space for the data-only clause, while working out how `coding-lessons` propagates to projects that want it.
why: A steering file travels with the repository, and a set travels only where someone has created and imported it, so the two diverge on every clone that skips the second step. A sentence written for the loaded case alone becomes an instruction whose target is absent. At best the session wastes a recall that returns nothing; at worst it improvises the missing procedure. Mentioning the absence once was agreed because a clone without the set otherwise loses the lessons with no sign, while repeating it every turn would be noise.

content: Decided 2026-09-06 by the human partner, at the 56-entry mark: a migrated entry gets a head **plus one or two members** when it is single-episode, and the fuller treatment only where it corrects itself across dates. The reason is compounding — four members per entry is roughly 4,000 characters of memory per entry, and across the ~120 entries then remaining that is a corpus somebody reads in recalls for a long time. **What the depth is *for* is the self-correction**: the entries that earned five to eight members are the ones where a measurement was later retracted as confounded, a diagnosis was reversed, or a fix was replaced — and in those, reading top to bottom puts the retraction *after* the number it retracts. A single-episode entry has no such ordering to preserve, so the detail buys nothing.
context: Migrating the tracking files into the memory set; the human partner set the depth after reviewing the first 56 issue entries.
why: A calibration decision with a stated cost model, made partway through so the first 56 entries are deeper than the rest. Recorded because the inconsistency is deliberate and would otherwise look like drift, and because the criterion — does this entry correct itself — is what a later session needs rather than a member count.

content: **A third skipped per-change recall on 2026-09-30**, before fixing `a-forgotten-replacement-reads-as-superseded-beyond-this-set`: the session went from the human partner's go-ahead to reading resolver code and writing tests, and noticed only when recording the fix. So the prescribed recall ran before two of six changes in one session of working through issues, and was skipped before three; the sixth, which had it skipped and a lesson carried over, is `01M3TF17N2…`. The skips cluster on changes taken straight after a design decision, where the next step feels like implementation rather than a new change.
context: Working through the supersession issues with the human partner, the sixth change of a session that began with the reembed-count mutation.
why: Evidence for the `adopting-coding-lessons` gate. Three instances in one session is the first point where a pattern is visible, though it is one session and one agent, so it stays an observation, not a generalisation. The clustering after a decision is the part a trigger could address: the moment the habit is lost is the hand-off from discussing to building.

content: Several memory files in one `scatterhoard_mem` directory, one `.json` per set, found by `set_id`. Decided 2026-09-25 under `one-repository-many-sets`. The `directory` form stops appending `memories.json` (`MEMORY_FILE` in `src/mcp.rs`). It reads the headers of `scatterhoard_mem/*.json`, takes the one match on `set_id`, refuses two, and matches on the declared name only for a set with no identity yet. Export with no match writes a new file named by the approximation rule. Bases stay keyed on the directory. Built when that ships with: the unexpected-contents warning narrowed to non-`.json` files; `.gitattributes` and SETUP.md changed to `**/scatterhoard_mem/*.json`; this repository's and `coding-lessons`' files renamed; and the refusals that name `memories.json` reworded. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `several-memory-files-per-directory`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Resolving `one-repository-many-sets` with the human partner, on the release gate.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, gathering the build for the resolved `one-repository-many-sets`. Release-gated itself, because it changes where a published set's file lives, and after publication that moves a file in every repository that carries one. It has to come before any repository but this project's own holds a memory file, which is what makes it cheap now.

content: **The measurements behind the 2026-08-25 resolution, and the one that mattered was a register statistic nobody had thought to take** -- history from that read. **Avoidable length, tested and absent:** 0.20% of the catalog's 2,955 served words were filler, mean word length was 4.59, and literal duplication between entries came to about 300 characters in total. **The predicted signature did appear, and it was small:** `route-where`'s reinforcement still carried a reason that had migrated into its text the day before -- the locally-right, globally-redundant shape the read was looking for -- worth roughly 200 characters. **What the read actually found was register.** `reinforcement` ran at **32.8 words per sentence with 42% of its sentences over 35 words**, against **24.2** in `text`: the shape of a design memo rather than a standing instruction, and a periodic sentence that arrives at its point after a dash makes the reader pay for the whole arc before delivering anything. Restructuring every entry but `recall-when` brought reinforcement to **22.9 words per sentence and 12% over 35**, and took 164 characters off the catalog.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the technique is reusable and the conclusion is not: the next session asking whether the catalog is bloated should take the register statistic first, since it is the one that found something, and should not repeat the filler and duplication passes, which found nothing and are the obvious things to try.

Every figure is a reading from 2026-08-25 and is stated as history rather than as the catalog's current state -- the word count in particular has moved, since the catalog has grown by roughly 3,000 characters since. Re-derive with `cargo test --test conventions report_catalog_size -- --ignored --nocapture` rather than quoting from here.

content: **How the command line reaches export was decided 2026-09-15 by publishing the operation, not by driving the tool surface from inside the binary.** `Server::export_set` and `Destination` were both private, and the three ways in were: build a `tools/call` request and read `isError` off the response envelope; publish a narrow `export_to` taking a public `Destination`; or two methods, `export_to_directory` and `export_to_file`, keeping the type private. The human partner chose the second, on the grounds that **correctness by construction is the project's theme and a strongly-typed, drift-resistant design serves it**. The envelope route would have made the binary depend on the shape of an MCP response rather than on the operation, and the two-method route would have split one idea in two that drift the moment a third destination form exists. `Destination` already carries the rules — `refusal`, `path`, `form` — so publishing it lets the caller *state* which form it means; inferring the form from the path was the thing to avoid, since that is the one fact only the caller holds.
context: Building command-line export, right after the human partner approved publishing the destination type.
why:
Recorded because the alternative is the one a later session would reach for first: going through `handle` looks conservative — it adds no public API — and its cost is invisible until the envelope changes. Naming what was traded keeps that from being re-litigated as an oversight.

The reasoning generalises past this call: where a private function is the only implementation of an operation, publishing it under a name for outside use beats reconstructing the call through a serialisation boundary, because the second path can silently stop agreeing with the first. What makes it safe here is that `export_to` delegates rather than re-implements — there is exactly one body.

content: Fixed 2026-08-26 **as the pair**, with `an-older-file-silently-resurrects-a-forgotten-memory` — the two were filed apart and had to be decided together, because **the duplicate-id explosion was the only thing making the resurrection visible at all**, so fixing this alone would have turned a loud corruption into a silent one. One statement in `write_memory` clears any tombstone for the id being written, which puts the invariant in the shared writer rather than in any caller: `insert`, `accept_from_file` and `replace_with` all go through it. It is `Store::forget`'s mirror — that deletes the memory row as it writes the tombstone — **and the asymmetry is what let this survive**. Placed at the table's level on purpose: `replace_with` having been repaired on its own, for the same invariant, is exactly how the record-at-a-time path went unexamined. The regression test drives the reproduction and then does the thing that failed — exports the result and reads it back.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Two defects that had to be fixed together because one was the only symptom of the other. The fix goes in the shared writer rather than the callers, since repairing one caller for this invariant is precisely what left the others unexamined.

content: **A shared set with no identity takes no records: the store refuses, and names how to give the set one.** Decided 2026-09-14 by the human partner, and built the same day as `Store::refuse_records_without_identity` in `src/store.rs`, reached from `Store::write`, `Store::replace_with` and `import_set` in `src/mcp.rs` after adoption; recorded in `documents/design/set-lifecycle.md` under *a shared set with no identity takes no records*. Forgetting is not refused. The refusal names `import` from a file carrying the identity, or `drop` with `save_to`, `create` and `import` from the saved copy — and not `hoard_sets` action `mint`, which makes an author record. **Tests choose explicitly**: `Store::open_in_memory` behaves like `open` and mints nothing; `Store::open_in_memory_and_mint_id` behaves like a set `create` just made.
context: Building the refusal for a shared set with no identity, after fixing identity-first link canonicalisation and rewording capture-before-ending.
why:
**Why an invariant.** Deciding whether a stored link is same-set compares the link's identity with the holding set's, which is sound only if every set holding records has one. Every tool path ensured it already; the store accepted callers that did not.

**Why refuse rather than mint.** The human partner offered both. Minting on the write is the rival-identity hazard a shared set's identity exists to prevent — two holders of one set each minting — so the session is told the way through instead. Existing tools cover both cases, so no new tool was needed.

**Why the constructor carries `and_mint_id`.** My first proposal made `open_in_memory` itself mint for shared scopes, with a separately named constructor for the tests needing no identity. The human partner objected that `open_in_memory` reads as `open` in memory, and nothing in that name says it also writes an identity. So the plain constructor stayed as it was and the minting one was named for what it does — which also removed the need for a special no-identity constructor.

**What the test suite cost, for whoever next tightens a store invariant.** The refusal failed 316 tests, every one tracing to a helper or first open that wrote to a shared store without an identity: 44 in-memory opens switched constructors, 39 file-backed first opens gained a mint, and three adoption tests now open without one on purpose. None was a regression.

content: **Measured 2026-09-07 over a full day of deliberate memory-writing, and it confirms the competing explanation cleanly: of 390 memories created that day, 9 carry an outbound link — 2% — and six of the nine are `supersedes`.** Three discretionary edges in 390. `supersedes` dominates because supersession *hands you the target id*: `correct-when` and the split rule march the caller to it. The BACKLOG migration never handed one over, so almost nothing was linked, even though the entries being migrated are densely related to each other. This is the cleanest test the corpus is likely to get — one author, one day, one uniform task, no id supplied — and it says the driver is **whether the workflow puts a target in hand**, not the vocabulary and not the author's judgement. What emerged instead, unprompted, was **cross-linking by keyword**: 52 of the day's memories carry more than one entry slug, because keywords are required on every store and links are not.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md, when the human partner asked whether the conventions would lead an LLM to link memories in different clusters discovered to be related.
why:
Filed as evidence for the hypothesis recorded 2026-08-24, which had a mechanism and no test. It now has one, and the effect size is larger than the earlier edge-classification suggested — 2% against the corpus-wide 18%, on memories written by an author who knew the hypothesis while writing them and still did not link.

The keyword substitute is the part worth carrying forward rather than treating as a workaround. It gathers correctly and cannot say *how* two things relate: `set-drop` and `set-restore` are the two halves of what a person does when a set has gone wrong, and a shared keyword carries none of that. It also only fires when the author notices at writing time, which is the case a later discovery does not meet.

content: Two servers on one store raced with no timeout: `Store::open` set only `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`, so the database ran in the default rollback-journal mode where a writer takes a lock that excludes readers outright. Fixed 2026-08-07 in `a2fd1f1` by configuring WAL and a busy timeout before the schema runs. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `store-is-not-configured-for-two-processes`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: A reserved keyword for things whose names hide their behaviour. Built 2026-09-04, absorbing `investigation-pipeline` rather than shipping beside it; the served text is `HOARD_WATCH` in [catalog.rs](src/conventions/catalog.rs) and the reasoning, the four agenda answers and the budget arithmetic are in [Served 2026-09-04](documents/design/conventions.md). Ready as of 2026-09-02, having been blocked on `a-keyword-cannot-be-retired-once-a-memory-has-been-exported` until that was fixed — a keyword the replacement drops stops matching, so a watch retires by superseding and leaving the mark off. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `watch-convention`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only.

**The slug is `watch-convention`, renamed from `hoard-watch` on migration 2026-09-07.** The old one sat inside the reserved keyword space — the same defect fixed for an ISSUES slug on 2026-09-06 and never applied here. `about-hoard-watch` was considered and rejected as the replacement: that term is the *subject* keyword and gathers eleven memories spanning three different tracking-file items — this build, the later `watch-push-is-an-index-per-set` rewrite, and the `about-hoard-watch-is-both-marker-and-subject` defect — so adopting it as a slug would claim the other two items' findings for this one. The subject keyword and the entry slug are different things, and conflating them is the marker-and-subject collision one level up.

content: The merge driver walks the three sides of a memory file in step, holding one record a side, rather than all three sides and the output in memory. Built 2026-09-22 the same day as filed: `merge::merge_streams` reads each side twice (check it parses and is in `file_position` order, then merge), `merge_files` wraps it for texts, and `cli::merge_file` writes beside `ours` and renames. A side out of file order — every file written before 2026-09-21 — is read whole, and the driver names it and says re-exporting ends it. Checked by `tests/merge.rs` and eight recorded mutations. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `streaming-merge-driver`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Filing and building the two follow-ups from the question about storing the hash that orders memory files. Restated 2026-09-24 as the first repair of step 2 of the out-link work, and the first live check of `link_delta`.
why: Superseded to record it as built. The whole-file path was kept rather than refusing an out-of-order side, because merge bases written by builds before the hash order are routine for now and refusing them would break merges that work today; naming the side is what keeps that path from being silent. Superseded again 2026-09-24 only to restate the link to the concurrent-additions decision, which the built version left behind and which still holds: the driver is how that decision mitigates the conflict.

content: Found 2026-08-11 exporting `local` during SETUP.md §5. A bare `false` is the boolean without the why, and **it would keep reading the same once the scan was built** — at which point a shared export that genuinely skipped the scan becomes indistinguishable from a local one that never needed it. **Fixed 2026-08-11**: a companion `prohibited_data_note` says which reason applies, leaving the boolean on the wire untouched, so `prohibited-data-scan` in [BACKLOG.md](BACKLOG.md) still describes the field it will change; noted in [Export Review](documents/design/export-review.md) so whoever builds the scan finds the field rather than deleting it as scaffolding. *The first version of the test asserted only that the two notes differed, and a recorded mutation walked straight through it by corrupting half of one message. It now asserts what each note actually claims.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A conflation that gets worse rather than better when the missing feature lands. The test that asserted only difference rather than content is the reusable warning: a mutation corrupting one message still leaves two messages differing.

content: Found 2026-08-11 running SETUP.md §5 item 7 against the real stores, **measured rather than inferred**: `limit: 2` returned four memories and `limit: 1` returned two, one from each set. The semantic path went through `recall_across`, which merges every store into one ranked list and applies the limit to that; the keyword path looped per store with nothing truncating the union. **Two consequences, the second easy to miss**: the response holds up to `limit × loaded sets` — `recall-limit-is-unbounded` arriving from the other direction, and the two compound, since the multiplier applies to whatever ceiling that entry eventually sets — and **there is no cross-store ordering at all**, so a two-keyword match in the second set sorts below a one-keyword match in the first. **Both are invisible with one loaded set, which is every test and was every real configuration until a shared set existed on this machine.**
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Two paths that should have shared a shape, with the divergence invisible to every test because the test fixture has one store. The count was measured and the ordering read from a loop that has no sort — worth distinguishing, since only one of the two was observed.

content:
**Built 2026-09-19: Scatterhoard encodes the whole text, and the recorded identity says so.** `StaticEmbedder::embed_each` calls `encode_with_args(texts, None, BATCH)` rather than `encode`, whose 512-token default was silently dropping the end of the embedding input — a memory's `why`, then its keywords. The identity is now `<weights hash>+whole` via `identity_with_encoding`, weights first so a reader comparing two servers sees whether the model differs or only the encoding does.

**Every existing store reports `Mismatched` on first contact with the new build**, because its vectors were built truncated, and the way out is `hoard_sets` action `reembed` per scope. That is correct rather than unfortunate: the vectors really are incomparable. The `status` note was reworded for it — it used to say the vectors "came from a different model", which would have sent a reader hunting for a model change that never happened, and it now describes the identity's two parts and names `reembed`.

Recorded in [documents/design/embeddings.md](documents/design/embeddings.md) under *The identity covers the encoding, not only the weights*. Guarded by `text_past_the_default_token_budget_still_reaches_the_vector` (needs a model, announces a skip without one) and `an_identity_records_how_the_text_was_encoded_and_not_only_the_model` (needs none), with a mutation apiece.</content>
context: Working memory-size-drift after the human partner asked to eliminate the truncation inside the encoding as well as cap the length, since a character cap is sensitive to language and model.
why: The re-embed is the part a later session will meet first and without context: four sets going `Mismatched` at once looks like a misconfiguration, and the fix is a one-line action that is easy to mistake for a workaround. Recorded with the identity format because the `+whole` suffix is the only visible trace of the change, and a reader who does not know what it means cannot tell a same-weights disagreement from a real model swap.

content: Found 2026-08-20 in passing, while working out where a link-target check could safely live. `Store::import` writes each record with `write_memory` directly, so **no cycle check runs at all**, and its doc comment says that is deliberate: *"a cycle can arrive from a hand-edited merge, and refusing the whole file would make one bad edge cost every memory in the set; resolution reports the cycle instead."* `Server::import_set` inserts each record with `store.insert`, which runs `check_no_cycle`; records stream in file order, so for a cycle A→B, B→A the first insert passes and the second fails, propagating out of the record loop as `could not store memory {id}` — **failing the import with the store already partly written**, half the file applied, no conflict report, and an error naming one memory rather than the cycle. So the documented stance held on the path nobody calls and was contradicted on the path everybody calls. The `supersession_cycle` resolution exists precisely so a cycle can be held and reported, which was unreachable through the client path.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery, and the exact asymmetry: one documented intention, two implementations, and the one carrying the intention is the one no client reaches.

content: **`violates` has never been used: zero edges across 1,023 memories, counted 2026-09-23.** The label counts are `related_to` 392, `supersedes` 166, `results_from` 82, `instance_of` 37, `supports` 31, `motivated_by` 14, `resolves` 11, `depends_on` 10, `contradicts` 9, `refers_to` 2, `causes` 1, `exception_to` 1, and nothing for `violates`, `precedes` or `follows`. This entry's condition was to revisit once there is real usage rather than a corpus, and that usage now exists — including the case the entry worried about, a memory set holding this project's issues, which produced no violation edges either. The evidence is on the side of removing the label; the decision is the human partner's.
context: The fuller second pass over the open questions, counting what the corpus actually does rather than reading what it was designed to do.
why: The entry rests on frequency — `VIOLATES` earned its place on it — so a count is exactly what settles it, and the count had never been taken. Recorded with every label's figure rather than the one, because the comparison is what makes zero meaningful: nine labels below twenty uses would make zero unremarkable, and that is not the shape.

content: **Where the server cannot ask the human for their publishing name, the model supplies it and the human is told afterwards**, decided 2026-10-11 by the human partner. On 2024-11-05, 2025-06-18, or any client without elicitation, `mint` keeps `author`, the first-write refusal uses the stop-and-ask-first wording, and the `mint` and `rename` results end with a sentence for the model to relay verbatim naming what was recorded and inviting a correction. On `gemma4:12b` that sentence was relayed with the correction offer 20 of 20 times, against 0 of 10 for today's note. Recorded in `documents/design/asking-the-human.md`.
context: Drafting the proposal for asking the human through MCP elicitation, after refusal wording failed on a small local model; settling what happens on protocol revisions that cannot ask.
why: Chosen over having the human run `scatterhoard mint <set> <name>`, which keeps the name out of the model everywhere, because the human partner judged that friction too high: capable agents have followed the instruction to ask without trouble, and `rename` supersedes one identity record, so a wrong name is cheap to fix once seen. The fallback therefore guarantees visibility of a wrong name, not its absence — which a later session must not mistake for the stronger guarantee the elicitation route gives.

content: **Default signpost selection for a project using a lessons set: the three lessons with the most instances among its last 20 recorded failures, ties going to the most recent instance, and at least two instances to qualify.** Decided 2026-09-28 by the human partner. A project with fewer than 20 recorded failures counts all it has. A signpost drops out when its lesson falls out of the top three. Instances are the project's own failure memories linked `instance_of` to the lesson, so the count is derived and never kept. These are defaults in the adoption guide; a project changes them with prompting of its own.
context: Designing how projects that opt in to `coding-lessons` catch failures before they are written: signpost selection, after testing it against this project's issues.
why: Tested on Scatterhoard's nine common causes. A threshold alone selected all nine, since each had at least four instances. The last 20 issues picked the three matching current work and dropped the three tied to finished work to zero; a window of 30 let a fourth in. Three bounds the lines pushed into every session, and the recall habit covers everything below the cut. The two-instance minimum keeps a young project from signposting one-off accidents, so the first threshold idea survives as a floor rather than as the selector. Retiring when a mechanical check makes the failure uncommittable was set aside as the main rule, because design-level causes recur after such checks exist.

content: `memories` meant two different things: `hoard_sets status` reported live memories while `export` reported records written to the file — memories plus tombstones — and nothing in either response said which measurement it was. Fixed 2026-08-20 by making `memories` the live count everywhere, with `forgotten` beside it and `records` naming what an export wrote. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `memories-count-means-two-different-things`; this record carries only its standing.

content: `Store::count` and `Store::identity_count` decided what an identity record is by the `hoard-author` keyword, so a memory carrying it as a subject vanished from the total and appeared among `identities`. Fixed 2026-09-30, at five sites rather than the two filed: both counts, `holds_any_author_record`, `author_records_named` and the floor's own-memories calibration in `src/store.rs` now ask whether the record attributes itself (`created_by = id`, or `Memory::is_identity_record`). Two of the extra sites changed behaviour: a set holding only a memory about `hoard-author` would not mint its first identity, and a memory whose text was a name made `mint_author` refuse. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `identity-counts-test-the-keyword-not-the-record`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through open issues with the human partner, after the numbered-opening summary fix and a measurement of whether the floor closes the two recall-limit issues.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed as its fixed-when asked, which named only the two counts. A search for `AUTHOR_KEYWORD` found three more sites with the same test. Measured before the fix in the live `scatterhoard` store: two records carry the keyword and one attributes itself; the other is `01M1WPCTJ4ERGTKHT14X82P25B`. The servers predate the fix, so `status` corrects itself only after a restart. Guarded by three tests in `tests/store.rs` and five mutations, one per site.

content: **These five entries must be settled before publication**; they are this memory's keywords. Gated 2026-09-23 by the human partner. Two have answers that would break something already in use if changed afterwards: the tool surface, the file format, or what an identity means. They are `set-settled-at-first-write` and `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`.
