content: An entry slug that is also a heavily-used subject keyword gathers the whole subject, not the entry's findings. Measured 2026-09-07 across the finished BACKLOG.md: of 55 clusters, 37 hold two members or fewer, but three slugs collide with common subject terms and over-gather — **`keyword-standards` returns 20 members, `investigation-pipeline` 17, `graph-traversal` 16**, where an entry's own findings are typically two or three. The row itself is unaffected, since its text is the head's opening; the damage is on recall, where *pull this entry's findings* returns every memory on the subject and the entry's own record is a minority of what comes back. Fixed when a slug cannot silently double as a subject keyword — by a rule at coining time, a check that reports the collision, or renamed slugs. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-slug-that-is-also-a-subject-keyword-over-gathers`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Wrapping up the BACKLOG.md migration and measuring cluster sizes across the finished file.
why:
Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. `misleads` rather than `costs` — the recall answers, and what it returns is not what was asked for, so a session surveying an entry's history draws conclusions from a population that includes memories the entry never produced.

Found by stepping back from the migrated result rather than from any single entry, and it is the same hazard avoided by hand earlier the same day: `about-hoard-watch` was rejected as a slug precisely because it gathers eleven memories spanning three tracking-file items. That judgement was made once, in conversation, and nothing carried it to the three entries that already had the problem.

content: **Whether a convention should require, before storing, that a memory carry or link to enough for a later reader to reconstruct it.** Raised 2026-09-07 by the human partner: *I know my mental state now, but if I write only from that state it will not make sense later — I need to project to the audience who will read it, at the time they will read it.* **The catalog is asymmetric here.** `recall-when` covers the read side — *lead with enough of its context to let the human place it before you rely on it* — and `context-gloss-on-recall` refines it. **Nothing covers the write side**, so a memory can be stored unreconstructable and nothing objects until someone retrieves it and cannot use it. **Note it is not the `context` field.** That field is an episodic handle for placing a memory in a person's own timeline, is deliberately excluded from the embedding, and is not for carrying the technical picture — the mechanism belongs in the claim. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `memories-must-stand-alone`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md, after a stored lesson failed on the reader it had just been explained to.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. Filed separately from `meta-observation-convention` under the split rule, because the two can be settled at different times for different reasons: that one governs **whether** something is recorded, this governs **what a record must contain**, and adopting either without the other is coherent.

**The drafting problem, and it is why this is not obviously a clause.** The obvious wording — *make sure a memory stands alone* — is a truism, and the author who under-specified was already trying to write well. What failed was detection rather than intent, since the referent is unambiguous from where the writing happens. So a usable rule has to name a mechanical test rather than an aspiration; the candidate is *does this record name its referents or point at them*, and whether that is checkable enough to survive contact with drafting is exactly what is open.

content: **Two over-claims about the non-match floor came in consecutive turns, in opposite directions, from one root.** On 2026-09-09 the design was called supportable on a benefit figure measured against probes I wrote, then called broken on an inversion test whose negative class was not negative. Both treated *different topic* as *unanswerable* — the assumption the investigation had spent its whole length disproving. Having documented the rule-shaped collision that morning did not stop me building a test that depended on its absence.
context: The human partner asking that the bylaws-analysis session be excluded from the harvest, which led to reading what the governance-docs store actually contains. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the memory was over the length limit.
why: Split from the correction of the second over-claim. Kept because the pairing is the lesson: a finding documented in the morning is not a finding applied in the afternoon, and an over-claim in one direction is no protection against the next one in the other.

content: **The resolution reversed one earlier decision and was taken against a measurement rather than an intuition -- 2026-08-29.** **`origin` is the reversal:** `origin-cannot-be-corrected`, decided 2026-08-21, is overturned on the human partner's reasoning that the field exists to clear up who supplied what, so a superseded wrong value costs little and the chain itself signals which record is current. **The measurement is held separately** as `01M18CDT5ZEQ0VMT1V97QCDZPW` and is not restated here: 16 supersessions, 10 tombstones and 2 amendments across 136 live memories, with both amendments inside 144 seconds of creation while supersessions ran to 12.4 days. **What it settled is the pricing of the objection.** Abolishing amendment would have added two records to 136, and a supersession copying content verbatim to move one `confidence` value has never occurred -- so the awkward object the whole question was waiting on turned out to be hypothetical. **Read the amendment figure as a floor on need rather than a measure of it**, which the measurement memory says itself: no convention triggers a later recalibration, so the corpus has never been asked whether it is still calibrated.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Recorded to link the decision to its evidence rather than duplicate it -- the measurement is a memory of its own with its method and caveats attached, and copying its numbers here would create the second copy that drifts. The `supports` edge is the point: a later session questioning the correction boundary should reach the measurement through this, and should re-measure rather than re-read, since the corpus has grown from 136 to over 600 since.

The `origin` reversal is kept because a reversed decision is exactly what a later session will trip over: `origin-cannot-be-corrected` reads as settled, was settled, and is no longer the rule.

content: **Two things the 2026-08-18 build found and deliberately did not decide.** First, **the collapsed-hit loose end dissolves, but not for the reason that had been recorded**: the code ranks *before* it resolves, so the gap cut having no quota is doing all the work — the earlier reading credited resolve-before-rank, which is not what the implementation does. Second, **a memory can inherit a decayed copy of its own score** along a path that leaves it and returns; that **ships as measured** and is filed as an open question rather than corrected in place, because the measurements that chose the combination rule were taken against this behaviour and changing it would invalidate them. **The weights are still unset, and the entry's standing reason for that expired.** *A weight layered onto a walk that runs without it* was written when no corpus existed; one does now, so a decay rate can be **measured** rather than guessed — and shipping a guessed constant is the *weight guessed to three decimals reads as reasoned about* failure the design warns against. Ship flat and recorded as untuned, or measure first, but do not invent one.
context: Migrating the graph-traversal entry out of BACKLOG.md, the last of the Recall section.
why:
Both findings are the kind that get quietly tidied. The collapsed-hit case looks settled and *is* settled — the loose end really does dissolve — so a later reader has no reason to re-check which mechanism does it, and would carry forward a wrong explanation that predicts wrongly the next time the ranking order changes. The self-inheritance looks like an outright bug, and fixing it in place would silently invalidate the answer-key measurements that chose `sum`.

The expired reasoning about weights is recorded because it reads as still-current: the entry states the justification without its date, and the fact that made it true — no corpus — stopped being true on 2026-08-15.

content: **Closed 2026-09-18 without a limit: `hoard_sets evaluate` reports what a review cost instead of capping what it may load.** The entry asked for a cap because embedding a whole file before returning could look like a hang. Measured that day, it cannot at any size this project will meet: 948 memories load in 0.63 s in release, so the failure needs a corpus around a hundred thousand memories. A record-count cap would also be wrong in the way the memory cap was — the right number depends on the machine and on whether the binary is a release or a debug build, and the build turned out to matter about nine times more than the model. **What shipped instead**: the response carries `took_ms` beside `memories`, so the cost is visible on hardware nobody here can test, and every real load adds evidence about the axis that stayed unmeasured. The probe that settled it is `probe_what_a_review_costs` in `tests/probes.rs`; the figures are in the measurement memory under `evaluation-load-size-limit`.
context: Closing the size-limit entry after timing a review load under both models.
why: Supersedes the entry as built rather than leaving it open for work the measurement showed is not needed. Recorded as a closure with its reason so that *there is no limit* reads as a decision rather than an omission — the next session to notice an uncapped embed should find this before adding one.

content: **Given Scatterhoard's read-only tools on a copy of the real stores, local `gemma4:12b` never passed an accidental large or zero `limit`.** Measured 2026-10-02 over 9 runs, thinking off, 16,384-token context, using Scatterhoard's published schemas through Ollama tool calling. Across 12 recall calls: 8 used the default with no `limit` (decision, lookup, an overview of "everything", a sweep "so nothing is missed"). A survey of what the set covers chose `limit: 50` with `detail: summary` unprompted. The only large limits, 1000 and then 100 in full detail, came when the task said to read every memory. No zero and no negative appeared. In both "read everything" runs, gemma resent a call refused for having no query, unchanged, before adding one.
context: Right after withdrawing recall-limit-is-unbounded; the human partner suggested hooking their local gemma4:12b to Scatterhoard to see whether a small model passes careless limits.
why: This is the evidence the withdrawal of `recall-limit-is-unbounded` names as the thing that would reopen it: callers passing limits they did not mean. The human partner nominated a small local model adding a zero as the likeliest source. None appeared, so it supports the decision without proving it: nine runs, one model, one setting, and the batch was cut short by the 30-minute limit on background jobs. The repeated refused call is recorded because it suggests the no-query refusal could give an example, which would need testing on a weak reader before any rewording.

content: One root cause, two symptoms, and the published schema stated it plainly in `absorbing`'s own description: *"needed again on every import of that file, since nothing records it."* Absorption was a receiver-side rewrite that left no trace, so **any operation that rebuilds a store from a file loses it** — restore is simply the one that does so while looking like a repair. The other symptom is `absorbing-on-one-import-and-not-another-puts-two-contents-under-one-id`, the falsification itself.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The generalisation that made restore one instance rather than the defect. Kept because the schema had documented the root cause as a caveat, where it read as an instruction to remember something rather than as a design fault.

content: **Where the trusted set name for a checkout comes from. Resolved 2026-09-25 by the human partner: nowhere, because no name needs trusting.** Whether a checkout's set is legitimate is its provenance: the user cloned it and names the `scope` on each call. Sameness is `set_id`'s job. The trust-on-first-use binding is dropped, and a rename is the same `set_id` under a new name. What the question had actually been guarding, a collision, is answered by identity: a mismatch is refused on import and export, each case with its own route. Built as `identity-mismatch-refusal`, with `open-a-set-under-an-alias` for two legitimate sets that share a name. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner, second of the checkout-and-sets pair after `one-repository-many-sets`.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. The question assumed Scatterhoard had to establish a set's legitimacy, and the human partner's point that git provenance does that removed the binding's purpose. The narrowings recorded under this question (remote versus path, the `bases` list as an accidental binding, Store Registry's registration) were answers to where a binding lives, so they fall with it. If auto-discovery is ever built, a binding may be worth reopening then.

content: **`DEVELOPMENT.md` became `CONTRIBUTING.md` on 2026-11-02, and `STANDARDS.md` stays as the rules it links to.** Decided with the human partner, over merging `STANDARDS.md` and `DEVELOPMENT.md`, which overlap little: one holds rules for code and 27 files link to it, the other held operating instructions. `CONTRIBUTING.md` adds how a contribution carries memories, reviewing a contribution (where the maintainer sentence about `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` now lives), and the mutation runner's reference material. `AGENTS.md` keeps every rule that applies at a particular moment -- `--stale` after a rename, the closing order in full -- and points to `CONTRIBUTING.md` for the rest.
context: Turning DEVELOPMENT.md into CONTRIBUTING.md during the going-public checklist, after the breaking-change audit and settling the beta tag.
why: GitHub shows `CONTRIBUTING.md` to anyone opening an issue or pull request, which is where a reviewer should meet the maintainer sentence, and the rename cost one link. Moving reference text out of `AGENTS.md` shrinks what every session loads; keeping the moment-bound rules there follows the earlier finding that a rule needing a lookup arrives too late.

content: `MAX_CATALOG_CHARS` counts bytes, not characters: the enforcement and `report_catalog_size` both sum `str::len()`, which is Rust's byte length. The name says characters, so headroom computed in characters is wrong wherever the served text is not ASCII — and a catalog served in a language costing two bytes a character would reach 18,000 at about half the content. Fixed when the name and the unit agree. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `catalog-budget-counts-bytes-not-characters`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Counting the catalog while adding a sentence to store-when, and noticing that an em dash cost three against the budget rather than one.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. `misleads` because nothing is lost or corrupted and the number is honest about itself — what is wrong is that the name promises a unit the code does not use, and every figure quoted from it since has been a byte count called a character count.

content: **Three unifying explanations were proposed and refuted on 2026-09-08, by the session that proposed them — the same pattern the previous day showed with four. The problem is still not understood.** (1) **`why` contaminating the embedding input**: refuted by its own control — the hub-rate rise across `why`-share quartiles is present with `why` removed. (2) **Question form**: refuted — question-shaped nonsense reaches p90 **0.192** where real off-domain questions reach 0.275, so the interrogative frame is not what lifts a score. (3) **Lexical overlap with the corpus**: refuted — pooled over 94 queries in seven families, Pearson **r = 0.317, r² = 0.100**, and `>>> <<< ||| ~~~ ^^^` has **zero** word-level overlap while scoring **0.478**; rule-shaped off-corpus queries carry *more* overlap than answerable ones (0.373 against 0.350) and score *lower* (0.415 against 0.522). **What survives is measurement, not theory**: the rule-versus-substance split is a robust empirical fact whose cause is unexplained, the `stale` collision is minimal-pair confirmed, and per-store calibration figures stand. **One caveat on (3)**: the measure is word-level document frequency, and the model tokenises to subwords, so a subword-level version is untested and would need tokenizer access.
context: Closing out a long session of recall measurements, after the human partner asked whether keyboard-mashing probes would help and the answer opened a third failed theory.
why:
Recorded because the honest state of the investigation is its most useful output, and because the failure has now recurred often enough to be data in itself. Seven mechanisms were ruled out on 2026-09-07, four explanations withdrawn on 2026-09-08 by the sessions that proposed them, and three more here — every one plausible when proposed, every one killed by a control or a counter-example that was cheap to run. A reader picking this up should expect their first unifying idea to fail and should build the falsifying test before reporting the result, not after.

The human partner's criterion for having bottomed out was that the *recommendations* would stop reversing while the numbers continued to vary. That has been met only in part and should not be read as met: controlling the off-corpus class does stop mechanisms swapping places between studies, but a pilot-sized draw still reverses, and three theories failed in the session that found the composition effect. The composition effect is real and is not the whole cause.

Confidence 0.9 on the refutations, which are direct measurements with named counter-examples, not on any positive account — there is no positive account. What would move this is a test at the subword level, which is the one operationalisation not yet tried.

content: Filed and withdrawn 2026-08-06: `amend` not reaching `why` is not an oversight, because `content` and `why` together are the claim while `keywords`, `links`, `context` and `confidence` are apparatus, and amend is apparatus only. The investigation accumulated under this entry carries the keyword `why-cannot-be-corrected`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster whose standing is withdrawn: the entry was wrong on both its claims, and this file keeps a withdrawn entry because the investigation is worth being able to find.

content: Found 2026-09-02 while building the durable author map, by writing the test the map exists for and watching it fail. **The suite had been working around it**: a test called a helper, `forget_the_set_identity`, that deleted the minted `set_id` by hand so adoption could be exercised at all — **that helper is the defect written down as a fixture**. **Why the rule is right and the outcome still wrong**: *never displace an identity already held* exists so two servers cannot oscillate, and that is sound for a set with a history — it over-reaches for a set with **no records at all**, since nothing was ever written under the minted identity, so adopting the file's cannot contradict anything, and after adoption the set has records and will not adopt again. **Fixed 2026-09-02 by that narrowing.** *Tombstones count as records*: a set whose memories were all forgotten has still been used, and its file carries tombstones written under the identity it holds. *The residual case is narrow and self-correcting*: an empty set that was exported leaves no trace, and does not need to — an empty set adopts whatever it is given, so two empty copies handed the same file reach the same identity, and divergence would need them handed different files, at which point they are different sets.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A correct rule that over-reached on the empty case, narrowed by asking whether anything had been written under the identity rather than whether one exists. The test helper that deleted the identity by hand is the tell: a fixture working around a defect is the defect written down.

content: **The personal-set exemption has a precondition that is not yet met, and getting the order wrong inverts the whole trust model.** The exemption is only safe **while scope is unforgeable**. If a memory set could talk its way into local scope, exempting `local` from the data-only rule would turn scope forgery from a trust *elevation* into straight **instruction injection**: a repository would need only to claim `local` to have its memories treated as directives. **What currently holds that shut is the File Format guard** -- the path establishes what a file is trusted to be, and a file's declared scope is checked against that expectation and can only ever agree with it, never widen it. **The part still missing is the set-name binding**, which is `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout` -- so the two entries are ordered rather than merely related: the exemption cannot be granted before that binding exists.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Recorded because the dependency runs the opposite way to how the entries read. The personal-set exemption looks like the safest of the four sub-questions -- it concerns only the user's own machine and their own writing -- and it is the only one that is actively dangerous to answer early.

The inversion is the part to keep: forgery that merely elevates trust is bounded by what the trusted thing may do, and an exemption is exactly a change to what the trusted thing may do. That reasoning applies to any future exemption granted by scope, not only this one.

content: `hoard_sets export` should say how many records are new relative to the file it is replacing — *94 records written, 4 not present in the file being replaced* — so an export that silently carries another session's work into a commit announces itself. Built when export reports the delta, with no new field and nothing persisted. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `export-reports-what-the-file-did-not-hold`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only, with the built-when since this one is unbuilt. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **Hash order's residual conflict rate, measured 2026-09-21** with `git merge-file` on random subsets of this project's set, 200 trials a cell, new ids shaped like real ones. FNV-1a over the id matched SHA-256 within noise. Conflict rates for 1 / 3 / 10 additions a side: **50 records** 3.5% / 32.5% / 96%; **200 records** 2.5% / 12.5% / 56.5%; **988 records** 0% / 2% / 21.5%. Id order conflicted in every trial. A conflict needs two additions in one gap, or in adjacent gaps, so the rate grows with the product of the two sides' additions and falls with the set's size.
context: Choosing between hash order and a file per memory for the end-of-file conflict.
why: The numbers behind accepting a residue, kept so a later session can judge whether the mitigation still suffices without re-running the simulation. The script lived in the session scratchpad and is not kept. The model is the parts of it worth reusing: rebuild the file three ways, sort by the candidate key, run `git merge-file`.

content: The refusal for a `hoard_recall` with neither a query nor keywords says what is missing but not what to send, and `gemma4:12b` resent the identical refused call before adding a query in both of the 2026-10-02 runs that asked it to read every memory. Found with `scripts/local_model.py agent`. Fixed when a weak reader adds the missing argument on its next call, as tested with that script, not as judged by reading the new wording. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-missing-query-refusal-gives-no-example`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Testing whether a small local model passes careless recall limits, after withdrawing recall-limit-is-unbounded; folding the gemma harnesses into scripts/local_model.py.
why: Head of an issue cluster. Severity is `costs`: a wasted turn, and the second attempt worked. Filed rather than fixed on the spot because the paging work showed a refusal reworded by eye can fail on exactly this reader, so the fix needs a test run, and two runs are a thin basis. The likely fix is an example in the refusal, such as a query in the caller's own words or `keywords` for an exact term.

content: `semantic_search_available` was a completeness flag read as an availability flag: `recall_across` computed `searchable.len() == stores.len()`, and when it was false the recall attached a note saying *"Nothing was searched by meaning"* while the response carried semantically-scored hits from every store that was searchable. content: **Two consequences of the 2026-08-13 recall-and-read decision, both about the half still unbuilt, and still true at migration on 2026-09-07.** First, **the software half is no longer blocked behind scoring**: a warning needs a threshold and would inherit `no-non-match-floor` and the cold-start question, while *surfacing the nearest few* asserts nothing and needs no floor. Declining to make the claim is what removed the dependency, so this can be built now rather than waiting for a corpus large enough to calibrate against. Second, **this is the detection moment `splitting-partly-stale` was waiting for.** That convention defers splitting to detection time on the grounds that at store time nobody can predict which half of a memory will rot first — but a store-time recall returning a partial overlap **is** detection, and its own test, *at detection the answer is already known*, is satisfied. The two are closer than their separate entries suggest and should be drafted with each other in view.

One caution the entry carried and it still applies: **watch the interaction with corrections.** A memory that supersedes another is *supposed* to resemble it closely, so a duplicate check that cannot tell supersession from duplication fires on exactly the records the corrections design is careful to preserve. content:
**Structural mechanisms beat conventions here, and that settles the site: export.** Established with the human partner 2026-09-12, before any convention text was drafted.

**The axis is theirs.** A convention is text a session is served and can be told to disregard, or edited out of a fork. A structural mechanism is something the *tool does*, which has to be patched out of the code — their example is the built-in ability to change an author's name, which is harder to remove than a convention edit. Against a determined actor, only the structural half is doing work.

**The charter was considered as the set-level surface and fails.** It is loaded first in every session and is the only place a set says what it is *for*, which looked promising. The human partner's counter-example: `This set contains memories about the Fluffy Cat project`, plus a session opening with *let's work on Fluffy Cat*, routes everything correctly while saying nothing about what Fluffy Cat is. **The charter can be contentless and still discharge its routing duty**, so there is no honest-charter-or-degraded-tool trade. Recall fails as a surface for the opposite reason: it is query-shaped and returns a slice sized to the question, so it never shows what a set amounts to.

**Export survives all three tests of a structural mechanism.** It runs whether or not a session chooses to reason about it; removing it means changing code; and it sits on the path to something the user wants for independent reasons. It is also the only moment the whole set is in view, which is what [decision-placement](documents/design/decision-placement.md) asks for — information and stake in the same place.

**Its coverage grows with the scale of the operation, which inverts the usual shape.** Export is avoidable only by never wanting portable memories, shared memories, or more durability than one SQLite file — so the actor it fails to reach is the solo, single-machine, never-shares case, which is also the least scaled. Most safeguards are strongest against the casual case and weakest against the determined one. This is the other way round, and that is why it may apply real friction even where defence is not a success criterion: the human partner's position is that B1, a party who could build their own memory system, is **not a criterion for success**, but that making Scatterhoard a meaningful nuisance to them is welcome if it comes free.

**One observed fact supports the whole arrangement**: an LLM has been a reviewer of every exported memory file in this project's history so far. The reviewer at that gate is a model, in practice and not only in principle.
context: Working through the risks behind the Golden Rule question the same day it was filed, after the threat report was read in full.
why:
Recorded because it settles the *site* before any text exists, and the site is what the whole question turns on. Two candidate sites were considered and eliminated on their merits rather than on taste, which is the part a later session would otherwise redo.

The scaling property is the reason to keep this rather than treat it as an interim note. Almost every safeguard is strongest against the casual case and weakest against the determined one; a gate on the path to portability inverts that, and an inversion of the usual shape is worth holding onto even if the specific mechanism proposed here is discarded.

Origin joint: the structural-versus-conventional axis and the charter counter-example are the human partner's, the three tests and the scaling observation are mine.

content: **Whether the gap sweep should run on writes, or only on recall by meaning.** Resolved 2026-09-22 by the human partner: **only before a search by meaning.** `write` no longer calls `prepare`, since it embeds its own memory and reads nothing the cache holds. The sweep's query now excludes identity records, so it can come back empty. A gap left by another server is filled at the next semantic recall rather than the next write, and nothing reads vectors in between. The findings gathered under this question carry the keyword `where-the-gap-sweep-runs`.
context: Pre-release review of open questions, straight after resolving link-only-write-after-export.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. The evidence is in the member checked the same day. content: Scatterhoard resolves supersession validity on two different paths, and they consult different lookups. Semantic recall goes through `recall_across` and `Neighbourhood::over`, which reads `Store::edges`. Keyword search goes through `Store::resolved_hit`, which calls `Store::resolve_supersession` directly and so consults `Store::incoming`. `Store::recall` is semantic even for a single store, because it delegates to `recall_across`. A guard placed in one of those lookups is therefore invisible to any test driven through the other path.
context: Found 2026-08-23 while building the fix for `a-set-can-suppress-another-sets-memory`. The test is `an_edge_naming_another_set_does_not_speak_about_a_colliding_local_id` in tests/cross_store.rs, whose doc comment records why it must use the keyword path.
why: This cost real time on 2026-08-23 and would cost it again. A test written to prove that `Store::incoming`'s cross-set filter worked was driven through `Store::recall`, passed, and proved nothing: the `edges` guard had already stopped the case earlier on that path, so the filter under test was never reached. Only a surviving mutation revealed it, and rewritten on the keyword path the same test caught the mutation immediately. Checkable in `src/store.rs` at `recall`, `resolved_hit` and `Neighbourhood::over`.

content:
A full mutation pass on 2026-09-19 found one guard untested, and it was untested in the documented way: two code paths refuse the same call, and the test took the other one. `evaluate` refuses a label this server already holds (`self.stores`/`self.withheld`) and separately refuses one whose file already exists because another server holds it. `evaluate_refuses_a_label_already_loaded` asserted only that the call errored and that the message named the label — and both messages name it, so disabling the in-process guard left the on-disk guard catching the same call and the test could not tell.

Fixed by asserting the distinguishing words, *already loaded for review* rather than *already held for review*. That is operational rather than cosmetic: **loaded** means drop it here, **held** means another server has it, and a reviewer told the wrong one looks in the wrong place.

Two things worth carrying. **The guard had been in place since evaluation mode shipped on 2026-09-18 with nothing proving it**, and a full pass is what surfaced that — the previous pass predates the mutation. And the runner's own note is worth heeding: `target-mutation` held 347,553 files and 32.3 GB, which slowed the pass to a 6.4s mean against about 1.6s on a clean tree. Roughly every third pass wants `rm -rf target-mutation`.
context: Running the first full mutation pass since the encoding change, at the end of the memory-size stretch.
why: Recorded because the rule it instantiates is already written in AGENTS.md — *suspect the test's route before concluding the guard is redundant* — and an instance of a rule actually firing is what tells a later session the rule earns its place. The wording assertion also needs its reason attached, or it reads as brittle and gets relaxed by whoever next edits that message.

content: **Decided 2026-09-17 by the human partner: an evaluation set's recalls do not feed floor calibration.** A recall that names a scope is logged with `scoped = 1` and the floor is a percentile over `WHERE used = 1 OR scoped = 1` (`src/store.rs`), so without this every query against an evaluation set would be a calibration signal — naming the scope is the only way to search one. Two reasons to exclude them: a reviewer's queries are exploratory rather than evidence the set answered well, and the measurement that made the scope label worth using treated it as a *noisy-but-frequent* signal, which an evaluation load makes universal instead. **The cost is small and was checked rather than assumed**: on 2026-09-17 no set on this machine held a floor at all — `scatterhoard`, `coding-lessons` and `local` each report none, with 36, 29 and 25 queries logged — so calibration is available and has never been run here. As the human partner put it, it would help but is not needed to perform a review. An evaluation store is also in memory and does not outlive the session, so any floor it calibrated would die with it.
context: Designing evaluation mode: cross-set links, then calibration.
why: Recorded because the interaction is invisible from both sides: the calibration code says nothing about load modes and the evaluation design says nothing about the query log. The empirical part is worth keeping because it bounds what the decision gives up — nothing that exists today — and because *no set here is calibrated* is a fact a later session would otherwise have to rediscover by reading the database, since no tool reports a set's floor.

content: Fixed 2026-08-25 by the test rather than by the deletion: `the_migration_gives_a_keyword_this_build_cannot_parse_a_lookup_key` in [tests/store.rs](tests/store.rs) plants `'memory view'` — whitespace, which `Keyword::new` refuses — in a store built at the previous schema, opens it, and reads the column back with `rusqlite`. The backfill fills that row; the refold `continue`s past it and then records its marker, so without the backfill it stays at `DEFAULT ''` for the life of the store. The mutation is now caught by that test and nothing else. **Asserted against the table rather than through a search, deliberately**: a query keyword must itself be a valid `Keyword`, so no search can be constructed that matches either the right value or the wrong one — the difference is real and currently unreachable through the API. What the test pins is the state a later relaxation of the constructor, or any second reader of that column, would find.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A test that asserts against storage because the difference it pins is unreachable through the API. Worth keeping because asserting on the table normally signals a test reaching past the interface, and here it is the only honest option.

The 52 are not a sample someone assembled to prove a point — each is a pair a session judged related **independently, at writing time, while doing something else**, and expressed by keyword only because keywords were the instrument being asked for. content: A keyword match count is comparable across Scatterhoard's memory sets where a cosine similarity is not, so keyword recall merges every searched set into one ranked list with no centring at all. The count counts the caller's own keywords, which mean the same thing in every set; raw cosines need the union centroid before they can be compared. This is the one place the design's cross-store incomparability rule does not bite. Ties break on memory id ascending -- most queries carry one keyword, so most hits score 1, and the alternative is store iteration order that no caller can see. Checkable at `search_keywords_across` in src/store.rs and the "Keyword search across sets is one ranked list" section of documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md.
context: Decided 2026-08-19 while fixing `keyword-recall-multiplies-the-limit-by-the-number-of-sets`, which had each set contributing its own limit and the union left unranked.
why: The incomparability rule is stated broadly enough in the design to look like it governs every cross-store merge, and applying it here would mean either refusing to merge keyword hits or inventing a normalisation for a scale that does not need one. What makes the difference is where the scale comes from: a similarity is measured against a corpus and therefore means something different in each store, while a match count is measured against the query the caller just wrote. Worth holding because the hybrid-search work deferred in open-questions.md will have to combine the two, and knowing which of them is already comparable is half of that problem.

content: Native confidence is deliberately left out of graph traversal's distance decay, and the reason is the evidence rather than the field. The design describes the walk as decreasing a memory's effective confidence by its native confidence and its distance from the seed; only distance is implemented. Nothing available can tune the confidence term: the evaluation corpus was authored with values spanning 0.8 to 0.95, and the live sets held five distinct values between 0.8 and 1.0 across 44 memories. A term whose entire observed range is the top fifth of its scale cannot be distinguished from a constant by any corpus this project currently has.
context: Decided 2026-08-16 by the human partner while settling the design questions the graph-traversal build would hit, after the walk's other parameters were measured against the evaluation corpus. Recorded in documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md.
why: Including it would mean guessing a second weight immediately after taking the trouble to measure the first, which is the failure the design names as a weight guessed to three decimals reading as reasoned about. Recorded so a later reader does not take the absence for an oversight and quietly add it back, and so the condition for revisiting is explicit: revisit with operating experience, once stored confidence values vary more than the test corpus and the early live sets do. Confidence may well belong in the decay; what is missing is data with enough range to say.

content: A reduced default detail level on the wire is allowed, but a full-detail mode must always exist, and the reduction must be expressed as one subtractive projection chosen in a single place — never as several call sites each re-listing the fields they send.
context: Stated by the human partner on 2026-08-02 while deciding how to fix recall's partial memories; recorded in ISSUES.md on `recall-returns-a-partial-memory` and load-bearing for the open `combined-recall-duplicates-content` work.

A field that no mode can show is a field whose corruption cannot be detected through the only interface that exists.

content: **Anything that scores a query against a summary of the corpus is measuring whether the query *sounds like* the corpus, and same-author off-topic text sounds exactly like it.** That rules out a family rather than one statistic: query-versus-corpus comparisons join query-versus-similarities and result-set coherence as measured failures on the non-match entry.
context: Running the CSLS re-test and the alignment-boundary trial the human partner asked for, across four set sizes plus the union.
why: Split on 2026-10-19 from the alignment-boundary result, whose reasoning it was, when that memory was restated over the length limit.

content:
**A second store refutes the early-floor stability: `coding-lessons` would have lost 10 of 53 later queries to a floor set from its first ten.** Same simulation, 2026-09-11, 63 labelled queries (37 scoped, 26 by later use) against 129 memories and the same 601 probes. Raw cosine: floor 0.469 from the first ten, against a true minimum of 0.307 reached later — 19% of subsequent real queries silenced. From 30 it is 0.336 and loses 1 of 33; from 40 it is 0.307 and loses none while silencing 66.7%. Centred on this store behaves better than on `scatterhoard` — 0.205 from 40, losing none and silencing 41.1% — but still worse than raw.

**What holds across both stores:** raw beats centred on benefit at the fully calibrated floor (62.7% and 66.7% against 2.7% and 41.1%); a floor wants **about forty labelled queries**, not ten; and a margin of 0.05 below the observed minimum loses nothing on either store from thirty queries onward.

**And a defect no run here can show: a floor conceals the evidence that would correct it.** Once it silences a query, nothing is returned, so no memory can be used afterwards and the query can never be labelled answerable — the floor protects its own mistakes, and the calibration data goes on looking clean.
context: Repeating the floor simulation on a second store at the human partner's suggestion, to see whether the first store's result held.
why:
Recorded because it corrects the reading of the first simulation rather than adding to it. `scatterhoard`'s raw minimum held from the first ten queries through eighty-five, which looked like stability and was the lowest-scoring query happening to arrive early; on a second store the same rule loses a fifth of the traffic that follows. One store was never enough to support *calibrate early*, and the caveat recorded with the first result is now an observation.

The self-concealing property is the part that should shape the design rather than the numbers. It argues for recall reporting that a floor silenced everything, and for letting a caller ask again without it: that keeps the over-recall bias honest and is the only way the evidence needed to lower a wrong floor can ever be produced.

content: Found 2026-08-02 driving the MCP surface against a disposable store: store A with keyword `alpha-marker`, supersede it with B carrying `beta-marker`, and a search for `alpha-marker` returns **B**. **Swapping the superseded memory for its replacement is correct and deliberate; reporting it as a direct keyword hit is not** — and on the keyword path that is the *only* signal available, since there is no score to look sideways at. The data was already there: the store populated `matched` on the keyword hit and the serialisation dropped it. *Two things this entry left open were answered much later.* Whether `matched_keywords` should report the matched memory's count or the returned one's was flagged here and not settled. And whether the keyword should still match at all was never argued — only inherited from the content rule — which is `a-keyword-cannot-be-retired-once-a-memory-has-been-exported`, filed a month later with this exact fixture.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: An entry that had the right fixture in front of it and answered the narrower question. Worth keeping because the sub-question it explicitly left open became a separate defect a month later, which is evidence that a noted-and-deferred question does not stay noted.

content: **The elicitation form is never pre-filled from a set's recorded export locations**, though the proposal planned it; dropped 2026-10-15 while building. A set records no `bases` until it holds memories, since exporting an empty set writes none, so a new set has no location at its first write; and the sets that do have locations before anyone here has written are sets taken on from someone else, whose repository owner is the publisher. The default would have offered exactly the stranger's handle the form exists to keep out. The hint stays as the field's description, for the human.
context: Implementing the elicitation proposal; tracing where a form default could come from.
why: The pre-fill reads as an obvious convenience to add later, and the reason it is harmful is not visible from the code. Checkable against `Store::set_bases`, which writes one row per memory. Decided by Claude while building, not reviewed by the human partner when written.

content: Of the walk's four constants, only `decay` is a weight; `seeds`, `hops` and `frontier` are bounds. That was deliberate, and both untuned-looking numbers are defended rather than guessed. The decay barely matters at the shape that ships: across 0.3 to 0.9 the configuration moves about one and a half points, which is a deliberate trade of a sensitive constant for an insensitive one. `frontier` did not bind at 429 memories -- 5, 20 and 40 give identical results -- so 20 is carried as the safety property it was defined to be, for a corpus larger than anything measured, rather than as a knob anyone tuned. `frontier` caps what may be expanded THROUGH at each hop and never what is admitted, because reaching a heavily cited memory is cheap while expanding through it is what branches.
context: Measured 2026-08-18 over 24 harvested queries labelled twice, blind, on different models. Checkable at `Walk::measured` and the `Walk` struct doc comment in src/traversal.rs, which carries the bound-versus-weight distinction. Note the constants were re-measured rather than carried over, because an earlier sweep had tuned against a walk that let a seed inherit back to itself.
why: These read as arbitrary constants to anyone who meets them cold, and the natural instinct on finding an untuned number is either to tune it or to treat it as an oversight and change it. Both are wrong here for different reasons: the decay is insensitive by design, so tuning it buys nothing, and the frontier is a bound whose whole point is not binding on any corpus yet seen -- an unbound safety limit looks useless precisely when it is working. Also corrects the closed `graph-traversal` BACKLOG entry, which predates the build and says the weights are still unset and should ship flat and recorded as untuned; the instruction was discharged by measuring instead.

content: **Investigated 2026-09-08, and the football query was never special: gibberish scores as well as a real question.** Controls against the 855-vector union — `"qwertyuiop asdfghjkl"` scores **0.359**, `"zzqxlp"` 0.295, `"xyzzy plugh frotz"` 0.275, against on-topic queries at 0.303 and 0.326. **Keyboard mashing outscores real questions.** So the offside result is one instance of a general property and not a vocabulary collision: any direction, meaningful or not, finds a nearest neighbour at roughly 0.25–0.36 among 855 vectors in 512 dimensions. Three candidate mechanisms were tested and all fail. **Not hubness**: measured properly by k-occurrence with every memory used as a query, `governance-docs` averages 11.00 against a corpus mean of 10.05, and its best member ranks 70th among hubs. **Not centroid removal**: the uncentred ranking still puts `governance-docs` 1st, 2nd and 4th, so centring amplifies `0.356` to `0.420` and reorders, but does not create the match. **Not word order either** — the gibberish controls have no word order to get wrong. What remains is structural: a small tight off-domain cluster in a mixed store acts as an attractor for any query not aligned with the corpus mass.
context: Investigating why a football query retrieved corporate bylaws, after splitting the non-match entry in two.
why: Recorded because the investigation was launched on the reasonable theory that *rule*, *league* and *interpretation* were matching governance vocabulary, and the control kills it in one line — a string with no words at all does the same thing. Naming the three refuted mechanisms is the point: each is the first thing a later session would try, each takes an hour to test, and each is now answered. The remaining explanation implies the fix is not in the scorer: if the nearest neighbour to an arbitrary direction is always something and always looks decent, then no threshold on that number can exist, and the question becomes what else a recall could say.

content: A correction to this entry's own measurement, and it matters for what gets built. *"Clearing does not measurably help"* — 2.4s per mutation before a clear, 2.6s after — is **not established**, because the two runs differ in more than the file count: the pass after the clear started with nothing cached and absorbed a full dependency rebuild, so it was not the same experiment. Read it as *no evidence either way*. **And the file count turns out to be the right quantity after all**: the bytes are wrong and also beside the point, because the cost is compile time and what bogs down is the filesystem as the inode count climbs — the human partner's reading on 2026-08-30, with which the runner's own history agrees, *"a pass at 159,000 files ran at twice clean speed"*. So the number to watch is the count; what is broken is the byte figure quoted beside it and the calibration of the threshold.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A measurement retracted by the session that made it, because the two runs it compared differed in more than the variable under test. Kept because the retraction has to travel with the number, or the number gets cited.

content: **Whether Scatterhoard should rename a set in place, keeping its identity and its machine state.** Raised 2026-10-18 by the human partner, who wanted to rename a set whose name identifies them. The only route today is the hand-edit procedure written for a hard fork in `documents/design/set-lifecycle.md`: export, edit `scope` in a copy's header, `drop`, `create` the new name, then `import`. Tested the same day, it keeps the identity, memories and links, but loses the set's query log and labelled queries, forgets which record is this machine's author until `identify` is run, and leaves links from other sets, which name the old set, pointing at nothing. Open because nothing decides whether a rename operation is worth building or what it should carry over. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `renaming-a-set-in-place`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Deciding how to handle the memories naming the governance set in the publication review: testing a set rename on a throwaway set in the test instance before considering it for the real one.
why: Head of a question cluster. It is a question rather than an issue because the procedure works as designed: it was built for a fork, which should get a new identity and has no history to keep. A rename of the same set has neither property. The live case is a set whose current name identifies the human partner. The losses are what turn a few minutes' hand edit into a reason to decide.

content: **The human partner's direction for `memory-size-drift`, given 2026-09-15: any convention should speak about general length *and about compression*, and should ask for dense text in memories and in queries, so semantic recall is efficient.** Density rather than a limit is the operative part — the target is text carrying more per token, not merely less text, which distinguishes it from a ceiling and from the shortening failure `EARLY-VALIDATION.md` already watches for. **It also reaches the query side**, which nothing in the catalog currently addresses: `recall-when` says when to search and in what language, and says nothing about how a query should be written.
context: Just after committing the memory-size question, as the session turned to the link-key collision test.
why:
Recorded because it narrows the question's open part — where a response belongs and what it would say — from any of measuring, advising or bounding, to a convention about how memories and queries are written. It is the human partner's stated direction rather than a decision: the question stays open, and what remains unsettled is whether density can be asked for in a way that is checkable at writing time, which is exactly the drafting difficulty `memories-must-stand-alone` already ran into with *make sure a memory stands alone*.

Kept separate from the candidate-cause memory beside it because the two can be settled independently: if drift follows the writing model, a density convention is still worth having for recall efficiency, and if it does not, this is still how the response would be shaped.

content:
**A set declares its languages as keywords on its charter, and sessions write and search in them.** Built 2026-09-14. Decided 2026-09-11 by the human partner and recorded in `documents/design/memory-data-model.md` under *Resolved 2026-09-11: a set declares its languages on its charter*: language tags ride on the `hoard-scope-topics` memory as `hoard-lang-*` keywords — lowercase BCP 47, several where a set is mixed — so they travel through export and appear in the JSON a maintainer reviews.

**What shipped:** `recall-when` tells a session to write a set's memories and phrase queries against it in a language its charter declares, translating when it can and keeping keywords and identifiers as spelled; `hoard_sets status` reports each set's `languages` from every live charter and adds a `language_note` to any set declaring none, `local` included; `create` asks for the declaration. Contract in `tests/set_languages.rs`. All four sets on the human partner's machine declare `hoard-lang-en`. **The human partner widened the purpose while building**: the declaration is first a findability instruction to the session — the shipping model barely separates meaning outside English, and almost not at all across languages — and only then a reviewed standard, which is why `local` is covered.

**Moved out, not dropped:** checking a declaration against the loaded model — the model-fit report, the write-door note and the coverage test — is `model-covers-declared-languages`, deferred. Adding the `hoard-lang-` family to the list of known control marks belongs to `reserved-keyword-block-list`, which builds that list. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `charter-declares-set-languages`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing charter-declares-set-languages after its declaration half was built and all four charters declared hoard-lang-en; the human partner asked for the checking half to move to its own entry.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because the entry is closed: its declaration half is built, and the checking half moved to its own entry at the human partner's direction, so this row reads done and the new row names what is left. Readiness facet dropped, as built entries carry none.

content: Each memory and tombstone row stores its `file_position`, so export is one `ORDER BY` over both tables holding one record at a time, rather than every id and whole tombstone sorted in process. Built 2026-09-22 the same day as filed: `file_position INTEGER` on both tables, stored sign-flipped (`stored_position` in `src/store.rs`), indexed with the id, filled on every open by `fill_file_positions`, and checked per record in `Store::stream_records` against the id's own position and the record before — a mismatch refuses with `StoreError::OutOfFileOrder`. Checked by `tests/store.rs` and seven recorded mutations. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `file-position-column`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Filing and building the two follow-ups from the question about storing the hash that orders memory files, straight after the streaming merge driver.
why: Superseded to record it as built — and built nullable, not the `NOT NULL` proposed when it was filed, which is the thing a later reader should not have to rediscover. SQLite's `ALTER TABLE` cannot add a `NOT NULL` column without a default, and a default is worse than no value: a row given `0` sorts to a wrong place quietly. So the protection a constraint would have given at write time is given at read time instead: open fills anything missing, and export refuses any position that disagrees with its id. That check also turned one id held as both a memory and a tombstone from an unreadable file into a refusal.

content: **Scatterhoard never changes a `README.md` that already exists in a memory directory, not even to add the project URL**: decided 2026-10-17 by the human partner, answering the overwrite question `readme-names-the-project-url` left open. The default README is written only when Scatterhoard creates the directory, and carries the URL from the start, so no Scatterhoard-written README ever lacks it; every README that predates the feature was written by a person, like this repository's own `scatterhoard_mem/README.md`, which stays as it is.
context: Starting on the default README for memory directories, building both README backlog entries together.
why: The entry required an answer rather than a default. Adding a line to a project's own file is what the do-not-overwrite rule in `memory-directory-readme` forbids, and Scatterhoard's own repository has no use for a pointer at itself. The coding-lessons repository is to get the default README by hand once its text is settled.

content: **Corrects an over-claim: the inversion test does not show the floor fails, because `governance-docs` is not an off-domain store for these queries.** It holds the governing documents of an association — a priority clause ranking Articles over By-Laws over Declaration, what percentage a rule requires, who may serve on which committee, how amendments take effect. Scatterhoard's own memories are about conventions, what a rule requires, amendment versus supersession, and which document governs which rule. **The two corpora share rule-shaped structure**, which this same investigation established is what actually drives the score — topic is not. So *record the losing argument alongside a decision so it can be revisited* scoring **0.589** there is plausibly a genuine match, not a false one. **"Unanswerable by provenance" was the error**: provenance establishes a different *subject*, and subject is precisely the thing shown not to govern these scores. `coding-lessons` is no cleaner — it overlaps by admission. **What stands from that test**: nothing about the floor failing. **What stands independently**: the floor is cheap on the answerable side, 1 of 142 on the store these queries are about; and the 53% figure remains suspect because authored substance probes may be unrepresentatively distant — that critique never depended on the inversion.
context: The human partner asking that the bylaws-analysis session be excluded from the harvest, which led to reading what the governance-docs store actually contains. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the memory was over the length limit. The earlier version's `contradicts` link to the 53% measurement was left behind, because this correction withdrew the over-claim that made it a contradiction.
why: Supersedes the inversion finding, exported and committed in `cff6386` before the flaw was seen. Found when the human partner asked that a bylaws-analysis session be excluded from the harvest: checking that meant reading what `governance-docs` holds, which exposed the larger error. Only two of the 142 queries came from that session and neither is about bylaws, so the contamination they asked about was absent; the test was invalid for a different reason.

content: Unpublished sets have no transport but a file syncer. Raised 2026-08-23 by the human partner. With `local` resolved as a single set, every other set is a symmetric `Shared` set — including those with no repository: a set across two of your own laptops, a household set, a volunteer board's institutional memory. **What is genuinely wrong with a syncer**: it produces conflicted copies rather than merges, where `git` produces a real three-way merge against a common ancestor. Per-record base checksums make two conflicted copies reconcilable by importing both, so it is recoverable rather than destructive — but manual, and it degrades exactly as a set gets more use. A SQLite store in a synced folder is a different and worse matter and stays prohibited. **What this is not**: a new scope class. A p2p-synchronised set is an ordinary `Shared` set whose file travels by something other than `git`, so nothing about `Scope` changes — and the scope question is settled in the negative, with no `synced:` or `p2p:` prefix. **Blocked deliberately until after the first release**, and until at least one unpublished shared set has been lived with long enough to say whether the syncer is inadequate or merely inelegant. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `built-in-sync`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Test and documentation debt section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. Filed while the reasoning that produced it was fresh, which is the entry's own stated reason for existing before it can be acted on.

Blocked on the release gate this entry depends on, and additionally on lived experience — two conditions rather than one, and the second cannot start until the first is met.

content: **Two corrections the entry made to itself on 2026-09-06, both found by writing the convention text rather than by review.** First, *the trigger moves next to the charter recall* rested on a misreading: `route-where`'s `hoard-scope-topics` recall fires when **routing a memory**, in one call across every set — not at startup and not per set. There was no existing habit to join, so the clause stayed in `recall-when`, which is where the only session-start instruction lives. Second, **the load-time trigger is not built**: an unreviewed set can arrive mid-session by `create` then `import`, which is what asking to read a set does today, so the convention says session start and nothing else. The load-time half waits for evaluation mode rather than shipping ahead of the rule that would bound it.
context: Migrating the watch-push-is-an-index-per-set entry out of BACKLOG.md; these are the corrections the entry recorded against itself after the build.
why:
Kept because both corrections read as omissions rather than decisions. A later session finding the watch recall in `recall-when` instead of beside the charter recall, or finding no load-time trigger despite the convention naming set-loading as a moment, would reasonably "fix" either — and both fixes are wrong: one relocates a session-start instruction to a routing-time call, the other opens the unreviewed-set surface deliberately left closed.

Worth noting how they were caught. Writing the served text is what exposed them, not reading the entry: the misreading survived being written down and being planned against, and only failed when someone had to state the instruction in the place it would actually run.

content:
**A description of each memory set, derived from its own contents, is built, 2026-09-12 into 2026-09-13**: shown at export, written into the exported file, recomputed at import, and owed at session start when an import could not give it. Designed in `documents/design/golden-rule.md` under demand C and `documents/design/export-review.md` section 4; contracts in `tests/summary.rs` and `tests/set_description.rs`.

What ships: spherical k-means over the stored embeddings, seeded by `k-means++` from a constant generator so every machine gets the same partition, with `k` from `round(1.2 · ln n)` clamped to 2..12; each cluster labelled by its most distinctive keywords; `describes` on the export response, after embedding anything missing; the header field `summary`, carrying the derivation and model; an import that recomputes rather than reads back and gives `against_the_claim`, comparing only under the same model and derivation and only when the set holds exactly what the file brought; an owed description, recorded when any arriving memory lacks a vector and reported by `hoard_conventions` at every session start until an export describes the whole set; and an `export-before-commit` clause telling a session to read the description against the charter, implying nothing about the motives of the memories' authors.

**`FORMAT_VERSION` stayed `0.4.0`**: an optional field an older reader skips takes no bump. **Still open, and deliberately**: the `k` rule is calibrated on two sets of one project; keywords are user-controlled, so labels can be steered by a deliberate act, which defence against a determined actor does not attempt to stop; and a file's `summary` can be deleted before shipping, which leaves the importing machine's own description standing but removes the comparison. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `derived-set-summary`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing the derived set summary after building the owed description, settling the format version and the export-before-commit clause with the human partner. Same stretch: diagnosing the previous session's [bio] refusals through flightlog.
why: Head of the backlog cluster, superseded because the entry is built. The standing moves from open and ready to built; the two decisions left for build time are settled in the design documents named above, and what remains open is recorded here as limits rather than as work.

content: Superseding an entry head moved its row to the bottom of the generated index: `genindex.py` sorted heads by id and a supersession mints a later one, so a one-character change of standing rewrote the row's position instead, and the file's original order — which the migration deliberately preserved — decayed into order-of-last-edit. Fixed 2026-09-18 by ordering rows on each entry's *earliest* ancestor, the oldest id reachable through `supersedes` links, which supersession cannot move. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `superseding-a-head-moves-its-row-to-the-end`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Restoring from the 2026-09-18 checkpoint and taking the first issue off the list: the ordering defect, fixed by walking supersession chains back to each entry's first version.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. Kept `costs` rather than `misleads` on the fix, as on the original — nothing false was ever asserted, the rows were all correct, and what was lost was an ordering a reader could take as meaningful plus a two-line diff per status change.

content: A reference that does not pin what it names resolves to whatever the name happens to reach. In this project the ambiguity took three forms. A spelling standing for an identity: a path string as a reconciliation target, a set named by a word that means two sets, a same-set link spelled the long way, a keyword folded by lowercase instead of casefold. An id without its set: memories keyed by id alone collapsing across sets, a link row keyed without its target's set. An identity resolved without a boundary: two sets sharing one identity, a link reaching the private `local` set by its identity. **The structural fix is to key every reference on what it names, qualified by where it lives** — canonicalise at the boundary, and refuse or reserve the spellings that could name two things.
context: Re-deriving the common causes of defects across all 104 issues, and moving them from a hand-written section of TRACKING.md into memories the index is generated from.
why: Not in the original analysis; it is the dominant cause of the multi-set work since 2026-08-20, which the first nine issues predate. Linked to the `coding-lessons` lesson about guards filtering on how something is written rather than what it is, which covers the spelling form and not the other two — so the general form is only partly written.

content: Filed 2026-09-06 on finishing the ISSUES.md migration, which made the staleness prominent rather than causing it. **The analysis is worth having and worth re-deriving, not deleting**: it is the thing that turned a list of defects into the single-source-of-truth argument this project now applies everywhere. **And it is cheaper than it was** — every entry is now a head memory carrying `issue-entry` with its severity as a facet, so the corpus can be enumerated by recall and grouped by cause without reading a 350,000-character file, which is the first thing the migration makes possible rather than merely tidier.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A stale analysis dated rather than silently fixed, because re-running it is analysis rather than migration. Recorded because it is the first concrete demonstration that the index migration bought capability and not only navigation.

content:
Observed 2026-09-14 while using the description, not history from building it. Exporting `shared:scatterhoard` at 838 memories (commit `62f6539`) and again at 840 — the only change two memories closing `a-healed-fork-reports-its-ancestor-as-a-cycle` — moved the cluster sizes from [190, 168, 126, 111, 91, 84, 48, 21] to [139, 126, 119, 115, 110, 86, 77, 69]. Matching each new cluster to the earlier cluster sharing most of its six labels: two kept all six, one kept five, two kept four, and three shared only one or two. Recompute by comparing the `summary` line of `git show 62f6539:scatterhoard_mem/memories.json` with the current file's first line.

**The cluster count did not change**: `round(1.2 · ln n)` is 8 at both sizes, so this is the partition moving, not `k`.

**Suspected mechanism, unverified**: `initial_seeds` in `src/summary.rs` draws `k-means++` seeds by index over subjects ordered by memory id. Inserting two ids shifts the index of every memory after them, so the constant-seeded draw lands on different seeds, and with several near-equal local optima the refinement settles somewhere else. Check by deriving with and without the two memories and comparing the chosen seed indices, before choosing a remedy.

**Candidate remedies, none decided**: keep the best of several deterministic restarts by within-cluster similarity, which is still reproducible on every machine; make seeding insensitive to insertion order; or accept some churn and say in `export-before-commit`'s neighbourhood that a description is compared within one commit, not across commits.
context: Found while exporting after fixing a-healed-fork-reports-its-ancestor-as-a-cycle, the first item taken from the open issues and backlog that session.
why: The evidence behind the issue head, dated and marked as an observation made in use. The measurement is kept checkable against a named commit; the mechanism is recorded as a hypothesis with the test that would settle it, so a fix does not start from a guess presented as a cause.

content: Fixed 2026-08-20: `Store::accept_from_file` is the write the import path uses — the same write as `insert` minus the cycle refusal, with both delegating to one private `write` so they cannot drift apart in anything else. **The difference named in the code is the caller, not the record**: a caller authoring a `SUPERSEDES` link holds both ends of it and can fix the one they meant, while a file is reconciled record by record and the refusal lands on whichever record the cycle happened to close on. **Reported, not merely tolerated**, which is the half that would have been easy to skip: after the writes, `import_set` resolves each record it wrote and reports any that come back `Resolution::Cycle` as `supersession_cycles`, with guidance saying no tool can resolve it and a merge combining two chains is the usual cause. Without that the fix would have traded an abort for silence. Only the records this import wrote are scanned, so the cost is proportional to the import rather than to the store. Two tests build the cycle by hand-editing an exported file, because no tool will produce one — which is the case itself — and two mutations pin the import path reverting to `insert` and the cycle scan reporting nothing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the discipline that kept it from becoming silence: removing a refusal has to be paid for with a report, or the condition simply stops being visible until it surfaces somewhere stranger.

content: The caller could not say what it already holds. Built 2026-08-18, with `graph-traversal` and in the same commit, which is the coupling the entry called for: `hoard_recall` takes `already_known`, and the ids are removed from the results after validity resolution and **before the cut**, and nothing else. That a suppressed memory still seeds the walk is pinned by a test that watches what it points at lead the results, against a control with the edge removed. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `recall-already-known`; this record carries only its standing.
