content: **Trust boundary on imported memory sets. Resolved 2026-09-25 by the human partner: every set is data, trust is decided per set, and nothing is inspected or weighted per memory.** The four sub-questions were settled that day. Personal-set exemption: none; `local` is data like every set. Import-side gate: none; import reports what arrived instead (`import-reports-what-arrived`). Provenance weighting: none; author and origin are reported, never weighted. Enforcement depth: structure plus a statement in the catalog (`data-only-rule-in-the-catalog`), never content detection. Found on the way and filed: `the-reserved-directory-accepts-the-local-set`. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `imported-set-trust-boundary`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner, after the checkout-and-sets pair.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. The four answers share one reason: trust belongs to the set and its checkout's provenance, so any finer grain would give different memories, or different readers, different standing, and people would confuse them. The human partner made that point twice, about prompts beside data and about readers seeing different truths. The old head called the file *a single well-known memory file*, no longer true since `one-repository-many-sets`. The core it named still holds: nothing instruction-shaped lives under `scatterhoard_mem`.

content: The convention catalog budget was raised from 8,000 to 16,000 characters on 2026-08-12, and the deciding argument was about what the budget is spending rather than about what the next convention needs: 16,000 characters is roughly 3,900 tokens against context windows of 128K to 1M. Decide that arithmetic at the identifier rate (about 4.1 characters per token) rather than the prose rate (about 5.5), because that is the direction the catalog drifts. The new figure is headroom to work towards, not space to fill.
context: Raised while restoring from the 2026-08-12 checkpoint, before drafting the keyword-standards convention, which did not fit under the old budget. Checkable at MAX_CATALOG_CHARS in src/conventions/mod.rs and the "Resolved: the budget is 16,000 characters" section of documents/design/conventions.md.
why: The old budget was about to be paid for by shrinking conventions against each other -- spending clarity and drafting effort to save something the context window does not notice. Choosing the pessimistic character-to-token rate is what keeps a character budget honest as a token proxy, since the constant's own documentation warns that the proxy gets more permissive the more the catalog shifts from prose toward tables of identifiers. The "work towards it" framing is the human partner's, and it matters because doubling the room is exactly when the record-everything failure gets its catalog form.

content: **An evaluation hit is marked by a per-hit field taken from the store's load mode, never parsed from the `eval-` name, and explained by a note in the response.** Decided 2026-09-16 by the human partner. Each memory returned from an evaluation load carries a field such as `"evaluation": true`, and the recall tool's description gains one clause saying what it means, as it already does for `inherited`. A response containing at least one such memory also carries a note, following `in_links_note` and `language_note` in `src/mcp.rs`, saying these are proposals under review and not the project's settled record. **The field comes from the mode because the name is not the source of truth**: parsing names would mean every return path has to remember to do it, and an omission would fail silently in the reassuring direction. The name and the mode cannot disagree anyway, since the evaluation constructor produces both. **The field goes wherever a memory is returned**: direct hits, memories reached through links in an evaluation-scoped recall, and `hoard_lookup` results. The conventions catalog was ruled out, both for its budget and because the note arrives at the moment it matters.
context: Revising the load-modes design: create defaults to read-write, the user chooses evaluation labels, and how evaluation hits are marked.
why: Recorded because the human partner asked whether the `eval-` prefix would trigger the flag, and the answer, that it must not, is the part a later implementation is most likely to get wrong: the name is the visible evidence, so it is the obvious thing to test. An unscoped recall cannot reach an evaluation memory even through a link, because an evaluation store is not among the stores such a recall searches. So the traversal case is limited to recalls that name the evaluation set.

content: **Whether Scatterhoard should manage how long memories are, against drift in either direction.** Raised 2026-09-15 by the human partner, who has watched the median memory size grow over time in other memory systems, expects that growth to degrade the embedding, and sees a risk in the opposite trend as well. **Nothing governs length today.** [memory-data-model.md](documents/design/memory-data-model.md) defines a memory as *a chunk of information small enough that the vector database can properly express its embeddings*, and nothing measures or enforces it: no served convention names length, `split-when-partly-stale` explicitly declines a rule against bundling at write time, and the only bound is `model2vec-rs`'s hardcoded 512-token cut in `encode`, which silently drops the tail of `embedding_input` — keywords first, since `src/embedding.rs` appends them last. **Both directions plausibly cost something, neither measured for retrieval.** Longer: a mean-pooled vector averages over more tokens, and past the cut loses its tail; recall also returns whole records into context. Shorter: a vector built from few tokens leans on its keywords, and a record can stop standing alone (`memories-must-stand-alone`). **Open:** whether to track size at all, what would count as drift (a ceiling, a band, a trend over time), and where a response belongs — a convention, a store-time note, a measurement in `hoard_sets status`. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `memory-size-drift`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Restoring from the checkpoint, before starting the link-key collision test; the human partner asked whether any convention manages memory sizes, having seen median size drift upward in other memory systems.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. Filed as a question rather than backlog because work cannot start until someone chooses what drift means and which layer answers it — measuring, advising, or bounding are different designs, and the choice between them is the open part.

**Why both directions are in one question.** The two risks share every candidate response: whatever measures growth measures shrinkage, and a band is one decision where a ceiling and a floor filed separately would be settled without reference to each other. The shrinking direction already has a live instance in this project — `EARLY-VALIDATION.md` watches whether rewritten `context` guidance produces contexts that are merely shorter — so it is not hypothetical.

**Why now, before Scatterhoard has seen drift of its own.** The measurement filed alongside suggests it already has: a baseline taken now is cheap, and one reconstructed later from `created_at` cannot separate drift from a batch migration, which is exactly what confounds the September figures.

content: One of four mutations survives and is recorded with its reason: the two resolution guards are belt and braces, and on the current code the `incoming` condition alone holds — reverting the `edges` guard leaves the foreign id entering `replaced`, but `incoming` then matches nothing and a store holds no links for an id it does not hold, so the chain resolves `Current`. **No test can separate them without removing the other guard.** The `edges` guard is kept because it states the rule at the layer the rule is about, and because it is what still holds if `incoming` is ever widened to answer a legitimate cross-set question — which reporting the edge will need. **The reporting half followed the same day**: ignoring the edge protects the reader, and naming it is what lets a session judge the dispute, so a hit now carries `disputed_by` — the claimant's set, id and label, and nothing that would let a rival put words in front of a reader.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A deliberately redundant guard, with the argument for keeping a line no test can prove: it states the rule where the rule lives, and it is the one that survives a future widening of its partner.

content: **`hoard_sets status` says nothing about calibration: neither a set's floor nor that a set is ready for one.** Noticed 2026-09-17, two halves of one missing report. **The floor**: `Store::floor` reads it, but the only tools that surface it are `calibrate`, which sets one, and `uncalibrate`, which names the previous value while removing it — so both ways of asking change the answer, and establishing that no set here had a floor took three direct database reads. **Readiness**: calibration sets nothing until `LABELS_PER_CALIBRATION` (20) labelled queries have arrived since the last one, and nothing tells a session or a human when a set has passed that. Measured the same day: `scatterhoard` held **26** labelled queries and no floor, having gone past the threshold unnoticed; `coding-lessons` held 9 and `local` 3. **Why it matters**: a floor decides whether recall answers *nothing* for a query no memory reaches, which is the one outcome a caller cannot tell from *this set holds nothing about that* — and an uncalibrated set silently forgoes that, while a set calibrated too high silently loses answers. **Built when** `status` carries each set's floor, absent where none is set, and how many labelled queries have accrued since the last calibration, with a test. The precedent for prompting is `owed_description`, which is reported at every session start until the set is next exported.
context: Designing evaluation mode; the human partner noticed nothing prompts that calibration is available.
why: Supersedes the entry filed earlier the same day, which covered the floor alone. The human partner pointed out the other half — that nothing prompts when calibration becomes available — and the two are one field in one report, so one entry is likelier to be fixed correctly than two filed hours apart. The counts are stated as *labelled* queries deliberately: an earlier message in the same session quoted total logged queries (36, 29, 25) while discussing the threshold, and that read as three sets being ready when only one was.

content: The 2026-08-24/25 convention tuning ran as a chain in which each repair exposed the next defect, and none was visible until the one above it was fixed. Order: `capture-before-ending`'s trigger was suspected and cleared by measurement — it fired three times on the day the fact was lost; `store-when`'s enumeration was suspected and only half-guilty, since `coding-lessons` is full of method under the same rule; the set charter turned out to be the operative filter; cutting the enumeration then exposed that `learn` excluded what a session decides; that exposed `correct-when` having no trigger at all, since an invalidation produces no write; and applying the new charter rule to the two live charters exposed that the rule condemned the charter that works.
context: Recorded 2026-08-25 at the human partner's request, from the session that made all four convention edits. The decisions themselves are in documents/design/conventions.md under the 2026-08-24 resolved section; this is the sequence, which that section does not carry.
why: Worth keeping because the shape argues against the way this work is naturally planned. Each layer looked like the whole problem while it was the current one, and every stopping point would have shipped a fix aimed at the wrong layer — the trigger patch, the sixth enumeration item, the charter rule as first drafted. What kept it moving was measuring the suspected cause before repairing it, twice finding the suspect innocent. The last step is the cheapest general lesson in it: a rule drafted from the failing case alone overshot, and the passing case had been in hand the whole time.

content: **`recall-is-latin-script-only` is fully built and marked fixed, as of 2026-10-04.** The last part was model recommendations. A `hoard-fit-model` memory must link to the set's hub when written, and is found by that link. `hoard_sets status` lists them as `recommended_models` whatever the scores and with no model loaded, and the band note for a language below 7 names the ones tagged for it or untagged. Still only proposed in the design: the write-door note, script histograms, and calibration probes in a declared language.
context: Finishing the declared-language check: built-in scores and bands, then a set's own sentences, then model recommendations, in three commits on 2026-10-04.
why: Replaces the in-progress note that said recommendations were missing, which would otherwise keep telling a later session there was work left on this issue.

content: **`off-corpus` is not one class, and that is why the verdicts swung.** Measured 2026-09-08 on the live union of 871 memories, live composition, raw cosine, three classes of twelve. Answerable in-domain: median **0.542**, min 0.448. Off-corpus **rule-shaped** — questions about how a formal rule system adjudicates a case, in another domain (offside, castling, hearsay exceptions, when a lease renews): median **0.421**, max 0.503. Off-corpus **substance-shaped** — physical objects and materials (sourdough, fertiliser, descaling, cast iron): median **0.138**, max 0.260. **The gap between the two off-corpus subclasses, 0.283, is more than twice the gap between in-domain and rule-shaped off-corpus, 0.122.** Three of twelve rule-shaped queries reach the worst answerable query; zero of twelve substance-shaped do. **The clean separation of the substance-shaped class did not survive a larger probe set**: at thirty probes, *why does bread go stale faster in the fridge* scores **0.476**, above the worst answerable query, on the strength of one term of art — see the lexical-collision finding. So the subclass split is real and large, but *substance-shaped separates perfectly* was a twelve-query result and is withdrawn. Re-run `probe_whether_the_form_of_a_question_decides_its_score` in `tests/probes.rs`.
context: Following up the human partner's observation that the recommendations, not just the numbers, swung between measurement setups — and that such sensitivity usually means we are looking in the wrong place.
why:
This is the mechanism behind the observation that the day's assessments of whole mechanisms shifted wildly between setups. A bimodal population sampled at n=6 or n=12 does not merely give wide error bars: it hands you one mode or the other, and each mode supports a different conclusion with apparent confidence. Every pilot on this entry drew its off-corpus queries without knowing the class had two halves, so the verdict was decided by how many rule-shaped questions happened to be in the set.

Amended within the hour of being written, before export, because a thirty-probe set falsified its strongest claim. That is worth keeping visible rather than tidying away: the claim *substance-shaped separates perfectly* was drawn from twelve queries, in the same session that recorded the bar of forty and the lesson that small sets manufacture separation. Documenting a failure mode does not stop you committing it, and the correction arrived only because the probe set was enlarged for an unrelated reason.

What survives is the subclass split itself, which is far too large to be sampling noise. What does not survive is any claim that either subclass is cleanly separable — there are at least three ways an unanswerable query scores high, and question form is only one of them.

Recorded at 0.85: one corpus, one model, and the exact thresholds are not portable.

content: Found 2026-08-31 while working out how a set UUID could be added without making existing files unreadable, read from the code rather than from a client: `check_version` compares `major_of(found)` against `major_of(FORMAT_VERSION)`, and `major_of` is `version.split('.').next()?.parse()` — the first dot-component. Every version this project has ever written begins `0.`, so every 0.x file passed the check against every 0.x build. The version number in the header was decoration: it recorded what wrote the file and refused nothing. Defensible while nothing incompatible had shipped, and `0.2.0` documents the one asymmetry it already produced — a new build reads an old file because `MemoryId::parse` still accepts the hex spelling, while an old build meeting a new file *"fails at the first id with a malformed-id error rather than at the version check, since minor versions are not gated."*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery and the mechanism, named where it can be checked. The existing comment is quoted because it shows the cost was known and accepted rather than missed — which is what makes the next paragraph's argument a change of circumstance rather than a correction.

content: **`mutate.py --stale` does not report a mutation whose `find` text matches its file more than once**, and the runner applies a mutation at the first match — so new code repeating an anchor's text silently retargets the mutation, and nothing short of a full pass notices. Decided 2026-09-14 by the human partner, after the first full pass in some time found `store: treat a cross-set supersession as resolved` retargeted onto `check_one_live_charter`, added by `acdc242` a session earlier (repaired in `7a11f7d`). The general form is the `coding-lessons` lesson on anchoring from 2026-08-25, which says a staleness check cannot catch it; this entry is that check. **Missing:** the count. `--stale` in `scripts/mutate.py` asks only whether `find` is `in` the file. **Built looks like:** `--stale` reports every mutation whose `find` occurs more than once, beside those that no longer match, and exits non-zero on either; and the **six already ambiguous** are resolved — at filing, `store: skip the write-time cycle check` (2), `store: drop the reverse index` (2, recorded `survives`), `bases migration: fire on every store, not only a faulty one` (4), `disputes: ask the memory's own store for claims against it` (2, recorded `survives`), `restore: save over the very file being restored from` (2, `src/mcp.rs`) and `embed: give identity records vectors like any other memory` (2). **To settle while building:** whether any of the six means the first match, and whether each survivor's recorded reason still describes the code its mutation actually lands on. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `ambiguous-anchor-check`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Running the full mutation pass before committing the prohibited-data scan subcommand, which found two mutations that no longer compiled. Same stretch: the export refusal and the reserved-keyword block-list.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness. Ready: the check is a count beside an existing membership test, and the six current cases are listed so the check's first run is not a surprise.

**Why the six are part of built rather than a follow-up.** A check that fails on its first run gets its exit status ignored or its condition weakened, and either undoes it. All six behaved as recorded in the full pass of 2026-09-14, but that proves only that each lands on *a* match, not the one it was written for.

**Why the two survivors matter most.** A mutation applied to the wrong copy survives there, so its written reason can describe code it never touched — and the copy it was meant for goes untested with nothing marking it. That is the masked half of the lesson this entry acts on.

**Why a tool and not the lesson alone.** The lesson has existed since 2026-08-25 and says to re-run existing mutations when adding a parallel function. The retarget found today happened anyway, because the lesson depends on being recalled at the moment the parallel code is written — the same reason `reserved-keyword-block-list` moved a served rule into software.

context: Building the set-supplied part of the declared-language check: the marks and write-time checks, then scoring from a set's own sentences. Committed alongside this memory.
why: The registered `hoard-fit-model` mark makes recommendations look supported when nothing reads them. A later session could close the issue on that appearance.

content: **Decided while building it 2026-08-20, and it is the reverse of what the entry assumed: the scan refuses at `hoard_memorize` and `amend`, and only *warns* at export.** Two independent reasons, and each would be sufficient. A set can hold memories that arrived by **import**, which `imported-memories-carry-no-arrival-provenance` means the exporter cannot identify — so refusing at export would ask a caller to rewrite somebody else's record in order to unblock their own work. And **the filter gains rules over time**, so a blocking export would let an ordinary improvement to the rules close a set that exported fine the day before: the same file, unchanged, suddenly unexportable because the checker got better.
context: Migrating the prohibited-data-scan entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the decision taken while building it.
why:
Recorded because export is the intuitive place to refuse — it is the moment data leaves — and the entry itself assumed that. What makes it wrong is not the principle but two facts about this system: that a set is a shared artifact whose contents you did not all write, and that the checker is expected to improve.

The second reason generalises past this scan: any gate whose rules tighten over time and which blocks an operation on **existing** data converts every improvement into a breaking change for someone. Warning leaves the improvement free to land.

content: `genindex.py` identifies an entry's slug by position, not by anything that distinguishes it: `rows_for` takes the first keyword that is neither the section keyword, nor the status keyword, nor a facet prefix. Any fourth keyword on a head can therefore become the row's title if it happens to be listed first — a watch mark, a subject term, anything — and `--check` is satisfied either way, because the file and the memories agree on the wrong slug. Fixed when the slug is recognised rather than counted to. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `genindex-picks-the-slug-by-position`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Noticed while filing the query-density question, whose head carries `hoard-investigation` beside its slug and produced the right row only because the slug was listed first.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. `misleads` rather than `costs` because the row that results is wrong and reads as right — the slug is what checkpoints, commits and memories reference, so a row titled by a watch mark points at nothing while looking like every other row.

content: **Closed 2026-09-18 without a limit: `hoard_sets evaluate` reports what a review cost instead of capping what it may load.** The entry asked for a cap because embedding a whole file before returning could look like a hang. Measured that day, it cannot at any size this project will meet: 948 memories load in 0.63 s in release, so the failure needs a corpus around a hundred thousand memories. A record-count cap would also be wrong in the way the memory cap was — the right number depends on the machine and on whether the binary is a release or a debug build, and the build turned out to matter about nine times more than the model. **What shipped instead**: the response carries `took_ms` beside `memories`, so the cost is visible on hardware nobody here can test, and every real load adds evidence about the axis that stayed unmeasured. The probe that settled it is `probe_what_a_review_costs` in `tests/probes.rs`; the figures are in the measurement memory under `evaluation-load-size-limit`.
context: Closing the size-limit entry after timing a review load under both models. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 2 links an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.
why: Supersedes the entry as built rather than leaving it open for work the measurement showed is not needed. Recorded as a closure with its reason so that *there is no limit* reads as a decision rather than an omission — the next session to notice an uncapped embed should find this before adding one.

content: A link inside a set that names that set by a name it no longer uses, and carries the set's identity, is stored as a cross-set link, so supersession inside the set silently fails: a `supersedes` link spelled that way leaves the memory it replaces resolving `Current`, and a `superseded_by` link resolves as replaced by something out of reach, though the replacement is in the same store. Found 2026-09-14, confirmed the same day by two parked tests in `tests/cross_store.rs`. The shape is what a pre-rename copy's links take once a set is renamed and that copy is imported. The cause: `write_links` in `src/store.rs` canonicalises a link to the compact same-set form only when `LinkTarget::is_foreign_to` finds the link's set *name* equals the set's current name, while `holder_of` and `edges_into_another_set` match a set by identity. Fixed when a link carrying the holding set's own identity resolves as a same-set link whatever name it carries — both parked tests pass — including rows already stored in that shape. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-link-naming-its-own-set-by-an-old-name-is-inert`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Re-anchoring ambiguous mutations for the anchor check, after a full mutation pass. Same stretch: the prohibited-data scan subcommand and the export refusal.
why:
Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing, severity and fixed-when. Misleads rather than corrupts: nothing is lost and the links are stored as written, but a corrected memory is presented as current with no report, which is the severity `a-hand-merge-into-a-new-set-name-leaves-supersessions-inert` was filed at for the same outcome by another route.

**How it was found**, since it came out of unrelated work. Building `ambiguous-anchor-check`, the mutation `disputes: ask the memory's own store for claims against it` turned out to have been landing on the scope guard in `referenced_from_other_sets` instead of `claims_against_hit`. Removing that guard left the whole suite green, and reading why showed the name-versus-identity disagreement. A third test added then — that such a link is not reported as a reference from another set — passes, and fails with the guard removed, so that guard is reachable and now covered.

**Not the 2026-08-23 fix regressing.** `a-same-set-link-spelled-with-its-set-name-is-inert` canonicalised by name when links carried no identity; set identities came later, and nothing extended the canonicalisation to them. The fix is not decided here: it is being discussed with the human partner, and whatever is chosen has to account for rows already in stores.

content: **The surface as settled 2026-08-30, and four of its five points are about what the operation must not be.** **It takes a file or directory, not a loaded set** — reading a file whose header declares *another* set is the point, since it inverts the usual check from *this file must declare S* into *this file declares another set and I mean to take it into S*, which is intentionality expressed as an operation rather than inferred from a header. **One operation, not a composed sequence**, with `restore` as precedent: the composed alternative — `create`, `import`, `absorb`, `drop`, `export` — has two failure modes, and **the dangerous one is stopping after the absorb**, which leaves the memories duplicated across two sets under one set of ids with nothing saying you are half done; it also uses `create` as a staging area for a set you intend to discard, which the tool cannot distinguish from the real thing. **A safety copy is written first and unconditionally**, even though the save-first rule is stated for *destructive* operations and this one is additive — **the rule's purpose is reversibility rather than deletion**, and this is a bulk change that is tedious to unpick. **Id collisions refuse before anything is written**, since both sides are in hand and collapsing two distinct memories onto one id is the one thing set-scoped ids make possible and nothing else prevents. **And `absorbing` was removed from `import`** — a published-schema removal, cheap then and expensive once another client depends on it.
context: Migrating the absorb-as-supersession entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the surface it settled before building.
why:
The save-first reasoning is the transferable part: a rule written for destructive operations that is really about **reversibility** applies to any bulk change, and reading it by its stated trigger rather than its purpose would have skipped the copy here on a technicality.

The composed-sequence rejection is the other. Every step of that sequence exists and each is individually correct, so the composition looks like reuse rather than a hazard — and its failure mode is not an error but a **stable, wrong intermediate state** that nothing reports.

content: **Several evaluation sets may be open at once for comparison during a review, so the evaluation naming scheme has to tell them apart. A read-only set is normally held as a single copy.** Stated 2026-09-16 by the human partner, withdrawing the same day's *one evaluation load at a time is enough*. Their examples for read-only: documentation for a piece of software, so the LLM can help someone use it; company policies; regulations with their case law. In each, one copy is all anyone needs. A review, by contrast, may want two or more versions of one set side by side. **Consequences for [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md):** evaluation names must be unique per load and must say which copy each is, not merely that it is an evaluation copy. The single-copy expectation supports withholding when two read-only holders of one identity load with no read-write one, since that case should be rare. Comparison through separate scoped recalls needs no new tool surface, but their scores are not comparable across calls, because each call scores against the sets it searched.
context: Revising the load-modes design after the human partner questioned asking users about read-only at create, and raised several evaluation sets open at once.
why: Supersedes the one-at-a-time half of `01M2PTAY…`, which the load-modes document had built on: its evaluation section says one at a time and suggests `eval-<declared name>`, which cannot tell two copies of one set apart. The use cases are recorded because they are the evidence for both halves, and a later session judging a design against *normally one copy* needs to know what *normally* was based on.

content: **Whether a memory may inherit along a path that returns to it. Resolved 2026-08-18: it may not, and the fix landed the same day.** Raised by the traversal build and settled by the human partner -- *resolve to a distinct set at the tips, and stay at the tips while walking* -- with the loop artifact fixed straight away, since the build that asked the question was the build that introduced it. **A walk origin now inherits nothing:** not along a path back to itself, and not from another seed, because both already carry their own similarity and the walk exists to reach what content similarity did **not**. **Each memory also takes one frontier slot per hop, carrying its best score**, so a later shortcut still propagates while a duplicate can never spend the expansion budget. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `inherit-along-a-returning-path`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

Kept whole in the head rather than split, because the entry is short and every part of it is the answer: the rule, the reason, and the frontier mechanic that makes the rule enforceable are one argument. Splitting would produce a member that restates the head.

*The walk exists to reach what content similarity did not* is the durable part -- it is the criterion that decides any future question about what a traversal should and should not return, and it is why a seed inheriting from another seed is wrong rather than merely redundant.

content: Found 2026-08-21 by `write-surface-matrix` — drawing every memory field against every write endpoint and looking for the empty cells. `origin` is required on `hoard_memorize` and records *whose reasoning produced the content*, and it could not be changed afterwards by any sanctioned means: not apparatus, since [Corrections](documents/design/corrections.md) defines that set as keywords, links, context and confidence, with no `origin` property in the schema; not claim, since the claim is `content` plus `why`, and superseding a memory whose claim did not change puts two identical claims in a chain and records a belief nobody ever held differently; and named nowhere in the design, so the three-instrument rule was presented as total while this field fell between all three. **Why it is worth more than a shrug**: [The Golden Rule](documents/design/golden-rule.md) leans on this field by name — *"recording whether the human or the LLM produced a conclusion is accuracy functioning as respect. It exists so the system doesn't tell someone 'you decided X' when the model decided it."* An LLM filling this in is exactly the party most likely to get it wrong, and the error it makes — claiming `human` or `joint` for its own reasoning — is the direction that misattributes a conclusion to a person.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A gap found by enumerating fields against endpoints rather than by hitting it, and the reason it is not cosmetic: the field is load-bearing for a principle about respect, and the likely error runs in the direction that misattributes reasoning to a person.

content: **On `gemma4:12b`, the reload-after-compaction sentence made no measurable difference, because the model already reloads whenever the catalog is missing from its context.** Measured 2026-11-02 with a scratch script on `scripts/local_model.py`'s server and chat helpers, judging only the first move. A compacted session reloaded 5/5 with the old wording and 5/5 with the new. A compacted session that had carried on for a turn reloaded 10/10 under both, even though its summary said the conventions had been loaded earlier. A fresh session with the new wording still loaded first, 5/5, and a session with the catalog still in context did not reload, 0/5.
context: Going-public checklist: testing the reload-after-compaction wording before changing SETUP, AGENTS.md and the tool description.
why: Shipped anyway because it did no harm and states the intent for models that might trust a summary's "already loaded". But it means this test cannot show the sentence working: a model that skips the reload would be needed to show the gain, and none has been found. A later session should not cite this run as evidence that the sentence is what makes models reload.

content: `hoard_sets calibrate` tells the caller a floor "lowers itself if a query naming this set ever scores under it", and nothing does: `Store::set_floor` is called only by `Store::calibrate`, so a contradicting scoped query changes the level only at the next calibration. The note describes the self-lowering rule that was reversed on 2026-09-12, the day the floor shipped. Found 2026-09-24 by reading the code while splitting the floor's backlog head. Fixed when the note describes what the code does, checked by a test that reads it. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-calibrate-note-promises-a-floor-that-lowers-itself`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Splitting over-length tracking heads in step 2 of the out-link work, and checking the floor head's claim about lowering on contradiction against the code before restating it. Same session: calibrating both shared sets, which is where the note was read.
why: Head of an issue cluster. Misleads rather than costs: a session that believes the floor corrects itself has no reason to recalibrate or uncalibrate after a scoped miss, which is the one remedy `Store::uncalibrate`'s own doc comment says exists for that case. The note is at `Calibration::Set` in `src/mcp.rs`; the note under `NotEnoughEvidence` was not checked.

content: **A person's keep-out lists also govern what their memories say about anyone else, and can only make the template's lists stricter for them, never looser.** Stated 2026-10-25 by the human partner, under the Golden Rule. If they keep their own sexuality out, they keep out everyone else's too. If they are open about theirs, that does not license anyone else's, since they cannot assume the other person is open: that person may store their own, and nobody may for them. So for a sentence about someone else, the review checks the template's lists together with the person's, and the stricter list wins. The person's exceptions and always-fine values apply only to the person.
context: Reviewing the scatterhoard set before committing the built judgement gate, then asking whether the review covers what store-when says about other people. Rolled into the same set of changes rather than filed.
why: The exporter cannot consent for someone who is not there, which `export-review.md` already says. A person's own openness is a fact about them, not about the people they write about. Before this, the built review flagged every sentence about someone else without saying which detail concerned it, so the person was deciding for the absent one unaided.

content: **To settle when evaluation mode is built: whether an evaluation set's recalls should feed calibration at all.** Raised 2026-09-17 by the human partner. Calibration treats a scoped recall as a labelled signal — `Question::in_a_session(scoped, ..)` writes `scoped = 1` into the store's query log, and the floor is taken from a percentile over `WHERE used = 1 OR scoped = 1` (`src/store.rs`). **An evaluation set is searched only when its scope is named**, so every query against one carries that label, where for an ordinary set the label marks the minority of queries a session aimed deliberately. **Two doubts, both the human partner's:** whether such a query deserves the weight, given that a reviewer's queries are exploratory rather than evidence the set answered well; and whether calibration should apply to an evaluation set at all, since the set is not adopted and its store does not outlive the session. Note also that the scope label was measured as *a noisy-but-frequent signal* worth using because a percentile tolerates noise — an evaluation set makes it neither noisy nor frequent but universal, which is outside what that measurement covered.
context: Finishing read-only mode; the human partner raised calibration before moving on to signposts.
why: Filed rather than decided, at the human partner's direction, while read-only was being built. Recorded now because the interaction is invisible from either side: the calibration code says nothing about load modes, and the evaluation design says nothing about the query log, so whoever builds evaluation meets it only if something points at it. Read from the code and not measured.

content: Recall's `limit` is a window, not a result count: how far down the ranking to look for the largest gap, and a ceiling on what may come back. It replaced `DEFAULT_LIMIT = 5`, which was measured and found low -- F1 peaks at eight to ten for a fixed cut. The default is 20 rather than 30 because F1 barely moves between them while the worst case falls from 28 memories returned to 13. It shipped deliberately coupled to `already_known`: shrinking the default result set is only safe if the caller has a way to ask for what was left behind, or "give me more" re-returns the same memories alongside the new ones and spends exactly the context the smaller cut just saved.
context: Decided 2026-08-16 by the human partner and built 2026-08-18. Recorded only in the closed `graph-traversal` entry of BACKLOG.md, which is why no recall could reach it -- harvested 2026-09-02 in the pilot that established closed entries carry unstored decisions. Also in documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md under the gap rule.
why: The coupling is the part that would be lost first and re-litigated. A later change that raises the default, or that ships a tighter cut without a way to ask for the remainder, breaks a trade made on purpose -- and nothing in the code states it. The numbers are the rejected alternative with its evidence attached: a fixed cut at 5 was not merely different from a window at 20, it was measured and beaten.

content: **These seven entries must be settled before publication**; they are this memory's keywords. Gated 2026-09-23 by the human partner. Four have answers that would break something already in use if changed afterwards: the tool surface, the file format, or what an identity means. They are `set-settled-at-first-write`, `several-memory-files-per-directory`, `identity-mismatch-refusal` and `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`. Three are gated because crafted files arrive with publication: `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity`, `the-reserved-directory-accepts-the-local-set` and `data-only-rule-in-the-catalog`. Every gated question is now answered; what remains is building.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner; the last open one.
why: Superseded 2026-09-25: `claude-md-in-the-repository` was resolved (its security half is outside Scatterhoard's scope), and nothing takes its place. The documents it pointed to, `publication-facing-docs`, are timed to publication rather than gated ahead of it. Retire an item by superseding this memory without its slug.

content: What 2026-09-02 added was mostly enabling rather than new design. **State transitions became implementable**: the open question on re-entry had already reasoned that transitions should be supersessions with the current state as the chain tip, and that could not work while a keyword survived supersession — marking a seed *answered* would have left it matching *open* forever. Keyword retirement shipped the same day, so dropping a state keyword on the superseding memory now retires it, and the store call reports the drop under `keyword_delta` so a transition is visible at the moment it happens. **This is the mechanism the pipeline was waiting on.** **`hoard-watch` is the nearest sibling and its signpost-length discipline transfers directly** — measured that day, the median memory in `shared:scatterhoard` is 1,383 characters, so fifteen ordinary memories pushed at session start cost roughly 5,200 tokens, more than the whole convention catalog, while fifteen signposts of ~350 characters cost about 1,300. **Anything this pipeline pushes has to be signpost-shaped for the same reason, and the seeds written so far are not.** Budget headroom also existed that had not: the reinforcement audit put roughly 3,540 of the catalog's 9,603 reinforcement characters in the *justifying* class, removable without deleting a rule, against 1,747 free.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A design that was fully reasoned and unbuildable until an unrelated defect fix landed, plus a measured length discipline the existing seeds fail. Both are why the convention shipped when it did rather than when it was decided.

content: **The export review's mechanical pre-pass flags email addresses, home paths carrying a user name, private addresses and internal host names, phone-number shapes, never-store words and the set's own author names.** Other personal names are left to the model's *who is this about*. Exact values listed under a new *Always fine to share* section of the preferences file are not flagged by the pre-pass, and the never-store list wins over it. Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public, after deciding categories come from the person's own file.
why: Only reliable shapes are scanned, because each false positive costs a glance and too many teach the person to wave flags through. Names have no shape: a capitalised-word heuristic is noisy and blind in lowercase scripts, while author records are exact. The allow-list stops a work phone number being put to the person in every new memory. It is literal and parsed like the never-store list, so the two cannot behave differently. Scatterhoard never writes the file; the review suggests the line instead. Project-owned values, such as a repository's `noreply` address, go to the project's `config.json`.

content: **Fixed 2026-09-16: an action-dispatched tool's `action` prose never named optional arguments, so it told a flattening client that `amend` took only scope and id.** The prose is built in `src/mcp.rs` (`branch_arguments` and `BranchArguments::sentence`) from each branch's `required` list and its `one_of` alternation. Nothing else was read, so `hoard_correct`'s description said *"`amend` takes scope and id"*, and every field `amend` replaces (confidence, content, context, keywords, links, origin, why) was listed as a top-level property with nothing saying which action takes it. That prose is the only place a client that drops `oneOf` learns what each action takes. **Found** when `hoard_sets` `create` gained its first optional argument, `mode`, and the generated prose left it out. **Fixed** by naming a branch's remaining properties as optional (*"`create` takes name, and optionally mode"*). The new test `every_published_argument_is_named_in_the_action_prose` in `tests/mcp.rs` covers every tool, and a recorded mutation proves it.
context: Implementing read-only load mode: adding `mode` to create, status and the write refusals.
why: Filed after the fix rather than before, because the fix was one step of the read-only work and was finished before filing came up. Filed anyway, because a fixed defect is evidence about where defects come from. This is the same class as `oneof-tool-schemas-present-no-parameters`: the published schema was correct while the view a real client uses was incomplete. Severity `misleads`: the prose said the wrong thing outright, rather than leaving a caller to guess.

content: **In the export review a memory is cleared by a `hoard_sets` `clear` action that accepts only ids a review in the same session has shown.** Agreed provisionally on 2026-10-22 by the human partner ("probably yes"), and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. Keeping a memory out is `hoard_correct` forget. Rewording is a superseding restatement, then forgetting the original, and the restatement is reviewed like any new record. Upgrading needs no migration: memories already in the file on disk count as reviewed.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public, after deciding the review set is grouped by subject.
why: The server cannot hear the person, so it checks what it can, which is that the memory was shown to the session. That rules out a model clearing everything unseen to get an export through. Confidence is 0.85 because the agreement was provisional. A wholesale clear was considered for the first export after upgrading and is unnecessary: the file on disk already holds every earlier export. The residue is a file exported before the upgrade and never reviewed.

content: `hoard_sets export` appends the reserved directory to its own argument, so passing the memory directory rather than the project root silently wrote `.../scatterhoard_mem/scatterhoard_mem/memories.json` and reported the doubled path as success. Fixed 2026-08-20 by refusing a `directory` whose last segment is already reserved. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `export-appends-the-reserved-directory-to-its-own-argument`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **The fifth defect was found by checking an assumption rather than an arm.** Confirming that a cross-set `SUPERSEDED_BY` is self-harm meant asking what the *same-set* spelling does, and it deletes the memory from every search path: `a-superseded-by-naming-an-absent-id-hides-its-memory`, Corrupts, and reachable by an honest mistake rather than a hostile file. **What the sweep is evidence for, beyond its own findings**: two of the three arms named as *probably self-harm* were, and the value came from the arm framed as least likely and from the assumption checked along the way. That is an argument for driving a threat model exhaustively rather than by likelihood — the same argument the write-surface matrix rests on.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The sweep's meta-result: the predictions about likelihood were accurate and therefore worthless as a guide to where to look, since everything of value came from the arm judged least likely and from an assumption checked in passing.

content: **Full export review of the `scatterhoard` set, completed 2026-10-19 before first publication: every record the export committed with this marker holds has been reviewed.** The read-through covered all 1,636 records of the three memory files at `39028a5`, and every record changed since was written during the review and checked as it was made. It applied the seven flagging conditions in `documents/design/export-review.md` as committed alongside this marker, with no private-only exceptions in force, since the repository is going public. A routine review starts from the export this marker is committed with.
context: Finishing the publication review: the last decision cleared, before exporting and committing.
why: The full-review marker `export-review.md` asks for: one per set, saying what was reviewed and against which conditions. Without it, the next routine review cannot tell where full coverage ends. The decisions it records: a fresh public history; restate-then-forget for a personal detail, the hypothetical recorded as fact, the governance set's name and five pronouns; and clearing the machine details, the Sub-Q clause and the log-hash anecdote.

content: Two processes making a set's first write at the same moment can each mint it an identity, and the later one wins: `Store::mint_set_id` in `src/store.rs` reads `set_id`, then writes with `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, so the two steps are not atomic. The earlier writer's record is then canonicalised under an identity the set no longer holds. Found 2026-09-28 by reading the code while building `set-settled-at-first-write` step 1, which makes every set's first write mint — the same race existed for `local` before, and now reaches shared sets. Not reproduced. Fixed when the mint fills an absence atomically (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, then re-read) and something proves it. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `concurrent-first-writes-can-mint-two-identities`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building set-settled-at-first-write step 1 — create stops minting, first write mints, export proposes an identity — after recalibrating the scatterhoard floor (unchanged at 0.360).
why: Head of an issue cluster. Corrupts rather than misleads: a record canonicalised under a vanished identity is silently wrong, and nothing reports it. Filed rather than fixed in step 1 because the guard has no deterministic test — two connections cannot be interleaved inside `mint_set_id` from a test — and this project records untested guards as survivors with a reason rather than adding them silently. Rare: it needs two sessions on one machine making the first write into one freshly created set at once.

content: **`two-sets-can-share-an-identity` reproduced 2026-09-16, and by a different route than its head names.** The head says *create + import the same file under two names*; that is refused, because import accepts only a file declaring the scope it is imported into (`import_refuses_a_file_belonging_to_another_set` in `tests/sets.rs`). Copying a database file under another name is refused too, since a store records its scope and `Store::open_at` returns `ScopeMismatch`. **The route that works is an exported file whose declared `scope` was edited before import**: `create` a second set, import the edited file, and `adopt_set_id` displaces the identity `create` minted, because the set holds no records yet. The import reports `adopted_set_id` and both sets then answer to one identity. **A machine left in that state loads both at every start**, so the rule has to hold at load as well as at import. Both are pinned by failing tests in `tests/sets.rs`: `an_import_does_not_give_a_second_loaded_set_an_identity_already_held` and `a_server_does_not_hold_two_sets_answering_to_one_identity`.
context: Resuming after the MCP restart; applied the AGENTS.md checkpoint clause, then wrote the reproduction tests for the duplicate-identity issue.
why: A finding in the issue's cluster rather than a supersession of its head, for now: the head's opening, which is what the tracking row shows, is still right, and superseding a head moves its row to the end of the index. The head will be superseded when the fix lands, to change its status, and the corrected route goes into it then. Recorded because a session trying the head's route would find it refused and could conclude the defect is not reachable, when it is. The author-map consequence is still unexercised, so the `corrupts` severity rests on reading the code.

content:
**The authored probes were twice as far off-domain as real off-domain questions, and every benefit figure taken against them was inflated.** Measured 2026-09-09 against the first genuinely independent negative class: 317 real questions harvested from the human partner's notes on an unrelated volunteer role, filtered of proper nouns, digits, identifiers, software terms and sensitive subjects. Against `scatterhoard`, 752 memories, raw cosine:

| negative class | median top-1 | p90 |
|---|---|---|
| authored substance probes | **0.145** | 0.263 |
| real off-domain questions | **0.294** | 0.395 |

A floor at the authored p90 (0.263) silences **57/159 (35.8%)** of held-out real off-domain questions and 1/142 (0.7%) of real in-domain queries. A floor at the real p90 (0.395) silences **140/159 (88.1%)** but costs **19/142 (13.4%)** of real queries. **So the honest benefit of the floor as previously calibrated is 35.8%, not the 53% measured against my own probes.**
context: The human partner offering notes from an unrelated volunteer role as a source of real off-domain questions, after every other source on the machine had turned out to overlap.
why: It corrects a benefit figure that had been quoted as settled. The figure was inflated because the negative class was authored by me, which made it a property of the author rather than of the store. Restated 2026-10-18 during the publication review, to take a personal detail out of the context. The original was forgotten and carried three claims, now three memories, each superseding it so that links into it follow to them with their labels intact. The claims are unchanged.

content: The hold on Scatterhoard catalog edits was lifted for one pass on 2026-08-25: every entry but `recall-when` was restructured, sentence architecture only, with wording and arguments held fixed. The human partner's reason was that the behavioural measurement then running is worth more against the wording that will be kept than against wording about to be replaced, so the confound is accepted once rather than measuring, rewriting and measuring again. The whole-file read the hold was waiting on is done: the catalog is not carrying avoidable length, and three Ready conventions compete for room at most one of them can use.
context: Decided 2026-08-25 by the human partner. Checkable in the dated comment above CONVENTIONS in src/conventions/catalog.rs, which records what the pass changed and what it deliberately left.
why: Recording the reason matters more than the permission: the standing rule against re-tuning is about acting on one session's impressions of text it just wrote, and this was the second sanctioned exception in two days, each granted for a stated reason. Left unrecorded, two exceptions in two days read as the hold having quietly lapsed. This splits the original memory rather than amending it, because the budget figure it also carried turned out to be wrong while this half was not — see the memory that supersedes it alongside this one. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 1 link an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.

content: **How `scripts/recall_nudge.py` fits into Claude Code: a `PreToolUse` hook that reads the session's own transcript and answers with context, never a block.** Claude Code passes the hook a JSON payload on stdin. The script reads `tool_name` and `tool_input` to decide whether the call writes under `src/` or `tests/`: by `file_path` for the edit tools, or by a write-shaped command for Bash. It then reads `transcript_path`, a JSON-lines file of the conversation, scanning `tool_use` blocks for the last `git commit` and for any `*__hoard_recall` call with the habit's shape after it. The server is named per machine, so it matches on the tool's suffix. If none is found, it prints `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext`, which reaches the model (confirmed 2026-10-06), and a `systemMessage` for the person, which the desktop app may not show. It keeps a once-per-commit marker per `session_id` in the temp directory, logs every decision to `~/.local/state/scatterhoard/recall-nudge.log`, and exits 0 on any error so it can never fail the edit it watches. It is wired per machine in `.claude/settings.local.json` under `hooks.PreToolUse`, matcher `Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash`, by absolute path. Not part of adopting `coding-lessons` (EARLY-VALIDATION.md, 2026-10-20).
context: After reading the `coding-lessons` release-gate evidence, recording the nudge before writing a cookbook recipe for building one.
why: The script's opening comment says why it nudges on timing. Nothing recorded how it plugs into the client: which payload fields it relies on, that the transcript is the only place a session's past calls can be read, and which output a model sees as opposed to a person. A later session adapting it to another client, or building the interruption mechanism in `interruptions-that-trigger-specific-recalls`, needs exactly that. Checkable in the script.

content: The prescribed per-change recall was skipped on 2026-09-30, before fixing `a-numbered-opening-summarises-to-its-number`: the session went from the human partner's go-ahead straight to a failing test, and noticed only after the change was written. Run late, the recall returned nothing that would have changed the fix. It had been run for the previous change in the same session, which it also did not change. An observation for the `adopting-coding-lessons` gate: the habit was dropped under momentum, two changes into a session working through issues one after another.
context: Working through the open issues with the human partner: the reembed-count mutation, the survivor audit, then the numbered-opening summary fix.
why: Part 6 of the adoption guide asks for what the habit catches, and a skip is evidence about whether it is held at all. That matters as much as a catch or a miss, because a habit kept only when remembered prevents nothing reliably. One instance, recorded as observed, not generalised.

content: **The set-identity check arrived as a report here too — the third instance of that shape, read 2026-09-23.** This question's 2026-09-07 member records that `set_id` travels in the file header while `check_scope` never looks at it, so two unrelated sets named alike still pass. Since then import and export gained `identity_note`, which names both identities and states outright that the records were imported as usual; `check_scope` is unchanged. So the accidental-import case is now *reported* rather than prevented, and the binding this question asks about — where it lives, what a legitimate rename is — is untouched.
context: Auditing the open questions for closure, after the issue family met the same shape twice.
why: Three entries in one audit met the same pattern — a hazard answered by a report rather than a refusal — which is enough to call it this project's habit rather than three coincidences. Worth recording under this question specifically because its member names `check_scope` as a few lines of work, and a session acting on that should know the surrounding behaviour changed while the function did not.

content: A field-aware `git` merge driver exists: `scatterhoard merge-file BASE OURS THEIRS`, positional in `git`'s `%O %A %B` order, writing the result over `OURS` and reporting conflicts through its exit status. Built 2026-09-16. The merge is `src/merge.rs`, a pure function over three texts — the shape `reconcile` has over three checksums — so the expensive part is testable without a repository. **Policy, decided with the human partner:** a scalar one side changed takes that side's value and one both changed differently conflicts; collections are **set-merged against the base, never unioned**, so a keyword one side retired stays retired; **`modified` takes the later attribution**, because every edit moves it and treating that as a conflict would mean nothing ever merges; `created` never moves and a disagreement conflicts. A conflicted record keeps the receiving side's version so the file still parses — conflict markers would make it unreadable to every tool here, the pre-commit scan included. [`.gitattributes`](.gitattributes) ships with the repository; the driver registration is per clone and does not. **This entry is still half of a pair**: whether that registration ever reliably fires is [EARLY-VALIDATION.md](EARLY-VALIDATION.md)'s half and is untouched by this. Written up in [multi-set-sync.md](documents/design/multi-set-sync.md), *the driver, and the policy it had to settle*; contract in `tests/merge.rs` and `tests/cli.rs`; mutations under `merge` in `scripts/mutations.py`. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `git-merge-driver`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building the merge driver after the checkpoint, in the session that fixed the link key and built command-line export.
why:
Head of the backlog cluster, superseded because the entry is built. The opening sentence is the generated index row, so it says what now exists rather than what was missing. The readiness facet is dropped, as built entries carry none.

**The pair is restated in the head deliberately**, because this is the moment it is most likely to be collapsed: an entry marked built invites someone to conclude the merge driver is done, and the half that has actually failed for other people — a driver registered nowhere, producing exactly the conflicts it exists to prevent while looking installed — is the other one. Marking this built must not close that.

Verified beyond the tests: eight mutations run against the merge policy and the driver's exit status, each caught by the test written for it, which is the check that matters here because all sixteen merge tests passed on the first run and this project has a recorded history of tests that pass without testing anything.

content: Where the eight had gone, and how they were repaired, 2026-08-23. Every one was a rename or a refactor that moved the anchored line without anyone noticing, spread across an unknown span — they were already stale at the 2026-08-21 checkpoint, and three more broke during the cross-set work that day and were repaired the same day, which is what surfaced the rest. **Two changed meaning rather than location, and were re-stated rather than re-pointed**: `recall: claim semantic search works with no model` was anchored on a `semantic_search_available` field that no longer exists, and the concept it guards now lives in `searched`; `store: adopt vectors of unknown provenance instead of rebuilding them` is renamed to `store: search vectors whose provenance is unknown`, because the guard's home moved from a rebuild path to `can_search_by_meaning` — same hazard, different sentence, and the old name would have described a line that is no longer where the decision is made. **What each is caught by is worth reading once**, because it is the evidence the re-anchor was honest rather than merely applied: `stop noticing keywords when deciding which search to run` fails eight tests, `assume semantic search is available on the keyword path` fails exactly one, and a re-anchor that failed nothing would have been an entry pointed at a line no test reaches.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
