content: **Splitting the template's keep-out list into "shared sets" and "every set, including private ones" did not stop `gemma4:12b` reporting allowed details as kept out of `local`.** Tested 2026-10-23 with numbered sentences, 3 runs each. Lone memories: 0 missed, 6 false alarms. Realistic groups: 0 missed, 9 false alarms. Every false alarm was the employer or the Lisbon address in `local`, apart from one: "users build from source" read as someone else. The figures are about what they were with the exception-based carve-out. The logs are in that session's scratchpad, `split-*`.
context: Testing the export review's per-memory questions on a small model, after the template's carve-out was restructured at the human partner's request.
why: The model reports any preference item it sees mentioned, whichever list it is on. It does not carry out the step of working out which list applies to this set, the same step it failed to carry from the framing to the moment of writing. That points to taking the step away from the model: ask only which items a memory mentions, and let the server work out what each item means for the set.

content: With no model loaded, a store bound to one reported a mismatch whose note blamed *another server running with its own model*. Fixed 2026-09-30 by giving `Mismatched { loaded: None }` its own wording at both places that describe it: `describe_model_state` in `src/mcp.rs` (status) and `Store::why_unsearchable` in `src/store.rs` (a recall's per-set reason). Each names the recorded model, says no model is loaded and that nothing is lost, and points at `SCATTERHOARD_MODEL` or `model` in the data directory. The recall reason had recommended `reembed`, which with no model is refused for having nothing to rebuild with. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-missing-model-reports-as-a-mismatch`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through open issues with the human partner, after fixing the target_set refusal.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed as its fixed-when asked, with no mention of another server. The open question, a separate `ModelState` variant or only a separate note, was already answered in the code: `Mismatched.loaded`'s doc comment says None and a different model are the same state wanting different wording. So no variant, and both general arms now match `Some` so the compiler checks the split. The second site was found by reading every consumer of the state. Two tests in `tests/sets.rs` take the remedy by loading the named model and requiring the set to be current and searchable; two mutations, and the swap mutation re-anchored.

content: **Re-measured at the end of 2026-09-07, and deliberate attention moved it a long way: 31 of the day's 472 new memories carry an outbound link — 6%, against 2% when measured mid-session — and only 7 of the 31 are `supersedes`.** So discretionary edges went from **3 to 24** across the day, on the same author doing the same task, once the gap had been named. **Label variety moved further than the count did**: eight distinct labels in one day — `instance_of` 8, `supports` 5, `results_from` 4, `depends_on` 4, `related_to` 3, `motivated_by` 2, `exception_to` 1 — against a corpus history in which `related_to` carried 58 of 155 edges. **`depends_on` and `exception_to` had *zero* live uses when the 2026-09-02 audit looked**, and now have four and one.
context: Wrapping up the BACKLOG.md migration session, re-running the mid-session linking measurement.
why:
This is the ceiling rather than the fix, and the distinction matters for drafting. It shows what an author produces when linking is actively in mind, which is what a trigger has to reach without requiring the author to be thinking about linking — so 6% is the number a mechanism should aim at, not evidence that a mechanism is unnecessary.

The label spread is the more interesting half and supports the 2026-09-02 finding directly: that audit concluded the vocabulary was not too coarse, since a more specific label existed in 22 of 30 `related_to` cases and was simply not chosen. A day of attention producing eight labels including the two that had never been used is the same conclusion from the other side.

content: `absorb` internalises links to memories that did not arrive: it supersedes every current memory here that links into the absorbed set by name, and makes that link same-set, without checking the target id is now held. For a whole set every target arrives. For a file carrying part of a set, which `absorb` reads without complaint, a working cross-set link is replaced by a same-set link to an id this set lacks, dangling, and the result does not say so. In `absorb_set` in `src/mcp.rs`, the `linked` filter tests `link.target.set() == Some(&absorbed)` and the rewrite loop repeats that test. Read from the code 2026-09-26, not exercised. Fixed when only links whose target is held after the records land are internalised, and the rest keep their cross-set form. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `absorb-internalises-links-to-memories-that-did-not-arrive`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building the release gate's directory-form group. The human partner was asking how `absorb` and `evaluate` fit the `directory` and `file` forms once a directory holds several sets, and then what a partial absorb would do.
why: Head of an issue cluster. Corrupts: a sound link is exchanged for a broken one silently, under a supersession that makes the broken version the current one. Found when the human partner asked what mechanically distinguishes absorbing six memories from absorbing a whole set; the answer was nothing but this step. Worth fixing beyond the defect: with it fixed, `absorb` means "take these records into this set", which would replace the hand-appending and importing steps of the manual procedure for moving memories between sets (set-lifecycle.md, *moving memories between sets*). Choosing what moves and checking supersession chains would stay with a person.

content: **Checked 2026-09-08, after the human partner asked whether the embedder or the similarity was simply broken: it is not, on four checks — and the check that rules it out also calibrates how sharp the space actually is.** The embedder is deterministic and 512-dimensional. Re-embedding a sampled memory's text today reproduces its **stored vector at cosine 1.000000, min median and max over 40** — so no stale vectors, no model mismatch, no drift in what `embedding_input` composes. A memory's own embedded text retrieves it at **rank 1, 40 of 40**, which exercises the similarity path end to end. And on a genuinely held-out query — each memory's `context`, which the design deliberately never embeds — the memory it came from ranks at **median 24 of 709, with 24 of 60 in the top 10, against a chance median of 355**. So the vectors carry real semantics, roughly fifteenfold better than chance, and misloaded weights would have shown as chance. **Treat the median of 24 as a lower bound rather than an estimate**: `context` is an episodic anchor chosen precisely for not being semantic, so it is the hardest query the corpus can offer. Re-run `probe_whether_the_embedder_is_working` in `tests/probes.rs`.
context: Probing the gap cut, when the human partner asked whether the embedder itself might be at fault.
why: Recorded because *the gap structure is indistinguishable from noise* and *the scores are noise* are different claims, and the first invites the second as an explanation. Separating them needed a measurement rather than an argument, and the result reverses the reading: the ranking is genuinely informative and still has no boundary in it, which means relevance in this corpus is continuous rather than that scoring is broken. Kept as its own record because it is the first thing anyone will re-ask when a scoring result looks disappointing, and re-deriving it costs a session what re-running the probe costs a minute. The stored-versus-recomputed check is the one worth keeping pointed at: it is the only one of the four that would catch a corpus quietly embedded under an older composition.

content: Recipes for Scatterhoard's users live in a published set, `scatterhoard-cookbook`, taken on read-only, with a short document pointing to it. Settled 2026-09-30 by the human partner. Each recipe opens with the reader's goal or symptom, since that is how a session phrases the query, and is published only after its procedure has been run end to end. The first is moving the data directories (`SCATTERHOARD_HOME`, `SCATTERHOARD_COMMON`), plus the symptom of personal memories seeming to vanish. The tracking system and lessons-set adoption follow. Recorded in `documents/design/load-modes.md`. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `where-user-facing-recipes-live`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through the stranded-local-store issue with the human partner, after they asked whether checkpoints record memory counts and suggested a cookbook recipe instead.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded because the question is resolved, in favour of the set the 2026-09-28 head leaned towards. Prompted by `moving-the-local-store-leaves-the-old-one-unmentioned`: a server-side check could see one of four routes to a stranded `local` store. A recipe for the deliberate move, plus one phrased as the symptom, reaches every route once someone notices, and noticing is what triggers the query. Still to decide: whether the set's file lives beside `scatterhoard`'s in this repository.

content: **The export review needs a capable model, and says so plainly, rather than being reshaped to run on small ones.** Decided 2026-10-24 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. The server's safeguards stay whatever model runs it: nothing is cleared without answers, an empty `clear` is refused, an unfinished one says it is not finished, and batches fit a small window. On a small model, the pre-pass and the never-store list are what protect the person.
context: Building the export review's judgement gate, step 8, after end-to-end runs on gemma with context use measured.
why: In the human partner's words, the tool had been bent and adjusted and still gave no useful results. Across four end-to-end runs, `gemma4:12b` never answered the memories through `hoard_sets`: not with the batch capped, not with empty clears refused, not with a ready-made call. It managed only in a short prompt with a small dedicated tool. A dedicated review tool was the alternative considered and not taken.

content: Fixed 2026-08-19 by deleting the catch-all arms rather than adding a flag beside them. `Found` carries the whole `Resolution` instead of a `Vec<MemoryId>` that had to mean three things, and `Recalled`/`KeywordHit` carry `in_cycle`. On the wire `hoard_lookup` distinguishes all three states — `superseded_by`, `superseded_beyond_this_set` (which was also being silently dropped) and `supersession_cycle` — and the semantic and keyword paths carry the cycle flag too. **A memory in a cycle is returned and named rather than withheld**: dropping it would hide a memory because its apparatus is broken. The tool description now also says how to walk a chain by hand, which is what prompted the question — `superseded_by` names the end, and `incoming` carries the immediate successor's `supersedes` edge.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the principle it turns on: a memory whose apparatus is broken is still the memory, so it is returned with the breakage named rather than withheld.

content: A malformed MCP tool call can store a damaged memory silently: a mis-closed parameter absorbs everything up to the next well-formed closing tag. The bound is that well-formed close, not a count of one -- occurrence five closed both content and why badly and lost two parameters, where the first four lost exactly one each because only one tag was wrong in each. Whether it is silent depends on whether a swallowed parameter was required. Do not repair it by making why required, which trades away a decided property, nor by ordering a required parameter after content, which depends on emission order nothing controls. As of 2026-08-13 hoard_memorize remarks instead: it scans stored text for tool-call framing, names the polluted fields in suspect_markup, and lists which text fields arrived empty so the caller can compare against what it believes it sent.
context: Superseding the 2026-08-12 record after occurrence five, which corrected the mechanic and prompted building the remark the same day. Checkable at TOOL_CALL_MARKERS in src/mcp.rs and the entry in ISSUES.md.
why: The two obvious repairs are wrong for reasons invisible from the defect itself, so anyone meeting this again will propose them unless the reasoning travels with it. The count correction matters because a remedy designed around "one parameter is lost" would under-report: the swallow runs through as many malformed closes as follow. Remark rather than refuse, because the failure is in emission -- refusing would discard a memory the caller cannot reliably re-send, and it would block a legitimate memory quoting tool-call markup, of which this one is an instance. The remark is a mitigation and not a cure: the damage still happens and is still stored, and a caller that ignores the response learns nothing.

content: **Decided 2026-09-16 by the human partner: read-only loading is built before evaluation mode; a set's load mode is chosen by the caller at `create`, stored in its own database's `meta` table, and can change only by one-way promotion to read-write.** **Order:** evaluation mode becomes a special case of read-only: a read-only load whose records come from a file, under a temporary name, pulling no watch marks, searched only when named, with every hit marked as evaluation. Built the other way round, the mode policy (refusing writes, the watch pull, dropping without a safety copy, *at most one writable holder of an identity*) would be written inside evaluation mode and then pried back out. Whether an evaluation set lives in memory or in a file is not part of that duplication, since a `Store` is the same code over either connection. **Storage:** `meta` never travels, because export writes records and a header, and `Store::replace_with`, which `restore` uses, clears record tables and leaves `meta` alone (checked in `src/store.rs`). `drop` deletes the database, so the mode goes with the set. **No demotion.** Read-only is chosen at birth, so a read-only set provably has never been written here, and that is what lets it be dropped without a safety copy with no guard stored in the database being destroyed. Every case that seemed to need demotion goes another way: a distributed set is created read-only and then imported; two read-write holders of one identity are resolved by dropping one (which writes its safety copy), creating it read-only, and importing the copy. **Promotion is one-way for a second reason, the human partner's:** promoting means a session reads the set's investigation and collection memories into context, which cannot be undone either. Whether promotion is offered at all is still open. **Read-only means no session writes** (memorize, correct, forget); allowing `import` to refresh a distributed set from a newer file was proposed and not objected to. Together these replace the provisional withhold-both rule for a read-write holder beside a read-only one.
context: Planning after the duplicate-identity fix: whether evaluation mode or read-only distribution goes first, and where a load mode is stored.
why: Recorded because it reverses the order the checkpoint and the `evaluation-mode` cluster imply, where evaluation was next and read-only distribution followed it. The human partner raised the reversal after seeing that an in-memory evaluation design was accumulating special cases read-only would need again. A separate settings file was the alternative for storing the mode, and was rejected for the cost of keeping it in step with the directories and the stale entries it would leave. Demotion was raised by the assistant for two cases, setting up a distributed set and resolving a two-holder conflict; the human partner did not see a need for it, and both cases turned out to have routes without it. Dropping it is what keeps the safety-copy exception structural rather than a stored flag. The `import` point carries less weight than the rest, since it was proposed rather than stated.

content: **A set's model-fit material uses three fixed reserved marks: `hoard-fit-hub`, `hoard-fit-sentences` and `hoard-fit-model`.** Decided with the human partner on 2026-10-04. They mark the hub, a sentence-set memory and a model recommendation. They are three fixed marks, not a `hoard-fit-` family, so a mistyped `hoard-fit-` keyword is still refused. Sentence sets are marked even though the hub's links identify them, so a reviewer can tell what one is on its own and status can report a set no hub links to. They are registered in `CONTROL_MARKS` in `src/store.rs`.
context: Starting to build set-supplied test sentences and model recommendations for the declared-language check, after committing the built-in-language part as `50d7f55`.
why: The names are permanent once they appear in exported files. The shared stem tells a reader the three belong together, and "fit" matches `language_fit` and `language_scores`. A prefix family would make any `hoard-fit-` keyword writable, which is the looseness the reserved-keyword check exists to prevent.

content:
Measured 2026-09-12 across every transcript in this project: the connect-on-recall clause appears to work on the half of the behaviour it can reach, and not at all on the half it was aimed at.

Controlling for `supersedes`, which any correction carries structurally, `hoard_memorize` calls carrying a **discretionary** link went from **198 of 965 (21%) before 2026-09-09** to **77 of 88 (88%) since**. Whereas adding a link by *amending an existing memory* — going back to what you just recalled and connecting it, which is what the clause distinctly asks for — went from 14 of 78 corrections to **1 of 7**.

**Read it with its caveats.** Two days, 88 memorize calls, dominated by a handful of sessions, and one of them is the session that ran this measurement after loading the conventions at its start — so the sample includes behaviour primed by the thing being measured. It is not a trend, and 88% will shrink. The direction is large enough to be worth having; the size is not.

Re-run it by scanning `~/.claude/projects/*scatterhoard*/*.jsonl` for `hoard_memorize` and `hoard_correct` tool calls, splitting on the timestamp and on whether a link's label is `supersedes`.
context: Building the query log's `used` label, when the human partner went looking for convention language they remembered adding and could not find.
why:
The human partner asked whether that language was effective, which is a question nothing in the project was set up to answer, and it turned out to be one scan of the transcripts. Recorded at 0.75 because the effect is large and the sample is two days: what should survive is the shape of the finding and the way to re-run it, not the percentage.

The negative half is the more useful one. The clause was added to feed a walk starved of edges, and links written onto *new* memories do feed it — but the memories already in the corpus stay isolated unless someone goes back, and that is the part that has not started happening.

content: **Without the driver registered, merging two branches that both exported conflicts twice, and the summary is only one of the two.** Reproduced 2026-09-21 with `git merge-file` on real exports. The files were `HEAD~1`'s `memories.json` as base, `34705fb`'s (eight memories added) as ours, and base plus one contributor memory with one cluster size moved as theirs. Result: two conflicts. One is the header line. The other is the **end of the file**: records are written in id order and ids are time-ordered, so memories added concurrently on two branches are insertions at the same point. Neither goes away if the header drops its summary. The same three files through `scatterhoard merge-file` exit 0: the contributor's record is kept and the header is ours verbatim. No code, and nothing in `SETUP.md`, registers the driver.
context: Reviewing what would stop other people using Scatterhoard ahead of release, starting from the human partner's suspicion that this question could cause a conflict after every merge. Straight after fixing genindex.py's slug pick and renaming the one `hoard-` slug.
why: The question was framed around the header alone. The tail conflict means removing or regenerating the summary would still leave an unregistered clone conflicting on every merge where both sides added memories, which is the ordinary case for two collaborators. A conflicted file does not parse either, so no Scatterhoard tool can read it until someone resolves it by hand.

content: A supersession cycle read as current: `Store::resolve_supersession` detected it and returned `Resolution::Cycle`, and **both callers discarded it** through catch-all match arms, so `lookup` reported `superseded_by: []` — byte-identical to a memory nothing supersedes. Fixed 2026-08-19 by deleting the catch-alls. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-supersession-cycle-reads-as-current`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **Both repositories have had a GitHub remote since 2026-10-04, and both are private.** They are `github.com/jtcours/scatterhoard` and `github.com/jtcours/coding-lessons`, shared with invited beta testers rather than published. Verify with `git remote -v`, and with `gh repo view <repo> --json visibility`. Making them public is a separate decision, still gated on `release-gate`. Its remaining entry, `adopting-coding-lessons`, waits on evidence from use that the human partner judges sufficient. Pushing now shares the sets with testers, so what a set holds still matters at every push, but it is no longer a one-way publication to the world.
context: Adding the first git remotes for the beta release, after rewriting the author address out of both histories and installing the GitHub CLI to authenticate the push.
why: Supersedes the no-remote signpost, which said to retire it once a remote existed and not to treat its absence as an oversight. The signpost mark is left off because the condition it guarded is over. What replaces it is a fact a later session can check: the repositories are private, and going public is still the human partner's call.

content: **Real in-domain queries and real off-domain questions separate at AUC 0.957, so the floor's mechanism works and its calibration method is what fails.** Measured 2026-09-09 against `scatterhoard`, 752 memories, raw cosine: 142 real in-domain queries against 317 real questions from an unrelated domain. `p90 of a probe set` inherits whatever distance that probe set happens to have, which is a property of whoever wrote it rather than of the store. **The design consequence:** both floors measured that day are points on one tradeoff curve, and neither was chosen, since each sat wherever a probe set's p90 fell. A better operating point exists, and the way to find it is to calibrate from the **answerable** side. A store has its own query history and can estimate where its real queries land, but it can never have a representative sample of the questions it will not be asked.
context: The human partner offering notes from an unrelated volunteer role as a source of real off-domain questions, after every other source on the machine had turned out to overlap.
why: It was the strongest separation result on the entry, and it was invisible while the negative class was either authored or drawn from a store sharing rule-shaped structure. The consequence inverted the calibration design and took the probe set off the shipping path, the component that had failed twice. Split out on 2026-10-18 from a memory restated during the publication review. The claim is unchanged.

content: **An item written inside a comment in the sharing preferences is reported, unless it is one of the template's own examples**, accepting that dash-style comments (` - ` carried down each line) are reported too. Decided 2026-10-31 by the human partner: a note a person does not need costs less than a never-store word added under the template's commented example that never took effect. The template's own rule follows: inside a comment, a marker appears only on a line meant to be copied, after its *An example* line. Checked by `the_template_marks_only_its_examples` in `tests/sharing_preferences.rs`.
context: Fixing the dropped bare-line issue in the preferences file, after restoring from the 2026-10-30 checkpoint and restarting the server.
why: Reporting lines inside comments looks like noise a later session might remove to quiet dash-style comments. The cost was weighed and accepted on purpose, and the template rule exists so a person can tell decoration from the shape to copy -- the human partner raised the dash-style comment convention as the hazard.

content: How many memories a recall returns is decided by the `limit` it was given rather than by the query: the same question answers with 2 memories at `limit: 17` and 17 at `limit: 18`, because the cut takes the largest gap *within the window* and a deeper gap of `0.0080` displaces the one at `0.0076` that had been winning. The live default of 20 sits past that flip. This contradicts what `Question::window` documents about itself — *not a result count… a query with two good answers returns two*. Fixed when the answer to a query does not change with the budget it was asked under. **The behaviour looks glitchy and is not**: the ranking either side of the flip is identical — the first five combined scores match to four decimals at both windows — so what moves is the cut alone, and the arithmetic of the largest-gap rule accounts for it completely. Nothing is left over that a deeper fault would be needed to explain. The findings behind this carry the keyword `no-non-match-floor`, which this entry was split out of; this record carries only its standing.
context: Splitting the non-match entry after the human partner questioned whether a smooth roll-off is a defect at all.
why:
Split from `no-non-match-floor` on 2026-09-08, which bundled two failures that are different in kind: how many results to return, and whether any of them are relevant. This is the first, and it is the one that needs no position on what relevance means — a query whose answer changes with the budget is inconsistent on the code's own documented terms, whatever one thinks about smooth roll-offs.

Amended the same day. The human partner's first reading was that a jump from 2 to 17 looks like a bug buried deeper than the cut rule, possibly shared with `an-unanswerable-query-returns-confident-hits`; that is recorded here as answered rather than dropped, because it is the natural suspicion and re-checking it costs a session an afternoon. The ranking's stability across the flip is the evidence.

The old entry's framing, *find the threshold that separates matches from non-matches*, is retired rather than inherited. It was a correct implementation of a wrong question: the ranking rolls off smoothly because relevance in a single-subject corpus is continuous, and no boundary exists to be found. That reading cost roughly a month, so it is stated here to stop it being re-derived.

content: An abnormal outcome returned in the shape of a normal one cannot be told apart from success, so it is acted on as success. In this project: an export written to a doubled path and reported done, memories stored with no vector and no warning, a supersession cycle reporting `superseded_by: []` — byte-identical to nothing superseding it — because both callers discarded `Resolution::Cycle` through catch-all arms, damaged tool calls stored whole, a missing merge driver leaving a file that reads as resolved, and a moved store indistinguishable from an empty one. **The structural fix is to give every distinct outcome a distinct shape** — an enum variant with no catch-all, a note naming what happened — so the caller has something to branch on. The project's *report, not refuse* designs are this fix where refusing would cost more than it saves.
context: Re-deriving the common causes of defects across all 104 issues, and moving them from a hand-written section of TRACKING.md into memories the index is generated from. Linked to its general form on 2026-09-24, alongside calibrating both shared sets.
why: Not in the original analysis, which saw nine issues; it surfaced across the 95 filed since. Its general form went to `coding-lessons` on 2026-09-24, kept distinct from the lesson that absence of a failure signal is not evidence of success, which is about checks rather than outcomes. Some of its instances plainly fit another cause as well; this attribution names the one a fix would have to address. Superseded only to add the `instance_of` link to that general form.

content: **A before-writing sentence reconstructed after a failure tends to describe the failure, not the change, so replaying it flatters ranked recall.** Seen 2026-10-05 while gathering cases for the `gut-feeling-recall` headroom measurement. On 2026-10-04 the reconstruction for a commit that left most of its change out read "staging files for a commit with a pathspec left most of the changes out of the commit". The genuine sentence from before that commit read "commit the language-fit work, staging the new module and its tests". The first shares its words with the lesson it is checked against, and the second does not. So a replay should take queries that flightlog shows were made before the change, and treat reconstructions as a separate, optimistic tier. This bears on part 2 of the `coding-lessons` adoption guide, whose "would the habit have caught it" check uses reconstructions.
context: Gathering cases for the gut-feeling-recall headroom measurement, the morning after the first beta, after fixing the read-only create note.
why: Any measurement of recall built on reconstructed sentences overstates how often the governing memory ranks in the top five. That would understate the headroom a broader signal could fill, the opposite error from the one the first replay's TF-IDF confound risked. One pair of sentences is the evidence, and that it is the general tendency is inferred, hence 0.6. Flightlog search, `tool_name` `mcp__scatterhoard__hoard_recall` from 2026-09-28, shows both sentences.

content: Fixed 2026-08-15 in `0e69123` and marked closed 2026-08-16 on finding the code had moved and the entry had not. `MemoryView` carries `incoming` on all three retrieval paths, unfiltered by label and on by default, with `IncomingEdge` living on the store's retrieval types rather than on `Memory` so that export stays **structurally unable** to carry a derived reverse. Verified against a live client. *This is the defect class the project keeps filing, in its own tracking file: the fix landed, the entry did not move, and anyone reading there would have concluded that `CONTRADICTS` still had an unmet precondition.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, with the placement decision that matters: putting `IncomingEdge` on the retrieval type rather than on `Memory` means a derived reverse cannot reach the export by accident. Kept together with the tracker lag, which is the recurring failure this project files most.

content: **Model recommendations are always listed in `hoard_sets status` as `recommended_models`, and are named in the band note when they bear on a low score.** Decided with the human partner on 2026-10-04. Each entry gives the recommendation's id, its summary line, and its language tags. When a language scores below 7, its note names the recommendations tagged for that language, plus any untagged ones. Recall does not repeat them. The server never parses a model name out of the prose, so a recommendation's opening sentence must name the model. A `hoard-fit-model` memory is refused when written unless it links to the set's hub, because that link is the only way the server finds it.
context: Building step 3 of the set-supplied part of the declared-language check, after committing the marks, the write-time checks and scoring from a set's own sentences as `b2bcf47`.
why: A recommendation is something a set's authors want passed along. A human setting up a new machine needs it before anything goes wrong, not only after a low score. Naming it in the band note turns a warning into a next step. On recall it would add length to every query without changing how the results read.

content:
**`CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0` is the obvious fix for a silting build directory and it is worse than the disease.** Measured 2026-09-20 on identical work — the same 88 mutations, from a directory cleared before each run: **535s with incremental compilation off, 340s with it on.** A 36% penalty.

It does stop the silt exactly. A rebuild adds 512 `.rcgu.o` codegen units with it on and none with it off, flat over four cycles, so the reasoning that leads to it is sound as far as it goes. What it misses is that a mutation pass is almost entirely rebuilds: a cold build costs about 1.7s more than a warm one, every mutation pays that, and it swamps the launch penalty the files cause.

**The silt does not bite as early as the accrual rate suggests.** Over those 88 mutations the directory went from empty to 45,000 files with no degradation in pace — 4.55s over the first eighth, which is the from-scratch build, then 2.6s to 3.6s with no upward trend. So there is room to let it accumulate and then clear, which is what shipped.

Recorded because the argument for turning it off is clean and wrong, and a later session will reconstruct it: each mutation is reverted immediately, so nothing can reuse the incremental state, so the state is pure cost. Every step of that is true and the conclusion still does not follow, because what incremental compilation saves is not reuse across mutations but reuse within one build.
context: Testing three ways to keep a mutation pass fast, after the human partner suggested clearing the directory periodically instead.
why: Kept as its own memory rather than a paragraph of the silting record, because it is the claim a later session most needs to find on its own terms — searching *should I turn off incremental compilation* should reach the measurement, not a record about directory sizes that happens to mention it. Splitting it out was prompted by the 2000-character refusal firing on the amendment that tried to bundle it, which is the convention working on its author.

content: Keyword recall ignored `already_known`, so ids a caller said it held came back anyway. Fixed 2026-09-29: the keyword branch in `src/mcp.rs` passes the held ids to `search_keywords_across_holding` in `src/store.rs`. That asks each store for `limit` plus the number held, leaves them out after substitution, then cuts, so the next page is still full. Pinned by `already_known_memories_are_left_out_of_a_keyword_recall` and `leaving_out_known_memories_still_fills_a_keyword_page` in `tests/mcp.rs`, and by three mutations. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `keyword-recall-ignores-already-known`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Taking the contained misleads-severity issues after the served-text indentation fix.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed by the first route the old head named, making the keyword path honour it rather than narrowing the schema. The over-fetch matters as much as the exclusion. Each store is cut to `limit` before the merge, so leaving held ids out afterwards returns a short page that reads as the end. A test and a mutation pin that separately.

content: **How to inspect a memory set without adopting it.** Raised 2026-08-26 by the human partner, from a maintainer reviewing a contributor's branch: import is adoption, and checking the branch back out does not undo it. **Designed 2026-09-16 in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md) as a special case of read-only, which was built on 2026-09-17.** Settled: an evaluation load comes from a file, once, through a `hoard_sets` action with no `create` step. Several can be open at once for comparison. Each is named `eval-<set>-<label>`, with the label chosen by the user, and `SetName::new` refuses the `eval-` prefix so no real set can carry it. It is searched only when its scope is named. Every memory it returns carries a field taken from the load mode, not parsed from the name, and the response carries a note explaining it. It pulls no watch marks, drops without a safety copy, and lives in memory. **Still open, and to be settled before building:** what a cross-set link does when an evaluation copy is a possible target, which turns largely on whether evaluation stores sit among the ordinary stores, since `hoard_lookup` resolves against all of those; and whether an evaluation set's recalls should feed floor calibration, since naming the scope is the only way to search one and a scoped recall is what calibration treats as a labelled signal. **Also open:** the size limit, and whether a returned memory carries its set's identity. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `evaluation-mode`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Finishing read-only mode; the human partner raised calibration before moving on to signposts.
why: Supersedes the head to add the calibration interaction the human partner raised on 2026-09-17, which belongs with the cross-set link question as something to settle before building rather than during. Also updates the read-only clause, since read-only is now built rather than merely designed.

content: Corrected twice the same day, and the second correction retracts the first. **First**: the human partner asked whether it could be how the servers are configured into the client, and it was — a fourth entry byte-identical apart from its name, added to the project `.mcp.json`, arrived with `scope`'s `oneOf` complete and accepted the object form where the original refused the identical call. The paragraph then blamed the *duplicate declaration*, on the reasoning that every server arriving intact was one whose name nothing else claimed. **That was a confound and the human partner called for isolating it**: every Desktop-declared server was also a collided one, so the two explanations fit the same evidence. A fifth server was added to the Desktop config only — a name the project does not claim — completing the grid, and it was reduced too. **Correlation with the Desktop declaration is perfect; with the collision it is zero.** A server declared in `claude_desktop_config.json` has every alternation stripped — `scope` on four tools, `links.items.properties.target` on two, `context` on one — and the duplicate name is irrelevant.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A confounded diagnosis isolated by completing the two-by-two grid rather than by arguing. Worth keeping because the first explanation fitted every observation available at the time and was still wrong.

content: Unify [ISSUES.md](ISSUES.md), [BACKLOG.md](BACKLOG.md) and [open-questions.md](documents/design/open-questions.md) into one file with a section per record type. Scope: per-type section tags, `genindex.py` taught to generate into each section, and the cluster-shaping guidance moved out of STANDARDS.md into the unified file. Blocked until the open-questions migration finishes, so the last 40 entries are not migrated into a file being restructured underneath them. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `unify-the-tracking-files`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Splitting CLAUDE.md into AGENTS.md, and writing the cluster-shaping guidance into STANDARDS.md, the evening after the BACKLOG.md migration finished.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. The opening sentence is the generated index row. Decided 2026-09-07 by the human partner as a deliberate deferral rather than an open question -- the *what* is settled and only the *when* was in doubt, which is what makes it a backlog item and not a question.

content: **An unresolved concern raised 2026-08-23 and deliberately left for the build to decide: a memory naming a cross-set successor removes itself from recall.** A chain that is superseded-but-unresolved resolves the holder to `Unreachable` — and the cross-set arm produces exactly that, since `LinkTarget::CrossSet { .. } => None` sets `unresolved` and leaves `superseded` true. **This fires when the successor's set is simply not loaded on this machine, which is the ordinary case rather than an exotic one.** It is self-inflicted rather than an attack, and it is the one place where *report rather than resolve* is not being applied: the honest answer looks more like returning the memory with a note that it has yielded to an id in another set, and letting the session decide, than like silently withdrawing it.
context: Migrating the edge-authority-across-sets entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the concern it flagged for whoever builds next.
why:
Recorded because it reads as correct behaviour from every angle except the one that matters. The memory *has* been superseded, the successor *is* unavailable, and withholding it is the conservative-looking choice — so nothing about the code invites a second look, and the symptom is a memory that quietly does not appear, which is the hardest failure in this system to notice.

It is also a live exception to a principle the project has arrived at from five independent directions, which makes it worth flagging rather than inheriting: everywhere else, an unresolvable situation is reported and left to the caller.

content: The schema stripped the field the refusal existed to catch: `amend` refused `content` and `why` with a message naming supersession, and `hoard_correct`'s published schema did not declare either — so a validating client dropped them, and the server answered with the unrelated *this amendment would change nothing* refusal. Fixed 2026-08-30 by dissolving the refusal rather than declaring it. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `amending-a-claim-is-refused-where-no-client-can-reach-it`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: The export review flagged the person's own published name in their own set. The pre-pass scans the set's author names so that a collaborator named in a memory's text is caught, and `Store::author_names` returned every identity record's name, the reviewing person's included; the served task gave the model no reason to read that name as anything but a mention of "my user names". Found 2026-10-29 on the `scatterhoard` set's full review, where every memory on the first page went to the person for `jtcours`. Fixed the same day: the pre-pass uses `Store::others_author_names`, which leaves out `Store::published_name`, the tip of the set's own author record; the first page serves that name as `published_as`, and the task says it alone mentions nothing. Past names and other authors are still flagged. Two tests in `tests/export_review.rs`, one in `tests/store.rs`, four mutations caught.
context: The scatterhoard set's full review, paused on its first page after the timestamp fix to settle and build this exception.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseding the open head now that the fix is built and tested. Costs: this project's memories cite `github.com/jtcours/...` throughout, so most flags would have been the person's own chosen name. The served task text was not tried on a small local model before shipping, though AGENTS.md suggests it; the review now recommends a capable model.

content: **The never-store word list was first written with `to_lowercase`, beside the `toNFKC_Casefold` that `Keyword::folded` in `src/memory/text.rs` already uses**, which is the `folding-is-lowercase-not-casefold` defect over again. Found 2026-10-22 before the list was committed, while adding full-width folding for Chinese users. Fixed by folding the list through the same function. The habit's recall before writing the list did not surface the earlier fix, so a trigger now exists in `coding-lessons`.
context: Building the sharing preferences' never-store list: adding full-width folding, optional spacing beside Chinese, and a Chinese example to the template.
why: EARLY-VALIDATION's `coding-lessons` entry asks for what the habit catches, and for what it misses. This is a miss: the lesson lived only as a fixed issue in this set, in words a recall about a word list did not reach.

content: **What earns a member slot is irreproducibility, agreed by the human partner 2026-09-07.** The depth rule caps how many members an entry gets — head plus one or two unless the entry corrects itself across dates — but it does not say *which* content fills them, and the criterion in use is: can this be re-derived later to answer the same question? Measurements usually cannot. The 120-character cap was measured against a 192-memory corpus that has since more than doubled; the 1,383-character median dated 2026-09-02 describes a population that no longer exists; the 411-character envelope was measured against a convention since rewritten. Re-running any of them today answers a different question. Outcomes are the opposite case — usually still visible in the code, the served text or a design document — which is why they survive without help and evidence does not. **Intended to fold into whatever change makes measurements and paths-to-a-conclusion get stored on an ongoing basis**, rather than remaining a migration-only habit.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md, after noticing that the criterion being used to choose members was not the one the depth decision records.
why:
Recorded because it is a criterion actually governing thirty-seven remaining migrations while not being the recorded rule, and an undocumented working criterion is how two sessions end up disagreeing about what a completed migration should contain.

It also sharpens the investigation it is filed under. *Record the method as well as the conclusion* is the broad version and is hard to act on, because almost everything has a method. **Irreproducibility is checkable at the moment of writing**: ask whether running this again next month answers the same question, and if not, it has to be written down now. That is a test an author can apply, where *is this a method or a conclusion* is a category judgement — and naming categories is precisely what the 2026-08-24 resolution found had rebuilt a whitelist and suppressed the intake in the first place.

content: This set holds knowledge about Scatterhoard itself: design decisions and what they rule out, measurements of how the system actually behaves, defects and the causes behind them, and constraints found while building it. A memory belongs here when it would still matter to someone working on Scatterhoard in a later session and would not matter to someone working on a different project. A lesson that would hold anywhere belongs elsewhere, even when Scatterhoard is where it was learned, though the Scatterhoard evidence for such a lesson does belong here.
context: Written 2026-08-12 while moving misfiled project memories out of the personal set, as the first use of the route-where convention.
why: Routing needs each set to say what it is for, so the rule can live in the sets rather than being compiled into the convention catalog as one user's taxonomy. This description was derived by sorting the 26 memories that had accumulated in the personal set: what the project-specific ones had in common, once separated, is what this set turns out to be about.

content: **The 30 open questions were audited on 2026-09-23 and one closed: `charter-recall-shape`.** Seven were checked against the code or the served catalog — this memory's keywords name them — and all seven stay open with their premises intact. The remaining 22 were read at their index rows and checked only for a shipped answer, which is a weaker pass than the issues got: a question goes stale through its premise moving rather than through code, and a row carries the claim but not the reasoning under it. Anything filed under those 22 today rests on that lighter reading.
context: The closure audit, continuing into the question family after the 18 issues were done.
why: Recorded with its own method stated, because a sweep that does not say how deep it went invites the next session to treat 22 row-level reads as verified. The one closure came from reading the served text against a head, which is exactly what the 22 did not get — so the honest reading is that the question family is half-audited, and a second pass over those 22 is still owed.

content: Unknown link labels carried opaquely through import, storage, export and supersession. Built 2026-09-28. `LinkLabel::Unrecognised` in `src/memory/link.rs` holds any spelling outside the vocabulary and is stored and exported exactly as read. `is_traversable` excludes it by an exhaustive match. `unknown_label_refusal` in `src/mcp.rs` lets `hoard_memorize` and `hoard_correct` carry one only when restating the same label and target id from the memory being superseded or amended. The label schema drops its `enum` and names the vocabulary in the property and tool descriptions. Pinned by `tests/unknown_labels.rs` and ten mutations. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`, the first release-gate item after `adopting-coding-lessons` closed.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded to record that it is built. The three proofs the old head named are met: a round trip that is byte-identical record for record, an unknown label that is not walked, and one kept across a supersession, each with a test and a mutation. Amend was added to the restating rule by the human partner, as were the schema change and naming the vocabulary in the tool descriptions.

content: **The question's shape changed on 2026-08-23, and the human partner's reframing turns a drafting problem into a retrieval one.** **The reshaped question is not *how do we let a household set hold memories about people*** -- the mild case shows that is real and fine. It is **whether any rule expressible in served text can separate the mild case from the movement log and the association map**, when all three pass the Golden Rule's demands individually and the distinguishing property belongs to the *set*. Candidates weighed: that the person must be incidental to a subject the set is actually organised around, which reads on the mild case and fails the other two; that a set accumulating repeated observations of one person **has become a dossier whatever its charter says**; and that served text may be able only to raise the question, leaving the judgement with the session. **The reframing:** demand C is about the *contents of a set*, and Scatterhoard is a system built to answer questions about the contents of a set -- *assuming we can figure out the correct question(s) to ask*. So a routing decision could recall against the destination set before storing and ask what it already holds about this person, detecting the dossier **by measuring the set rather than by a rule inspecting one memory**. That is the move `route-where` already makes with charters -- derive from the set rather than compile into the catalog -- applied one layer deeper. **What must be settled before it is a mechanism:** what the question actually *is*, since *how much does this set already say about this person* is not a similarity query and may not be expressible as one; what threshold means anything, given aggregation is a matter of degree; whether the check runs at store time, costing a recall on every person-memory, or at export, where the set already exists and the review gate is the natural home -- and note the second is where the *set* is visible, which is where C says the property lives; and that a check keyed on a person's name inherits every spelling problem `keyword-standards` describes, which makes the naive version weakest exactly where it matters. **Do not treat the mildness of the first case as licence to relax the clause** -- its whole value is that it holds where relaxing it is most tempting.
context: Migrating open-questions.md, recovering content a faulty deletion boundary had left orphaned after the entry's head was already stored.
why:
Recorded because the reframing is the most promising line the question has and is not derivable from the entry's headline: it converts *no rule can express this* into *this is a query against the destination set*, which is the one kind of problem this project is equipped for.

The four settling conditions are kept because each is a genuine obstacle rather than a checklist, and the store-time-versus-export-time choice in particular has an argument attached that points the opposite way from the cheap option.

The closing warning is preserved verbatim in force because it is the entry's own guard against the most likely misreading of its own findings.

content:
**Both embedding models Scatterhoard supports may be redistributed under MIT, but neither fits in an ordinary git repository.** Checked 2026-10-04 against Hugging Face's model metadata and cards:
- `minishlab/potion-base-32M` and `minishlab/potion-multilingual-128M` are MIT.
- So are the models they distil, `BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5` and `BAAI/bge-m3`.
- They were trained on C4, which licenses the dataset, not models trained on it.
- Neither Hugging Face repository carries a LICENSE file. The model2vec project's own reads "Copyright (c) 2024 Thomas van Dongen", so redistribution should carry an MIT notice naming that holder.

Each `model.safetensors` is over GitHub's 100 MB per-file limit: 129 MB and 512 MB. The tokenizers are 1.5 MB and 18.6 MB.
context: Preparing the first beta release: rewriting SETUP.md and filling in the README's quick start, which wrongly said the models ship with Scatterhoard.
why: The human partner asked whether the models could be redistributed with the repository for the beta release. Licensing allows it. Where they live is a separate decision with lasting costs: committed files stay in every clone's history, and Git LFS has storage and bandwidth quotas.

content: **These eight entries must be settled before publication**; they are this memory's keywords. Gated 2026-09-23 by the human partner. Three have answers that would break something already in use if changed afterwards: the tool surface, the file format, or what an identity means. They are `set-settled-at-first-write`, `several-memory-files-per-directory` and `identity-mismatch-refusal`. `unrecognised-link-labels-on-import` decides whether every later label is a format break. `claude-md-in-the-repository` gets a look, though it is easier to change afterwards. Three are gated because crafted files arrive with publication: `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity`, `the-reserved-directory-accepts-the-local-set` and `data-only-rule-in-the-catalog`.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner, closing `imported-set-trust-boundary`.
why: Superseded 2026-09-25, adding two entries by the human partner's decision. `the-reserved-directory-accepts-the-local-set` fixes the gap a crafted repository would use to reach the personal set, and its fix refuses a call that works today. `data-only-rule-in-the-catalog` is gated for security, not compatibility. The human partner expects the first public users to try "disregard all previous instructions" inside a memory soon after release, and until the catalog says a recalled memory is data, whether that works depends on the client. Retire an item by superseding this memory without its slug.

content: **Whether *violates a decision* belongs in a memory system — resolved 2026-09-23: yes, `violates` stays.** Zero uses across all four sets on this machine is an artifact of this project rather than a verdict on the label: Scatterhoard keeps its defects as issue clusters, so its corpus is exactly the one where a violation has somewhere else to live. A user without an in-memory tracker is the case the label was built for, and without it their only label for a deviation is `exception_to`, bringing back the documented trap of defects recorded as sanctioned exceptions. The worry the question raised, a memory set accumulating violation edges and doing a tracker's job, did not happen in seven weeks. Keeping it costs about a dozen tokens of schema.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner, starting with the quickest.
why: Decided by the human partner, who also named where the label is likeliest to earn its place: `governance-docs`, a set about governing documents, where a proposed bylaw that breaks a recorded statutory requirement is exactly a violation rather than a sanctioned exception. Settled before publication because the label set is closed — an unknown label fails import — so removing it afterwards would break files that use it, which is what put this on the release gate.

content: Confirmed 2026-08-04 against the renamed variant, and the second half of the message was worse than the first. `{"shared": "coding-lessons"}` was refused with *"no memory set is loaded for scope … Loaded scopes have to be imported before they can be used; check the set name."* Two problems beyond the one recorded: **it names a second action the caller cannot take** — there was no import tool on the surface, import being designed in [set-lifecycle.md](documents/design/set-lifecycle.md) and unimplemented, and per that design the bootstrap answer is `create` rather than `import`, so the advice would still be wrong once import shipped, since a set that has never existed anywhere cannot be imported from anything. And **"loaded scopes have to be imported" is circular**: a loaded scope is precisely the one needing no import. The sentence means "a set has to be imported before it can be used".
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Two further faults in one sentence, kept because each is a distinct way for guidance to fail: naming a remedy that does not exist, and naming a precondition that contradicts the state it describes.

content: A memory *about* a `hoard-` mechanism takes `about-` in front as of 2026-09-06 -- `about-hoard-watch`, never the reserved term -- because a reserved keyword is a control mark and whatever carries one is put in a list something acts on. Measured that day: `hoard-scope-topics` returned nine memories of which four were charters, the other five being design memories about charters, which `route-where` has a session match candidates against as though they described a set. `hoard-author` was clean at four of four. The five can be repaired by superseding each with a replacement carrying `about-hoard-scope-topics`, since a keyword hit follows the tip's keywords.
context: Correcting a claim about keyword retirement that had propagated into an issue, a design section and this memory within one afternoon.
why: Supersedes the version stored hours earlier, whose last clause said the five could not be repaired because superseding does not retire a keyword. That was false and came from a stale memory of pre-fix behaviour; the repair is an ordinary supersession pass. The measurement is the part worth keeping either way, because it shows the hazard is live rather than theoretical and shows which way it leans -- the impostors outnumbered the real charters. Worth knowing before anyone proposes another reserved keyword: the namespace rule has to arrive with the keyword, since the discussion accumulates fastest while the mechanism is being designed.

content: Fixed 2026-08-05: `hoard_sets` answers both halves. Action `status` enumerates every loaded set with its memory count and whether it can be searched by meaning; action `create` brings a new shared set into existence, so the caller who could not discover a usable name can now make one. The refusal was rewritten to name both actions, which is the part that closes the defect as filed — it previously named *"check the set name"* with nothing to check against and *"have to be imported"* with no import tool, two dead ends in one sentence. **`create` takes a name rather than a scope**, so `local` is unrepresentable: the local set always exists and creating it is not a thing anyone can mean. This is the `oneOf`-per-action schema shape rather than a flat `action` enum with every optional argument beside it, so `{"action": "status", "name": …}` cannot be constructed and believed — which is what `schema-underspecifies-scope-and-links` was.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the schema shape that came with it: per-action `oneOf` makes an impossible combination unconstructible rather than merely undocumented, which is the lesson the earlier schema defect taught.

content: **`recall-when` gained a connect-on-recall clause 2026-09-09, funded by trimming editor-facing rationale out of four served conventions.** The clause: *"When what you recall should be linked to a memory you already hold, or needs a keyword you can now see it wants, connect them before moving on: the connection is visible only while both are in front of you."* Plus one reinforcement sentence. **The catalog had 320 characters of headroom and a convention averages ~1,600**, so this had to be a clause and had to be paid for. Four trims freed 385 characters by moving *drafting* rationale into source comments, where `Convention`'s own doc comment already says it belongs: `store-when`'s note on how its people clauses relate to its general ones, `route-where`'s explanation of why the overrides are served rather than delegated plus an ordinal that would not survive reordering, `hoard-watch`'s reason the three actions are a closed set, and `capture-before-ending`'s reference to the boundary it exists to catch. Ends at **17,624 of 18,000, 376 spare**. Two approval snapshots were updated deliberately; `report_catalog_headroom` in `tests/conventions.rs` now prints the figure so `AGENTS.md`'s *derive it, never quote it* has something to derive it with.
context: Drafting the connect-on-recall clause the human partner asked for, and trimming served justification to fund it.
why:
Recorded because the trimming is reusable and the criterion took a while to state cleanly: **rationale that helps a session apply a rule is served; rationale that explains why the rule is worded as it is belongs to whoever edits it.** Every sentence removed was true and worth keeping — none was deleted, all four moved to comments beside their entries — and each was about the convention rather than about the work. The sharpest test found: a sentence that indexes the clause list ("the third is the one...") is always editor-facing, because it describes an arrangement rather than a hazard, and it silently rots when the clauses are reordered.

**The clause deliberately does not name the instrument, and that hides a cost worth watching.** `correct-when` already decides between amend and supersede, and it decides expensively here: `amend` is refused after export, so connecting two exported memories means storing a full copy of one carrying a `supersedes` link, purely to add an edge. That overloads supersession — a claim about *validity* — with something that is only a claim about *adjacency*. With 603 of 762 memories isolated and most of them exported, the clause will meet that case often. Left unpapered rather than worded around: if the cost bites, the fix is a link-only write, not a rewording.

Confidence 0.9: the clause and the trims are in the served catalog and pinned by snapshot, and the headroom figure is derived. What is not established is whether the clause changes behaviour — `already_known` is the standing evidence that it may not.

content: Found 2026-08-30 by acting on the note and measuring the result. `mutate.py` ends a slow pass blaming the size of `target-mutation` — *"One full pass leaves roughly 35,000 files behind, so about every third one wants `rm -rf target-mutation`"* and *"A healthy pass on a clean tree averages about 1.6s per mutation."* Against a deliberately cleared directory: 138,529 files (claimed 10.2 GB) and 2.4s per mutation before, **132,907 files and 2.6s per mutation** after `rm -rf` and one full pass. **One pass from empty produces ~133,000 files, not ~35,000**, so the directory is above the note's own alarm threshold the first time it is ever used, and the note prints on every pass including the one immediately after the remedy it recommends. **Why this is worth an entry rather than a shrug**: the note is an instrument whose reading is constant, so a caller who follows it spends a minute on `rm -rf`, sees the same warning and the same pace, and learns nothing about their tree — and it attributes a real observation, that passes are slower than 1.6s, to a cause now ruled out, so the next person to look at pass duration starts from a wrong hypothesis this file endorsed.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: An instrument whose reading cannot vary, and the second-order cost: it explains a real symptom with a cause that has been eliminated, so it sends the next investigation the wrong way.

content: **The same resolution works on a superseded memory's outbound links, so a supersession cannot withdraw a relation from the walk.** Read from the code 2026-09-23, not reproduced: building the neighbourhood in `src/store.rs` passes *both* ends of every walkable edge through `tip_of`. So if A carries `A CONTRADICTS C` and B supersedes A without restating it — deliberately, because B's author no longer holds it — the walk still follows `B CONTRADICTS C`. The record and the walk then disagree: looking B up shows no such link. Unlike keywords, which a supersession must restate and whose losses `keyword_delta` reports, links are neither required nor reported, so nothing tells the author the omission will not take effect.
context: Answering whether supersession drops a memory's links, after building the causes region, whose attribution counts every version of a chain for exactly this reason.
why: This entry's head and members cover only in-links, where the harm is a claim nobody reauthored. The outbound case differs in who could have acted: B's author did see A, and did choose, and the walk overrides the choice. Found when the human partner asked whether superseding a memory drops its links, and the honest answer turned out to depend on whether you read the record or the walk.

content: **What an evaluation copy does and does not do once loaded, as built 2026-09-18.** An unscoped recall does not search it; every memory it returns carries `evaluation: true`, taken from the load mode, in summaries and `hoard_lookup` alike, with a response note explaining the mark. Its cross-set links are surfaced as `cross_set_targets` — label, set name, target id, identity, and every loaded scope answering to that identity with its mode — and never resolved. It logs no query, so it calibrates nothing; it drops with no safety copy; and it pulls no watch marks.
context: Moved 2026-09-24 out of the entry's head, which was over the length limit, in step 2 of the out-link work.
why: The behaviour of a loaded review copy, moved out of the head so each part can change without superseding the entry's standing.

content: **Two ingredients are already identified for when the blockers clear -- named 2026-08-03.** **Similarity computed for keyword hits too**, which is cheap because the query vector and the memory vectors both already exist: a keyword hit that is also semantically close is exactly the doubly-found case the separation currently hides, and it costs no new machinery to detect. **And rarity weighting**, so that matching a precise identifier counts for more than matching a broad word -- `matched_keywords` is currently an unweighted count that cannot tell a precise tag from a broad one, which is the same limitation `keyword-standards` warns about from the authoring side. **The two are complementary rather than alternative:** the first gives a keyword result a score on the semantic scale so the two can be ranked together at all, and the second stops that ranking being dominated by memories carrying many common terms.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because they are the design work already done, and because the first one changes the cost estimate substantially -- a hybrid ranking sounds like it needs a new scoring model and mostly needs an existing vector comparison run over a different candidate set.

The rarity point connects to a limitation that shows up in two other places -- unweighted `matched_keywords` in ranking, and the convention's advice against broad keywords -- so a fix here would retire a recurring complaint rather than serve only this question.

content: **Centroid removal was adopted 2026-07-31 to fix hubness, and its cost could not have been visible in the measurement that adopted it.** The case is in `documents/design/embeddings.md`: removing the mean from both query and memory lifted `potion-base-32M` from 71.7% to 77.5% at r@5 and 83.3% to 87.5% at r@10, and cut the worst hub from 13 of 20 queries to 6. Hubness was established as a general high-dimensional property rather than a static-embedding artifact, since MiniLM showed it too at 8 of 20. **The trade nobody knew they were making:** centring subtracts the same component from both sides, so the score becomes blind to how far the *query* sits from the corpus mean — and that quantity, `cos(query, centroid)`, is the one thing measured on 2026-09-08 that separates an answerable query from one the corpus cannot answer. **The spike could not have seen this.** It ran on 45 single-domain memories with 20 on-topic queries, so it contained no unanswerable query to lose, and recall@k measures ordering while the discarded signal is a level. **Nothing is destroyed, only unused**: the query vector and the centroid are both to hand at scan time, so the signal can be reported beside the score without undoing the centring that earns the ranking.
context: Banking the probe findings, when the human partner asked why the centroid adjustment was introduced in the first place.
why:
Recorded because the natural response to *centring discards the signal we need* is to question the centring, and that would trade a measured 5.8-point ranking gain for a quantity that can be recovered for free. Stating the trade and its remedy in one place is what stops that.

The second reason is about method rather than centroids: this is the third time in this project a decision measured in one regime has been carried into another where it means something different — the traversal crossover at 170 memories, CSLS rejected at 45, and now this. The spike was honest and its number was right; it simply could not contain the case that later mattered. **The corpus is now 855 memories, so both the centroid decision and the CSLS rejection are due a re-run at scale**, and the CSLS entry in `EARLY-VALIDATION.md` names exactly that precondition and can now be met.

content: **The absolute floor was ruled out by a measurement whose own recorded caveat said it could not support the ruling, and at corpus scale it works — but not as a constant.** The 2026-08-03 rejection was taken on a **five-memory store** using **centroid-relative** scores, and its context line asked for a re-measurement on a larger store before anything was built on it. That never happened; the floor then appeared on the 2026-09-08 list of seven failed mechanisms. Re-measured on the live union of 875 memories with **raw cosine**, 18 answerable queries against 24 unanswerable: **AUC 0.944**, the highest of the eight ruled-out statistics, and the most robust of them in every condition tested. A single threshold at **0.447** makes 4 errors of 42. Raw beats centred, 0.944 to 0.884, and centring on a five-memory store is what produced the original "narrow, low band, negative scores". **The original memory's actual conclusion — that a floor cannot be a hand-picked constant — is upheld**: across seven corpora the p90 floor runs 0.089 to 0.286 and the max floor 0.125 to 0.476, so any constant is wrong somewhere. What is refuted is the broader reading that no floor works at all. Re-run `probe_whether_controlling_question_form_stabilises_the_verdict` in `tests/probes.rs`.
context: Testing the human partner's prediction that the swinging verdicts would subside once their cause was found, by re-running the ruled-out mechanisms against form-controlled query sets.
why:
Supersedes the 2026-08-03 measurement rather than sitting beside it, because that memory has been read for a month as *the floor was tried and failed*, which is not what it measured. The measurement itself is kept above rather than split into a second memory: the two halves are one subject here, since the correction is precisely that this measurement does not support that reading, and splitting them would leave a reader holding either an obsolete conclusion or a number with no bearing.

Amended before export to withdraw a claim that a larger probe set falsified. The first version said a threshold at 0.332 makes zero errors against substance-shaped non-matches; that rested on twelve of them, and at thirty one scores 0.476 through a single term of art. The distinction that matters for the design is the one now stated: the floor is real, the constant is not, and the 2026-08-03 memory was right about the second even while being read as settling the first.

The general shape is worth as much as the result. A caveat written into the record at the moment of measurement — *re-measure on a larger store before building on this* — did not survive being cited. Each later reference carried the conclusion and dropped the condition, and by the time it reached a list of ruled-out mechanisms it read as a settled negative. A caveat that lives only in a `context` line is not attached to the claim in any way a later session will feel.

Scoped carefully against the open entry. This does **not** close `an-unanswerable-query-returns-confident-hits`, whose text says no statistic separates *the football case*, and that remains exactly true.

content: Writing a check that follows a memory's links and matches `LinkTarget::SameSet`. A link whose `target_set` names the set itself is same-set too, and `write_links` stores it as one; ask `LinkTarget::is_foreign_to` with the set's scope and identity, as the write does, or reuse `targets_in_this_set`.
context: Recording the model-fit link failure under the coding-lessons adoption guide, part 5.
why: A project trigger for the `coding-lessons` lesson on guards keyed to spelling, phrased in this project's nouns because a session about to write such a check says "SameSet" and "links", which the general trigger matches only loosely. content: **Three constraints were settled when the question was raised on 2026-08-30, before any design existed, and each rules out an obvious shortcut.** First, the digest is **derived, never stored**: a second checksum living inside the record would have to be excluded from the record's own canonical form, and would become a second thing to keep in step. Second, it carries **its own algorithm identity**, for the same reason `checksum::ALGORITHM` exists -- verified 2026-09-07 as `"fnv1a64/json-sorted-v1"` in `src/checksum.rs` -- so that a build meeting digests it cannot reproduce detects that rather than comparing garbage. Third, a match is a **report, never an action**: an absorption fork, a deliberately re-stated memory, and two people independently writing the same thing all look identical to a digest, all are worth surfacing, and none is safe to resolve automatically. **The connection to `convention-text-evaluated-objectively` is load-bearing rather than incidental** -- exact-duplicate counting is one of the avoidable-work instruments that question needs, and it falls out of this one with no counterfactual replay at all, which is the expensive part of every other instrument proposed there.
