why:
The three constraints are the reusable part: each is an argument against a design that would otherwise look reasonable, and all three would have to be re-derived from scratch by anyone starting the build from the entry's headline alone. Recorded with the second one re-verified rather than quoted, since it asserts something about the code as it currently stands.

The cross-question link is kept because it changes build order: the measurement question is blocked on instruments that are mostly expensive, and this is the one cheap instrument, so building the digest unblocks a piece of that question as a side effect rather than as a separate project.

content: In a UUIDv7 from `uuid`'s `now_v7`, the 74 bits after the millisecond timestamp hold a 42-bit counter, then 32 random bits. The counter is reseeded randomly each millisecond and incremented within it. The randomness is what makes ids unique across servers; the counter is what keeps one process's ids in order. Ids minted by two processes in the same millisecond interleave arbitrarily, and nothing in Scatterhoard depends on their order. Check in `uuid`'s `src/timestamp.rs` (`ContextV7`) and `src/v7.rs` (`new_v7`).
context: Diving into the flaky id-ordering test, picked from the seven open issues right after restoring the 2026-10-01 checkpoint.
why: This is the half of the 2026-09-22 account that is still true, split out now that its claim to have ruled out every cause has been corrected separately. The human partner's question at the time, whether the random part is what guarantees uniqueness across servers, is what this answers. The source was read again on 2026-10-01 while reproducing the ordering bug.

content:
**Re-embedding on 2026-09-19 cleared `scatterhoard`'s calibrated floor, and that is correct rather than damage.** `Store::reembed` clears it whenever the model identity actually changes, because a level is entirely the model's — every set's floor moved 0.10 to 0.16 under a different one — so a level calibrated under the displaced encoding describes nothing about the arriving one.

What it cost: the floor of 0.3755, the first ever set here from real traffic and read from 26 labelled queries, is gone. `non_match_floor` reads null and the set is back under the 20 labelled queries a calibration needs, at 3. Until those accumulate again, an unanswerable query gets the best of a bad ranking instead of nothing.

**The new thing to know is that a re-encode now counts as a displacement.** Before the encoding entered the identity, only different weights could clear a floor. Any later change to how text is fed to the model discards every set's calibration too. That is the honest behaviour — the level really is invalid — and it is worth budgeting for rather than meeting by surprise, because the evidence it destroys takes weeks of ordinary use to rebuild.
context: Rebuilding all four sets right after restarting the server on the build that encodes whole text.
why: A session reading the first-calibration record will expect a floor in place and find none, and the tempting reading is that something went wrong. Recorded so the answer is one recall away. The forward-looking half matters more: the encoding is now a thing that can change, and whoever changes it next should know it costs every set's calibration rather than discovering that afterwards.

content:
**Several of the operations Anthropic blocked had hand-built the thing Scatterhoard is — and one detail makes the point far sharper than that.** Read 2026-09-12 from the full report, superseding a version written an hour earlier from the published summary page alone. An observation made while filing `golden-rule-beyond-person-harm`, not history from building anything.

**The sharpest finding: splitting work across sessions is an evasion technique, and the report names it as one.** Of the conventional-weapons actors generally it says they *split their work across many sessions to conceal the full nature of their programs*; of the Yemen guided-weapons cell (GTG-87001), that they *split their work across multiple sessions so no single session revealed their full intent*. The safeguards act per request and per session, and fragmentation is what defeats them. **A project-scale cross-session memory tool is structurally fragmentation repair** — it hands back the coherence an actor deliberately gave up in order to evade detection. That is a far narrower and more uncomfortable claim than *a memory tool could be misused*.

Three supporting patterns, all from the conventional-weapons section:

- **Multi-instance role division.** GTG-87001 ran several Claude instances at once with assigned roles — one writing code, one researching, one reviewing what the first produced. A shared memory set is the coordination substrate for exactly that arrangement.
- **Deliberate extraction of artifacts that persist without the model.** The same cell compiled its simulation toolkit into a standalone executable, and had already built an offline toolkit independent of Claude. An exported memory set is that kind of deliverable.
- **The individually-mundane record.** Of the Russian procurement case (GTG-27006): detection is *particularly challenging, because each of the actor's requests ... seem individually mundane*.

**On practicality it cuts the other way, harder than the superseded version said.** Every detection ran on signals a hosted service has — account metadata, regional-access evasion, reseller and proxy infrastructure, classifier hits, cross-account correlation, and in one case a journalist's tip. The biological section concludes that in dual-use domains a classifier *cannot simultaneously enable benefit and prevent harm*, and that the answer is trusted user programmes, meaning account and institutional signals. Scatterhoard is local, with no accounts, no telemetry and no server-side view, so none of those routes exists here. Whatever friction is possible is a convention read by the session doing the work, and nothing else.

Source: `~/Downloads/Anthropic-Detecting-and-countering-091026.pdf`, 154 pages, published 2026-09-10; conventional weapons at pp. 111–128, biological misuse at pp. 129–138.
context: The morning the question was filed. Superseding a version of this memory written an hour earlier, once the PDF could actually be read.

Splitting would put the surviving claim and its own provenance into two records that always have to be read together, which is the cost the rule exists to avoid rather than an instance of it. The original stays readable.

The superseded version said no tool on this machine could extract the PDF. That was false in a way worth noting: nothing had been installed, but macOS ships PDFKit, and the general lesson went to `coding-lessons` rather than here.

content: The third change shipped 2026-09-02 with the other two: `hoard_memorize` returns `keyword_delta` — one entry per superseded target, naming `added`, `dropped` and `retained` — plus a note. **Reported, never refused**, because dropping a keyword is legitimate and is the only way to retire one; the server states the fact where the caller can still act on it. Three details worth keeping. **It reports when nothing was dropped, too**: a caller who re-typed the old set faithfully learns so from `dropped: []`, and suppressing the report in that case would remove exactly the confirmation and leave a faithful re-typing indistinguishable from a server that did not look — a recorded mutation pins it. **Same-set targets only**: a cross-set target's keywords are not ours to read and may not be held here, and an empty delta would say *nothing was dropped* where the truth is *nothing was checked*, the shape `prohibited-data-scanned-conflates-skipped-with-unbuilt` was filed for. **Compared on the folded form**, because that is what matching uses, so two spellings differing only in case are one term and reporting them as a drop plus an addition would be a change the search path cannot see. The response shape is recorded in [tests/snapshots/memorize_supersession.json](tests/snapshots/memorize_supersession.json).

why: A report designed so its silence is never ambiguous: it fires on the empty case so a confirmation exists, and it refuses to cover targets it cannot inspect rather than reporting nothing found.

content: Measured 2026-09-02: harvesting a closed tracking-file entry into memory works for symptoms and fails for decisions. A symptom written symptom-first -- leading with what the trouble looks like from outside, before the cause is known -- went from unreachable to rank 1 at 0.307 on the query "a memory I know exists has vanished from search results and I cannot work out why", against a previous top of 0.178 with nothing relevant returned. The same harvest of three DECISION memories from the closed `graph-traversal` entry did not come back at all on a broad query naming its own subject ("how the walk was designed, what was tried and rejected"), while a targeted query naming the specific mechanism returned one at 0.526, the session's highest score. So a harvested decision is findable by someone who already knows what they are looking for, and not by someone about to repeat a mistake.
context: Run as a deliberate pilot on two closed entries: `graph-traversal` in BACKLOG.md and `a-superseded-by-naming-an-absent-id-hides-its-memory` in ISSUES.md, with both probes re-run verbatim afterwards. Symptom vocabulary is distinctive and nothing in the corpus competes for it, and a stuck person genuinely arrives with a query, which is the rare case where a pull interface is the right shape. content: **The calibrated floor bounds a recall's size but does not make it independent of the window**, measured 2026-09-30 on the 1,298-memory `scatterhoard` set at floor 0.360. The one-word query `memory` returned 5 at `limit: 20`, 28 at 100, and 28 at 5000, so a huge limit no longer returns the whole store. A narrow query returned the same 3 at 17, 18, 50 and 1000. The floor runs before the largest-gap cut, so once the window reaches past every hit above the floor the count stops moving; below that, it still follows the window. The bound holds only where a floor does: uncalibrated sets, `ignore_floor`, and keyword recall have none, and `limit` is still taken unclamped in `src/mcp.rs`.
context: Working through open issues with the human partner, just after recalibrating both shared sets' floors and fixing the numbered-opening summary.
why: The human partner asked whether the floor closes the two limit issues. It closes neither: the window-dependent count reproduces, the first reproduction since the 2026-09-23 audit could not, and the unbounded limit is bounded only on calibrated semantic recall. Kept so a later session does not re-derive this, and so whoever takes either issue knows the floor narrowed it. That matters for the design: summary mode makes large windows a deliberate use, so a hard maximum now cuts against something the project built.

content: **Three constraints on the remark, all load-bearing, decided 2026-08-29.** **Scope it to `content` and `why`**: apparatus correction cannot invalidate a label, because the text the edge's author judged has not moved — unscoped, it fires on every confidence change and teaches callers to skip it. **A remark, never a refusal**, applying the rule the code already follows — *remark when the caller can still act, refuse when they cannot* — and here the caller can act in the same turn, holding both texts; the malformed-parameter guard was converted from one to the other on exactly that ground. **Not a block on in-links**: measured over the live sets, `related_to` dominates at 24 of 51 edges in `scatterhoard` and 37 of 48 in `coding-lessons`, and it asserts least about content, **so a block would refuse most often where it protects least**.
context: Migrating the in-link-remark entry out of BACKLOG.md; these are the constraints that shaped it.
why:
The third constraint is the one that needs its measurement attached, because the intuition runs the other way: an inbound edge looks like a reason to protect the text, and the distribution says the commonest inbound edge is the one that cares least what the text says. Blocking would have been the conservative-looking choice and would have produced a guard that mostly obstructs.

The first constraint is the general form of a failure this project keeps meeting — a signal that fires on cases it does not apply to trains its reader to ignore it, and then it is absent when it matters. Scoping it to the fields that can actually invalidate a judgement is what keeps it worth reading.

content: **Whether convention text can be evaluated objectively, and against what.** Raised 2026-08-30 by the human partner, whose own best answer so far was subjective, alongside two values a memory system should be judged on: **avoidable work** -- work a session did that a proper store or recall would have saved -- and **information that exists only across sessions**. Neither has a measure, and the catalog has never been evaluated at all. **What makes it genuinely open is that the confounds are severe and the population is one.** The corpus grows, the work changes, the model changes, and -- the hard one -- **the same LLM is subject and experimenter**, so *the convention worked* cannot be separated from *the session that wrote it was thinking about it anyway*. A before-and-after across a convention's ship date is objective and is not controlled. Whether that is worth having, or whether it manufactures false confidence in exactly the way the mutation-count caution warns about, is the question. **The immediate stake:** `cold-reread-of-the-catalog` is judgement-based precisely because removal is unmeasurable, which is what makes the catalog ratchet upward. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `convention-text-evaluated-objectively`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The confounds are in the head rather than a member because they are what makes this a question rather than a task: the instruments are mostly designable, and a session reading only the row would otherwise take this for *build a measurement* when the open part is whether any measurement here can mean anything.

content: **Controlling the off-corpus class stops verdicts diverging *between* studies, but does not stabilise a pilot-sized one — so the swings had two causes, not one.** Tested 2026-09-08 by scoring the eight ruled-out statistics against 400 pilot-sized draws (6 answerable against 6 unanswerable) from four differently-composed pools. **Between-study divergence is large and is the composition's doing**: at full power, result-set coherence scores AUC **0.949 against substance-shaped non-matches and 0.588 against rule-shaped**, and `cos(query, centroid)` **0.991 against 0.634** — the difference between adopt and reject, from the query set alone. **Within-pilot instability is not fixed by controlling form.** Draws from substance-shaped only produce one winner 100% of the time; draws from rule-shaped only produce **seven different winners, the top one taking 71%** — less stable than the uncontrolled mix at 78%. Balanced draws sit at 75%. So *small query sets manufacture separation* survives as an independent cause, and controlling question form addresses the other one. The absolute floor wins 71–100% of draws in every condition and is the only statistic robust to both.
context: Testing the human partner's prediction that the swings would subside once their cause was found — the session after the off-corpus class turned out to be two populations.
why:
Recorded because it is a partial confirmation reported as one, and the half that failed is the more useful half. The prediction under test — made by the human partner before the cause was known — was that finding the cause would leave ordinary numeric variation while the recommendations stopped reversing. Half of that holds: mechanisms no longer swap places between studies once the off-corpus class is composed deliberately. The other half does not, because six queries against six is too few for any composition to rescue, and rule-shaped queries are the worst case since their scores land inside the answerable range where small changes reorder everything.

The practical consequence is a rule for future trials on this entry rather than a finding about the system: state the rule-to-substance ratio of the unanswerable class, because a verdict is not interpretable without it, and keep the forty-query bar, because composition and size are separate requirements and satisfying one does not buy the other.

Confidence 0.85: the resampling is deterministic and reproducible from the recorded seed, and the between-condition gaps are far too large to be noise, but the whole study rests on 18 answerable queries built by hand in one session, which is the part most likely to be flattering.

content: The fix is two changes and **their order is a precondition rather than a preference**. **Authoring**: where a store call carries a `supersedes` link, the keyword set must be *stated* — absence refused, an explicit empty list accepted as a deliberate choice. **Search**: a keyword hit follows the tip's keywords rather than the matched memory's. **Doing the second without the first manufactures the very bug this entry cites**: omitting keywords on a superseding memory is survivable today *because* the old terms still reach, so cutting the reach while the keyword set can still default to nothing makes supersession silently destroy findability. *Note for drafting: a conditionally-required parameter is a required choice, so [decision placement](documents/design/decision-placement.md) governs it — and there is a standing reluctance to reach for required-ness, from the malformed-call work, "do not repair this by making `why` required, which trades away a decided property." Conditional on `supersedes` is narrower than that, and the argument still has to be made rather than assumed.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Two fixes whose order is load-bearing: the safe one first, because the current defect is what makes the unsafe default survivable. Recorded because either change alone reads as the whole fix.

content: Observed 2026-09-22: `ids_sort_into_creation_order` generates 1,000 ids with `MemoryId::generate` (`Uuid::now_v7`, `uuid` 1.24.0) on one thread and asserts they sort in creation order. It failed in one `cargo test --no-fail-fast` run and passed 30 of 30 runs alone; the assertion's output was not captured. **Both candidate causes are ruled out by `uuid`'s source** (`src/timestamp.rs`): an earlier clock reading keeps the last timestamp and increments the counter, and the shared context is a `std::sync::Mutex`, a time read before the lock being handled the same way. So the failure is unexplained. The next occurrence needs the out-of-order pair and their timestamps.
context: The human partner asking whether UUIDv7's random component is what guarantees uniqueness across servers, just after the flaky test was filed.
why: Supersedes the first account, which named a backward clock step and cross-thread sharing as the candidates; the human partner's question about UUIDv7's random component prompted reading the crate. The 74 non-timestamp bits hold a 42-bit counter, reseeded randomly each millisecond and incremented within it, plus 32 random bits: randomness gives cross-server uniqueness, the counter gives in-process order. Ids from two processes in one millisecond interleave arbitrarily, which nothing here depends on.

content: **Whether `hoard_sets create` should refuse to make a shared set without a charter. Resolved 2026-09-24 by the human partner: no — the first memorize into a shared set with no charter is refused instead, unless the memory being stored is the charter.** What kept it open was that `create` could not tell a new set from one about to be taken on by `import`, which overwrites any charter given at creation. Settling it at the first write removes that: a set taken on from a file brings its own charter, and a new one is asked at the moment its creator is writing to it and holds the remedy. An empty set with no charter is valid, and `status` already says it has none. Built as `set-settled-at-first-write`. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `charter-at-set-creation`; this record carries only its standing.

content: **The reconciliation model already handles a partial file correctly, which is why only two things are missing -- established 2026-08-11 and re-verified against the code 2026-09-07.** A recipient holding no bases for a target reconciles a partial file correctly, because a record the file omits with no base resolves to `KeepLocal` -- confirmed at `reconcile.rs`, where the `None` base arm returns exactly that. So a partial import does not silently delete what it omits, which is the failure that would otherwise make the whole idea unsafe. **What is missing is a way to name which records travel, and a base rule for a target that agrees with only part of a set.** Only the first is mechanical. `Store::set_bases` is written as `DELETE FROM bases WHERE target = ?1` followed by inserts -- it replaces a target's whole base set, on the stated assumption that an export writes the whole file -- so a partial export under today's code would discard the bases for every record it did not carry.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Recorded because *most of it already works* is the load-bearing and least obvious fact: a session picking this up would reasonably budget for a reconciliation change and does not need one. Naming the two gaps precisely, and which is hard, is what stops the estimate being wrong in either direction.

Both claims are re-verified rather than carried over, since each asserts what the code does today: `set_bases` and the `KeepLocal` arm were read on 2026-09-07 during migration. Check them again before relying on this -- `grep -n "fn set_bases" src/store.rs` and the `None` arm in `src/reconcile.rs`.

content: **Confirmed by test 2026-09-15: a memory linking with one label to the same id in two different sets keeps only the second link, and nothing reports the loss.** `two_links_to_one_id_in_different_sets_both_survive` in `tests/store.rs` stores one memory with two `RefersTo` links to a single generated id, one naming set `left` and one naming `right`, then reads it back: the stored links are `["right"]` where `["left", "right"]` was written. `insert` returns `Ok`, so the write looks successful from every caller. The mechanism is as filed — `links` is `PRIMARY KEY (source, label, target)` with `target` the id alone, and `write_links` in `src/store.rs` writes with `INSERT OR REPLACE` — and `target_set`, `target_keywords` and `target_set_id` are all outside the key. The test asserts on the set names recovered from `links_of`, so it fails on the loss rather than on a count that a duplicate could also satisfy.
context: Picking up the checkpoint's next step, after filing the memory-size question and committing it.
why:
Recorded because the entry was filed on a reading of the schema, and the first step it named was a test that would confirm or refute it. It confirms, so the entry stands as a defect rather than being withdrawn, and the test is the proof that was asked for.

Written as a failing test before any fix, per the project's test-driven standard: the assertion is what the fix has to turn green, and it discriminates — comparing recovered set names rather than a link count, so a fix that kept two rows by duplicating one would still fail it.

What remains unmeasured is exposure: no count exists of how many live memories hold two such links, and the ordinary way to get one is a memory copied between sets keeping its id, which no store here is known to have done.

content: The reserved directory was mandatory even where nothing reads it. Built 2026-08-25, pulled forward by `set-drop` and `set-restore`, whose shared safety copy must by construction write somewhere that is *not* the set's normal export path. `export` takes `directory` **or** `file`, never both and never neither — **the alternation lives in the type**, since `ExportSet` flattens a `Destination` enum so *both* and *neither* are not values it can hold, and the branch schema's `one_of` key refuses them at dispatch. **An explicit file is its own reconciliation target**, keyed on the file rather than its parent: two sets backed up into one synced folder are two replicas, and keying on the shared parent would hand each import the other file's ancestor. The directory form's target is byte-identical to before, because changing it would orphan every existing base. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `export-may-name-a-file`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Test and documentation debt section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only. Resolved in [set-lifecycle.md](documents/design/set-lifecycle.md), which had settled it 2026-08-23 with nothing implementing it.

Why the fixed path existed at all is worth keeping, since removing it looks like relaxing a safety rule: it exists for **auto-discovery in a checkout** — *a file found here is a project set no matter what its header claims* — and nothing auto-discovers a backup or a synced folder, where trust comes from the caller's stated expectation through `check_scope` instead.

content: **A store that imports from repository A and exports to B does not make A's memories read as the local user's own.** Import writes `created.by` and `modified.by` exactly as the file carries them (`write_memory` in `src/store.rs`), so the records still name their authors. B's commit truthfully names who committed them, and the export-before-commit convention puts every arrival in that person's diff before the commit. What no record holds is only *which repository* they came from — the gap any copy of code between repositories has, which nobody treats as a defect. Corrects the 2026-08-20 claim that such memories "read as the local user's own additions."
context: Settling whether the set-identity note closes the arrival-provenance issue, after calibrating both shared sets and graduating four common causes to coding-lessons.
why: The human partner asked on 2026-09-24 whether B's `git commit` would not record who committed the memories; checking the import path showed the original claim was wrong on authorship too. The corrected residue is small enough that it bears directly on whether the issue should close.

content: Scatterhoard keeps two lookups over the links table that read the same rows for opposite purposes. `Store::incoming` refuses cross-set rows (`target_set IS NULL`) and feeds resolution, so no foreign edge can change a memory's standing. `Store::claims_against` reads exactly those refused rows (`target_set = ?`) and feeds a report, so a dispute can be named without being obeyed. Keeping them separate is what lets the design report an edge it will not act on; collapsing them would restore the suppression defect.
context: Built 2026-08-23 closing `a-set-can-suppress-another-sets-memory` and the reporting half of `edge-authority-across-sets`. The report is the `disputed_by` field on a recall or lookup hit, carrying the claimant's set, id and label and deliberately not its content.
why: The pairing is easy to mistake for duplication and delete, and deleting either one is a silent regression in a different direction: without the filter on `incoming` a rival set suppresses memories it does not hold, and without `claims_against` a dispute becomes invisible. It is also the shape the design's `report rather than resolve` principle takes in code -- one lookup that acts and one that only describes -- so it is worth recognising as a pattern rather than as an oddity of this table. Checkable in `src/store.rs`; four mutations pin the reporting half and two pin the resolution half.

content: An abnormal outcome returned in the shape of a normal one cannot be told apart from success, so it is acted on as success. In this project: an export written to a doubled path and reported done, memories stored with no vector and no warning, a supersession cycle reporting `superseded_by: []` — byte-identical to nothing superseding it — because both callers discarded `Resolution::Cycle` through catch-all arms, damaged tool calls stored whole, a missing merge driver leaving a file that reads as resolved, and a moved store indistinguishable from an empty one. **The structural fix is to give every distinct outcome a distinct shape** — an enum variant with no catch-all, a note naming what happened — so the caller has something to branch on. The project's *report, not refuse* designs are this fix where refusing would cost more than it saves.
context: Re-deriving the common causes of defects across all 104 issues, and moving them from a hand-written section of TRACKING.md into memories the index is generated from.
why: Not in the original analysis, which saw nine issues; it surfaced across the 95 filed since. No general form exists in `coding-lessons` yet — the nearest, that absence of a failure signal is not evidence of success, is about checks rather than outcomes — so this one is a candidate to graduate. Some of its instances plainly fit another cause as well; this attribution names the one a fix would have to address.

content: **This entry is to be done early, ahead of the questions-first order, and in a session of its own.** Decided 2026-09-23 by the human partner: *we need the ability to drop links*. Until it lands, every supersession has to restate links by hand to avoid carrying ones that no longer hold, and the same day's work already had to be arranged around it — nine entries gated through one list memory rather than nine supersessions. It is context-intensive, touching the store's walk, the memorize path's reporting and the causes region's attribution rule, so it starts a fresh session rather than being fitted into the end of one.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner, after correcting which entry had been forcing the day's workarounds.
why: An exception to the recorded route to release, and recorded as one so the route is not read as violated: questions come first in general, but work that every other piece of work is currently routing around pays for itself by going first. It carries `release-gate` so the next session's recall of that term finds it beside the gated list.

content: A memory *about* a `hoard-` mechanism takes `about-` in front as of 2026-09-06 -- `about-hoard-watch`, never the reserved term -- because a reserved keyword is a control mark and whatever carries one is put in a list something acts on. Measured that day: `hoard-scope-topics` returned nine memories of which four were charters, the other five being design memories about charters, which `route-where` has a session match candidates against as though they described a set. `hoard-author` was clean at four of four. The rule prevents new instances and cannot repair those five: they are exported so amendment is refused, and superseding does not retire a keyword. The `hoard-watch` case escaped only because its recall stopped asking for the reserved term at all, which is not available here.
context: Being told that memories about the watch mechanism should never have been in the reserved space, and measuring how far that had already gone.
why: The measurement is the part worth keeping, because it shows the hazard is live rather than theoretical and shows which way it leans -- the impostors outnumbered the real charters. The unfixability is the other half and is the reason this is filed as an open issue rather than closed with the rule: a later session will reach for a supersession pass, and it does not work, which is documented behaviour rather than a bug. Worth knowing before anyone proposes another reserved keyword: the namespace rule has to arrive with the keyword, since the discussion accumulates fastest while the mechanism is being designed.

content: **The public release is `0.9.0-beta.2`, tagged `v0.9.0-beta.2`**, settled 2026-11-02 by the human partner and set in `Cargo.toml` the same day, so `serverInfo`, `--version` and `server_version` report it. It continues the beta counter from `0.1.0-beta.1` rather than restarting at `beta.1` under the new number, so no two builds share a label, and semver ranks it above the earlier build. The beta label tells everyone the production release will bump the memory file's format version. The pre-release keeps its dot (`beta.2`, never `beta2`), because semver compares dot-separated numeric identifiers as numbers.
context: Going-public checklist: settling the version before publishing, after verifying the GitHub steps.
why: Supersedes `01M6A583TGF0GSJ25PTKTKAJ9T`, which held the number as provisional. `0.1.0-beta.N` understated the tool's maturity, and the public tag is the first most people will see. The earlier scheme memory, `01M4513Z94EA0VQ4FQD6DP63ZV`, still describes the builds tagged so far and is superseded when this tag is cut.

content: A set's derived description reshuffles on a small change: adding two memories to a set of 838 relabelled most of its clusters, so a reader comparing descriptions across commits sees a set that changed character when it did not. The import comparison is unaffected, since it compares identical memories. Fixed when a small change to a set leaves most of its description recognisable, so that a change in the header reflects a change in the set. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-set-description-reshuffles-on-a-small-change`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Found while exporting after fixing a-healed-fork-reports-its-ancestor-as-a-cycle, the first item taken from the open issues and backlog that session.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, severity and fixed-when only. Misleads rather than costs, because the harm is a wrong belief — drift read into a set that did not drift — at the export gate `export-before-commit` now points a session at. The evidence is the member that follows.

content: **The 22 open backlog entries were audited on 2026-09-23 and one was built: `linking-has-no-trigger`.** The other 21 — this memory's keywords — were checked against the code, the served catalog and the corpus, and stay open. Premises verified rather than assumed: the `vectors` table is still `(memory_id, vector)`, `edges()` still reads every link row per recall, nothing writes a README into a memory directory, a store still returns only `summary` and `keyword_delta`, and recall still names one scope. This completes the first `audit-open-entries-for-closure` pass over all three families: 70 entries read, two closed.
context: The closure audit's third and last family, after the issues and the questions.
why: A backlog entry goes stale by being built, which is checkable in a way a question's premise is not — so these were read against the code rather than against their own prose. Two closures in 70 entries is the audit's actual yield, and worth stating plainly: the pass is cheap and mostly confirms, which is an argument for repeating it on a schedule rather than for having skipped it.

content: A reconciliation target was the caller's directory argument as typed, so `/p/proj` and `/p/proj/`, an absolute path and a relative one, and a symlinked route to the same checkout were four targets with four independent base sets — and import reconciled an unrecognised spelling with no ancestor while saying nothing. Fixed 2026-08-26 by normalising at the store boundary and making import say it. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `target-identity-is-an-unnormalised-path-string`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Eight recorded mutations no longer matched their file, so they were guards that ran nothing while the corpus counted them as coverage. Fixed 2026-08-23: all eight re-anchored on text that exists and each confirmed caught by running it. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `eight-mutations-no-longer-match-their-file`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: A seed and a trap are the same object: both are session-start push, so the trigger difference `hoard-watch`'s drafting agenda assumed does not exist, which is what let one convention replace two and needed no budget raise. Advancement is spawning a new head that draws on the observations, not superseding: one observation set can drive several questions and supersession affords one successor. And push is the marked case -- most accumulation stays passive and is reached by ordinary recall -- which is the budget story push had been missing. This is the part of the original memory that survives the 2026-09-06 rewrite; how a memory is marked changed, and is the memory alongside this one.
context: Rewriting the watch convention around the index line, and finding the memory that recorded how it was built had gone half stale.
why: Split rather than amended because only part of the original went stale: it also said one keyword marks push while a second names the kind, and that is now false. The three corrections here are untouched by the rewrite and are the ones a later session would otherwise re-derive expensively -- the spawning one especially, since the re-entry question said transitions are supersessions and following that would fork a chain deliberately.

content: **The breaking-change audit of the open backlog before publication, 2026-10-31, found no entry that changes the memory file's record shape.** Of 20 open entries, `content-hash-keyed-vectors` changes only the store schema, which migrates in place locally as earlier columns have. `in-call-references-for-memorize`, `open-a-set-under-an-alias`, `recall-across-several-evaluation-sets`, `recall-before-storing`, `import-reports-what-arrived`, `forget-is-silent-about-in-links`, `status-reports-which-build-is-running` and `promotion-to-read-write` are additive to the tool surface. The rest are conventions, documents, process or internal caching, apart from `built-in-sync`, which is blocked. The exposure sits in open questions instead: `occurred-time` would add a field, `claim-digest` would if the digest were stored rather than computed, and `merge-without-a-recorded-ancestor` would change how two builds merge.
context: Working through the going-public checklist after the bare-line preferences fix: item 2, the breaking-change audit.
why: A record-shape change is what publication makes expensive: below 1.0 any shape change bumps the minor version, and `check_version` in `src/memory_file.rs` refuses a file whose minor is newer than the build's, so after publication everyone sharing a set would have to upgrade together. Store and tool-surface changes do not have that cost. Recording the result spares the next session from re-reading twenty heads to reach the same answer.

content: **`context` doubles as this project's only answer key, and batch migration broke it: 70% of `scatterhoard` memories share their context word for word, one string appearing on 224 of them.** Measured 2026-09-08 — 719 memories carry a context and only 257 are distinct, the largest groups holding 224, 77 and 75. `coding-lessons`, written one at a time, is 116 distinct of 119. **Nothing in retrieval is harmed, since `context` is deliberately never embedded**, but two other things are. As a held-out answer key it silently becomes unanswerable: asking which single memory a context came from when 224 share it cannot be got right, and a known-item measurement that includes them reports the retrieval as far worse than it is. And as the thing `context` exists for — a handle helping a human place a memory later — *Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry* on 224 memories places nothing. **Always filter to unique contexts before using them as queries**, and prefer a spread sample to a prefix, since ids are chronological and the early memories predate the batches.
context: Running the CSLS re-test, when the scale sweep's numbers collapsed and the answer key turned out to be the cause.
why:
Recorded because the answer key is the instrument every retrieval measurement here depends on, and its flaw looks exactly like a retrieval result: the first run of the scale sweep reported median rank 199 of 721 and it was the key failing, not the scoring. The project has no hand-labelled key for any corpus written since 2026-07-31, so this is the only evaluation material that scales, and knowing how to use it correctly is worth more than any single number taken with it.

The second half is a note about writing practice rather than about code. A per-entry context that says which batch the entry was in is cheap to produce and carries almost nothing; the convention asks for what was being worked on, named the way a person would say it, which a batch label technically satisfies and practically does not.

content: **A single Latin-script keyword lets a Chinese memory store, with a vector built from that keyword alone.** Observed 2026-09-11 UTC on a disposable home: `这个汤需要多放点盐`, with `why` `测试` and the one keyword `soup`, stored as `findable_by_meaning: true`, and the English query *soup salt* ranked it first at **0.461**. `embedding_input` joins content, `why` and keywords before embedding, and `[UNK]` pieces are dropped before pooling, so the Chinese contributes nothing and the vector is `soup`. **So the loud Chinese failure on this entry needs every embedded field to be out of vocabulary**, which ordinary use will rarely produce — identifiers, file names and borrowed terms are Latin. The common Chinese case is therefore a fourth quiet mode: stored, findable, and matched only on its English fragments. When every field is Chinese, the write fails and stops the store — `one-unembeddable-memory-stops-the-store`.
context: Restoring from the checkpoint and starting on the Latin-script recall issue, after the human partner pointed out that English off-domain probes might not calibrate a floor for a store in another language. Reproducing the Chinese write failure on disposable homes.
why:
Recorded because it changes the shape of the language question. The discussion so far had treated Chinese as the loud, safe failure and Russian, Hindi and Japanese as the quiet ones; with any Latin token present Chinese joins the quiet group, and in a worse form than collapse, because the matching looks plausible — the English fragment is often a memory's most specific term.

Found by accident: it confounded the first two attempts to reproduce the store failure. Worth knowing for any later probe of script handling — vary every embedded field, not only `content`.

One memory and one query. The mechanism is read from `embedding_input` and the independently verified forward pass, so its direction is secure; the magnitude is not measured.

content: Sweep the memories that already sit in two clusters and give them real edges. Raised 2026-09-07 by the human partner as the deliberate half of `linking-has-no-trigger`. **The candidate set is already identified and bounded**: 52 memories created on 2026-09-07 carry more than one entry slug, out of 111 entry slugs in the set — co-membership written unprompted, because keywords are required on every store and links are not. Each is a pair a session already judged related at writing time and expressed with the only instrument that was asked for. The pass reads each and asks which of the fourteen labels states the relation, which the 2026-09-02 edge audit found available in 22 of 30 cases. **Built when the multi-slug memories have been read and given the relation they carry, or the pass has reported which ones genuinely have none.** The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `cross-link-the-multi-slug-memories`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Filed while migrating BACKLOG.md, from the human partner's suggestion of an explicit cross-linking pass.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. Filed as its own entry rather than mentioned inside `linking-has-no-trigger`, per the `set-restore` lesson that a tracking file does not catch work named in the prose of an entry about something else.

Ready: the candidate set is derivable today with a keyword count, and the labels all exist. It is reading work rather than design work, which is what makes it separable from the trigger question — and doing it would produce the first real evidence about how much relation the corpus is actually carrying unexpressed.

content: **A set's description is shown at import as well as at export, and at import it is derived from what arrived, never read from the file.** Decided with the human partner 2026-09-12. Their reasoning for import as a second surface: if the receiving model has safeguards, the aggregate picture can engage them there too. And import is the harder gate to skip, since a received set is useless until imported, where export can be declined by anyone content with one SQLite file. Deriving rather than reading is what stops an edited file presenting a self-attested description as a measurement.
context: Retiring the header summary and its comparison, which made the 2026-09-12 decision on where the description lives partly stale.
why: The part of the 2026-09-12 decision still in force, split out when the stored copy and its comparison were retired on 2026-09-21. The two surfaces and the rule against reading a description from a file are unaffected by removing it: the retirement took away what was compared against, not what is shown.

content:
**Acted on 2026-09-07: the steering file was split three ways, which is the shape the entry's own second half was asking about.** `CLAUDE.md` became `AGENTS.md` by `git mv` -- the project's working notes in a form any coding agent reads -- and a new `CLAUDE.md` holds an `@AGENTS.md` import plus only what is Claude Code specific, which turned out to be exactly one thing: the `PreCompact` hook wiring. The import is the documented cross-agent arrangement; Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` and not `AGENTS.md`, so one copy serves both without a second file to maintain. **The third tier is the one the entry did not have a name for and is the reason the split matters:** a Scatterhoard *user* has no checkout at all, so neither file reaches them -- what reaches them is the served catalog plus one line in whatever steering file their own client loads. This makes *interface-neutrality* concrete rather than aspirational: `AGENTS.md` names no client, and the one file that does is the one that may.

Three checks the move needed, none of which any tool reported: `AGENTS.md` had no remaining occurrence of *Claude*; four references elsewhere cited `CLAUDE.md` for content that had moved (two in `open-questions.md`, one in `conventions.md`, two comments in `precompact-checkpoint.sh`) and still resolved while being wrong; and `checklinks.py` cannot see that class, because the target exists.
context: Restarting the MCP client onto a current binary, then splitting CLAUDE.md and writing the cluster-shaping guidance into STANDARDS.md.
why:
The entry asks whether the whole file should travel, and whether it should be split so the parts a contributor needs travel and the parts a working style wants do not. This is that split, performed, with the answer that the Claude-Code-specific residue is far smaller than expected -- one hook -- which is itself evidence about the question, since it means almost nothing in the file was ever client-specific and the coupling was in the filename alone.

Stored under the entry's slug although the entry is not yet migrated and has no head memory, so a slug recall returns this before the head until it does. Recorded here rather than left to the migration because the finding is the action taken today, which the migrated entry body cannot contain: the body predates it.

Not settled by this, and left open deliberately: the security half the entry raises, that a committed steering file is instruction-shaped text arriving by `git pull` and loaded unconditionally with no gate. The split does not address it and arguably sharpens it, since `AGENTS.md` is now read by more tools rather than fewer.

content: A set can be exported from the command line: `scatterhoard export SCOPE --directory DIR`, or `--file PATH`. Built 2026-09-15, so a backup can run on a schedule — export was reachable only from inside a session. It goes through `Server::export_to`, a public wrapper over the same `export_set` the tool calls, so there is no second implementation for a later rule to miss. **The bare invocation still serves MCP.** Argument parsing is `src/cli.rs`; contract in `tests/cli.rs`; written up in [set-lifecycle.md](documents/design/set-lifecycle.md), *export from the command line*. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `export-subcommand`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building command-line export after the link-key fix, in the session that filed the memory-size question. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the head was over the length limit: the head keeps the claim and standing, and the detail moved to members under the slug.
why: Head of the backlog cluster, superseded because the entry is built. The opening sentence is the generated index row, so it says what now exists rather than what was missing. The readiness facet is dropped, as built entries carry none.

content: Measured, then recorded as checked-in fact on 2026-08-05. A `limit: 100000` recall returned thirteen memories: twelve carried `similarity`, one carried `matched_similarity: -0.273` and no `similarity` at all, and nothing in `tools/list`, the tool descriptions or `hoard_conventions` says that entry can occur. [tests/snapshots/tools_list.json](tests/snapshots/tools_list.json) contains zero occurrences of `outputSchema`, so any tool that starts publishing one shows up as a diff; [tests/snapshots/recall_substituted.json](tests/snapshots/recall_substituted.json) puts the whole problem in one file — three entries in one ranked list, the first carrying `matched_similarity` with no `similarity` field at all, the other two carrying `similarity`. **The envelope is inconsistent too, which the snapshots made visible**: `hoard_recall` returns `semantic_search_available` on both paths, `hoard_lookup` returns no such field and no envelope beyond `memories`. Defensible, since lookup does not search, but it is a second undocumented shape difference between two tools returning the same kind of payload.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Turning a claim about an absent contract into a snapshot that fails when it changes — the only available way to guard a shape nothing publishes. The envelope difference is recorded because it was invisible until the two snapshots sat side by side.

content: History from the unification, 2026-09-08: **the human partner asked for the filing prompting to move out of `AGENTS.md` into `TRACKING.md` itself**, so the rules for filing an entry live in the file the entry goes into. Three sections and the four-state table left `AGENTS.md`; what remains is a pointer. **This trades a discovery cost the previous day's reasoning had bought deliberately.** On 2026-09-07 the cluster-shaping guidance was placed in `STANDARDS.md` and reached by proximity -- a link from a path already walked -- with a `hoard-signpost` rejected as spending session budget on something recall reaches once you know to ask. `AGENTS.md` is read at the start of every session and `TRACKING.md` only once a session knows to open it, so the prompting now sits one hop further from the moment it applies. The mitigation is the pointer paragraph and nothing else, and it says so in its own text: if filing ever stops happening, suspect the pointer before suspecting the rules.
context: Unifying the tracking files into TRACKING.md, the morning after the open-questions migration finished.
why: Recorded because a later session finding `AGENTS.md` thin on tracking will reasonably read it as an omission and be tempted to restore a summary there, which is how the three-copies problem this same commit removed would come back. The cost is named rather than hidden so that the mitigation can be judged against evidence later: what would settle it is entries stopping being filed, not an argument.

content: **A moment now reliably produces links between memories already stored, so this is built.** `d66541e` on 2026-09-09 added `recall-when`'s closing clause — when what you recall should be linked to a memory you already hold, connect them before moving on — funded by trimming served rationale, two days after the gap was filed. Measured 2026-09-23 over the corpus, counting links other than `supersedes`: **before 2026-09-09, 99 of 738 memories carried one (13.4%); from 2026-09-09, 247 of 293 (84.3%)**. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `linking-has-no-trigger`; this record carries only its standing.
context: The closure audit's backlog family, after the issues and the questions.
why: Closed on a measurement rather than on the clause existing, because the entry asked for a moment that *reliably* produces links and a served sentence is not evidence that anyone follows it. The 2026-09-07 baseline was three discretionary edges in 390 memories; six times the rate across 293 memories is not a reading that a confound explains away, though the before-period does include migrated heads which carry few edges by construction.

content: Every export-review page recomputed work over the whole set that cannot change between pages, so reviewing a large set timed out. `review_set` in `src/mcp.rs` clustered the subject vectors of the whole set to group a page's few memories, and ran the pre-pass over every pending memory to sort flagged ones first. Found 2026-10-29 on the `scatterhoard` set's full review (1,526 memories), where the client's first two calls timed out. Fixed the same day: the review state keeps the grouping beside `summary::fingerprint` of the subjects it came from, and each memory's pre-pass answer beside its checksum and a digest of the preferences, always-fine values and author names. A change to any input is seen, by this process or another. On a copy of that set, debug build: the first page 21s, later pages 0.6s, from 20s. Three tests in `tests/export_review.rs` and one in `tests/summary.rs`; seven mutations caught.
context: Starting the scatterhoard set's full review under the judgement gate; parked it to fix this, intending to test the fix on that review.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseding the open head now that the fix is built and measured. Blocks: the review gates publication and could not be run on the set the project means to publish. Keyed by inputs rather than invalidated on a signal, because a signal has to be raised by every writer, including another server process, and the code-that-assumes-one-process cause shows how that fails. The first page still pays the full cost once per review; whether 21s fits the client's timeout is to be seen on the real review.

content: **Every mutation-runner run clears a crowded build directory, `--only` and `--start-at` included, since 2026-09-29.** Until then only a whole pass cleared, on the reasoning that `--only` exists to be fast and a from-scratch build costs about fifteen seconds. That reasoning ran the wrong way. Clearing happens only above `CROWDED`, which at about 520 files per mutation is roughly once per 190 mutations' worth of runs, while a crowded directory slows every mutation of every run. `--only` is a name filter that often matches twenty or thirty mutations, so the occasional fifteen seconds is the fast choice. `should_clear` in `scripts/mutate.py` now asks only whether the count is above `CROWDED`.
context: Fixing `the-mutation-runners-crowding-note-fires-on-every-pass` with the human partner.
why: The corrected part of the 2026-09-20 build record, split out following split-when-partly-stale. Decided with the human partner, who asked whether `--only` should clear too. Making it clear on every run is also what removed the last case the end-of-run crowding note had, so the two changes go together.

content: **Two of hybrid search's three blockers have cleared, unnoticed — read 2026-09-23.** The entry blocks on scoring worth ranking with, on the non-match floor, and on a corpus large enough to test against empirically. The corpus was six memories when that was written and is 1,023 now. The floor was built on 2026-09-11 into 2026-09-12 and has been calibrated once for real, at 0.3755 from 26 labelled queries. What has not cleared is the scoring half: nothing has re-measured whether an exact keyword hit and a semantic near-miss can be ranked against each other on a corpus this size. So the entry is a measurement away from being answerable rather than blocked behind unbuilt work.
context: The fuller second pass over the open questions, checking each entry's blockers against what has since shipped.
why: Blockers clear silently: each of the three was someone else's work, none of it done for this entry, and nothing reports to a question that its conditions were met. The entry itself flagged the corpus half as worth watching, which is why it is worth saying outright that the watching has now happened and found two of three gone.

content: **The characterisation of `an-unanswerable-query-returns-confident-hits`, after a day of measurement: seven mechanisms were tried and all seven failed, and they failed for one reason.** Ruled out, each with numbers recorded separately under this slug: an absolute similarity floor; a ratio to the top hit; the largest gap in the ranking; gap-to-median against a null; a per-query z-score; the coherence of the result set; `cos(query, centroid)`; and matching the query against a set's `hoard-scope-topics` charter. **Every one is a function of the same embedding, and the football-versus-bylaws confusion is in that embedding** — so no rescoring of those vectors recovers what they do not encode. Two of the seven fail in ways worth remembering rather than merely recording: **result-set coherence** measures whether a cluster was found and not whether it was the right one, so the off-domain query scores highest of twelve; and **charter matching** measures how abstract a query is, because charters are abstract, so it ranks a football question above *what is the link traversal mechanism*. **What was never tried until the end is changing the embedding itself**, and the first attempt at that reordered the failure. Read that as the direction, not the answer: the entry is not fixed and the ruled-out list is what stops the same ground being covered again.
context: Writing up the day's investigation before deciding what to build.
why:
Recorded as the entry's index because eight separate findings are more than a later session will read, and the useful part is not any one of them but that they share a cause. Without the shared cause the list reads as bad luck and invites a ninth mechanism of the same kind.

The two named failures are singled out because both looked correct on most of their test cases and were killed by one or two queries — coherence by the football query, charters by two narrow technical ones the human partner supplied. That is the pattern of the whole day: every candidate survived the queries that happened to be lying around and died to a case chosen deliberately. Anything proposed here next should be shown the hard cases first rather than last.

content: A rule saying what a returned `context` is for, on the read side. Unblocked 2026-10-03, when `response-shape-is-unpublished` was fixed in `9c62e5c`: recall and lookup now publish output schemas, and `context` has a description there, so the field a client receives can be documented. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `context-gloss-on-recall`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Right after publishing output schemas and restarting the client; updating the entry that issue had been blocking.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded to move readiness from blocked to ready: its named blocker is fixed. One caveat for whoever builds it. An output schema is read by programs, and a host may never show it to the model this rule addresses; whether this client does is unknown. So the schema is a home for documentation but not a guaranteed channel to the reader, and `recall-when`'s served clause, phrased as always, stays the channel known to reach a session at recall time.

content: **Whether the gap sweep should run on writes, or only on recall by meaning.** Resolved 2026-09-22 by the human partner: **only before a search by meaning.** `write` no longer calls `prepare`, since it embeds its own memory and reads nothing the cache holds. The sweep's query now excludes identity records, so it can come back empty. A gap left by another server is filled at the next semantic recall rather than the next write, and nothing reads vectors in between. The findings gathered under this question carry the keyword `where-the-gap-sweep-runs`.
context: Pre-release review of open questions, straight after resolving link-only-write-after-export. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 2 links an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. The evidence is in the member checked the same day. Guarded by `tests/gap_sweep.rs` and a mutation restoring `prepare` to the write path, and by a two-connection test writing through a stale cache. The broader reservation the human partner deferred on 2026-09-11, about the special case's cost, is corrected separately rather than closed.

content: Scatterhoard's live similarity scores sit in a narrow, low band, and negative scores are returned as results. Measured against a five-memory store: a query written specifically to hit one memory scored it 0.32, while a plainly unrelated memory scored 0.135, and a full recall ran 0.110, 0.075, 0.024, -0.045, -0.084. A non-match floor therefore cannot be a hand-picked constant — there is under a factor of two between a deliberate hit and an unrelated memory.
context: Measured 2026-08-03 driving the MCP surface from a client, in the first session after recall began returning whole memories. Recorded as evidence on `no-non-match-floor` in ISSUES.md; scores are centroid-relative, so they depend on corpus composition and should be re-measured on a larger store before anything is built on them.
why: The obvious fix for the no-non-match-floor defect is to drop everything below some threshold, and this measurement says that will not work: any constant that excludes the unrelated memory at 0.135 is uncomfortably close to the 0.32 that a good hit earns. It is why the floor has to be settled together with the cold-start scoring question rather than on its own.

content: **Why it is worth building rather than relying on the convention.** `export-before-commit` already mandates reading the diff, and that is what caught the original incident — but **the gate's own reasoning is about scope errors the exporting session made itself, and it had never met a record the session had not written.** Reporting the delta makes the surprise announce itself instead of depending on the review being done carefully: the same move as putting a length check where the length can be seen. *Where there is no prior file, everything is new and the report should say that rather than reporting a count of zero, since those are different answers.*
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A convention that caught the incident and was not designed for it. Making the condition announce itself rather than relying on a careful reader is this project's standing preference, and the no-prior-file case is the one where a zero would be a lie.

content: **Whether `local` is one set across a person's machines, and what that does to the identity it now mints.** Raised 2026-08-31 by the human partner immediately after `local` was given an identity on the argument that it *never leaves the machine it was written on* -- so there is one store by construction and nothing to fork against. **That premise is load-bearing and has a known expiry.** `local` cannot sync through `git`, which is the whole reason it is exempt from the export gate; but peer-to-peer sync would suit two laptops belonging to one person exactly, and it is the arrangement most likely to be wanted first. **The sharp part is the timing, not the principle.** `Store::claim_set_id_if_local` mints on the first write -- verified 2026-09-07 in `src/store.rs` -- so by the time any sync exists **both machines have already minted, independently, long ago**: precisely the auto-mint hazard this design named and rejected for shared sets, reached through the mechanism added to stop `local` being unable to acquire an identity at all. Changing the rule later does not help, because the rival identities already exist. **So the remedy has to be a reconciliation of two minted values, not a different minting policy** -- and it must be decided *before* peer-to-peer sync is built, not as part of it. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `local-across-machines`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The *decide before building* instruction is carried in the head because it is the entry's operative demand and the one a session would skip: peer-to-peer sync is a feature someone will pick up as a feature, and by the time they meet the rival identities the decision will look like an implementation detail of the thing they are already halfway through.

The timing argument is also the clearest instance in the corpus of a hazard being reached *through* the mechanism added to avoid a different one, which is worth having on record independently of `local`.

content: **A person's sharing preferences are built, 2026-10-20 to 2026-10-22, and served at session start.** When no file exists, `src/preferences.rs` writes `sharing-preferences.md` into the common directory from a template, and never touches it again. `hoard_conventions` then serves the file, with its framing, as the catalog's final JSON field. Its *Never store these words* list is enforced by `hoard_memorize` and `hoard_correct` themselves, because tests on `gemma4:12b` showed that served text alone did not hold a small model to it. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `sharing-preferences-served-at-session-start`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Finishing the one release-gated item: template, framing, route-where and export-before-commit revisions, the never-store list with Chinese support, then committing.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because the entry is built. It meets the old head's test: the template is written once and never changed, and `hoard_conventions` returns the file with its framing. Six local-model runs are recorded under the slug. They found that served text moves a small model only where the file gives a detail another place, and that a refusal works. That is why the build also has the word list, decided along the way in `documents/design/export-review.md`. Localising the template is left open as `preferences-template-language`.

content: A memory *about* a `hoard-` mechanism takes `about-` in front as of 2026-09-06 -- `about-hoard-watch`, never the reserved term -- because a reserved keyword is a control mark and whatever carries one is put in a list something acts on. Measured that day: `hoard-scope-topics` returned nine memories of which four were charters, the other five being design memories about charters, which `route-where` has a session match candidates against as though they described a set. `hoard-author` was clean at four of four. The five were repaired by superseding each with a replacement carrying `about-hoard-scope-topics`, since a keyword hit follows the tip's keywords.
context: Running the re-keying pass and finding the memory that announced the rule among the memories that broke it.
why: Supersedes a version that carried `hoard-scope-topics` itself -- the memory stating the rule was the sixth violation of it, written an hour after the rule shipped and caught by the verification recall rather than by care. Worth keeping as the record of the repair and of how easily the reserved term is reached for: the term is what the memory is *about*, so it is the obvious keyword, which is exactly why the rule has to be a rule rather than an intention. Also worth knowing before anyone proposes another reserved keyword: the namespace rule has to arrive with the keyword, since the discussion accumulates fastest while the mechanism is being designed. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 1 link an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.

content: **The public release will be tagged as a beta, with a version number chosen to reflect its maturity -- probably `0.9.0-beta.2`, tagged `v0.9.0-beta.2` -- rather than continuing `0.1.0-beta.N`.** Stated 2026-10-31 by the human partner; the exact number is not final, but the pre-release keeps its dot (`beta.2`, never `beta2`), as the earlier tags do. The beta label tells everyone that the production release will bump the memory file's format version. Update `version` in `Cargo.toml` when the number is settled; it reaches `serverInfo`, `--version` and `server_version` from that one constant.
context: Working through the going-public checklist: after the breaking-change audit, settling versioning and the history wipe.
why: `0.1.0-beta.N` understates how far the tool has come, and the next public tag is the first most people will see. The dot matters because semver compares dot-separated numeric identifiers as numbers, so `beta.10` follows `beta.2`, where `beta10` would sort before `beta2` as text. Recorded beside the earlier versioning decision rather than superseding it, because the number is still provisional and that memory still describes the builds tagged so far; supersede it when the tag is cut.

content: Found 2026-08-03 attempting to file a genuinely project-scoped memory. The refusal was *correct* — only `local` existed — but **"check the set name" names an action the caller has no way to perform**: no tool listed loaded sets, `tools/list` published the *shape* of a scope but not which values were live, and `hoard_recall`'s "omit to search every loaded set" gave no way to enumerate them either. This is the residue of `schema-underspecifies-scope-and-links` one level down: that issue was about the schema not being constructible and is fixed, while this is about the **inhabited values** — a caller could build a syntactically valid scope and still not discover a usable one except by trying names and reading errors. It gets worse rather than better: with one loaded set the answer is always `local`, but once set names are arbitrary strings chosen by whoever exported them, guessing is the only strategy a client has.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery, and the distinction that makes it a separate defect from the schema one: a schema can be complete about shape and say nothing about which values exist, and only the second is what a caller needs to make a call succeed.

content: **Decided 2026-09-16 by the human partner: read-only loading is built before evaluation mode; a set's load mode is chosen at `create`, stored in its own database's `meta` table, and can change only by one-way promotion to read-write.** **Order:** evaluation mode becomes a special case of read-only. Built the other way round, the mode policy (refusing writes, the watch pull, dropping without a safety copy) would be written inside evaluation mode and then pried back out. Whether an evaluation set lives in memory or in a file is not part of that duplication, since a `Store` is the same code over either connection. **Storage:** `meta` never travels, because export writes records and a header, and `Store::replace_with`, which `restore` uses, clears record tables and leaves `meta` alone (checked in `src/store.rs`). `drop` deletes the database, so the mode goes with the set. **No demotion.** Read-only is chosen at birth, so a read-only set provably has never been written here, and that is what lets it be dropped without a safety copy with no guard stored in the database being destroyed. A distributed set is created read-only and then imported. **Promotion is one-way for a second reason, the human partner's:** promoting means a session reads the set's investigation and collection memories into context, which cannot be undone either. Whether promotion is offered at all is still open. **Read-only means no session writes** (memorize, correct, forget); allowing `import` to refresh a distributed set from a newer file was proposed and not objected to. Design in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md).
context: Settling whether a set can be loaded more than once, after revising the load-modes design.
why: The part of `01M2PTQ6…` that still stands, split out under `split-when-partly-stale`. The stale part, which resolved two holders of one identity by recreating one read-only and let a read-write holder load beside read-only copies, was replaced the same day by the rule that a set identity loads only once, and is superseded separately. Kept because the ordering, storage and no-demotion reasoning are what a session building read-only needs, and none of it changed.

content: **A continuous recall signal read from recent conversation did not discriminate, tested offline 2026-10-05.** Moments: 6 before changes where a helpful memory existed, 7 where none did, and 216 background actions, from session transcripts 2026-09-28 to 2026-10-05. Windows were the last 700 or 3000 characters, either prose alone or prose with commands and edits. The readings were scored against both sets as they stood at each moment: top raw similarity, centred density, confidence-weighted density, supports/contradicts links among the top 10, and peakedness. Against the moments where nothing would have helped, every reading scored AUC 0.37–0.63. The conversation window also never brought the governing memory near: ranks 15–1000, where the session's own written sentence placed it at 2–13.
context: Testing the continuous recall nudge offline from session transcripts, after the gut-feeling-recall headroom result, the morning after the first beta.
why: This answers the human partner's discrimination test before more effort was spent on the idea. The one lead is that top raw similarity beats background actions (AUC 0.69–0.77) but not the known-negative moments, which are also just before a change. So it senses *about to change something*, not *something here to recall*. The value of the per-change recall lies in the session compressing its intent into one sentence, which ambient text does not do. Caveats: 13 labelled moments, thinking blocks redacted in transcripts, and one static model. That rules out a strong signal, not a weak one, hence 0.75.

content: **Whether the publish boundary is three-valued rather than two.** Raised 2026-08-23, falling out of the scalar-scope resolution. `Scope::exports_to` answers `Some(name)` or `None` and the export-review gate keys on it -- but **three situations are being sorted into those two slots**. **(1) No person boundary at all:** a backup, or your own second laptop; no gate is clearly right. **(2) A boundary to known people, no repository:** a household set shared with a spouse, a volunteer board's institutional memory. There is no maintainer for maintainer review to serve, but memories genuinely do reach someone else -- so the mechanical prohibited-data scan arguably still earns its place while the judgement gate plainly does not. **(3) A repository:** the full gate. **Today (1) and (2) both answer `Some(name)` whenever the set is shared**, because a shared set can acquire a repository at any moment, and *publishing later changes nothing structural* is the property protecting the user from a binding choice. **So the current collapse is over-strict in the safe direction and is not a defect** -- the question is whether the middle case deserves its own answer, and the honest reason to hold off is that it cannot be decided from one instance. **Note the trap:** any answer making the gate depend on a *declaration* by the set reintroduces the instruction-shaped channel, since a set describing itself as private would be asking to skip its own scan. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `publish-boundary-three-valued`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

*Over-strict in the safe direction and not a defect* is carried in the head because it decides how urgent this is -- someone finding three cases collapsed into two slots would otherwise file it as a bug and fix it, and the fix is the thing that needs a real instance behind it.

The trap is in the head rather than a member because it rules out the obvious design, and it is the same self-declaration hazard that appears in the trust boundary question -- a set cannot be trusted to describe its own exposure.

content: **A set's own language material is shaped as a hub memory per language, rather than as one long memory.** Agreed with the human partner on 2026-10-04. The hub is short prose carrying a new reserved mark and the `hoard-lang-` tag. It links out to ten memories, each holding one `[anchor, paraphrase, unrelated]` JSON array. Model recommendations link in to the hub, so adding one never supersedes it. The memory length limit stays without exceptions: one long memory of all ten sets would have been its first carve-out, which the human partner declined. Test sentences are embedded like any memory. One that intrudes on ordinary recall is superseded with something less intrusive. Still open: whether a hub may hold recommendations with no sentence sets.
context: Designing agent-supplied test sentences for languages with no built-in ones, after the declared-language check shipped for eight languages (uncommitted).
why: Ten sets of JSON reach about 1,850 of the 2,000 characters in French with `why` and keywords, and six times that if an agent escapes non-ASCII as `\uXXXX`.
