content: **Whether conventions should steer an LLM toward a project's single sources of truth.** Raised 2026-08-03, after ISSUES.md found that a majority of the defects in the built system came from one fact being written down twice and the copies drifting silently. **The engineering rule is now in STANDARDS.md, but a rule in a standards file only helps a session that reads it.** The proposal is a convention pair: **record** a project's authoritative sources as memories when they are established, and **recall** before writing anything that might duplicate one -- a serialiser, a schema, a fixture, a constant, a documented path. **This is a good test of whether Scatterhoard earns its keep**, because it is exactly the class of knowledge that is expensive to rediscover, invisible in the code (the whole problem is that the second copy looks self-consistent), and cheap to state once. **Open:** whether this is one convention or two, and whether it generalises past duplication into *what this project has already decided about how to build*. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `conventions-steer-toward-one-way`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

**One of the entry's three open sub-questions is dropped rather than carried across, because its premise expired.** The entry asks *whether it should wait, since Conventions deliberately keeps the set small until the basic system works, and this would be the first convention added for a reason found by using Scatterhoard rather than by designing it.* That precondition expired on 2026-08-12, when three conventions shipped against it, and what binds now is the character budget. The *first convention found by use* framing is also no longer true -- several have been since. Keeping the sub-question would have preserved a reason to defer that no longer exists.

The *good test of whether Scatterhoard earns its keep* line is kept because it is a claim about the project's own value that can actually be checked, and this question is the check.

content: Three Scatterhoard defects with separate issue numbers share one cause: a store is keyed on the set name alone, so every checkout of a repository shares one store. That forced the reconciliation base to grow a `(record, target)` key, made an unnormalised path string serve as an identity, and left nothing binding a set name to a repository. Giving each checkout its own store, selected through a machine-local registry, dissolves all three instead of fixing them one at a time.
why:
Each defect looked local and had a plausible local fix, and two were filed separately before the shared cause was visible. It came into view by asking what would happen if the store moved into the checkout -- naming the many-to-one mapping directly rather than reasoning forward from any one defect. Worth keeping because the local fixes are still tempting and each would leave the cause in place.</why>
<parameter name="context">Worked out 2026-08-06. Drafted as documents/design/store-registry.md, which is a proposal and is not implemented; the affected issues in ISSUES.md must not be closed on the strength of it.

content: **Where a shipped non-match floor gets the answerable queries it is calibrated from. Resolved 2026-09-11: from a query log the server keeps in the store, locally, and never exports.** The gap that raised it was real — nothing records queries, and the 142 behind every earlier floor figure were recovered from session transcripts after the fact. The answer keeps the history out of the export entirely: the log holds the raw top score per store, the `scope` argument, the ids a recall would have returned and whether the floor silenced it, recorded *before* the floor applies, and no query text. Designed in `documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md`, built as `calibrated-non-match-floor` in the backlog. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `floor-calibration-source`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing the floor question after the signal-frequency measurement, the walk-forward simulations on two stores, and the write-up. Split 2026-09-24 in step 2 of the out-link work, because the head was over the length limit: the head keeps the claim and standing, and the detail moved to members under the slug.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. The answer is a design rather than a choice among the candidates first listed: the human partner's query-log-in-the-export supplied the idea, their question about what would be distributed ruled out harvesting the client's transcripts, and the measurements they asked for set the parameters. Deliberately not closed over: whether a floor is worth shipping at all, because no genuinely off-domain corpus exists on this machine to measure its benefit against.

content:
**The non-match floor works on raw similarity and fails on the centred score the floor stage actually reads.** Walk-forward simulation 2026-09-11, `probe_simulate_a_floor_calibrated_from_labelled_queries`: 85 queries labelled answerable for `scatterhoard` — 59 by naming a scope, 26 by a later use of a returned id — replayed in the order they were asked, against 601 off-domain probes, with the store at 795 memories.

| composition | floor | later real queries lost | off-domain silenced |
|---|---|---|---|
| shipping, centred, from the first 10 | 0.303 | **6 of 75** | 85.7% |
| shipping, centred, from the first 60 | 0.205 | 0 of 25 | **2.7%** |
| **raw cosine, from the first 10** | **0.301** | **0 of 75** | **62.7%** |

**Centred, the admissible floor sinks as queries accumulate** — 0.303 to 0.205 as the lowest real query score falls — and the benefit collapses with it, so under *lose no real query* the floor converges on buying nothing. **Raw, the minimum found in the first ten queries was never undercut by the next 75**, so the floor is stable at 0.301 and silences 62.7% at no cost. Medians agree: labelled 0.526 against a probe median of 0.277 raw, and 0.437 against 0.262 centred.
context: Returning to the floor after the language decision; the human partner asked for the frequency of the answerability signals and a simulation of what recalibration would produce.
why:
The strongest evidence yet that the floor has been asked of the wrong quantity. `Stages::floor` compares `hit.similarity`, which recall reports with the corpus centroid removed, and this investigation already recorded that centring removes the one direction marking a query as out of domain. Ranking can stay centred — that is what centring was measured to improve — while the floor reads the raw content similarity beside it, which means carrying both numbers through the scan rather than choosing between them.

It also answers what a query log would need to store, which was the open question on `floor-calibration-source`: the raw top score per store, not the centred one.

Caveats: one store at today's size, 85 labelled queries from one project, and English probes. The stability of the raw minimum rests on the lowest-scoring of the 85 having arrived in the first ten, which is luck as much as structure — what it supports is that the raw minimum did not drift downward across a month of use, not that it cannot.

content: **A fixed-issue task in `how-much-scatterhoard-lifts-a-small-model` must use the memory set as it stood at the pre-fix commit, not the current one.** The current set remembers the fix itself: its cause, its design and often the code. Recalling it would credit memory with knowing an answer it was handed. The exported `scatterhoard_mem/scatterhoard.json` is committed alongside the code, so checking out the pre-fix commit and importing that file into a scratch home gives the set exactly as a session working on the issue would have had it.
context: After folding the gemma harnesses into scripts/local_model.py; a conversation about running models locally on fixed RAM.
why: The contamination is invisible in the results: an inflated lift looks like success. The fix depends on a project habit, committing the export with the code under `export-before-commit`, which makes the historical set available at no cost. A later session designing the experiment might not connect the two. Inferred while sketching the design, not tested, hence 0.8.

content: **This entry names `adjacency_over`, which no longer exists: the function is `Store::edges`, and the claim still holds.** Read 2026-09-23 — `edges()` prepares `SELECT source, label, target, target_set, target_set_id FROM links` with no scoping and no cache, on every semantic recall, and throws the result away. The `cache_built_at` field on `Store` is the vector cache and does not cover it, which leaves the invalidation the entry proposes — keying the graph to the same `PRAGMA data_version` counter — exactly as available as when it was written.
context: Auditing the backlog family, checking each entry's named symbols against the code.
why: A stale symbol name in an otherwise-correct entry costs the next session a grep that returns nothing, and invites the reading that the work was already done. Recorded rather than fixed by supersession because the claim and the standing are both right; only the pointer moved.

content: `imported-memories-carry-no-arrival-provenance` is a recovery problem rather than a trust problem, and was reduced from Corrupts to Costs on 2026-08-20. Where a store imports from and exports to one checkout, git already records which commit introduced a memory, so an arrival record in the store would be a second copy of that fact. What survives is one store serving two different repositories, which the set-name binding would remove -- so prevention is the load-bearing fix here and the arrival record is the fallback if the binding is refused.
context: Reduced 2026-08-20 while restoring from the previous checkpoint, at the human partner's questioning. Checkable in ISSUES.md under that slug, which keeps the superseded reasoning deliberately, and in documents/design/export-review.md, which gained the matching note about its judgment gate.
why: The entry had argued the reverse, that attribution is the one of detection, prevention and attribution that survives the other two failing. It rested on the upstream-poisoning vector, which is precisely the vector git attributes completely. What separated the two questions was asking what the missing record would be used for rather than what it would prove: three of the four uses turned out to be held by git, by backup hygiene, or by nothing anyone can have without signatures at store time.

content: Found 2026-08-26 testing a prediction of the human partner's — that the graph already carries ancestry through inserts and supersessions, and that **`amend` and `forget` are the two exceptions**. The prediction was right, and following it to `forget` reached this in one step. **Reproduced end to end from a sequence with no thumb drive in it**: store and export, `forget` and export again so the agreement is the tombstone, put the *earlier* file back at the same path, import. Three failures in a row, and the third is the one that matters — **this project wrote a file its own reader refuses**: the import reported an ordinary `took_from_file`, status showed one memory and one tombstone, the export half-succeeded and then failed on the primary key because `stream_records` yielded one id twice, leaving the set exported to a file nothing can import and with no recorded agreement. **Step three is ordinary**: a `git checkout` of an earlier commit, a `git revert`, a file restored from backup, a colleague force-pushing an older state. **`replace_with` already got this right and this path did not** — the replace path had been repaired for the same invariant, and the record-at-a-time path was not examined at the same time.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A defect found by following a prediction about where ancestry is missing, reproduced with only ordinary git operations. The invariant — an id is a memory or a tombstone, never both — is one the file format depends on and no layer enforced.

content: **History from designing the convention, 2026-09-02: two independent reasons a marked memory must be short**, which is usually a sign the constraint is right. A signpost pointing at a README does not rot when the scheme changes, because the README stays the source of truth. And the startup cost only works at signpost length — measured that day, the median memory in `shared:scatterhoard` was **1,383 characters**, so fifteen typical memories is roughly **5,200 tokens, more than the whole convention catalog**, while fifteen signposts of ~350 characters is roughly 1,300. **Marking the memories rather than keeping a list of terms is the load-bearing choice**: a separate list is a second copy of a fact the store already holds, free to drift silently in exactly the way the mechanism exists to prevent — the objection `hoard-scope-keywords` is stuck on in open-questions.
context: Migrating the hoard-watch entry out of BACKLOG.md under its new slug; this was its cost argument.
why:
The median figure is the one thing here that cannot be re-derived to answer the same question: it dated 2026-09-02 and the corpus has since more than doubled, mostly through migration, so today's median measures a different population. It is what justified a length constraint at all, and the constraint it justified was later replaced — the length rule gave way to the derived index on 2026-09-06 — so this records the reasoning of a decision that has since been superseded in the catalog but not refuted.

The marking-not-a-list choice outlived that replacement and still holds: it is why the watch mark lives on the memory rather than in a registry.

content: **Result of the trigger trial, 2026-09-07: the candidate rule — *before writing the summary, check what you worked out rather than looked up* — was run against the last fourteen migrated entries and produced roughly six captures that would otherwise have been conversation-only.** The split-versus-fold counterweight, the per-clone activation lesson, the unnamed filing discipline, the ratchet's general form, the completeness-matrix technique, and the reasoning-versus-probing symmetry. None was a restatement of an entry; each came from noticing one entry re-arguing what another had already argued, which is the cross-entry synthesis that had been evaporating all day. **It also failed once, in a way worth keeping**: it fired correctly on the per-clone activation lesson and the *stored memory was still unusable* — under-specified for a reader who had just been told the same thing. So the trigger governs whether something is recorded and says nothing about whether the record can be read, which is why `memories-must-stand-alone` is filed separately rather than as a clause of the same rule.
context: Wrapping up the session that migrated BACKLOG.md, reporting on the trigger proposed earlier the same day.
why:
Recorded because the result of a stated experiment is exactly the class this session kept finding unrecorded — a trial that is run, works, and is then described only in passing. Six captures across fourteen entries is a rate worth quoting when the convention is drafted, and it was measured under favourable conditions: one author, aware of the hypothesis, on uniform work.

The failure is the more useful half. It separates two checks that would naturally be written as one clause, and it did so before either was drafted, which is cheaper than discovering it after.

content: **A competing explanation that must be settled in the same pass, and if it holds this entry is the wrong instrument.** Recorded 2026-08-24: the labels that actually get written may be the ones whose **target id the workflow already put in the author's hand**, rather than the ones the vocabulary makes easiest to reason about. `supersedes` gets written because `recall-before-storing` and `correct-when` march the caller to the target; `related_to` gets written because it is about whatever is already in context. `motivated_by`, `supports` and `instance_of` each need a separate lookup first. If that is what drives the distribution, **no wording fixes it** — the change would be to the tool surface, not to a convention, and drafting `link-label-choice` would be spending catalog budget on the wrong layer.
context: Migrating the link-label-choice entry out of BACKLOG.md; this was the alternative reading the entry insisted be settled alongside the evaluation.
why:
Recorded at 0.7 because it is a hypothesis with a mechanism and no test yet, and it is the kind that is easy to lose: it does not contradict the measurement, it reinterprets it, so nothing about the numbers will surface it later.

It matters because it changes what the bounded evaluation has to look for. Reading the 26 `related_to` edges for *was a better label available* answers whether the fallback is overused; it does not distinguish an author who chose badly from an author who would have needed a lookup to choose at all. Both questions have to be asked of the same edges, or the pass will be run again.

content: **Immutability applies to memories, not to forgetting -- the answer that reconciled the Golden Rule objection, supplied by the human partner 2026-08-26, and it changes what `forget` is.** The requirement is that a memory mischaracterising a person can be *removed*, and the same for personal information or a secret that reached a set, because mistakes will happen and the escape hatch has to exist. So forgetting must make the harmful text **unreadable** rather than merely stop it being recalled -- which keeps the property the proposal was for, since a memory's checksum still never changes: the memory stops existing and a tombstone takes its place rather than the record being mutated. **What is removed is the text, not the record.** *If the memory record says `Joe is a jerk`, the harmful part is not the UUID or the links, it is the statement.* So `content`, `why` and `context` go -- and **`keywords` with them**, since those are authored free text carrying the same hazard, and a cross-set link's `target_keywords`, the one part of a link that is prose rather than structure. **What is kept is what the graph needs, and that is not a nicety:** a memory's supersession edge is its ancestry, and under an immutable design the chain would be the *only* history a memory has. **The design principle that falls out: keep what the graph needs and remove what a person wrote.**
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
The principle in the last sentence is the durable output of this whole question and is stated nowhere else so compactly. It answers, for any future field, whether forgetting should clear it -- prose a person wrote goes, structure the graph traverses stays -- without needing the field enumerated in advance.

One thing in the entry has since changed and is corrected here rather than carried across: it cited `forgetting-a-chains-middle-makes-a-stale-conclusion-current-again` as *a defect today*, warning that an immutable design would make it fatal. That issue is now marked fixed in ISSUES.md, checked 2026-09-07. The argument still holds -- the reason to keep the edges is unchanged -- but the standing example is no longer live, and a session quoting it as a current defect would be wrong.

content: The convention catalog's length is sentence architecture, not verbosity. Measured over the served text on 2026-08-25: 0.20% of 2,955 words were filler and mean word length was 4.59, so there is nothing to squeeze at the word level -- but `reinforcement` ran at 32.8 words per sentence with 42% of its sentences over 35 words, against 24.2 in `text`. That is the register of a design memo rather than of a standing instruction. Moving sentence boundaries and word order with the wording held fixed brought reinforcement to 22.9 words per sentence and 12% over 35, and took 164 characters off the catalog. Word-level trimming is not a budget lever here.
context: Measured 2026-08-25 across the ten served entries, before and after the restructuring pass. Checkable in the dated comment above CONVENTIONS in src/conventions/catalog.rs, and re-derivable by parsing the string literals out of that file.
why: The open question asked whether 18,000 is too small or the catalog is carrying avoidable length, and the tempting answer to either reading is to cut words. The measurement rules that out and supplies a third answer: the length is in how the sentences are built. It also sets what the change is worth -- 164 characters is a tenth of what a convention needs, so restructuring settles the style question and leaves the budget question exactly where it was.

content: **The question underneath is whether two machines' `local` sets should reconcile at all, and it is a question about the person rather than about the software -- posed 2026-08-31.** Two laptops' personal memories may be one set the person wants unified, or two sets that both happen to be called `local`. **The name cannot distinguish them:** `local` is a scope *kind* here rather than a chosen name, so unlike a shared set there is no naming act carrying the owner's intent. **If they are one set**, one identity has to win and the other be superseded -- and *which* is a judgement no software has grounds for making. **If they are two**, the identities are already correct and what is missing is a way to hold both, which the current design forbids: `local` is one set rather than a class of them, resolved 2026-08-23.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the two branches need different *code*, not just different settings -- one needs identity supersession, the other needs the single-`local` decision reopened -- so this is the fork that has to be settled before anything is built, and the entry's headline about minting timing does not convey it.

Recorded also because it is a case where the software genuinely cannot decide: both readings are coherent and the difference is what the person meant by keeping two machines. That makes it a question for the human partner rather than a design to be worked out, which is worth flagging so a later session does not try to derive an answer.

content: Building a Scatterhoard traversal fixture large enough to have non-seeds is not enough: you must also control *which* memories become seeds, and content intuition will not do it. Scores are cosines against a centroid-removed query, so the centred query points away from the corpus mean and an outlier in the query's own direction routinely ranks below the crowd — with the marker embedder in tests/cross_store.rs, four different content arrangements each put the wrong memories in the top five. The reliable arrangement is to add a purpose-built crowd that outranks the memory under test and pass its ids to `Question::already_holding`, which suppresses them from the results without removing them from the seeds.
context: Found 2026-08-24 while sweeping the hand-edited-file threat model, measuring whether a cross-set EXCEPTION_TO edge carries score to the memory that wrote it.
why: Observing what an edge contributes means reading `inherited` on a memory the walk reached, and a seed never inherits, so a fixture whose subject is accidentally a seed reports 0.0 and looks like an edge that was never walked — indistinguishable from the defect you might be probing for. Four attempts were spent on this before the crowd-plus-already_known arrangement worked; `already_known` suppresses output and not participation, which is exactly the property needed. Checkable at `a_cross_set_dispute_does_not_carry_score_to_the_memory_making_it` in tests/cross_store.rs and at `Question::already_known` in src/store.rs.

content: **Deferred 2026-09-11 UTC: the human partner finds the gap sweep architecturally unsatisfying, and chose to keep it for now.** The objection: a store keeps its model's vectors when a server that cannot supply that model writes, the gaps such a server leaves are the case `reconcile_embeddings` exists for, and the price of that one case is a sweep query on every write and every recall by meaning. Their standing instinct is to be suspicious of special cases, because they tend to distort an architecture. **Kept because every alternative examined costs something the design already rejected:** re-tying the store to whichever model last wrote brings back the two-server tug-of-war; refusing writes from a server without the store's model loses memories; a store-level *has gaps* flag is a second record of what the missing rows already say. **Revisit if the sweep causes problems.** Recorded alongside, so the framing is not lost: the case is not specific to a *missing* model — a server holding a *different* model leaves gaps the same way, since `embed_all` writes nothing into a mismatched store.
context: Designing the fix for the store-stopping embed failure: whether a marker row is needed to tell a tried-and-unrepresentable memory from a genuine gap, and what the gap sweep is for.
why:
A design reservation that is stated and deliberately parked leaves no trace in the code: the sweep will read as settled to any later session, and the person who doubted it will not be there to say so. The trigger for reopening is the human partner's, stated as "if it causes problems" — plausible forms are the sweep showing up in recall or write latency, or a new source of gaps making its per-call query expensive.

The discussion that produced it: the human partner framed a missing model as the null model, which made gaps look like the two-model mixture the design forbids. The resolution was that the mixture rule protects comparisons, and an absent row enters none — but that resolves the rule, not the discomfort, which is about where the cost of the case lands.

content: **Measured 2026-09-28: queries phrased as what a session is about to write find short trigger memories phrased the same way, where they miss the hindsight lessons.** Against `coding-lessons` as written, three activity-phrased queries found none of their target lessons, while hindsight-phrased queries found each at rank 1. In a scratch set holding four triggers (the activity at the moment before the mistake), the three lessons, and two distractor triggers, 7 of 8 activity queries ranked their own trigger or lesson first. The miss was the most realistic query, taken from real work that session: it shared the word "file" with the loading trigger and ranked its own third. Model `potion-base-32M`, a static model that matches largely on shared words; one run, one person's phrasing. The scratch set's contents are in the session scratchpad and were not kept.
context: Discussing with the human partner how `coding-lessons` could help prevent failures in projects that opt in, and whether a habit of recalling before writing could replace signposts.
why: Settles part of whether a set's lessons need a separately written trigger to be found before a mistake, not after it. They do: a lesson is about the failure, and a query formed while writing is about the activity. Whether a recall habit could replace pushed signposts turns on this. It shows triggers are necessary, and not that they are sufficient; that caveat is recorded separately.

content: **Whether to raise the catalog budget a third time, and on what evidence.** Raised 2026-08-25 by the human partner on resolving `catalog-budget-too-small`, which established that drafting is not the constraint. **Gated deliberately on two things, in order:** that the restructured wording has been observed performing across several sessions, per the standing rule that tuning a convention takes living with it rather than reading it; and that the work of adding the conventions needing the room is actually in hand, so the number is argued against a real draft rather than an estimate. The standard is unchanged -- the second raise set *well under 4% of the smallest context window in range* -- and so is the objection: **a budget raised whenever it binds is not a budget.** **As of 2026-09-04 the case expected to force a raise did not**, and the cheaper answer was tried for the first time and worked, so the standing objection is unspent. Never quote a headroom figure from this cluster: the catalog's free space is derived, never written down, and this entry's own figure had drifted to overstate the room by 1,793 characters before being caught. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `third-catalog-budget-raise`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

Deliberately carries no headroom number, which is unusual for this entry and is the point: the entry's history is largely a history of its own figures going stale, so a head that quoted one would be reproducing the defect the cluster records. The two gates are in the head because they are what a session tempted to raise the budget needs to meet, and they are easy to skip past when the free space is small and the pressure is immediate.

content: **A floor from self-queries reproduces the label-derived floor on the two sets that have one, and cannot place a useful floor on an eight-memory set.** Measured 2026-09-24 by `probe_a_floor_without_labelled_queries` in `tests/probes.rs`: each current memory's index line asked against the rest of its set, floor at the 5th percentile less 0.05. It gave 0.372 against a real 0.360 on `scatterhoard` and 0.332 against 0.333 on `coding-lessons`, silencing 1 of 78 real labelled queries. **Negatives from real unscoped traffic fail as a floor**: above every one silences 16 of 50 and 12 of 28 labelled queries, because a query about a neighbouring subject scores like an answerable one. On `governance-docs` the self-query floor is 0.159, below both football queries, and the offside query's 0.376 sits inside the set's own self-query range (median 0.523).
context: Discussing the shape of a backup calibration mode with the human partner, and testing the two candidate sources of evidence against the sets with real labels before building either.
why: The first test of a backup mode against ground truth. It supports self-queries as the backup's rule for a set of any real size, rejects the traffic-negative rule the discussion had favoured, and shows the case that prompted the backup is not a calibration problem at all on a set this small: no floor read from the set separates the offside question from its own answers. The first run counted superseded memories and identity records and flattered the result; restricting to current claims is part of the method.

content: **Trust here is doing three jobs and an in-file identifier can only do two -- the analysis behind the proposal, 2026-08-26.** *Decide whether to read this file at all* is answered by the path and cannot be answered by anything inside the file, since Trigger and Loading settles trust before reading contents: a header token verifies and can never gate. *Is this the same set?* it answers decisively. *Is this the same copy of that set?* it cannot, and that is the gap. **What it closes is more than it first appears:** renaming becomes free, so *the harm is collision, not naming* becomes mechanically checkable rather than a human judgement; the fork case sharpens, with a contributor keeping the identity and a divergence re-minting, one deliberate act at the moment the person knows which they are; and `check_scope` -- which exists in `src/memory_file.rs` -- becomes an identity check rather than agreement about a name. **What it does not close is `a-target-path-can-come-to-mean-a-different-volume`, and the reason is structural:** an identity names the *set*, while a base must distinguish two checkouts of one repository -- which is the entire reason the base is per-target -- so set identity can never be target identity. Two backups of one set at one mount point match throughout and reconcile against the wrong one anyway. That issue was still open when checked on 2026-09-07.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the three-jobs decomposition is the reusable part and is easy to lose: the natural reading of *give it a UUID* is that identity problems go away, and the value of this analysis is stating precisely which one does not and why it structurally cannot.

The negative result matters more than the positives. A later session hitting the target-path defect will reach for set identity as the fix, and this records that the two are different axes rather than that the work was not done.

content: Fixed 2026-08-08 (`f07535e`, and the sweep after it): `meta` carries `embedding_model`, **written when a vector is produced rather than when an embedder is handed over** — holding a model is not what binds a store to one. The identity is the **content hash of the weights file**, because the substitution being caught is a different model arriving at the same configured path, where nothing but the bytes changes. Detection drives the re-embed: a mismatch discards every vector and rebuilds with the model in hand, so the store never holds two models at once. `Embedder::identity` is **required rather than defaulted**, which cost seven test doubles a line each — a default would have to invent a value, and every embedder that did not override it would claim to be the same model as every other, which is the silent agreement this whole mechanism exists to prevent.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and two decisions worth reusing: identity by content hash rather than by configured name, because the attack is a different file at the same path; and a required trait method rather than a defaulted one, because a default identity is an assertion of sameness nobody made.

content: **Evaluation sets are named `eval-<set>-<label>`, and no real set may have a name starting `eval-`.** Decided 2026-09-16 by the human partner. The refusal is what makes the name a trustworthy mark on recalled hits. The alternative was carrying the evaluation status outside the name, as in `scatterhoard (evaluation: issue-3)`, which a real set's name could never counterfeit. **The user chooses the label**, confirmed by the human partner; the LLM passes it on. The software adds the prefix, makes the label valid as a set name, reports the result, and refuses a duplicate. **Proposed enforcement, not yet agreed:** `SetName::new` refuses the prefix everywhere it is called (`create`, file headers, cross-set links), and evaluation names come only from a separate constructor used by the evaluation load. That way a file cannot claim to be an evaluation set and a link cannot name one. It makes counterfeiting unrepresentable without adding a third `Scope` kind, which would reopen the 2026-08-23 resolution that there are exactly two.
context: Revising the load-modes design: naming evaluation sets so several can be open at once, and whether create asks about read-only.
why: The prefix is a namespace reservation in a name that means the same thing on every machine, so it has to be refused at every entry point, not only at `create`, or a file or a link could carry the mark falsely. No set on this machine starts `eval-` (the `hoard_sets status` listing holds `scatterhoard`, `coding-lessons`, `governance-docs` and `local`), and the project has no remote, so the reservation strands nobody known.

content: route-where gained a third compiled override on 2026-08-13: no shared set takes people as its subject, whatever its hoard-scope-topics description claims, so a memory about a person goes with the work it concerns or to the personal set. It is scoped to shared sets because the personal set is the acknowledged catch-all and never travels. Accepted consequence, not an oversight: this forbids a team set whose charter is personnel notes.
context: Decided 2026-08-13 resolving the open question about a set whose declared charter is people. Checkable in ROUTE_WHERE in src/conventions/catalog.rs and the "Resolved: the person clauses" section of documents/design/conventions.md.
why: It closes the hole the rejected keyword clause could never have closed, and it had to go in the compiled overrides rather than the topical descriptions because this is the one set description whose faithful execution produces the artefact the Golden Rule exists to prevent. The placement argument is decision-placement applied to a safeguard: aggregation harm is a property of the set, since a dossier can be assembled entirely from individually answerable, work-serving memories, so no rule examining one memory at a time can see it and routing is the only layer that can. The transparency argument on the other side is real -- a charter is visible and reviewed like any other memory -- and is the thing to revisit if the trade ever looks wrong.

content: **Whether `store-when`'s person material should be a convention of its own.** Raised 2026-08-13 after it came up three times in one session without being written down, which is the signal open-questions exists to catch. **What makes it genuinely open is that the obvious fix has a real cost.** The person clause works precisely because it restates `store-when`'s own two demands -- earn its place, name where it can be checked -- applied without the exemption a judgement about someone quietly gets. Split into its own convention it must either restate them a second time, which is two copies of one rule free to drift, or refer to them, which reintroduces exactly the derivation leap the restatement was written to remove. **Reduced by decision placement to a question about paging and the tool surface**, not about drafting: a session reads the whole catalog either way, so the split changes nothing for any reader that exists -- and the question is whether there is ever a reader who gets `store-when` without the rest. Not a defect: nothing in the entry is wrong, and the 2026-08-13 rewrite is why it is right. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `store-when-person-material`; this record carries only its standing.

content: Keyword recall ignored `already_known`, so ids a caller said it held came back anyway. Fixed 2026-09-29, and at the human partner's request retrieval was rebuilt in the shape it should have had. Each store is read by a `KeywordCursor` in `src/store.rs`, in rank order, `KEYWORD_BATCH` ids at a time, skipping held and superseded ids before loading a record. `search_keywords_across_holding` merges the cursors one hit at a time and stops at `limit`, so a page is full whenever enough matches exist. Ties now break on the id of the memory that matched. Pinned by two paging tests in `tests/mcp.rs`, a multi-batch test in `tests/other_paths.rs`, a substituted-and-held test in `tests/cross_store.rs`, and mutations. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `keyword-recall-ignores-already-known`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Taking the contained misleads-severity issues after the served-text indentation fix; the human partner questioned the first version before it was committed.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed. The fix first shipped as a filter after the per-store cut, with each store over-fetched by the number of held ids. The human partner asked whether retrieval pulled every hit into memory. It did read every matching id, loaded up to `limit` records per store, and computed claims for all of them, and the over-fetch made it load the held records it then discarded. They asked for a bounded fetch-filter-repeat loop instead. The tie-break moved to the matched memory's id so the merge can stream; ordering by the replacement's id would need a whole tier read first, and a one-keyword query is one tier.

content: The first attempt at the fix redefined `semantic_search_available` as *did the semantic path run*, which broke the keyword path — that field is deliberately a **capability** statement there, since keyword search runs no semantic search and cannot report whether one happened. That is the already-fixed *keyword-only recall lies about semantic_search_available*, reintroduced. What surfaced it before it landed was the **approval diff flipping one value from `true` to `false`**; nothing else in the change looked wrong. `recall_partial_coverage` now records the case that had no fixture — real hits from one set, the other named with its reason — and three mutations are recorded, all caught.

why: A regression that reintroduced an already-fixed defect and was caught only by a snapshot diff, not by a failing assertion. Recorded because it is the argument for approval tests over hand-written assertions on response shape.

content: **Every figure in the original argument had moved by 2026-09-07, and they moved in opposite directions -- observation made on migrating the entry, re-derived that day.** The size argument is weaker and the proportion argument is much stronger. `store-when` is **2,410 characters**, essentially unchanged from the 2,400 recorded in 2026-08-13. But the catalog is now **17,680** rather than 14,632, so it holds **13.6%** rather than *a sixth*; and the next largest, `route-where`, has grown to **2,053**, so the lead is **17%** rather than 60%. Meanwhile the person clause is now **63%** of the entry -- 48% of `text`, 74% of `reinforcement` -- against the *roughly 40%* first recorded. So the convention has stopped being conspicuously large while becoming mostly about people. **And one of the two triggers named as hypothetical now exists:** `conventions::get(id)` is implemented at `src/conventions/mod.rs`. It has **no callers**, so no reader yet receives `store-when` without the rest and the reduction still holds -- but the entry's *could change that* has become *is built and unused*, which is a much shorter distance. Re-derive rather than quote: `cargo test --test conventions report_catalog_size -- --ignored --nocapture` for the total, and `grep -rn "conventions::get" src/` for the callers.

A later session reading only the 2026-08-13 member would argue from a 60% size gap that no longer exists.

Confidence is high because every figure was measured rather than inferred, and the commands that produced them are named so the next reading can disagree with this one.

content: **Set identity shipped and did not dissolve this question, because nothing checks it -- verified 2026-09-07.** `set-uuid` predicted it would *largely dissolve* this entry, on the reasoning that renaming becomes free and *the harm is collision, not naming* becomes mechanically checkable rather than a human judgement. **Identity did ship**, and it does travel: `set_id` is a field on the file header in `src/memory_file.rs`, deliberately `Option` so a file written before identity existed still reads. **But `check_scope` compares only the declared `Scope`** -- `Expectation::Exactly` against the scope, `AnyShared` against the kind -- and never looks at `set_id`. So two unrelated sets both named `notes` still satisfy the check, which is precisely the accidental-import case `set-uuid`'s own cluster records as the one thing identity remains the only answer to and *no operation added since does any part of*. **The prerequisite is built and the check is not**, which is a much smaller gap than the entry describes but is not the same as being closed.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Recorded because the prediction is in the corpus and would otherwise be believed: a session reading `set-uuid` would reasonably conclude this entry had lapsed, and the file would agree with them by saying nothing. Naming the exact function that does not do the check makes the remaining work a few lines rather than a design.

Verify before relying on it -- `check_scope` in `src/memory_file.rs`, and whether `set_id` appears anywhere in the import path -- since this is the kind of gap that gets closed without the question being updated, which is how the entry got into this state in the first place.

content:
**A description of each memory set, derived from its own contents, is built, 2026-09-12 into 2026-09-13, with its seeding corrected 2026-09-14**: shown at export, written into the exported file, recomputed at import, and owed at session start when an import could not give it. Designed in `documents/design/golden-rule.md` under demand C and `documents/design/export-review.md` section 4; contracts in `tests/summary.rs` and `tests/set_description.rs`.

What ships: spherical k-means over the stored embeddings, seeded by `k-means++` with each memory's draw keyed by a hash of its id, keeping the most cohesive of ten seedings — so a small change to a set leaves its grouping largely intact, and every machine computes the same partition (derivation `clusters/2`; `clusters/1` drew by position, see `a-set-description-reshuffles-on-a-small-change`); `k` from `round(1.2 · ln n)` clamped to 2..12; each cluster labelled by its most distinctive keywords; `describes` on the export response, after embedding anything missing; the header field `summary`, carrying the derivation and model; an import that recomputes rather than reads back and gives `against_the_claim`, comparing only under the same model and derivation and only when the set holds exactly what the file brought; an owed description, recorded when any arriving memory lacks a vector and reported by `hoard_conventions` at every session start until an export describes the whole set; and an `export-before-commit` clause telling a session to read the description against the charter, implying nothing about the motives of the memories' authors.

**`FORMAT_VERSION` stayed `0.4.0`**: an optional field an older reader skips takes no bump. **Still open, and deliberately**: the `k` rule is calibrated on two sets of one project; keywords are user-controlled, so labels can be steered by a deliberate act, which defence against a determined actor does not attempt to stop; and a file's `summary` can be deleted before shipping, which leaves the importing machine's own description standing but removes the comparison. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `derived-set-summary`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Fixing a-set-description-reshuffles-on-a-small-change, the second item taken from the open issues that session, after the healed-fork fix.
why: Head of the backlog cluster, superseded because the seeding it described changed: it said seeds came from a constant generator, which was the positional draw `a-set-description-reshuffles-on-a-small-change` found and replaced. Standing stays built; only what ships changed.

content: The mutation "reembed: report the memories offered rather than the vectors written" is recorded as caught and survives: it no longer changes anything any test sees. Its reason, and the comment beside `let embedded = self.embed_all(&borrowed)` in `src/store.rs`, say the rebuild's input includes identity records and so overstates by one per set. But the input now comes from `memories_without_vectors`, whose query excludes identity records (`m.created_by <> m.id`), so input and output differ only by memories the model cannot represent, and no reembed test builds one. Found 2026-09-27 by a full mutation pass; it survives at `b74929c` too, so it predates that session. Fixed when a reembed test includes a memory the model refuses and asserts `vectors_rebuilt` excludes it, and the comment says why the count is the output's. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-reembed-count-mutation-no-longer-changes-anything`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Reading the results of a full mutation pass after building the local-set refusal on the release gate, while discussing how `coding-lessons` signposts propagate to projects.
why: Head of an issue cluster. Misleads: the corpus claims coverage for the reembed count that the suite does not have, and a later change reporting the intended count instead of the written one would pass. The mechanism is the shape `a-check-that-cannot-fail` names: a guard moved upstream, and the mutation proving the downstream count kept its `caught` label with nothing left to catch.

content: Fixed 2026-09-06 by recognising an identity record structurally: `Memory::is_identity_record` asks whether the record **attributes itself** — `created.by == id`, which both mint paths produce via `Memory::self_attributed` and which `hoard_memorize` cannot produce, since it mints a fresh id and attributes it to the author record's. Five sites asked the keyword question and all five now ask the structural one. The keyword still marks these records for *search*, which is how a caller finds the identities to choose between; nothing branches on it, so using it as a subject now costs a stray hit and nothing else. The misleading note needed no separate fix: `hoard_memorize` never stores an identity record, so a false `findable_by_meaning` from that tool can now only mean model trouble, which is what the note says.

why: The fix, and the shape of it worth reusing: the filter now keys on something a caller cannot write. Recorded with the site name so a later session can check whether it still holds.

content: **Whether 18,000 characters is too small for an effective catalog, or the catalog is carrying avoidable length. Resolved 2026-08-25: neither, and the third answer is the useful one -- the length was sentence architecture.** A whole-file read, with a mechanical n-gram pass across entries behind it, found no avoidable length to speak of and no case that the budget was wrong. What it found instead was **register**: `reinforcement` was being written in the shape of a design memo rather than a standing instruction, and restructuring it -- sentence boundaries and word order only, wording and arguments held fixed -- recovered 164 characters. **So drafting was not the constraint, and neither was it free.** 164 characters is about a tenth of what one new convention needs, which settles the style question and leaves the budget question standing exactly where it was. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `catalog-budget-too-small`; this record carries only its standing.

content: The detector was built 2026-08-13 as a **remark rather than a refusal**, and the reasoning is worth keeping because it was later reversed. `hoard_memorize` scanned the stored prose for tool-call framing and added `suspect_markup` naming the polluted fields plus a note explaining the cause, **listing which text fields arrived empty**, and naming the remedy. **Naming what did *not* arrive is the actionable half**: the server cannot know what was intended, the caller can, and the swallow eats the parameters *after* the one closed badly. A remark and not a refusal because the failure is in emission, so refusing would discard a memory the caller cannot reliably re-send. **Two repairs are wrong and both are the first thing anyone reaches for.** Making `why` required would trade away a decided property — it is optional *"deliberately so: a type that demanded reasoning would make the LLM invent some when it has none, which produces a worse memory than an honest omission"* — and reversing a quality decision to catch a parsing bug is the wrong trade. Ordering a required parameter after `content` depends on emission order nothing here controls, since the published schema's properties come out alphabetical, and a parameter added *only* to be swallowed would be a control with no decision behind it.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The first mitigation, with the two obvious fixes ruled out for reasons that still hold. Kept as written because the remark-not-refusal argument was overturned six days later, and the reason it was overturned only makes sense against the reason it was adopted.

content: **The name collision is the lesser half**: `check_scope` makes the file's header agree with the caller's stated scope, and two unrelated sets legitimately named the same thing agree — but [Open Questions](documents/design/open-questions.md) already settles that *"the harm is collision, not naming"*, and an empty store adopting a stranger's set contaminates nothing. The corruption is the stale base, not the shared name. **`drop` is what makes the human partner's original scenario safe, and the safety does not generalise**: dropping destroys the store *and its `bases` table*, so a re-created set importing from the new drive resolves every record `(None, None)` → `NewFromFile`. Remove the drop from the scenario and nothing protects it. **A content fingerprint per target does not fix this, and the reason matters** — it was the obvious proposal and the human partner's next question retired it: a maintainer checking out a contributor's branch changes the file at that path too, and [Set Lifecycle](documents/design/set-lifecycle.md) already records that a branch switch, a checkout or a `git clean` does exactly that. Identical evidence, opposite required responses — the base is merge ancestry, and the file moving on afterwards is the situation an ancestor *exists for*, not evidence against it. What needs identifying is the **replica**, not the file's contents.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Three things a reader would otherwise re-derive: why the shared name is not the problem, why the scenario as first told is safe for a reason that does not transfer, and why the obvious fingerprint fix is defeated by an ordinary git operation producing identical evidence.

content: Two recorded mutations were disturbed by the change and both were repaired rather than explained away. `keywords: skip validity resolution` went **stale** when the loop became a `let ... else`, and was re-anchored. `view: stop reporting the substitution behind a keyword hit` began **surviving**, because the only covered producer of a keyword substitution had left that path — the *adding a layer un-tests a guard* shape — and was re-covered by a new test on the cross-set concession. A third test, `keyword_search_substitutes_a_superseded_memory`, passed before and after the change for different reasons, its name naming a mechanism it no longer exercised; it was renamed, and the case it never covered added beside it.

content: Do not quote Scatterhoard's convention catalog size from a document; derive it. The enforced figure is what `catalog_fits_context_budget` in tests/conventions.rs sums — `id + text + reinforcement` over every entry — and it is not the same as the paging measure, `text + reinforcement`, which is 166 characters smaller because the ten ids are excluded. On 2026-08-29 the enforced total was 16,988 of 18,000 with 1,012 free, and the paging measure 16,822. Three design-document sites recorded 16,978 and 1,022, which was wrong, and the paging figure beside it did not reconcile with it either, so two figures were adrift at once and their errors partly hid each other.
context: Re-derived 2026-08-29 while recording the corrections rework, by running the catalog-size report added beside the budget test. content: Filed as Corrupts and downgraded to Misleads the same day, after the human partner asked whether a newly stored memory would really conflict. It does not. A memory the file has never held never reaches `resolve` at all — store-only ids route to `resolve_absent_from_file`, which with no base returns `KeepLocal`. Supersession leaves the superseded record's checksum untouched, because `superseded_by` is derived from links at read time rather than written back onto the old row, so the new memory is `KeepLocal` and the old one is `Converged`. With no base, identical content is `Converged` and anything else is `Conflict` — and a conflict is reported, never resolved, so nothing is lost either way. **What is left is one spurious conflict per `amend` or `forget` applied to an already-exported memory since the last agreement with that target**, and zero if the session only added memories. The reconciliation model degrades safely with no base; the defect is that nothing says why.

why: A severity downgrade established by reading the code rather than by argument, prompted by one question from the human partner. Worth keeping because the reasoning bounds the blast radius exactly, and a later reader meeting the entry would otherwise re-derive it.

content: Offer an identity default from the origin's remote URL. **Blocked: neither repository has a remote, and this cannot be exercised until one does** — which is a decision rather than an omission, recorded in the release-gate signpost this entry depends on. The defaults today are settled — `SCATTERHOARD_AUTHOR`, `$USER` for `local` alone, and an honest blank otherwise, with `git config` deliberately not among them. **What is missing is the one automatic source shaped correctly**: the owner component of a remote URL (`jtcours` in `git@github.com:jtcours/scatterhoard.git`) is a handle *in the origin's namespace*, which is the kind of string an author record wants, and it varies per repository, which is the granularity identity-as-a-function-of-origin calls for. `git config user.name` has neither property. Built when a set whose repository has a remote offers the owner component as the pre-filled answer to *which record is you*, above `$USER` and below `SCATTERHOARD_AUTHOR`, with the offer **suppressed rather than guessed** when the remote is absent or the URL does not parse. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `author-default-from-remote-url`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; the last entry of the Configuration and process topology section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only.

**Why it is only ever an enhancement, and this belongs with the standing rather than in a member because it bounds what the entry may become.** The owner is not the author for an org repo, a fork, or anything you contribute to without owning, so it can offer *someone else's* handle — which means it must be offered and never written, and must be droppable when it looks wrong. And it is unavailable at the moment it is most wanted: the identity question has to be answerable **before** publication, because the record-shape window closes at the first push. A source that needs a remote cannot be the mechanism.

content: **The goal is not equal response across sets. A store scoring low on a question it is not about is the system working, and the payoff is saved cycles and context.** Stated by the human partner 2026-09-09 while the non-match floor was being worked up: asking *how often do directories change* against `governance-docs` **should** answer poorly, because that store is not about directories; and if *what are the current bylaws* scored low against `scatterhoard`, that would be a good outcome, not a defect — nothing would be spent on answers that do not match the question. **This corrects a drift in how the calibration work was being framed.** Per-store floors had begun to be justified as compensating for stores that behave differently, which reads as though the differences were a fault to normalise away. They are not: the floors differ **because the stores legitimately differ**, and the measured spread (p90 from 0.089 on an 8-memory set to 0.286 on a 429-memory one) is the signal rather than the noise. The property that matters is entirely **within** a store — that its unanswerable queries score below its answerable ones — and no comparison of levels **between** stores is a target.
context: Wrapping up a long session on the non-match floor, just before checkpointing and committing, when the human partner set out what the feature is actually for.
why:
Recorded because it is a statement of what the feature is for, made by the person whose call that is, and because it was needed: a day of cross-corpus measurement makes between-set comparison feel like the object of study, and it is not. The tables comparing `scatterhoard` against `coding-lessons` against the traversal corpus answer *how much does a floor vary*, which is a question about implementation cost. They do not define success, and read without this they could easily be mistaken for defining it.

Confidence 0.95: stated outright by the human partner, in their own framing.

content: Found 2026-08-21 by `write-surface-matrix`: every property on `hoard_memorize` and `hoard_correct` carried a description except `keywords`, so a caller reading the published schema learned the field exists and takes strings and nothing else — not that keywords are the exact-match path, not that they are the only path that works with no embedding model loaded, not that a coined spelling should match one already in use. Most of that belongs to the `keyword-standards` convention rather than to a schema, and a schema should not restate a convention; but the other seven properties manage a sentence each, and the field with a whole convention behind it was the one that said nothing. Fixed 2026-08-21 with *"Terms for exact-match search, and the only path that still works with no embedding model loaded. See the `keyword-standards` convention for how to choose and spell them."* — **pointing at the convention rather than restating it, because that convention is served into the same session and is already in front of the reader**, the boundary recorded on 2026-08-13: restate what the reader does not have, point at what they do.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The gap and the fix together, kept for the boundary rule they turn on: restate what the reader does not have, point at what they do. That is what makes a one-sentence schema description the right size rather than a summary of the convention.

content: Found 2026-08-09 by the human partner, noticing `target/debug/deps` at 159K files and asking whether the alerts should have fired by now. They should have; neither did. Measured across three full passes in one session: **+28% between two runs about eight minutes apart** — 1.66s then 2.12s per mutation, comparing only the 88 mutations applied in both, so not an artifact of the six added since — roughly 2× the recorded healthy figure, with the file count at 80% of its threshold and the pace at 42% of its. **The file-count assumption is falsified outright**: its comment read *"a busy day of building reaches roughly 40,000, so this leaves plenty of room"*, and one day of this session's work reached 159,000, about four times that rate. **Mutation testing is the heaviest contributor**, because every mutation is a fresh link — so the tool that watches for the problem is the main thing producing it, and its own threshold was tuned as though it were a bystander. *The workaround was already visible and is the tell: full passes had moved to the background during that session because they take four minutes, which is the accommodation behaviour the `coding-lessons` set names.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A threshold calibrated on the assumption that the tool holding it is a bystander, when it is the main producer of what it measures. The accommodation — moving passes to the background — is the signal that arrived before the alert did.

content: The general shape is worth noting for whatever is built next: `store.insert` is shared by an **authoring** path, where refusing is cheap and correct, and an **import** path, where refusing costs the file. A write-time check added to `insert` inherits both callers whether or not that was intended. So the fix was deliberately **not** removing `check_no_cycle` from `insert` — it is correct for `hoard_memorize`, where a caller is authoring one edge and can fix it.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: One write function serving two callers with opposite tolerances for refusal. Recorded on its own because it predicts the next occurrence rather than describing this one, and because the tempting fix — drop the check — is wrong for the caller it was written for.

content: **Four open questions each resolve into new convention text, and the catalog has 24 characters free — but the budget constrains shipping, not reasoning.** `meta-observation-convention`, `memories-must-stand-alone`, `conventions-steer-toward-one-way` and `store-when-person-material` can be worked through now: the human partner stated on 2026-09-12 that headroom must not constrain reasoning — establish whether a solution exists and what it costs, then decide whether it can be afforded — and that they would raise the budget for something important enough.
