content: **First live calibration, 2026-09-17: `scatterhoard`'s floor is 0.3755, read from 26 labelled queries.** The human partner asked for it immediately after `status` began reporting calibration state, wanting run-time with a floor in place. Before this, no set on this machine had ever been calibrated, though the query log had been running since 2026-09-11. State straight afterwards: `scatterhoard` at floor 0.3755 with 0 labelled queries since; `coding-lessons` and `local` still uncalibrated, with 9 and 3 labelled queries accrued — both short of the 20 a calibration reads. **What to watch, since this is the first level ever set from real traffic rather than simulation**: whether recall starts answering *nothing* for questions the set can in fact answer, which would say the 5th percentile and the 0.05 margin are too tight on a corpus this size; and whether a scoped query lowers the floor on the spot, which is the self-correcting path and has never fired outside tests. Both bear on `floor-calibration-source`, whose open part is whether those constants, read off two stores of one project, generalise.
context: Calibrating scatterhoard right after building the calibration report, before starting evaluation mode.
why: Recorded because it is the zero point for every later judgement about the floor: a level that looks wrong in a month is only interpretable against what it was set from and when. The numbers are from the calibration's own response and a direct read of the three databases, not carried forward from earlier in the session — an earlier message in this session quoted total logged queries where labelled ones were meant.

content:
Measured 2026-09-14, confirming the suspected mechanism: **drawing k-means++ seeds by index is what makes the set description reshuffle**, and drawing them by a key that belongs to each memory almost removes it. `probe_how_stable_a_set_description_is` in `tests/probes.rs` partitions each live set whole and again with one memory removed at eight spread positions; its copy of the algorithm reproduced the shipped cluster sizes exactly on both sets, in both runs.

Two runs the same day. The first compared seeding by index against a key hashed from each memory's **vector**; the human partner then asked whether a vector hash survives machines whose embeddings differ in the last bit, which it would not, so the second added a key hashed from the memory's **id**. Figures below are adjusted Rand against the whole-set partition (mean / min), labels kept of 6, cohesion, from the second run unless marked.

`shared:scatterhoard`, 845 memories, k=8:
- as shipped: 0.608 / 0.439, 3.83, 0.7876 (the first run, at 844 memories, gave 0.499 / 0.395 — the baseline itself flaps)
- run to convergence instead of 25 passes: 0.609 / 0.439 — **the pass cap is not the cause**
- by index, best of 10 restarts: 0.453 / 0.407, 3.14
- by vector key: 0.923 / 0.702, 5.62; best of 10: 0.889 / 0.425, 5.42
- **by id key: 0.973 / 0.932, 5.78, 0.7886; best of 10: 0.974 / 0.946, 5.91, 0.7894**

`shared:coding-lessons`, 136 memories, k=6: as shipped 0.878 / 0.508, 5.40, 0.7855; by index best of 10 0.455 / 0.342; by vector key 0.933 / 0.871, 5.71; **by id key 0.923 / 0.572, 5.52, 0.7806; by id key best of 10 0.992 / 0.983, 5.96, 0.7860**.

**Restarts help only when each restart's seeds are themselves stable.** With index draws every restart shifts on an insertion, so choosing the best of ten flips between near-equal optima and is worse than one run. With id keys the ten candidate partitions barely move, so the best of them is chosen consistently, and it was the most stable and among the most cohesive variant on both sets. An id-derived key also needs no floating-point agreement between machines and puts no id into the output, since it is used only to choose seeds.
context: Taking a-set-description-reshuffles-on-a-small-change as the next item after the healed-fork fix, at the human partner's request, because a description that flaps gets ignored.
why: The measurement that turns the issue's hypothesis into a cause and chooses the remedy. It records the negative result for restarts together with the condition under which it reverses, since "restarts make it worse" stated alone would have ruled out the variant that measured best. Kept reproducible by the probe, since the numbers move as the sets grow — the baseline moved by a tenth of ARI between two runs one memory apart.

content: **A recalled lesson changed what got written, 2026-09-28: the first part-6 observation under `coding-lessons`.** Before building `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`, a query asking whether clients enforce a tool schema's `enum` returned the lesson on making a test be the client. That showed the restating rule would be unreachable while `links_schema` publishes the label as an `enum`, and the schema change was decided before any code was written. It surfaced from a deliberate question, not from the per-change recall: the per-change query for the same work returned only the entry's own records.
context: Starting to build `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`, right after closing `adopting-coding-lessons`.
why: Part 6 of the adoption guide: observations like this are the only evidence the habit prevents anything, and the release gate waits on them. The distinction between which recall found it matters for judging the habit itself: the prescribed per-change query missed, so this counts for recalling in general rather than for the per-change sentence.

content: A convention prompting the LLM to expose fresh memories before committing. Built 2026-08-12 as `export-before-commit`, and split in two on the way. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `pre-commit-convention`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: The failure is healing a fork, and the cause is one visited set doing two jobs. Where `X` was superseded independently by `A` and by `B` — which the design explicitly expects when two people advance the same record — and a later `C` supersedes both, `resolve_supersession(X)` returns `Cycle`. `A` and `B` still resolve to `C` correctly; only the shared ancestor breaks, and that is the memory every older link points at. The walk in `resolve_supersession` in [store.rs](src/store.rs) guards with `if replacement == id || !seen.insert(replacement) { return Ok(Resolution::Cycle) }`: reaching a node twice is a cycle *or* a diamond, and that guard cannot tell them apart. The write-time cycle refusal does not catch it either — inserting `C` is accepted.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The cause, named where it can be checked, and the reason the blast radius is the worst possible one: the ancestor is precisely the id that older links still point at, so the damage lands on the memories nobody has reauthored.

content: **`violates` has no stored reverse, and the one case that would want one is a rule recorded after the practice that breaks it.** The in-link is derived: a lookup on the rule shows `incoming` `{label: "violates", source}`, read as *is violated by*, or `referenced_from` across sets; `exception_to` is the same. Stored reverses exist only where the newer memory's side is free — `causes`/`results_from`, and `superseded_by` for a scope reason — resting on the measurement that 29 of 29 edges pointed outbound from the newer memory. That corpus was about design, where a violation is found after its rule. A set analysing documents, such as `governance-docs`, learns in reading order rather than logical order, so the rule can arrive second and the only recourse is superseding the older memory to add the link.
context: Settling `violates-belongs-in-memory` with the human partner, who asked what its in-link counterpart is.
why: Raised by the human partner asking for the in-link counterpart of `violates`. Recorded at modest confidence because nothing has yet happened: it names where the direction assumption is likeliest to fail and what the failure would cost, so the evidence is recognisable when `governance-docs` grows. A reverse label would be a format change, which `unrecognised-link-labels-on-import` would make cheap if it resolves toward tolerating.

content: To measure whether graph traversal can earn its cost on a given corpus, read the stored vectors straight out of each store's SQLite `vectors` table — raw little-endian f32 blobs keyed by memory id — subtract the union centroid across every set being considered, then for each link rank all memories by cosine against the link's source and record where the target lands, as a percentile of the corpus rather than as a rank. Exclude `supersedes` and `superseded_by`, which validity resolution never traverses. The percentile is the scale-invariant quantity; a rank means nothing without the corpus size beside it.
context: Devised 2026-08-15 and first run against the scatterhoard and coding-lessons sets, then against the pilot design-document corpus. The script itself is corpus/measure_link_percentiles.py, kept in the repository rather than a scratchpad because the first version was written to /private/tmp, which is how the seed-quality corpus was nearly lost.
why: This is the acceptance check for any corpus proposed for traversal evaluation, and it runs before any query is authored, which is the expensive half. It needs no embedder, because the vectors are already in the store, and no tool-surface change, because SQLite is readable directly. Reporting rank instead of percentile is the trap: at 70 memories a linked target ranking 2nd looks like traversal is redundant, and the same percentile at 1,000 memories ranks 29th and looks essential.

content: **Read-only loading is built; evaluation is not.** As of 2026-09-17: `LoadMode` in `src/store.rs`, stored in `meta` under `load_mode`; `Store::choose_read_only`, refused once a set holds records; the write refusal on `insert`, `carry_forward` and `forget`, with early refusals in `Server::author_for`, `absorb` and the author actions; `create`'s optional `mode`, defaulting to read-write; `status` reporting it; `drop` with an optional `save_to`, skipping the safety copy for a read-only set and honouring a path given anyway; and **one copy of each identity loaded, in `Server::settle_identity`** — a lone copy loads whatever its mode, the single read-write copy wins among several, and otherwise every copy is withheld and `status` lists them. Dropping a copy settles the identity again, so a survivor loads without a restart. **Not yet built:** how a read-only set's signposts get recalled, which needs a decision between convention text and a `status` field; promotion to read-write; and evaluation mode, which also needs the cross-set link question answered first. Check the status line in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md), which is kept current as slices land.
context: Finishing the load-once slice of read-only mode. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 1 link an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.
why: Supersedes the partway record written on 2026-09-16, which named the drop and load-once slices as unbuilt and pointed at an unused `owes_a_safety_copy` and a withhold-all `add_store` as signs of it. Both are now built, so that memory would send a session looking for work that is done. What remains is listed for the same reason the old one listed it: the state shows, the deliberate stopping does not.

content:
**The build directory silted up again, and the rate is now measured: `target/debug/deps` reached 543,052 files by 2026-09-20, five weeks after being cleaned to 861 on 2026-08-15.** 541,228 of them are `.rcgu.o` codegen units, 282,853 written since 2026-09-01.

Confirmed by alternating trials, same binary, same machine, only the directory differing — first launch of a freshly linked `checksum` test binary took 2.37s, 2.45s, 2.56s from the crowded directory against 0.27s, 0.26s, 0.27s from a fresh `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` holding 1,125 files. Roughly nine-fold, with 0.00s user and 0.00s sys throughout: it is wait, not work. A warm second launch is 0.00s, so only the first run after linking pays.

**This is what made the 2026-09-19 mutation pass take 53 minutes at a 6.4s mean.** Every mutation relinks the test binaries it names, so every one pays. `01M03V427A…` in `coding-lessons` records the same condition diagnosed on 2026-08-09, with a full pass at 129 minutes falling to two after `cargo clean`.

What to do about it is `01M3160C9GEB9VXZ1RG8RZ4ZDK`; why the obvious remedy is worse than the disease is `01M3161JP7EPS9V077CMJX2AJH`.
context: Testing the mutation runner's own claim that directory crowding slows launches, at the end of the memory-size stretch.
why: The general lesson already exists and is not restated here; what is new is the recurrence rate, which the earlier record predicted but could not quantify. Five weeks from 861 files to 543,052 says periodic manual cleaning is not a reasonable answer — the accrual is faster than anyone will remember to counteract.

content: **Whether a link may be added to an exported memory without superseding it.** Resolved 2026-09-22 by the human partner: **no, not now** — supersession stays the only route (option B). In twelve days of the connect-on-recall clause, no connection needed one: links went on the memory being written, which is not yet exported, and traversal ignores direction. **Reopen if** link-only supersessions start appearing in the set, a session reports skipping a connection between two exported memories, or a pass to connect the older isolated memories is decided on. The findings gathered under this question carry the keyword `link-only-write-after-export`.
context: Pre-release review, right after serving the cost-framed recall-when wording. Superseded 2026-09-24 to restate 1 link an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`, and to point its two links at the rationale-criterion memory's trims half, which is the half they concern now that it is split.
why: Head of a question cluster, superseded to record its resolution. Option A lost its main recorded objection when the merge driver began set-merging links, but it would still need an additions-only rule, a whitelist excluding labels that change another memory's standing, a decision on `modified.by`, and served text the catalog has no room for. Nothing measured pays for that. Option C was only ever about the cost premise, which the 2026-09-09 examination removed. The reopen conditions are the cases where A would earn its cost, so a later session can tell when to look again.

content: Two figures circulate for the convention catalog's size and they differ by 166, the sum of the ten ids. `catalog_fits_context_budget` sums `id + text + reinforcement`; `conventions::page` sums `text + reinforcement` only, because ids are not charged against a page. The test's figure is the one that binds. Quoting the paging figure understates the pressure: the 2026-08-25 06:38 checkpoint reported 1,024 characters free where the enforced budget had 858.
context: Found 2026-08-25 while re-deriving the checkpoint's counts. Checkable at `catalog_fits_context_budget` in tests/conventions.rs and at `page` in src/conventions/mod.rs.
why: The two numbers are close enough to read as the same number, and neither function is wrong, so nothing flags the substitution -- a session planning a convention against the paging figure drafts 166 characters it cannot land. The restructuring done later the same day made this worse rather than better: the enforced total came to 16,978, within two characters of the paging figure the stale handoff quoted, so a note carrying the wrong measure now reads as confirmed by the right one.

content:
**Built 2026-09-19: a memory over 2000 characters is refused, at both write doors.** `over_length_refusal` in `mcp.rs` measures `embedding_input_of` — content, `why` and keywords — and runs in `memorize` after decoding and in `amend` on the memory as it would stand afterwards, since amend replaces some fields and leaves others. A door that skipped it would be the way around the other.

**The limit is not the embedder's budget.** It was one while `encode` truncated at 512 tokens, and stopped being one the same day. What it bounds is what a memory is: a record that long is usually several claims whose relationships, which link labels exist to carry, are buried in prose. So the refusal says to split, and says that shortening while keeping every claim meets the number and misses the reason.

**Characters, not tokens, and the reason is the no-model path**: tokenising needs the model, keyword search does not, and a store that refused by tokens could not answer where it matters most. A character is a Unicode scalar, so a script costing more bytes per character is not given a shorter memory. 2000 came from the corpus — nothing in the project's first five weeks reached it, median 998, longest 1565.

`embedding_input` was split so the door and the embedder measure one text, not two. Recorded in [documents/design/memory-data-model.md](documents/design/memory-data-model.md); one mutation raises the constant out of reach and both doors' tests catch it.
context: Building the length refusal after the human partner settled on 2000 and accepted that this project's own corpus will feel it while no other user will.
why: A later session meeting this refusal will want to know whether shortening is a legitimate answer, and it is not — the limit exists to produce several linked memories, so text cut to fit while keeping every claim defeats it. Recorded with the characters-versus-tokens reasoning because that looks like an approximation someone should tighten later, and it is a deliberate choice about which failure mode matters.

content: **MCP elicitation lets a server ask the human directly, and Claude Code supports it; Scatterhoard's server cannot use it yet.** Claude Code shows form and URL elicitation as a dialog (code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp, *Respond to MCP elicitation requests*). Up to revision 2025-11-25 the server sends `elicitation/create` as its own request in the middle of a tool call; revision 2026-07-28 replaces that with multi round-trip requests, an `InputRequiredResult` the client answers by retrying the call, and also drops `initialize`. The server negotiates only 2025-06-18 and 2024-11-05 (`PROTOCOL_VERSIONS` in `src/mcp.rs`), ignores the client's capabilities, and its stdio loop in `src/main.rs` only answers, never asks. Claude Desktop's chat support was not found on 2026-10-10.
context: Researching whether the server could ask the human for a shared set's publishing name itself, after refusal wording failed on a small local model.
why: Elicitation is the one route found by which a name can reach `mint` without passing through the model, which is what text alone could not achieve. Recorded so the next session starts from what the protocol and the client offer, and where the server falls short, rather than researching them again. The docs and the spec are where to check, since both change between revisions.

content: The proposal on the table, from the human partner 2026-08-30: **a derived baseline instead of a threshold.** On finding `target-mutation` empty, let the first compilation establish a baseline set of file paths — essentially the external dependency artifacts plus whatever the first mutation contributes as noise — and thereafter periodically delete everything outside the baseline before a compilation run. **Why it beats recalibrating `CROWDED`**: it deletes only what was about to be rebuilt anyway, since mutations touch this crate and never the dependencies, so the churn is our own `.rcgu.o` objects and test binaries — throwing those away costs seconds where `cargo clean` throws away the dependency build and costs minutes, and that asymmetry is the whole argument; the baseline is derived rather than configured, so there is no number to drift, which is exactly how the current threshold failed; and a wrong trigger is cheap, since cleaning too often costs one rebuild of this crate, which makes *periodically* a tuning question rather than a correctness one. **Three things to settle before building it**: whether cargo tolerates having outputs removed underneath it, since deleting an artifact while leaving `.fingerprint` intact could leave cargo believing something fresh is present — probably it rebuilds, but that must be proved, and it is the one failure that would corrupt a pass rather than merely slow it; what invalidates the baseline, since a dependency upgrade or toolchain change makes the recorded set stale and a stale baseline is the bad case, so key it on a hash of `Cargo.lock` plus the `rustc` version; and where the baseline lives, under `target-mutation` so it is deleted with the directory, an empty directory correctly meaning *establish a new baseline*.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A design that replaces a drifting constant with a derived one, with the three unresolved questions that gate building it. Recorded because the argument — delete only what was going to be rebuilt anyway — is the reusable part, and because the cargo-fingerprint question is the one that could corrupt rather than slow a pass.

content: **Resolved 2026-09-17: a set is loaded read-only by choosing that mode at `create`, and read-only distribution is built.** The question was how to hold a set someone else publishes — documentation, policies, regulations — so its memories can be read and never written here. The design is [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md): `create` takes an optional `mode` defaulting to read-write; the mode lives in the set's `meta`; a read-only set refuses session writes, takes and refreshes its records from its publisher's file by `import` or `restore`, drops without a safety copy unless `save_to` is given, and pulls the `hoard-signpost` mark alone, which `hoard_sets status` names per set. A set identity loads once, a read-write copy winning over read-only ones. The publisher cannot declare read-only-ness in the file, because a header is contents. **What it left behind is one backlog entry, `promotion-to-read-write`**, deferred: the design settles what promotion would do, and nothing implements it. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `read-only-distribution`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Closing out read-only mode, deciding what comes next after it was finished.
why: Supersedes the head to mark the question resolved. Its last open part, whether promotion is offered, is decided-but-unbuilt rather than undecided, so it moves to the backlog as `TRACKING.md` says a resolved question's residue should, instead of holding this entry open.

content: A seed and a trap are the same object: both are session-start push, so the trigger difference the watch convention's drafting agenda assumed does not exist, which is what let one convention replace two and needed no budget raise. Advancement is spawning a new head that draws on the observations, not superseding: one observation set can drive several questions and supersession affords one successor. And push is the marked case -- most accumulation stays passive and is reached by ordinary recall -- which is the budget story push had been missing.
context: Rewriting the watch convention around the index line, and finding the memory that recorded how it was built had gone half stale.
why: Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claims are unchanged. These are the three corrections untouched by the 2026-09-06 rewrite, and the ones a later session would otherwise re-derive expensively -- the spawning one especially, since the re-entry question said transitions are supersessions and following that would fork a chain deliberately. How a memory is marked changed separately, and is the memory alongside this one. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 2 links an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.

content: **The change improves the constant and does not remove the trap, and what shipped reflects that -- 2026-08-20, verified 2026-09-07.** A prefix still constrains *time* rather than identity, because the leading bits are a timestamp; six base32 characters still collided 61 times in the corpus measured. **The design's original answer had been to accommodate the habit** by letting `hoard_lookup` accept a prefix -- and that accommodation is precisely what `lookup-prefix-selectivity-is-time-correlated` reports as a defect. **So the real question was which of two coherent designs to hold:** accept prefixes and make them selective and self-announcing, or remove the provocation and delete prefix lookup rather than fix it -- which STANDARDS.md prefers on principle, since making an error impossible to express beats detecting it at run time. **What shipped is the second, in a sharper form than *removed*:** `id` takes a whole 26-character id and **refuses a short one rather than guessing**, while substring search moved to an explicitly named `fragment` parameter that also advises taking characters from the *end*, since the leading ones are a timestamp. **Note what this does and does not promise.** It does not stop a model truncating -- nothing will. It stops truncation **silently succeeding**, which is the whole of the harm.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Recorded because *prefix lookup removed* understates what happened and would mislead: the capability still exists, under a name that cannot be reached by accident, with guidance attached about which end of an id is selective. That is the correctness-by-construction move rather than a deletion, and the distinction matters to anyone tempted to restore convenience by letting `id` accept a prefix again.

The closing distinction is the reusable one: the goal was never to prevent the behaviour, only to stop it failing quietly, and that is the achievable version of most guards against model habits.

content: **The constraint that decides the wording, and it is not obvious: the default text must describe and never direct.** [trigger-and-loading.md](documents/design/trigger-and-loading.md) resolves that Scatterhoard **provides no location for instruction-shaped text at all**, on the grounds that an auto-loaded instruction channel is the sharpest attack surface available and one Scatterhoard would be *introducing* to the ecosystem rather than inheriting. A README is prose sitting in a directory that has just declared it contains no instructions, and it is exactly the shape — a markdown file — that the same document's tripwire treats as a weak smuggling signal. **So the item is not done if the wording drifts into telling a reader or a model what to do**; the proposed default passes as written, and any expansion of it has to be checked against this rather than against readability. Note the tripwire this depends on is itself designed and unbuilt — no code searches the directory for unknown entries today — so the item does not need it built, but the two want to land knowing about each other, since the second is what would otherwise complain about the first.
context: Migrating the memory-directory-readme entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the constraint that governs its text.
why:
Recorded because the natural instinct with a README is to make it *helpful*, and helpful prose slides into imperative — *run this*, *put your memories here*, *see the docs for how to* — without anyone noticing a line was crossed. The line is a security property of the whole design, not a style preference, and it is invisible from the file being written.

The self-tripwire point is the other half a later session would miss: Scatterhoard writing a file its own unknown-entry check would flag is a system complaining about itself, which reads as a bug in the checker rather than as an unregistered file.

content: Observed 2026-10-28, the first compaction seen to fire the hook. Session `8a53d486`'s transcript shows: last turn ends 05:45 UTC at 542,551 tokens, about 54% of a 1M window; hook stub `2026-10-28-0639-precompact.md` at 06:39; summary written 06:40 with no turn running; compaction applied at 07:07 when a background task's notification arrived, marked `"precomputed": true`, `"trigger": "auto"`, 99 ms. So the hook can fire on an idle, half-full session, against the design's premise that auto-compact means a full window. Idle time alone does not trigger it: two later idle stretches of about 6 and 16 hours at about 100k tokens produced no compaction and no stub. The threshold is unknown. The hook's text appears nowhere after the boundary, and the summary carries none of it. Claude Code issue #71625 says `PreCompact` fires during summarization; it was closed "not planned". #40138 reported a sub-agent's compaction firing the main agent's hook, a risk here though this session had no sub-agents.
context: Re-reviewing the published memory sets under the export review's judgement gate. Investigated on 2026-10-29 from the raw session transcript, because flightlog had not indexed this session.
why: The evidence behind the head, kept apart so the head stays a claim. The idle firing and the unknown threshold matter beyond this hook: a session can be compacted long before it is full, which changes how much a long review can count on keeping. The external issues are why the fix should not wait for a blocking `PreCompact`.

content: **The argument that decided it was the human partner's, and it is not the one the entry was filed on.** Whatever is said against folding-alone applies to lowercase-alone: either the lookup does a *complete, specifiable* normalisation, or it does *none* and the convention says matching is byte identity. Doing part of it is the worst arm — a caller cannot treat matching as exact, and it still misses what a non-English author writes. And **naming a standard is more compact in served text than describing a bespoke mapping**, which matters because the reader is a model deciding, at the moment it coins a keyword, whether two spellings are one subject. That reframing moved this from *lowercase is nearly enough* to *lowercase is the one arm with no defence*. **A sampling-bias correction the human partner supplied**: an earlier measurement — 12 of 514 live keyword rows differ from their folded form — was presented as if it bounded the cost, and it bounds *one English speaker's* cost. The users this affects are the ones absent from the corpus, and the strongest case is one no English corpus contains: an IME emits fullwidth Latin, so the same keyword typed in two input modes was two keywords.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Two arguments that reframed the decision: partial normalisation is the one option with no defence, and a corpus measurement bounds the cost only for the population that produced the corpus.

content: Give a session a way to see that the running MCP server is older than the binary it was launched from. Candidate mechanisms: the server comparing its own process start time against the binary's mtime, a build stamp it reports, or a version in a tool response a session can check cheaply. The need is operational rather than theoretical -- a restart mid-session disrupts live work, so restarts get deferred, and a server deferred past the end of a session is simply never restarted at all. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `detect-a-stale-running-server`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Restarting the MCP client after finding the served conventions were a day behind the source, then splitting CLAUDE.md into AGENTS.md.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. The opening sentence is the generated index row. Filed 2026-09-07 by the human partner after a session loaded a day-old convention catalog without noticing. Ready rather than blocked: nothing has to be decided first, and every candidate mechanism is implementable today.

content: **Neither static model tested reads Italian kitchen terms in English text: `potion-base-32M` scored 1 of 10 and `potion-multilingual-128M` 2 of 10 on a set's own sentences.** Measured 2026-10-04, end to end on a disposable set, with ten triplets. Each anchor used an Italian term, such as "finish the risotto with a proper mantecatura", and its paraphrase explained the term in plain English. The same set's English scored 10 on the built-in sentences. So a set's own sentences do catch what the built-ins miss, but switching to the multilingual model did not fix it. The ten triplets were not kept; one is the example in the cookbook recipe for borrowed terms, `01M42PXNHAEZSRYTER48CG8KTN`. Keyword recall found such a memory by its term where semantic recall scored it 0.15.
context: Running the terms-of-art procedure end to end before writing a cookbook recipe for it, after adding the model-fit how-to to status's band notes. The same stretch tested that how-to on gemma4:12b.
why: The design and the plan for a cookbook recipe both assumed a multilingual model would help a set full of borrowed terms. This measurement does not support that assumption. For terms of art, the honest advice is to measure and then lean on keywords, not to switch models. One set and one domain, so confidence is moderate. A static model may simply be unable to connect a term with its explanation in any language.

content: The prohibited-data scan cannot be run against a file. The scan itself is built as `scatterhoard::prohibited::scan`; this is reaching it from outside a running server. **The path nothing covers**: `hoard_memorize` refuses a credential and `export` warns about one, so both routes through the tools are handled — a `scatterhoard_mem/memories.json` that is **hand-edited and committed with no re-export** passes neither. That is a real path rather than a hypothetical, because [set-lifecycle.md](documents/design/set-lifecycle.md) specifies renaming a forked set as a hand-edit of the file header, so the design itself tells people to edit this file by hand. Built when the binary takes a subcommand that scans a memory file and exits non-zero on a find, the no-argument invocation is unchanged with a test saying so, and the rules come from `prohibited::scan` rather than a second copy. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `prohibited-scan-subcommand`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Storage and correctness section.
why: Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only. Worth a line in [SETUP.md](SETUP.md) showing the pre-commit hook when it lands, since a check nobody installs protects nobody.

content: **Measured 2026-09-08: `scatterhoard`'s link graph is an archipelago, not a web, so associative drift is structurally unavailable in it.** Of 713 memories, **only 122 appear in the traversable link graph at all and 591 are isolated**; the graph breaks into 34 components whose largest holds **21 memories, 2.9% of the corpus**. `coding-lessons` is better connected and still fragmented: 87 of 121 in the graph, 14 components, largest 33 at 27.3%. **The walk is therefore bounded by component size long before it is bounded by its three-hop limit** — from any seed, there is nowhere further to go. This matters for a specific reason: it rules out drift as the explanation for the smooth roll-off in the merged ranking. Five in six `scatterhoard` memories can only ever be reached by content similarity, so the smoothness comes from the similarity side over a single-subject corpus, and not from following associations until everything is distantly related. Re-derive by walking the `links` table undirected, excluding `supersedes` and `superseded_by` and cross-set targets.
context: Probing the gap cut, when the human partner questioned whether the filed defect is a defect at all — since walking an associative web drifts by nature.
why: Recorded because *a web of memories you can walk arbitrarily far through* is the natural mental model for this system and it is not yet true of this corpus — the human partner raised drift as a candidate explanation for the smooth roll-off, and the graph cannot produce it. Keeping the number is what stops the same reasonable hypothesis being re-raised and re-argued instead of re-measured. It also puts a figure on how far the memory set is from the design's own premise: the traversal machinery is built, measured and shipping, and 83% of the memories it runs over have no edge for it to follow. That is an argument about linking practice rather than about the code, and it is invisible from any single recall.

content: **`capture-before-ending` fires before handing control back to the human after work that used tools, as well as before a commit or an export and when the human signals they are wrapping up.** Decided 2026-09-14 by the human partner, who proposed the rewording, and served the same day; recorded in `documents/design/conventions.md` under *Served 2026-09-14: `capture-before-ending` fires before handing control back*, with the wording's history in the comment above `CAPTURE_BEFORE_ENDING` in `src/conventions/catalog.rs`. The session must write *"worth remembering from this: ..."* with what it worked out rather than looked up, or *"worth remembering from this: nothing"*, and then store what survives, in the same turn. It answers the trigger half of `meta-observation-convention`; the half about stepping back to judge a result in its larger context remains open.
context: Rewording capture-before-ending with the human partner, after they asked whether the conventions had prompted recording what a long investigation of set identity had found. Same stretch: the link identity fix and the scan subcommand.
why:
**Why the hand-back.** The old first trigger, a multi-turn piece of work finishing, was the least observable moment in the list, and material worked out on the way to a question handed back went unrecorded on 2026-09-07 and 2026-09-14. The 2026-09-07 finding had named the moment before handing back as the candidate; the human partner proposed it again after the second instance.

**Three wording choices, each settled in conversation.** *After work that used tools* replaced the proposal's *after any operation across multiple turns*, because tool use is observable and the prompting investigation ran within one of the human's turns. *What you worked out rather than looked up* is the bound the open question required, so the line does not fill with status. And the moments are joined by *or* with *before* kept on commit and export: the human partner asked whether their draft's *and* would read as a compound condition, and it would have; a tighter draft's *at a commit* read as after it.

**The required *nothing* line** is the human partner's, and it keeps the original decision's rule that *nothing* is a sanctioned answer while giving the step evidence of having run — the 2026-09-07 measurement found this convention firing on one commit in ten beside a tool-call convention firing on all ten.

**Not yet tested.** Whether it changes what gets recorded is an observation for later sessions, which belongs under `meta-observation-convention` and `charter-rewrite-intake-measurement` as it arrives.

content: Scatterhoard's live memory graph is far sparser and less varied than the corpus its link vocabulary was chosen on. Measured over the 36 memories of the shared:scatterhoard set: 16 edges carrying only four distinct labels — SUPERSEDES 7, RELATED_TO 7, RESULTS_FROM 1, RESOLVES 1. MOTIVATED_BY, SUPPORTS, CONTRADICTS and INSTANCE_OF have no instances at all, though the fitted corpus used all twelve labels with MOTIVATED_BY dominant at 8 of 29 edges. Counting both directions, 11 of the 36 memories are isolated and the highest incident degree is 3.
context: Measured 2026-08-14 over scatterhoard_mem/memories.json while reopening the graph-traversal design. Recorded in the "What the corpus can currently support" section of documents/design/recall-mechanisms.md; the comparison corpus is corpus/link-label-findings.md. Re-measure after any bulk memory import, which would change it.
why: The link vocabulary was validated against a corpus labelled retrospectively, in a pass whose purpose was labelling. These memories were written through the tool during other work, which is the condition traversal will actually run under. The gap matters because per-label traversal behaviour cannot be designed, tuned or measured for labels that nothing writes — three of the open traversal questions currently concern labels no stored memory uses.

content: **How to inspect a memory set without adopting it.** Raised 2026-08-26 by the human partner, from a maintainer reviewing a contributor's branch: import is adoption, and checking the branch back out does not undo it. **Designed 2026-09-16 in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md) as a special case of read-only, and built after it** (`read-only-distribution`). Settled: an evaluation load comes from a file, once, through a `hoard_sets` action with no `create` step. Several can be open at once for comparison. Each is named `eval-<set>-<label>`, with the label chosen by the user, and `SetName::new` refuses the `eval-` prefix so no real set can carry it. It is searched only when its scope is named. Every memory it returns carries a field taken from the load mode, not parsed from the name, and the response carries a note explaining it. It pulls no watch marks, drops without a safety copy, and lives in memory. **Still open, and to be settled before building:** what a cross-set link does when an evaluation copy is a possible target. That covers the copy as the only holder of the link's identity, the copy beside the real set, and evaluation memories linking into real ones. It turns largely on whether evaluation stores sit among the ordinary stores, since `hoard_lookup` resolves against all of those. **Also open:** the size limit, and whether a returned memory carries its set's identity. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `evaluation-mode`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Revising the load-modes design after settling how evaluation hits are marked; the human partner raised cross-set links into evaluation sets.
why: Supersedes the head written earlier the same day, whose open list lacked the cross-set link cases the human partner raised immediately afterwards. That is the most consequential open part, and a head is where a session reads what remains. The previous head's claim that an evaluation load does not count as a holder outside its own searches is dropped from the settled list, because that is exactly what the new open part puts in question.

content: **`hoard_sets create` splits into `create`, for a new set, and `adopt`, for taking on a set from its exported file.** Decided 2026-09-24 by the human partner. `create` takes a name and, once the two residues are drafted, a charter and an author, and mints the identity. `adopt` takes a file and an author, with an optional mode, and gets name, identity and charter from the file in one step instead of `create` then `import`. Renaming a fork stays `create` then `import`, because a fork is a new set whose contents come from a file. Whether `restore` folds into `adopt` is being examined next.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner, the first being how far `create` should differ from opening an existing set.
why: The overloading had already produced a defect: `create` mints an identity at what its own comment calls the one moment a set is known to be new, which is false on the adoption path, and `adopt_set_id` gained a rule letting an empty set's identity be displaced purely to undo it (`a-re-added-set-cannot-recover-its-identity`). Split, every required parameter is load-bearing on every call. A single `create` switching on an optional file was rejected because the conditional requirement is invisible to a flattening client. `adopt` rather than `open`, which suggests loading a database already on the machine.

content: **Cap how long `hoard_sets evaluate` may run, not how much memory it uses.** An exported file carries no vectors, so `evaluate` embeds every memory in the file before returning; on a large file that is a tool call which appears to hang, and a hang is the shape a caller retries. There is no memory question any more: since 2026-09-18 a review copy is a database file under the home rather than a store in memory, so what a review costs is time and disk, and disk is the directory the user already chose for their stores. **Built when** `evaluate` either refuses a file whose record count is above a limit, naming both numbers, or reports progress as it embeds — with the limit set by timing a full embed of a real set rather than guessed. Measured 2026-09-16 for the memory question that no longer applies: about 3–4 KB per memory beyond the vectors.
context: Building evaluation mode; the human partner reversed the in-memory storage after the first version shipped.
why: Supersedes the entry filed hours earlier, whose case rested on holding the copy in memory. The human partner moved review copies to disk, which removes that argument entirely and leaves a smaller, different one: the embed is slow and silent. Kept open rather than dropped, because the failure it names survives the change.

content: **Whether this issue needs a fix at all was questioned on 2026-09-24, and left open for the human partner to think about.** The case for: `local` holds personal preferences, and a session that recalls nothing from it acts on defaults with no sign anything was missed; the new store takes every later write, so the personal record splits across two files nothing merges; and the likely causes are accidental rather than a deliberate move — `SCATTERHOARD_COMMON` set in one client's MCP config and not another's, a shell profile one launch path reads, a typo. The case against: `status` already names every set's file, and a warning must guess, since a fresh install beside an old store is legitimate. If per-client disagreement is the real risk, an alternative to a startup remark is `status` flagging a `local` store at the default path that this server is not reading.
context: Settling the two issues whose prevention arrived as a report rather than a refusal; the other, arrival provenance, was closed. Just before starting the out-link supersession work.
why: Recorded so the question is resumed from where it stood rather than re-derived. The accidental causes shift what the fix is for: a deliberate move needs no warning because the mover knows, so the fix is only worth building for the causes nobody notices — and the two-clients case suggests a different fix from the one the fixed-when describes. Confidence reflects that this is an argument not yet weighed by the human partner, not a decision.

content: A personal store split across two directories had no route back: `import` of a stray `local` backup into `local` is refused for its different identity, with advice to "use action absorb", and `absorb` refused every `local` file. Reproduced 2026-09-30 on a disposable home, by setting `SCATTERHOARD_COMMON` without moving `local.sqlite3` and writing into the new store. Fixed the same day: `absorb_set` in `src/mcp.rs` takes a `local` file into `local` and nowhere else. For `local` it tells the same set by identity, and it makes no links internal, since nothing links into `local` from another set. Rerun end to end, the original identity holds all memories, the stray one included, and a second absorb changes nothing. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `a-split-local-store-cannot-be-merged-back`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Testing the data-directory move procedure for the first scatterhoard-cookbook recipe, from the stranded-local-store issue.
why: Head of an issue cluster, found and fixed in one session, so amended rather than superseded: it never left this machine open. Blocked: the refusal's advice led to a second refusal, the shape the coding-lessons lesson on testing a remedy by taking it describes. Found by running the recovery procedure before writing it as a cookbook recipe, the rule the human partner settled that day. They chose to fix it before creating the cookbook, since a symptom recipe that diagnoses a split with no way back leaves its reader worse placed. A shared set still never takes a `local` file. Three tests in `tests/sets.rs`, the split test taking `import`'s named remedy; five mutations, three re-anchored; `documents/design/set-lifecycle.md`.

content: Any project store silently stored memories that could never be found by meaning: the server loaded the model and called `set_embedder` on the local store only, so a memory written to a project store was stored successfully with no vector and no warning. Fixed 2026-08-03, and guarded structurally the same day. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `project-stores-get-no-embedder`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry, in file order.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: Checkpoint filenames in `checkpoints/` are stamped **UTC**, settled 2026-09-08 by the human partner and written into `AGENTS.md` beside the naming rule. The filenames are the only ordering these files have, so a single local stamp among UTC ones does not merely look inconsistent -- on 2026-09-07 a mid-session checkpoint named in local time sorted *before* the checkpoint that superseded it, so *most recent file* named the wrong one and a session restoring from it would resume from superseded state. `scripts/precompact-checkpoint.sh` was changed in the same commit to `date -u`, for both the filename stamp and the derivation time it prints; check that the script and the rule still agree, since the rule is only as good as the tool that writes most of these files.
context: Unifying the tracking files into TRACKING.md; the timezone question came from the previous checkpoint's open list.
why: Recorded because the failure is silent and reads as something else: a session that picks up the wrong checkpoint finds stale-but-plausible state rather than an error, and the natural diagnosis is that the previous session recorded badly rather than that the sort order lied. The mixed-timezone directory that produced it was noticed only because one file superseded another on the same day.

content: `hoard-watch`'s length clause was replaced on 2026-09-06, not tightened: *keep a marked memory short enough to read fifteen of* is gone and *make its opening 120 characters say what it is for and when it applies* stands in its place, with the reinforcement's per-record cost arithmetic removed alongside it because it priced pushing records rather than lines. The rule is now one an author can follow without arithmetic, and both write paths show them the result -- `hoard_memorize` and `hoard_correct`'s `amend` echo the derived line. The convention is no longer provisional in any part.
context: Finishing the watch rewrite and clearing out the warnings written while it was still provisional.
why: Supersedes a memory whose whole purpose was to warn that the shipped length clause was wrong and being replaced. That warning has done its job and is now worse than nothing: it tells a session not to follow a rule the catalog no longer contains, which sends them looking for text that is not there. Recorded rather than simply retired because the *shape* of the replacement is the durable part -- a rule stated as a length nobody can measure became a rule stated as an opening the tool shows you, which is the move worth repeating the next time convention text asks for arithmetic.

content: Two routes forward, one built. **A third route, proposed 2026-08-30, would dissolve this rather than fix it: stop keeping bases.** [The graph is the ancestor](documents/design/multi-set-sync.md) argues that with correction gated on service, the per-record merge is a lattice join over *absent → memory → tombstone* and needs no recorded ancestor — and since **the damage here is caused by the base**, an import with no ancestor to consult cannot commit it, so the same thumb-drive scenario resolves loudly instead of silently. That is a much larger change and has a falsification step outstanding, so it is the shape of a possible end rather than the plan. **The cheaper half is built**: an import names any `TakeFile` whose incoming version is older than the one it replaces, under `taken_backwards`, with guidance listing *"an older copy of the set read from a location this set has agreed with before"* among the causes — this scenario, detected and reported, needing no replica identity, no new state and no format change. **So the realistic half — an older backup of the same set at a familiar path — is covered**, and what remains open is the different-set half, which the set UUID proposal would refuse outright. *The entry stays open because detection is not prevention: the store still takes the older content and the caller still has to notice a report and act on it. What changed is that the damage is no longer silent, which was the whole of the Corrupts severity.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The state of the fix: detection shipped, prevention blocked on what identifies a replica, and a third proposal that would remove the mechanism causing the damage entirely. The distinction between detection and prevention is why the entry stays open despite the severity being addressed.

content: Say what points here before the text moves under it. Built 2026-08-30, in the session after `correction-gated-on-service` shipped: the response carries `in_links` and `in_links_note`, and `Store::incoming_edges` became public so the write surface reports the shape the read surface already publishes rather than growing a second projection of it. **The problem it answers**: widening correction to `content` lets a rewrite leave another memory's `SUPPORTS` or `INSTANCE_OF` edge asserting something nobody would author, and only the caller can tell whether it did. **It has no dependency** — `incoming-edges-invisible-on-the-wire` is fixed, so inbound edges already ship, and a session following `recall-when` before correcting has them in context already; **the remark is the backstop for the session that did not look**. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `in-link-remark-on-a-content-correction`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Test and documentation debt section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only. It is the correction half of a pair whose supersession half is `supersession-silently-repoints-an-in-link-nobody-reauthored`.

Its Built-when carries a testing point worth keeping in the head: the test must cover **both** directions, since a remark that always fires and one that never fires are equally useless, and only the pair of tests tells them apart.

content: **Every stage of the shipping scorer is relative, which is why an unanswerable query still returns about four confident memories.** Measured 2026-09-09 over 886 memories at window 10: with the gap cut in force a question about sourdough returns **3.80** hits on average, a rule-shaped off-corpus question **4.67**, and pure word salad **4.40**, against **5.56** for a genuinely answerable query. Turn the cut off and every family returns the full window of 10 — so **the cut is the only stage that decides how many results come back**, it removes 4 to 6 of 10, and it removes them from answerable and unanswerable queries alike. This is by design rather than by oversight: `cut_at_largest_gap`'s own doc comment rules out an absolute threshold, citing `no-non-match-floor` and the cold-start problem, and argues that a gap "needs no number anyone would have to defend". A gap, a rank and a ratio are all relative, so **there is no stage anywhere in the pipeline that can say *nothing here answers this*** — the scorer is constitutionally incapable of it, and no tuning of the existing stages changes that.
context: Reading the stage-by-stage ablation of the shipping scorer the human partner asked for.
why:
Recorded because it converts the open entry from a defect report into a structural statement, and because it is the argument for the floor that does not depend on any of the day's contested measurements. The entry `an-unanswerable-query-returns-confident-hits` reads as though something is going wrong; what is actually happening is that a pipeline built entirely from relative comparisons is doing exactly what it says, and an absolute question was never asked anywhere in it.

That reframes the floor from a fix to an addition. Nothing needs backing out for it to work — the gap cut can keep deciding how many of the survivors to return, and a floor would decide whether there are any survivors at all. The two operate on different questions and the ablation shows they do not overlap: the cut's behaviour is nearly identical across families, so it is not doing any of the work a floor would do.

It also retires the reason the floor was ruled out in that doc comment. The cold-start objection — a small store's absolute scores carrying no information, a one-memory store scoring 0.0 — is real and remains a genuine constraint, but it argues for a floor **calibrated per store** rather than against a floor as such, which is the design now on the table.

Confidence 0.9: measured through the shipping path with a pinned default, and the mechanism is visible in the source rather than inferred from the numbers.

content: **Three lines of the existing design already pointed at requiring a charter and had never been connected to it** -- noticed when the question was raised, 2026-08-24. Set Lifecycle says the set name *comes from whoever runs `create`, which is the only participant that knows what the set is for* -- and a charter is exactly *what it is for*. It also says *`create` fixes what every copy must agree on, `export` states what only this machine knows* -- and a charter travels in the file, so every copy agrees on it. Tool Surface already refuses to guess a one-way-door choice, which is why `Scope` has no `Default`, confirmed 2026-09-07 as a documented deliberate absence in `src/memory/scope.rs`. **The refusal boundary from Cross-Set References fits too:** refusal is right *where the caller holds the remedy and the mistake is theirs to fix*, and at `create` the caller holds it entirely. **A set arriving by `import` with no charter is a separate case and should be reported rather than refused** -- there the remedy belongs to the set's author, not to the caller, so the same boundary gives the opposite answer. **One sub-question if it is required:** whether the parameter takes the charter text alone, with the reserved keyword and scope minted by the tool, or whether it also takes the `why`, which is where *how this charter was arrived at* would be recorded.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Kept because the argument is already made and merely scattered: three separate documents each imply the answer, and the value of the entry is the assembly rather than any new reasoning. A later session would have to re-read all three to reconstruct it.

The import case is recorded alongside deliberately. It is the same refusal principle producing a different answer on a neighbouring path, which is the clearest available demonstration that the principle is doing real work rather than being invoked to justify a preference.

content: Nothing records which file an imported memory came in from, so a repository claiming a set's name contributes memories with no conflict, no warning, and attribution it wrote itself — `origin`, `created.by` and `confidence` are all file contents. Fixed when the set-name binding lands so one store cannot serve two repositories, or failing that when arrival is recorded unwritably from the file. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `imported-memories-carry-no-arrival-provenance`; this record carries only its standing.

why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only, with the fixed-when since this one is open. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content:
**Several of the operations Anthropic blocked had hand-built the thing Scatterhoard is** — which is what changes the question's shape. An observation made 2026-09-12 while `golden-rule-beyond-person-harm` was being filed, not history from building anything.

One cluster is described as maintaining *persistent campaign memory* across sessions while running autonomous loops around the clock; two others as building reusable multi-session workflows carried between engagements; the influence operations as embedding standing instructions in reusable templates and fixed output formats. So the demand for durable cross-session project memory is documented **inside the misuse itself**, independently of this tool. The question is therefore not whether a memory tool *could* be turned to such work in the abstract: Scatterhoard supplies that capability ready-made, exports it, and makes it shareable through a repository — the one thing those operations were assembling by hand.

**It cuts the other way on practicality.** Detection in every case ran on signals available to a hosted service — API-key usage patterns, coordinated publication timing, matching generated text against what appeared in the world — plus, in one case, a journalist's tip. A local tool with no telemetry and no server-side view has access to none of that. Whatever friction the design could add is a convention read by the session doing the work, and nothing else.

**Sourcing, and it is one step removed.** Read from the published page at `https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026`. The human partner's local copy is `~/Downloads/Anthropic-Detecting-and-countering-091026.pdf`, 154 pages — **no tool on this machine could extract its text** (poppler, pypdf, pdfminer and PyMuPDF all absent), so this summarises the page and not the document. Re-verify against the PDF before relying on any specific here.

**What I did not see**, and the human partner named both: the missile-guidance case and the biological and chemical weapons cases. Those categories are named in what I read, but their case studies were not in the portion I got. Treat the specifics above as covering the cyber, influence and fraud cases only.
context: Reading the threat-intelligence report on the morning the question was raised, before any other work in the session.
why:
Recorded separately from the head because it changes what the question is about. The human partner's framing was *could this tool be misused for such work*; the report's own case descriptions answer a stronger version — the demand for cross-session project memory is documented inside the operations themselves, and Scatterhoard is that capability, packaged and made shareable. Anyone picking the question up should have that before deciding it is hypothetical.

Kept at 0.7 and with its sourcing stated in the text because the reading is one step removed from the source, and the two cases the human partner named are exactly the ones I did not see a case study for.

content: **A client that shows an elicitation form retries the call itself, so the model never sees the question or the answer**, observed 2026-10-16 in Claude Code 2.1.299 in an interactive terminal, the first time Scatterhoard's form reached a person. The model made one `hoard_memorize` call and got one successful result; the set's author, the name the human typed, turned up only when the session called `status`, and it could not account for it. Since then a write that settles identity from the form carries an `author_note` naming what the human answered (`Exchange::settled` in `src/mcp.rs`).
context: Testing the publishing-name form across Claude hosts; the interactive terminal was the last row, after the desktop chat and Code tab.
why: It overturned the proposal's claim that the model sees a question was asked, and any later use of elicitation will meet the same thing: whatever the human answers is invisible to the model unless the final result says it. Checkable in that session's transcript, 39be3b6a-8908-4ec8-a07d-f03199c74882.

content: A `hoard-` keyword is a control mark, so whatever carries it lands in a list something acts on — and five Scatterhoard design memories discussing the charter mechanism answered to `hoard-scope-topics`, arriving as though they described a set. Fixed 2026-09-06 by re-keying fifteen memories to `about-`. The findings and measurements accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `reserved-keywords-carry-subject-memories`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set entry by entry, in file order, after the index marker regions went into the other two tracking files.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, severity and fixed-when only, so its status can be superseded without re-transcribing the entry. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content:
Fixed 2026-09-18 by `earliest_ancestor` in `genindex.py`: the sort key is the oldest id reachable through `supersedes` links, taken as the minimum over everything the walk reaches, which needs no special case for the two shapes that would otherwise want one — a head superseding two entries, and a supersession cycle. A link target absent from the file still counts, so pruning a superseded record cannot move a row. The one-time regeneration moved 18 rows of 218 and left every row's text byte-identical, which is the check to repeat: only positions may change.

The key was chosen by measuring each candidate's review diff against the file as it stood — earliest ancestor 18 rows moved, status-then-ancestor 62, slug alone 200. Slug alone was rejected for scattering an entry away from the work it was found with as much as for the diff. Status-first was proposed by the human partner, open rows floating to the top against 16 open of 96 issues, and dropped once the measurement showed it re-creates move-on-close and splits each stretch's entries apart as they close — which is the clustering that made ancestor order attractive in the first place. Both rejections are now written into the docstring, which had been detailed about its five guards and silent about order.

Found in passing and fixed in the same change: `main` returned a status nothing read, because `if __name__ == "__main__": main()` discards it, so the new `--self-check` would have exited 0 while printing its failures. Now `sys.exit(main())`.
context: Restoring from the 2026-09-18 checkpoint and taking the ordering defect off the issue list, the first work of the session after the load-mode stretch.
why: The measurement is the whole of the decision and nothing re-derives it: the three candidates all look defensible in prose, and only the diff sizes separate them. Recorded with the rejected alternatives because the next session to dislike alphabetical-by-slug will otherwise re-propose it, and because the status-first option is the one that reads best and measures worst. The byte-identical check is recorded because it is what distinguishes this regeneration from a damaging one.

content: Two processes making a set's first write at once could each mint it an identity, and the later one won, leaving the earlier writer's records under an identity the set no longer held. Fixed 2026-09-28 in `src/store.rs`: minting goes through `Store::claim_set_id`, a single insert-if-absent followed by a re-read that returns whatever the set holds. `adopt_set_id` is that one statement with no read before it. Proved deterministically by interleaving the steps by hand across two connections on one file, both reading and then both claiming, in `two_claims_after_two_empty_reads_agree_on_the_first` in `tests/concurrency.rs`, with no threads. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `concurrent-first-writes-can-mint-two-identities`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Working through the open corrupts-severity issues, the last of the three, after making a forget one-way at import.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed. It had been filed rather than fixed on the belief that no test could interleave two connections inside `mint_set_id`. The human partner suggested the classic answer: factor the critical section into steps a test can call independently. Here the factored step is the fix itself, so no untested guard was needed. The mutation `set identity: mint a fresh identity over one already minted` now survives with a recorded reason, because the read it deletes is a shortcut; the claim is the guard.

content: The mutation "reembed: report the memories offered rather than the vectors written" was recorded caught and survived, because it ran only `tests/sets.rs`. Fixed 2026-09-30 by adding `unrepresentable` to its `tests` in `scripts/mutations.py`: `a_rebuild_reports_the_memories_its_model_cannot_represent` in `tests/unrepresentable.rs` already rebuilds one refused memory beside an ordinary one and asserts one vector, and fails under the mutation. The comment beside `let embedded = self.embed_all(&borrowed)` in `src/store.rs` now names refused memories, not identity records, as what the input overstates by. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-reembed-count-mutation-no-longer-changes-anything`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Fixing the reembed-count mutation, right after recalibrating the recall floors on the scatterhoard and coding-lessons sets.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed — though not as its fixed-when asked, which was a new reembed test. That test already existed, outside the one binary the mutation ran, so the defect was routing rather than missing coverage. Verified by running the mutation before and after: survives with `sets` alone, caught with `unrepresentable` added.

content: **Observation 2026-09-07, from migrating the first five BACKLOG entries: outcomes were recorded in memories and evidence was left in the entry body.** In all five, some evidence existed only in the file — `recall-summary-output-mode` had its three shipped decisions stored and nothing about the 120-cap measurement, the 192-memory corpus test or the invariance finding; `watch-push-is-an-index-per-set` had the convention outcomes and nothing about the 411-character envelope its whole design rests on; `watch-convention` had neither its originating case nor the median-memory figure that justified a length constraint. **All of that was authored after the 2026-08-25 rewrite.** Two qualifications that keep this honest: it is a tendency and not a rule — `recall-before-storing` already carried two members from drafting the convention, so it is not *nothing recorded* — and the material was written under a backlog-entry habit, where an entry body is the obvious home for evidence, rather than freely.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md entry by entry; this is the pattern that showed up across the first five and prompted the human partner to ask for observations to be accumulated.
why:
Evidence against the hypothesis, recorded at 0.75 because it is suggestive and not the classification the investigation actually asks for. If it holds across the remaining thirty-seven entries, the rewrite did not reach the behaviour it was aimed at, and `store-when-names-method` may deserve reopening despite being resolved.

The confound is worth stating rather than discounting: a tracking file that invites long entries competes with the store for the same material, which is the boundary `checkpoints/` was already found to lose at. So this may be evidence about *where evidence goes when a file is available* rather than about the charter gloss — and separating those is something the migration is now, incidentally, well placed to do, since the file is being removed as an option.

content: The field-versus-endpoint matrix was never reapplied to the write surface. Done 2026-08-21: every memory field drawn against every write endpoint — `hoard_memorize`, `amend`, `forget`, `import` — looking for the empty cells. **Output was four findings, as the entry predicted**: `origin-cannot-be-corrected` (blocks), `crockford-left-stale-prefix-text-behind` (misleads, fixed in the same commit), `keywords-is-the-one-field-with-no-published-description` (costs), and `edge-authority-across-sets`. The same exercise on the *read* surface had previously found a `Corrupts` defect, which is why it was worth repeating. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `write-surface-matrix`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; Test and documentation debt section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim and standing only. The four findings are each recorded in their own issue clusters and are not restated; the member carries what the exercise is good at, which is the part that governs whether to run it again.

An analysis task whose output is issue entries rather than code — worth noting as a shape, since its Fixed-when is *the analysis was done* and it produces work rather than closing it.

content: **These three entries must be settled before publication**; they are this memory's keywords. Gated 2026-09-23 by the human partner. Two have answers that would break something already in use if changed afterwards: the tool surface, the file format, or what an identity means. They are `set-settled-at-first-write` and `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely`. One is gated because crafted files arrive with publication: `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity`. Every gated question is answered; what remains is building.
context: Drafting the data-only clause with the human partner, after the directory-form group shipped.
why: Superseded 2026-09-28: `data-only-rule-in-the-catalog` was built, so it leaves the gate. Retire an item by superseding this memory without its slug.

content: One of the fifteen re-keyed memories was the memory announcing the `about-` rule itself, written an hour after the rule shipped and carrying `hoard-scope-topics`. It was caught by the verification recall rather than by care, which is the argument for verifying a namespace rule by enumeration instead of trusting the authors of it — the reserved term is what such a memory is *about*, so it is the obvious keyword to reach for, and knowing the rule is no protection against reaching for it.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The rule was broken by the memory that announced it, within the hour, by the session that wrote it. That is evidence about what a namespace convention can and cannot buy: prevention needs enumeration, not attention.

content: **Decided 2026-09-18 by the human partner: a copy loaded for review is a database file under `SCATTERHOARD_HOME`, loaded again at every start — not a store in memory.** Two reasons, both theirs. **Memory**: Scatterhoard is meant to run beside a model on the user's own machine, so the server must be sparing with it; and **no portable way exists to ask how much memory there is**, so an in-memory limit is a number nobody can pick — an 8 GB laptop and a 128 GB workstation want different answers, and a file wants none. **Under the home rather than the system temp directory**: the home already holds the user's stores and so is known to be sized for them, where `/tmp` is commonly a small root partition; supporting a `SCATTERHOARD_TEMP` would add a setting to answer a question the home already answers. **Loaded again at every start**, from `reviews/` under the home, which makes `drop` the single way a copy goes: never loading them left a file after every restart that only a person would remove, and made a reviewer re-embed someone else's whole set to carry on. A forgotten review is then a set `status` lists, rather than a stray file nobody sees; a user who wants reviews closed promptly can say so in their own prompting. **Two servers share a home**, so a label another server holds a review under is refused here too. `StoreLayout::reviews` and `Server::evaluate_set`; `REVIEW_DIRECTORY` is excluded from nothing — discovery reads it deliberately.
context: Building evaluation mode; the human partner reversed the in-memory storage after the first version shipped.
why: Reverses the in-memory design the assistant proposed on 2026-09-16 and built on 2026-09-18, and the reversal's grounds are worth keeping because they are not about this feature: a tool that shares a machine with a local model cannot treat RAM as free, and Rust gives it no way to find out how much is free. The restart half was decided separately, after the human partner asked whether *gone at restart* had ever been decided — it had not; it was a property of storing the copy in memory, and on disk it became a choice between two cleanup stories.

content: **Claude Code in print mode declares form elicitation and declines every form unseen**, observed 2026-10-16 on version 2.1.299 in the Claude desktop app's Code tab. It declared `elicitation: {form, url}` on `server/discover` and on each call, received Scatterhoard's form, and answered `decline`; its log for the server reads *Elicitation request received in print mode*. No setting for it was found. A server cannot tell that decline from a human's, since the answer is identical and nothing on the request says print mode.
context: The first live test of asking the human for their publishing name, on a throwaway set through the `scatterhoard_a` test instance, after a restart onto the new build.
why: It is why an unanswered form has to fall back rather than be final, and it will look like a Scatterhoard defect to anyone testing in the desktop app. Checkable in Claude Code's per-server log under `~/Library/Caches/claude-cli-nodejs/<project>/mcp-logs-<server>/`. Whether the desktop app could route forms to the person and simply does not is unknown; reading the client binary found the message among its print-mode strings but not the logic.

content: **Read-only loading was built in part on 2026-09-16, and stopped deliberately after its first slice.** Built: `LoadMode` in `src/store.rs`, stored in `meta` under `load_mode`; `Store::choose_read_only`, refused once a set holds records; the refusal on `insert`, `carry_forward` and `forget`; `create`'s optional `mode`; `status` reporting `mode`; and early refusals in `Server::author_for`, `absorb` and the three author actions. **Not yet built, in the intended order:** `drop` skipping the safety copy for a read-only set (`LoadMode::owes_a_safety_copy` exists but nothing calls it); the one-copy-per-identity rule at load, where a read-write copy wins over read-only ones, which replaces today's withhold-all in `Server::add_store`; how a read-only set's signposts get recalled; promotion; and evaluation.
