Check the current state against the status line in [load-modes.md](documents/design/load-modes.md), which is kept up to date as slices land.
context: Implementing read-only load mode after designing it the same day; also fixed the action prose that omitted optional arguments.
why: Recorded because the state will show in the code and the stopping will not. An unused `owes_a_safety_copy`, and an `add_store` that still withholds every copy, read as deliberate settings unless something says they are step one of several. The design document's status line is the maintained copy; this memory is how a session that does not open that document learns the work is partway.

content: Fixed 2026-08-26: `Store::normalise_target` resolves a target fully — symlinks included, the same treatment `Store::file` already gives a database path — applied at the **store** boundary in `set_bases`, `merge_bases` and `bases_for`, so no route into or out of that table can carry a second spelling. It is idempotent, so callers that normalise for their own comparisons pay nothing and neither site needs to know about the other. **The open decision was what to do with a path that cannot be resolved, and it answers by construction rather than by choosing**: such a target keeps the spelling it came with and nothing fails, because a base is only ever consulted by exact key, so an unresolvable key can be matched by nothing but the path it names — it is inert, not wrong. *A second reason originally given was stated too strongly — "it comes back to the same path" assumes a path re-identifies the same volume, which `a-target-path-can-come-to-mean-a-different-volume` is the case where it does not. The decision stands on the first reason alone.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, placed at the store boundary so the invariant cannot be bypassed, and a correction to the entry's own justification kept rather than quietly dropped — one of its three reasons was unsound and the decision survives without it.

content: **Whether one mechanism should replace two: supersede throughout, and abolish amendment. Resolved 2026-08-29: neither -- the boundary moves instead.** Decided by the human partner: correction survives, its *occasion* narrows to a record that **never entered service**, and its *reach* widens to the whole record, `content` and `why` included. Supersession takes the update load. **This gets what abolition was for without paying what abolition cost.** A record that has never been exported exists on one machine, so correction after export is refused and concurrent correction becomes structurally impossible -- which means every change a second replica could see is a supersession or a forget, both of which carry ancestry. Reconciliation gets its `git` property without the corpus duplication, and without reversing the Golden Rule answers that blocked abolition. **The apparatus-supersession puzzle this question was waiting on is dissolved rather than solved:** nothing ever needs to copy content verbatim to move a `confidence`, because a record that entered service is superseded with its claim rewritten, and one that has not is simply corrected. Recorded in Corrections and Multi-Set Sync, which also record the two mechanisms this makes unnecessary so they are not rebuilt. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `supersede-throughout`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

*The boundary moves instead* is carried in the head because the question is posed as a binary -- one mechanism or two -- and the answer is neither, which a row saying only *resolved* would hide. The never-entered-service criterion is the operative rule a session will actually apply, and it is the part that makes concurrent correction structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged.

content: **Under `potion-multilingual-128M` every set's floor rises by 0.10 to 0.16 and the spread between sets roughly halves — and for English the floor no longer separates.** Measured 2026-09-11 UTC with `probe_how_much_a_calibration_floor_varies_across_corpora`, both models back to back over the same live sets and 30 authored probes. p90 floor by set, base → multilingual: `governance-docs` (8 memories) 0.089 → 0.251, `local` (10) 0.200 → 0.320, `coding-lessons` (129) 0.248 → 0.369, `scatterhoard` (789) 0.275 → 0.367, traversal corpus (429) 0.286 → 0.376. **Spread across sets:** p90 rule 0.197 → 0.126, max rule 0.351 → 0.156. The ordering by size mostly survives — the 8-memory set is lowest under both — and the size ladder on `scatterhoard` drifts less: p90 +0.054 from 30 to 789 memories under the base model, +0.028 under the multilingual one. **Headroom:** the worst of 18 verified answerable queries scores 0.361 base and 0.338 multilingual, against the set's own p90 floor of 0.275 and 0.367 — **+0.085 under the base model, −0.028 under the multilingual one**, with five authored off-domain probes outscoring the worst real query where the base model had one.
context: Testing the multilingual model at the human partner's direction, to see how much of the per-set floor variation comes from the model itself before choosing how to calibrate the floor.
why:
Answers the human partner's question of how much per-set floor variation comes from the model. The level is entirely the model's, and between a third and a half of the spread moved with it. That undercuts candidate (3) under `floor-calibration-source`: a floor modelled on set size from one model's measurements would not carry to another model.

The headroom result agrees with the English fixture's 23-point drop at r@5, from a different direction: this model separates English less well, in ranking and in scoring alike.

Thin: 30 authored probes, which were already shown to sit unrepresentatively far off-domain, and only 18 answerable queries.

content: **Observation 2026-09-07, after migrating 25 BACKLOG entries: the single most common thing an entry body held that no memory held was the divergence between the plan and the built thing.** Roughly ten of the twenty-five carry one, and they are the passages a session would most want: `prohibited-data-scan` refuses at the write and only warns at export, *the reverse of what the entry assumed*; `content-hash-keyed-vectors` is a correctness mechanism and was filed as a speed one; `scatterhoard-local` shipped and was widened the same day; `set-drop` first read a contamination episode as an argument for a non-searchable scope and then withdrew it; `graph-traversal` found two loose ends and deliberately decided neither; `recall-eval-harness` corrected itself four times. **The pattern is structural rather than incidental**: an entry is written before the work and revised during it, so it is the artifact present at the moment a plan turns out to be wrong — while the memory, if one is written at all, is written afterwards and records the outcome, by which time the divergence reads as simply how the thing works.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md, when the human partner asked whether the cross-entry trends were being recorded anywhere.
why:
Filed as evidence for the investigation, and it sharpens the hypothesis rather than merely supporting it. *Outcomes get memories and evidence does not* is the broad version; this says **which** evidence, and why that class specifically. A measurement can at least be re-run against a new corpus. A decision that reversed the plan cannot be recovered from the code at all, because the code shows only what was chosen — the rejected alternative and the reason leave no trace in the artifact.

That makes this class the highest-value thing the migration is rescuing and the most complete loss if the entry body is deleted without it, which is what the head-only depth would have done.

content: **The backfill is not thereby redundant, and this is the part worth being careful about.** `refold_keywords` skips any row whose spelling today's `Keyword::new` rejects — whitespace-containing or empty — with a bare `continue`. For such a row the backfill is the only thing that puts anything in `folded`: with it, the verbatim old spelling, still matchable by an exact search; without it, `''`, and permanently, because the refold records its marker on the way out and never runs again. A legacy multi-word keyword is exactly the shape a tightened constructor leaves behind, and nothing in the suite held one. **Deleting the backfill was the option to avoid**, and it was the one the survivor invited: it reads as the obvious response — a later repair covers the same rows — and it would have taken the unparseable case with it silently.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The reason the redundant-looking line is load-bearing: the later repair skips exactly the rows a tightened constructor leaves behind, and it records a marker so it never runs again. The survivor invited the deletion that would have lost that case.

content: A set can be exported from the command line: `scatterhoard export SCOPE --directory DIR`, or `--file PATH`. Built 2026-09-15, so a backup can run on a schedule — export was reachable only from inside a session. It goes through `Server::export_to`, a public wrapper over the same `export_set` the tool calls, so there is no second implementation for a later rule to miss; `Destination` is public so the caller states which destination form it means rather than having it inferred from the path. Refusals exit `2` with the reason on stderr — a destination that does not exist, a set this machine does not hold, a missing or duplicated destination — because a scheduled job is watched by its exit status and read by nobody; the JSON report goes to stdout. It builds the same server a session gets, model included, since export uses the model to describe the set, and it records bases and discharges the description as any export does, against a store a running server may hold open — safe under WAL. **The bare invocation still serves MCP.** Argument parsing is `src/cli.rs`; contract in `tests/cli.rs`; written up in [set-lifecycle.md](documents/design/set-lifecycle.md), *export from the command line*. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `export-subcommand`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building command-line export after the link-key fix, in the session that filed the memory-size question.
why:
Head of the backlog cluster, superseded because the entry is built. The opening sentence is the generated index row, so it says what now exists rather than what was missing. The readiness facet is dropped, as built entries carry none.

The three things the entry asked to settle while building were settled as follows. **A refused scheduled backup is noticed by its exit status**, which is why every refusal is non-zero rather than a message alone. **It loads the model**, because export uses it to describe the set and a subcommand without one would write a file whose description was silently missing. **It writes to a store the MCP servers may hold open**, which WAL already makes safe between processes — the same property that lets two servers share a store.

Superseded rather than amended because the head was exported when it was filed.

content:
Fixed 2026-09-11 in two halves, and only one of them is a mechanism.

The reformat is `2797118`, alone in its own commit and verified to change nothing: 772 tests pass, clippy clean, no mutation's `find` text moved, and the convention catalog still measures 17,678 of its 18,000 characters, so the served text is untouched. The catalog file's share of the diff was two blank lines.

The other half is a paragraph in AGENTS.md telling a session to run `cargo fmt --check` at the *start* of its work rather than only before committing — run first it names the files you will otherwise sweep up and you can put them back; run afterwards you are reverting by hand and the diff is unreviewable until you do. **Nothing executes it.** There is no CI and no remote here, and a written rule is exactly what failed the first time: STANDARDS.md had required the formatter before every commit throughout. So if the tree drifts unformatted again, the answer is a pre-commit check wired per machine, the way this project already wires its hooks, and not a firmer sentence in a document.
context: Committing the query log, then clearing the reformatting it turned up.
why: The fix is worth recording mostly for its weak half. Marking this fixed on the strength of a rule invites the next session to trust that the tree is clean because something is watching, and nothing is — so the condition that would reopen it is written down beside the fix, along with what to build instead of restating the rule.

content: **`charter-at-set-creation` and `author-name-or-reference`'s residue are one question about the tool surface: how far it should distinguish creating a new set from opening an existing one.** Framed 2026-09-23 by the human partner. Both residues want `create` to require something — a charter, an author — and both stall on the same overloading: `create` is how a fresh set is made *and* how a set someone else exported is adopted before `import` replaces its contents, so a parameter load-bearing for the first is inert or wrong for the second. Settling whether those are one operation or two answers both entries at once, which is why they are examined together rather than drafted separately.
context: Reviewing the open questions with the human partner for what must be settled before a first release.
why: Each entry names the overloading from its own side — the charter entry says `create` cannot tell which of its two uses is running, the author entry that `create` still requires no author — and neither points at the other, so taken one at a time each would get a local answer the other then contradicts. Pre-release because a required parameter added to `create` after publication breaks every existing caller.

content: A set's declared languages are checked against the loaded model and reported where they do not fit. Built 2026-10-04, taken up from deferral as the fix for `recall-is-latin-script-only`. It is built differently from what this entry first proposed. The vocabulary-by-script coverage test was rejected after Russian and Greek tokenised fully and still collapsed (2026-09-19). In its place is a paraphrase-rank score of 0 to 10 per language, with three bands. That score comes from built-in sentences for eight languages, or from the set's own sentences under a `hoard-fit-hub`, which take precedence. Not built: the note at the write door, script histograms, and calibration probes in a declared language, which are still proposals in the design. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `model-covers-declared-languages`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Finishing the declared-language check: built-in scores and bands, then a set's own sentences, then model recommendations, in three commits on 2026-10-04.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because the model-fit report it asked for is built. The proposals it listed and that were not built stay recorded as proposals in `documents/design/memory-data-model.md`, not under this entry, because none is needed for the report to work.

content: **Both repositories have had a GitHub remote since 2026-10-04, and both are private.** They are `github.com/jtcours/scatterhoard` and `github.com/jtcours/coding-lessons`. **No beta testing took place**: as of 2026-10-17 no invited tester is active, so the private beta has no users, and the next step the human partner plans is to make the repositories public and see who comes -- with versioning to be discussed then, since `0.1.0`, though accurate, reads as far less mature than the software is. Verify the remotes with `git remote -v`, and visibility with `gh repo view <repo> --json visibility`. Going public is still the human partner's call, gated on `release-gate`.
context: Starting on the default README for memory directories, after clearing the open issues; the human partner said no testers had taken part.
why: Supersedes the memory that said the repositories were shared with invited beta testers, which a later session would otherwise plan around -- writing docs for testers, or treating a push as sharing with them. The decision to go public, and the versioning question, are deferred to that point by the human partner rather than settled.

content: **The per-change recall missed an earlier decision the change would have reversed, 2026-09-28: the first part-6 miss under `coding-lessons`.** Before building *a memory never replaces a tombstone at import*, the one-sentence query returned two memories about the merge driver. It did not return `an-older-file-silently-resurrects-a-forgotten-memory`, whose fix had decided on 2026-08-26 that such a resurrection is reported, never refused, to honour a reverted forget. A text search of `TRACKING.md` for *resurrect* found it, and the build was stopped before any code was written. The query and the decision shared the idea but not the words: the query said *tombstone* and *TakeFile*, while the decision's head says *resurrects a forgotten memory*.
context: About to build the tombstone-wins step for `a-target-path-can-come-to-mean-a-different-volume`, right after filing `merge-without-a-recorded-ancestor`.
why: Part 6 of the adoption guide asks for each time a session realises a recall should have surfaced something. This is the case the habit exists for, a decision an earlier decision governs, and the habit missed it. What caught it was a second lookup in different words. That argues for recalling in both the mechanism's words and the user-visible effect's words before reversing behaviour, and it is one instance.

content: **Whether a memory needs an `occurred` time distinct from `created`.** Surfaced by the link-label corpus test: `PRECEDES`/`FOLLOWS` exist to express world-event order, and with no `occurred` field they are currently the only way to express it -- verified 2026-09-07, the record carries `created` and `modified` and nothing else temporal, and neither label is in the live link vocabulary. **A field is cheaper when absolute times are known; edges are better when only relative order is**, which is the usual situation for an LLM reconstructing a history after the fact. **Decide alongside the deferred `PRECEDES`/`FOLLOWS` pair in EARLY-VALIDATION.md** -- the two are one decision, since choosing the field would leave the labels with little to do and choosing the labels leaves the field unmotivated. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `occurred-time`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only, kept whole rather than split -- the entry is four sentences and every one is load-bearing, so a member would restate it.

The cheaper-when trade is the part worth preserving: it is the criterion, and it is easy to lose behind the framing of *should we add a field*, which invites a yes/no answer rather than a look at which kind of information is actually available at writing time.

The dating rule matters here in an unusual way: the entry carries no date at all, which is why none is stated. It was surfaced by the corpus test rather than raised on a day, and inventing one would be worse than the gap.

content: **The per-change recall surfaced a lesson that changed the fix, 2026-09-28: the second part-6 observation under `coding-lessons`, and the first from the recall the guide prescribes.** Before fixing `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity`, the one-sentence query returned this project's cause `a-reference-that-does-not-pin-what-it-names`, which links `instance_of` to the lesson on guards keyed to one spelling. Following that link changed two things. Every route by which a link could reach a store was enumerated, which confirmed `holder_of` was the only open one. And the guard was keyed on whether a store is addressable at all, rather than on `Scope::Local`, so a future unnamed scope is covered too. The lesson arrived through a link from a project memory, not as a direct hit.
context: Fixing `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity`, after building `unknown-labels-carried-opaquely` the same day.
why: Part 6 of the adoption guide: the gate waits on evidence that recalling changes what gets written. The route matters when judging the guide. The query matched the project's cause, not the lesson or any trigger, so the lesson was reached because the cause links to it. That supports linking project causes to lessons, and says nothing yet about how triggers perform.

content: **Replaces `recall-gloss-convention`, retired 2026-09-04 — it was two rules, and the other one has shipped.** What remains is one rule: when surfacing a recalled memory to a human, lead with what was going on at the time rather than restating content cold, and expand when asked. Whether it should be continuous rather than on demand is deliberately left to the optional-conventions mechanism if that is ever built, since always-glossing is output styling a user should be able to decline. **A version already ships**, which is why this is not urgent: `recall-when`'s final clause says to lead with enough of a memory's context to let the human place it, phrased as *always* and kept that way until this entry's home exists, since it is currently the only channel reaching a session at recall time. **Done 2026-09-04, the capture half**: what to write *into* Context now lives in the `context` parameter description rather than in the catalog, **because that string was measured to be what drives the behaviour** — the previous wording produced 98% adoption of an optional field and returned its own vocabulary. It reaches every client, is pinned by a snapshot, and costs nothing against the convention budget.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Half of a retired convention that shipped as a parameter description rather than as catalog text, because the description was measured to drive the behaviour at 98% adoption. That measurement is why the remaining half waits for a place to live rather than being forced into the catalog.

content: Found 2026-08-03 reading `src/mcp.rs` to answer what the current ceiling is: `let limit = params.limit.unwrap_or(DEFAULT_LIMIT);` — `DEFAULT_LIMIT` is 5, and there is no clamp. A caller passing `limit: 10000` gets up to ten thousand full memories in one response, and since `store.rs` scans `limit * 2` per store to leave room for validity substitution, the work scales with it too. The schema says only *"How many memories to return."* Harmless while the corpus was five memories and the only caller was careful; it stops being harmless in exactly the situation Scatterhoard is for — a large store, an LLM choosing the argument, and a context window the response is now competing for. **A limit that exists to protect a budget should not be settable to a value that destroys it.**
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The discovery and the principle it turns on, which is what makes this a defect rather than a missing nicety: the parameter's whole purpose is to bound a budget, and an unbounded setting inverts it.

content: **`link_delta` caught two real incomplete restatements on 2026-09-30.** Superseding the `where-user-facing-recipes-live` question head and the Windows SETUP issue head, the session restated the supersession and its new links but not the old heads' `related_to` links. Each would have been silently dropped from the walk. Both times the response's `left_behind` named them before export, and an amend restored them. The first observed catch of the slip this report was built for, in ordinary use rather than a test.
context: Closing issues and resolving the cookbook question with the human partner, the same day the in-link remark for supersession was built.
why: Evidence that step 1 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`, reporting what a supersession leaves behind before inheritance was cut, earns its place: writing a superseding head from scratch, the obvious way, drops links nobody meant to drop. Recorded as observed, two instances by one agent in one session; it says the report works, not how often authors slip.

content: **In the export review the person decides in conversation, with the model presenting memories in batches, not through a server form per memory.** Decided 2026-10-22 by the human partner, and recorded in `documents/design/export-review.md` under *The procedure*. Decisions are recorded as they are made, so a long review can span several sittings, and export waits only on what is left.
context: Designing the export review's judgement gate before going public: the file on disk is the clearance record, and local is reviewed with a session-start reminder.
why: A person clicking through fifty forms reaches the point of fatigue and lets things slip. Batching worked in the 2026-10-17 read-through. The cost accepted is that the server hears the model's account of each decision rather than the person's own answer, so whatever the mechanical pre-pass catches is always put to the person. The rejected alternative was MCP elicitation, already used for the author name, which would have made the person's answer the record.

content: When every set with a floor declines a question and every hit comes from sets without one, recall now says so. Built 2026-09-24, the day it was filed: `Recall::answered_only_without_a_floor` in `src/store.rs` names those sets, computed after the gap cut, and `hoard_recall` returns it with a note that the hits may be background and that `scope` asks one set alone — joining any note already there rather than replacing it. Marked rather than withheld, by the human partner's decision. Not marked when a floored set also answered, when no searched set has a floor, or when the caller waived the floors. Two tests in `tests/mcp.rs` and three recorded mutations. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `note-when-only-uncalibrated-sets-answer`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building the two backlog entries from the backup-calibration discussion, note first; the self-query calibration is next.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because the entry is built. The condition deliberately does not ask whether the floored sets were silenced or merely outranked: either way the answer came only from sets that cannot tell a non-match from an answer, which is the fact the reader needs.

content: **How memories written during a code review reach the set.** Raised 2026-08-05 by the human partner while settling the reconciliation base, from a configuration they actually run: one repository checked out twice on one machine, one checkout for development and one for review. The reviewing session is exactly the kind that *produces* memories worth keeping -- why a change was rejected, a constraint the author had not noticed -- and there is no reliable moment for it to write them. **Source-code precedent does not transfer.** A reviewer does not alter the files under review; they flag issues and the author acts. A memory set is different: the observation belongs to the set rather than to the review comment, and routing it through the author to re-record loses both the reasoning and the attribution. **But the reviewer's only dependable opportunity to change files is immediately before merging** -- earlier, and the author can revert them without noticing, or force-push over them. That points at a merge-time step nothing in the design has: the export gate is the *author's* pre-commit gate, and Multi-Set Sync settles how two files reconcile but not who is entitled to write one and when. **This is about authority and timing, not mechanism** -- the base-per-target decision already makes the two-checkout case reconcilable. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `review-memories-reach-the-set`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The closing distinction is in the head because it is the thing most likely to be mistaken: the entry describes a two-checkout setup and a reconciliation problem, and a session skimming it would reach for the sync machinery, which already works. What is missing is a *rule about who may write and when*, which no amount of mechanism supplies.

content: **The non-match investigation spent a day on scoring rules over one model's output and never touched the cheapest variable.** Seven mechanisms were tried and rejected on the premise that the information was absent from the space; a different static model of the same size, same format and same loader puts enough of it back to reorder the failure — which means the premise was about *that embedding*, not about embeddings.
context: Answering whether a contextual embedder is available, which turned up a cached retrieval-tuned static model first.
why: Split on 2026-10-19 from the retrieval-model measurement, whose reasoning it was, when that memory was restated over the length limit.

content: A set too little used to gather the twenty labelled queries a calibration reads now gets a floor from its own memories. Built 2026-09-24, the day it was filed: when `Store::calibrate` finds too few new labels and the set has no floor read from labels, it asks each current claim's index line against the rest with itself left out and sets the floor at the 5th percentile less 0.05. It needs twenty current claims, the same count labels need, so `local` at twelve and `governance-docs` at eight stay without one. Labels outrank it both ways. The source is stored beside the level as `FloorSource`, reported by `calibrate` and `status`, and `status` offers the backup to a set big enough for it. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `calibration-from-self-queries`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building the two backlog entries from the backup-calibration discussion, straight after the note for answers only from sets without a floor.
why: Head of a backlog cluster, superseded because the entry is built. The minimum left open at filing was settled at the label count on the reasoning that it is the same amount of evidence either way and makes the percentile something other than the weakest memory. Five tests in `tests/floor.rs` and two in `tests/sets.rs`, six recorded mutations; one test had to earn its labels with scoped queries, because a floor silences the uses that would otherwise label an unscoped one.

content: Superseding an entry head moves its row to the bottom of the generated index: `genindex.py` sorts heads by id and a supersession mints a later one, so a one-character change of standing rewrites the row's position instead. The diff shows a deletion and an insertion rather than a toggled checkbox, and the file's original order — which the migration deliberately preserved — decays into order-of-last-edit. Fixed when a row keeps its place across a supersession. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `superseding-a-head-moves-its-row-to-the-end`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Adding a release-gate keyword to an existing issue head, which moved its row 79 lines and exposed the ordering.
why: Head of an issue cluster: claim, standing and severity only. `costs` rather than `misleads` because nothing false is asserted — the rows are all correct — but the ordering a reader may take as meaningful stops meaning anything, and every status change costs a two-line diff to review instead of one character.

content: **Whether a set should be able to declare its own keyword conventions, via a reserved `hoard-scope-keywords`.** Raised 2026-08-12 by the human partner as the obvious sibling of the `hoard-scope-topics` memory that `route-where` matches against. It would let a project say how it spells things, and would make `keyword-standards`' reuse rule cheap: *use the spelling already in use* currently costs a recall per candidate keyword and cannot be answered at all for a set with no memories yet. **What makes it genuinely open is that the two cases differ exactly where it matters.** A set's *charter* is not derivable from its contents -- nothing but a declaration can say what a set is for, which is what defeated keeping the taxonomy in the catalog. A set's *vocabulary is* derivable: the keywords in it are the keywords in it, so a declared list is a second copy of a fact the store already holds, free to drift from actual usage -- the single-source-of-truth failure this project names as its largest cause of defects, invited into the memory format. **So the question reduces to whether there is normative content that usage cannot supply.** *We spell issues `issue-NNN`* is a rule about keywords not yet written and no amount of reading existing ones yields it; *this project talks about embeddings a lot* is derivable and should be derived. If the normative half is real the feature is a small declaration rather than a vocabulary dump; if it is not, the honest answer is a query over existing keywords and no new reserved keyword at all. The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `set-declares-its-own-keywords`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

The derivable-versus-declared distinction is in the head because it is the whole question and it is counter-intuitive: the feature looks like an exact sibling of `hoard-scope-topics`, and the reason it is not is a property of vocabulary rather than anything about the design. A session reading only the row should not come away thinking this is a straightforward symmetry to implement.

content:
**Raw cosine plus a per-store floor silences 53% of unanswerable queries at zero cost to answerable ones — the first thing tried on this entry that has no downside.** Measured 2026-09-09 through the shipping scorer via `Stages`, 890 memories, window 10, floor calibrated at p90 on **fifteen held-back probes** and evaluated on the other fifteen plus every other family.

| variant | unanswerable silenced | answerable results | top hit kept | 2nd hit kept | rank first lost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| centred, no floor (**ships**) | 0/32 (0%) | 5.56 | — | — | — |
| centred + floor 0.296 | 18/32 (56%) | 3.06 | 17/18 | 12/18 | 2.6 |
| raw, no floor | 0/32 (0%) | 3.83 | — | — | — |
| **raw + floor 0.263** | **17/32 (53%)** | **3.83** | **18/18** | **18/18** | **none** |

Word salad goes to **0.00 results** under either floor. Held-out substance queries drop from 4.40 to 0.80 under raw. **The centred floor cuts into real answers** — it takes the top answer for one query of eighteen and the second for six, first removing at mean rank 2.6 — while the raw floor removes **nothing** from any answerable query. **What neither fixes is rule-shaped off-corpus**: unchanged at 3.83 under raw, and centring only reduces it by cutting everything. Re-run `probe_raw_plus_a_floor_against_centred`.
context: Testing raw cosine plus a floor against centring, after the ablation and the cross-store tests left the two complementary rather than competing.
why:
Recorded because it is the first positive result on this entry after eleven refuted explanations, and because it resolves the raw-versus-centred question that three earlier measurements could only characterise. Raw had won on separation, split-invariance and subset-invariance and lost on result-count ratio; the floor is what closes that last gap, and it closes it in raw's favour rather than merely evening it up — the two are complementary, which is what the previous measurement guessed and this one shows.

**The held-out split is what makes it believable.** Calibrating and evaluating the floor on the same probes would have guaranteed the substance family looked separated, and this investigation has already lost three pilots to exactly that shape of error. Fifteen probes set the floor and never appear in the evaluation.

**Two things stop this being a finished design.** Rule-shaped off-corpus questions are untouched — a question about the offside rule still returns 3.83 memories — and that is the case established as a genuine semantic similarity rather than a scoring error, so it may not want fixing. And the answerable set is 18 hand-built queries against one corpus and one model, which is the part most likely to be flattering: a floor that removes nothing from queries chosen by the same person who set the floor is exactly what a wider query set would test.

Confidence 0.85 rather than higher: measured through the shipping path with a pinned default and a held-out calibration, but on one corpus, one model, and a query set of my own construction.

content: **The first write into a set with no author is refused until one is named for that set**, pointing to `hoard_sets` `mint` for a new contributor or `identify` where the set already holds the writer's record. Decided 2026-09-24 by the human partner over two alternatives: accepting `SCATTERHOARD_AUTHOR` as deliberate while dropping only the `$USER` fallback, and reporting the author in `status` while keeping today's default. It closes the residue of `author-name-or-reference`: a set's author was whatever name the server was configured with, which is how a corpus came to be attributed to a machine account.
context: Settling what `create` versus opening a set should require, after deciding the set operations are primitives with charter, author and identity settled at first write.
why: The name is how a person is known where this particular set is published, which varies by set, so a machine-wide name is wrong for anyone who publishes in more than one place — the reason the second alternative lost. Asked at first write, per set, by the person, it is stated at the moment it is used. The machinery largely exists: a set holding identity records that this machine has not claimed already refuses its next write and points to `identify` or `mint`.

content: **Meaning survives in every language tested under `potion-multilingual-128M`, and across languages too; under `potion-base-32M` it survives only in Latin script, and weakly outside English.** Measured 2026-09-11 UTC with `probe_whether_paraphrases_outscore_unrelated_text_in_each_language`: three triplets per language — an anchor, a paraphrase worded to share as little with it as possible, and an unrelated sentence — raw cosine. **Multilingual:** the paraphrase wins in 24 of 24 triplets, with mean margins English 0.355, Spanish 0.396, German 0.281, French 0.297, Russian 0.345, Chinese 0.391, Hindi 0.354, Japanese 0.237. **Across languages** — the English anchor against each language's paraphrase and unrelated sentence — 24 of 24, margins 0.219 (Hindi) to 0.342 (Russian). **Base:** English 0.404, but Spanish 0.141, German 0.137, French 0.119; Russian −0.003 and Hindi 0.029, with related and unrelated pairs both near 0.85–0.9; Chinese 0.029 with one of three triplets unembeddable; Japanese 0.261 on an unrelated baseline of 0.48; cross-language margins 0.016 to 0.081.
context: Testing the multilingual model at the human partner's direction; the related-pair probe written to answer what the unrelated-pair test could not.
why:
Closes the half the unrelated-pair probe could not answer. The multilingual model represents meaning in every script tested, rather than merely not collapsing, and it lets an English query find a memory written in another language — which matters for a shared set whose contributors write in different languages, the collaborator case the vision is built around.

English is not where that model loses on this test (0.355 against 0.404), so its 23-point r@5 drop on the labelled fixture is about ranking among many similar in-domain memories, not the gross separation measured here. The result also sharpens the picture of the shipping model: Latin-script European languages separate at about a third of English's margin, so they are degraded rather than simply working.

Thin: three triplets per language, with translations written by the LLM that wrote the probe, and some languages cannot avoid a shared word — Chinese 车, and 会 in both 会议 and 聚会 — so those margins are upper bounds.

content: Observed 2026-08-12 writing the `hoard-scope-topics` descriptions: a `content` parameter closed with the wrong tag absorbed the parameter that followed it, so the stored content ran on into `<parameter name="why">` and no `why` was recorded at all. **The call succeeded**, and it was caught only because the recall output was read afterwards. **The mechanic, as first recorded**: the swallow is bounded by the next well-formed close, so normally exactly one parameter is consumed and everything after it parses normally — which is why `confidence`, `origin`, `keywords` and `context` all arrived intact. **Whether the damage is silent therefore depends entirely on whether that one swallowed parameter was required**; here it was `why`, which is optional, so nothing complained. **It is silent in both directions**: the call returns `findable_by_meaning: true` and an id, which reads as full success, and the damage is visible only to a lookup nobody has a reason to make.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The first occurrence and the mechanic derived from it — later corrected. Worth keeping as written, because the *exactly one* reading held for four occurrences and shaped the early remedies before occurrence five falsified it.

content: **Re-run 2026-09-08 as `corpus/seed-quality-provenance.md` asked: raw cosine reproduces the published spike figures exactly, and the centroid-removal row does not.** Raw came back at **39.2 / 65.8 / 71.7 / 83.3 with worst hub 13** — every cell and the hub count identical to the table in `documents/design/embeddings.md`, which validates the fixture, the `content + why + keywords` composition, the per-query averaged recall metric and the top-5 hub definition all at once. Against that, the centred row reproduces in **one cell only**: r@5 of 77.5% is exact, and the rest is not. Measured for the variant that ships — query and memories both centred — r@1 is **34.2% against a published 39.2%**, r@3 **57.5% against 66.7%**, r@10 **83.3% against 87.5%**, worst hub **8 against 6**. Centring memories only, or the query only, does not close the gap either. **Two claims do not survive.** *Centroid removal lifted r@10 from 83.3% to 87.5%* does not reproduce — centring leaves r@10 unchanged at 83.3% in every variant tried. And centring is **not free**: it costs 5.0 points at r@1 and 8.3 at r@3 to buy 5.8 at r@5, where the published row shows r@1 unchanged.
context: Answering whether `context` was a valid search target, which sent the evaluation back to the real 45-memory fixture.
why:
Recorded because the headline number is fine and the row around it is not, and only the headline is ever quoted. 77.5% at r@5 appears in two design documents and in `EARLY-VALIDATION.md` as validated; it is confirmed. What is not confirmed is the shape of the trade beside it, and that shape is the argument for the decision — a row showing r@1 unchanged says centring is free, and a row showing it down five points says centring buys mid-ranking precision by spending top-1 accuracy.

That raw reproduces to the decimal is what makes this worth acting on rather than filing as a curiosity: the same code, corpus, metric and hub definition produce an exact match on one row and a mismatch on the next, so the difference is in the centring step and not in the apparatus. This is `ISSUES`' own Common Cause #1 in the documentation rather than the code — a measurement hand-copied into a table, kept in step with nothing.

content: **The embedder is sound — that stands — but the *median rank 24* figure recorded with it on 2026-09-08 was optimistic and should be read as roughly 40.** The four soundness checks are unchanged and still hold: deterministic; stored vectors re-embed at cosine 1.000000 over 40 samples; self-retrieval rank 1 for 40 of 40; and held-out retrieval far above chance. What was wrong is the last number's sample. It was taken over the first 60 ids, which are the **oldest** memories and predate the batch migrations, and it counted memories whose context is shared with up to 223 others, where naming the single source is impossible by construction. Re-measured properly — unique contexts only, spread across the corpus rather than a prefix, 218 queries — the memory a context came from ranks at **median 42 under the scoring that ships, with 31.7% inside the top ten**, against a chance median of about 360. So the conclusion is intact and about ninefold better than chance rather than fifteenfold. **`context` remains a floor rather than an estimate**: it is an episodic anchor chosen for not being semantic, so it is the hardest query the corpus can offer.
context: Running the CSLS re-test, when the scale sweep exposed the sampling flaw in the earlier held-out measurement.
why:
Supersedes the 2026-09-08 record because it was exported and committed in `dab1fe7` before the sampling flaw was found. The claim that mattered — the embedder is not broken — is unchanged, which is why this corrects the figure rather than retracting the memory.

Worth keeping as an instance rather than a silent fix: the flaw was a prefix sample, taken because iterating and breaking at 60 is the obvious way to sample and gives no sign that ids are chronological. Both halves of the error pushed the same way, and a number that is wrong in a flattering direction is the kind that gets quoted.

content: Found 2026-08-25 while working out what `set-restore` would have to build. **It is an adaptation artifact, not a decision**: `MemorySet` arrives in the first commit to define the memory file at all, when a record could only be a memory; the commit that introduced tombstones updated `validate` to count both shapes and gave `read` the minimum edit that kept `Vec<Memory>` compiling — an `if let`. Nothing in that commit argues tombstones do not belong in a `MemorySet`; the filter preserves a type that predates them by one commit. **Currently harmless by accident**: the tool surface's `import` does not use `read`, and the only production caller is the eval binary loading a corpus with no tombstones. **What it breaks the moment a writer uses it**: a tombstone is a graph node, deliberately — `forget` cascades a memory's keywords, links and vector, so a forgotten memory's *inbound* edges survive pointing at an id that now holds only a tombstone, and `holds_record` counts a tombstone for exactly that reason. Discard it and every inbound edge reads as dangling, and forgetting stops propagating: an agreed removal comes back as an anomaly on the next reconciliation.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A filter that exists to preserve a type one commit older than the thing it filters out, harmless only because of which caller production happens to use. The tombstone-as-graph-node argument is what makes the discard a correctness fault rather than a missing count.

content: Before letting a set declare something about itself in a reserved memory, ask whether the store already holds that fact. A set's charter is not derivable from its contents, which is why `hoard-scope-topics` had to be a declaration; a set's keyword vocabulary is derivable, so declaring it would be a second copy free to drift. The test that separates them is whether the content is normative: "we spell issues `issue-NNN`" is a rule about keywords not yet written and cannot be read off existing ones, while "this project talks about embeddings" can.
context: Reached 2026-08-12 while filing the proposed `hoard-scope-keywords` reserved keyword as an open question, by asking why the `hoard-scope-topics` precedent did not simply carry over.
why: `hoard-scope-topics` is a tempting template because it worked, and the next proposal to copy it will not automatically be a case where declaration is the only source. Scatterhoard's largest recorded cause of defects is one fact written down twice with the copies drifting, so a memory format that invites a second copy of derivable state is that failure moving into the data. Stating the normative test rather than the conclusion is what makes this reusable for whatever the next declaration proposal turns out to be.

content: A design document may derive a convention's rules; served convention text must state them. When store-when's person clause was redrafted on 2026-08-13, the elegant finding was that its demands are the convention's own general rules applied without exemption -- so the clause could have referred to them. It does not: it restates them. The human partner's constraint is that a weaker model, without an extended reasoning session, will not make that leap, and served text is read by whatever model is running.
context: Stated by the human partner 2026-08-13 while accepting the four demands, and applied immediately in the store-when redraft. Checkable in the comment above STORE_WHEN in src/conventions/catalog.rs.
why: This cuts against the drafting instinct that the elegant compression is the better text, and against the context budget, which rewards brevity. It is the same failure in a new place as compiling a clause from a principle's conclusions: both save words by assuming a reader who will reconstruct what was left out. The budget is the wrong thing to spend here -- the catalog sits at 10,195 of 16,000 characters, so restating cost about 1,300 characters of headroom that was bought for exactly this.

content: The mutation runner's crowding note fired on every pass, so its reading was constant and told the reader nothing. Fixed 2026-09-29 by removing it, along with `SLOW_MUTATION`, from `scripts/mutate.py`. Its pace half had drifted below a healthy pace: 2.0s was calibrated at 1.63s in 2026-08, and the grown suite ran 4.9s per mutation on 2026-09-28. So the conjunction was the file count alone. Once every run clears above `CROWDED`, `--only` included, a crowded directory at the end of a run is only the last stretch before the next check. The mis-counted byte figure went with it. Pace is watched relative to the run instead, by photographing a step far slower than its neighbours. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-mutation-runners-crowding-note-fires-on-every-pass`; this record carries only its standing.
context: The last issue of a long session; the human partner asked whether the note still served its purpose now that the runner clears itself, and why it fired at all.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded because the defect is fixed, though not by the old fixed-when, which asked for a recalibrated threshold or a derived baseline for the note. Clearing on every run removed the situation the note existed to explain, so the note had nothing left to report. The human partner's derived-baseline design stays in this cluster as the longer-term replacement for `CROWDED` as a clearing threshold. It is not needed to close this.

content: **The migration was measured rather than estimated, 2026-08-20, and two parts came in under it.** Scope as measured beforehand: **219 id-bearing rows** across the live stores (`memories`, `links`, `tombstones`, `bases`, `vectors`), about **2,400 occurrences** across the machine-generated corpus and labelling files, five in tests, and the approval snapshots — and **no memory quotes a full id in its prose**, since cross-references live in the `links` structure, so there was nothing to chase by hand. **Under estimate:** the corpus and labelling files were not rewritten at all, because hex still parses through the compatibility window, so those ~2,400 occurrences now serve as a live exercise of that path rather than as migration work. And the approval snapshots did not move, because ids were already normalised to `<id-N>` tokens — **though that only held after the normaliser was taught the new shape, and the first regeneration wrote raw ids into every snapshot.** A `format_version` bump came with it and **the reader must still accept the hex form**, since a set travels between machines that upgrade at different times; that compatibility window is the real cost of doing this late rather than early, and it is cheap only while one machine holds every set.
context: Migrating the crockford-base32-ids entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the migration scope and what it actually cost.
why:
The snapshot near-miss is the transferable part: a normalisation that makes tests id-agnostic protects them only while it recognises the id shape, so changing the shape silently disables the protection and the first regeneration bakes real ids in. Nothing fails — the snapshots simply stop being about what they were about.

**Two things the entry asked the build to get right, and both still apply to the substring search.** Its ambiguous-result message should say that fragments from the **end** of an id are far more selective, since the head is what a caller reaches for first and is the only unselective region — a timestamp prefix, shared by everything written nearby. And the ordering property is load-bearing: Crockford is order-preserving over the same bits, and both the file format's sort and keyword recall's tie-break depend on it, so a test should assert that ordering survives the encoding rather than trusting it.

content: **These seven entries must be settled before publication**; they are this memory's keywords. Gated 2026-09-23 by the human partner. Three have answers that would break something already in use if changed afterwards: the tool surface, the file format, or what an identity means. They are `set-settled-at-first-write`, `several-memory-files-per-directory` and `identity-mismatch-refusal`. `unrecognised-link-labels-on-import` decides whether every later label is a format break. `imported-set-trust-boundary` is gated because trust decisions have repeatedly shaped the file format. `claude-md-in-the-repository` gets a look, though it is easier to change afterwards. `a-link-can-reach-the-local-set-by-its-identity` is gated because crafted files arrive with publication.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner.
why: Superseded 2026-09-25: `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout` was resolved (no name binding; identity mismatches refused), and its build, `identity-mismatch-refusal`, takes its place, because it adds refusals to the tool surface. The alias feature it also produced is additive and stays off the gate. Retire an item by superseding this memory without its slug.

content: **Every hit recalled from an evaluation load must be marked as coming from one.** Decided 2026-09-16 by the human partner. The reason is what evaluation mode is *for*: the set is loaded because the LLM is exploring it, so its memories are not the project's settled record and must not be taken as ground truth. The opt-in rule decides whether such a hit appears at all; this decides how it reads once it does. **A set name that itself says it is an evaluation copy is an acceptable mark**, which holds only if no real set can carry such a name, so the prefix an evaluation name uses has to be refused by `create`.
context: Revising the load-modes design after the human partner questioned asking users about read-only at create, and raised several evaluation sets open at once. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 2 links an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.
why: Split from `01M2PTAY…`, which also said one evaluation load at a time was enough. The human partner withdrew that part the same day, and it is superseded separately. This half still stands. The condition about refusing the prefix is the assistant's addition: a name is a trustworthy mark only if a real set cannot counterfeit it.

content: **An unknown link label is carried opaquely on import, restated only by copying, and added to the vocabulary under ordinary semantic versioning.** Decided by the human partner on 2026-09-25, resolving `unrecognised-link-labels-on-import`. Import stores an unrecognised label as text, re-exports it unchanged, shows it as written, and never walks it. A write may carry an unknown label only when it restates a label-and-target pair from the memory it supersedes. Authoring a new link with an unknown label is still refused. Whoever adds a label decides whether that is compatible or breaking. The test: an older build that does only the above still leaves a set the newer build accepts. `compatibility_of` in `src/memory_file.rs` already reads a minor bump as compatible from `1.0`; below `1.0` a compatible addition is a patch.
context: Working through the release-gated questions with the human partner, after closing `imported-set-trust-boundary`.
why: A closed vocabulary would make every addition after publication break every older reader, fixed on the day the first build ships. The restating rule answers the human partner's supersession case. The tool surface restates links, and `link_delta` reports those left behind, so without it a build could never keep a link it cannot name, such as `is_sketch`, across a supersession. Copying needs no knowledge of the label, and refusing new authoring still catches typos. The session had proposed that any label carrying behaviour must force a breaking bump. The human partner replaced that with semver, because only a future author knows whether an older build carrying a label opaquely is safe. A label that only improves ranking or display on newer builds is. This reverses the 2026-08-02 reasoning in `documents/design/memory-data-model.md` that an unknown label should fail at import where a person can see it. Not walking it keeps that point: nothing guesses at an edge it does not understand.

content: **Whether a checkout's set is the legitimate one is settled by the repository's provenance, which is outside Scatterhoard.** Stated by the human partner 2026-09-25. The user trusts the `scatterhoard` set because they cloned the `scatterhoard` repository, and `git` can answer where the memory file came from. Inside Scatterhoard, `set_id` is the set's identity and is what guards against two sets colliding. The declared name is a label the server will usually honour but need not: an evaluation copy is reported under a name of its own. So anything that makes a checkout's set easier to identify, such as naming the file after the set, improves transparency, not trust.
context: Working through the release-gated questions: `one-repository-many-sets`, deciding between one set per directory and a file named per set, ahead of `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout`.
why: This corrects a claim made in the same session: that naming each file `scatterhoard_mem/<name>.json` would be a trust gain, because the path would then yield the name and the header would have to agree. It would not. The file's name and the header are written by the same hand, and neither says whether that hand is legitimate. It extends the three-jobs analysis (path gates reading, identity answers "same set?") with a fourth question Scatterhoard does not own. It also changes what `trusted-set-name-for-a-checkout` has to answer: if the name is not what establishes trust, a binding that protects the name may be protecting the wrong thing.

content: On Windows, a server started without `SCATTERHOARD_AUTHOR` attributed every write to the name `unknown`. `whoami` in `src/main.rs` fell back from that variable to `USER`, which Windows does not normally set, and then to the literal `"unknown"`. Found 2026-09-24. **Fixed 2026-09-28** by `set-settled-at-first-write` step 3. `main.rs`'s `account_name` reads `USERNAME` on Windows, and with no name available `local`'s first write is refused rather than recorded as `unknown`. Shared sets no longer take a machine name at all. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `the-default-author-is-unknown-on-windows`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Building set-settled-at-first-write step 3.
why: Head of an issue cluster, superseded to record the fix. The fix is untested because `main.rs` is startup wiring, which `STANDARDS.md` exempts from test-first development, and this project has only ever run on macOS. The refusal that replaces `unknown` is tested in `local_with_no_account_name_is_refused_until_one_is_minted`.
