content: Filed 2026-08-21 at the human partner's prompting — *"There are probably also other, similar questions related to intentional edits to memory stores that we should also consider and pin."* The confirmed defect came from one primitive, a hand-written cross-set edge plus a lookup that does not filter by set, and the same primitive had four untested neighbours: a cross-set `SUPERSEDED_BY`, which `resolve_supersession` maps to `None` so the holder resolves `Unreachable` — reachable only against a memory in one's own set, so it looks like self-harm and was worth confirming rather than assuming; **cycle injection**, an edge from another set closing a loop through a memory you hold, where `check_no_cycle` guards the write and nothing guards a file; **`EXCEPTION_TO` and `CONTRADICTS`**, which the design names as also changing a target's standing, with traversal behaviour unverified; and **id collision**, a file reusing an id already held in another loaded set. The value was framed as the sweep rather than any one answer — the write-surface matrix exercise pointed at a threat model instead of at an API.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A threat model enumerated from one confirmed primitive rather than from likelihood, with each arm's expected answer written down before it was driven — which is what made the surprises legible afterwards.

content: The default README cannot point anywhere yet. **Blocked on a fact that does not exist: Scatterhoard has no published home** — which is the release gate this entry depends on rather than an oversight. Once the project has a URL, the default README should carry it, so a person meeting the directory can reach an explanation rather than a sentence. That is the whole item. Built when the default text names where to read more, **and the overwrite question has an answer rather than a default**. The findings accumulated under this entry carry the keyword `readme-names-the-project-url`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Migrating BACKLOG.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order; the last entry of the Sync and export section.
why:
Head of a backlog cluster: claim, standing and readiness only.

**Filed separately from `memory-directory-readme` rather than folded into it, because the blocker is external and open-ended and a Ready item should not sit behind one** — the same reasoning that keeps a ready driver out from behind an unproven registration risk.

The open question inside it is real rather than an oversight: whether an **already-written** README gets the URL added is the *do not overwrite* rule from the other entry pulling the other way, and whoever unblocks this has to answer it rather than pick a default. Adding the URL to a README a project has edited is exactly the overwrite that rule forbids; not adding it leaves the older directories the ones that most need the pointer without it.

content: **The entanglement this entry names as blocking it no longer exists -- checked 2026-09-07.** The entry says the budget question is *still entangled with graph traversal, which remains unimplemented*: semantic search produces seeds, the design's walk outward with confidence decaying by distance does not exist yet, so how much a caller must walk for itself is undecided. **Traversal is built.** `src/traversal.rs` exists, the recall result carries an `inherited` field -- *what this memory inherited from a memory the query matched directly, decayed by distance* -- and the walk's scoring was measured and decided across 2026-08-15 and 2026-08-18, ending at a blend with a quarter weight on the inherited term. **So the caller no longer walks anything for themselves**, and the open part narrows to what it always was underneath: whether the default detail level should be narrower than full. **What that changes about the question is the cost side** -- links are not merely a field to serialise now, they are what the traversal already used to reach the result, so trimming them from a default hides the reason a memory came back at all.
context: Migrating open-questions.md into the memory set, entry by entry in file order.
why:
Recorded because a blocker that has quietly cleared leaves an entry looking harder than it is: a session reading this would defer the budget decision on the grounds that traversal must land first, and traversal landed weeks ago.

The consequence in the last sentence is the part worth having beyond the correction. Before traversal, links were payload; after it, they are provenance -- which is a new argument against trimming them by default, and it did not exist when the constraint was written.

content: Keyword recall ignores `already_known`, so ids a caller says it holds come back anyway. The `hoard_recall` schema promises they are left out, with no mention of which search path. In `src/mcp.rs` the semantic branch hands them to `Question::already_holding`, while the keyword branch calls `search_keywords_across` without them. Observed 2026-09-25: a keyword recall passing three ids returned exactly those three, and a second passing one returned it first. The same exclusion on a query recall worked. Fixed when the keyword path leaves them out too, or the schema says it applies only to `query`. The findings accumulated under this defect carry the keyword `keyword-recall-ignores-already-known`; this record carries only its standing.
context: Resolving `one-repository-many-sets` with the human partner, recalling the question's cluster at the start of the discussion.
why: Head of an issue cluster. Misleads: a caller paging past what it holds by keyword gets the same tranche back and may read it as all there is, and it pays for the repeated records in context. Found while resolving `one-repository-many-sets`, when a cluster recall returned the very head it had been told to skip. Untested because the parameter's tests go through the semantic path, the only one that reads it: two routes to one behaviour, guarded on one.

content: **Measured 2026-09-22 against the exported set: the connect-on-recall clause needed no link-only write.** Of 156 supersessions in the file, **none** changed only links: 154 changed content or reasoning, one only keywords, and one nothing. Current memories created since the clause (2026-09-09) number 171, of which 13 are isolated, against 519 of the 683 created before it. The connections went on the new memory: 56 links from memories written since the clause to memories written before it, and none needed the old side changed. Traversal is direction-blind (`src/traversal.rs`: *"crossing every label the same way in both directions"*), so a link on either end reaches both.
context: Evaluating whether link-only-write-after-export was worth implementing, straight after serving the cost-framed recall-when wording.
why: The evidence the question lacked when it was filed, a day after the clause, with one link-only case in the corpus. It answers option B's recorded objection, that the costly path would be the common one. The common path turned out to cost nothing, because the memory being written is where a connection is noticed and it is not yet exported. Derived by a script over `scatterhoard_mem/memories.json` classifying each `supersedes` pair by which fields differ; re-derive before relying on the counts.

content:
**Bias toward over-recalling: a missed memory costs far more than a surplus one.** Stated by the human partner 2026-09-09, and it settles the non-match floor's operating point, which no measurement could. The reason is the user's experience of the failure: a memory that should have surfaced and did not is disorienting and produces *but you knew this last session* — where an extra result is merely ignored. **So a floor is admissible only if it loses no real query, and then silences what it can.** Measured on `scatterhoard`, 752 memories, raw cosine, 142 harvested real queries against 601 public-domain probes:

| floor at | value | off-domain silenced | real queries lost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **minimum real query score** | **0.256** | **47.9%** | **0 / 142 (0.0%)** |
| p01 of real queries | 0.286 | 62.1% | 1 (0.7%) |
| p05 of real queries | 0.344 | 83.9% | 7 (4.9%) |
| p90 of off-domain probes | 0.369 | 89.9% | 14 (9.9%) |

**This also flips the calibration source.** The floor should come from the *answerable* side — a store's own query history, which it has — not from a probe set, which is the component that has failed twice. A shipped floor wants a margin below the observed minimum, since `p00` is fitted to the 142 queries seen so far and the 143rd may score lower.
context: The human partner settling the floor's operating point, after the measurements produced a curve but no way to choose on it.
why:
Recorded because it is a design intention only the human partner can supply, and because it does work no amount of further measurement could: the whole investigation could produce a separation curve but never a point on it, since choosing one is a judgement about which failure hurts more. The AUC of 0.962 says a good point exists; this says which one.

**The stated reason matters more than the ruling.** The cost of a false silence is not the lost result but the user's model of the tool — a system that forgets what it plainly knew is worse than one that returns too much, because the second is a nuisance and the first undermines the reason to keep memories at all. That reasoning generalises past the floor: it argues against any future mechanism that trades recall for precision, and should be recalled before proposing one.

Recorded at 0.95 because it was stated outright, and not 1.0 only because it is a design intention that could be revised.

content: A control mark that doubles as vocabulary makes whatever discusses the mechanism behave as though it were marked. In this project: memories about the charter mechanism carrying `hoard-scope-topics` and arriving as charters, `hoard-watch` both marking memories for push and naming the design, `hoard-author` as a subject keyword silently disabling embedding and skewing identity counts, a watch mark listed first becoming an index row's title, and entry slugs that are also common subject terms gathering a whole subject. **The structural fix is a reserved prefix plus a separate spelling for talking about a mark** — `hoard-` for marks, `about-` for discussion — enforced where a mark is recognised rather than left to whoever writes the keyword.
context: Re-deriving the common causes of defects across all 104 issues, and moving them from a hand-written section of TRACKING.md into memories the index is generated from.
why: Not in the original analysis; every instance postdates the watch and charter mechanisms. The general form is already in `coding-lessons` — a marker with control mechanics needs a spelling for talking about it — which is linked rather than restated. Two instances are still open, which says the rule prevents new cases only where it is applied.

content:
Fixed 2026-09-14 by keying each memory's seeding draw to its id and keeping the most cohesive of ten seedings, under derivation `clusters/2`. History from implementing the fix. In `src/summary.rs`, `Subject::new` now takes the memory's id, hashes its text form with FNV-1a and keeps only the number; `initial_seeds` draws by weighted sampling with keys — the memory maximising `ln(u) / w` wins with probability proportional to its weight, where `u` hashes the key with the seed being chosen and the restart — and `cluster` runs ten such seedings through `refine` and keeps the highest cohesion, earliest on a tie. The refinement cap rose from 25 to 300, which the measurement showed was never the cause; runs settle in 14 to 17 passes. `probe_how_stable_a_set_description_is` checks that its copy of the chosen variant reproduces production's cluster sizes exactly, and it did on both live sets.

**A key hashed from the id rather than the vector**, on the human partner's point that a vector hash depends on every machine agreeing on the last bit of every component; the id key measured better as well.

**The test that pins it had to be rebuilt once.** `the_order_memories_arrive_in_does_not_change_how_they_are_grouped` in `tests/summary.rs` clusters the same memories forwards and reversed. Its first fixture had loose group structure, ten restarts found the same partition from any seeds, and the mutation putting positional draws back survived it. The fixture is now structureless, so near-equal partitions compete and the seeds decide; the mutation is caught. Keeping the first seeding instead of the best is recorded as surviving, with the probe as its evidence.
context: Fixing a-set-description-reshuffles-on-a-small-change, the second item taken from the open issues that session, after the healed-fork fix.
why: History from fixing the defect: the mechanism and where each part can be checked, the reason for the id key, and the fixture that first passed without testing anything — the failure mutation testing exists to find, and a plausible one to repeat on any statistical property.

content: **The exported file format gained its first approval recording here, 2026-08-30 — something STANDARDS.md had asked for all along and nothing provided.** `sets_export` records the response to an export and **never the bytes**, so the artifact the whole design turns on had no recorded shape at all. **Two format changes shipped the same day with no recorded artifact showing either.**
context: Migrating the tombstone entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is the coverage gap it closed in passing.
why:
Recorded because the gap is the kind that looks covered. An export *had* an approval snapshot, and it asserted the wrong thing — the response, which is a report about the operation, rather than the file, which is what other machines read and what a format version describes. A reader checking whether exports were covered would see a snapshot named `sets_export` and stop.

It is also the same shape as the migration's other findings: the artifact that travels is the one nothing was watching, and the fact that two format changes had already shipped under that gap is the measure of how long it can persist without anything failing.

content: **Blindness was made a property of the artifact rather than of anyone's discipline, 2026-08-15 — and the queries turned out to be harvestable rather than authorable.** *Author queries blind to the link structure* had been recorded as the one step with no mechanical shortcut. True of the **labels**, false of the **queries**: this project's own session transcripts hold real `hoard_recall` calls issued during ordinary work by sessions that had no idea a corpus would be built from the design documents. `corpus/harvest_queries.py` recovers **29 distinct semantic queries and 12 keyword searches** spanning 2026-08-03 to 2026-08-14 — blind **by construction** rather than by procedure. **The cutoff is the safeguard and must not be relaxed**: only calls made before 2026-08-15 are included, which excluded six, and the exclusions are exactly the ones that needed excluding — three from the session that built the corpus and one from the session writing the entry. **The worksheet leaks structure three ways and only the first is obvious**: the `links` field; the `context` field reading *Extracted from documents/design/X.md*, which gives away most of what the links would since three quarters of edges are within-document; and **the record order**, since ids are UUIDv7 over per-document timestamps, giving 429 records in **91** contiguous same-document runs, shuffled to 394, what a random arrangement of 21 documents gives.
context: Migrating the recall-eval-harness entry out of BACKLOG.md; this is how the evaluation was kept honest.
why:
Built from an **allowlist rather than a denylist**, because a denylist is correct only against the fields existing when it is written: add a field carrying structure and a stripping script keeps emitting it silently while passing every test it has.

Three things worth carrying to any similar harness. **The seeded shuffle is safe here and the distinction matters**: a fixed seed buys reproducibility rather than stability, and this project was bitten by exactly that when ids from one seeded stream shifted on every insertion — but that hazard is about *identities*, and an ordering is not one. **A check that searches output for the words `links`, `target` and `context` fires on prose**: the corpus is *about* a memory system with links, so those words are its subject matter — 23 memories discuss links, 37 discuss targets — and it was replaced by structural questions instead, every memory's fields within the allowlist and no memory naming another's id anywhere, both holding at zero. **And whoever has seen both the corpus links and the harvested queries must not do the labelling**, which disqualifies the author of the entry and is a constraint on staffing rather than on method.

content: Scatterhoard's rule for `ON DELETE CASCADE` in the store schema, learned twice: cascade only what can be rebuilt from something else. `vectors` and `keywords` cascade from `memories` and should -- both are derived, or go with the text. `bases` had a cascading key and lost the record of agreement on every amendment; `links` had one and destroyed a forgotten memory's supersession edges, breaking any chain that lost its middle. Neither is derived: a base records what two replicas agreed, and a link records what somebody said. Both keys are now gone, and the schema comments in src/store.rs say why beside each table.
context: The `bases` case is 2026-08-05, `amending-destroyed-the-reconciliation-base`; the `links` case is 2026-08-30, `forgetting-a-chains-middle-makes-a-stale-conclusion-current-again`. Checkable in the CREATE TABLE batch in src/store.rs and in the two migrations that removed the keys, `drop_cascading_bases` and `drop_cascading_links`.
why: Both defects were written by copying a clause from a neighbouring table, which reads as consistency and is really an untested assumption that the new table has the same relationship to its parent -- and the second happened after the first was recorded, because that memory was about `bases` rather than about the choice. The general form is the useful one at the moment a table is added, which is the moment nobody is thinking about deletion. Note the failure mode both share: nothing breaks visibly, because the cascade fires only on an operation no test runs until the day it matters.

content: **A `hoard-` term the set already holds counts as a known control mark, on any memory, superseded ones included.** Decided 2026-09-14 by the human partner while building `reserved-keyword-block-list`, and recorded in `documents/design/conventions.md` under *Decided 2026-09-11: the write path guards the reserved namespace*. Built as `Store::check_control_marks_known` in `src/store.rs`, with the contract in `tests/store.rs`. What this version knows on its own is `CONTROL_MARKS`; `hoard-lang-` and `hoard-proj-` are `CONTROL_MARK_FAMILIES`, where any non-empty suffix is accepted.
context: Building the reserved-keyword block-list after committing the two memory files left from the previous stretch, and fixing a summary test that wrote the retired `hoard-watch` mark.
why:
The human partner's reason: copies of a set run different versions of Scatterhoard, and keyword structure has to be able to change between them, as `hoard-watch` gave way to the three watch-list marks. A check knowing only its own list would paint that into a corner twice over. An older version could not write a mark a newer one introduced, even after importing it. A newer version could not amend a memory still carrying a term it does not know: counted from the export on 2026-09-14, twelve live memories in this set do — six carrying `hoard-watch`, six carrying the old slug `hoard-author-as-a-subject-keyword-silently-disables-embedding`. With the set vouching for its own terms, amending or superseding restates rather than introduces.

Families are prefixes rather than lists because the embedding model is the user's choice, so the languages a set is written in are too — also the human partner's point, made before the design was proposed.

Costs accepted with the decision: a typo that arrived before the check, or by import, stays writable in that set; and a retired mark can still be put on new memories where the set holds it, with the served `about-` rule standing against that. The alternative offered and not taken was to check only `memorize` of a brand-new memory, leaving amendment and supersession out entirely.

content: **How much does Scatterhoard raise a model's effective capability, measured on models small enough to run locally?** Raised 2026-10-03 by the human partner. They want a sense of what the memory adds, on a machine whose RAM cannot grow, against an industry expecting a RAM shortage through 2028. Open because nothing decides whether to build the measurement, or how its answers would be scored. content:
**What the `used` label can see, and what it structurally cannot.** A memory counts as used when the session names its id again — a lookup, a link, a correction, `already_known`. But the commonest way a recalled memory is useful is being read in the recall response and acted on with no further call, and no call-based signal can ever see that. So `used` is strong evidence when it fires and badly incomplete when it does not, which is the reason `scope` stays in the label set despite being only evidence of intent.

The counts behind that, from `corpus/labelled-queries-*.json` 2026-09-12: `scatterhoard` 85 labelled = **59 scoped, 26 used**; `coding-lessons` 63 = **37 scoped, 26 used**. Drop `scope` and each store has 26 labelled queries from about a month of work, below any usable threshold — neither would ever have calibrated anything.

**Rates, which is what every cadence decision rests on**: 19-20 labelled queries a week on both stores with both signals, against 5.9 and 8.3 a week on `used` alone. So a window filling to forty triggers roughly every two weeks per active set with both signals, and every five to seven weeks without `scope` — slower than the store changes.

Re-derive with `first_seen` spans in those files; the labels are exclusive, one per query.
context: Choosing the floor's labelling signals with the human partner, who asked why the signals were limited to scoped queries.
why:
The temptation with a noisy signal is to drop it for a cleaner one, and these numbers say what that would cost: the clean signal is a fifth to a third of the volume and arrives too slowly to track a growing store. The deeper point is that its cleanliness is partly illusory — it is not a better sample of usefulness, it is a sample of the usefulness that happens to require another tool call.

Recorded because the argument recurs every time someone looks at `scope` and finds it weak, and the answer is not in the code.

content: Fixed 2026-08-20: `memories` is the live count in both responses, `forgotten` sits beside it in each and is **present at zero**, and `export` reports `records` for what it actually wrote, so `records == memories + forgotten` is checkable from one response. **Both counts are asked of the store rather than one derived from the other by subtraction** — a derived number cannot disagree with its source, so it could never report a real inconsistency, and being able to see one from a single response is the whole point. `Store::forgotten_count` is a sibling of `count` for the same reason: they answer different questions, and conflating them is what this entry is about. The fix was not primarily *report tombstones*; it was that one field name must not mean two things, and the vocabulary was already settled by the file format, where a tombstone record carries `forgotten`. It cost two reconciliations in the session that fixed it, once at the gate on 2026-08-19 and again on 2026-08-20 — the shape the entry predicted. Two mutations recorded, both caught.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The fix, and the reasoning worth reusing: deriving one count from the other would have made the two agree by construction, which destroys the only thing that makes a discrepancy visible. A field present at zero exists so a reader need not first decide whether an absent field means none or not-reported.

content: **An import that cannot describe what it brought owes the description, and pays it at session start until the set is next exported.** Decided with the human partner 2026-09-13. At import, if any non-identity memory in the set lacks a vector, the response describes nothing, says so in `description_owed`, and records the debt in the store. At the start of each session (`hoard_conventions`, first page) the server catches up the embeddings of any store that owes one, and once every memory has a vector it reports the derived description beside the catalog. It repeats until the set is next exported with nothing unembedded, because the export shows the description itself when the set becomes portable. The condition is coverage, not the arrival of a model: a mismatched model leaves the same gap. Contract in `tests/set_description.rs`.
context: Retiring the header summary and its comparison, which left this decision describing a verdict that no longer exists.
why: Without it the gate is defeated by importing first and installing the model afterwards; the human partner raised this when a no-model fallback was proposed. Clearing on export was chosen over clearing on the first report, and coverage over a model being attached. Superseded 2026-09-21 only to remove the verdict on the file's own description, retired that day with the description the file carried; the deferral is unchanged, and the note that it is owed moved from the verdict's field into `description_owed`.

content: **Do not fix it by resolving `target_set: "local"` to `Scope::Local`** — that would make the local set addressable from a shared memory's link. **The reason changed on 2026-08-23 and the conclusion did not.** It used to be that this inverted the trust gradient, which [Cross-Set References](documents/design/cross-set-references.md) has since withdrawn in favour of a symmetric rule — *no edge changes the standing of a memory in another set, in either direction* — so a shared memory pointing a `SUPERSEDES` at a local one would now be ignored at resolution like any other cross-set edge, and the standing hazard is gone. What remains is the reason the rule keeps refusing the edge anyway: **`local` names a different set on every machine**, so a link recorded against it is not globally meaningful and resolves to a stranger's private notes wherever it travels. Making it addressable would mint links that are wrong by construction rather than merely inert.
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A conclusion that survived the withdrawal of the argument that originally supported it, on a different and better reason. Worth keeping because the withdrawn argument is the one a later session would reconstruct, and would then find no longer holds.

content: **Trust boundary on imported memory sets -- remaining sub-questions.** **The core is resolved in Trigger and Loading:** project memories are always data and never instructions, enforced structurally by path -- a single well-known memory file and bounded config alongside it, with nothing instruction-shaped living under `scatterhoard_mem` at all. **Four sub-questions remain.** *Personal-set exception:* should the personal set be exempt from the data-only rule, given its contents are authored by the local user? Plausible, not confirmed. *Import-side gate:* is a counterpart to the export review gate warranted on import, and if so does it inspect content or just surface what changed? *Provenance weighting:* should origin or author affect how much trust a recalled memory carries -- memories authored outside the local user's own history treated more skeptically? *Enforcement depth:* is the data-only rule carried by convention text alone, or does the software also refuse to surface memory content in a way that reads as directive? The findings accumulated under this question carry the keyword `imported-set-trust-boundary`; this record carries only its standing.

Head of a question cluster: the question and its standing only. The opening sentence is the generated index row.

content: **The rule for naming a set's first memory file, agreed 2026-09-25 by the human partner.** The name must be legal on every operating system, not just the one exporting, because the repository goes wherever it is cloned. Normally it is `<set-name>.json`, which is almost always legal while `SetName` is ASCII-only. A Windows-reserved name (`con`, `nul`, `aux`, `prn`, `com1`–`com9`, `lpt1`–`lpt9`) gets a suffix, so `con` becomes `con-set.json`. A name already used in that directory by another set's file, compared ignoring case, gets a numeric suffix such as `notes-2.json`. If set names are ever widened beyond ASCII, the rule grows to normalize to NFC and replace any character some OS forbids; that is not to be built now.
context: Resolving `one-repository-many-sets` with the human partner, after they asked whether matching names would fail for Chinese or Japanese.
why: A decision within `several-memory-files-per-directory`. The file name only has to point people's habits the right way, since nothing enforces that it keeps matching. So the rule only has to be safe and close, never exact. Comparing names ignoring case is what stops `Notes` and `notes` from sharing a file on a Mac. Legality everywhere is what stops an export made on one OS from breaking a checkout on another.

content: Found 2026-08-02 exercising SETUP.md §5. `by_keyword` entries carried only `id`, `content`, `matched_keywords` and `scope` — no `why`, `confidence` or `context`, all of which the `memories` list carried. **Keyword search is the degradation path when no embedding model is installed**, so on the configuration most likely to be someone's first encounter with Scatterhoard, every recalled memory arrived without its reasoning. The `store-when` convention requires every memory to have a `why` on the grounds that reasoning *"is what lets a later reader judge whether a memory still applies instead of following it blindly"* — and then the fallback path stripped exactly that field. **A memory system whose degraded mode invites blind following has degraded further than intended.**
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: A degradation path that removed the field a served convention says is what makes a memory judgeable. The severity turns on which path it is: the same omission on the primary path would be a cost, and on the fallback path it meets first-time users.

content: A proposed clause in `keyword-standards` forbidding a person's name as a keyword was rejected on 2026-08-12. The legitimate uses are ordinary -- "the third pull request from jbrown carrying this error", "jbrown is the subject matter expert on XYZ" -- and the dossier hazard is contained by routing rather than by spelling: a topical set returns what someone did on that project, not who they are. The keyword layer knows how a term is spelled and not what it aggregates, so a safeguard placed there sits where the information is not. `store-when`'s content rule is the right home, and it is already there.
context: Decided by the human partner while reviewing the keyword-standards draft, 2026-08-12. Checkable in the "What was left out" section of documents/design/conventions.md and the comment above KEYWORD_STANDARDS in src/conventions/catalog.rs.
why:
Recorded because the clause is tempting and will be proposed again: it looks like a cheap safeguard, and what defeats it is not that the harm is unreal but that this layer cannot see it. That is decision-placement applied to a safeguard rather than to a parameter, which is the less obvious half of that principle. Two holes in the routing containment were left open rather than closed -- the personal set, which is the catch-all but never travels, and a set that declares itself for dossiers on people, which no keyword rule would stop anyway.</why>

content:
**Semantic recall is Latin-script only: other scripts either match meaninglessly or, with no Latin token at all, cannot be embedded.** Raised 2026-09-09 by the human partner asking whether an English calibration set could serve a Chinese or Hindi user. It cannot, and the reason is upstream of calibration. `potion-base-32M` is distilled from `baai/bge-base-en-v1.5`, whose WordPiece vocabulary is **58,548 of 63,091 tokens Latin (92.8%)** — 492 CJK characters against the three to five thousand common usage needs, **71 Devanagari**, 111 Cyrillic. `model2vec-rs` **discards `[UNK]` before pooling**, so unrecognised text contributes nothing rather than noise, and `Vector::new` refuses the direction-less result.

**The failure modes, measured.** One question against an unrelated statement in the same language, where near zero is healthy:

| language | unrelated-pair similarity | storable |
|---|---|---|
| English | **0.071** | yes |
| Spanish / French | 0.158 / 0.162 | yes |
| German | 0.276 | yes |
| Japanese | **0.721** | yes |
| Hindi | **0.880** | yes |
| Russian | **0.908** | yes |
| **Chinese** | — | **only with a Latin token somewhere** |

Russian, Hindi and Japanese store and then **cannot be told apart** — every query matches everything, because the script has collapsed onto the few tokens the vocabulary holds. **Chinese splits two ways, corrected 2026-09-11 UTC:** with any Latin token in content, `why` or keywords it stores with a vector built from that token alone; with none, the write reports failure, commits the memory anyway and stops the store — `one-unembeddable-memory-stops-the-store`. Keyword search is unaffected; it matches on `toNFKC_Casefold` and is script-agnostic.
context: Restoring from the checkpoint and starting on the Latin-script recall issue, after the human partner pointed out that English off-domain probes might not calibrate a floor for a store in another language. Reproducing the Chinese write failure on disposable homes found the store-stopping defect filed beside this.
why:
Filed as an issue rather than a question because nothing here is a design choice awaiting a decision: a store that returns everything for any query in three of the world's most-written languages, and either misindexes or cannot hold a fourth, is behaving wrongly by any reading. What to *do* about it is a design question and a large one — a multilingual model, a script check at the write door, an honest refusal that says why — but the defect stands independently of that.

**The severity is `misleads`**, because the modes that remain on this entry all store successfully and recall confidently while nothing reports that the numbers are meaningless: Russian, Hindi, Japanese, and Chinese carrying any Latin token. That is the same shape as `an-unanswerable-query-returns-confident-hits`, one layer down and far worse. The loud mode — Chinese with no Latin token — was read here as *the better failure*; it is not, and it is filed separately as `corrupts`, because it commits the memory it reports refusing and takes the store down with it.

**It also answers the calibration question conclusively.** A floor cannot be calibrated for a Hindi store because there is nothing to calibrate: the separation the floor would sit inside does not exist at 0.880. The probe set is irrelevant to that. Any work on multilingual calibration is downstream of a model that separates meanings in the script at all.

The measurement is thin in one respect worth stating: one sentence pair per language, chosen by me. The vocabulary counts are facts; the exact similarities would move with other sentences, though not by enough to change the reading.

Superseded 2026-09-11 UTC to correct the Chinese row. The original said Chinese fails hard at the write and called that the better failure. Reproducing it on disposable homes showed it wrong in both directions: it usually does not fail at all, and when it does, the write has already been committed.

content: A shared set whose database another server process created after this one started could not be reached until a restart. **Fixed 2026-10-16, the day it was found**: before every tool call the server rescans its directories with the startup scan (`StoreLayout::discover`) and opens any set it does not already hold, loaded or withheld, through `add_store`, so a colliding copy is withheld as after a restart (`Server::pick_up_new_stores` in `src/mcp.rs`). content: **The `uuid` v7 ordering bug was reported upstream by the human partner on 2026-10-01**, by hand, to https://github.com/uuid-rs/uuid. The report covers `ReseedingTimestamp::advance` pairing the stored seconds with a later reading's fraction, and includes a four-call `Timestamp::from_unix` reproduction. The human partner filed it by hand rather than from a draft I wrote, because some projects are sensitive about AI-drafted reports. The issue's URL was not recorded here.

content: **Corpus integrity does not trade against context budget, and that is what reframed the fix.** The question had looked hard because it traded caller usefulness against the budget and reasonable people could differ — but you cannot verify that memories survive supersession intact without being able to see them intact, so visibility is a precondition for trusting the store at all and should be settled ahead of the budget question rather than as part of it. **Constraint from the human partner, 2026-08-02**: the default detail level may well be reduced later, but **a full-detail mode must always exist**, and the default should err toward exposing bugs early rather than toward economy — *a field that no mode can show is a field whose corruption cannot be detected*. Decide the default separately from the capability, and build the capability first. *Checked 2026-08-02 and clean — a superseded memory retained all four keywords and its inbound link — but it took direct database access to establish, which is the point.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: The argument that dissolved an apparent tradeoff, and the constraint it produced: capability before default, because a field no mode can show is a field whose corruption is undetectable. Both outlive this defect and govern any later reduction of the default projection.

content:
Fixed 2026-09-14 by giving the two jobs the visited set was doing to two separate steps. `resolve_supersession` in `src/store.rs` still walks every memory reachable from the one being resolved, but `seen` now only stops a memory being walked twice; the walk records each replacement edge it crosses, and `Store::closes_a_loop` then runs Kahn's algorithm over what was reached. A diamond empties completely, since the healing memory becomes removable once both branches are gone; anything left over sits on a loop and the answer is `Cycle`. The question is asked of everything reachable rather than only the path to a tip, so a loop anywhere downstream still makes no replacement trustworthy — the behaviour `a-supersession-cycle-reads-as-current` depends on.

Checkable in `tests/store.rs`: `a_healed_fork_resolves_to_the_memory_that_healed_it` fails on the old guard with `Cycle`, and `a_loop_past_a_healed_fork_is_still_a_cycle` is what the obvious repair — simply ignoring revisits — would break. In `scripts/mutations.py`, the old revisit mutation was retargeted onto the new loop verdict, and `store: treat a memory reached twice as a supersession loop` puts the defect back and is caught by the healed-fork test. The write-time check `supersedes_transitively` never had the flaw: its visited set only prevents revisits and never returns a verdict.
context: Working through open issues and backlog items after closing derived-set-summary; this was the first one taken, at the human partner's choice.
why: History from fixing the defect: the mechanism, the trap the regression tests were built around, and where each part can be checked. The row shows only the claim, so how it was fixed has to live in a member.

content: Superseding a memory does retire a keyword, since `a-keyword-cannot-be-retired-once-a-memory-has-been-exported` was fixed: a keyword hit follows the **tip's** keywords rather than the matched record's, so a term the replacement drops stops matching. Verified 2026-09-06 by recalling the two terms the original defect was measured on, `max-catalog-chars` and `remark-not-refuse` -- both return nothing. `hoard_memorize` also says so on every supersession, in the `keyword_delta_note`: *nothing answers to them here any more*. Amendment is still refused after export, so supersession is the instrument; stating the replacement's whole keyword set is required alongside a `supersedes` link, which is the authoring half of that fix.
context: Being asked why a fixed issue was being cited as open, and finding the answer in a memory that had gone stale.
why: Re-keyed 2026-09-06 under the `about-` rule; the claim is unchanged. It supersedes a measurement of the pre-fix behaviour that outlived the fix by two days and was then believed, producing a filed issue, a design section and a stored memory all asserting that a keyword cannot be retired, with the contradicting evidence in the same session twice. That is the failure `store-when` names -- a structural claim keeps reading as authoritative after the code has moved -- so the correction is worth more than the fact: when a memory describes how something currently works and the answer matters, check it against the code or the tool before building on it. Superseded 2026-09-24 only to restate 1 link an earlier version wrote, in step 2 of `out-links-stay-with-the-record-that-wrote-them`.

content: Measured 2026-08-30: `memory_file::absorb` is the **only** way to put two different memory contents under one id in Scatterhoard, and every other write path leaves the author's bytes unchanged. Adoption, restore and re-import were each driven and asserted; absorb reaches it because its set list is an `import` argument that nothing records, so two holders of one set importing identical bytes land on different content and reconcile as a `Conflict` on a memory record. Checkable as `absorbing_on_one_import_and_not_another_puts_two_contents_under_one_id` and `every_other_write_path_lands_the_authors_bytes` in tests/sets.rs. The legacy route -- an amendment predating the service gate, met by a restore from an older file -- is unreachable through the surface, because two files differing for one id would need an amendment between two exports.
context: Run as `falsify-record-immutability` from BACKLOG.md, after `correction-gated-on-service` made an exported memory immutable. The second finding of the same attempt is `restore-silently-reverts-an-absorption` in ISSUES.md.
why: This is the premise the whole *graph is the ancestor* proposal rests on, and it had been reasoned from reading rather than tested. Running it changed the standing of the proposal twice over: it is false as the code stands, which is what justifies building `absorb-as-supersession`; and it is false for exactly one reason, which is what makes that one change sufficient rather than a first instalment. Recorded because re-deriving it means re-enumerating every write path, and because the qualifier matters as much as the result -- the invariant holds going forward and cannot be assumed for records written before 2026-08-30.

content: Found 2026-08-30 from a client, storing a memory with a link while wrapping up `correction-gated-on-service`. **Both fields are right on their own terms**: `scope` says *which set this call is about*, where `local` and a shared set are alternatives and the prefix is what distinguishes them; `target_set` is only ever a shared set's name, so a prefix there would be noise. The design has no defect — the refusal is where the two meet and it explains neither, so the caller learns the fields disagree only by guessing, and the whole call is refused, so a memory with several parameters has to be resent. *Also from the same call: `target_set` was sent for a link within the caller's own set, which its description says to omit. That is a caller error, and the refusal is exactly the moment to say so.*
context: Migrating ISSUES.md into the memory set, entry by entry.
why: Two individually correct field designs meeting at a refusal that explains neither. The cost is not the rejection but the resend, since the whole call is lost and the caller has no way to know which spelling to try next.
